title: Collision Free Navigation of a Multi-Robot Team for Intruder Interception
evidence: Ch.11 Theorem 11.1: the robot 'updates its heading and the linear velocity based on updating rule (11.11) at any time t' - avoidance is the navigation law itself, not a layer over a nominal decision.
method: Report/thesis: decentralized sliding-mode navigation laws for boundary intruder interception, leader-follower safest-path switching among obstacles, and a virtual source/sink force field for one robot among dynamic obstacles.
evaluation: Simulation only (MATLAB); 5-10 robots, 1-3 intruders, 1-4 obstacles; min obstacle distance tables (0.9866 m vs eps 0.9965 m; 7.17 dm vs eps 5 dm); only baseline is swiping coverage for detection (96% vs 17%).
contribution: Collects decentralized control laws for multi-robot intruder interception and obstacle-avoiding formation navigation, with proofs and single-run simulations but no runtime safety layer and no safety baseline.
flag: Multi-chapter report (about 260k chars, read in 3 fetches). Primary claim is interception/coverage, collision avoidance is a property of the planner. Would also fail minimum evaluation (E2): no collision rate, no baseline for avoidance, single runs. Ch.8 table shows first-step distance 0.9866 m slightly below the stated safety margin 0.9965 m; Ch.9 obstacle distance 0.82 below margin, called 'acceptable'. Chapter 12 cites '79% success in intrusion detection' while Ch.7 table gives 96% vs 17% (79 looks like the difference). Intruder speed stated as both 4.5 and 4.2 in Ch.5.

title: Toward Verifiable Real-Time Obstacle Motion Prediction for Dynamic Collision Avoidance
evidence: Sec. V: 'v_safe is guaranteed to avoid a collision for the next m timesteps with a given probability'; Algorithm 3 applies v_safe in place of the desired velocity.
method: Online-trained LSTM with dropout predicts obstacle motion as uncertainty ellipsoids; a nonlinear probabilistic velocity obstacle then picks the collision-free velocity closest to the hand-designed desired velocity.
evaluation: Stage-ROS simulation, single obstacle; GP and plain-RNN prediction baselines compared only qualitatively (Fig. 5, no error numbers); statistical model checking Table I SAT-UNSAT over theta=0.9-0.75 and sigma2=0-0.05 (N=20, alpha=beta=0.1); proved bounds 1-theta, (1-theta)^2, 1-theta^N; 2 Hz on an i7 laptop; no collision rate, no ablation.
contribution: Wraps an online-learned LSTM obstacle predictor in a probabilistic velocity-obstacle filter and uses statistical model checking to approximately verify that real motion stays inside the predicted bounds.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: no - the LSTM sits inside the filter as its predictor; what is guarded is a hand-designed desired-velocity controller, which is what the 2026-11-13 scope ruling calls E1. Check whether the maintainer counts the learned predictor as enough to keep (a). E2 is the alternative: no collision or violation rate, no numeric prediction error against GP or RNN, no ablation, so the only safety result is the theorems plus Table I SAT-UNSAT. Proofs of Theorems 1-2 are deferred to a longer arXiv version, the multi-agent reciprocal case is theory with no simulation, and the abstract's 'real-time' is 2 Hz on a 32 GB i7 laptop.

title: Collision-Free Multi Robot Trajectory Optimization in Unknown Environments using Decentralized Trajectory Planning
evidence: Sec VI-B.2: "We require that the generated trajectory also remains within the feasible convex region" - inter-robot avoidance is a hard constraint inside the planner.
method: Decentralised receding-horizon QP trajectory planner: each robot forward-simulates neighbours' broadcast states (constant acceleration), builds convex safe regions from hyperplanes, and penalises obstacle proximity as a soft cost.
evaluation: Gazebo/ROS only, up to 8 quadrotors and 10 TurtleBots at a walled intersection; no baselines or ablations; success/failure rates only in Figs 4-5; planner 25 Hz on a Xeon E5-1630 workstation.
contribution: A decentralised trajectory optimiser that keeps multiple ground and aerial robots collision-free in unknown environments via convex safe regions, shown in Gazebo without baselines.
flag: Collision avoidance is the titled claim, so (c) is nominally met, but there is no baseline or ablation, so the minimum-evaluation rule fails (E2); E1 as a planner paper is equally defensible. I could not read the success/failure values - they exist only in Figs 4-5, not in the text. Authors report some runs where robots hit obstacles (LIDAR 5 Hz vs planner 25 Hz). No per-solve computation time; 25 Hz is a loop rate, not a measured latency. Simulation only.

title: Towards Safety-Aware Computing System Design in Autonomous Vehicles
evidence: Sec. 3.1: 'once LiDAR perception latency exceeds 100ms, the system response time increases at a much higher rate'; Sec. 4.1 derives a situation-dependent response-time window theta from distance and vehicle dynamics.
method: An RSS-derived 'safety score' mapping computing response time to nominal safety, a fitted perception-latency model, and offline-planned plus online-monitored heterogeneous CPU-GPU resource management for an AV pipeline.
evaluation: In-house AV and architecture simulators replaying 200+ hours and 2000 miles of industrial L4 fleet traces; against CPU and CPU+GPU baselines the scheme gives 4.6x and 1.3x safety score, 2.4x and 35% lower response time, 2.6x and 45% lower LiDAR perception latency; latency-model MSE 1.7e-4; perception is 74% of response time; Xeon CPU plus Volta GPU; no ablation, no collision rate.
contribution: Defines a safety score that ties an autonomous vehicle's computing response time to RSS-based nominal safety and uses it to drive latency-aware CPU-GPU resource management on the vehicle.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: partly - the pipeline contains deep perception modules, but the contribution is classical scheduling and it budgets compute rather than intercepting a decision, so (a) is no and the record rests on (d) alone. Check that a safety score is accepted as a safety metric: no collision or violation rate is reported, the paper only says the score is 'in line with' collision probability in simulation, and there is no ablation. Simulators and traces are proprietary and in-house, the latency model is fitted for LiDAR perception only, and the score's shape depends on user-set sigma=0.05 and eta=0.1.

title: Online monitoring for safe pedestrian-vehicle interactions
evidence: Sec. IV-C: when predicted vehicle and pedestrian reach sets overlap the Decision Module "sets the mode for the controller to brake to avoid possible collision".
method: Particle-filter pedestrian intent estimator feeds online reachability analysis; a decision module switches the speed controller from trackspeed to brake when vehicle and pedestrian reach sets intersect.
evaluation: Gazebo and a Polaris GEM car indoors, one pedestrian, two scenarios; no baseline; reach-set time 0.096-0.163 s for 3-5 s look-ahead; containment accuracy 92-98%. No collision rate.
contribution: An online reachability monitor that predicts pedestrian and vehicle reach sets from estimated intent and commands braking on overlap, computing reach sets in about 0.1 s on a real vehicle.
flag: Genuine runtime interceptor (brake override) with measured compute time, but it fails the minimum evaluation: no collision, violation, false-positive or intervention rate, no trial counts and no baseline or ablation (not even the distance-based stop the intro names). If the maintainer accepts reach-set containment accuracy (Table II, 92.078-98.161%) plus the look-ahead sweep as sufficient, it would be an include under (a);(d). Text claims max "about 99%" accuracy; legible table values top out near 98% and the high-confidence column was garbled in extraction. Only one pedestrian and one vehicle - multi-agent state not credited. Authors tested only cases where intent was predicted correctly. Compute hardware unspecified; no stated deadline, 0.1 s is a measurement. Time-to-irreversibility cell is generous (look-ahead horizon and stopping reach set, not an explicit TTI). Safety-driver presence not stated.

title: Reciprocal Collision Avoidance for General Nonlinear Agents using Reinforcement Learning
evidence: Abstract: 'safety is ensured by introducing linear constraints from the optimal reciprocal collision avoidance (ORCA)'; Sec. III-B: the agent selects the action closest to the RL-combined action subject to those constraints.
method: A two-agent RL policy trained by evolution strategy; at runtime the pairwise outputs are distance- and velocity-weighted and then projected by a convex program with ORCA linear constraints for nonlinear bicycle-model agents.
evaluation: Simulation only, 3 to 42 agents, 0.05 s steps, 450-parameter policy trained in about 20 minutes on an eight-core i7-7700K; no tables and no collision, success, distance or per-step computation numbers; no numeric baseline and no ablation, only trajectory figures called free of collision, congestion and deadlock.
contribution: Combines a tiny two-agent RL policy with an ORCA-derived convex projection applied at execution time to give decentralised reciprocal collision avoidance for agents with general nonlinear dynamics.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - an ORCA convex projection filters the RL policy's action before it is executed, so (a) and (c) both hold on reading and this would otherwise be a strong include. It fails the evaluation floor: the paper has no results table and reports no collision rate, success rate, minimum distance or runtime, compares no baseline numerically (ORCA and prior RL work are discussed only in prose) and runs no ablation, so 'ORCA significantly improves system safety' is unmeasured. The authors also concede that linearising the nonlinear dynamics 'can introduce small errors' and suggest inflating the agent radius.

title: MAMPS: Safe Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning via Model Predictive Shielding
evidence: Sec. 3/Alg. 1 (closely paraphrased): MAMPS uses the learned policy whenever safety can be guaranteed and otherwise switches individual agents to a backup/recovery policy, iterating per-agent recoverability flags until convergence.
method: Model predictive shielding for MARL: simulate backup policies to check joint recoverability, switch only irrecoverable agents to recovery, iterate, fall back to all-backup if no convergence.
evaluation: Multi-agent particle env, 3-4 agents, 3-4 obstacles, 500 episodes; MADDPG vs MADDPG+naive joint shield; safety 100% vs under 50% unshielded (4A4O); goal rate in Fig. 4. No latency.
contribution: A multi-agent model predictive shield that overrides MADDPG per agent with a verified backup policy, keeping all episodes collision-free while reaching goals far more often than a whole-system shield.
flag: Direct shielding baseline for RQ5: reports safety and task-performance cost against both no shield and a naive joint shield. Caveats: exact safety and goal-reaching numbers are only in Fig. 4 - text gives under 50% safe for unshielded MADDPG at 4 agents/4 obstacles and "all agents in all episodes" safe for both shields, and MAMPS beating naive "often by an order of magnitude"; none of these could be read as numbers. No per-step computation time or backup-usage frequency despite forward simulation each step; hardware (Xeon Gold 6148, RTX 2080 Ti) is for training. Guarantee assumes deterministic, accurate dynamics and full observability. Workshop-length paper; fetched text was partly garbled and the Appendix A proof was cut off. Non-generative cell credited because the check is deterministic model rollout - maintainer may disagree.

title: Learning to Optimize Autonomy in Competence-Aware Systems
evidence: Sec. 4.2: at level 1 (verified autonomy) the agent must request and receive human approval before acting, and at level 2 a human supervisor can override the action; feedback signals are approval, disapproval and override.
method: A competence-aware system composing a stochastic shortest path domain model with an autonomy model and a learned human-feedback model, so the planner picks an autonomy level per action and learns its own competence online.
evaluation: Simulated campus delivery robot (fixed and random tasks) and AV obstacle passing, means over 10 trials; level-optimality about 100% by episode 150 after about 275 feedback signals (about 375 for random tasks) and about 90% with under 60 signals on the AV; level-1 approval actions fall 45.8% to 0.0% while unsupervised actions rise 41.7% to 87.5%; convergence proved in Prop. 5.6 and Thm. 5.7; no baseline, no ablation.
contribution: Learns online, from human approval, disapproval and override signals, the level of autonomy at which an agent should execute each action, converging to the agent's true competence.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - the system's own planned actions are gated, with level 1 requiring human approval before execution, so (a) and (e) hold and the Pillar 3 deferral test passes on hand-off plus sequential setting. Check the evaluation floor: there is no experimental baseline or ablation, so it rests on the convergence theorems, which assume an epsilon-consistent stationary human and no starved state-action pairs, plus the feedback-count curves; expected cost is shown as a curve with no numeric values, and no unsafe-action, violation or separate takeover count is reported. Single agent with one human authority, so no multi-agent aspect; transfer of control is explicitly not modelled; the intro mentions an AV prototype but every reported result is simulated.

title: Implicit Multiagent Coordination at Unsignalized Intersections via Multimodal Inference Enabled by Topological Braids
evidence: Sec. VI: 'The main decision variable of our scheme is the speed with which an agent tracks its path'; collision avoidance enters via the collision probability in the cost (eqs. 1, 13-14), and abstract claims collision frequency reduced 'by >65%' over trajectory-reasoning baselines.
method: Decentralized planner for noncommunicating agents: forward-simulates rollouts, extracts topological braid words, picks high or low speed minimizing entropy of the predicted braid distribution plus collision cost.
evaluation: Simulated 4-way intersection, 2/3/4 agents (144/125/81 runs); baselines C1 no avoidance, C4/C5 trajectory reasoning; collisions vs C4 down 95%/65%/66%; no hardware, no latency.
contribution: Shows that reasoning over topological braid modes of joint multi-agent behaviour, rather than raw trajectories, cuts simulated intersection collision frequency by 65-95% for noncommunicating agents.
flag: Borderline c: it is a planner (not a runtime interceptor), so (a) fails, but collision frequency against baselines is the headline measured outcome alongside max experiment time; maintainer should judge the primacy test, exclude-E1 is defensible. Absolute collision rates and times are only in figures, text gives relative reductions only. One run per speed combination, error bars from a Bernoulli assumption. Text cites S3 result as Fig. 11a and says C4 'consistently' better than C5 (likely typos). Inattentive-agent claim: 'less than half' the collisions of C4'/C5' in S2 and S3. Simulation only, no latency figures; authors say they did not exploit projected computation gains. Read via one summarised full-text fetch.

title: Energy-Optimal Motion Planning for Agents: Barycentric Motion and Collision Avoidance Constraints
evidence: Sec. IV-D: 'we may write a safe distance constraint for agent i relative to agent j' (eq. 81); Introduction describes the result as 'a coarse high-level plan for many systems'.
method: Analytical optimal-control derivation of energy-minimizing double-integrator trajectories under a barycentric (stay within a disk of a reference) state constraint, extended to a pairwise safe-distance constraint.
evaluation: None: purely analytical (Theorem 1, Corollary 1, lemmas on finite-time arrival and invariance); an announced case study has no reported results; no baselines, metrics, hardware or latency.
contribution: Derives closed-form optimality conditions for energy-minimal agent trajectories under barycentric and pairwise collision-avoidance state constraints, as a building block for high-level multi-agent motion plans.
flag: E2 applies equally: no simulation, experiment or quantitative metric; the text promises 'a case study for Theorem 1 and Corollary 1' but I found no results. Collision avoidance is a constraint inside the optimal control problem, not a runtime mechanism; control barrier functions appear only as related work. Collision case assumes the other agent's reference has zero fourth derivative (Assumption 3) and no disturbances (Assumption 2). Real-time numerical solution is stated as future work. Read via one summarised full-text fetch.

title: Multimodal Trajectory Prediction via Topological Invariance for Navigation at Uncontrolled Intersections
evidence: Sec. 4: a GraphNet encoder over a directed graph of agents (node attributes position and velocity, edge attributes relative position with a one-hot winding-number sign) predicts the future states of all agents under each topological mode.
method: MTP predicts multimodal joint future trajectories by conditioning a graph-network and GRU encoder-decoder on winding-number topological modes; MTPnav then scores the predicted modes in a cost-based planner that hands a trajectory to a tracking controller.
evaluation: Simulated 2-4 agent datasets plus a CARLA Town04 four-way intersection, 50 trials per condition; minADE-minFDE 0.301-0.611 to 0.264-0.588 m against GRU 0.929-1.578, MFP 0.834-0.825 and the MTP-fc ablation 0.523-1.063, i.e. 78.24% better minADE than MFP and 33.82% better than MTP-fc, Wilcoxon p<0.001; navigation collisions near zero at 2-3 agents, still high at 4; no inference-time or hardware figures.
contribution: Uses winding numbers as topological invariants to enumerate interaction modes, letting a graph network predict multimodal joint futures at uncontrolled intersections and feed a cost-based navigation planner.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: not applicable - this is a criterion (b) prediction record with no interception; the planner selects its own minimum-cost trajectory and overrides no nominal action, so (a) is no, and (c) fails the primacy test because displacement accuracy is the primary outcome and collision frequency is reported next to time to destination. RQ5 is capped at 2 per the protocol for predictor papers. The non-generative inference cell is a judgement call, since the mode predictor is described as VAE-like. Table 2's navigation numbers are garbled in the PDF text layer so per-method collision rates could not be assigned reliably, the four-agent collision rate stays high (attributed to 162 possible modes and a small dataset), and the reported '1,180M' three-agent trajectory count looks like a typo that disagrees with Appendix B.1.

title: Rules of the Road: Safety and Liveness Guarantees for Autonomous Vehicles
evidence: Sec. V-D: an agent that loses the conflict cluster resolution "must take its backup plan action"; Sec. III-B: the agent "will always be able to safely take its backup plan action".
method: Assume-guarantee behavioural protocol: precedence rules, token-based conflict-cluster resolution and an action selection strategy that replaces the intended action with a maximal-braking backup plan; safety and sparse-traffic liveness proofs.
evaluation: Custom RoSE grid simulator, 3 maps, 100 trials each of 250 steps; zero collisions; 77%, 36%, 43% of agents reach destinations; no baseline, ablation, hardware or timing.
contribution: Decentralised assume-guarantee protocol for autonomous vehicles with a proved collision-freedom guarantee and sparse-traffic liveness, in which a losing agent is forced onto a maximal-braking backup plan.
flag: Borderline, maintainer call. Applied literally the paper fails minimum evaluation: the only safety number is zero collisions over 100 trials on each of 3 maps with NO baseline or ablation, and agent counts and spawn probability are not given. Against that, multi-agent collision-freedom is the primary claim and is supported by a formal proof (Thm 6.1), so it may merit inclusion as a formal result if the protocol admits proofs in place of a baseline. Interceptor is yes only in the sense that the action selection strategy substitutes the backup plan at execution time; it is built into the agent protocol, not a separate monitor, and the paper never uses the words shield or monitor. Guarantees assume no communication error and synchronous turns; liveness holds only for sparse traffic (N < M-1) and some simulations ran outside that condition. Appendix proofs read via second fetch; no further experiments there.

title: Safe Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning through Decentralized Multiple Control Barrier Functions
evidence: Sec. III: 'the composite CBF corrects the action of an agent only if it tends to violate safety constraints'; Algorithm 1 overwrites the MADDPG action with the QP solution before execution.
method: Decentralized multiple control barrier functions combined by Boolean intersection; a per-agent QP projects each MADDPG action to the nearest action satisfying cooperative and non-cooperative barrier constraints at every step.
evaluation: Multiagent Particle Environment, 2 patrolman agents, 3 obstacles and a wall; 5 runs x 5000 episodes; baseline MADDPG; collisions 0 vs 12,634 (50.5% of episodes); reward stable near 40,000; no hardware or latency reported.
contribution: Decentralized multi-CBF safety filter that corrects each learned MADDPG agent's action at execution time, eliminating collisions (0 vs 50.5% of episodes) while keeping reward high from the first episode.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - two MADDPG policies filtered by a per-agent CBF QP. Check: no ablation separating cooperative from non-cooperative CBFs, only 2 agents in one toy environment, the baseline's reward value is never stated so the reward comparison is not like-for-like, no latency or hardware figures, and the Sec. IV guarantee covers only the pairwise collision case.

title: Latent Variable Nested Set Transformers & AutoBots.
evidence: Sec. 3: a discrete latent variable with alternating temporal and social multi-head attention decodes scene-consistent joint future trajectories for all agents in a single forward pass (AutoBot-Joint).
method: Latent variable sequential set transformer: encoder alternates temporal and social attention, seed-matrix decoder emits one mode per latent value as bivariate Gaussians, trained by exact likelihood plus an entropy regulariser.
evaluation: nuScenes, Argoverse, TrajNet and TrajNet++, Omniglot; baselines Trajectron++, WIMP, GOHOME, CoverNet, Scene Transformer; nuScenes minADE(10) 1.05, off-road 0.03, Argoverse minADE 0.89 and minFDE 1.41, TrajNet++ scene collisions 139 vs 1144 ego-only; one GTX 1080 Ti, above 30 FPS.
contribution: Latent variable set transformer that predicts joint, socially consistent multi-agent futures in one forward pass, cutting scene collision counts roughly 8x versus ego-only prediction at a fraction of the compute.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: n/a - nothing is guarded, this is a pure predictor with no runtime interception, so only (b) holds and RQ5 is capped at 2 per protocol. Check: the record title 'Latent Variable Nested Set Transformers & AutoBots' is the v1 title of the same arXiv id, later renamed 'Latent Variable Sequential Set Transformers for Joint Multi-Agent Motion Prediction', so this is not a wrong paper. The collision counts are offline prediction metrics, not hazard rates of an acting system, and the maintainer may read this as a generative trajectory regressor (exclude-E1) rather than a Pillar 2 world model; the 30 FPS figure is a throughput claim with no per-step latency budget.

title: Approximate Computing for Robotic path planning -- Experimentation, Case Study and Practical Implications
evidence: Table 2 (warehouse, two robots): collision cases 5% at perforation rate 0.6, 20% at 0.75 and 20% at 0.8 versus exact A*; safety check only ensures 'the path does not force the robot to collide with static obstacles'.
method: Loop perforation (modulo skipping of iterations) applied to centralized A* path planning for multiple warehouse robots; studies resulting speedup, path growth and inter-robot collisions. No mitigation implemented.
evaluation: 2-D grid warehouse and room scenarios, 2 robots; baseline exact A*; perforation rate sweep 0.2-0.88; speedup 1.85x-3.4x, path increase in 0-20% of cases, failures 0-15%, collisions 5-20%. No hardware or latency.
contribution: Shows that approximating A* by loop perforation gives 1.85x-3.4x planning speedup but introduces inter-robot collisions in 5-20% of two-robot warehouse cases, a hazard absent with exact planning.
flag: BORDERLINE c, maintainer should decide between include and exclude-E1. It is a hazard characterisation, not a detector or safety mechanism; collision rate vs exact-A* baseline is reported but speedup is the co-primary outcome. Only 2 robots; trial counts behind percentages not stated; simulation not explicitly stated; no hardware. Energy savings are claimed as motivation but no energy number is reported. Text says path increase 'not more than 10%' while Table 1 shows 15-20% at rates 0.8-0.88; text says 10-20% collisions while Table 2 has 5% at 0.6. New tag approximate-computing added; sampling-based-planning is a loose fit for grid A*. One fetch covered the whole text.

title: Least-Restrictive Multi-Agent Collision Avoidance via Deep Meta Reinforcement Learning and Optimal Control
evidence: Sec. IV-A: a single learned policy chooses per step between letting each agent's default controller run unchanged and overriding it with a maximum-actuation left or right turn, triggered by the pairwise Hamilton-Jacobi safety value.
method: Least-restrictive collision avoidance module trained with PPO and MAML over an LSTM-VAE encoding of a variable number of observed neighbours; it overrides the default controller only when the HJ reachability value signals conflict.
evaluation: Gazebo/ROS simulation plus TurtleBot3 Burger hardware, 3-6 agents and an unseen 8-agent task, 100 trials per scenario repeated 5 times; baseline HJ plus mixed-integer programming of Chen et al.; success above 90% and at least 30 points above baseline, 0.85-0.91 on 8 agents, interruption fraction 0.46 vs 0.54 for the distance-reward ablation; Jetson Nano, no latency given.
contribution: Learned least-restrictive supervisory layer that overrides any default controller with maximum-actuation evasion only when Hamilton-Jacobi reachability signals conflict, raising multi-agent success while intervening on under half of steps.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: which - the interceptor itself is a learned meta-RL policy, but the guarded default controller may be classical, learned or even human-driven, so the protected system is not necessarily learned. Check: no standalone collision, deadlock or travel-time metric (success is defined as reaching the goal without collision), baseline numbers are only legible in figures, the Jetson Nano is named but no inference latency or control frequency is reported so the edge deployment cell rests on hardware alone, and the 6-agent restrictiveness ties the ablation (0.48 vs 0.48) so the claimed 10% restrictiveness gain holds only for 4-5 agents.

title: Social Coordination and Altruism in Autonomous Driving
evidence: "The policy is trained offline and deployed into all agents to be executed in a distributed and online fashion" (Sec. V-D); safety enters only through the social reward, no monitor or override.
method: Decentralized multi-agent deep Q-learning with a social-value-orientation reward (egoistic, cooperation, sympathy terms) so autonomous vehicles learn altruistic coordination with human-driven vehicles in highway merging.
evaluation: Modified highway Gym simulator, 4 AVs and 20 IDM-MOBIL human vehicles, 2000 test episodes; egoistic and cooperative-only variants, single-agent and observation ablations; crash and mission-failure rates; no hardware or latency.
contribution: Shows that autonomous vehicles trained with a social-value-orientation reward learn implicit altruistic coordination that lets a merging vehicle enter mixed highway traffic, cutting crash and failed-merge rates versus egoistic agents.
flag: Borderline (c): crash rate is a reported outcome with ablations (single SC agent 74.5 pct crashed and 74.4 pct mission failed vs multi-agent SC 12.8 and 12.2 pct; autonomy flag 10.4 vs 8.9 pct crashed; mission-vehicle observation 9.2 vs 8.3 pct), but the primary claim is social coordination and optimal altruism, and a failed merge is scored as a crash by scenario rule. Safety sits in the training reward, so (a) is not met. Main egoistic-vs-altruistic comparison (Fig. 5) is graphical only, no numbers in text. Text says 15000 training episodes, Table III says 10000. Human drivers are simulated models, not participants.

title: Group-based Motion Prediction for Navigation in Crowded Environments
evidence: Sec. 4.2 (paraphrase): a 3D-convolutional encoder-decoder predicts future group-space shapes from a history of group-space images; Table 1 reports ETH mIoU 86.66% vs 83.52% for constant velocity.
method: Pedestrians clustered into groups (DBSCAN); conv encoder-decoder predicts future group shapes; sampling MPC for a single robot scores 12 rollouts by goal and group-proximity cost.
evaluation: Simulation on ETH/UCY replay and ORCA pedestrians; baselines ped-nopred, ped-linear, ped-sgan, group-nopred; success, comfort, min distance, path length; IoU vs constant velocity; no hardware or latency.
contribution: Group-level prediction of pedestrian formations fed to a sampling MPC yields larger clearances and fewer group intrusions than per-pedestrian prediction in simulated crowd navigation, at some cost in path length.
flag: Borderline. Only (b) is arguable: predictor over multi-pedestrian group state with IoU against a constant-velocity baseline (e.g. ETH fIoU 78.64% vs 76.32%), so it meets the predictor minimum as method evidence only; RQ5 capped at 2. Prediction is in image space, not a graph or latent world model, and there is ONE robot - multi-agent only in the sense of the crowd; maintainer may prefer E1. No runtime interceptor (cost inside planner). No separate collision rate; collisions folded into comfort metric. Example values: UNIV Flow offline comfort 86.79% (group-pred) vs 68.87% (ped-nopred). No compute time reported. ETH trial counts missing in Table 2. Read via PDF-to-text summary; appendix tables not fully transcribed.

title: Safe Deep Reinforcement Learning for Multi-Agent Systems with Continuous Action Spaces
evidence: Sec. 2.3: 'we augment the policy networks by introducing an additional centralized safety layer' - a QP projects the joint MADDPG action onto a linearised safety set before execution, and the filter is still required at test time.
method: Centralized safety layer solving a QP that projects joint MADDPG actions onto a linearised collision-constraint set learned by a neural sensitivity model, with a soft-constrained variant that penalises otherwise infeasible projections.
evaluation: Multi-agent particle environment, 3 agents and 6 pairwise constraints, 8000 episodes over 10 seeds, unsafe-initialisation and exogenous-disturbance cases; baselines unconstrained and hard-constrained MADDPG; test collisions 52.8 soft vs 137.4 hard vs 1386.5 MADDPG (unsafe init) and 40.8 vs 678.1 vs 1499.8 (disturbance); no hardware or solve-time figures.
contribution: Centralized QP safety layer over learned MADDPG actions that cuts training collisions by about 98% versus unconstrained MADDPG and stays feasible where a hard-constrained projection fails.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - the MADDPG actor networks. Check: the projection is soft and the authors say it 'does not necessarily guarantee zero constraint violations', 20.9% (unsafe init) and 56.7% (disturbance) of hard-constrained episodes hit infeasible QP conditions, the filter is centralized and still needed at test time so there is no decentralised runtime story, the soft variant's reward is far worse under unsafe init (-136.4 vs -84.1) and goes undiscussed, there is no separate ablation beyond the hard/soft comparison, and no QP solve time is reported.

title: UMBRELLA: Uncertainty-Aware Model-Based Offline Reinforcement Learning Leveraging Planning
evidence: Sec. 3.2: the conditional VAE dynamics model 'models the stochasticity of other agents' behavior at time t with a continuous latent variable' and is rolled out inside a sampling-based MPC loop that executes only the first action; no layer sits between plan and execution.
method: Offline model-based RL: CVAE stochastic dynamics model, behaviour-cloned policy prior ensemble and truncated value function combined in return-weighted sampling-based MPC; the pessimistic variant keeps only the worst ensemble head's rollouts.
evaluation: NGSIM I-80 (5,596 trajectories) and CARLA Town04 unprotected left turn with 6 other agents, 30 in-distribution and 30 out-of-distribution scenarios; baselines MBOP, 1-step IL, MPUR, human, no-action; success 0.60 vs 0.50 (NGSIM), 0.63 vs 0.27 (CARLA ID), 0.43 vs 0.20 (OOD); Titan X and i5-3550, authors state the planner is not real-time capable; no prediction error reported.
contribution: Uncertainty-aware offline model-based RL that plans through a generative model of other agents' futures, roughly doubling collision-free success over MBOP in CARLA while remaining too slow for real time.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: no - nothing is intercepted, safety lives inside the MPC objective and model, so (a) fails per the runtime-override rule. Criterion (b) scope is arguably met (a generative latent model of other agents' future behaviour) but the protocol's predictive floor is not: prediction quality appears only as qualitative videos (Fig. 7) and no prediction error is reported, hence exclude-E2. This is the record most likely to be overturned: the closed-loop collision-free success rates do beat MBOP (2.33x CARLA ID, 2.15x OOD) with baselines and a pessimism ablation, so the maintainer may prefer include as method and architecture evidence with RQ5 capped at 2, or exclude-E1 since other agents are non-reactive logged trajectories and the multi-agent safety property is not the primary claim. Also a NeurIPS 2021 workshop paper, and Fig. 8 runtime has no numeric values.

title: Multi-UAV Conflict Resolution with Graph Convolutional Reinforcement Learning
evidence: "Sec. 5.1: the model manages to always avoid near misses in both cases, as the NMAC distance is never breached" - conflict resolution among 3-4 UAVs is the paper's sole objective and sole measured outcome
method: Cooperative MARL with graph convolutional communication (DGN) over a UAV relation graph; each agent picks turn-left, turn-right or do-nothing every 2 s; conflicts and severity penalised in the reward
evaluation: BlueSky ATC simulator, 3 then 4 UAVs, 10k episodes each; only comparator is the average unmitigated case; average LOSS per episode <1, zero NMAC breaches; trained on Tesla K80, no inference latency
contribution: Graph convolutional cooperative MARL resolves multi-UAV conflicts, holding losses of separation below one per episode with no near-midair-collision breaches in 3-agent and 4-agent airspace.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes, the RL policy is the actor but nothing guards it - safety is reward shaping only, so (a) fails and runtime_interceptor is no. Check the evaluation floor: the only comparator is a dashed "average unmitigated case" line in Fig. 2, with no rule-based or learned baseline and no no-communication ablation, so exclude-E2 is defensible. Table 1 counts of solved compound conflicts (5650 for 3 agents, 4461 for 4 agents) are not normalised to an episode total, and the claimed "time in LOSS <5 s" appears only in prose.

title: MDPFuzz: Testing Models Solving Markov Decision Processes
evidence: "Abstract: We present MDPFuzz, the first blackbox fuzz testing framework for models solving MDPs" - the Sec. 7.4 abnormal-behaviour detector flags activation patterns offline and is never described as intervening in a live action
method: Blackbox fuzzing of sequential decision models: mutate initial states, keep seeds that crash, cut cumulative reward or add fresh state sequences (GMM density); offline anomaly detector and fine-tuning repair
evaluation: Five targets (CARLA RL and IL, ACAS Xu, MARL cooperative navigation, BipedalWalker), 12 h campaigns, 3 runs, 598 crashes; freshness ablation adds 37 crashes; detector AUC-ROC >0.78; repair cuts ACAS Xu crashes 139 to 29; RTX 3090
contribution: MDPFuzz fuzzes models solving MDPs by mutating initial states under a state-sequence freshness measure, exposing hundreds of collision-triggering states in RL, imitation, MARL and ACAS Xu policies.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes (RL, IL, DNN and MARL policies are the systems analysed), so the Pillar 1 scope ruling is satisfied, but this is offline test-case generation with no execution-time override, so (a) fails, and multi-agent is 1 of 5 benchmarks rather than the primary claim, so (c) fails the primacy test. Most likely record in this batch to be overturned: the Sec. 7.4 detector (AUC-ROC >0.78 on 6000 samples) reads as a runtime monitor if the maintainer relaxes the intervention requirement, and the repair result (139 to 29 crashes at unchanged reward 30.73 to 30.74) is exactly RQ5 evidence. No external fuzzer baseline is compared quantitatively; the abstract's 598 crashes do not match the Table 3 per-model means, which sum to about 590.

title: Multi-Agent Vulnerability Discovery for Autonomous Driving with Hazard Arbitration Reward
evidence: "Abstract: Safety Test framework by finding Av-Responsible Scenarios (STARS) based on multiagent reinforcement learning" - attack success rate, i.e. the rate of AV-responsible collisions produced by 1-3 learned adversaries, is the primary measured outcome
method: Multi-agent RL (MAPPO, parameter sharing) trains 1-3 surrounding vehicles as adversaries; a Hazard Arbitration Reward penalises collisions the attackers themselves caused, isolating AV-responsible hazards
evaluation: highway-env Highway, Merge and Roundabout against four defender policies (Value Iteration, Robust VI, PPO, D3QN); ablation over 1, 2, 3 attackers; attack success rises e.g. 47.88 to 76.08 to 72.75 percent on Highway VI and 20.20 to 87.98 percent on Merge VI; no hardware or latency reported
contribution: STARS trains cooperating adversarial traffic agents with a hazard arbitration reward so that discovered collisions are attributable to the autonomous vehicle, exposing vulnerabilities even in safety-enhanced planners.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes, two of four defenders (PPO, D3QN) and all attackers are learned, though Value Iteration and Robust VI are dynamic programming over a finite MDP abstraction and carry the highest reported attack rates, so the headline numbers lean on the non-learned defenders. Scenario generation only, no runtime override, so (a) fails. Check the evaluation floor: the only ablation is attacker count, there is no ablation removing the Hazard Arbitration Reward and no quantitative comparison with prior single-attacker or multi-attacker attack methods, which are discussed qualitatively only. The acceleration threshold lambda in HAR is never specified, and AV-responsibility is judged by the authors' reward design rather than independent rating.

title: Detecting danger in gridworlds using Gromov's Link Condition
evidence: "Abstract: Serendipitously, we discover these failures occur exactly where undesirable or dangerous states appear in the gridworld" - Theorem 5.2 (Sec. 5) characterises Link Condition failures as knight-move or 2-step-bishop-move agent pairs
method: Modified Abrams-Ghrist-Peterson state complexes with added dance generators for multi-agent gridworlds; failure of Gromov's Link Condition (positive curvature) is proved to coincide with collision-prone agent configurations
evaluation: Exhaustive enumeration of small rooms (3x3 with 0-9 agents, plus 2x2, 2x3, 4x1, 4x4) in a custom Python tool on a laptop; comparison is original versus modified complex; e.g. 3x3 with 3 agents gives 84 states and 184 link failures, mean 2.19, max 14; Remark 6.1 notes infeasibility at scale
contribution: Filling in agent dance squares makes gridworld state complexes fail Gromov's Link Condition exactly at collision-prone configurations, giving a proved, bounded-foresight geometric signal for multi-agent danger.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: no - the gridworld agents are abstract tokens with no policy, the authors state that mapping this geometry to neural network representations is ongoing work (Sec. 7), and no learned planner is guarded or analysed, so the Pillar 1 scope ruling of 2026-11-13 makes criteria (a) and (c) fail and this is exclude-E1 rather than exclude-E2. It does clear the evaluation floor on its own terms (Theorem 5.2 plus Table 1 enumeration against the unmodified complex), and the proposed "detour" response and bounded-foresight remark in Sec. 6 are future work only, so there is no runtime interception. Second most likely overturn in this batch if the maintainer counts gridworld RL environments as learned systems by setting; note the authors themselves "caution against hasty real-world implementation" (Sec. 7).

title: Deadlock Resolution and Recursive Feasibility in MPC-based Multi-robot Trajectory Generation
evidence: Sec. III, Algorithm 1: collision avoidance is enforced as hard separating half-space constraints (MBVC-WB) inside each robot's MPC; no supervisor or fallback when the optimisation is infeasible.
method: Distributed infinite-horizon MPC with warning-band buffered Voronoi constraints; deadlock detected as terminal overlap and resolved by adapting repulsion weights; proofs of recursive feasibility and collision-freedom.
evaluation: Sim 2D 2-14 and 3D 8-60 robots, 100 trials each; 20 and 8 Crazyflies; baselines BVC, iSCP, DMPC; success rate 100% vs 41/12/63% at 14 robots; 0.75 s cycle for 60 robots.
contribution: A distributed MPC that detects impending deadlocks from predicted terminal overlap and resolves them by adaptive repulsion, with proven recursive feasibility, reaching 100% success where BVC, iSCP and DMPC fail.
flag: Deadlock and feasibility are the primary claim and outcome (success rate, completion time, infeasibility counts) - the protocol names this case as E1; safety is a constraint inside the planner, so not (a). Does prove collision-freedom (Corollary 1) but reports no collision rate. Deadlock detection ahead of time, about (K-2)h, is loosely adjacent to RQ2. Reported 0.75 s cycle time for 60 robots exceeds the 0.2 s sampling interval and the paper does not address it. Tables II-IV infeasibility rows and some Table III entries were garbled in extraction - verify numbers before citing. Theorem 2 needs target-separation and non-collinearity assumptions.

title: Velocity Obstacle Based Risk-Bounded Motion Planning for Stochastic Multi-Agent Systems
evidence: Abstract: 'collision-free trajectories are generated under a prescribed collision risk bound'; Sec VI-C: 'The minimum distance between each pair of agents and the success rate are treated as the safety metrics.'
method: Distributed chance-constrained MPC per agent with velocity-obstacle collision constraints reformulated as mixed-integer constraints; a risk budget is split across neighbours so collision probability stays under a prescribed bound, without communication.
evaluation: Simulation, 4-20 agents, Gaussian noise; vs pure VO and position-based MPC; success 100% vs 91-78% (PB-MPC), min distance 0.447-0.491 m vs 0.412-0.436 m; Intel i5 3.3 GHz, within 50 ms step.
contribution: A distributed chance-constrained MPC using velocity obstacles that keeps stochastic multi-agent collision risk under a prescribed bound, holding 100% success where position-based MPC drops to 78% under noise.
flag: Borderline: this is a planner with collision constraints inside the optimisation, not a runtime filter, so (a) is not met and runtime_interceptor is no; I credit (c) because risk-bounded collision avoidance is the primary claim and the measured outcome (success rate, min distance) has a baseline - maintainer may prefer E1. No collision rate as such; trial count for Table I not stated; PB-MPC cells at highest noise were illegible in extraction and the text's 78% does not match the 84% I could read at mid noise - check the PDF table. Computation time only in plots, the sole numeric claim is within the 0.05 s sampling period at N=50. Internal inconsistencies between Table II and Sec VI-A (run time, radius). Simulation only.

title: Decentralized Safe Multi-agent Stochastic Optimal Control using Deep FBSDEs and ADMM
evidence: Sec. on SCBF: 'a safe optimal control can be obtained by solving the resulting Quadratic Program (QP) at every time step'; barriers guarantee safe operation 'with a high probability'.
method: Decentralized stochastic optimal control: Deep FBSDE network with an embedded merged consensus-ADMM/OSQP QP layer enforcing stochastic control barrier functions for neighbouring agents.
evaluation: Sim, unicycle agents: swapping (16), bottleneck (8), moving obstacle (8), formation (32); vs centralized Safe Deep FBSDE; memory 1586 vs 17879 MiB, 14.75 vs 1306 s/iter; violations only plotted.
contribution: A decentralized Deep FBSDE controller with an ADMM-based barrier-function QP layer scales safe stochastic multi-agent control to 32 agents, cutting memory by 91% and iteration time by 99% against a centralized formulation.
flag: Borderline E2 vs include. Safety is a constraint in the QP layer that generates the control, not a filter over a nominal action, so not (a). The only quantified comparison against the baseline is constraint count, memory and training time; barrier violations and collisions appear only as curves in Fig. 3 (h vs h_pos) with no numbers in the text, described as 'much lower or even zero for some tasks'. If the maintainer can read usable violation counts off Fig. 3 this could be include on (c). Abstract says safe operation of all agents 'is ensured during the entire training process', but the body reports nonzero barrier violations during training and a probabilistic guarantee only. No hardware named, no per-step latency. Quotes relayed via the fetch tool.

title: Probabilistic Symmetry for Multi-Agent Dynamics
evidence: "Instead of predicting the position directly, PECCO outputs a Gaussian distribution over velocity" (Sec. 4.3), for all agents in the scene jointly
method: PECCO: SO(2)-equivariant continuous-convolution network predicting per-agent Gaussian velocity distributions for all agents in a scene, integrated through dynamics to give calibrated position uncertainty.
evaluation: Argoverse, TrajNet++, synthetic particles; vs LSTM-NLL, CtsConv-NLL, Trajectron++, MFP, conformal variants; Argoverse minADE6 1.39, minFDE6 3.41, coverage@3s 84.5%; TrajNet++ 0.59/1.06. No inference latency.
contribution: An equivariant probabilistic forecaster for multi-agent trajectories that improves accuracy and coverage calibration over Trajectron++ and MFP on vehicle and pedestrian benchmarks.
flag: Enters under (b) as predictor/architecture evidence only; no safety mechanism or hazard metric, RQ5 capped. Predicts explicit trajectories, not latent state, so non-generative cell not claimed. Coverage numbers disagree between tables (Table 2 84.5% at 3 s vs 87.5% in Tables 4-5; Table 3 differs again). PECCO NLL on Argoverse (4.26) is worse than Trajectron++ (2.48). Training on 4 RTX 2080 Ti; ablation tables partly garbled in the PDF text I read.

title: Cooperative Multi-Agent Trajectory Generation with Modular Bayesian Optimization
evidence: Conclusion: the algorithm "requires between two and three hours to optimize a multi-vehicle trajectory" - an offline optimiser, nothing sits between decision and execution.
method: Modular Bayesian optimisation of time allocation for min-snap multi-quadrotor trajectories; per-vehicle feasibility and per-pair collision GP classifier surrogates; rejection sampling inside the offline search.
evaluation: Six sim environments plus four real quadcopters in mocap; baselines formation control and MILP; metric trajectory time (mBO 5.2-8.1 s vs MILP 7.0-12.3 s); 2-3 h offline compute.
contribution: Offline Bayesian optimisation with modular Gaussian-process constraint surrogates produces faster cooperative quadrotor trajectories than MILP and formation baselines, but with no runtime safety layer.
flag: Offline trajectory optimiser; outcome is flight time, no collision-rate metric. Paper admits vehicle contact in real flights on trajectories 1 and 2. Multi-fidelity results are figures only. No runtime latency. Surrogate tags are approximate - no project tag fits Bayesian optimisation.

title: The Before, During, and After of Multi-Robot Deadlock
evidence: Sec. 2 states the QP is formulated with "safety constraints taking precedence over task-satisfaction", and Sec. 3 that "Manual intervention is needed to resolve deadlock"
method: KKT analysis of decentralized CBF-QP collision-avoidance filters characterises deadlock as a force balance; a three-phase controller detects deadlock, rotates robots at the safety distance, then resumes goal control.
evaluation: Simulations with 2 and 3 single-integrator robots and Khepera-IV experiments; no baseline or ablation; no collision, success or timing metrics; only deadlock-configuration counts {1,1,4,18} for N=1-4.
contribution: Characterises when and how CBF-QP safety filters deadlock multi-robot systems and gives a provably relapse-free three-phase resolution controller for two and three robots.
flag: The protocol names deadlock papers as E1 and that is the subject here; exclude-E2 applies independently (no quantitative safety metric, no baseline, results are figures and videos). Still worth a background citation: it is a formal account of a known failure mode of the very runtime filters the review covers - the CBF-QP does override the nominal command, hence runtime_interceptor yes, but the paper analyses the filter rather than proposing or evaluating it as a safety mechanism. Proof of relapse-freedom is for N=2, with N=3 asserted as a trivial extension; only Category A deadlock is handled; single-integrator model without actuator limits; two-robot hardware deadlock could not be reproduced and a virtual deadlock was initialised instead. The manual-intervention remark is motivation only, no human handoff is studied. No hardware latency. Detection thresholds not given numerically. Read via a summarising fetch tool, so check quotes against the PDF.

title: A Benchmark for Unsupervised Anomaly Detection in Multi-Agent Trajectories
evidence: "The spatial graph embedding layer transforms the trajectories of all agents into an embedding space" (Sec. V, Methods, STGAE)
method: R-U-MAAD benchmark plus 11 unsupervised baselines - linear and deep reconstruction auto-encoders (Seq2Seq, STGAE, LaneGCN-AE) and OC-SVM and DSVDD one-class variants - scoring multi-agent trajectory anomalies.
evaluation: Argoverse 205,942 train sequences, unsupervised; 160-sequence annotated test set, sliding window T=16; 11 baselines; AUPR-Abn best 59.65 (STGAE) vs CVM 47.19; no hardware or latency reported.
contribution: Provides a public benchmark with human-annotated anomalies for unsupervised multi-agent driving-trajectory anomaly detection, together with eleven reconstruction and one-class baselines.
flag: Enters as predictor evidence only (criterion b), so RQ5 is capped at 2 per protocol v1.6 and it should not be credited with preventing anything. Criterion (c) is arguable: the primary outcome is AUPR, not a hazard or collision rate. No latency, hardware, inference-time or online-deployment statement appears anywhere in the body, so the edge and real-time angle is entirely absent. The interaction-aware graph models (STGAE 59.65, LaneGCN-AE 57.19) barely beat or lose to the single-agent Seq2Seq (59.21), which weakens the multi-agent framing. OC-SVM variants were tuned on 20% of the annotated test data, a supervised advantage the authors acknowledge.

title: DMCA: Dense Multi-agent Navigation using Attention and Communication
evidence: Sec. III-B assumes "the request-reply is fast and executed within a single planning cycle"; collision avoidance is learned only via the reward in Eq. (7), with no runtime filter.
method: End-to-end GA3C policy with multi-head attention over neighbour observations and Gumbel-Softmax link prediction choosing which neighbours to query for hidden state; collision penalty in reward only.
evaluation: gym-collision-avoidance, up to 30 agents; baselines ORCA, CADRL, GA3C-CADRL, BVC, BUAVC, Long et al., SelComm, TarMAC; success/collision rate, time-to-goal; ~6 ms per agent on RTX 2080 Ti; 2-3 real robots qualitative.
contribution: An attention-and-selective-communication RL navigation policy reaching 0.99 average success with zero collisions at up to 30 agents in circle scenarios, computing each action in about 6 ms on a desktop GPU.
flag: Borderline (c): collision rate is tabulated against six baselines (Table II DMCA 0 at all counts vs ORCA 0.02, CADRL 0.31 at 30 agents), but the paper is a learned navigation policy with safety in the reward, not a safety mechanism or certificate - I read it as failing the primacy test; maintainer may disagree. Abstract 'up to 24%' success improvement could not be traced to a table row. The '2-10x lower than broadcast' claim rests on estimated broadcast counts; Table IV gives about 1.5-2.3x. Table II mislabels rows as NavSIC. 6 ms is on Xeon plus RTX 2080 Ti, not edge. Real-robot runs have no metrics.

title: Decentralized Deadlock-free Trajectory Planning for Quadrotor Swarm in Obstacle-rich Environments -- Extended version
evidence: Contribution statement (section not confirmed, likely Sec. I): "the first decentralized MATP algorithm that guarantees the feasibility of the optimization problem, collision avoidance, and deadlock-free in a dense maze-like environment."
method: Decentralized quadrotor trajectory planner: grid-based PIBT waypoint, LP subgoal optimization for deadlock resolution, then QP trajectory under safe flight corridor and linear safe corridor constraints, replanned at 5 Hz.
evaluation: Simulation (forest, sparse and dense maze, 10 agents, 30 trials) and 10 Crazyflie 2.1; baseline LSC-PB; success rate, flight time, distance; 7.2-9.1 ms per replan on i7-9750H laptop.
contribution: A decentralized quadrotor swarm planner combining PIBT waypoints, subgoal optimization and linear safe corridors that reaches 100% success in dense mazes where its predecessor deadlocks, at about 8 ms per replan.
flag: Planner with collision avoidance as a constraint; the paper is about deadlock resolution and flight time, so it fails the (c) primacy test. Success rate is 100% for both methods except dense maze (LSC-PB 0% from not reaching the goal, not collisions); no separate collision or deadlock rate. Headline 27.6% shorter flight time and 7.4% shorter distance at infinite range is not reproducible from a single Table I row (random forest gives about 25.7% and 5.9%); averaging basis unstated. Computation time 7.24-9.05 ms is measured on a laptop, not onboard; no explicit latency constraint, so (d) not credited. Hardware demo is one flight with 'no collision or deadlock', no counts. This is the extended version of a conference paper - check for a duplicate queued record.

title: Learning Control Admissibility Models with Graph Neural Networks for Multi-Agent Navigation
evidence: Sec 2.3: "we choose the action that has the highest preference score in the admissible set"; Sec 3.2: "the safety rate of CAM remains nearly 100% for all the environments, up to 512 agents"
method: GNN control admissibility model scores sampled candidate actions per agent; inadmissible ones are filtered and the best-preference admissible action executes; subgraph decomposition composes models by intersecting admissible sets.
evaluation: Simulated UR5 (PyBullet), Car, Dynamic Dubins, Drone; train 3 agents, test to 512; baselines GNN-DDPG and MACBF; safe rate and reward; desktop RTX 3080, about 4.3 ms per agent-step max.
contribution: Learned graph admissibility model that filters each agent's sampled candidate actions at run time, trained on 3 agents and composed to 512 with near-100% safe rate at about 4.3 ms per agent-step.
flag: Runtime-interceptor call is a judgement: CAM filters 2000 sampled candidates against a goal preference score rather than overriding a separate nominal controller, and it is learned with no guarantee (appendix reports about 0.4-0.9 percent forward-invariance violations in single-agent examples). Main baseline comparison (Fig 4) is image-only - no numeric safe rate for DDPG/MACBF in text; only numbers are Table 1 chasing game at 64 agents: safe rate 0.99 vs 0.90 without decomposition (Car), 0.989 vs 0.988 (Drone). The 4.3 ms figure is a desktop GPU, not edge hardware, and reported as a maximum after acceleration - latency is measured but not a design constraint, so the latency cell is generous. No real robots. Abstract has no numerals. RQ4 score rests on agent-count/density generalisation, not hazard combinations.

title: Scalable Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning through Intelligent Information Aggregation
evidence: Future work includes "adding a safety guarantee layer for the actions of the agents to avoid collisions" (Sec. 5); collisions enter only as a -5 reward term (App. B.1).
method: InforMARL: MAPPO-style actor-critic where a graph neural network aggregates each agent's local neighbourhood (agents, obstacles, goals) into a fixed-size vector for decentralised actor and centralised critic.
evaluation: Modified MAPE, 3-15 agents, 4 tasks, 100 test episodes; vs RMAPPO, MADDPG, QMIX, DGN, GPG, EMP; Target N=10: reward 429.14, success 100%, 4.73 collisions vs RMAPPO 6.93; no hardware or timing.
contribution: A graph-aggregation architecture for decentralised multi-agent reinforcement learning that scales navigation policies to more agents than seen in training using only local observations.
flag: Coordination/scalability paper with no safety mechanism: the paper itself defers a safety layer to future work. The GNN aggregates current neighbourhood state for the policy; it is not a predictive world model, so (b) is not met. Collision counts are reported but are not the primary outcome and are not uniformly better (N=3: 1.45 vs RMAPPO 0.67; collisions per agent rise with density, 0.40 at m=3 to about 1.2-1.3 at m=15). Multi-agent-state cell credited only for the graph encoder; drop it if the cell is reserved for safety mechanisms.

title: A Hierarchical Variable Autonomy Mixed-Initiative Framework for Human-Robot Teaming in Mobile Robotics
evidence: Sec. III-B: the controller transfers control between operator and robot at runtime, and cognitive availability is used "to assure they provide driving input only when they are attending the Operator Control Unit (OCU) screen".
method: HierEMICS: AHP-ranked fuzzy rule base over operator cognitive availability (head pose), navigational intent, motion error and speed that switches level of autonomy between teleoperation and autonomy.
evaluation: Gazebo simulation, one robot, 13 participants within-subject vs EMICS; collisions M=0.23 vs 1.23, conflicts 4.77 vs 9.92, AI switches 5.54 vs 11.62, time 272 vs 283 s; no latency.
contribution: A hierarchical mixed-initiative controller that uses operator attention and intent to decide when to switch control, reducing collisions, human-robot conflicts and unnecessary autonomy switches against EMICS in a 13-person study.
flag: Single robot only (multi-robot is future work), so multi-agent is absent; inclusion rests on (e) handoff. Collision result is internally inconsistent: text calls it significant but prints Z=-2.266, p=0.23 (likely .023) - verify in the PDF. No situation-awareness measure and no takeover-time measure; NASA-TLX overall 40.00 vs 43.66 n.s.; completion time n.s. Total LOA switches 16.38 vs 28.15 (p=.003). NASA-TLX frustration figures were garbled in the extracted text. Only baseline is EMICS, no ablation of individual modules; simulation only, n=13, no latency or control-rate figures. Whether attention gating blocks or defers commands is not stated.

title: AVstack: An Open-Source, Reconfigurable Platform for Autonomous Vehicle Development
evidence: Appendix A: "AVstack is not proposed as a real-time solution"; also (section not identified) "We have not performed experiments evaluating latency."
method: Open-source modular Python platform for building and evaluating AV perception, tracking and prediction pipelines across datasets and CARLA, with a V2I collaborative-sensing case study.
evaluation: KITTI, nuScenes, CARLA, 5 passive agent configs over 10 sequences; CARLA V2I with 40 infrastructure LiDARs, ego-only baselines; precision/recall, HOTA, MOTA, MOTP, ADE, FDE; no hardware or latency.
contribution: Presents AVstack, a reconfigurable open-source AV development platform, and uses it to compare perception-tracking-prediction stacks across KITTI, nuScenes and CARLA and to study infrastructure-to-vehicle sensor fusion.
flag: Tooling/platform paper; no safety mechanism, no collision or hazard metric (RSS listed as an available metric in Table 2 but no values). V2I study reports tracking metrics only, e.g. C1-Base HOTA 0.47 vs C1-Ideal 0.55, FDE 6.40 vs 3.23; infrastructure detections are simulated and passed with zero latency. Methods tag is a loose fit (no graph learning; nothing in the list fits a perception/tracking platform) - maintainer may blank or retag. Internal inconsistencies: text says 5 CARLA scenes and 9 collaborative cases, Table 6 caption says 10 trials and Table 5 lists 7 plus 2 baselines.

title: Structural Attention-Based Recurrent Variational Autoencoder for Highway Vehicle Anomaly Detection
evidence: Abstract and Sec. 3.2.4: 'a stochastic Koopman operator-propagated latent space predicts the next states of vehicles', over a graph of vehicle and lane nodes.
method: Unsupervised VAE with vehicle-vehicle and lane-vehicle attention, GRU encoder and stochastic Koopman latent propagation; the one-step prediction error maximised over vehicles is the anomaly score.
evaluation: MAAD simulated highway set, 11 anomaly classes; four baselines and four ablations; AUROC 87.0, AUPR-Abnormal 65.5, FPR at 95% TPR 57.7 against STGAE-KDE 86.3, 55.2, 50.0; V100 training, no inference latency.
contribution: Unsupervised highway anomaly detector that adds road-structure attention and stochastic Koopman latent prediction, lifting wrong-way-driving detection AUROC from 73.2 to 99.3 over a spatio-temporal graph autoencoder baseline.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: no - the monitored agents are human-driven vehicles in the simulated MAAD dataset, so under the 2026-11-13 scope ruling (a) and (c) both fail and the include rests on (b) alone; this is the record the maintainer is most likely to overturn to exclude-E1. (a) also fails on its own terms: the anomaly score is computed offline and 'integrating with a vehicle controller' is listed as future work (Sec. 5), so there is no runtime override. For (b), check whether detection AUROC counts as a direct predictive measure - no ADE, FDE or any trajectory-accuracy figure is reported, and the prediction horizon is a single step. Hyperparameters were selected on a 20% validation split taken from the test data (Sec. 4.1), a leakage risk. The deterministic ablation SABeR-AE matches or beats the proposed SABeR-VAE on AUROC (87.2 vs 87.0) and AUPR-Abnormal (69.0 vs 65.5), so the variational component is not clearly earning its place and the headline 18% AUPR gain over STGAE-KDE is smaller than the ablation's 25%. RQ5 capped at 2 per the (b)-only rule.

title: Shared Information-Based Safe And Efficient Behavior Planning For Connected Autonomous Vehicles
evidence: "If all the actions in A are not safe in the worst case, then the controller will apply the emergency stop (ES) process." (Sec. 5)
method: Connected vehicles share pruned-CNN vision features over V2V; a multi-agent actor-critic policy's chosen action passes a safe action mapping that substitutes a safe alternative or triggers emergency stop.
evaluation: CARLA mixed traffic, 30 vehicles, CAV ratio 0-1; vs MADDPG and IDM; unsafe actions 0 vs 4,416-242,976; headway >=18.5 m; velocity 60.06 to 66.15 mph; i9-10900X, four RTX 2080 Ti.
contribution: A safe action mapping over a multi-agent actor-critic policy, fed by V2V-shared vision, executed zero unsafe actions in CARLA mixed traffic where unshielded MADDPG executed thousands, while raising average velocity.
flag: Check: (1) Table 4 values for CAV ratio 0.5-0.8 were not readable in the extracted text; only 0.1-0.4 (MADDPG 4,416/9,510/21,897/43,491, safe MARL 0) plus a text figure for 0.9 (242,976 vs 0), and 0.9 is not a column of the table. (2) Safety metric is a count of unsafe actions and minimum headway, not a collision rate; zero unsafe actions is partly true by construction of the mapping. (3) No count of emergency stops or substitutions, so no intervention or false-halt rate. (4) Only safety baseline is unshielded MADDPG; no ablation of the mapping or of V2V sharing beyond a qualitative obstacle-at-corner test. (5) Execution-time use of the mapping rests on one sentence in the Conclusion ("guarantees the safety of the training and execution process"); there is no separate test-time protocol. (6) Safety is one-hop headway above 18.5 m only. (7) Throughput figures (99 img/s after pruning, 3.5x speedup) are for the vision models on desktop GPUs; no decision-loop latency, so edge and latency cells not credited. Simulation only.

title: ForceFormer: Exploring Social Force and Transformer for Pedestrian Trajectory Prediction
evidence: Sec.III-B: backbone is AgentFormer, a CVAE Transformer with latent variable Z, to which per-agent driving and repulsive social-force sequences are fed as inputs to predict multi-pedestrian futures.
method: Adds goal-derived driving force and elliptical repulsive social force (group-aware via DBSCAN) as input features to the AgentFormer CVAE Transformer; U-Net estimates goals from heatmaps and scene maps.
evaluation: ETH/UCY leave-one-out, 8 obs/12 pred steps, K=20; 9 baselines; avg ADE/FDE 0.20/0.29 (Dr), 0.19/0.30 (Re) vs AgentFormer 0.23/0.39; collisions 548-588 vs 683; Tesla P100, no inference time.
contribution: ForceFormer feeds social-force features into a CVAE Transformer for multi-pedestrian trajectory prediction, cutting average FDE from 0.39 to 0.29 m and predicted collisions by about 20% versus AgentFormer on ETH/UCY.
flag: Enters under b only (predictor, method evidence); RQ5 capped at 2 per protocol. Generative CVAE with K=20 sampling, so non-generative inference NOT credited. Interaction is attention plus hand-crafted forces, no graph. Test-time goal is picked from sampled candidates by smallest L2 error to GROUND TRUTH, so results are oracle-optimistic. Collisions are raw counts within predictions (threshold 0.1 m), not a rate, dominated by Univ (655 of 683). Text claims beating Y-net on all subsets but ETH; Table II shows Y-net better on Hotel for Dr and on Univ FDE for Re. Pedestrian forecasting may be outside intended scope: maintainer may prefer exclude-E1. New tag social-force. One fetch covered full text.

title: Planning and Control of Uncertain Cooperative Mobile Manipulator-Endowed Systems under Temporal-Logic Tasks
evidence: Ch. 4 Sec. 4.2 'Adaptive Robot Navigation with Collision Avoidance Subject to 2nd-order Uncertain Dynamics': collision avoidance is built into the control law through navigation functions with barrier-like obstacle terms; Ch. 2 handles obstacles as constraints inside nonlinear MPC.
method: PhD thesis (KTH 2020): adaptive, prescribed-performance and NMPC control for cooperative manipulation, formation control and multi-robot navigation under temporal-logic tasks with uncertain dynamics.
evaluation: Simulations (V-REP, 3-4 manipulators, 6 UAVs) and UR5/UAV experiments; comparisons of grasp-matrix choices, PID, RRT variants; convergence plots only in text read; no collision rates or latency.
contribution: A doctoral thesis on provably convergent adaptive and MPC control of cooperating mobile manipulators and multi-robot teams under temporal-logic tasks, with collision avoidance embedded in the control laws.
flag: PARTIAL READ: this is a full PhD thesis and the fetched text is capped at 500000 characters, ending mid Sec. 4.2.5; I read offsets 0-100k, 200k-300k and 400k-500k (not 100k-200k or 300k-400k), and Chapters 4 (results), 5 (temporal-logic multi-agent planning) and 6 were seen only as outlines and figure lists. In everything read, collision avoidance is a constraint inside the controller or planner (not a runtime override) and no quantitative safety metric against a baseline appears, so (a) and (c) fail; maintainer may want to confirm Ch. 4-5 do not contain a collision-rate comparison. Barrier-type terms are part of the nominal control law, not a safety filter. Event-triggered communication with minimum inter-event times in Ch. 2 but no delay model. Check whether a thesis counts under E3; constituent papers may be queued separately.

title: Parallel Optimization with Hard Safety Constraints for Cooperative Planning of Connected Autonomous Vehicles
evidence: Safety is "enforced as hard constraints" (Abstract) via linearised collision and road-boundary constraints solved inside a dual consensus ADMM trajectory optimisation (Sec. IV-A, IV-D)
method: Cooperative trajectory optimisation for connected vehicles: collision and road-boundary conditions convexified into hard constraints, solved in parallel per vehicle by dual consensus ADMM with LQR subproblems.
evaluation: CARLA Town03 roundabout, N=8/12/16; vs IPOPT and a CARLA tracking controller; multi-process time per step 1.56/4.11/8.76 ms vs IPOPT 0.109-7.09 s; mean speed 9.1-10.0 vs 5.5-7.8 m/s; Xeon server.
contribution: Solves cooperative trajectory planning for up to 16 connected vehicles with hard collision constraints in under 9 ms per step by splitting the problem across vehicles with dual consensus ADMM.
flag: Borderline. Safety lives inside the planner, so (a) fails. For (c): hard-constraint safety is a headline claim but the measured outcomes are computation time and average velocity; safety evidence is qualitative only ("collisions between vehicles are avoided"; baseline "fails to avoid collisions", Sec. V-B) with no collision counts, so it would be E2 if (c) were granted. For (d): 1.56-8.76 ms per step on a 2-socket Xeon 6348 server is fast but no explicit latency budget is set and it is not edge hardware. The claim of at least two orders of magnitude over IPOPT holds only against one-stage IPOPT; against two-stage it is about 58-70x. Single runs, no variance, k_max = 2 ADMM iterations and no constraint-violation statistics. Assumes complete communication graph.

title: Multi-agent Distributed Model Predictive Control with Connectivity Constraint
evidence: Sec 3: connectivity enters only as an optimisation constraint (10k), lambda_2(L(x(j|k))) >= lambda_2, alongside collision-avoidance constraints inside the finite-horizon problem.
method: Distributed tracking MPC for multi-agent systems with an algebraic-connectivity (Fiedler eigenvalue) constraint and collision constraints inside the optimisation, solved by SQP amenable to ADMM distribution.
evaluation: MATLAB/CasADi simulation: 10 agents crossing an obstacle, 4-agent leader-follower; only comparison is with vs without connectivity constraint; lambda_2 plots, no tables; Intel i7, no solve times.
contribution: A tracking MPC that keeps a multi-agent communication graph connected by constraining the Laplacian's Fiedler eigenvalue, with recursive-feasibility arguments and two simulated examples.
flag: Constraint inside a planner, so (a) fails by the strict-runtime rule; subject is connectivity maintenance, not hazard detection. Would also fail on E2: no collision or violation rate, results are qualitative plots (lambda_2 falls to 0 without the constraint, stays >= 0.1 with it), no baseline method. No comm delay or asynchrony modelled, no solve times despite real-time relevance. Extracted text had duplicated/misnumbered equations (extraction artefacts).

title: Rate-Tunable Control Barrier Functions: Methods and Algorithms for Online Adaptation
evidence: "Algorithm 1 presents an update law that minimally modifies Theta to ensure the feasibility of the CBF-QP controller" (Sec. VI-A); QP of Eq. 30 minimally modifies a reference input designed without regard to constraints
method: Rate-tunable CBFs: class-K parameters of each barrier evolve online so the CBF-QP filter stays feasible; trust scores about neighbours relax or tighten constraints in decentralized multi-robot control.
evaluation: Simulations: 1D pointwise study, adaptive cruise control, decentralized multi-robot with adversarial/uncooperative agents; vs fixed-parameter CBF-QP, which becomes infeasible; time-to-failure shown in Fig. 4 only. No hardware or timing.
contribution: Lets control-barrier-function parameters adapt online so a decentralized safety filter remains feasible and less conservative among cooperative, uncooperative and adversarial agents where fixed-parameter filters fail.
flag: Borderline E2: baseline (fixed-parameter CBF-QP) is present but safety evidence is feasibility/infeasibility and trajectory plots; normalized time-to-failure appears only in Fig. 4 with no numeric values in text, and no collision or violation rates. (c) is weak - multi-agent trust is one section, the primary claim is QP feasibility. Agent count ambiguous (5 in scenario 1 text, caption suggests otherwise; about 6 in scenario 2). Assumes perfect observation of neighbours. No compute times.

title: Model-based Dynamic Shielding for Safe and Efficient Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
evidence: Sec 4.2: shields 'reject agents' unsafe actions and replace them with safety actions'; Sec 3.3: a shield 'monitors the control input of agents and corrects any unsafe control input instantaneously'.
method: Reactive shields synthesised from LTL safety games (Slugs) over local agent groups; shields merge, split and recompute as agents move; model-based variant learns RSSM-style dynamics to build shields without prior model.
evaluation: Gridworld (4 agents) and MPE spread/adversary, N=4,8,12; baselines factored shielding, MADDPG+CBF, safety-reward MADDPG/DDPG; collisions 0.0 vs up to 43.5; no hardware or timing reported.
contribution: Dynamic shields that merge, split and recompute around interacting agents replace unsafe MARL actions at runtime, giving zero test collisions in MPE at up to 12 agents with reward comparable to CBF baselines.
flag: Table 1 test collisions: DS 0.0 at N=4/8/12 vs MADDPG+Safe 1.3/10.0/38.2 (spread) and 1.1/6.8/43.5 (adversary); MADDPG+CBF also 0.0, so safety gain over CBF is nil and reward gain small (CBF better at N=4). Abstract claims 'formal safety guarantees with high probability' for MBDS but body gives no probability bound and puts cascading model error out of scope. 'Real-time' synthesis claimed, no synthesis time, hardware or latency measured; authors admit no time-complexity analysis. Learned model appears per-agent kinematics, so (b) not credited. Text inconsistent: four vs six gridworld maps; 5 vs 10 runs. Fig 10 'safety rate' is defined as a collision-step ratio; MBDS results (4 to 8 agents, above 90%) only in figures. No ablation of merge/split.

title: Multi-Layer Continuum Deformation Optimization of Multi-Agent Systems
evidence: The collision bound "assigns a lower bound on alpha_i(t) for every i in W_1 at any time t" (Sec. 4.1); simulation states only that inter-quadcopter collision avoidance is guaranteed (Sec. 5).
method: Multi-layer continuum deformation coordination: leaders' time-varying weights are set by a quadratic program with inter-agent collision-avoidance and containment constraints; followers tracked by feedback linearisation.
evaluation: Single MATLAB R2022b simulation, 67 quadcopters (7+6+54) tracking a helix for 1000 s in obstacle-free space; no baseline, no ablation, no numeric safety metric; desktop i7, no timing.
contribution: A hierarchical continuum-deformation formation scheme whose quadratic program bounds deformation to guarantee inter-agent collision avoidance, shown in one 67-quadcopter simulation without baselines or measured safety outcomes.
flag: Safety constraints live inside an offline/planning QP, not a runtime interceptor. Abstract claims "improvements in safety and efficiency" but the body has no comparison and no quantitative safety or efficiency value, only plots and design parameters (alpha range 0.6-5.0). One scenario, no trials. Could equally be coded E1 (formation coordination); E2 chosen because safety is claimed but unevaluated.

title: Decentralized Multi-Agent Planning for Multirotors: a Fully Online and Communication Latency Robust Approach
evidence: Algorithm 1/latency handling: the planner "will skip planning at the start of the current planning period and wait for the next period"; Conclusion: "a 0% collision rate"
method: Decentralized synchronous MIQP/MPC multirotor planner with time-aware safe corridors; agents broadcast timestamped trajectories, estimate communication delay and skip a planning period when peers' trajectories are stale.
evaluation: Simulation only, i7 CPU: 10-agent swap, 100 runs at 0/50/100 ms latency vs EGO-Swarm, MADER, RMADER; 8/12 agents with 70 obstacles to 150 ms; collision %, flight time, compute 10.6 ms mean.
contribution: A fully online decentralized multirotor planner robust to communication latency: 0% collisions at 0-100 ms delay versus 15-42% for MADER, with about 18% shorter mean flight time than RMADER.
flag: Borderline: this is a navigation planner, and the (c) carve-out sends planners to E1 unless safety is the primary claim and outcome. Here latency-robust collision safety is the headline and collision % vs baselines is the first table column (EGO-Swarm 64/84/84, slow EGO-Swarm 14/25/22, MADER 15/38/42, RMADER 0/0/0, proposed 0/0/0 at 0/50/100 ms), so I lean include - but RMADER also reaches 0%, so the incremental gain over the best baseline is efficiency (flight time 6.77/6.79/7.1 s vs 7.28/7.95/10.4 s; zero stops vs 0.46/0.347/1.75), not safety. runtime_interceptor set to no: the only runtime gate is skipping a planning cycle when trajectories are stale (a deferral of replanning, with a stop-at-horizon-end fallback), not a filter between a nominal decision and its execution; maintainer may read this as yes. (d) is weak: latency is communication delay, compute is 10.6 ms mean but 70 ms max on a desktop i7 (up to 86.6 ms max with 12 agents), no onboard/edge hardware. Simulation only, no real flights. Assumes synchronized clocks and symmetric communication. 150 ms latency tested only in the obstacle scenario with 10 runs, no baselines and no explicit collision count. MADER/RMADER compute times are quoted from another paper. No ablations. Abstract has no numbers.

title: SocNavGym: A Reinforcement Learning Gym for Social Navigation
evidence: Sec. III.A: the environment is "lightweight, fast, easy to use"; collisions enter only through the reward (Eq. 1 and Eq. 2 assign -1 on contact), with no layer that overrides the agent's action.
