method: A 2D social-navigation gym extending the Multi-Agent Particle Environment: randomised rooms, human groups and interactions, ORCA or SFM humans, configurable rewards including a learned SNGNN-v2 discomfort reward.
evaluation: Dueling-DQN trained 50K episodes under two rewards, three scenarios, 100 test episodes; collision rate 0.01-0.13, SPL 0.27-0.87; no latency or hardware specs.
contribution: An open, lightweight reinforcement-learning gym for social robot navigation among simulated humans, with configurable scenarios, rewards and standard social-navigation metrics.
flag: Benchmark environment, not a safety mechanism; single learning robot among scripted humans, so multi-agent is nominal. Safety exists only as a reward term, which the protocol says does not meet (a). Results are mixed: the SNGNN-reward agent has a HIGHER collision rate in Exp. 2 (0.12 vs 0.02) despite the paper's social-compliance claim. No seeds or variance reported. No success rate is reported directly. Could be cited as a testbed only.

title: We Need to Talk: Identifying and Overcoming Communication-Critical Scenarios for Self-Driving
evidence: Sec. III (evaluation): 'We assess performance by analyzing collision rates'; Intro claims the method 'reduces hard collisions by up to 62.5%'.
method: Ego vehicle picks which neighbours to query using a scalar concern value from forecast occupancy confidence, then fuses their trajectory-candidate scores with uncertainty-aware weighting and re-ranks candidates.
evaluation: CoBEV-Sim on the Interaction dataset with adversarial occluder/pedestrian, 0-3 communicators, 64 candidates; baselines ego, random, all-agents, ground-truth ego; top-1 and top-k collision rate, link count; no hardware/latency.
contribution: Selective, uncertainty-aware vehicle-to-vehicle querying cuts the top-1 collision rate of ranked trajectory candidates from 5.8 to 2.2 (37.5% of single-agent) while using 2.08 of 3 possible links.
flag: Borderline (c): open-loop re-ranking of trajectory candidates, not a monitor or shield; nothing can veto or halt. Short workshop-style paper, scenario count not reported, units of collision rate not stated. Table I was garbled in extraction: the k=1 values for the concern-only rows (3.6/4.3/4.3) are uncertain. Reader noted top-k for full method (5.5) is below the ground-truth oracle (12.5), which the text does not explain. Section label of the evidence quote is my best guess. Communication latency is future work only.

title: Deadlock-Free Collision Avoidance for Nonholonomic Robots
evidence: Sec. III: "Constraint (1a) describes the half-planes of permitted velocities for the current robot"; collision constraints are "always met with a minimized velocity violation".
method: Decentralized per-cycle QP over velocity-obstacle half-planes with slack; MCCA adds masked-velocity half-planes so normal-priority robots yield to head-priority ones; second QP maps to differential-drive wheel inputs.
evaluation: Webots simulation, 7 scenarios, 10-40 differential-drive robots, noise 0.01 m and 1 deg. No external baselines; one qualitative angular-control ablation. No numeric collision, deadlock or timing results.
contribution: A decentralized QP collision-avoidance scheme for nonholonomic robots that propagates masked velocities between robots to avoid deadlock in narrow passages, shown qualitatively in simulation.
flag: No quantitative safety metric and no baseline: results are figures plus a claim of collision-free and deadlock-free runs over 'hundreds of simulation hours' with no counts. QP solve 'in less than one millisecond' is asserted, not measured. Abstract claim of being first with stable deadlock avoidance is not backed by any comparison. Primary emphasis is deadlock, so (c) primacy is doubtful too (E1 would also be defensible). The QP minimally modifies a preferred velocity each cycle, so runtime_interceptor could be argued yes; I scored it no as an ORCA-style reactive planner.

title: Counterfactual Fairness Filter for Fair-Delay Multi-Robot Navigation
evidence: Sec 3.1: the sampled navigation action "is filtered by f_t^i to stop agents that are not allowed to move" (Eq. 4, a_t^i = f_t^i * nu).
method: NCF2: learned navigation module plus a counterfactual fairness filter (CF2) outputting a binary go/stop gate per robot, trained with counterfactual default-action rewards to equalise delays.
evaluation: Simulated lidar robots, 128x128 map, 8-16 agents, UNIFORM and CORNER maps; baselines FEN, SOTO, Nav-Only; SR, makespan, delay variance/max/mean; 3 ablations; V100 GPU, no latency.
contribution: A learned per-robot stop/go gate multiplies the navigation action to make decentralised robots yield fairly, cutting delay variance (e.g. 133.9 to 74.6 on CORNER-12-25) while keeping success rate.
flag: Gate is structurally a runtime halt (zeroes the action each step) but its purpose is fair delay, not safety; no collision/violation rate is reported, only success rate (86.4 vs 77.6 Nav-Only on CORNER-12-25), so (a) and (c) not met on my reading - maintainer may judge (a) borderline. Paper claims NCF2 did well on every metric but Table 1 shows exceptions (e.g. Uniform-8-50 VD 24.1 vs 21.1 Nav-Only). No named simulator, no latency, deterministic transitions, no comm delay.

title: Distributed Hierarchical Distribution Control for Very-Large-Scale Clustered Multi-Agent Systems
evidence: Sec II-B: collision and obstacle avoidance enter as probabilistic chance constraints inside the steering optimisation; Sec V-D: "DHDC outperforms DCS in terms of safety as well".
method: Hierarchical ADMM-based distribution estimation (bottom-up) and distribution steering (top-down) of Gaussian clique distributions with affine disturbance feedback, with chance-constrained collision and obstacle avoidance inside the optimisation.
evaluation: Matlab/MOSEK simulation, 20, 144 and 2,097,152 double-integrator agents; baselines centralised and distributed covariance steering; computation time and collision percentage shown in plots; i7-11800H laptop.
contribution: A hierarchical distributed covariance-steering framework that plans chance-constrained trajectories for clustered swarms of up to about two million agents, scaling beyond centralised and flat distributed steering.
flag: Scalability of offline distribution steering is the claim; safety is a chance constraint (theta 0.997) inside the planner, with no runtime mechanism. A collision-percentage comparison against DCS exists (Fig 7, axis up to about 4.5%) but the text gives no values, and computation time (Fig 6) is also plot-only. No convergence guarantee (listed as future work). Fails the primacy test for (c).

title: Multi-Robot Path Planning Combining Heuristics and Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
evidence: The stated objective is "to minimize the total length of all paths L that all agents travel" (problem formulation); rules are added "to the output layer of the real-time planner to avoid some actions inconsistent with common sense" (Sec. 4.1).
method: MAPPOHR: MAPPO real-time planner that treats a D* Lite heuristic replan as an action, with empirical rules embedded in the action output layer and reward to prune implausible actions.
evaluation: Grid airport ground 111x171, two planes, 20 training and 10 test cases; vs D* Lite (total cost 508.6 vs 372.7, success 1.0 vs 0.9), MADDPG and ablations MAPPOH, MAPPO, PPOHR; RTX 2070.
contribution: A multi-robot path planner combining D* Lite heuristics with rule-embedded MAPPO, cutting total path cost versus D* Lite on ten two-aircraft test cases at a 0.9 success rate.
flag: Path-efficiency paper; no collision or violation rate measured, so fails the primacy test for (c). One rule ("the robot is forbidden to continue to move forward" on next-step collision risk, Sec. 4.4) resembles action masking, but the paper does not say whether it acts at execution or only in training and never evaluates it as a safety mechanism. Proposed method has LOWER success than the D* Lite baseline (0.9 vs 1.0). Only two agents; no seeds or variance; "collision rate of 0.9" in Sec. 5.1 is undefined. Ablation results are curves only. Replanning budget 3 s is the only timing.

title: iPLAN: Intent-Aware Planning in Heterogeneous Traffic via Distributed Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
evidence: Sec 4.1: behavioral-incentive loss is 'given by an average L1-norm error between the predicted state' sequence and ground truth; Sec 4.2 uses a Graph Attention Network and RNN to predict opponents' trajectories.
method: Decentralised MARL (PPO per agent, no communication or weight sharing); GRU behavioural-incentive and GAT+RNN instant-incentive encoders trained by predicting opponents' future states, fed to the policy. No runtime override.
evaluation: Sim only: MPE Non-Cooperative Navigation (3 agents) and Highway-env (5 learners, 50 scripted cars); vs QMIX, MAPPO, IPPO plus two ablations; chaotic success 67.81% vs 42.50% IPPO; no hardware or latency.
contribution: iPLAN lets each decentralised driving agent infer neighbours' long-term behaviour and short-term intent from local observations alone, raising collision-free success in chaotic simulated highway traffic from 42.5% (IPPO) to 67.8%.
flag: Borderline E2 vs E1. Criterion (b) is met only in topic: latent opponent-state prediction over a GAT, but NO predictive-accuracy metric (no ADE/FDE/MSE) is reported, so the v1.6 minimum for (b) fails; prediction is judged only via reward. Criterion (c) fails the primacy test in my reading: collisions are a reward penalty (-1) and the paper is about planning performance, though success rate (share of vehicles collision-free at episode end) and survival time are in Table 1 with baselines and ablations - maintainer may judge that enough for include under (b)/(c). No shield, fallback or human takeover; simulation only; authors admit no theoretical safety foundation (Sec 6). Abstract numbers: 48.1% and 25.3% success gains are percentage-point differences vs QMIX and IPPO in Table 1, not relative gains; 80.6% longer survival does not reproduce exactly (76.20 vs MAPPO 42.31 gives about 80.1%, vs QMIX 39.38 about 93.5%); 13.7% vs IPPO does reproduce; reward gains (4.3%, 38.4%, 12.7%, 6.3%) appear only in figures and could not be verified. Navigation results are curves only. Rebuttal appendix experiments (H.2) use 1 seed. Paper read via WebFetch summariser over the full PDF text (3 fetches), not by eye.

title: Decentralized Social Navigation with Non-Cooperative Robots via Bi-Level Optimization
evidence: Sec. on local planning: priority enters the planner as 'a linear maximum velocity scaling of' V_MAX/sigma^i; the robot 'with the highest bid is allocated the highest priority'.
method: Bi-level decentralized navigation: a sponsored-search auction assigns priority order; a DWA-style local planner scales each robot's maximum velocity by its priority.
evaluation: SocialGym 2.0, 3-10 robots, 25 trials, doorway and intersection; vs CADRL, CADRL-LSTM, Enforced Order, Only Local, RVO, Social Forces; success 76%/96%, collisions 0.17/0.14; real F1/10, Jackal, Spot.
contribution: An auction-based priority order combined with a priority-scaled local planner lets decentralized robots pass doorways and intersections with 76-96% success, outperforming multi-agent reinforcement learning baselines in simulation and on real robots.
flag: Navigation/scheduling planner about success rate, deadlock and social compliance; collision rate is one of four metrics, so the primacy test for (c) fails, and there is no runtime filter. Collision rate is reported against baselines though (door 0.17 vs CADRL 0.00, Only Local 2.32; intersection 0.14 vs 1.20, 2.48), and CADRL beats it on collisions at the doorway, so a maintainer reading (c) more loosely could argue include. Real-robot trial counts are inconsistent in the text (5 trials vs 6 trials). Fig. 7 crowd-model values are not given numerically. '44% better' matches 76 vs 32 success only by inference. No compute or latency data.

title: Runtime Safety Assurance of Autonomous Vehicles used for Last-mile Delivery in Urban Environments
evidence: Sec. 3.2.1: after a fail-safe stop 'only remote operator (via the HMI of the CCC) has the authority to select the next appropriate driving mode'; Sec. 5: the monitor 'triggers immediately an emergency brake'.
method: Onboard Dependability Cage monitor (safe zone, lidar detector, camera validator, mode control) triggers an emergency stop, then a remote command control centre operator selects the next driving mode.
evaluation: One real-vehicle demonstration on a closed test track in Hamburg, parked car blocking path; no baselines, ablations, repeated trials or latency; only figure is a 1 m stopping distance.
contribution: Dependability-cage runtime monitor that emergency-stops a delivery vehicle and hands mode selection to a remote operator, demonstrated once on a closed track without quantitative evaluation.
flag: On topic for (a) and (e) and a real fast-halt then human-handoff architecture, but evaluation is a single qualitative demo: no safety rate, no baseline or ablation, no operator response time or workload. Single vehicle; fleet supervision and vehicle-drone cooperation described only as design/future work. Quantitative novelty monitor was not implemented. Worth citing as background for RQ3 even if excluded.

title: CaRT: Certified Safety and Robust Tracking in Learning-based Motion Planning for Multi-Agent Systems
evidence: "we slightly modify it using our CaRT distributed safety filter" (Sec. II-B.1); the filter minimises the squared deviation from the learned input subject to a log-barrier safety constraint, in closed form (Sec. III-B, Theorem 1)
method: Two-layer hierarchy: an analytical, distributed log-barrier safety filter minimally modifies a learned motion-planning policy at runtime; a contraction-based robust filter then tracks the certified safe trajectory under disturbance.
evaluation: Simulation only: 6-spacecraft simulator, 10-spacecraft LEO reconfiguration, 50 runs; vs CLF-CBF QP and filter-only ablation; success 100% vs 31.6% (94.0% filter-only); no compute times or hardware.
contribution: Introduces a hierarchical analytical safety filter plus contraction-based robust tracking filter that certifies learned multi-agent motion planners, keeping 100% task success under large disturbances where a CLF-CBF QP achieves 31.6%.
flag: Clear runtime safety filter over a learned policy in a multi-agent setting, with a baseline and an ablation. Weak points: the only quantitative safety figure is success rate over 50 simulations (Table I); no collision or violation rate is reported numerically, and in the illustrative example violations are shown only as markers in Fig. 3 - maintainer should decide whether success rate satisfies the safety-metric requirement. Table I is not a controlled comparison: filter-only was run at small disturbance (1.0e-2), CLF-CBF QP and CaRT at large (5.0e-2). Control effort J: optimal 1.26, filter-only 4.93, CLF-CBF 10.36, CaRT 5.86; simulator text gives 4.96x less effort than CLF-CBF. Claimed faster evaluation time is never measured; no hardware, no latency, simulation only (dt at least 0.1 s). No false-halt or throughput measure, so RQ5 rests on the control-effort comparison. PDF text extraction was garbled in parts of Sec. II and the Theorem 3 proof.

title: Deadlock-free, Safe, and Decentralized Multi-Robot Navigation in Social Mini-Games via Discrete-Time Control Barrier Functions
evidence: Algorithm 1 (Sec. 5): "Perturb u_t^i via Equation (23)" after the MPC output; Sec. 7: barrier certificates let robots "preemptively perturb their state in a minimally-invasive fashion" onto liveness sets.
method: Decentralized receding-horizon MPC with discrete-time CBF collision constraints plus a liveness-set mechanism that detects impending deadlock geometrically and minimally perturbs robot speeds (projection or liveness CBF) before execution.
evaluation: Simulation and real F1/10, Jackal, Spot at doorway, intersection, hallway; 10+ baselines (ORCA-MAPF, CBF-QP, NH-ORCA, NH-TTC, CADRL, IMPC-DR, GBPPlanner, DWA). Collision and deadlock rate, delta-V, path deviation, makespan. No latency.
contribution: A decentralized MPC-CBF controller that predicts deadlocks in doorway, hallway and intersection encounters and minimally perturbs robot speeds to prevent them, with 0% collisions and deadlocks and lowest velocity change among baselines.
flag: Borderline on primacy: the headline claim is deadlock prevention; collision rate is reported (Table 3) but is 0% for every method except CADRL at the doorway (50%), so the discriminating outcomes are deadlock rate (NH-ORCA, NH-TTC, MPC-CBF 100%), delta-V (0.001-0.002 vs 0.008-0.38), path deviation and makespan ratio (1.005). Table 3 gives no agent counts or trial numbers. The post-MPC override applies to single-integrator dynamics; for double integrators liveness is a constraint inside the MPC, which alone would not meet (a). Real-robot liveness test: 5 runs, 3 succeeded and 2 failed; SocialGym velocity-scaling success 76% and 96% without clear condition labels. Real doorway flow rate 2.0 (m s)^-1 with no trial count; human-robot result is qualitative and is interaction, not handoff. Fig. 11 caption (deadlock around t=4) conflicts with text (near t=10). Hardware AMD Ryzen 2.90 GHz 16 GB; no solve time. Scaling to 1024 agents (Sec. 6.6) reports input-constraint violations only qualitatively.

title: MRNAV: Multi-Robot Aware Planning and Control Stack for Collision and Deadlock-free Navigation in Cluttered Environments
evidence: Short-horizon module (SH-NDM): a safety barrier certificate filter turns desired accelerations into safe ones 'in a minimally invasive manner', and lower layers 'will override higher level decisions in order to enforce safety'.
method: Three-layer multi-robot stack: centralised A* long-horizon planner, on-board DREAM receding-horizon planner, and a safety-barrier-certificate filter that overrides the controller's desired acceleration at runtime.
evaluation: RotorS, 8 quadrotors, 300 s, forest and maze with 0-400 dynamic obstacles; ablation of all 7 layer subsets; collisions 102/220 without filter vs 0/158 full stack; no latency or hardware.
contribution: A three-layer multi-robot navigation stack whose barrier-certificate safety filter overrides planner output at runtime; only the full stack gives zero collisions and zero deadlocks across four simulated environments.
flag: Meets (a) via the SBC filter and (c) via the layer ablation on collision rate, but it is a system paper with co-equal deadlock and collision claims, so check primacy. Useful for RQ5: the filter alone or with the on-board planner removes most collisions but deadlocks up to 8/8 robots in the maze, i.e. a measured throughput cost of filtering. Weaknesses: apparently a single run per configuration, no external baseline, no timing or hardware figures (real-time operation is asserted, not measured), simulation only. The filter acts on intermediate accelerations, not final motor speeds, and the paper says this does not guarantee actuator-level safety. Robustness to message drops and delays is a stated design goal that is not tested.

title: Collision Avoidance and Navigation for a Quadrotor Swarm Using End-to-end Deep Reinforcement Learning
evidence: Sec III-B: 'The action of robot i at time t is a_t^i in [0,1]^4, corresponding to the thrust levels at each of the four rotors' - end-to-end policy, no filter; Sec V Limitations: safety 'is not guaranteed'.
method: End-to-end deep RL policy with attention over neighbours and SDF obstacle observations maps local observations to rotor thrusts for decentralised quadrotor swarm collision avoidance; compressed to 1,820 parameters onboard.
evaluation: Sim 8-32 quadrotors with obstacles vs SBC and GLAS: success 0.97, collision 0.03, inference 5 ms (SBC 21, GLAS 15). Real Crazyflie 2.1, 8 robots, 0.35 ms on-board.
contribution: Learns decentralised collision-avoiding quadrotor swarm control end to end and runs it on a 168 MHz microcontroller in 0.35 ms, at a collision rate close to a barrier-certificate baseline.
flag: No runtime interceptor; relevant as learned-avoidance baseline and edge evidence. (d) is a stretch: compute limit (168 MHz, 192 KB) is explicit but no stated latency deadline. Barrier-certificate baseline SBC is safer (collision 0.01 vs 0.03). Base-setting success reported inconsistently (0.88, 0.95, 0.97) and inference 5 ms in Table I vs 0.35 ms on-board (different model size/platform, not reconciled). Real flights use Vicon and a stored obstacle list; no physical collision rate found. Primacy: paper is also about navigation.

title: Safe multi-agent motion planning under uncertainty for drones using filtered reinforcement learning
evidence: Sec. III-B: the safety filter "computes safe control inputs ... that minimally deviate from the corresponding RL control inputs"; "Only the first safe control ... is applied for each agent i, and then (12) is solved again at time t+1 in an MPC-like fashion."
method: Single-agent PPO policies propose controls; a centralised chance-constrained QP safety filter with set-based terminal constraints minimally corrects them each step for inter-agent and obstacle avoidance under Gaussian uncertainty.
evaluation: 100 Monte Carlo sims vs filter without terminal constraints and pure MPC: success 99% vs 92% vs 55%; six Crazyflie 2.1; QP 0.05 s mean at 10 Hz.
contribution: A chance-constrained QP safety filter overrides independently trained single-agent RL plans at every step, giving probabilistic collision avoidance for drone teams; 99% success in simulation and real-time on six Crazyflies.
flag: Clean runtime filter. Safety metric is task success % plus minimum-separation percentiles, not an explicit collision rate; failures lump collisions with timeouts. Filter is centralised (one QP for all agents) despite decentralised RL. Latency is measured (0.05 s vs 0.1 s period, workstation Ryzen CPU, ECOS) but not an explicit constraint and not edge hardware, so latency cell is generous and (d) not claimed. Pure MPC with terminal constraints failed numerically in all trials. Scaling timings to 24 agents only in Fig. 9. Hardware safety reported only as 'distances are always positive'. No human takeover.

title: Asymmetric Design of Control Barrier Function for Multiagent Autonomous Robotic Systems
evidence: Sec. 2.2-2.3 (eq. 18): each robot solves a QP minimising ||u_hat_i - u_i||^2 subject to its decentralised CBF constraint, so the nominal input is corrected at every control step; Sec. 5: "in the proposed method (asymmetric), the minimum value was greater than zero in all steps".
method: Decentralised CBF safety filter whose pairwise inequality constraints are split asymmetrically by speed-based weight functions summing to two, restoring QP feasibility; a damping fallback input provably satisfies the constraint.
evaluation: 1D three-robot and 2D 20-robot simulation (100 runs per gamma) plus three rail-mounted omni robots at 10 Hz; baselines symmetric and prior asymmetric CBF; no-solution count 0/100 vs 74-100/100.
contribution: Speed-based asymmetric splitting of decentralised control-barrier-function constraints removes the QP infeasibility that makes symmetric decentralisation fail, giving zero no-solution events in 300 multi-robot runs where baselines failed 74-100% of the time.
flag: The headline metric is a solver feasibility count ("no solution" returned by fmincon), not a measured collision or distance, so the safety reading depends on accepting infeasibility as a violation proxy; the only safety-margin claim is "the minimum value was greater than zero in all steps" with no number, and no collision count or minimum distance is reported anywhere. The hardware test was 1D on guide rails with three robots and is purely qualitative (Figs. 10-13, no numbers, no trial count), yet the conclusion claims validation "in 1D and 2D planes and real robots"; the 2D case is simulation only. The prior asymmetric baseline fails 100 of 100 runs at every gamma, worse than the symmetric baseline, and the paper never explains this, so check whether that baseline was implemented fairly. Theorem 2's fallback input relies on the precondition ||x_ij|| - r_s >= 0 and the text does not address what happens when it fails. No solve time or latency anywhere, so (d) is unmet. Note the violation quote in Sec. 6 describes the symmetric baseline, not the proposed method. Publication year is not printed in the PDF; the record says 2023 and the newest reference is 2021.

title: Learning Hyperplanes for Multi-Agent Collision Avoidance in Space
evidence: Abstract: "These constraints ensure collision avoidance by defining separating hyperplanes"
method: Rotating separating-hyperplane collision constraints inside a generalized Nash game for spacecraft; hyperplane parameters (rotation rate, keep-out radius) learned from expert trajectories by differentiating through the equilibrium solve.
evaluation: Simulated Hill-Clohessy-Wiltshire dynamics, 2 robots learning, 6-robot generalization; noise sweeps only, no baseline method; trajectory reconstruction error and success plotted, no collision rate; no hardware or timing.
contribution: Inverse game method that learns rotating-hyperplane collision-avoidance constraint parameters for multi-spacecraft games from expert demonstrations, evaluated in simulation by parameter recovery under noise.
flag: Collision avoidance is a constraint inside the equilibrium solve, not a runtime filter. No comparison baseline and no quantitative safety metric: the only numbers in text are settings (true omega 0.015 rad/s vs initial 0.008; true radius 30 m vs initial 10 m; 30 gradient steps); results are figures (parameter recovery, reconstruction error, success over 20 trials) without tabulated values. Text and Table I disagree on the noise range (sigma 0-20 vs 0:5:40). If the maintainer counts the noise sweep as an ablation and reads success off Fig 8, this could be argued as (c), but it fails the v1.6 minimum as read. Read via WebFetch summariser; appendix garbled.

title: Neural Graph Control Barrier Functions Guided Distributed Collision-avoidance Multi-agent Control
evidence: Sec 3: the method uses 'the learned GCBF as a detector to detect unsafe scenarios and use a switching control policy' between the nominal controller and the learned safe controller.
method: GNN jointly learns a graph control barrier function and distributed controller; at execution the GCBF checks the nominal LQR/PID action and switches to the learned controller, with online gradient refinement.
evaluation: Simulation: SimpleCar, DubinsCar, SimpleDrone, trained on 16 agents, tested to 1024 (2D) and 4096 (3D); baselines MDCBF, MAPPO; safety 0.993-1.000 for 16-128 CrazyFlie-model agents; no GCBF latency.
contribution: Learns a graph control barrier function with a GNN and uses it at run time to detect unsafe nominal actions and switch to a learned distributed controller, scaling collision avoidance beyond 1000 agents.
flag: Abstract claims (up to 3x success below 500 agents, >50% success above 1000 agents) were not matched to a specific body table in my read; check against the figures. Minimum success reported 97.1%/99.7%/99.5% (SimpleCar/DubinsCar/SimpleDrone); obstacle setting min safety 99.12%, success 84% at 128 agents with 32 obstacles; refinement ablation safety 0.977 to 0.984 at 64 agents. My read found simulation only (CrazyFlie dynamics in Appendix B.4) - verify whether real hardware flights exist. Timing (0.009-0.244 s centralised, 0.00047-0.00156 s decentralised per step) is for the handcrafted-CBF comparison in Table 3, not for GCBF. Switch is a controller swap, not a halt or deferral. No formal verification of the learned certificate. Likely superseded by GCBF+ (same group) if that is queued.

title: Learning Safe Control for Multi-Robot Systems: Methods, Verification, and Open Challenges
evidence: Abstract: "In this survey, we review the recent advances in control design methods for robotic multi-agent systems (MAS)"
method: Survey of learning-based safe control for multi-robot systems: shielding (CBFs, predictive safety filters, HJ reachability, automata shields), learned CBFs, safe MARL, and verification of learning-enabled MAS.
evaluation: No original experiments; quantitative figures are quoted from cited works only; no baselines, hardware or latency of its own.
contribution: Survey of safe learning-based control for multi-robot systems covering shielding, learned control barrier functions, safe multi-agent RL and verification, with open challenges.
flag: Self-described survey (Sec 1.3 claims first survey on robot MAS with explicit safety focus). Useful for citation chasing: Sec 3 shielding and Sec 4 learned CBFs. Only the first 100000 of 128531 characters were read; the remainder is the reference list.

title: Bidirectional Temporal Plan Graph: Enabling Switchable Passing Orders for More Efficient Multi-Agent Path Finding Plan Execution
evidence: Sec. on BTPG execution: for a bidirectional pair "either agent in the pair is allowed to enter the conflict location first"; evaluation metric is execution-time improvement over TPG, collisions not measured.
method: Bidirectional Temporal Plan Graph: post-processes a MAPF plan so some passing orders are switchable at execution (first arrival goes first), with two anytime construction algorithms (BTPG-n, BTPG-o).
evaluation: 3900 simulations, six MAPF benchmark maps, random delays; baseline TPG and ideal bound; mean improvement 8.9-20.9% (BTPG-o), max 63.6%; construction 0.04-181 s; i7-12700KF; no collision metric.
contribution: Lets agents executing a multi-agent path finding plan switch passing orders on a first-come basis, reducing unnecessary waits under delays by 8-20% over temporal plan graphs while provably avoiding deadlock.
flag: Efficiency paper (fewer unnecessary waits under delay); collision/deadlock freedom is proved as a validity condition (Properties 3-4), not measured - fails (c) primacy test. The wait rule is an execution policy, not a safety interceptor; agents are merely assumed to have onboard stop-on-obstacle. Abstract 8-20% matches body medians (8.1-20.0%, Table 1). MAPF-runtime row in Table 1 did not align cleanly with map columns in the extracted text; plots not inspected. Delay handling is simulated timestep delay, not latency/jitter-aware inference.

title: Multi-Agent Dynamic Relational Reasoning for Social Robot Navigation
evidence: "Sec. IV-A: the encoder infers relation graphs and hypergraphs in the latent space" from historical states without relation supervision, and the decoder predicts future displacements conditioned on those evolving latent structures
method: Latent-variable encoder infers dynamically evolving relation graphs and group-wise hypergraphs among agents, with smoothness, sharpness and sparsity regularisers; predicted trajectories feed a PPO social navigation policy
evaluation: ETH-UCY, SDD, NBA and a synthetic group dataset against MID, GroupNet, Graph-TERN and EigenTrajectory; ETH-UCY minADE20/minFDE20 0.18/0.30 versus 0.21/0.36, NBA 1.16/1.64 versus 1.46/2.19; crowd simulator 96.31 percent success and 3.59 percent collision versus CrowdNav++ 93.21 and 6.66; real RosMaster X3 robot; RTX A6000, no latency reported
contribution: Inferring dynamically evolving relation hypergraphs among agents improves multi-agent trajectory prediction and, fed to a reinforcement learning policy, lowers collision and group-intrusion rates in dense crowd navigation.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: which - nothing is guarded; safety comes from reward penalties and learned behaviour, and the authors concede it "still cannot achieve a zero collision rate in very dense scenarios" (Conclusion), so (a) fails and runtime_interceptor is no. (c) fails the primacy test because collision rate is one of seven navigation metrics alongside success, path length and group intrusion. Admitted under (b) as Pillar 2 method evidence, not safety evidence, so RQ5 is capped at 2 - check whether the maintainer counts a latent-hypergraph VAE decoder as a world model or dismisses it as a trajectory regressor, which is the pivot for this record. Text claims state of the art on SDD but the table shows minADE20 8.1 tied with EigenTrajectory, and claims shorter path length though 20.53 m exceeds CrowdNav++ 20.37 m. No inference latency or onboard compute figure, so edge deployment and latency cells are not claimed despite the real-robot trial.

title: TrustAgent: Towards Safe and Trustworthy LLM-based Agents
evidence: 'the inspection method interrupts the trajectory whenever the agent repeats a mistake after being notified and criticized' (Section 4.2); the post-planning inspector vets each action before execution.
method: Agent Constitution of safety regulations enforced in three stages: pre-planning hindsight finetuning, in-planning retrieval of relevant regulations, and a GPT-4 post-planning inspector that vets every action.
evaluation: 70 tool-use cases in 5 domains (ToolEmu sandbox); 5 LLM backbones vs no-strategy baseline; GPT-4-judged safety 0-3 rose GPT-3.5 1.22 to 2.02, Claude-2 1.83 to 2.57, GPT-4 2.15 to 2.56, Mixtral 1.33 to 2.44; helpfulness also up; prompting-only vs inspection-only ablation on medicine; no hardware or latency reported.
contribution: TrustAgent wraps an LLM tool-using agent in a rule-based Agent Constitution plus a runtime action inspector, raising judged safety across five backbones without reducing helpfulness.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - an LLM tool-calling agent. Check (c): this is one planning agent plus an inspector, so the multi-agent primacy test fails; safety is GPT-4-judged inside a GPT-4-emulated sandbox over only 70 cases; no latency, cost or false-halt analysis, and no human handoff; body says GPT-4 average safety is about 2 while Table 2 gives 2.15; Mixtral has no with-strategy results for food or chemistry.

title: MADRL-based UAVs Trajectory Design with Anti-Collision Mechanism in Vehicular Networks
evidence: Sec 3.1: "we introduce two novel collision avoidance mechanisms, namely flat and rank masking, which rely on constraining the agents' action space to entirely avert collisions"
method: Central controller computes binary action masks removing moves that could bring UAV pairs within a safety distance; rank masking lets the higher-ranked UAV act freely and masks the lower-ranked one.
evaluation: SUMO/3GPP simulation, 3 UAV base stations, 80 ground users, 3DQN; baseline penalty-based training vs flat and rank masking; collision counts, reward and satisfied users in figures; no hardware or latency.
contribution: Rank-based action masking for multi-UAV reinforcement learning removes unsafe moves before selection, cutting collisions from 17% of training and 28% of evaluation episodes under penalty training to zero.
flag: Action masking is a pre-emptive shield on the action set rather than a post-hoc override of a chosen action; I counted it as (a) but the maintainer may read it as a constraint inside the learner. The paper never states explicitly that masks stay active at deployment, though evaluation shows 0 collisions with masking. Table 2: penalty 170 (17%) collisions in training and 14 (28%) in evaluation; flat and rank masking 0 (0%) in both; caption says "average number" and the denominators (1000 training episodes, about 50 evaluations) are inferred, not stated. Reward and satisfied-user gains of rank over flat masking appear only in Figs. 3-4 with no numeric values, so the throughput cost of the shield is unquantified. Masks are computed centrally and sent over a C2 link assumed always reliable; no delay, latency or compute figures despite a real-time execution claim. Only 3 UAVs, simulation only, short paper, no ablation beyond flat vs rank. Abstract has no numbers.

title: Reinforcement Learning with Ensemble Model Predictive Safety Certification
evidence: Sec 4.4: the goal is "to certify an action u_t proposed by an RL-based policy"; Sec 1: actions "are modified to safe ones if necessary".
method: X-MPSC: tube-based MPC safety filter over an ensemble of 5 probabilistic NN dynamics models minimally corrects each MBPO action; reuses previous solution, then soft constraints, when infeasible.
evaluation: Pendulum, Cart Pole, Two-Link-Arm, Drone sims, 5 seeds; vs CPO, SQRL, SL, LBPO, Lag-TRPO; returns and total constraint violations; 676 ms per solve at N=5 on one i7 core.
contribution: An ensemble-model predictive safety filter that corrects a model-based RL agent's actions at every step, cutting training-time constraint violations versus constrained-RL baselines in four simulated control tasks.
flag: Single-agent only, so E4 is arguable; kept as include because the filter is sequential and timing is reported. Returns and violation counts are only plotted (Fig 2), no numeric table; text gives only 'approximately an order of magnitude' fewer violations with a prior model and infeasibility 0.0-2.0% of steps (about 39% worst case in TwoLinkArm). Solve times 676 ms to 71,982 ms (Table 1, pendulum, no warm start) are far from real time at the stated 50 Hz. No false-intervention rate. Backup controller for the pendulum is described inconsistently (Sec 7.2 vs App 9.1.1). No hardware deployment.

title: Distributed Safe Navigation of Multi-Agent Systems using Control Barrier Function-Based Optimal Controllers
evidence: agents aim at "remaining as close as possible to their nominal controller" subject to CBF obstacle and inter-agent constraints (Sec. III)
method: Distributed algorithm solves a network CBF-constrained optimisation that keeps each robot's input close to its nominal controller while enforcing obstacle and inter-agent avoidance during formation navigation.
evaluation: Unity simulations with 5 and 3 Husky robots; hardware with 3 Jackal robots, onboard computation. No baseline, no ablation, no collision rate, success rate or timing reported.
contribution: Designs a distributed CBF-based optimal controller that lets a robot team follow nominal waypoint and formation commands while avoiding obstacles and each other, shown in simulation and on three Jackal robots.
flag: Qualitative demonstration only: text says robots 'successfully complete the task by avoiding collisions and reaching all the waypoints' with no numbers; Fig. 3 distance plots not readable as text. No baseline or ablation. Safety is conditional on feasibility (Assumption 3) with no runtime fallback, and optimiser assumed 'instantaneously available' (Assumption 4) - no latency measured despite onboard hardware. CBF constraints sit inside the controller's optimisation rather than a separate filter, so runtime_interceptor=yes is arguable (min-deviation from nominal input).

title: Agent Smith: A Single Image Can Jailbreak One Million Multimodal LLM Agents Exponentially Fast
evidence: Section 4.2 reports that seeding one adversarial image into 1024 agents jailbreaks almost all of a million "before the 32-th chat round", measured as infection ratio against prompt-injection baselines.
method: Universal adversarial image optimized with MI-FGSM over retrieval, query and answer losses, seeded in one agent's album and spread by pairwise agent chats; epidemic transmission model.
evaluation: 256-agent and extrapolated million-agent LLaVA-1.5 and InstructBLIP societies; baselines visual and textual prompt injection and sequential jailbreak; infection ratio; 64 CPU cores and 8xA100 40GB.
contribution: One adversarial image passed between multimodal agents produces exponential cascading jailbreak across a simulated million-agent society, which prompt-injection baselines never achieve.
flag: Attack and hazard-model paper with no mechanism and no runtime interceptor, so it enters only as threat evidence; it cannot support RQ5 beyond showing that model-level alignment (95.12% and 96.69% refusal success) fails to stop the spread, and Section 1 concedes that "how to design a practical defense that meets this principle remains an open question". The million-agent headline is extrapolated by seeding 1024 agents at c0=1/1024, not simulated at that scale, and the authors say the full run would need 8xA100 for nearly a month. Numbers I could not find values for: retrieval success rate, JSR and minCLIP are all defined but never given a figure in any part I could read; the roughly 100% at 27-31 rounds claim is a Figure 1 caption, while Figure 19 gives 95.03-96.23% at round 22. Inclusion hinges on reading cascading multi-agent failure as the primary measured outcome, which it is, but a maintainer who reads criterion (c) as requiring detection rather than demonstration of hazard would exclude it.

title: Formal Synthesis of Controllers for Safety-Critical Autonomous Systems: Developments and Challenges
evidence: Sec. 5.4 (survey text on others' work): safety shields are used "to regulated plans generated by neural networks such that formal safety guarantees can be obtained".
method: Survey of formal controller synthesis for safety-critical autonomous systems: abstraction-based methods, supervisory control, MPC, barrier functions, temporal-logic planning, learning-enabled synthesis, multi-agent scalability.
evaluation: None of its own: no experiments, baselines, metrics, hardware or latency. Only a worked state-count illustration for five agents in Sec. 6.
contribution: Survey of formal synthesis methods for safety-critical autonomous systems, covering supervisory control, barrier functions, temporal-logic planning and shields for learned controllers, with open challenges in scalability.
flag: Survey, so E3 regardless of topical fit. Read characters 0-100000 of the body; the remainder (100000 onward) was bibliography only. Useful as a snowballing source for shielding and CBF references. Minor: Sec. 6 says five agents with 100 states each give at most one hundred billion states, but 100^5 is ten billion.

title: ARMCHAIR: integrated inverse reinforcement learning and model predictive control for human-robot collaboration
evidence: "Avoidance of collisions between elements of the group and with obstacles is enforced by (10h)." (Sec 3.3 MPC-MIP Formulation)
method: Centralised receding-horizon MPC-MIP plans trajectories and target allocation for robots supporting a human, using an AIRL-learned policy to predict the human; collision and connectivity are planner constraints.
evaluation: Simulation, 2 robots + synthetic human, 2 environments x 1000 Monte Carlo runs; baselines open-loop MIP, no robot support; collisions, disconnections, targets, redundant visits. No hardware or solve time.
contribution: ARMCHAIR couples an adversarial-IRL human prediction model with a mixed-integer MPC so a robot team supports a human explorer without commands, cutting collisions and disconnections versus open-loop planning in simulation.
flag: Safety is a constraint inside the planner, not a runtime interceptor, so (a) fails; (c) primacy doubtful: paper is about collaboration and task allocation, collisions are one of four metrics. Env 1 collisions 0.001 vs 0.58 open-loop, but in Env 2 ARMCHAIR is WORSE (0.013 vs 0.004). Human is a synthetic PPO agent, no real humans; AIRL prediction is single-human grid policy, not a multi-agent world model, so (b) not met (Table B3 compares recovered vs surrogate policy only). No recursive feasibility; on infeasibility robots just stop. No timing reported (T = 1 s). Text labels a figure 'Simulation 101' but refers to it as 111.

title: Collision Avoidance Verification of Multiagent Systems with Learned Policies
evidence: Sec III-B: Eq. (14) 'is a LP that does not involve NN controllers, as thus can be solved efficiently, enabling our method to provide a safety guarantee online'; Sec IV-A: 'ReBAR correctly alerts that a collision could occur in the next timestep'.
method: ReBAR: offline MILP computation of relative backprojection over-approximations for each agent pair under neural-network policies, then a cheap online LP membership check that flags possible next-step collisions.
evaluation: Simulated 2-10 agents with NN policies; compared against 2M Monte Carlo samples. Offline 201-322 s per pair, online LP 1.3-1.6 ms per pair; Gurobi, i9-13900K.
contribution: Verifies collision avoidance for multi-agent systems with learned policies by backward reachability, with offline pairwise set computation and an online check costing about 1.5 ms per agent pair.
flag: Borderline E2: no collision or violation rate; evidence is verification runtime and enclosure of Monte Carlo unsafe sets, forward reachability compared only qualitatively, no ablation. Online check alerts only - it does not override or halt, so not (a). Latency is reported, not a design constraint, and on a desktop CPU, so (d) not claimed. Online cost is per pair; total scales O(n^2). Horizon 5 steps; 10-agent policies were not trained to avoid each other.

title: Safe Road-Crossing by Autonomous Wheelchairs: a Novel Dataset and its Experimental Evaluation
evidence: 'crossing is not recommended until the vehicle slows down or surpasses the crossing location' (Sec. 3); the danger function only issues a recommendation and is itself analytical, not learned (Sec. 4).
method: Analytical explainable danger function over car distance, velocity and acceleration, thresholded to tag unsafe road-crossing states, with fusion across wheelchair range sensors, wheelchair camera and a drone camera using YOLO detection.
evaluation: 15 lab runs of three RoboMaster robots (car, wheelchair, drone) with 18-camera OptiTrack ground truth; three single sensors vs distance, danger and voting fusion; best results distance fusion accuracy 0.92, recall 0.91, precision 0.95, danger fusion RMSE 0.361 vs 0.582 range-only; sensors at 10-30 Hz resampled to 100 Hz; no decision latency and no compute platform given.
contribution: A multi-sensor laboratory dataset and an analytical, explainable danger function for autonomous-wheelchair road crossing, with a preliminary comparison showing distance fusion most accurate.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: no - the crossing decision and the danger function are hand-designed; only the YOLO perception stage is learned. Most likely record in this batch for the maintainer to overturn: hazard detection over three agents is the primary measured outcome and he may count the autonomous wheelchair as an AI system; against that, there is no runtime override (recommendation only), no ablation, 15 short runs, and Table 1 vs Table 2 disagree on camera resolution.

title: Self-organizing Multiagent Target Enclosing under Limited Information and Safety Guarantees
evidence: "the distance between the two closest pursuers never reaches zero" (Sec. IV, Simulation Results, Fig. 7d) - the only safety evidence, and it is qualitative.
method: Sliding-mode guidance law for constant-speed non-holonomic pursuers enclosing a stationary target, with a Gaussian repulsive term switched on only for the nearest colliding pursuer; Lyapunov proofs.
evaluation: Numerical simulation only: 6 pursuers at 40 m/s, 100 m orbit, 50 m sensing, two scenarios; plots only. No baseline, no ablation, no numeric safety metric, no hardware or latency.
contribution: A decentralised guidance law lets pursuers enclose a stationary target using only relative measurements, switching on repulsion from the nearest colliding neighbour, with Lyapunov-based safety and convergence proofs.
flag: Fails minimum evaluation: collision avoidance is shown by trajectory and distance plots only, no collision or violation rate, no baseline or ablation. Not a runtime interceptor - the repulsive term is part of the single control law, not a filter over a nominal command. A maintainer could also read this as E1 (formation control with safety as one property). Theorem-level guarantees are for a 2D stationary-target case; opposite-side neighbours are excluded (Remark 4). Videos with 10 and 20 pursuers are mentioned but not analysed.

title: Multi-Agent Coverage Control with Transient Behavior Consideration
evidence: "Our algorithm incorporates this aspect by carefully designing episodes using the doubling trick." (Sec. 1); safety variant restricts planned paths to the estimated safe set (Sec. 5.2), no runtime filter.
method: MAC-DT: episodic GP-UCB multi-agent coverage on a graph; greedy oracle assigns destinations, agents sample en route, doubling trick ends episodes; sublinear approximated-regret bound that accounts for transient travel.
evaluation: Grid simulations with 3, 6, 10 agents over 10 reward maps vs MacOpt-SP and Voronoi; safe variant vs SafeOpt-SP and SafeMaC-SP; 3 Crazyflie drones; metric is regret; no timing.
contribution: MAC-DT learns an unknown reward map while covering it with multiple agents, with a regret bound of order sqrt(T) up to logs that accounts for agents' transient travel between destinations.
flag: Coverage and exploration efficiency paper; the only measured outcome is regret, shown as curves with no numeric values in text. Safe-exploration extension is a constraint inside the planner, argued heuristically (App. E.3.1) and outside the theory, with no violation rate reported. Only numbers: safe variant reaches no-regret coverage after about 50 samples (no baseline within 200); hardware run reaches optimal coverage in 19 steps with 57 samples. Needs a centralized coordinator. Intro states O(sqrt(T)) while the theorem gives it only up to log factors. Onboard collision avoidance on the drones is mentioned without detail.

title: Characterization and Mitigation of Insufficiencies in Automated Driving Systems
evidence: 'the ADS has to perform an emergency brake or disengage from the AD mode to hand over control to the human' (Section 4); the DMV and video studies count human takeovers caused by output insufficiencies.
method: Taxonomy of 16 output-insufficiency types for automated driving in four categories, plus Daruma, an unimplemented design pattern using cross-channel analysis, safety fusion and a high-level arbiter to switch between heterogeneous driving channels.
evaluation: DMV 2021 reports (over 2500 disengagements, insufficiency-caused five times more often than fault-caused), 32 road-test videos over 10h17m giving 71 insufficiency scenarios of which 62 (87%) safety-critical, and open-loop LGSVL runs of Apollo 5.0, Autoware.Auto and openpilot with 42 insufficiencies and 23 missed objects; no baseline or ablation for Daruma, which is never implemented.
contribution: Characterises the output insufficiencies behind automated-driving disengagements using DMV reports, road-test videos and simulation, and sketches Daruma, an arbiter that switches between heterogeneous driving channels.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: which - the analysed Apollo and openpilot channels contain deep networks, but Daruma itself is unimplemented and unevaluated, so no safety metric is reported against a baseline or ablation and (a) fails. Maintainer may instead prefer E3 since the paper is part survey and part position paper, or may argue the takeover analysis under (e) earns inclusion. Channels were run sequentially in open loop, so switching was never tested; body says Autoware and openpilot missed twice as many objects as Apollo while Table 5 gives 4 and 17 vs 2.

title: Stability Certificates for Receding Horizon Games
evidence: "We derive a sufficient condition for the closed-loop stability of RHG controllers" (Sec. I, contributions); no state constraints, no monitor or override is described.
method: Receding-horizon game control (v-GNE each step, no terminal ingredients) for stable LTI systems; LMI stability certificate from dissipativity and monotone operator theory, with a distributed local-LMI corollary.
evaluation: Numerical only: 2-agent example (K=10) and 3-consumer battery-charging game over 48 h with real demand data; weight and horizon sweeps; no baseline controller, no hardware or timing.
contribution: Gives the first LMI-based sufficient condition for closed-loop stability of receding-horizon game controllers on stable LTI systems, with a distributed check and tuning rules.
flag: Stability analysis of a multi-agent game-theoretic MPC, not a safety mechanism; input constraints hold by construction, no hazard, collision or violation metric and no baseline. Reported numbers are parameters only (rho(A)=0.954 and 0.727, mu=0.498 unstable vs 0.125 stable). Certificate is conservative per the authors. E2 would also apply if judged as a safety paper.

title: Delay-Aware Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning for Cooperative Adaptive Cruise Control with Model-based Stability Enhancement
evidence: Algorithm 1 lists the step 'Output action with stability check': Eq. (15) replaces the RL acceleration with a model-based ideal acceleration whenever the latter scores at least as well (Sec. IV-C).
method: Multi-agent delay-aware MDP for cooperative adaptive cruise control; attention-based CTDE policies emit acceleration and filter gains, and a velocity-optimisation action filter can replace the learned action at execution time.
evaluation: Catchup and Slowdown platoons of 5, 8 and 10 vehicles, 0.5s total delay (k=5 steps), 50 test trials, 3 seeds, vs MADDPG, ConseNet and NeurComm; collisions at size 8 are 0 vs 27 and 50 (Catchup) and 3 vs 12, 50, 50 (Slowdown); average reward -36.6 vs -30.9 to -667.8; Xeon Silver 4214R and RTX 3090; no inference or control latency measured.
contribution: Delay-aware multi-agent RL for vehicle platooning adds a model-based action filter that overrides unstable learned accelerations, cutting collision counts to zero or near-zero against MARL baselines.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - a MARL platoon policy whose action is filtered at execution. Check (d): the 0.5s delay is actuation and communication delay inside the environment, not inference latency, and no compute latency is reported, so (d) is weak. (c) is borderline: the primary claim is delay handling and stability, with collisions one of three metrics. There is no ablation isolating the action filter, so its contribution is unproven; the filter selects by reward, not by a formal guarantee; the paper claims it beats all baselines in every scenario but ConseNet has higher reward at Catchup size 5; only one delay setting is tested despite the abstract's 'various delay conditions'; collisions are counts, not rates.

title: Cooperate or Collapse: Emergence of Sustainable Cooperation in a Society of LLM Agents
evidence: 'all but the most powerful LLM agents fail to achieve a sustainable equilibrium in GOVSIM' (Abstract); five LLM agents share one common-pool resource and the measured outcome is collapse (Sections 2.3, 3.1).
method: GOVSIM, a common-pool-resource benchmark where five LLM generative agents harvest and negotiate over 12 simulated months in fishery, pasture and pollution scenarios; universalization prompting is proposed as a mitigation.
evaluation: 15 LLMs, 5 seeds, 3 scenarios; survival rate 53.3% GPT-4o, 46.7% Claude-3 Opus, 20% Qwen-110B, 6.7% GPT-4, 0% Llama-3-8B; ablations remove communication (over-usage +22%, p<0.001) and add universalization (about +4 months survival, +24% efficiency, p<0.001); greedy-newcomer test drops GPT-4o to 33.3%; sub-skill accuracy correlates with survival (R2=0.92); up to 4x RTX 3090 or 2x A100, about 4h per run.
contribution: GOVSIM shows that most societies of LLM agents collapse a shared resource within months, and that communication and universalization reasoning measurably extend sustainable cooperation.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - societies of LLM agents are the analysed system. No runtime interception of any kind, so (a) fails and this enters as emergent multi-agent failure evidence, not safety-mechanism evidence. All three scenarios are logical simulations, so there is no physical domain and no cross-domain cell; humans in the loop are future work only; the reported hours and GPUs are wall-clock simulation cost, not decision latency; metrics are judged on 5 seeds per model-scenario pair.

title: Certified Policy Verification and Synthesis for MDPs under Distributional Reach-avoidance Properties
evidence: "Finally, the algorithm feeds the resulting system to an off-the-shelf SMT solver." (Sec. 5)
method: Offline template-based synthesis and verification of memoryless policies with distributional reach-avoid certificates for MDPs, reduced to SMT constraints; swarms are modelled as a distribution over states, not individual agents.
evaluation: Gridworld swarm, Insulin and PageRank models (5-88 states); Yices 2.6, Ryzen 3600; no baseline; 7/7 verification, 3/5 synthesis tasks solved; invariant generation 1-238 s, 10-minute timeout.
contribution: Gives a sound, relatively complete SMT-based method to synthesise and certify MDP policies under distributional reach-avoidance specifications, solving all seven verification and three of five synthesis benchmarks.
flag: Design-time verification and synthesis only: no runtime monitor, shield or override, so (a) is not met; the appendix confirms no mention of monitoring or shielding. Multi-agent is nominal - a swarm is abstracted as a probability distribution over MDP states (at least 90% reach target, at most 10% in limited cells) under one policy, with no inter-agent hazard, so (c) is not met either. Even on topic it would fail minimum evaluation: authors state they know of no existing automated method, so there is no baseline; the only comparison is among SMT solvers (Yices vs z3 vs MathSAT, unquantified). Does not scale: synthesis times out on Grid 8x8 (32 states) and Grid 20x10 (88 states). Main-text PDF was truncated in Appendix E; tail read separately. Background citation at most for certificate-based verification.

title: AI Algorithm for Predicting and Optimizing Trajectory of UAV Swarm
evidence: Sec. 3.3: "we assume that all UAVs take off and fly simultaneously, following predefined trajectories"; Conclusion: "This activation function substantially outperforms commonly used counterparts in terms of trajectory accuracy."
method: One-hidden-layer MLP (15 neurons, 201 linear outputs, Levenberg-Marquardt) predicts UAV waypoints using a new AdaptoSwelliGauss activation; a separate offline pipeline detects sphere collisions, nudges trajectories and batches takeoff times.
evaluation: 500 simulated UAVs in MATLAB UAV Toolbox, 201 waypoints, 70-15-15 split, 1000 epochs; baselines seven standard activations; best MSE 3.059e-14; 262 collisions detected at R=0.5, 41 remaining after avoidance, 0 after batching; Intel i7 12th gen, no latency.
contribution: Proposes the AdaptoSwelliGauss activation for UAV-swarm waypoint regression, reporting far lower MSE than seven standard activations, plus an offline collision-detection, avoidance and takeoff-batching pipeline for 500 UAVs.
flag: The subject is an activation function for trajectory regression, so none of (a)-(e) is the paper's subject: avoidance is pre-flight trajectory editing plus takeoff batching, never a runtime interceptor, and the Conclusion ranks collision handling third of three contributions, which fails the (c) primacy test. If the maintainer is tempted to credit (b), note each UAV is regressed independently from its own start and destination with no multi-agent or graph input, so there is no multi-agent latent state and no world model of dynamics - my multi-agent state cell refers only to the all-pairs offline collision check. Internal inconsistency to verify: the text reports 41 remaining collisions at safe radius 0.5 while Table 9 gives 47 at the same radius. The abstract's "substantially better accuracy than all existing activation functions" is not supported on the Z axis, where AdaptoSwelliGauss (1.739e-13) barely beats Swish (2.182e-13). No repeated runs, variance or significance tests anywhere, and no inference-time or latency figure despite the real-time framing (real-time sensing is future work only).

title: LNS2+RL: Combining Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning with Large Neighborhood Search in Multi-Agent Path Finding
evidence: "Only valid actions are sampled during training and evaluation" (Replanning Tasks as a MARL Problem) - collision handling is inside the planner; no runtime safety mechanism is described.
method: Large Neighborhood Search for multi-agent path finding that uses a MARL replanner in early iterations to reduce colliding pairs, then switches to prioritized planning with SIPPS; action dependency graph for robot execution.
evaluation: Grid MAPF maps 10x10 to 50x50, 50-77.5% agent density; baselines LNS2, EECBS, LaCAM, SCRIMP; success rate, sum of costs, colliding pairs (-26.3% vs LNS2 at 65%); 90 virtual plus 10 real robots, qualitative.
contribution: Hybrid MARL and large-neighborhood-search planner that raises success rates on dense, structured multi-agent path finding instances where LNS2, EECBS, LaCAM and SCRIMP fail.
flag: Offline MAPF planner about solvability and path cost; collisions are a planning constraint (colliding pairs in a not-yet-feasible plan), not a runtime hazard, so the protocol v1.2 coordination rule gives E1. The action dependency graph does make real robots wait for dependencies at execution time, but the paper does not frame or evaluate it as a safety mechanism and the real-robot result is qualitative. Text says MARL replanner is about 7x slower while Table 3 shows +1175% time at iteration 1 (about 12.8x). Tables 4 and 10 were garbled in extraction; per-cell success rates not verified.

title: BELLS: A Framework Towards Future Proof Benchmarks for the Evaluation of LLM Safeguards
evidence: Section 5.1 Baseline detection: 'It achieves a 0.97 AUPRC score after 80 steps in the environment.' - the only implemented test supervises an LLM agent's trace.
method: Benchmark framework of three test categories for LLM input-output safeguards; implements one next-gen-architecture test on MACHIAVELLI plus a trajectory-harm detector that flags unethical steering.
evaluation: 200 MACHIAVELLI traces (134 games, 33.6k API calls); detector thresholded against 100 random agents; AUPRC 0.97 at step 80, above 0.9 after step 29; no safeguard compared, no ablation, no hardware or latency.
contribution: BELLS proposes a three-category benchmark structure for LLM input-output safeguards and contributes the first next-gen agent test, a MACHIAVELLI trace dataset and a trajectory-harm baseline detector.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - safeguards over an LLM application/agent. Check: safeguards only produce reports from traces, nothing overrides or halts an action, so (a) fails; the single quantitative result (AUPRC 0.97) has no comparator safeguard and no ablation, so the evaluation floor fails; existing tools (Lakera Guard, Llama Guard, GPT-4 moderation) are discussed but never run with numbers; only one agent, multi-agent is named as future work, so exclude-E4 is also arguable, as is E3 for a framework/position paper with one implemented test.

title: Safe, Out-of-Distribution-Adaptive MPC with Conformalized Neural Network Ensembles
evidence: Abstract: "When an OOD situation is detected, SODA-MPC triggers a safe fallback control strategy based on reachability"; Sec. 5: "We use the maximum singular value of the empirical covariance among the ensemble as the OOD signal."
method: SODA-MPC: ensemble of pedestrian predictors; spectral norm of ensemble covariance is a conformally calibrated OOD monitor that switches the vehicle MPC to a reachable-set fallback controller at runtime.
evaluation: Simulated pedestrian crossing (1 vehicle, 1 pedestrian), 20 runs each, vs SPDE, MARC, ensembles-only, reachable-only; nominal success 60-70%; OOD detection 91.3-91.7%, false positives 4.4-13.9%; no hardware or timing.
contribution: A conformally calibrated ensemble-disagreement monitor detects out-of-distribution pedestrian behaviour at runtime and switches the planner to a reachability-based fallback, avoiding collisions that conformal MPC baselines incur.
flag: Borderline on level: one ego vehicle and one scripted pedestrian, so multi-agent only nominally (E4 arguable); kept because it is a sequential runtime monitor with fallback. Collision outcomes are stated qualitatively ('avoids collisions in all settings') with no counts; the quantitative safety evidence is detection/false-positive rates (Tables 1-2) and nominal success (SODA 60%, ensembles-only 70%, so the monitor costs throughput). Trajectron++/nuScenes test is detection only, ego not under MPC. No solve times or hardware. Paper says 66 parameters per MLP but App. C.1 describes two 32-unit layers. Published at L4DC 2025 (PMLR 283).

title: A Superalignment Framework in Autonomous Driving with Large Language Models
evidence: Section I Contributions: the framework is a guardrail 'effectively censoring the data interacting with cloud-based LLM'; Section V adds 'a safety assessment agent', but no module is specified.
method: Conceptual security layer between vehicle and cloud LLM: driving-safety, data-safety and alignment conditions over models P_phi, P_psi, P_omega, stated as subset and limit requirements with no rejection rule.
evaluation: AutoGen harness, 250 nuScenes-QA pairs, 11 published LLM-driving system prompts on gpt-3.5-turbo and llama2-70b-chat; accuracy 16.4-93.0 percent, GPT-4-assigned alignment 45-92; the proposed framework itself is never evaluated; no hardware.
contribution: Sketches a cloud-LLM autonomous-driving security framework with driving-safety, data-safety and alignment conditions, and benchmarks eleven published LLM driving prompts on nuScenes-QA for accuracy and alignment.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - a cloud LLM in a driving stack, but the guardrail is only a sketch: no module list, no architecture detail, no threshold or veto rule, so (a) fails. Check: the abstract's claim that the framework's efficacy was 'successfully demonstrated' is unsupported - every experiment benchmarks other papers' prompts, and Table III safety rates are copied from those papers rather than measured. Multi-agent is nominal (Section III sets P_phi=P_psi=P_omega for a single-agent structure). Table IV and V 'Time' columns have no units and no hardware. exclude-E1 is arguable if the maintainer reads it as a prompt benchmark rather than a safety mechanism.

title: Multi-Task Lane-Free Driving Strategy for Connected and Automated Vehicles: A Multi-Agent Deep Reinforcement Learning Approach
evidence: "any action causing leftward movement during diverging at off-ramps is suppressed" (Sec. 3.4); collision avoidance is otherwise a reward term (Sec. 3.5.3, Eq. 20).
method: MADDPG lane-free driving policy for connected automated vehicles with a multi-objective reward covering collision avoidance, desired speed, overtaking, merging/diverging and comfort; centralised training, decentralised execution.
evaluation: SUMO sublane sim: 6 agents trained on a 400 m ring road, tested on ring road and 4 km freeway with ramps at 7200 veh/h; no baseline or ablation; ring flow about 17000 veh/h; no hardware or latency.
contribution: A multi-agent deep reinforcement learning policy for lane-free driving of connected automated vehicles that learns collision-free overtaking, merging and diverging in SUMO, without comparison to any baseline controller.
flag: Safety enters through reward shaping, which does not meet (a); the paper is a multi-task driving strategy (speed, overtaking, merging, comfort, capacity), so (c) primacy fails. Would also fail E2: no baseline or ablation, and collisions are reported only as a training curve reaching zero (Fig. 5b), with no test-phase collision rate, seeds or trial counts. The single off-ramp action-suppression rule is not evaluated and it is unclear whether it runs at execution. Speed deviation under 0.01 m/s and reward about -3 are the only other numbers.

title: Multi-UAVs end-to-end Distributed Trajectory Generation over Point Cloud Data
evidence: The approach "consistently achieves a remarkable success rate of 100% for obstacle densities up to 15%" and has "an average computational time of 1.3ms with a maximum of 1500 points sensed" (Sec. V).
method: Decentralised end-to-end GNN planner: PointNet-DMoN point-cloud encoder, message-aware graph attention among neighbours, and a final QP layer enforcing velocity, acceleration and a learned collision constraint on MINVO trajectories.
evaluation: Sim, 4-25 UAVs, forest and corridor, obstacle density 5-25%, 50 repetitions; vs MADER and four ablations; success 100-85% (MADER 85% at 25%); travel time 11.8 s; 1.3 ms on i7-9750H with RTX 2080Ti; Crazyflie SITL.
contribution: A decentralised graph-neural trajectory generator over raw point clouds that plans for up to 25 UAVs in 1.3 ms on average, keeping collision-free success between 100% and 85% as obstacle density rises.
flag: Borderline. It is a learned planner, not a runtime interceptor: the QP layer refines the network's guess and no execution-time fallback or infeasibility handling is described, so (a) is not met. (c) rests on collision-free mission success being the main measured outcome against MADER and ablations, but the paper also sells scalability, deadlock avoidance and speed - maintainer may judge it E1 under the primacy test. (d) is weak: 1.3 ms is on a laptop CPU with an RTX 2080Ti, not edge hardware, and there is no stated deadline, only a 0.056 s communication delay margin and 15 Hz replanning. At 25% density it only ties the MADER expert (85%). No real flights (Crazyflies in Unity+MuJoCo SITL; hardware is future work). Fig. 3 "safety rate" has no values in the text. Not a world model, so (b) not claimed.

title: Robotic Shepherding in Cluttered and Unknown Environments using Control Barrier Functions
evidence: Sec. V-D: when infeasible 'the herding constraint is allocated as a soft constraint' - CBF constraints sit inside the herding QP itself, with no separate nominal action being filtered.
method: Robot-dogs herd uncontrollable Reynolds-model sheep along a planned trajectory by solving a QP with herding, obstacle and dog-dog control barrier function constraints over a LiDAR occupancy map.
evaluation: Matlab simulation only, three single-run scenarios (11 sheep/3 dogs, 3/2, 7/3), 100 Hz control; no baselines, no ablations, no collision or violation statistics, no timing.
contribution: CBF-constrained QP controller letting a few robot-dogs herd a flock through cluttered unknown environments, shown in three Matlab simulations without baselines or safety statistics.
flag: Would also fail as E2: single runs, no baseline or ablation, only qualitative claim that herd radius stays below R^d. Primary claim is herding/containment, dog-dog collision avoidance is one constraint among several. Reference velocity u_d^ref (Eq. 35) does not appear in QP Eq. 39 as extracted, so filter-vs-controller reading is uncertain. Feasibility proven only for n=m without other constraints, sims use n>m. Read via one summarised fetch of the PDF.

title: EARBench: Towards Evaluating Physical Risk Awareness for Task Planning of Foundation Model-based Embodied AI Agents
evidence: Section 2.1: EARBench is 'the first automated physical risk assessment framework specifically designed for EAI scenarios'; average Task Risk Rate over 12 foundation models is 95.75 percent.
method: Automated four-module pipeline (safety-guideline generation, risky-scene generation, embodied task planning, GPT-4o plan assessment) producing EARDataset, which scores physical risk in foundation-model embodied task plans.
evaluation: 2636 textual and visual scenarios, 28 scenes, 7 physical domains, 12 LLMs and VLMs; TRR 95.75 percent average and 94.03 for GPT-4o; mitigation ablations cut TRR to 67.85 (Llama-3.1-70B) and 45.64 (GPT-4o); human kappa 0.85; no latency.
contribution: EARBench automates physical-risk assessment of foundation-model embodied planners, finding a 95.75 percent average task risk rate and showing prompt-level mitigation still leaves risk above 40 percent.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - foundation-model embodied planners are the system assessed. Check: there is no runtime interception at all (RM-Implicit and RM-Explicit are prompt text, plans are judged after generation and never executed), so (a) fails and inclusion rests on the 'safety evaluation of LLM agents' clause of (c); the multi-agent cooperative system is the evaluation harness, not the system under test, and planning is single-agent, so exclude-E4 is arguable. GPT-4o generates the scenarios, judges the plans and is itself evaluated. No robot or simulator execution; visual scenes are Midjourney-V6 images. GPT-4o TRR is reported as 94.03, 94.12 and 94.53 textual with 93.52 visual in different places.

title: MAPPO-PIS: A Multi-Agent Proximal Policy Optimization Method with Prior Intent Sharing for CAVs' Cooperative Decision-Making
evidence: Section 3.3: 'if the intention trajectory of CAV overlaps with that of other vehicle, the intention is considered unsafe, and it will be replaced with a new safe intention'; Algorithm 1 replaces it before execution.
method: MAPPO for connected-vehicle merging plus an Intention Generator Module (8-step PID rollout of each agent's intent) and a Safety Enhanced Module that priority-checks shared intents and substitutes a max-min-margin action.
evaluation: highway-env merging, easy and hard, homogeneous and heterogeneous human drivers, 2M steps, 3 seeds; baselines MAPPO, MAACKTR, MAA2C and a module ablation; collision 0.01 vs 0.03 hard and 0.04 vs 0.09 heterogeneous-hard, reward 33.27 vs -36.58, speed 21.61 m/s, PET 1.6 s; no latency.
contribution: MAPPO-PIS shares predicted intent among connected vehicles and adds a runtime module that replaces conflicting intentions, lowering collision rate from 0.09 to 0.04 against MAPPO while delaying merge bottlenecks.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - the Safety Enhanced Module vetoes and replaces the MARL policy's own chosen intention before it is executed, so (a) is clear. Check: (c) is arguable but I did not claim it - the headline gains are reward, average speed and bottleneck delay, and collision rates sit between 0.00 and 0.04 with little separation from MAA2C. No module-isolating ablation exists (only full MAPPO-PIS vs MAPPO, i.e. both modules together), no SEM intervention-frequency or false-halt figures, and no latency or onboard hardware despite the CAV framing. Text and tables disagree: Section 4.4 says hard-mode collision 'grow to 0.02' while Table 1 gives 0.01, and Section 4.3 cites speeds 24.5 vs 22.5 m/s against 25.69 vs 25.06 in Table 1. PET is used without definition. Gap cell non-generative inference is my judgement because intent prediction is PID plus IDM-MOBIL rollout, not a generative model - drop it if too generous.

title: XP-MARL: Auxiliary Prioritization in Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning to Address Non-Stationarity
evidence: Sec. IV-C: XP-MARL "improves the safety of a baseline model by 84.4%" (collision rate, median, vs MAPPO baseline 1.09%).
method: XP-MARL: MAPPO agents jointly learn priority scores and driving policies; agents act in priority order and lower-priority agents condition on communicated actions of higher-priority neighbours.
evaluation: SigmaRL simulator, trained with 4 vehicles, tested with 15 on CPM map, 32 one-minute runs; baselines MAPPO, perfect opponent modelling, random priorities, noisy actions; collision rate, speed -2.2%; no hardware.
contribution: Learned priority ordering with action propagation among connected vehicles cuts the collision rate of a MAPPO baseline (1.09%) by 84.4% for a 2.2% loss in average speed.
flag: Not a runtime interceptor: safety comes from a learned coordination scheme, so only (c) applies. Primacy test is borderline - paper is framed around non-stationarity in MARL, though collision rate vs baseline is the headline outcome. Absolute XP-MARL collision rate is not stated in text (only relative 84.4%); other reductions: perfect opponent modelling 12.8%, random priorities 22.0%, 10% action noise 35.8%. Assumes communication delay under one 50 ms step; no inference time or hardware reported; simulation only. Abstract figures 84.4% and 2.2% are in the body. Figure-only values not seen.

title: Decentralized Nonlinear Model Predictive Control for Safe Collision Avoidance in Quadrotor Teams with Limited Detection Range
evidence: Sec. IV-B, eq. 5d: pairwise ECBF conditions enter the NMPC as inequality constraints 'G_ij(x_i, x_j, u_i) >= 0'; conclusion claims the derived detection-range bound 'does not affect the overall safety of the system when compared to an infinite detection range'.
method: Decentralized NMPC per quadrotor with pairwise exponential CBF constraints under thrust limits; derives minimum robot and obstacle detection ranges that preserve the ECBF guarantee.
evaluation: Sim: up to 10 quadrotors, 20 obstacles, 10 runs per setup; detection-range ablation (infinite, bound, 2.0 m, 1.0/1.5 m); barrier-violation counts; 3 real quadrotors, VOXL 2, ~160 Hz.
contribution: Decentralized NMPC with pairwise exponential barrier constraints keeps quadrotor teams safe under thrust limits, and a derived minimum detection range matches unlimited-range safety in simulation and on three real quadrotors.
flag: Borderline. Safety constraint sits inside the planner, so (a) is not met; inclusion rests on (c) only. No external baseline controller, only a detection-range ablation. Violation counts are mostly in Fig. 4; text gives only 'safe for N<=5, No<=5' and total '<=4' at N=10, No>=10, and no figure for the restricted-range case. Unlimited range is not violation-free (NMPC infeasible in deadlocks). ~160 Hz is a loop rate, no solve-time or latency data. Real-world result is qualitative. Quotes relayed via the fetch tool, verify wording.

title: Realizable Continuous-Space Shields for Safe Reinforcement Learning
evidence: Sec. 3: the shield does not intervene when the policy's action satisfies the specification; on a violation it "overrides a with a corrected action".
method: Stateful continuous-space shield from a temporal specification; realizability checked offline so a safe action always exists; overrides PPO action with nearest satisfying action via optimiser, solver fallback.
evaluation: Sim mapless navigation (5 policies, 5 seeds x 100 runs) and 4-agent Particle World; no-shield, shield variants, Lagrangian-PPO; collision 0.03-0.78 to 0.00-0.01; 0.35-0.49 to 0.00; no latency.
contribution: Realizable continuous-space shields guarantee a safe corrective action always exists, cutting collisions to about zero in navigation and a four-agent particle task without lowering success rates.
flag: Mostly single-agent; multi-agent only in the 4-agent Particle World (success 0.53-0.66 to 0.93-0.97, collision to 0.00), so multi-agent state cell is thin and E4 is arguable. No shield query time reported; paper's own Table 4 marks real-time capability as unmet. Residual 0.01 collisions for the Unsafe policy attributed to partial observability. Text's realizable configuration (30, 13) does not match Table 1 labels. Lagrangian-PPO collision 0.05-0.09 (App. F). Simulation only; compute is a 255-CPU cluster for training. Abstract has no numbers. Read via summarising fetch of the PDF.

title: Collaborative Safety-Critical Formation Control with Obstacle Avoidance
evidence: Sec III Eq. 14: each agent solves a QP minimising the deviation between nominal formation command u_i^f and safety correction u_i^s under CBF obstacle constraints; Sec IV-A: any action from the returned set 'will also be safe for all neighbors'.
method: Distributed CBF safety filter for formation control: neighbours exchange requests and adjustments over communication rounds to restrict each agent's admissible action set so one agent's avoidance stays safe for neighbours.
