evaluation: 2D mass-spring simulation only: 7-agent tree and 8-agent fully connected networks, static and dynamic obstacles, 100 Hz. No baseline or ablation. Only metric: max 13 communication rounds.
contribution: Collaborative control-barrier-function filter in which neighbouring agents negotiate admissible action sets so formation control and obstacle avoidance stay jointly safe, with a bound on communication rounds.
flag: Runtime filter and on-topic for (a)/(c), but fails minimum evaluation: no collision or violation rate, no baseline, no ablation; only round counts and trajectory plots. Maintainer may keep it as a formal result (Theorem 2 round bound). No fallback when terminally infeasible; delays unmodelled, synchronised rounds assumed; authors note the dynamic-obstacle test reaches an unsafe state at higher speeds. No latency or hardware.

title: Learning responsibility allocations for multi-agent interactions: A differentiable optimization approach with control barrier functions
evidence: Sec I: responsibility is "an agent's willingness to deviate from its desired control to accommodate safe interactions with others"; Sec VIII leaves use in robot policy construction to future work
method: Responsibility-weighted multi-agent CBF quadratic program used as a descriptive model; per-agent responsibility weights learned from interaction data by bi-level inverse optimization through the differentiable QP.
evaluation: Synthetic 2-agent 1D and 6-agent 2D systems (128 samples) plus a two-human traffic-weaving simulator dataset; internal model variants only; results in figures, no tables; MacBook Pro M2, no timings stated.
contribution: Differentiable-optimization method that learns how responsibility for collision avoidance is shared among interacting agents by fitting a responsibility-weighted control barrier function program to data.
flag: The CBF-QP is only a data-fitting and interpretation model here; nothing filters or overrides an action at run time and no collision, violation or intervention rate is measured, so (a) and (c) both fail; E2 would be an equally defensible code. No numeric results anywhere in the text - convergence, timing-vs-batch-size and learned weights are figures only; the "great potential for realtime applications" remark (Sec VI) is unquantified. No external baseline (SVO, VR-ORCA discussed only in related work). Could be background for responsibility-aware filters.

title: NetSafe: Exploring the Topological Safety of Multi-agent Networks
evidence: Abstract and Table 1: under misinformation injection the Star topology falls from 95.03 to 66.80 on Fact, a 29.7 percent decrease; Section 4.2 names 'Agent Hallucination' spreading through the network.
method: NetSafe models an LLM multi-agent system as a graph with a RelCom iterative communication protocol, injects misinformation, bias or harmful content at chosen nodes across five topologies and measures network safety.
evaluation: GPT-4o-mini agents, 6-node Chain, Cycle, Tree, Star and Complete graphs, 0-5 attackers, 3 runs, datasets Fact 153, CSQA 127, GSMath 113, Bias 103, AdvBench; Star 95.03 to 66.80, Complete GSMath 89.38 to 44.25, moderation 0.097 vs 0.920 attacker; static-metric Kendall tau APV 0.367, NE 0.067, EC -0.567; no defended baseline, no latency.
contribution: NetSafe shows that an LLM multi-agent network's safety depends on its topology, with misinformation in a star graph cutting accuracy 29.7 percent, and names Agent Hallucination and Aggregation Safety.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - the agents are LLMs and multi-agent safety is both the primary claim and the primary measured outcome, so (c) holds. No defense, filter or monitor is proposed, so (a) fails and runtime_interceptor is no. Check: the comparison is across topologies and attacker counts rather than against a defended baseline, so the maintainer may hold that the evaluation floor's baseline requirement is unmet; outcomes are task accuracy and OpenAI Moderation scores, not a hazard or intervention rate; every network has 6 nodes averaged over 3 runs with no scaling study; the proposed static topology metrics correlate weakly (NE Kendall tau 0.067, EC -0.567 i.e. inverted); text-only agents, no physical or robotic setting, so no cross-domain cell.

title: Multiple Ships Cooperative Navigation and Collision Avoidance using Multi-agent Reinforcement Learning with Communication
evidence: Sec 3.2: 'We assume that ships are invisible to each other, so they have to communicate to alleviate partial observation'; COLREGs compliance enters only as a reward term.
method: MADDPG (centralised critic, decentralised actors) with learned 3-bit inter-ship messages on a 3-DOF MMG ship model; collision avoidance and COLREGs shaped by reward only, no runtime filter.
evaluation: Custom MPE-based simulator, two ships; baselines MAPPO, DDPG, no-communication MADDPG; avoidance success 79.3% vs DDPG 52.7%; navigation 84.2% vs <5% blocked; no hardware or latency.
contribution: Shows two simulated ships can learn a 3-bit communication protocol with MADDPG that lifts cooperative collision-avoidance success to 79.3% against 52.7% for independent DDPG.
flag: Borderline (c): half the paper is collision avoidance with a success rate against baselines, but the claim is learned communication and cooperation, safety is a reward term and no collision rate is reported separately. Only two ships. Per-encounter success: head-on 79.8%, crossing 77.3%, overtaking 83.4%. Cooperative vs non-cooperative success not significantly different (p>0.05). Maintainer may prefer include under (c) if primacy test is read loosely.

title: A Systematic Study of Multi-Agent Deep Reinforcement Learning for Safe and Robust Autonomous Highway Ramp Entry
evidence: Abstract: "collision-free controllers are theoretically impossible in fully decentralized, non-coordinated environments"; collision percentage tables are the only reported outcome (Sec. 4.5 and 5.2)
method: Game-theoretic multi-agent deep RL (DDPG actor-critic, two 30-unit layers) trained by self-play; ego vehicle controls acceleration only in [-5,4] m/s2; collision avoidance comes from reward penalties, no runtime filter.
evaluation: Unnamed vehicle simulator, three-vehicle and full-scene taper merges; reference is an idealized optimal collision table plus an exploration-rate ablation; metric collision percentage; 100 ms control step; no hardware or latency reported.
contribution: Game-theoretic multi-agent DDPG self-play learns longitudinal control for taper-type highway ramp entry, reporting collision-percentage tables against an idealized optimal-controller bound across ramp lengths, gaps and traffic policies.
flag: No runtime interceptor at all - safety is a training-time reward penalty, so criterion (a) fails and (c) is the only route in; maintainer should decide whether a learned driving policy counts as a safety mechanism under protocol v1.2. The only baseline is an idealized unavoidable-collision bound, not a competing method: prior work (Schester and Ortiz, Kamran et al.) is discussed with no numerical comparison, so check whether this satisfies the baseline-or-ablation requirement of protocol v1.6. The abstract claims controllers are "nearly ideal" but I could not find any single aggregate collision percentage for the best three-vehicle network in the body; the best full-scene network is reported only as a raw count, "total collisions of 4,389". The simulator is never named. My time-to-irreversibility gap cell rests on the ideal table marking cells where collision is already unavoidable - drop it if that reading is too generous.

title: Barriers on the EDGE: A scalable CBF architecture over EDGE for safe aerial-ground multi-agent coordination
evidence: Sec. I: the CBF-filtered signal "is minimally invasive on the nominal controller"; Sec. V (Conclusion): "The validation of the proposed controller and theoretical evaluation will be included in the extended version."
method: Onboard CBF-QP safety filter per robot minimally modifies the nominal input; an edge-hosted Watcher node sends each UAV/UGV its constraint matrices (A, b) over ROS/Wi-Fi in a star topology.
evaluation: None. Preliminary version: no simulation, no robot experiment, no baseline, no measured metric, no latency or hardware figures. Only analytical link counts (2N star vs 2N(2N-1) fully connected).
contribution: Proposes an edge-coordinated control-barrier-function safety filter architecture for N UAV-UGV pairs, with constraints distributed from an edge Watcher node, but reports no evaluation.
flag: Runtime filter and topic fit (a)/(c), but the paper has NO evaluation at all (authors defer validation to an extended version) - E2 under minimum-evaluation rule. Check whether the extended version exists and is queued. Edge cell is architectural only: no latency measured, latency discussed qualitatively; Kubernetes not mentioned. Filter adjusts input, no halt/veto described. No human role.

title: LiveNet: Robust, Minimally Invasive Multi-Robot Control for Safe and Live Navigation in Constrained Environments
evidence: Sec 4: "a differentiable QP layer which solves a standard QP problem with inequality constraints"; Sec 1: perturbs "the speed of a robot by the smallest amount necessary, without changing its direction"
method: Decentralized neural controller per robot outputs a reference control and CBF penalty terms; a differentiable QP layer enforces safety and liveness dCBF constraints, minimally altering speed at execution.
evaluation: Simulation only, 2 robots, doorway and intersection, 50 runs each; baselines MPC-CBF, SMG-CBF, MACBF, PIC, BarrierNet; collisions, deadlocks, makespan, delta-V, cycle time; no hardware.
contribution: LiveNet embeds a CBF quadratic-program layer in a learned decentralized controller, giving 0 collisions and 0 deadlocks in 50 two-robot doorway and intersection runs while perturbing velocity less than MPC baselines.
flag: Borderline. The QP layer is trained end-to-end inside the policy (BarrierNet style), not a separate filter on an independent nominal controller; maintainer should decide if that meets (a). Paper is as much about deadlock/liveness as collision, so (c) primacy not claimed. Only 2 agents, simulation only. Results: LiveNet 0/50 collisions and 0/50 deadlocks in both scenes; MACBF, PIC, BarrierNet 50/50 collisions; MPC-CBF 50/50 deadlocks; robustness 25/28 vs SMG-CBF 16/28. Intro claim of "30% more scenarios" has no table; nearest support is 25/28 vs 16/28 (about 32 points) against one baseline. Cycle time column is labelled seconds (LiveNet 7.5 and 9.3, SMG-CBF 81.1 and 157.0) which is implausible for a 0.2 s step; units probably ms or mislabelled, compute platform not stated. Text says QP "maximize" (u-uref)^2, likely typo. No ablation.

title: SafeAgentBench: A Benchmark for Safe Task Planning of Embodied LLM Agents
evidence: Sec. 5.6: the GPT-4 chain-of-thought safety filter "inspected each planned step and terminated execution if unsafe"; Table 2 reports rejection rates on 450 hazardous tasks.
method: Benchmark of 750 tasks (450 hazardous, 300 safe) in AI2-THOR-based SafeAgentEnv with execution-based and GPT-4 semantic evaluators; a chain-of-thought safety filter is tested as an add-on runtime defense.
evaluation: 9 embodied LLM planners and 5 LLMs in SafeAgentEnv; rejection of hazardous tasks only 0-10 pct, risk rate up to 0.69, unsafe completion up to 0.28; RTX 4090, 21-97 s per task.
contribution: SafeAgentBench shows embodied LLM planners execute most hazardous instructions, rejecting at most 10 percent, and that a chain-of-thought safety filter over-rejects safe tasks without fixing long-horizon hazards.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - embodied LLM task planners. Check that criterion (a) is not over-credited: it rests only on the add-on chain-of-thought safety filter in Sec. 5.6, whose numbers live in Figure 6 and not in the text, so the over-rejection and no-improvement claims could not be verified from the body; the benchmark itself intercepts nothing. Multi-agent only incidentally (CoELA, MAP are two-agent). Text calls the semantic evaluator GPT-4 while App. C.4 names gpt-4o-2024-08-06, and Table 14 renames CoELA as Co-LLM-Agent.

title: xSRL: Safety-Aware Explainable Reinforcement Learning -- Safety as a Product of Explainability
evidence: Sec. 4.3: a shield is triggered when Q_risk(s_t,a_t) exceeds an environment-specific threshold and the task action is replaced by a safety-policy action (closely paraphrased).
method: xSRL augments a CAPS policy graph with post-hoc Q_task and Q_risk critics, uses it to find safety-critical states for adversarial attack, then patches the agent with a risk-threshold shield.
evaluation: MuJoCo Navigation 2 and Maze, single SAC agent; patches AdvExRL, RRL-MF, SQRL; local vs global explanation baselines; fidelity NRMSE, 270-person user studies; safety only in Fig. 2. No latency.
contribution: An explainability framework for safe RL that combines local risk critics with a global policy graph, letting developers locate vulnerabilities and patch a single agent with an existing risk-threshold shield.
flag: Borderline. Single-agent CMDP despite the AAMAS venue; the shield is the existing AdvExRL safety policy and the paper's claim and measured outcomes are about explanation (fidelity, user accuracy), so I read it as wrong level, but it is sequential RL with a runtime override so a strict reading of E4 could admit it under (a). Safety(%) for attack/patch appears only in Fig. 2 - I could not read numeric values. Intro claims "less than 33.5% error in risk estimation" but Table 1 Q_risk NRMSE is 43.1-62.8% for SAC-under-attack, RRL-MF and SQRL (33.2% only for AdvExRL). Intro claim of about 72% safety drop at 50% attack rate not found as a table value. Appendices (Maze results, user-study design) were not in the fetched text. Humans are explanation consumers, not takeover operators - not (e).

title: Scaling Safe Multi-Agent Control for Signal Temporal Logic Specifications
evidence: The low-level controller is "a learnable MA collision avoidance controller" (GCBF+, Sec. 4.3) and Fig. 1 says it "ensures that the agents do not collide while following the generated goals"; no runtime filter or QP is described.
method: GNN-ODE planner generates per-agent goal sequences satisfying Signal Temporal Logic specifications; a pre-existing learned GCBF+ controller tracks them with collision avoidance; planner trained end to end, decentralised.
evaluation: JAX sim, DubinsCar/single/double integrator, N=8-32, 30 seeds; vs STLPY MILP, CE, ODE ablation; branch N=32 success 88.12% vs 18.12%, plan 0.03 s vs 87.92 s; 5 Tello drones qualitative; T4 training.
contribution: A graph-neural planner that produces goal sequences satisfying signal temporal logic tasks for up to 32 agents in milliseconds, paired with a learned barrier-function controller for collision avoidance.
flag: Borderline on (c). The contribution is the scalable STL planner; primary outcomes are success rate and planning time. A safety rate is reported against STLPY (e.g. branch N=8 100.00 vs 85.00) but the collision-avoidance component is the earlier GCBF+ controller reused unchanged, and Sec. 7 concedes the planner ignores obstacles. A maintainer who counts the safety-rate column as a primary outcome could include under (c). GCBF+ is a learned policy with a learned certificate, not a filter between decision and execution, so (a) fails. Numbers are inconsistent: Table 8 vs Table 2 for the same setting (branch N=8 plan time 0.01 vs 0.05 s; seq N=8 success 97.92 vs 95.00). Claimed "70-1000x faster" does not hold for seq N=8 (about 49x) and the "average 65% improved success rate" could not be reproduced from the tables; STLPY beats it at seq N=8 (97.50 vs 95.00). Drone experiment is qualitative only; timing hardware for plan times is unstated.

title: MARL-OT: Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning Guided Online Fuzzing to Detect Safety Violation in Autonomous Driving Systems
evidence: Sec. 3.4: "Once the online fuzzer is triggered, it takes control of the surrounding vehicle."; violation rate against GA, single-agent RL and random baselines is the primary outcome (Table 3).
method: MADDPG trains surrounding vehicles to cooperatively encircle an ego ADS; its high-level guidance triggers a rule-based finite-state online fuzzer running four pre-crash action patterns to expose ego safety violations.
evaluation: MetaDrive, IDM and PPO ego policies, 7 scenario types, 200 runs x 5 repeats; violation rate 9.3-14.9 pct vs GA 0.2-6.7, single-agent RL 4.7-11.0, random 0.1-5.4; RTX 3090, about 15 min training.
contribution: MARL-OT couples MARL high-level guidance with a rule-based online fuzzer over surrounding vehicles, roughly doubling the detected safety-violation rate of autonomous driving systems versus offline genetic and single-agent RL fuzzers.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes for the PPO end-to-end ego policy, no for the hand-designed IDM policy. Check (a) is correctly denied: there is no runtime interception anywhere - the fuzzer controls only surrounding vehicles and never overrides the ADS, so this is adversarial testing, and a maintainer who reads the review as about safety reflexes rather than hazard discovery could call exclude-E1. Included on (c) because the multi-vehicle collision rate is both primary claim and primary measured outcome against three baselines. The abstract's up to 136.2 pct improvement does not reproduce from Table 3, where the best pairwise gain over single-agent RL is about 94 pct. No ablation other than the stripped single-agent RL variant; no human role beyond a 5-tester realism rating.

title: One Stack, Diverse Vehicles: Checking Safe Portability of Automated Driving Software
evidence: Sec. V-D: the safe sets "can be used as customized supervisors for legacy ACC" - stated as a possibility only, not implemented or evaluated.
method: Design-time portability check: robust controlled invariant sets per vehicle hardware configuration with actuation delay, then CBMC bounded model checking of ACC controller code (MPC and neural) against the set.
evaluation: Three hypothetical vehicle configurations, MPC and DDPG-trained ACC code; RCIS time 7.5-29.5 min, BMC verdicts or counterexamples in minutes; Threadripper PRO 7955WX; no baseline, no simulation, no runtime latency.
contribution: Offline check of whether ACC controller code stays inside a delay-aware robust controlled invariant set when ported across vehicle hardware configurations, using bounded model checking.
flag: Offline verification, not a runtime interceptor; the supervisor use of the safe set is only suggested. Single ego plus one lead vehicle, no multi-agent hazard. Actuation delay (tau 0.1-0.4 s) is modelled in the plant, which touches (d) only loosely since nothing is inferred at runtime. No collision or violation rate and no baseline, so it would also fail minimum evaluation (E2) if a criterion were granted. Table II is garbled in the PDF text: MPC verified on VHC 1 and 2 (7.0 min), counterexample on VHC 3 (5.2 min); NNC verified on VHC 2 (35.4 min), counterexample on VHC 3 (30.1 min) and on VHC 1 (time not legible) - check against the PDF. DNN verifier not named.

title: Discrete GCBF Proximal Policy Optimization for Multi-agent Safe Optimal Control
evidence: Sec 4.2: the policy is trained to "satisfy the DCBF conditions instead of using the safety filter framework"; Sec 5.2 reports a safety rate close to 100% against penalty and Lagrangian baselines.
method: DGPPO jointly learns a discrete graph CBF and a distributed GNN policy with PPO, decoupled CRPO-style constraint updates and gradient projection; no execution-time filter.
evaluation: Sim only: LiDAR, MuJoCo, VMAS tasks, N=3 (5 and 7 on LINE); baselines InforMARL penalty/schedule, MAPPO-Lagrangian; safety rate and cost; RTX 4090 training about 12 h; no latency.
contribution: Learns a discrete graph control barrier function jointly with a multi-agent PPO policy, reaching near-100% safety rates in simulation without a nominal policy or a runtime safety filter.
flag: Safety enforced through training, not a runtime filter, so (a) is not met; inclusion rests on (c) as a learned certificate. Main-result numbers are in figures only; the body says only "close to 100%". The only tabulated values are Table 3 (App C.8, TARGET, trained on 8 agents): safety 1.000 at 8, 0.992 at 16, 0.982 at 128, 0.985 at 512 agents. Hand-crafted DGCBF lowers safety by about 15% on TRANSPORT2. Ablations C.6 are qualitative in text. No hardware, no inference time. Authors concede the guarantee is hard to achieve by learning (Sec 6).

title: Safe Multi-agent Satellite Servicing with Control Barrier Functions
evidence: Trajectory-following/CBF section: 'the resulting safe control is used for each TPODS agent'; hybrid logic: 'Otherwise, the produced control signal is discarded, and the DCOL framework is used to prevent any TPODS-RSO collisions.'
method: Linear MPC tracks fuel-optimal references; a centralised HOCBF-QP minimally modifies the control for inter-agent safety and switches to DCOL polytope re-optimisation for agent-RSO collisions; margins inflated by MEKF covariance.
evaluation: Simulation, 2 CubeSat modules on a tumbling RSO; CBF vs DCOL vs hybrid; 500-run Monte Carlo: 97.6% trials with no violation; CBF 0.0144 s vs DCOL 0.0229 s average solve; impulse 1.01 vs 1.59 Ns.
contribution: A hybrid CBF-QP filter plus differentiable-collision re-solve keeps two servicing CubeSats violation-free in 97.6% of 500 Monte Carlo runs on estimated states, with CBF filtering cheaper than polytope re-optimisation.
flag: Multi-agent only just: two agents plus mothership/RSO, and the CBF-QP is centralised (all agents solved simultaneously); authors say pairwise constraints do not scale. The baseline is a comparison of the two component mechanisms (CBF-only vs DCOL-only, Table 1), not an unfiltered controller, so there is no no-safeguard collision rate. Authors concede the covariance inflation 'no longer retains the safety guarantees offered by CBFs'. Table 2 minimum constraint values (about -0.002 to -0.017, at most 5 violations per constraint) were garbled in extraction - verify. Compute platform unstated; solve times are simulation timings, not flight hardware, so no latency/edge cell ticked. Simulation only.

title: AttentionSwarm: Reinforcement Learning with Attention Control Barier Function for Crazyflie Drones in Dynamic Environments
evidence: Sec. IV-B and Table I: AttentionSwarm reports a 0% collision rate against 30% (MAPPO), 30% (A2C) and 15% (MPC) over 20 four-drone trials, with success 100% in case 1 and 95% in case 2.
method: Multi-agent RL for drone swarms where an attention network replaces the Lagrangian multipliers of the constrained objective, emitting per-agent safety penalty weights over swarm and obstacle state during training.
evaluation: gym-pybullet-drones, four drones, 20 trials, two cases; baselines MAPPO, A2C, MPC; success 100% and 95%, collisions 0% vs 15-30%; two real Crazyflies with Vicon, qualitative; no latency reported.
contribution: An attention network standing in for Lagrangian multipliers in constrained multi-agent RL drives a four-drone swarm through obstacle and gate courses with zero reported collisions, against 15-30% for MAPPO, A2C and MPC.
flag: Criterion (a) is NOT met and runtime_interceptor is no despite the title: Sec. III-D says "we replace the traditional Lagrangian multipliers with an Attention-based CBF Neural Network" whose "attention weights serve as safety penalties", "effectively enforcing the safety constraints as a soft constraint", and Algorithm 1 executes the sampled action directly with no projection, QP or override. That is a safety term in the training objective, which the protocol explicitly excludes from (a). No barrier function or barrier condition is ever written down for the so-called CBF, so the claim that "this attention mechanism ensures that the actions selected by the policy adhere to predefined safety constraints" is unsupported; the maintainer may want to downgrade or re-tag barrier-functions. Include therefore rests entirely on (c) and on Table I, whose column header reads "Precision (%)" while the text calls the same numbers success rates. There is no ablation of the attention module against plain MAPPO under the same reward, so the attributed gain is not isolated. Obstacle counts are inconsistent: the text says eight static obstacles, Table I says one and three, and Sec. III-A with Fig. 2 describe a moving obstacle that the reported trials do not use. Abstract claims about safe landing and about Crazyflie 2.1 are not substantiated in the body. Real-world results are qualitative only, with no numeric success rate, clearance, separation or mission time, and no inference time or control-loop rate is given, so (d) is unmet; compute is an RTX 4090 workstation with Vicon, not edge.

title: Reach-Avoid-Stay-Collision-Avoidance Negotiation Framework for Multi-Agent Systems via Spatiotemporal Tubes
evidence: Sec. 4: "the agent's tube is spatially 'frozen' before the start of the collision zone" - colliding spatiotemporal tubes are renegotiated so that no tube intersections remain.
method: Token-based sequential negotiation over spatiotemporal tubes: on predicted tube intersection one agent's tube is frozen before the collision zone, then re-extended; closed-form tube-tracking controller.
evaluation: Simulation only: 3 ground robots (2D, 4 obstacles, 200 s) and 6 drones (3D); no experimental baseline or ablation; only a qualitative feature table; no collision rate, timing or hardware.
contribution: A negotiation scheme assigns non-intersecting spatiotemporal tubes to agents for reach-avoid-stay with inter-agent collision avoidance, shown in two simulations without quantitative comparison.
flag: Topic fits (c) but fails minimum evaluation: no quantitative safety metric and no baseline or ablation (Table 2 is a qualitative feature comparison asserting zero collisions). Only numbers are collision-interval timestamps. Freeze acts on reference tubes during negotiation, not on executed actions, so runtime_interceptor set to no - maintainer may read the tube freeze as a halt. Termination of negotiation not proven; stalemates conceded (Sec. 7). Controller proof omitted. Abstract has no numbers. Read via summarising fetch of the PDF.

title: HALO: Fault-Tolerant Safety Architecture For High-Speed Autonomous Racing
evidence: Sec. 10.2: on a failed heartbeat the Node Health Monitor escalates from Graceful Stop to zero velocity to Long Control, to a direct brake command to the SSC Interface, to engine shutoff; Sec. 11: 'we were unable to rigorously test each module'.
method: Four ROS2 safety nodes on an Indy racecar: graceful stop latch, heartbeat node-health monitor, covariance-based localisation multiplexer, and behavioural monitor that defers the post-overtake merge until 30 m separation holds.
evaluation: Real AV-21 logs from IMS and LVMS, one illustrative scenario per fault class; no baseline, no ablation, no aggregate rates; thresholds only (500 ms timeouts, covariance 0.1225); compute unspecified.
contribution: HALO layers heartbeat, data-health and behavioural monitors over a 175 mph autonomous racecar stack, escalating from graceful stop to engine shutoff, shown on three real-track fault scenarios without aggregate safety metrics.
flag: Genuine runtime interceptor on a real vehicle but evaluation is qualitative: three single-scenario plots, no detection/false-stop/collision rate, no baseline or ablation, run counts not reported, so it fails the v1.6 minimum evaluation. Multi-agent only nominally (one opponent in the merge check; n-of-k window values not given). Operator can override throttle/brake and kill the engine from the base station in testing but no handoff study. Paper itself notes margins cause unnecessary stops. No latency measurements, only timeout thresholds.

title: LIVEPOINT: Fully Decentralized, Safe, Deadlock-Free Multi-Robot Control in Cluttered Environments with High-Dimensional Inputs
evidence: "This formulation ensures that the control input u* minimally deviates from the nominal input k(q)" (Sec. IV-B); the liveness filter "only changes the speed of the robot and not its planned trajectory" (Sec. V-B).
method: Decentralized CBF-QP safety filter with barriers synthesized directly from depth point clouds, plus a symmetry-angle deadlock detector that projects one robot's speed onto a liveness set so the other passes first.
evaluation: Python quadrotor simulator, 2 robots, doorway and intersection, 50 runs each; baselines ORCA, MPC-CBF, MPNet, single-agent Depth-CBF, no-liveness ablation; collisions 0/50 vs 50/50, success 100% vs 0%; no hardware or compute time.
contribution: Point-cloud control barrier functions with a speed-only liveness filter let two decentralized quadrotors pass doorways and intersections with zero collisions or deadlocks in simulation where five baselines fail every run.
flag: Abstract claim "35% smoother than baselines" is NOT found or derived in the body; Table I velocity-change values even show LIVEPOINT less smooth than ORCA for robot 1 in the doorway and worst for robot 1 in the intersection. Results are suspiciously binary: every baseline collides in 50/50 runs (or deadlocks 50/50), LIVEPOINT 0/50 - suggests near-deterministic scenarios, so 50 runs are not 50 independent trials. Only 2 robots, simulation only; the 0.04 s figure is the simulated control cycle, not a measured compute time. Paper is about deadlock as much as safety; primacy for (c) holds on collisions being the first reported outcome but is arguable.

title: Safe and Efficient CAV Lane Changing using Decentralised Safety Shields
evidence: Sec. III-B: the shield works 'by overriding the possibly unsafe control input' from the motion planning layer; if lateral constraints fail, 'a new steering input ... is evaluated using a feedback controller to follow the current lane instead'.
method: Decentralised Hybrid Safety Shield per vehicle: a CBF-QP minimally corrects longitudinal acceleration for dynamic time-headway, and a rule vetoes or aborts unsafe lane changes, wrapped around a MAPPO behavioural policy.
evaluation: highway-env on-ramp merge, 2-8 CAVs, 100 evaluation episodes; vs unshielded MARL-CAV; mean crash count 0 vs 6.3 (light) and 0 vs 5 (moderate); speed 28.36 vs 27.70 m/s; shield at 15 Hz, latency unmeasured.
contribution: Decentralised CBF shields wrapped around multi-agent RL lane changing remove all crashes in simulated on-ramp merging while matching or slightly exceeding the unshielded policy's average speed.
flag: Clean runtime shield with a no-shield baseline, so useful for RQ5 (speed +2.4% light, -0.78 m/s moderate - my arithmetic from Table I; contributions say 'outperforms' but moderate traffic is only 'comparable'). Weaknesses: one baseline, no ablation of longitudinal vs lateral shield, no shield intervention rate, single scenario, simulation only, pure-CAV traffic. 'Crash count' unit is not clearly defined (text says averaged over evaluation episodes; unclear if also over the 3 seeds). The shield is trained in the loop, so the comparison mixes shielded training and shielded execution. Stated time budgets (0.2 s MARL, 0.0667 s shield) are design rates, not measured latency, so I did not tick latency/jitter aware. Slack penalty value unreported, so 'guarantee' is soft.

title: Characterizing the Robustness of Black-Box LLM Planners Under Perturbed Observations with Adaptive Stress Testing
evidence: App. D.2: timesteps whose entropy exceeds a first-quartile threshold are flagged to alert engineers; Sec. 4.2: "we use MCTS to intelligently search for perturbation action trajectories".
method: Adaptive stress testing with MCTS over prompt perturbations (sensor-field removal, noise, prompt style, few-shot removal), scoring LLM driving-action diversity as a black-box uncertainty proxy; offline trees reused for runtime alerting.
evaluation: highway-env with Llama 3.2, Dolphin 3.0 and DeepSeek-R1 planners; OPD tree-search comparator on unperturbed driving; alert rates 0.57-0.88 across MCTS depth and iteration settings; 24000 generations; no latency reported.
contribution: Adaptive stress testing with MCTS over prompt perturbations exposes unsafe black-box LLM planner behaviour and yields an entropy threshold that flags unpredictable timesteps at runtime without access to model internals.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - black-box LLM driving planners. Title check: the fetched PDF carries the earlier title Adaptive Stress Testing Black-Box LLM Planners, while the abs page shows the record title and four versions through 2026-05-11, so the figures above may come from an older version - worth re-reading v4. Criterion (a) fails: the runtime flag only alerts engineers and cannot veto, halt or defer. Primary metrics are action-diversity and entropy proxies plus alert rate with no baseline for the uncertainty method itself; collision, speed and inconsistency numbers appear only in figures, so the evaluation floor is met only if alert rate counts as a detection rate and the MCTS-setting variants count as ablations. A single planner in traffic, so (c) is multi-agent only nominally; exclude-E2 or exclude-E1 is defensible.

title: PRISM: Complete Online Decentralized Multi-Agent Pathfinding with Rapid Information Sharing using Motion Constraints
evidence: Sec.5 Theorem 2: 'PRISM is complete and can resolve all solvable deadlock situations.' Collisions are handled as CBS constraints inside local-network replanning (Sec.4.3.4).
method: Online decentralized multi-agent pathfinding: agents in communication range form local networks, replan with modified CBS, and relay motion constraints via info packets with flush times.
evaluation: MAPF benchmark maps, 10-30 agents; baselines CBS and TPTS; success rate, runtime, cost, max tasks (maze: 215 vs 85 tasks; 92% vs 60% success); 10 TurtleBots on Raspberry Pi, no timing or collision data.
contribution: PRISM is a complete decentralized online pathfinding planner that shares motion constraints through info packets, solving 3.4x as many agents as CBS at minimum connectivity and up to 2.5x the tasks of TPTS in mazes.
flag: Fails primacy test for c: primary claims are completeness, deadlock resolution and scalability; collision count is never a reported metric and collision avoidance is a planner constraint. Not a runtime interceptor. Edge deployment NOT credited: Raspberry Pi robots appear only in a qualitative 10-robot demo with no latency or collision numbers. Completeness proof is a sketch under perfect communication. Text says TurtleBot2, Fig.8 caption says TurtleBot3. TPTS beats PRISM on open warehouse map (1000 vs 495 tasks). Table 3 partly garbled in extraction. Tags are loose fits (CBS is search-based, not sampling-based).

title: MC-Swarm: Minimal-Communication Multi-Agent Trajectory Planning and Deadlock Resolution for Quadrotor Swarm
evidence: Sec. V: the trajectory QP is said to ensure 'collision avoidance even with the asynchronous planning updates of neighboring agents' - safety is a constraint inside the planner, with no separate filter or monitor.
method: Decentralised quadrotor swarm planner: PIBT waypoints, safe flight corridor and modified buffered Voronoi cell constraints in a QP, with subgoal optimisation for deadlock resolution; no or minimal communication.
evaluation: Simulation, 5-20 agents, 30 trials per setting, vs DREAM, MADER, EGO-v2, GCBF+: success 100% vs 0-93%; runtime 2.0-9.6 ms on i7 laptop; 8 Crazyflies with NUCs, 2.2 ms.
contribution: A minimal-communication quadrotor swarm planner that reaches 100% success in forests and mazes where MADER, EGO-v2 and GCBF+ deadlock, at 2-10 ms per agent.
flag: Coordination and deadlock planner: collision avoidance is a constraint inside the QP and the headline metrics are success rate and flight time, so it fails strict (a) and the (c) primacy test. Collision rate is not reported separately from success. Per-agent solve time (2-10 ms, onboard NUC i7-1260P) could interest RQ1 as a timing reference but there is no explicit latency constraint, so (d) not met and edge cell not claimed. Assumes delay-free perfect position sensing. Paper inconsistency: planning step given as 0.1 s and as 0.2 s.

title: VLMLight: Safety-Critical Traffic Signal Control via Vision-Language Meta-Control and Dual-Branch Reasoning Architecture
evidence: Sec. 3.2: "Rather than issuing control actions directly, AgentModeSelector interprets the set of textual scene descriptions"; AgentCheck rejects an unvalidated LLM phase after N_check attempts and the system falls back to the RL action.
method: A VLM turns four camera views into text; an LLM meta-controller routes each decision interval to a PPO policy or to three reasoning LLM agents for safety-critical scenes, with RL fallback.
evaluation: SUMO-based image simulator on three real intersections; 9 baselines plus component and backbone ablations; emergency-vehicle wait 7.48, 2.17, 2.60 s vs best RL 22.04, 5.17, 7.81 s; 9.4-11.5 s decision latency on A100s against a 13 s phase buffer.
contribution: VLMLight routes traffic-signal decisions between a fast RL policy and a slow multi-agent LLM reasoning branch, cutting emergency-vehicle waiting time by more than half at small routine-traffic cost.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - a PPO traffic-signal policy and the LLM reasoning branch. Criterion (a) rests on the AgentCheck validator plus RL fallback, which vetoes an LLM phase at execution time; the meta-controller otherwise only routes, so a maintainer could read the whole thing as architecture rather than interception. No collision, violation, intervention or throughput metric is reported - the only safety evidence is emergency-vehicle delay - so exclude-E2 is defensible under a strict reading of the floor. Abstract claims over 60 pct reduction in both AETT and AEWT and under 1 pct routine degradation; tables give about 29 pct AETT at Songdo and about 5 pct ATT degradation at Yau Ma Tei and Massy. Sec. 4.3 quotes a 48 s to 58 s ablation as AEWT where Table 2 places those values under AETT. Latency of 9-11 s on five A100s is real-time only against a traffic phase buffer, not edge.

title: Robust and Safe Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning with Communication for Autonomous Vehicles: From Simulation to Hardware
evidence: Sec. 3.2: the CBF-QP safety shield is used to 'filter unsafe commands prior to actuation'; Fig. 2 caption: 'If no safe action exists, an emergency stop is triggered.'
method: Robust CTDE PPO agents with worst-case Q-network and V2V communication, trained under delay models, with a per-vehicle CBF-QP shield filtering actions and falling back to emergency stop.
evaluation: CARLA 50 episodes plus 1/10-scale F1TENTH fleet on Jetson Orin Nano; vs Safe-RMM, no-shield, no-comm, MARL-DR; collisions, return, completion time; shield 10 Hz, V2V latency 10-20 ms.
contribution: Delay-robust multi-agent RL with a CBF safety shield for connected vehicles: 0-2 collisions over 50 CARLA episodes versus 42 without the shield, and zero collisions on F1TENTH hardware.
flag: Number of agents and number of hardware trials not stated; completion-time units not stated. Table 2: no-shield RSR-MARL 42 and non-robust 45 collisions vs 2 (F-2) for the full method, Safe-RMM 15, MARL-DR 10. Text says F-5 keeps 'near-zero collisions' while Table 2 lists 1. CBF intervention rate 18.7% without communication vs 11.4% with. Algorithm 1 shows the CBF-QP only in the PID branch, so shield use under MPC is underspecified. No per-step compute time; MPC horizon unspecified. Delay units (F-1..F-5, TV 0-5) presumably steps - check. 50-200 ms V2X figure is cited, not tested. Criterion (d) not claimed: delay is modelled in communication, no latency budget for the safety decision.

title: Q-ARDNS-Multi: A Multi-Agent Quantum Reinforcement Learning Framework with Meta-Cognitive Adaptation for Complex 3D Environments
evidence: Obstacle hits are handled only by a -2 reward penalty (Sec. 5.1); no shield or override is described
method: Two-agent reinforcement learner using simulated 2-qubit action circuits, dual short/long-term memory, shared memory and a meta-cognitive network adapting learning rate and curiosity.
evaluation: 10x10x3 GridWorld, 2 agents, 5000 episodes; vs MADDPG and SAC; success 99.6%/99.5% vs 98.6%/99.2% and 49.7%/49.9%; steps to goal 210 vs 227 vs 912; Colab CPU, 2818.8 s total.
contribution: A quantum-inspired two-agent reinforcement learning framework for 3D grid navigation reporting higher success rates than MADDPG and SAC.
flag: Off-topic: cooperative navigation RL, no safety mechanism. A 2.1% collision rate is quoted for the method only, with no baseline collision figures. No ablations. Internal inconsistencies (MADDPG 98.6/99.2% in Table 2 vs 98.9% in Fig. 3; circuit outputs 4 actions, environment lists 6). Circuits simulated, no quantum hardware.

title: From Virtual Agents to Robot Teams: A Multi-Robot Framework Evaluation in High-Stakes Healthcare Context
evidence: Sec. V-A: "Overall, these results suggest that a detailed KB helped increase performance across most dimensions"; Issue Handling scores 0 in both conditions.
method: Stress test of a four-robot CrewAI hierarchy (manager plus navigation, information-collection and display robots) driven by GPT-4o in a simulated emergency-department onboarding task, with and without a knowledge base.
evaluation: Simulation only, no real robots and no participants; 5 runs per condition; overall success 45.29 pct baseline vs 72.94 pct with knowledge base; delegation accuracy 0.333 vs 0.733; issue handling 0 in both; cost 0.077 vs 0.154 USD per run.
contribution: Stress-testing a CrewAI robot team in a simulated emergency department exposes five persistent failure modes of multi-agent LLM frameworks and yields three design guidelines for embodied deployment.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - a GPT-4o multi-robot team - but nothing guards it. No runtime override, veto or halt, and the primary measured outcomes are task-success and delegation-accuracy scores rather than any hazard, collision or violation rate, so the (c) primacy test fails and I recommend exclude-E1. Escalation to a human supervisor exists only as prompt and knowledge-base text and is never implemented or evaluated, so (e) fails. If the maintainer instead reads a multi-robot LLM failure-mode study in a high-stakes healthcare setting as (c), the evaluation floor still fails for lack of any safety metric, which would make it exclude-E2. Only 5 runs per condition, no hardware or latency figures, and the healthcare stakes are asserted rather than measured.

title: DURA-CPS: A Multi-Role Orchestrator for Dependability Assurance in LLM-Enabled Cyber-Physical Systems
evidence: Step 7 of the orchestration loop: "Controller may halt, log details, or activate the RecoveryPlanner", and the RecoveryPlanner "overrides the Generator's decision" with emergency_brake (Sec. III.C, Fig. 3).
method: Multi-role LLM orchestrator (generator, safety monitor, security assessor, fault injector, performance oracle, recovery planner) wraps a fine-tuned Llama 3.2 11B CARLA driving planner; unsafe flags trigger an emergency-brake override.
evaluation: CARLA, six scenarios x 15 runs (90 total); no baseline and no ablation; unsafe-flag rate 38.9% average, collision rate 8.9% average; 100 ms simulated steps; no hardware or latency values.
contribution: Shows an LLM-driven cyber-physical planner can be wrapped in a multi-role assurance loop whose safety monitor and recovery planner veto unsafe driving actions at runtime in CARLA.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes, a fine-tuned Llama 3.2 11B tactical planner. Genuine runtime override, so this is my most likely overturn candidate, but it fails the protocol v1.6 floor: collision rate 8.9% and unsafe-flag rate 38.9% are reported with no baseline and no without-monitor or without-recovery ablation, and the recovery benefit is asserted only by manual inspection of near-misses. The paper lists processing time per role as a metric but no value appears in the body, and no hardware is named. Multi-agent exists only as CARLA traffic; the other roles are evaluators, several rule-based, not multiple learned acting agents, so (c) not credited.

title: Very Large-scale Multi-Robot Task Allocation in Challenging Environments via Robot Redistribution
evidence: Sec. 5: 'our research aims to find a task allocation that is likely to prevent deadlocks but does not set out to find collision-free paths directly.'
method: MRTA-RM: GVD roadmap split into components, demand-supply analysis, Hungarian-based robot redistribution with route-aware revision and flow prioritisation, then first-come task assignment inside components.
evaluation: Unity with NavMesh and RVO, three maps, 5-500 robots; vs CBS-TA, ECBS-TA, TA-CCBS, TA-CECBS, Greedy-TA, Hungarian-TA; makespan, sum of costs, success rate, compute time; AMD 5800X.
contribution: Centralised task allocation for hundreds of robots that redistributes robots across roadmap components to reduce deadlocks, cutting makespan by up to 70-92% against Hungarian and greedy allocation in simulation.
flag: Efficiency/deadlock paper: objective is makespan, no collision or violation rate is reported, success rate means reaching goals without deadlock. Sec. 4.6 admits conflict-free paths are not guaranteed. No ablations. Allocation time 0.02-0.15 s small scale, 8.99 s at 500 robots (planning time, not a safety latency). Table cells were partly garbled in extraction; figures here come from the prose.

title: Trust-MARL: Trust-Based Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning Framework for Cooperative On-Ramp Merging Control in Heterogeneous Traffic Flow
evidence: Sec. 6.2 (paraphrase): at full CAV penetration and high density the collision rate is 5.2% for Rule-Based, 4% Non-Coop MARL, about 3.2% Trust-Sensitive HVs and 2.5% for Trust-MARL.
method: Decentralised MASAC with LSTM encoder; exponentially smoothed inter-vehicle trust sets a cooperation factor blending selfish and cooperative reward; game-theoretic cooperative/non-cooperative switching at a trust threshold.
evaluation: SUMO on-ramp merge, 300-900 veh/h, 0-100% CAV penetration, 10 seeds; baselines rule-based, non-coop MARL, trust-sensitive HVs; ablation table; collision rate, travel time, jerk, recovery time; no hardware or latency.
contribution: A trust-weighted multi-agent RL policy for cooperative on-ramp merging of connected vehicles in mixed traffic, reporting lower collision rate, travel time and jerk than rule-based and non-cooperative baselines in SUMO.
flag: Coordination policy, not a safety mechanism: safety enters through reward terms only, no shield, mask or supervisor; collision rate is one of three outcomes (with travel time and jerk), so (c) primacy fails in my reading - maintainer may judge (c) borderline since collision rate vs baselines is reported. Numbers are unreliable: Table 3 labels columns as reductions (Trust-MARL 1.2/3.8/7.4%) with the full model smallest, while Sec. 6.1 reads 1.2% as a collision rate; these conflict with Sec. 6.2 (2.5% collision, 10% travel time, 46.7% jerk); bottleneck drop is said to be both postponed and 15 min earlier. Claims no explicit communication yet states 10Hz state exchange. Read via PDF-to-text summary.

title: eCAV: An Edge-Assisted Evaluation Platform for Connected Autonomous Vehicles
evidence: Sec. 4.2.1: vehicle clients 'include support for over-riding the edge node super-sensor input' based on data staleness - a platform feature, not an evaluated safety mechanism.
method: eCAV: distributed CARLA-based co-simulation platform where an edge node runs user algorithms (A*, constrained k-means) and sends waypoints to many vehicle clients, with barrier synchronisation across nodes.
evaluation: CARLA Town06 and highway on Azure VMs, up to 256 vehicles (64 with perception); vs OpenCDA, AutoCastSim; step time, 99th-percentile network overhead 45 ms, mean velocity; Tesla M60/V100 GPUs.
contribution: Simulation platform for edge-assisted connected vehicles that scales to 256 vehicles (64 with perception at under 800 ms step time), several times beyond OpenCDA.
flag: Evaluation infrastructure paper, not a safety method: no collision or violation metric ('none were observed', metric explicitly omitted). Possible (d) reading rejected: latency figures (45 ms and 35 ms p99 network overhead, 51 ms case causing missed control deadlines, 200 ms control loop) describe simulator scaling, not a safety decision under a latency bound, and 'edge' means a cloud-VM edge server. Vehicle-side staleness override and waypoint validation are described but never evaluated. Conclusion says 'at least 5x faster' while abstract says 1.5x faster with perception; accuracy claim is qualitative.

title: Safe Multi-Agent Navigation via Constrained HJB-Informed Learning
evidence: Sec. V-B: the learned policy needs 'a single forward pass at inference, with no online optimization'; Sec. IV-B: the CBF loss 'encourages the satisfaction of safety constraint (4)'; Table II reports safe-reaching rate against QP-GCBF+, DGPPO and Def-MARL.
method: HJB-GNN jointly learns a value function, a graph CBF and a distributed GNN policy, with KKT-derived graph-dependent Lagrange multipliers trading safety against goal reaching; no QP or nominal controller at runtime.
evaluation: Sim: double integrator, surface vessel, Crazyflie; train 8 agents, test to 1024; vs QP-GCBF+, DGPPO, Def-MARL; safe-reaching 99.65->89.59% (32->320 agents) vs 74.45% QP-GCBF+; 8 Crazyflies, offboard PC.
contribution: A jointly learned graph barrier certificate and GNN policy keeps safe-reaching near 90% at 320 agents after training on 8, where the QP-filter baseline GCBF+ drops to about 74%.
flag: Included on (c) as a learned safety certificate with safety rate as primary outcome; it is NOT a runtime interceptor - it explicitly removes the QP filter and nominal controller, and safety is a training loss, so (a) is not met. Theorem 1 guarantees hold only if the learned CBF satisfies its conditions, which training merely encourages (Remark 2). The 'few milliseconds on Jetson Orin Nano' statement is asserted, not measured; hardware runs used an offboard PC with OptiTrack, so I did not tick edge deployment or latency cells. Hardware result is qualitative (8 drones reach goals without collision). Several safety figures are read from prose/plots ('near 100%', 'below 85%'), only Table II values are exact. No ablation removing the KKT multiplier. Sim step 0.03 s.

title: Time-Varying Coverage Control: A Distributed Tracker-Planner MPC Framework
evidence: "we employ a partition update verification to ensure recursive feasibility" (Sec. VI-A)
method: Distributed two-layer coverage control: a slow planner optimises reference trajectories over Voronoi partitions for a time-varying density; per-agent nonlinear tracking MPC follows them within tightened partitions.
evaluation: Four 1:28 RC cars with mocap, 33 ms sampling; periodic vs nonperiodic planner, K=30 vs 60; planner solve 96.69-944.24 ms mean, tracker 0.418 ms; no safety metric.
contribution: Proposes a distributed planner-tracker MPC scheme for time-varying coverage control with recursive feasibility and convergence guarantees, demonstrated on four miniature cars.
flag: Coverage-control paper; collision avoidance is a constraint inside the MPC via tightened partitions, which the protocol says does not meet (a). The partition-update check can reject a new partition and keep the old one, but it is a feasibility condition within the planner, not an interceptor of a nominal action, so I scored runtime_interceptor no; a maintainer could argue otherwise but there is no safety metric or baseline either way. Safety is a single sentence that the minimum inter-agent distance is always ensured, with no number. No external baseline. Coverage cost values appear only in figures. Solve times are reported (planner max 2030 ms, tracker all under 10 ms) but the compute hardware was not identified in what I read. Read via a summarising fetch tool, so check the quote against the PDF.

title: Multi-Robot Cooperative Herding through Backstepping Control Barrier Functions
evidence: "we adopt the safety filter approach proposed in [46], wherein a nominal controller is first constructed" and the QP of Eq. (27) minimally modifies it under CBF constraints (Sec. 4.3).
method: Backstepping control barrier functions for herders steering evaders into a goal region; a CBF-QP safety filter adjusts each herder's nominal control to keep evaders from colliding with each other.
evaluation: MATLAB sim and Vicon-tracked Mecanum robots, 3 herders and 3 evaders, 20 Hz centralised control over MQTT; no baseline, no ablation, no collision or violation rate, single runs, no timing.
contribution: A backstepping control-barrier-function safety filter that lets robot herders drive evaders to a goal while keeping evader-evader distances positive, demonstrated qualitatively with three herders and three evaders.
flag: Genuine runtime CBF-QP filter, but evaluation is qualitative only (distances "remain strictly positive"); no quantitative safety metric, no baseline or ablation, number of runs not reported - fails v1.6 minimum evaluation. Filter covers evader-evader pairs only; herder-herder avoidance not addressed and herder-evader assumed intrinsic. Authors concede constraints may conflict in dense scenes. Computed centrally on a control station, no latency figure.

title: DREAMS: Density Functional Theory Based Research Engine for Agentic Materials Simulation
evidence: "a hierarchical, multi-agent framework for DFT simulation" (Abstract); the paper's measured outcomes are lattice-constant and adsorption-energy accuracy, not any hazard, violation or intervention.
method: Hierarchical LLM multi-agent framework (planning supervisor plus DFT and HPC ReAct worker agents on Claude 3.7 Sonnet via LangGraph) with shared canvas memory automating density functional theory workflows.
evaluation: Sol27LC lattice constants, MAPE 0.36% BCC, 0.51% FCC, 1.00% diamond, and CO on Pt(111) adsorption energies versus human expert and literature; no framework baseline or ablation; no latency or hardware.
contribution: Automates density functional theory screening with a hierarchical LLM agent team reaching expert-level accuracy on lattice-constant and adsorption-energy benchmarks, with no safety or hazard mechanism.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: no, nothing is guarded. Likely WRONG FILE for Pillar 1: scientific-automation accuracy paper with no safety monitor, hazard metric, runtime override or human gate; multi-agent means an LLM task pipeline. The only gate-like features are tool validation checks and a canvas that asks for confirmation before overwriting a key, which is not safety interception, and self-correction after seven of eight jobs failed is reliability, not hazard prevention. I read the main text (first 100k of 308k characters); the remainder is supporting information and canvas logs.

title: Manipulating LLM Web Agents with Indirect Prompt Injection Attack via HTML Accessibility Tree
evidence: "We show that adversaries can embed universal adversarial triggers in webpage HTML to hijack agent behavior" (Abstract); the measured outcome is attack success rate on an LLM web agent.
method: GCG-optimised universal adversarial triggers embedded in webpage HTML, reaching the agent prompt through the BrowserGym accessibility tree, to force a chosen action from a Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct web agent.
evaluation: Five real websites plus eleven held-out login pages, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct; lowest targeted-site universal-instruction success 0.83, unseen-page success 0.55, leaks on 7 of 8 training sites; no defense, baseline or hardware.
contribution: Demonstrates that universal adversarial triggers hidden in HTML can hijack an LLM web agent through its accessibility tree, transferring to unseen login pages at 0.55 success, with no defense tested.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: nothing is guarded; this is an attack on a learned agent, with input sanitisation and prompt hardening only recommended in the conclusion, never implemented or measured. Single agent and a single injected input, hence wrong level; the maintainer may prefer E1 because no criterion really holds, or may argue the web agent's multi-step action loop supplies a sequential aspect. Transfer to Llama-2-7b-chat and Mistral-7B failed. The targeted-website targeted-instruction attack success rates are never given numerically in the text, and the Appendix B ablations time trigger optimisation (search width 128 under three hours) rather than any safety outcome.

title: Hierarchical Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning with Control Barrier Functions for Safety-Critical Autonomous Systems
evidence: Sec. 5.2: 'we formulate the low-level policy as a Constrained Optimal Control Problem (COCP)' with CBF constraints per neighbour; Table 1: success 0.99 in bottleneck versus 0.75 for CoPo and 0.09 for IPPO.
method: Hierarchical MARL: a centrally trained high-level policy picks a skill per agent, and each skill is executed by a decentralised QP with control barrier function constraints against every sensed neighbour.
evaluation: MetaDrive five scenarios, 15-45 vehicles, 5 seeds, plus a LiDAR suite; baselines IPPO, CL, MFPO, CoPo; success 0.97-0.99 vs 0.00-0.85; ablation with LQR low level; RTX A5000; no latency.
contribution: Hierarchical multi-agent RL whose low-level skills are CBF-constrained quadratic programs reaches 0.97-0.99 success across five dense MetaDrive traffic scenarios where penalty-based MARL baselines score 0.00-0.85.
flag: Not (a): the CBF constraints are inside the low-level policy QP, there is no separate filter over a nominal action, no infeasibility handling and no safe stop; included on (c) only, and the maintainer may judge it a constrained controller (E1). Headline metric is success rate (success-weighted time and energy), not a separately reported collision rate; safety rates for the LiDAR suite are only in Figs. 7-8. Safety theorem assumes an accurate model but the paper uses an approximate bicycle model in PyBullet and is inconsistent about kinematic vs dynamic. Baselines trained 1M iterations vs 300k for the method. Table 3 ablation columns could not be mapped reliably from the extracted text. No QP solve time despite a real-time claim. Abstract 'within 5%' vs contribution '>= 95%' both consistent with Table 1.

title: ReCoDe: Reinforcement Learning-based Dynamic Constraint Design for Multi-Agent Coordination
evidence: Sec. 2: the policy's action space consists of the constraint parameters "rather than the actual control input", which is output by the solver; slack is added only to learned constraints so "safety is unaffected".
method: MARL policy outputs parameters of one learned quadratic constraint added to each agent's handcrafted QP controller; solver computes control; handcrafted safety constraints retained.
evaluation: VMAS sim, 4 scenarios, 75 starts; baselines handcrafted, RVO, pure MARL, online CBF, shielding; reward 0.55/0.40/0.73/0.25; 6 RoboMaster robots; no latency figures.
contribution: ReCoDe learns situation-dependent constraints for optimisation-based multi-robot controllers, gaining about 18% reward over the next-best hybrid baseline while keeping handcrafted safety constraints.
flag: Constraint inside an optimisation controller, not a filter over a nominal action, so (a) fails as written; primary outcome is reward, so (c) primacy fails. No collision rate reported - 'near-zero collision' rests on training collision-penalty averages (-0.0001 ReCoDe, -0.06 online CBF, -9.4 pure RL, Fig. 3c). Shielding appears only as a baseline. Real-robot result is qualitative (no trial count). Agent counts outside the corridor scenario not found. Abstract has no numbers. Read via summarising fetch of the PDF.

title: Multi-Agent Path Finding Among Dynamic Uncontrollable Agents with Statistical Safety Guarantees
evidence: Probabilistic Collision Avoidance and Corollary 1: plans avoid collisions with uncontrollable agents at confidence 1-delta; Table 3 reports closed-loop safety violations of 1/100, 3/100, 4/100 for 1, 3, 5 uncontrolled agents.
method: LSTM predicts trajectories of uncontrollable agents; conformal prediction intervals become avoided vertices inside a modified ECBS planner; rolling-horizon replanning every H steps in lifelong setting.
evaluation: Three warehouse and two game grid maps, 5-50 controlled and 1-40 dynamic agents; baselines IGNORE-, OBSTACLE-, PRED-ECBS; CP coverage 0.962-0.987; violations 0-4/100; i9-9900K, no latency figures.
contribution: Conformal prediction regions around uncontrollable agents are embedded as constraints in ECBS, giving 1-delta collision-avoidance guarantees for one-shot MAPF and at most 4/100 closed-loop violations in tests.
flag: Not a runtime interceptor: safety is a planner constraint plus periodic replanning, so (a) not met; included on (c) only. Tables 2 and 3 give violation counts for CP-Solver alone; baseline collision, throughput and runtime comparisons are in figures and described only qualitatively in the text I could read, so the baseline half of the minimum evaluation needs checking against Fig 4. Authors concede 'OBSTACLE-ECBS produces fewer collisions on average'. Guarantee holds only for one-shot setting under no distribution shift from controlled agents (Assumption 2); deadlock pauses counted as collisions. Abstract has no numbers. Dynamic agents are simulated A* walkers, not humans. Results averaged over only three random initialisations. Predictor is per-agent LSTM, (b) not credited. Tag sampling-based-planning is a loose fit for search-based MAPF.

title: BlockA2A: Towards Secure and Verifiable Agent-to-Agent Interoperability
evidence: "updates the task's ILC guard to halt execution" (Sec. 5.2, Algorithm 2, Task Halt Upon Prompt Tampering, closely paraphrased); abstract: "Byzantine agent flagging, reactive execution halting, and instant permission revocation"
method: Blockchain trust layer for LLM agent-to-agent protocols (DIDs, access-control, interaction-logic and governance contracts) plus a Defense Orchestration Engine that flags agents, halts tasks and revokes permissions at runtime.
evaluation: Prototype on Hardhat testnet and IPFS, Intel 2.60 GHz server, 10 runs; no baseline or ablation; latency: flagging 135.0 ms, halt 87.0 ms, revocation 91.8 ms; no detection rates.
contribution: Proposes a blockchain-anchored identity, access-control and audit layer for LLM agent-to-agent protocols, with an engine that halts tampered tasks and revokes agent permissions in roughly 90-135 ms on a local testnet.
flag: Fails minimum evaluation, not topic: a genuine runtime halt/revoke mechanism for multi-agent LLM systems, but no quantitative safety metric (no attack success, detection or false-positive rate) and no baseline, no-defense run or ablation; Sec. 6.1 defense effectiveness is a qualitative table. Only numbers are operation latencies (Table 2: 0.2-64.0 ms per operation; Table 3 DOE totals 135.0/87.0/91.8 ms) on a local Hardhat testnet with network latency deliberately excluded, so real-chain figures would be far worse; I did not credit latency/jitter aware for that reason. Abstract says only sub-second overhead. Table 3 components sum to 134.5 and 86.3 ms, not the stated 135.0 and 87.0. Self-described position paper under active development. Humans only receive alerts; no approval gate or takeover. Number of agents never stated. If the maintainer treats latency of a safety action as criterion (d), there is still no explicit latency constraint.

title: A Robust Cooperative Vehicle Coordination Framework for Intersection Crossing
evidence: "Obtain the control input U by Equation 20 and execute the first command" (Algorithm 1, Section III-C)
method: Intersection manager running a robust chance-constrained receding-horizon cooperative trajectory planner over vehicle position distributions, plus a Lyapunov-index context-aware scheduler allocating limited state-update sub-channels.
evaluation: MATLAB with YALMIP and MOSEK, 5-20 CAVs, 1.2 vehicles per lane per second, 200-500 runs; vs STRS, Re-STRS, SMPC, round robin, AoI; collision probability 5.0% vs 11.0%.
contribution: A robust chance-constrained cooperative intersection-crossing framework that cuts both collision probability and total passing time under measurement noise and scarce communication sub-channels.
flag: The closest call in the batch: collision probability is reported first in every table against three coordination baselines, so a maintainer could read the primacy test as met. I excluded it because safety is enforced by chance constraints inside the planner, which the prompt says does not meet (a), and nothing can override or halt the executed command (Algorithm 1 step 11), leaving it coordination-only under protocol v1.2. No measured solve time or latency appears anywhere despite the multi-access edge-computing-server framing; only asymptotic complexity is given, and the authors' own future work admits computational cost. The scheduler's "around 25%" collision-probability reduction is a Figure 7a claim with no tabulated value. The headline 54.5% safety advantage simply restates Table III (0.05 vs 0.110).

title: Integrating Symbolic RL Planning into a BDI-based Autonomous UAV Framework: System Integration and SIL Validation
evidence: Sec. 3: "soft integration in which symbolic planning complements BDI decision-making only when necessary"
method: BDI multi-module UAV autonomy framework (AMAD) whose plans call a symbolic-RL (PDDL plus RL) Dynamic Planner over ZeroMQ request-response; no monitor, veto or fallback described.
evaluation: SIL simulation, one target-acquisition scenario (3 km x 3 km search); baseline coverage path plan; ~75% travel-distance reduction in one highlighted case; run count, hardware and latency not reported.
contribution: Integrates a symbolic RL planner into a BDI UAV mission framework and reports about 75% shorter travel distance than a coverage-path baseline in software-in-the-loop simulation.
flag: Mission-planning integration paper, no safety mechanism or safety metric. Single UAV; 'multi-agent' refers only to software modules of the architecture. The 75% figure comes from one highlighted case (Fig. 5), no per-run values or run count; abstract calls it mission efficiency but it is distance reduction. Threat penalty exists only in RL training reward.

title: MATRIX: Multi-Agent simulaTion fRamework for safe Interactions and conteXtual clinical conversational evaluation
evidence: Experiment 3: five clinician-agent LLMs are run on 14 hazard scenarios across 10 use cases, 2100 dialogues, and scored pass/fail on hazard handling by BehvJudge (Fig. 1: 'outputs a binary pass/fail assessment, along with reasoning for verdict').
method: Offline simulation framework: an LLM patient simulator (PatBot) converses with a clinical LLM agent and an LLM judge (BehvJudge) grades the finished transcript against a structured hazard taxonomy.
evaluation: 240 HazMAT transcripts, 10 clinicians as baseline: judge F1 0.96 vs clinician 0.94, sensitivity 0.999; 2100 dialogues, hazard-handling accuracy 20-69% across five LLMs; no hardware or latency.
contribution: A simulation benchmark for clinical dialogue agents in which an LLM judge matches clinicians at hazard detection (F1 0.96 vs 0.94) and five agents handle 20-69% of hazard scenarios safely.
flag: Borderline. Meets (c) only through the 'safety evaluation of LLM agents' clause; it is post-hoc grading of completed transcripts with no interception, and multi-agent only nominally (one agent under test plus a simulated patient and a judge), so E4 is defensible. Emergency escalation exists only as a prompt instruction, not a tested handoff, so no human-handoff cell. Paper is internally inconsistent: Llama3.3-70B judge sensitivity 0.80 in Table 1 vs 0.79 in text; Gemini F1 CI upper bound 0.977 in body vs 0.980 in Appendix G. Decision-time plot (App. J) gives no numbers.

title: Discrete-Guided Diffusion for Scalable and Safe Multi-Robot Motion Planning
evidence: Sec 4.4: "If any constraint in (1a)-(1b) is violated, we run a constraints-aware diffusion model to obtain the feasible solution" - repair happens inside offline trajectory generation, not at execution.
method: Discrete-Guided Diffusion: convex decomposition, MAPF spatiotemporal assignment, MAPF-guided diffusion sampling with projection onto convex regions, then augmented-Lagrangian constraint-aware repair when violations are detected.
evaluation: Sim only: Basic, Dense, Room, Shelf maps, 3-18 robots, 25 instances each, 900 s limit; baselines MPD, MMD, SMD; success rate, runtime, path length, acceleration; RTX A6000.
contribution: A multi-robot motion planner that steers diffusion sampling with a discrete MAPF plan and repairs constraint violations, keeping success rates high at 18 robots where prior diffusion planners fail.
flag: Borderline (c): title claims safety but the measured outcome is planning success rate and runtime, not a collision or violation rate, and all constraint handling is inside an offline planner, so I read it as a planner (E1); maintainer may disagree. Figures: DGD 100%/12.2 s at Basic 6, 96%/65.7 s Basic 18, 76%/47.8 s Dense 18, 100%/219.0 s Room 18, 84%/324.8 s Shelf 18; MPD and MMD 0% on Room and Shelf 18; SMD 254.3 s at Basic 6 and N/A at 18. Text says 76% for Shelf 18 but the table shows 84%. The 100-robot scalability claim has no numeric success rate or runtime in the text I read. Theorem 2 bounds expected violation only. Tag diffusion-models is new. No hardware experiments, no per-step latency.

title: SAFE--MA--RRT: Multi-Agent Motion Planning with Data-Driven Safety Certificates
evidence: "abort (safety violated)" (Algorithm 2, step 8); candidates with infeasible SDP are rejected: "If feas = false, reject and resample" (Sec. IV.A, step 4)
method: Multi-agent RRT whose edges carry data-driven affine feedback controllers and invariant ellipsoids certified by SDP from input-state data; space-time reservation table resolves inter-agent conflicts at planning time.
evaluation: Noise-free Clohessy-Wiltshire spacecraft simulation, 2 agents, 7 debris squares, one run; baseline data-driven LQR on same path; violations 0% vs 7/45 and 3/45 layers; no hardware or timing.
contribution: Builds multi-agent RRT plans whose every edge has a data-driven invariant-ellipsoid safety certificate, giving zero violations where an LQR tracker on the same path violates safety in two-agent spacecraft simulation.
flag: Weak include, E2 is defensible: the whole evaluation is ONE noise-free run per scenario with two agents, no seeds or statistics, and violation is not defined. Baseline is a single LQR variant on the same path; no ablation and no comparison with RRT, CBS or velocity obstacles. Safety is certified offline at planning time; the only execution-time action is an abort check in Algorithms 2 and 4 with no recovery, so I set runtime_interceptor no and did not credit (a) - a maintainer could argue the abort is a halt monitor. Provably safe claim holds only without noise; probabilistic safety is future work. Synchronous lockstep agents assumed, no delay model. No solver, planning time or hardware reported. Mean motion printed as 1.1e-1 s^-1 looks like a typo.

title: Dual-Stage Safe Herding Framework for Adversarial Attacker in Dynamic Environment
evidence: safety is internal to the controller: "a saturation function, which makes sure that" the control stays within its bound (Sec. IV-A); no filter, shield or override layer is described
method: Two-stage herding: defenders use a barrier-based pursuit-evasion game judgment to capture an attacker, then escort it to a safe area in a formation with potential-field obstacle avoidance.
evaluation: Numerical simulation only, 3 defenders and 1 attacker, 0.05 s control period, AMD R5-4500H PC. No baseline run, no ablation, no collision, success or timing metric.
contribution: Proposes a dual-stage capture-then-escort herding framework that steers an adversarial attacker away from a protected area around dynamic obstacles using game-theoretic judgment and potential fields.
flag: Herding/pursuit-evasion coordination; 'safe' in the title refers to guiding the attacker to a safe area, not a safety mechanism over an acting system. 'Barrier' is a differential-game barrier, not a control barrier function. Would also fail E2: no quantitative outcome, comparison with fixed-formation herding is qualitative only, 'computationally lightweight' is asserted without measurement. Figs 6-8 not readable as text; Table I speed ratio garbled in extraction (read as 0.65).

title: Distributed Event-Triggered Distance-Based Formation Control for Multi-Agent Systems
evidence: Sec IV-B: the distributed CBF quadratic program "deviates from the nominal controller ... only when collision avoidance constraints become active".
method: Event-triggered distance-based formation controller, updating only when measurement error exceeds a state-dependent threshold, wrapped by a distributed CBF-QP that overrides the held nominal input for pairwise collision avoidance.
evaluation: Robotarium, 6 robots, and a 200-agent 3D simulation; periodic-triggered baselines (Ts 0.033-1 s), topology and alpha/sigma sweeps; trigger counts, filter-activation counts, formation error. No timing.
contribution: An event-triggered distance-based formation controller with a distributed barrier-function filter that reaches formation error comparable to fast periodic control while counting how often the collision filter must intervene.
flag: Weak include, maintainer should consider E1: the paper is about event-triggered formation control and the CBF filter is a component, not the primary claim. The only safety-related metric is tau2, the count of collision-avoidance filter activations (complete graph: ET 4 vs periodic 20 and 7; cycle: 0 vs 20 and 0; 200 agents: 2); no collision count or minimum distance is reported, so the v1.6 minimum is met only if an intervention count qualifies. The stated roughly 80% reduction in control updates is not supported by Table I as I read it (ET 313 and 380 triggers vs 152 periodic); in the 200-agent test ET 356 vs 500 at Ts 0.05 s. Zeno exclusion is not proven. QP called real-time with no solve time. Table values came through a text extraction; verify against the PDF.

title: SMART: Scalable Multi-Agent Reasoning and Trajectory Planning in Dense Environments
evidence: "The process continues until all conflicts are eliminated or no feasible plan exists" (Sec. 3.2, priority-based search) - conflicts are resolved inside the planner before execution
method: Hierarchical multi-vehicle trajectory planner: priority-based search with spatio-temporal hybrid A* front end and selective replanning, then distributed SQP back-end optimisation within trust regions.
evaluation: Custom C++ simulation, 5-100 Ackermann vehicles, 60 instances per setting; baselines SCC, PP, FOTP, CL-CBS; success 90-100% up to 25 vehicles, solve time 0.03-0.90 s; Xeon CPU; real vehicles.
contribution: Scales cooperative multi-vehicle trajectory planning to dense maps by combining priority-based hybrid A* search with distributed sequential quadratic programming, keeping high planning success within about one second for 25 vehicles.
flag: Clear E1 under protocol v1.2: an offline coordination planner measured on planning success rate, solve time and task completion time; no collision, violation or intervention rate, no execution-time monitor or emergency stop, no ablation of its own components. Abstract claim of over 90% success within 1 s up to 25 vehicles is only exactly 90.00% (0.90 s) on 50 m random maps. Test-case count is inconsistent: 2100 stated vs about 7200 implied by the stated design. Conclusion claims one to two orders of magnitude real-world speed-up; Sec. 4.2.3 gives 0.014 vs 0.332 s and 0.623 vs 10.075 s. SMART task completion times are longer than baselines. FOTP ran in Matlab on a different CPU with unspecified normalisation. CPU printed as Xeon Gold 622R (probably 6226R). 4G/V2X mentioned but no delay model; real-world trial counts not stated.

title: Hierarchical Reinforcement Learning with Low-Level MPC for Multi-Agent Control
evidence: Sec IV: "the RL provides the reference input for an MPC execution layer" - the RL output is a tracking target, not a proposed action that is filtered; only the Shielding MPC baseline (Sec VI) "only intervenes upon constraint violations".
method: MAPPO high-level policy picks a target inside a region of interest; decentralized MPC (horizon 5, IPOPT) tracks it with slack-penalized separation and obstacle constraints.
evaluation: Simulated predator-prey, 2 predators/3 prey, 3 layouts, 1000 episodes; baselines end-to-end MARL and shielding MPC; capture rate, capture time, collisions; Ryzen 9 9950X/RTX 5080, no solve times.
contribution: ROI-guided hierarchical RL with a low-level MPC matches a shielding-MPC baseline on collisions (6 per 1000 episodes) while roughly halving capture time in a two-predator pursuit task.
flag: Proposed method is constraint-inside-planner, which the protocol says does not meet (a); primary claim is sample efficiency and capture performance, so (c) primacy fails. BUT the paper contains a head-to-head against a genuine runtime shield (Layout 3 collisions per 1000 episodes: ROI 6, shielding MPC 6, end-to-end 986; capture rate 99.4/96.57/0.8%; capture time 75.25 vs 144.7 steps; steps to 80% reward 2.288M/4.039M/7.125M) - maintainer may want it as RQ5 comparator evidence and include under (a) via the baseline. Only 2 learning agents; dt=1 s sim step, no MPC solve time reported. Other values: Layout 1 capture 100/98.89/98.76%, time 65.02/98.45/96.21; Layout 2 capture 99.98/81.41/93.13%, time 75.18/194.7/171.8; randomized ROI radius: 78.61 steps, 99.5%, 5 collisions. One full-text fetch pass.

title: MAD-PINN: A Decentralized Physics-Informed Machine Learning Framework for Safe and Optimal Multi-Agent Control
evidence: Sec IV: safety rate is "The fraction of agents that remain collision-free for the entire horizon, quantifying per-agent safety."; Sec I: "integrates performance optimization with strict safety guarantees"
method: Decentralized physics-informed network learns an epigraph value function for state-constrained optimal control on a 3-agent system; HJ-reachability pairwise values select neighbours; receding-horizon policy via binary search.
evaluation: Simulated double-integrator drone navigation, 3-256 agents, 100 initial conditions x 5 seeds; baselines DEF-MARL, SafeMARL (CBVF filter), MPPI; neighbour-selection ablation; safety rate, safe scenarios, cost; no hardware or latency.
contribution: MAD-PINN learns a decentralized safe-optimal value function on three agents and scales to 256, keeping 98.3% of agents collision-free at 16 agents versus 44-51% for DEF-MARL and MPPI.
flag: Meets (c) only: safety is intrinsic to the learned value function and policy, there is no filter over a nominal action, so not (a). Table I safety rate/safe scenarios at 3, 8, 12, 16 agents: ours 100/100, 99.5/98, 99.3/96, 98.3/86; SafeMARL 100/100, 99.8/99, 99/96, 97.5/90; DEF-MARL(8) 100/100, 95.4/82, 75.2/37, 50.9/13; MPPI 98/97, 89.5/72, 72.9/35, 48.8/9. Note the SafeMARL safety-filter baseline is statistically level and beats it on safe scenarios at 16 agents (90 vs 86), so the advantage over an existing safeguard is in cost, which is shown only in Fig. 2 without numbers.
