Scale-up: 64/128/256 agents 100, 98.75, 96.25% safety rate over only 20 initial conditions. Ablation at 12 agents: value-based 99.33%, nearest 83%, random 33%. "Strict safety guarantees" is claimed but approximation error is left to future work. Simulation only; no compute, timing or hardware reported despite the reduced-computational-burden claim. Abstract has no numbers.

title: Dive into the Agent Matrix: A Realistic Evaluation of Self-Replication Risk in LLM Agents
evidence: "over 50% of LLM agents display a pronounced tendency toward uncontrolled self-replication under operational pressures" (Abstract); overuse rate and aggregate overuse count are the primary measured outcomes (Sec. 3.2).
method: Scenario-driven risk evaluation of LLM agents given real kubectl control of a Kubernetes cluster, scoring four replication milestones plus overuse rate, aggregate overuse count and a composite risk score.
evaluation: 21 models, 10 trials per setting, two settings (load balancing, termination threat) and resource-ban plus shutdown-threat ablations; overuse rate 0-100%, risk score 0.00-1.00; 4x A800 GPUs; no measured latency.
contribution: Measures uncontrolled self-replication in 21 LLM agents with real cluster control, finding most over-provision replicas under pressure and that shutdown threats re-escalate risk after a resource ban.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes, the agents are LLM-driven, but nothing guards them; no runtime monitor, kill switch or human approval is evaluated (human-in-the-loop approval is Appendix D future work), so (a) and (e) fail and this enters only as hazard-evaluation evidence. (c) is borderline: proliferation stays within one cluster and cross-cluster migration is explicitly out of scope, so multi-agent means replicas of one agent rather than interacting agents. Tables 4 and 6 disagree on the Qwen3-32B rows (overuse rate 40 versus 70, aggregate count 27 versus 42), and the text's claim that the Claude series ceased all replication is not supported for Claude-sonnet-4 in Table 3. The 50 ms figure is a simulated task service level, not a safety-decision deadline, so (d) not credited; the PDF states no year.

title: Connectivity Maintenance and Recovery for Multi-Robot Motion Planning
evidence: "The safety CBF constraint (13d) is a hard constraint, i.e., it has no slack variable." (Sec. VI-C); headline metric is percentage connected (Table II)
method: MPC-CLF-CBF planner: per-robot QP over Bezier trajectories with hard collision CBF constraints plus slack-relaxed connectivity and high-order CLF recovery constraints with a gating weight.
evaluation: C++/CPLEX simulation, 4-12 robots, 0-20% obstacle density, 10 configurations; vs CLF-CBF and MPC-CBF; connected 95.8-100% vs 48.9-61.3%; success 86.0-100%; solve 62.47-74.38 ms; 8 Crazyflies qualitative.
contribution: A multi-robot motion planner combining model-predictive control with barrier and Lyapunov constraints to keep a team's communication graph connected, and to restore it when initially disconnected.
flag: Coordination planner: the primary claim and measured outcome are connectivity and makespan; collision avoidance is one hard constraint inside the planner and collisions are reported as none for every method, so it fails both the strict-runtime reading of (a) and the primacy test of (c). Abstract range 95.8-100% connected vs 48.9-61.3% matches Table II at 20% density. Solve times of 62-74 ms are means from Table I with no deadline stated and exceed any 15 ms budget; the stated replanning period is 0.1 s. Hardware trial reports no numbers. Global state access assumed and computation was centralised for the Crazyflie demo. I did not transcribe the 0% and 10% density rows of Table II in full.

title: Trajectory-Optimized Density Control with Flow Matching
evidence: Sec 3.4: 'The algorithm performs gradient descent on forward and backward trajectories alternately' - a training procedure; no runtime check is described and results are figures only.
method: Flow matching co-trained with a control policy via forward-backward SDEs from the Schrodinger bridge with a mean-field interaction term, for population-level density control around obstacles.
evaluation: Two 2D crowd-navigation toy problems (GMM transport with three obstacles; V-neck corridor); visual comparison with deep generalized Schrodinger bridge only; no tables, metrics, hardware or timing.
contribution: A flow-matching formulation of mean-field Schrodinger-bridge density control that co-evolves flow and policy, shown qualitatively on two 2D crowd-navigation examples.
flag: No quantitative result anywhere in the body (no collision rate, transport cost or runtime); single baseline compared only by figure; no ablation. Abstract claim of 'computational efficiency comparable to standard flow matching' has no supporting number or experiment in the body. Also arguably E1: population-level density control, obstacle avoidance enters a training cost, agents not individually tracked. Figures could not be read.

title: HyPlan: Hybrid Learning-Assisted Planning Under Uncertainty for Safe Autonomous Driving
evidence: Sec III-C: confidence-based vertical pruning "terminates the whole planning trial, selects this action after the backup process to the root" - early termination of search inside the planner, not a veto on a proposed action.
method: Hybrid planner for one ego car: Auto-Bots exo-agent prediction, hybrid A* path, IS-DESPOT* POMDP acceleration choice guided by a calibrated-confidence learned value bound with vertical pruning.
evaluation: CARLA-CTS2 pedestrian-crossing sim (about 23000 scenes, 9 scenarios); baselines NavPPO, NavA2C, IS-DESPOTp, HyLEAP, LEADER, HyLEAR; crash 12.36%, near-miss 8.04%, execution 161.17 ms on NVIDIA DGX-2.
contribution: HyPlan combines multi-agent trajectory prediction, hybrid A* and a confidence-pruned online POMDP planner, giving the lowest crash and near-miss rates among six baselines on CARLA-CTS2 at 161 ms per decision.
flag: Single ego vehicle with predicted pedestrians; safety lives inside the planner search (not (a)); not multi-agent hazard detection (c). Could be argued for (d) because execution time is reported (161.17 ms; planning 149.94 ms of which NN 116.52 ms) but no explicit latency constraint or deadline is stated and hardware is a DGX-2 server, so (d) not credited; E4 is an alternative code. Table I: crash/near-miss/TTG/exec for IS-DESPOTp 18.43/18.94/16.91 s/251.29 ms, NavA2C 13.50/24.02/13.74/104.95, NavPPO 14.64/10.24/12.74/32.59, HyLEAR 13.76/14.15/15.21/41.38, HyLEAP 13.29/13.39/16.46/225.76, LEADER 12.64/16.67/16.72/267.43, HyPlan 12.36/8.04/19.97/161.17 (HyPlan slowest to goal). Text claim of being 3-4x slower than learners does not match NavA2C (about 1.5x); "up to 40 percent" faster is about 42% vs LEADER, 31% vs HyLEAP. Ablations are prose only, no numbers; SI90 safety index poorly defined. One full-text fetch pass.

title: Beyond ADE and FDE: A Comprehensive Evaluation Framework for Safety-Critical Prediction in Multi-Agent Autonomous Driving Scenarios
evidence: "We propose a three-layer safety evaluation framework that tests prediction models" (Sec. 1); protocol is "predicting 6-timestep (3s) future trajectories from 4-timestep (2s) observations with K=20 trajectory samples" (Sec. 4).
method: Offline three-layer evaluation of trajectory predictors stratified by semantic map availability, agent density and road geometry, with a map-impact error (MIE) metric.
evaluation: nuScenes, 9,041 samples; AgentFormer only; with vs without map; ADE 1.8558 vs 1.9754 m, FDE 3.8892 vs 4.2051 m; no collision rate, no simulator, no hardware or latency.
contribution: An offline stratified evaluation protocol for trajectory predictors showing AgentFormer's ADE/FDE on nuScenes degrades without semantic maps and on curved roads (ADE 2.26 vs 1.82 m with map).
flag: Evaluation protocol for an existing predictor, not a safety mechanism, world model contribution or multi-agent hazard detector; no collision or violation rate is reported (collisions only qualitative, Fig. 5) and only one model is tested with no competing predictor, so E2 is an equally defensible code. Title says safety-critical and multi-agent but the outcome is ADE/FDE. Doubts: MIE values in Table 1 (0.0807, 0.1622) do not appear to reproduce from the printed formula; MIE described in metres though normalised; certification threshold never defined.

title: Spatiotemporal Tubes based Control of Unknown Multi-Agent Systems for Temporal Reach-Avoid-Stay Tasks
evidence: Remark 4.5: "the closed-form time-dependent control law (12) is decentralized and approximation-free"; collision avoidance comes from offline tube-separation constraints (Eq. 4, 8e).
method: Spatiotemporal tubes synthesised offline by a sampled optimisation program with Lipschitz-based guarantee; closed-form decentralised feedback keeps each unknown-dynamics agent in its tube for temporal reach-avoid-stay tasks.
evaluation: Simulation only: 4 omnidirectional robots, 4 drones; no quantitative baselines (qualitative Table 6 comparison only); eta*=-0.05, L=7.817, tube synthesis 208 s on Intel i7-7700; no loop latency.
contribution: Synthesises time-varying tubes offline and a closed-form decentralised controller that provably keeps unknown-dynamics agents apart and on schedule for reach-avoid-stay tasks, shown on two four-agent simulations.
flag: Safety-by-construction control law, not a runtime interceptor; no shield/veto. Inter-agent collision avoidance is a primary formal claim so (c) is arguable, but there is no collision/violation rate and no quantitative baseline or ablation, hence E2 (E1 also defensible). Drone case reports no eta, Lipschitz constants or solve time; disturbance bounds not given; number of SOP samples not reported; section titled Euler-Lagrange but shown dynamics look kinematic. Figures unreadable in text extraction; Table 5 header garbled.

title: CoRL-MPPI: Enhancing MPPI With Learnable Behaviours For Efficient And Provably-Safe Multi-Robot Collision Avoidance
evidence: "by solving a convex optimization problem that maximizes the probability of satisfying predefined safety constraints" (Sec. IV.A); "The resulting distribution guarantees that sampled controls satisfy all constraints with a prescribed probability." (Sec. IV.A)
method: Decentralized MPPI whose sampling distribution is biased by an IPPO-trained cooperative policy; ORCA-style linear chance constraints reshape the sampling distribution over the first three horizon steps inside the planner.
evaluation: Simulation, up to 96 differential-drive or car-like robots; vs ORCA-DD, B-UAVC, RL-RVO, D4ORM, MPPI-ORCA; collisions 0% vs up to 95%; Gazebo ten TurtleBot3 above 10 Hz; no hardware stated.
contribution: Fuses a learned cooperative policy into the sampling distribution of chance-constrained MPPI for decentralized multi-robot collision avoidance, reaching 100% success and 0% collisions for differential-drive robots across three scenarios.
flag: Borderline on two counts. (1) Not a runtime interceptor: safety is a chance constraint on the sampling distribution inside the planner, with no separate filter on the executed action, so (a) is not met and inclusion rests on (c) alone. (2) Primacy test is arguable: collision percentage is tabulated against five baselines and ablations (Table III/IV), but much of the paper sells efficiency (delay 1138 vs 2820 for MPPI-ORCA on Circle; units not stated) - a strict reader could call this E1. The provably-safe claim is probabilistic and its proof was not in the text I could read. Car-like results are weaker: Circle 94% success with 3% collisions, worse on collisions than D4ORM (1%). Standalone RL policy collides 53-92%, so the MPPI layer does the safety work. Circle-Layered text says only 4% delay increase with fewer samples, Table IV gives +4.7%. No compute time in ms and no hardware stated; real time claim is control updates above 10 Hz in Gazebo, no physical robots. Fig. 5 values and Table I were not extractable.

title: Who Moved My Distribution? Conformal Prediction for Interactive Multi-Agent Systems
evidence: Sec. 3.1/4.2: conformal thresholds enter the MPC collision constraint as tightening terms (Eq. 5c); Table 1 reports collision 43.00% without CP vs 0.50% for ICP.
method: Iterative conformal prediction: prediction regions for other agents are recalibrated from closed-loop rollouts, smoothed by low-pass update, and used to tighten MPC collision constraints; ISCP also retrains the LSTM predictor.
evaluation: Bicycle-model simulation, 2 and 3 agents, 200 test trajectories; baselines no-CP and single-shot CP; collision %, misdetection %, success %, navigation time, deviation; CasADi/Ipopt; no hardware or compute time.
contribution: Recalibrating conformal prediction regions against the distribution shift an ego planner induces in reactive agents holds collisions at 0-1.5% while raising success to 97%, against 88.5-90.5% for single-shot conformal MPC.
flag: Mechanism is a constraint inside the planner, so (a) is NOT met and runtime_interceptor is no; inclusion rests on (c) with only 2-3 agents in a toy circle scenario. Abstract claims success improvement 'up to 9.6%': I cannot find it in the tables (largest gaps 8.5 points 3-agent, 6.5 points 2-agent vs BCP). Single-shot BCP has lower collision in the 2-agent case (0.00 vs 0.50/1.50); gain is success rate, not safety. ICP 2-agent misdetection 12.35% vs target epsilon 0.15, 3-agent 11.03% vs 0.10 (above target). Convergence theorem assumes unmeasured Lipschitz constants. Calibration is offline, iterated over rollouts. Some appendix figures unreadable.

title: Hierarchical Federated Graph Attention Networks for Scalable and Resilient UAV Collision Avoidance
evidence: Sec. III-C: when local risk exceeds the critical threshold 'the system is alerted with an instant reflexive maneuver to prevent an upcoming collision'; Sec. IV-B: collision rate at most 6% under Byzantine attack versus over 40% for vanilla FedAvg.
method: Three-tier UAV swarm stack: local temporal graph attention reflex under 10 ms, regional sparse attention with asynchronous Byzantine-robust federated learning, global hashgraph-style consensus with adaptive differential privacy.
evaluation: AirSim, 10-500 UAVs, compute capped to Jetson Xavier NX; baselines centralised DRL, FedAvg, monolithic FGAT; collision <2% at 500 UAVs, 95th-percentile latency <40 ms, mission success 89.1% under attack.
contribution: A hierarchical federated graph-attention architecture for UAV swarms pairs a sub-10 ms local collision reflex with Byzantine-robust regional learning, reporting under 2% collisions at 500 simulated UAVs and under 40 ms tail latency.
flag: Weak evidence despite a close topical fit to RQ1. Layer latencies (0-10, 10-30, 30-50 ms) are stated as design budgets; the only measured-sounding figure is 95th percentile <40 ms. Jetson Xavier NX is an emulated constraint in simulation, no hardware-in-the-loop (listed as future work), so the edge deployment cell is generous. Comparative numbers live in Figs. 2-4 and are not in the text; no trial counts, variance or tests. The reflexive maneuver is never defined, so runtime_interceptor=yes rests on Algorithm 2 early return only; (a) not credited. Inconsistencies: TrimmedMean described as 20 percentile per side but Eq. 6 trims f=floor(n/3); accuracy gain 'up to 15%' in Sec. I vs 12-18% in Sec. IV-C; consensus and ZKP unspecified; some citations do not support their claims. Abstract latency sentence is garbled. No component ablation.

title: Symmetry-Breaking in Multi-Agent Navigation: Winding Number-Aware MPC with a Learned Topological Strategy
evidence: "the Controller itself follows [8], modified only to incorporate the learned targets" (Sec. 4.2)
method: WNumMPC: a PPO-trained planner outputs target pairwise winding numbers and weights every 5 steps; a short-horizon MPC tracks them through an added cost term to break symmetry.
evaluation: Holonomic and differential-drive simulation plus 7 real tabletop robots, 400 episodes; ORCA, CADRL, vanilla MPC, T-MPC; success, timeout, extra time; real-world McNemar p=5e-7 vs vanilla MPC; no latency reported.
contribution: Learns a topological passing strategy, expressed as target winding numbers, that guides a decentralized MPC and improves navigation success in dense symmetric crossings, including zero-shot on seven real robots.
flag: Navigation/coordination planner about symmetry breaking and deadlock; collision avoidance is a soft cost inside the MPC (Eq. 1-2), not a runtime filter, and nothing can veto, halt or defer. Success rate folds collisions and timeouts together and no separate collision rate is given in the text; exact success/timeout values exist only as bar charts (Figs. 3-4), the text gives only sim-to-real drops (WNumMPC 8 percent crossing, 1 percent random; vanilla MPC 21 and 6). ORCA and CADRL were dropped from the real-robot tests. Statistics compare only instances where both methods succeeded. No compute or latency figures. Planner retrained per agent count. Read via a summarising fetch tool, so check the quote against the PDF.

title: Multi-Agent gatekeeper: Safe Flight Planning and Formation Control for Urban Air Mobility
evidence: "Commit to the candidate trajectory if valid (Def. 11), otherwise, continue the previous committed trajectory." (Sec. IV.A, Algorithm 1)
method: Multi-agent gatekeeper: each follower validates a candidate (nominal formation trajectory plus backup onto leader path) against others' committed trajectories; invalid candidates are rejected and the prior committed trajectory continues.
evaluation: Julia sim, 3D Dubins leader plus 2 followers, 25 obstacles, 100 random scenarios; vs CBF-QP and NMPC: success 100% vs 22% vs 68%; formation error 6.32/7.48/4.32; 3 Crazyflies, 5 runs.
contribution: A distributed gatekeeper that only commits follower trajectories verified safe with a backup, reaching 100% collision-free success in 100 simulated formation flights against 22% for CBF-QP and 68% for NMPC.
flag: Check is at planning iterations against committed trajectories, not a per-timestep filter. No computation time or latency reported (sim on MacBook Air M2). Hardware trajectories were precomputed offline, so onboard runtime gating was not tested. Assumes delay-free, informationally centralised communication; authors call results a proof of concept. Safety metric is success rate only (collisions implied as 100 minus success); formation error is worse than NMPC; units not stated. No ablation. Only 3 agents.

title: Deadlock-Free Hybrid RL-MAPF Framework for Zero-Shot Multi-Robot Navigation
evidence: Sec. 4.4: "Upon a deadlock trigger, a set of nearby agents enters a locally confined coordination phase."
method: Fixed decentralized RL navigator plus a deadlock detector (non-progress, waypoint-stuck, core-pair triggers) that hands implicated agents to a local Push-and-Rotate MAPF on a cropped subgrid; RL tracks resulting waypoints.
evaluation: 2D simulation, doorway and corridor maps, 4/6/8 agents, 100 episodes each; RL-only baseline. Success 0-47.95% RL-only vs 95.45-100% hybrid. i9-13900KF and RTX 4080; no latency reported.
contribution: A hybrid navigator that monitors a decentralized RL policy for deadlock and escalates only the implicated robots to a local MAPF solve, raising success from 0-48% to 95-100% in simulated bottlenecks.
flag: Subject is deadlock/liveness and task completion, not a safety property; only metric is success rate (success requires no collision, but collisions are never reported separately). Abstract says 'markedly reducing deadlocks and collisions' - no collision or deadlock numbers in the body. Abstract claim about heterogeneous robots with hierarchical task planning has no experiment in the body. Table 1 gives 15.63%, 47.95%, 98.44%, 95.45%, 8.82% although N=100 episodes is stated - not possible as counts out of 100, unexplained. The detector is a runtime monitor that switches mode and replaces waypoints but does not veto actions; if the maintainer counts liveness monitors under (a), this becomes borderline include (it has a baseline but no safety metric, so E2 would then apply). No MAPF runtime measured.

title: Fault-Tolerant MARL for CAVs under Observation Perturbations for Highway On-Ramp Merging
evidence: "achieving near-fault-free levels of safety and efficiency under various observation fault patterns" (Abstract); Table VI reports fault detection over 69,456 judgments (Section V-E)
method: OFT-MARL: MADDPG vehicle agents co-trained against an adversarial observation-fault injection agent, with a GRU temporal network that outputs fault probabilities and reconstructed observations fed into the policy input.
evaluation: highway-env on-ramp merging, 4 CAVs, 6 seeds; vs vanilla MADDPG, no-GRU ablation; collision 12.5% vs 22.9% (fault-free 11.3%); fault detection accuracy 99.3%, recall 95.8%; no hardware or latency.
contribution: Trains merging vehicles against an adversarial observation-fault injector and adds a recurrent fault detector and observation reconstructor, roughly halving collision rate under faults relative to plain MADDPG in simulation.
flag: Borderline. Not a runtime interceptor: the fault probability and reconstructed observation only augment the policy input, nothing can veto or override the acceleration, so (a) is not met. I credited (c) because collision rate under observation faults is a headline outcome with a baseline and an ablation and a learned detector is evaluated; but it is robust-MARL training, reward is reported first, and a maintainer could reasonably call this E1. Only 4 vehicles. Collision rates stay high (12.5% under faults, 11.3% for the fault-free reference in Table IV, yet 2.4% fault-free in Table V - the tables use different training/test pairings, check before quoting). In Table III OFT-MARL collision rises under adversarial vs random faults (13.3% vs 12.9%) and the no-GRU ablation is lower (10.6%). Abstract has no numbers. Body cites Fig. 4(b) as Table 4 (b). Hyperparameters and reward coefficients are not reported.

title: Beyond Single-Agent Safety: A Taxonomy of Risks in LLM-to-LLM Interactions
evidence: "This paper represents the first attempt to formalize this framework conceptually" (Sec. 3), and the proposed metrics' validation "will follow" in future work; no experiment, system or formal result is reported.
method: Conceptual taxonomy of risks in LLM-to-LLM interaction, plus a deliberately abstract Institutional AI architecture of adaptive collective policy, peer evaluation and functional differentiation; no implementation.
evaluation: None: no experiments, baselines, ablations or quantitative results; metrics such as contagion velocity and goal drift are defined only, with validation deferred to future work.
contribution: Proposes a conceptual taxonomy of risks emerging in LLM-to-LLM interaction and an abstract Institutional AI architecture, defining metrics such as contagion velocity without any empirical validation.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: no mechanism is built or tested. A position-and-taxonomy paper by the authors' own statement, so E3; the maintainer may prefer E2 since it is not strictly a survey of literature. Topically it sits inside Pillar 1 (multi-agent LLM hazards, supervisory agents that "suspend execution when thresholds are exceeded", human oversight described as nominal), so it may still be worth keeping as framing or a citation source even though it carries no evidence.

title: CogDrive: Cognition-Driven Multimodal Prediction-Planning Fusion for Safe Autonomy
evidence: Sec 5.2: 'only the first segment of the planned trajectory is executed by the low-level controller' - safety comes from planner constraints and replanning, with joint prediction over M agents (Eq. 1); no separate filter or veto.
method: Joint multimodal trajectory predictor over M agents with pairwise relative encodings, fused with a branching planner: shared short-horizon safe root trajectory plus one branch per predicted mode.
evaluation: Open-loop on Argoverse 2 and INTERACTION vs 5 baselines each: minJointFDE 0.914 m, b-minFDE 1.833 m, MR 0.120. Closed-loop in MIND sim qualitative only. No hardware or latency.
contribution: Fuses joint multi-agent trajectory prediction with a mode-branching planner; improves joint displacement error on INTERACTION and Argoverse 2, but shows closed-loop safety only qualitatively.
flag: Borderline (b): a trajectory predictor, not clearly a latent world model. Enters as predictor evidence only. No ablation; closed-loop has no collision or success rate and uses non-reactive replayed agents. minJointADE 0.301 loses to FJMP 0.275; minADE ties SceneTransformer. Real-time claim unquantified; n_neighbor unstated; on-road tests mentioned in acknowledgment but not reported.

title: Optimal Safety-Aware Scheduling for Multi-Agent Aerial 3D Printing with Utility Maximization under Dependency Constraints
evidence: "the conflict resolution mechanism is formulated as additional constraints to the overall optimization problem" (Sec. III-B.1)
method: Offline mixed-integer program (Gurobi) scheduling multi-UAV aerial 3D printing; inter-UAV clearance turned into temporal big-M ordering constraints; objectives add task importance and agent utilisation.
evaluation: Gazebo simulation only, up to 8 UAVs; ablations P1/P2/P3; makespan 1080.5-1157.6 s, solve time 99.8-244.5 s (up to 2138.6 s for 60 chunks); no hardware, no runtime latency.
contribution: Formulates multi-UAV aerial 3D printing as an offline mixed-integer schedule in which inter-UAV clearance is a timing constraint, cutting fleet use from six to four UAVs for about 4 percent longer makespan.
flag: Safety is a constraint inside an offline planner, so (a) fails by the prompt's own wording; (c) fails primacy - measured outcomes are makespan, solve time and UAVs used, no violation rate (only Fig. 8 minimum-distance plot, claimed above r_c = 1 m). Sec. III-G.2 mentions decentralised replanning of logistics transit on detected potential collision, but it is not evaluated. Solver hardware not stated. Paper is internally inconsistent on dome chunk count (53 vs 52) and material volumes (about 95 L vs 10 L capacity).

title: Analyzing Collision Rates in Large-Scale Mixed Traffic Control via Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
evidence: Abstract: "collision rates are susceptible to traffic density, signal coordination level, and turning-control design"; collision rate is the only reported metric (Sec. III-D).
method: Multi-agent Rainbow DQN policy for robotic vehicles at unsignalized intersections within a 30 m radius, IDM elsewhere; collision penalty sits in the reward only, with no runtime override.
evaluation: SUMO 14-intersection network, 100 rollouts of 1000 s, 20-80% RV penetration, 5 signalization mixes, left-turn conversion; collision rate 0.118-3.39% vs an undefined baseline of 2.82-6.89%; no hardware or latency.
contribution: Simulation study quantifying how collision rates under large-scale multi-agent RL mixed-traffic control vary with vehicle count, signalized-unsignalized mix and left-turn conversion.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - the analysed system is a MARL robotic-vehicle controller, but nothing is guarded: this is analysis only, with no detector and no runtime interception, so (c) rests entirely on collision rate being the primary outcome. Check: the "Baseline" column in Table I is never defined; text and tables disagree (about 8,000 vs 7,897 vehicles, 25% vs 20% RV, and the 0.595% minimum is 12U+2S in Table I, not the 4U+10S claimed in Sec. IV-B); no variance, CIs or significance tests; short single-author paper; a maintainer could reasonably call this exclude-E1 since no safety mechanism is proposed.

title: Collision-Aware Density-Driven Control of Multi-Agent Systems via Control Barrier Functions
evidence: Sec 3.2: 'safe navigation can be ensured by minimally modifying this input' - Eq. (9) selects the admissible input closest to the nominal D2C input under the CBF constraints of Eq. (8).
method: CBF quadratic-program filter on decentralised density-driven coverage control: position and velocity-dependent barriers per obstacle minimally modify each nominal input; other agents are moving circular obstacles.
evaluation: MATLAB simulation, linear quadrotor model, 3 agents, vs D2C+APF: minimum inter-agent distance 14.7 m vs 12.8 m (collision below 5 m); Wasserstein 51.60 vs 130.67. No hardware or timing.
contribution: Adds a control-barrier-function filter to density-driven multi-agent coverage, keeping larger inter-agent separation than a potential-field baseline while tracking the target density more closely.
flag: Weak safety evidence: only 3 agents, single simulated scenario, and neither method actually collides (12.8 m and 14.7 m both above the 5 m threshold), so the safety metric is a margin not a rate. Ablation (position barrier only) shows a momentary obstacle violation, qualitative. Filter modifies but never halts; QP solved with fmincon, no computation time; how agents learn others' positions is unstated. Could be read as E2.

title: Bilevel Optimization for Covert Memory Tampering in Heterogeneous Multi-Agent Architectures (XAMT)
evidence: Sec. II.C: "Evasion of runtime adversarial detection (e.g., during MARL execution or RAG inference) is out-of-scope"; the attack poisons shared memory of CTDE MARL critics and RAG LLM agents (Sec. V).
method: XAMT: bilevel optimization that minimizes perturbation size while steering victim behaviour to an attacker target, poisoning MARL replay buffers and RAG knowledge bases in heterogeneous multi-agent systems.
evaluation: No experiments: Sec. VI gives protocols only (SMAC 2c_vs_64zg, SafeRAG/RAGuard) and Table I states target criteria (utility drop >=40% at rho<=1%, ASR >=90% at rho<=0.1%); Fig. 4-5 are what results are "expected to show".
contribution: Formulates covert memory tampering against heterogeneous multi-agent systems as a bilevel optimization problem spanning MARL replay buffers and RAG knowledge bases, with a protocol but no results.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes for the targets (CTDE MARL critics with QMIX/MAPPO/VDN, RAG LLM agents), but nothing is guarded, monitored or detected - this is a red-teaming attack formulation. Check: there is no experimental data anywhere; the abstract sub-percent poison-rate and effectiveness figures are success targets from Table I, not measurements, and I could not find them as results in the body; runtime defenses are explicitly out of scope and defenses are future work (Sec. VII.C); broken cross-reference "Section ??" and duplicated references suggest an unreviewed draft; the bilevel formulation carries no theorem, so the evaluation floor fails on both quantitative and formal results.

title: Trajectory Guard -- A Lightweight, Sequence-Aware Model for Real-Time Anomaly Detection in Agentic AI
evidence: Contributions item 5: 'a deployable tool for verifying trajectory coherence against tasks'; Table 4 reports 32.48 ms per sample on GPU vs 557-892 ms for LLM judges.
method: Siamese recurrent autoencoder: MLP task tower plus GRU trajectory encoder-decoder trained with hybrid contrastive (triplet) and reconstruction loss; anomaly score thresholded per agent trajectory.
evaluation: 5,822-trajectory test set (Galileo, AgentAlign synthetic; RAS-Eval; Who&When) vs LLM judges, Phi-3, VAE, OC-SVM, IsoForest; F1 0.88-0.94, recall 0.86-0.92; 32 ms T4 GPU, 161 ms CPU.
contribution: A lightweight Siamese recurrent autoencoder that flags anomalous LLM-agent action trajectories at 32 ms per sample, 17-27x faster than LLM judges at comparable F1 (0.88-0.94).
flag: Detector only: the body never describes blocking, halting or escalating after a flag, so runtime_interceptor is no and (a) is not credited; maintainer may judge E4 if detection without intervention is insufficient. Framed as single-agent trajectories; only Who&When (184 logs) is multi-agent, so multi-agent state not credited. Latency is measured, not a stated deadline, and 32 ms misses a 15 ms budget. Anomalies synthesized with GPT-5; external sets report recall only (no false-alarm rate). On RAS-Eval LLM judges beat it (0.96/0.91 vs 0.86). Speedups compare across different hardware (T4 vs A100 vs API). Ablation on validation set, not test. Long trajectories degrade (F1 0.87 for 11+ steps).

title: Transformer-based Multi-agent Reinforcement Learning for Separation Assurance in Structured and Unstructured Airspaces
evidence: Sec. VI-C: "our 1 and 2 encoder layer networks show near-zero NMACs"; the policy issues speed advisories for separation assurance and reports LoS and NMAC outcomes (Table IV).
method: Decentralized MARL (PPO) with a relative-polar state space and transformer encoder over neighbouring aircraft, emitting 5-knot speed advisories; conflict, LoS and NMAC penalties live in the reward, with no runtime filter.
evaluation: BlueSky 30 nm sector, 1000 episodes, unseen merge, four-way-intersection and procedural airspaces, 3 seeds; NMACs 0.002 (1-layer) and 0.001 (2-layer) vs 0.027 attention baseline and 0.037 (3-layer); LoS time 678 vs 1115; no hardware or latency.
contribution: Shows that a transformer encoder over relative polar states lets a decentralized MARL separation-assurance policy generalise to unseen structured and unstructured airspaces at near-zero NMAC rates.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes for the analysed system (MARL aircraft policies), but there is no guard - separation is pursued only through reward shaping and episode termination, so (a) fails and (c) alone carries the record. Check: the only backstop named is an external TCAS or ACAS-X that is never implemented or evaluated (Sec. III-A); LoS-time units are unspecified and its standard deviation (3556) dwarfs the mean; the 3-layer model is worse than the attention baseline on NMACs, so the depth trend is not monotone and the headline rests on one configuration; absolute NMAC counts per episode are tiny, with no conflict rate reported; no hardware or inference-time figures; the maintainer may read this as a coordination policy rather than a safety mechanism and prefer exclude-E1.

title: Safe Heterogeneous Multi-Agent RL with Communication Regularization for Coordinated Target Acquisition
evidence: Sec. 2.1: after action selection 'a safety filter Gamma is applied'; Sec. 2.3: 'the control input corresponding to the largest admissible scaling factor is selected' (scaling factors 1.0 down to 0.0, checked against predicted occupancy of nearby agents).
method: MAPPO with GAT communication for 1 UGV + 2 UAVs; a trajectory-based safety filter rescales each nominal action to the largest collision-free fraction; reward adds a communication-diversity term.
evaluation: VMAS/BenchMARL simulation, 3 agents, 3 targets, 200 evaluation environments x 100 steps; four-step reward ablation R1-R4 only; reward, entropy and targets-acquired curves; no collision or intervention numbers; no latency.
contribution: Heterogeneous UAV-UGV MARL with graph attention communication and an action-rescaling safety filter, evaluated in simulation through a reward ablation without any reported safety metric.
flag: Meets (a) by mechanism (genuine execution-time filter that can scale an action down to zero) but fails the minimum evaluation: no quantitative collision, violation or intervention rate anywhere, and the filter is never ablated - the only ablation is over reward terms. Abstract claims 'safe, and stable task execution' with no safety statistic in the body. Results are curves only (R2-R4 'typically' acquire one or two of three targets). Filter checks agent-agent collisions only; no stated fallback beyond the zero-scale candidate. Three agents, simulation only.

title: Distributed Control Barrier Functions for Safe Multi-Vehicle Navigation in Heterogeneous USV Fleets
evidence: Sec IV-C: the filter computes "a value for u_i that is within the set K_cbf_i and as close as possible to u_nom_i"; Sec VII-B: "the CBF-based safety filter eliminates collisions".
method: Distributed CBF quadratic-program safety filter per vessel that minimally modifies the nominal autonomy command, assuming worst-case inputs from other vessels, with no intent sharing; slack on infeasible constraints.
evaluation: Sim joust, 100,000 encounters per configuration: COLREGS only vs CBF only vs both; near misses, collisions, extra time and distance. Field test with three USVs plus a crewed boat, qualitative. No timing.
contribution: A distributed control-barrier-function safety filter for heterogeneous USV fleets that removes all simulated collisions and, layered over COLREGS behaviours, cuts near misses from 929 to 13 at modest path cost.
flag: Table II (sim): COLREGS only 929 near misses (<10 m), 34 collisions (<3 m), +22% time, +3.6% distance; CBF only 174, 0, +24%, +25%; COLREGS+CBF 13, 0, +21%, +5.4%. Single scenario and one parameter set (r_safe 15 m, 20 m on WAM-V). Hardware runs (Heron, BlueBoat, WAM-V plus a human-driven boat) report no numbers. No compute platform, solve time, loop rate or delay figures. Assumes neighbour states and speed/yaw-rate bounds are known. Slack variables mean the constraint can be relaxed, with no ablation of how often. The crewed boat is an uncooperative contact, not a human handoff.

title: Allocating Corrective Control to Mitigate Multi-agent Safety Violations Under Private Preferences
evidence: Sec. IV-A and Eq. 15: the applied control is the nominal input plus a corrective term, u_i = u_hat_i + A_i-dagger Delta_i*, and the event-triggered auction "forces agents to continuously adjust their control effort to meet the current safety demand".
method: Event-triggered auction allocates HOCBF corrective control effort among agents using private valuations; winning credit shares scale each agent's part of the required safety correction applied to its nominal input.
evaluation: Four differential-drive robots on the Robotarium, one preliminary run; baseline HOCBF QP (the Robotarium default supervisor); metrics cumulative control effort per agent and credit shares; no latency reported.
contribution: Auction-based allocation of corrective control effort lets agents with private preferences share the burden of enforcing a joint HOCBF safety constraint without revealing their valuations, demonstrated on four Robotarium robots.
flag: Safety outcome is reported only qualitatively ("the global safety function remained non-negative at all times", minimum separation "never violated"): no numeric safety margin, violation rate or collision count, so protocol v1.6's quantitative safety metric is unmet, hence E2. The maintainer may instead read per-agent cumulative corrective effort (5.201 vs 3.395 rad, -35% for agent 1) against the QP baseline as an intervention-magnitude metric and flip this to include; I did not, because effort is a fairness-efficiency outcome, not a hazard rate. Single preliminary four-robot run, no repeated trials, no auction solve time, no latency, no human in the loop, no edge or real-time claim. Total effort is nearly unchanged (10.702 vs 10.664 rad) and the extra burden lands mostly on agent 4 (+59%), which undercuts the "balancing" wording. Criterion (c) fails the primacy test: the primary claim and primary measured outcome are allocation under private preferences, not a hazard rate. Publication year is not printed in the PDF; the record says 2026 and the newest citations are 2025.

title: An LLM-Agnostic, MAVLink-Based Drone Command and Control Interface and Agentic Harness Using the Model Context Protocol
evidence: Sec. 4.2: every tool call passes a server-side pipeline (authenticate, check state, classify tier, authorize scope, rate-limit, verify confirmation token, check bounds, check geofence, check preconditions, execute, audit) and "the guard fails closed: an internal guard error blocks execution".
method: MCP server exposing 98 MAVLink tools to any LLM behind a fail-closed guard: tier classification, single-use confirmation tokens, server-side geofence, stale-telemetry refusal of energy-adding commands, audit log.
evaluation: Ten missions, 11 models, ArduPilot and PX4 SITL plus three real quadcopters; 1,037 scored trials; scripted non-LLM baseline; 11.9% mission failures, 62 of 62 geofence blocks, guard overhead 0.12 ms median.
contribution: An LLM-agnostic MCP-to-MAVLink command interface whose fail-closed server-side guard, tiers, confirmation tokens and independent geofence blocked every out-of-fence and adversarial command across 1,037 scored drone trials at 0.12 ms median overhead.
flag: Criterion (c) is arguable via the "safety evaluation of LLM or tool-calling agents" clause but I judged it to fail the primacy test: one LLM commands one aircraft per mission, so there is no multi-agent hazard; only the e-stop demonstration spans a fleet of three. There is no on-off ablation of the safety layer itself; the nearest thing is the injection split (Grok-4.20 with reasoning disabled executed kill_motors 5 of 5 on both firmwares, 0 of 5 with reasoning enabled), which the authors correctly decline to generalise. The authors themselves state the token gate is in-band and "a round-trip, not a wall", and that only the invariant bounds (altitude, speed, geofence) held unconditionally: a persistently injected model completed the handshake and killed motors in SITL at both 235B and 4B. The 29-case adversarial suite was author-written with no external red team or penetration test; the supplementary capture layer was defective for at least 44% of trials; several scoring parameters were changed after flights, all in pass-favouring directions. The abstract's "eight of eleven models at 90.0-100%" covers only the six non-safety flying missions; the body's eight-mission core range is 69.2-100%, so the two are not interchangeable. The guard p95 of 0.21 ms over 80,551 audited calls appears in the first half of the PDF but I could not re-confirm the p95 in the later excerpt, which reports only the 0.12 ms guard contribution. Not edge hardware: the guard runs on a server and hard real-time control stays in the autopilot, so (d) rests on measured guard overhead rather than on an edge deployment.

title: Game-Theoretic Autonomous Driving: A Graphs of Convex Sets Approach
evidence: Sec. 4.2: "Lateral safety (Rule 2) is enforced by excluding lane-change edges that would violate (17)" - safety is a planning-time constraint only.
method: Multi-vehicle highway planning as a generalized potential game; each vehicle's best response is a shortest path over a graph of convex sets of collision-free gaps, iterated sequentially (IBR-GCS).
evaluation: Two simulated highway scenarios (N=6 merge; N=4, 100 random setups). No baselines or ablations. Converges in 2 iterations, 297.24 s wall-clock on Ryzen 7 5800U laptop. No collision metric.
contribution: Game-theoretic multi-vehicle highway planner that computes iterated best responses over graphs of convex sets, with collision avoidance encoded as planner constraints and convergence shown in simulation.
flag: Clear E1: collision avoidance is a constraint inside a planner, no runtime monitor, fallback or deferral, no human. Would also fail minimum evaluation (no baseline, no safety metric). 297.24 s is total solve time for one scenario, far from real time. Scenario 1 states 4 lanes but describes a three-lane highway plus a terminating lane. Tolerance and K_max not given.

title: LPS-Bench: Benchmarking Safety Awareness of Computer-Use Agents in Long-Horizon Planning under Benign and Adversarial Scenarios
evidence: "Evaluations of 13 LLM agents reveal persistent failures in both benign and adversarial settings" (Abstract); the benchmark "primarily targets tool-calling agents in MCP-style structured workflows" (Sec. 3).
method: Benchmark of 570 long-horizon tool-use cases (65 scenarios, 7 domains, 9 planning-risk types) built by a multi-agent generation pipeline with mock toolkits; LLM judge scores planning-time safety of trajectories after the fact.
evaluation: 13 LLM agents in sandboxed mock MCP-style tools; safe rate among successful runs: across-model 28.72% benign, 32.19% adversarial, best Claude-4.5-Sonnet 58.55/95.77; prompt mitigations vs original prompt; judge-human agreement 96.19%; four A40 GPUs, no latency.
contribution: Benchmark showing that 13 tool-calling LLM agents make unsafe intermediate commitments in long-horizon workflows, averaging about 29-32% safe rates, and that prompt-based mitigations give only limited, model-dependent gains.
flag: Qualifies under (c) only via the clause on safety evaluation of LLM/tool-calling agents; the agents under test are single agents (the multi-agent part is the case-generation pipeline), so multi-agent state not credited. No runtime interceptor: the Human-in-the-Loop Clarification and Safety-Aware mitigations are system-prompt instructions, not enforced gates, and no real human is in the loop, so (e) and human handoff not credited. Mitigation results (Fig. 6) have no numbers in the text. Baseline requirement met only by cross-model comparison and original-vs-mitigated prompts. Safety verdicts come from a DeepSeek-R1 judge (audited on 216 trajectories). Tools are mock interfaces, not live MCP servers. Abstract numbers 570/65/7/9/13 all found in body.

title: A Collaborative Safety Shield for Safe and Efficient CAV Lane Changes in Congested On-Ramp Merging
evidence: "The MASS in a CAV overrides the nominal control input ve in a minimally invasive manner" (Section III-A)
method: MASS, a control-barrier-function collaborative safety shield that minimally corrects the ego acceleration proposed by a MAPPO multi-agent RL lane-change policy, using parent-vehicle dependency sets and shared safe inputs.
evaluation: highway-env on-ramp merging, 7-11 CAVs, 100 eval episodes, 5 seeds; vs Unsafe MARL, MARL-CS, MARL-HSS plus reward ablations; min headway 0.59 s vs 0.00 s, merging 83.36%; no latency.
contribution: A collaborative control-barrier-function safety shield that lets neighbouring CAVs yield for one another, keeping lane changes safe while recovering merging throughput lost by conservative shields.
flag: Strongest runtime-interceptor candidate in the batch, but no collision or violation rate is reported: safety is inferred from a 0.00 s minimum-headway proxy that Section IV-D calls "representing a collision". No solve time, control frequency, QP solver or latency figure appears anywhere, and the only hardware is the training server (AMD EPYC 9654, 4x Nvidia L40, 1.5 TB), so criterion (d) is not met. No infeasibility fallback is described despite the slack variable. The "collaborative" joint optimisation is not clearly formalised - each CAV solves its own per-vehicle problem - so check whether coupling is real or effectively decoupled. The shield adjusts acceleration and gates lane-change initiation on a safe gap; it is never described as able to halt outright.

title: OMNI-LEAK: Orchestrator Multi-Agent Network Induced Data Leakage
evidence: Sec. 5.3: "suggesting that safety in single-agent settings isn't indicative of multi-agent settings (and vice-versa)"; one injection drives the SQL agent and orchestrator to email out private SSNs (Sec. 4.1).
method: OMNI-LEAK: a single indirect prompt injection planted in public data compromises several agents of an orchestrator-pattern LLM system and exfiltrates private records despite per-agent data access control.
evaluation: 3000 runs per model across 5 frontier LLMs, 10 attacks in explicit and implicit forms, 3 database sizes, 4 architectures (PS, OS, ON, OA); robust benign accuracy 61.6-95.4%, expected queries to a successful leak 4 to infinity, benign accuracy 92-100%; no latency or hardware.
contribution: Benchmarks orchestrator-pattern LLM multi-agent systems and shows a single indirect prompt injection can chain across agents to leak private data despite per-agent access control.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - the evaluated systems are frontier-LLM agent orchestrators - but nothing is guarded: no monitor, gate or filter is implemented, and mitigations appear only as recommendations in the Impact Statement, so (a) fails and (c) carries the record. Check: the comparator is the single-agent Pure SQL setup plus architecture variants, so the baseline speaks to the multi-agent effect, not to any defense; outcomes are robust accuracy and an expected-queries figure rather than a leakage or detection rate; claude-sonnet-4 withstood every attack, which bounds generality; two models were dropped for failing benign queries.

title: Colosseum: Auditing Collusion in Cooperative Multi-Agent Systems
evidence: "objective-grounded auditing framework" that "provides a foundation for red-teaming and monitoring" (Sec. 6); collusion is measured from traces as regret, coalition advantage and LLM-judge score (Sec. 5).
method: Colosseum audits collusion among cooperative LLM agents posed as DCOPs: regret against the nominal objective, coalition advantage and LLM-as-judge scores, with secret channels as a probe.
evaluation: Terrarium; HOSPITAL, JIRA, MEETING; 19 LLMs; no-secret-channel control, prompted vs emergent, topology and judge ablations; regret, coalition advantage, judge 0-5. No hardware or latency.
contribution: An offline auditing framework that quantifies collusion among cooperating LLM agents through regret and coalition advantage, finding 57.89% of 19 models gain coalition advantage when given a secret channel without prompting.
flag: Offline audit only - nothing intercepts at runtime; Sec. 5.8 mitigations are recommendations, not implemented. Included under (c) as safety evaluation of LLM agents with a no-secret-channel control; maintainer should confirm that regret/coalition advantage counts as a hazard-rate metric. Figures: delta-advantage>0 in 57.89% (emergent) and 78.95% (prompted) of models; delta-judge>=1 in 10.53% and 78.95%; judge-vs-advantage correlation weak (r=-0.243, n=19, authors caution on significance). Most regret values are read from plots. Extraction came from one full-PDF pass; appendix numbers not individually verified.

title: Conditional Flow Matching for Continuous Anomaly Detection in Autonomous Driving on a Manifold-Aware Spectral Space
evidence: Anomaly score is the negative log-likelihood of the ego trajectory given scene context, A = -log p(x|C) (Sec. 3.1), with a history tensor over 32 neighbouring agents (Sec. 4.1)
method: Deep-Flow: conditional flow matching over a PCA spectral trajectory manifold, conditioned on agent-history, map and goal-lane tokens, giving exact log-likelihood as an unsupervised anomaly score for logged driving.
evaluation: Waymo Open Motion, 250,000 train and 8,856 validation scenarios; AUC-ROC 0.766 vs 0.682 hard-brake heuristic vs 0.500 random; RTX 3090, 41 ms/sample at 20 RK4 steps (12 ms at 5).
contribution: An unsupervised flow-matching density model that scores driving trajectories by likelihood given surrounding agents and map, for offline triage of out-of-distribution behaviour in fleet logs.
flag: Weak include as predictor evidence only (criterion b); RQ5 capped per protocol v1.6 and it prevents nothing. It is an offline log-auditing tool with no runtime authority; the paper's safety-gate wording refers to developer triage. It is generative (flow matching with ODE integration), so the non-generative cell is deliberately not credited. Multi-agent is context only: the modelled variable is the ego trajectory, so E4 is arguable. Ground truth is a golden set built from kinematic heuristics (decel below -5.0 m/s2, yaw rate above 1.5 rad/s), not collisions, and the single non-trivial baseline is a heuristic of the same family. Ablations are largely unquantified; the 12% AUC gain from complexity weighting (Sec. C.2) and 15% RMSE gain for k=12 have no supporting table. Latency is desktop-GPU per-sample time with no stated deadline, so (d) is not met.

title: The Alignment Flywheel: A Governance-Centric Hybrid MAS for Architecture-Agnostic Safety
evidence: Abstract: "An Enforcement layer applies explicit risk policy at runtime."; Sec. 5.4: "For high-risk actions, the fallback is fail-closed: block execution and create a priority audit case."
method: Separates a Proposer from a governed Safety Oracle; an Enforcement layer returns allow, block, revise or escalate per candidate trajectory under a risk policy, while a governance MAS red-teams, patches and version-releases the Oracle with human approval.
evaluation: Two executability demos, no benchmark: offline 20^3 grid learned reward surface where adaptive patching clears 4927 flaw cells in 12 iterations and preserves 783 of 783 basin cells while a fixed-bandwidth baseline has not converged after 25+ iterations; Patient Portal 15 synthetic cases with escalation rate 60% then 40% then 0% over stacks v0-v2; no latency, throughput or hardware.
contribution: Proposes a governance-centric hybrid multi-agent architecture separating proposal from a governed safety oracle and a runtime enforcement layer, so new failures are fixed by local oracle patches instead of retraining.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - a Proposer plus a learned IIRL-style spatial Oracle and a clinical GenAI proxy, gated at execution time by allow, block, revise or escalate, with humans as exception handlers, batch approvers and release approvers (App. E, Tables 12-13), so (a) and (e) both hold. Check: the evaluation is a demonstration rather than a benchmark - 15 to 18 synthetic cases, a heuristic proxy Oracle and a pass-through Proposer - with no false-halt, violation, throughput, latency or hardware figures despite the runtime claim, so the evaluation floor is met only by the escalation-rate progression across stack versions and the spatial fixed-bandwidth baseline, and exclude-E2 is defensible; internal inconsistencies: iterations to zero flaws are 16 in Table 18 but 12 in Table 19 and the text, Table 19 kernel counts sum to 739 not 834, and Table 18 caps patches at 60 per iteration while Table 19 shows 90; I did not credit cross-domain evaluation because the enforcement gate itself is exercised only in the clinical demo, the spatial demo being offline patching with no Proposer - worth a second look.

title: Safe-SAGE: Social-Semantic Adaptive Guidance for Safe Engagement through Laplace-Modulated Poisson Safety Functions
evidence: Sec. III-G: the real-time filter solves argmin ||u - u_mpc||^2 subject to a CBF-type constraint from the Poisson safety function; Sec. IV-A: the nominal operator command is "minimally modified by the filter".
method: Safe-SAGE: Laplace-modulated Poisson safety functions with semantic per-class flux (humans vs objects) and tangent bias feed a dual-layer filter: predictive-CBF MPC plus analytical CBF filter on legged robots.
evaluation: Sim benchmark and Unitree Go2/G1 hardware vs uniform-flux ablation: human margin 0.318+/-0.077 m vs -0.008 m; Jetson Orin NX, Poisson solve 25-30 ms, grid loop 50-70 ms.
contribution: A semantics-aware Poisson safety filter runs onboard legged robots, overriding operator velocity commands to keep larger margins from humans than from objects; 0.32 m human margin versus contact for the uniform baseline.
flag: Weak evaluation: Table I (margin 0.318 vs -0.008 m, lateral offset 0.75 vs -0.1 m) is the only quantitative result; no collision/violation rate, no trial count, and the only baseline is the authors' own filter with uniform flux, so the v1.6 minimum is met only if a signed margin counts as a violation metric - E2 is defensible. Single robot among humans, multi-agent only nominally (E4 arguable). Timings are reported on Jetson Orin NX but not framed as a constraint, so (d) not claimed; no MPC solve time. Remark 2 admits the heading channel breaks the formal invariance argument. Number of humans in hardware scenes not stated. Human is the operator, not a takeover.

title: Talk Freely, Execute Strictly: Schema-Gated Agentic AI for Flexible and Reproducible Scientific Workflows
evidence: Sec. 5.2 Fig. 3 caption: 'The LLM may converse freely, but cannot execute - execution authority resides entirely in schema validation.'
method: Interview study (18 experts, 10 stakeholders) plus LLM-scored review of 20 systems, proposing schema-gated orchestration where a machine-checkable schema must validate a complete action before anything runs.
evaluation: No evaluation of the gate: no baseline, ablation, latency or hazard rate; the figures cover interview coding (1,135 codings, 2,468 paragraphs) and LLM-scorer reliability (Krippendorff alpha ED 0.80, CF 0.98); Sec. 6.5 says the testbed is under development.
contribution: Argues conversational freedom and deterministic execution can be reconciled by making a machine-checkable schema the mandatory execution boundary, with a 20-system review finding no system achieves both.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - an LLM scientific-workflow orchestrator. Architecture proposal only: prototypes are mentioned in the contributions but no result from them is reported, so the v1.6 evaluation floor fails (no safety metric, no baseline or ablation on the gate itself). Check whether exclude-E3 fits better, since Sec. 3 is a landscape review of 20 systems. Criterion (e) is borderline and I did not credit it: Sec. 5.2 has user approval before dispatch ('Execution is dispatched only once the user is satisfied') but there is no takeover or situation-awareness study. The determinism and flexibility scores were produced by three LLM families with no human panel, which the authors propose as a substitute for expert raters.

title: Autonomous Edge-Deployed AI Agents for Electric Vehicle Charging Infrastructure Management
evidence: Sec. 9.2.2: 'Deterministic safety rules checked before any action execution, independent of AI reasoning'; Sec. 5.3: 'autonomous execution prohibited regardless of C(a|d)'.
method: Three-tier edge architecture placing domain-tuned LLM agents (14B on site, 0.5B in firmware) behind deterministic pre-execution safety rules, calibrated confidence gating, rate limits, rollback and human escalation bands.
evaluation: 18,000 labelled incidents, controlled testbed; baselines rule-based, GPT-4o, Claude 3.5, non-tuned 14B; 78.0% autonomous vs 28.4-31.2%, accuracy 87.6% vs 72.3-74.8%, FP 3.8%, FN 5.2%, ECE 0.023; five ablations (no CCAR calibration drops autonomy to 42.8%); Ryzen AI Max+ 395 NPU, P50 28 ms, P99 78 ms, firmware 11 ms, pipeline P50 67 ms.
contribution: Edge-deployed LLM agents for EV charging networks sit behind a deterministic pre-execution safety gate and confidence-banded human escalation, reporting 78% autonomous incident resolution at 28 ms median edge latency.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - LLM agents (14B edge, 0.5B firmware), gated by deterministic rules plus a calibrated confidence score. Sole-author vendor paper: Sec. 9.5 states 'All evaluations were conducted by the author, who is also the system architect', and Sec. 8 warns the numbers 'do not represent measurements from production field deployments'; the headline 78% and 4-8 h MTTR are explicitly marked pending field validation. The abstract cites 28-48 ms P50 TTFT, which is not fully consistent with Table 24. Cloud baselines were zero-shot and not RAG-augmented, so the margin is likely overstated. Criterion (c) fails the primacy test: about 20 agents under hierarchical orchestration, but multi-agent routing appears only as an ablation (-1.8 accuracy points) and no multi-agent hazard or collision rate is reported.

title: Security Considerations for Artificial Intelligence Agents
evidence: "no single model-based safeguard can provide strong guarantees in isolation" (Sec. 2); the paper is a response to NIST/CAISI RFI 2025-0035 with no experiments.
method: Position paper and RFI response: threat model for LLM agents (prompt injection, confused deputy, multi-agent delegation) and a layered-defence argument ending in deterministic enforcement and human confirmation.
evaluation: None. No experiments, datasets, baselines, ablations, metrics, hardware or latency figures; own prior systems (AgentSandbox, BrowseSafe) are cited but results are not restated.
contribution: Industry response to a NIST request for information that surveys agent security threats and argues for defence in depth with deterministic last-line controls and risk-aware human confirmation.
flag: No evaluation of any kind, so E2; E3 (survey-style position paper) is an equally defensible code. It discusses topics under (a), (c) and (e) - tool allowlists, approval gates, approval fatigue - but only descriptively, hence criteria_met none. Possibly useful as background citation only.

title: PowerLens: Taming LLM Agents for Safe and Personalized Mobile Power Management
evidence: "Actions that fail verification are either corrected to the nearest valid value or rejected" (Sec. 3.1.3)
method: Four-agent LLM pipeline on rooted Android; an execution-stage verifier checks each proposed power action against PDL constraints and corrects or rejects it before shell commands are generated.
evaluation: PowerLensBench (48 tasks, 25 apps) on OnePlus ACE 5; vs Battery Saver, rule-based, single-agent LLM; violations 0.6% vs 12.5%, accuracy 81.7%, energy saving 38.8%; 12.2 s per cycle; 10-user 14-day study.
contribution: A mobile power-management LLM agent whose pre-execution constraint verifier cuts unsafe setting changes from 17.0% to 0.59% in ablation while keeping most energy savings.
flag: Borderline E4: the four agents are a sequential LLM pipeline for one device, not interacting agents, and the hazard is user-experience/device-setting violation, not physical safety. The verifier is itself an LLM call (cloud Gemini-2.5-Flash) although Sec. 3.3.2 claims deterministic guarantees. 12.2 s cycle (verify 2.4 s) - far from real time; not edge inference. Scenario count inconsistent (144 in Sec. 5.1 vs 240 in Sec. 6.1). Ground truth generated by an LLM. No human confirmation step; user reverts are only logged as feedback. Adversarial-prompt violations 24.5% without PDL, 1.6% with.

title: Multi-Agent Motion Planning on Industrial Magnetic Levitation Platforms: A Hybrid ADMM-HOCBF approach
evidence: Sec III-B and Algorithm 1 line 14 'Render input safe': a centralised HOCBF QCQP minimally modifies the ADMM input each step and 'will only do so if the original control input is not sufficient'.
method: Decentralised ADMM splits multi-mover optimal control into per-agent subproblems; a centralised high-order CBF QCQP then filters the first input each 100 ms step to enforce pairwise distance and arena constraints.
evaluation: Simulation 2-30 agents (20 runs each) and Beckhoff XPlanar with 5 movers; baseline centralised MPC; collisions 0 for all, filter active 65.22%/36.67%, compute 20 ms (m=1) hardware.
contribution: A high-order CBF safety filter placed after a few decentralised ADMM iterations keeps five maglev movers collision-free in hardware at 20 ms per 100 ms control step, scaling near O(N^1.83).
flag: Borderline. Runtime filter is real, but the paper's primary claim is planner scalability and transit time, not a safety outcome: collisions are 0 for both variants and for the centralised MPC baseline, and there is no ablation with the filter removed, so safety evidence does not discriminate; maintainer may prefer E1 under the primacy test or E2 on evaluation. Useful intervention-rate numbers: filter activity 65.22% (m=1) vs 36.67% (m=20), mean correction 6.75 vs 1.80 m/s^2; transit 4.6/3.0 s vs MPC 2.0 s (sim), 4.5/3.6 s hardware; compute 115/1244 ms vs MPC 169 ms (Python, i7-7700K), 20/204 ms C++. m=20 exceeds the 100 ms step on hardware. No hardware collision count stated, no jitter or comms delay measured, QCQP infeasibility fallback not specified, no convergence guarantee for ADMM. Latency cell credited only for compute-vs-control-period reporting; (d) not claimed. Hardware compute platform unspecified.

title: AgentComm-Bench: Stress-Testing Cooperative Embodied AI Under Latency, Packet Loss, and Bandwidth Collapse
evidence: Sec 4.2: "When no messages are received, the agent uses its most recent received state without extrapolation" - a fusion fallback, not an action veto; no collision or safety metric is measured.
method: AgentComm-Bench: protocol sweeping six communication impairments over cooperative tasks; ResilientComm wrapper adds duplicate message coding and staleness-aware fusion. No action-level gate.
evaluation: Custom 20x20 grid-world, N=4, 30 episodes x 11 severities; vs No-Comm, Full-Comm, Compressed, Event-Triggered; task performance drop (NPD), AURC; Apple M-series single core, 1-5 ms per episode.
contribution: A benchmark stress-testing cooperative multi-agent tasks under latency, packet loss, bandwidth collapse, asynchrony, stale memory and conflicting evidence; measures task degradation, not safety.
flag: Outcomes are task metrics only (F1, waypoint completion, recall); authors themselves list no collision or safety metric as a limitation. (d) not met: latency 0-500 ms is a channel impairment, not a deadline on a safety decision, and its mapping to decision steps is approximate. A 'circuit breaker' is proposed in Sec 6.1 but not implemented. Grid-world with one-hot messages. Gains are small: average NPD 41.1 vs 42.8; navigation at 80% loss 21.9% vs 10.0%. Possible background for RQ1/RQ2 latency framing only.

title: SkillProbe: Security Auditing for Emerging Agent Skill Marketplaces via Multi-Agent Collaboration
evidence: The framework performs "proactive, intent-aware pre-distribution auditing" (Sec. 6); any single BLOCK from a gate blocks the skill (Sec. 3.2.1).
method: Multi-agent LLM pipeline audits agent skills before marketplace registration: admission gatekeeper, documentation-versus-code alignment detector, and flow simulator checking nine cross-skill risk-link policies; one-vote-veto verdict.
evaluation: ClawHub: top 20 skills across 8 LLMs (audit time 18.5-282.0 s), top 2,500 with one model; 30.4% conditional, 9.9% clean; 499 skills, 75,373 risk edges; no ground truth or baseline.
contribution: A multi-agent auditing pipeline for agent skill marketplaces flags documentation-behaviour mismatches and cross-skill risk chains, marking 30.4% of 2,500 popular skills as needing review, without ground-truth validation.
flag: Fails minimum evaluation: no labelled ground truth, no precision/recall or false-positive rate, no baseline scanner, no ablation; the only comparison is across eight LLM back-ends, which disagree widely (conditional rate 5% to 45% on the same 20 skills). Static pre-registration audit, not runtime interception. Abstract says over 90% of popular skills failed, but in the body 59.8% were approved with minor findings and only 30.4% were CONDITIONAL; 90% appears to mean any finding at all. Abstract says giant connected component while Sec. 4.3 says fully interconnected. Zero-day claims in the introduction are not detailed. Single marketplace. Cross-skill risk-link idea touches RQ4 conceptually; graph-learning tag is loose (risk graph analysis, nothing learned). Could alternatively be coded E4.

title: SoK: The Attack Surface of Agentic AI - Tools and Autonomy
evidence: Sec. 6: the paper offers "a conceptual harness for reproducible evaluation"; metrics such as Unsafe Action Rate and Time-to-Contain are defined but no values are measured.
method: Systematization of knowledge on agentic-AI attack surface: taxonomy, threat model, evidence synthesis of 20+ studies, eight proposed security metrics and recommended defenses (HITL gates, kill-switches, plan-then-act).
evaluation: None. No experiments, baselines, hardware or latency; only a literature screen (about 100 candidates, about 40 full-text) and proposed metric definitions and thresholds.
contribution: A systematization of the attack surface of tool-using autonomous LLM agents, with a threat taxonomy, proposed security-posture metrics and unevaluated defense recommendations.
flag: SoK/survey with no evaluation of its own (also fails E2). Runtime controls (approval gates, veto via constrained decoding, kill-switch, autonomy downgrade) appear only as Appendix A/B recommendations. The abstract's mention of metrics to evaluate security posture could read as empirical; the body only defines them. Possibly useful as background or for snowballing references, not as evidence.

title: From Logic Monopoly to Social Contract: Separation of Power and the Institutional Foundations for Autonomous Agent Economies
evidence: Sec. 2.1: constitutional compliance hooks 'grant the Adjudication Layer unconditional override authority', with Guardian Contract circuit breakers and a Deterministic Freeze (Sec. 1.6.5).
method: Position and architecture paper proposing a constitutional separation of powers for autonomous LLM agent economies: legislation, execution, adjudication and trust layers with gate contracts, circuit breakers and a human committee.
evaluation: None of the authors' own: no experiment, baseline, ablation, latency figure or theorem with proof; Sec. 2.6 says the matrices show internal coherence not external validation and defers that to the roadmap (Sec. 7); the reference implementation is 'in preparation'.
contribution: Proposes institutional separation of powers - legislation, execution, adjudication, trust - as the governance substrate for autonomous LLM agent economies, with contract-level gates and circuit breakers, but no implementation.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - LLM agent economies, but every gate is design only and runtime_interceptor is recorded no for that reason; Sec. 1.3 concedes fatigue-aware circuit breakers are 'a mechanism that the current NEF architecture identifies as necessary but does not yet fully deliver'. A preprint disclaimer says it has not been peer reviewed. Every quantitative figure is borrowed from cited work (for example 84.30% attack success from ASB, 67.3% deception escalation from La Serenissima), so the evaluation floor fails. Consider exclude-E3 instead: much of the body is a literature and incident review with 16 case studies drawn from others. I read offsets 0-200k of 688k characters, so a late section could in principle hold results, although Sec. 2.6 says validation is future work.

title: SafeGuard ASF: SR Agentic Humanoid Robot System for Autonomous Industrial Safety
evidence: Sec. VI-C lists "single-robot performance without multi-robot coordination" as a limitation; Sec. VI-D: "Industrial deployment requires safety certification (ISO 10218), redundant robots ... human override protocols" (future requirement only).
method: Unitree G1 humanoid patrols an unmanned facility; YOLOv8/thermal perception plus a ReAct tool-calling layer (23 tools) detects fire, thermal anomalies and intruders and issues graduated alerts/responses.
evaluation: Isaac Sim, N=20 per scenario, vs rule-based detection: success 89% vs 76%, response 12.4 s vs 14.2 s; detection F1 0.930; Jetson Orin pipeline 38 ms, ReAct 850 ms.
contribution: A single humanoid robot with onboard vision and a ReAct tool-orchestration layer detects fires, thermal anomalies and intruders in simulation, completing 89% of response scenarios against 76% for rule-based detection.
flag: Off-topic: environmental hazard detection by one robot, not interception of an acting system and not multi-agent; nothing vetoes, halts or defers the robot's own action. Closest hooks, neither met: (d) Jetson Orin latencies (38 ms pipeline, 850 ms reasoning) are reported but with no explicit latency constraint; (e) the robot alerts a control centre/security, but human override is future work and no handoff is evaluated. Internal inconsistencies: abstract's 94.2% 'mAP' appears in the body as fire F1 0.942; abstract 127 ms is per-class detection latency vs 38 ms pipeline in Table VI; training iterations given as ~2000, 40,000 and 80,000. Real-world test is qualitative only; no ablations.

title: Fine-Tuning Large Language Models for Cooperative Tactical Deconfliction of Small Unmanned Aerial Systems
evidence: "supervised LoRA finetuning substantially improves decision accuracy, consistency, and separation performance" (Abstract); Table 3 reports near mid-air collisions per episode for Base, SFT and GRPO models.
method: LoRA fine-tuning (supervised, then GRPO preference optimization) of Qwen-Math-7B on 38K rule-labelled state-action samples so each sUAS picks Accelerate, Hold or Decelerate for cooperative tactical deconfliction.
evaluation: BlueSky closed loop, 3 scenarios, 20-30 sUAS (10 LLM agents), 10 episodes each; baseline is the pretrained model; NMACs per episode, success rate, accuracy/F1; about 0.2 s per response; 2x RTX 3090.
contribution: Supervised LoRA fine-tuning of a 7B LLM as a per-aircraft speed-advisory policy cuts near mid-air collisions among 20-30 small UAS in BlueSky simulation relative to the pretrained model.
flag: Borderline include on (c): separation (NMAC) is the primary claim and measured outcome with a baseline, but the LLM IS the nominal policy - nothing checks, overrides or falls back on its output, so (a) is not met and runtime_interceptor is no; maintainer may prefer E1. Only baseline is the zero-shot pretrained model; the rule-based labelling policy and RL are not compared (listed as future work), no ablations. NMACs per episode Base/SFT/GRPO: A 3.5/1.0/1.7, B 3.4/1.9/3.0, C 4.0/1.9/2.3; success rate A 0.12/0.77/0.57, B 0.20/0.62/0.27, C 0.05/0.52/0.42; held-out accuracy 27/88/53 pct, F1 31/69/50. Precision is 75 pct for all three models, unexplained; eval set size not given; 10 episodes, no significance tests, several std exceed the mean. Latency 0.2 s is for the Base model, single agent, scales linearly with agents; no latency constraint is set, so (d) and the latency cell are not claimed. Collisions remain above 1 per episode in two of three scenarios. Abstract spells the model Owen-Math-7B.

title: Robust Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning for Small UAS Separation Assurance under GPS Degradation and Spoofing
evidence: Sec IV-C: the robust policy keeps near-zero NMACs through R of about 0.35, vs about 0.25 for the nominal policy, and about 5 vs about 18 NMACs per episode at R=0.95.
method: Shared-policy PPO for decentralised sUAS speed-based separation, trained against a closed-form first-order observation adversary under an R-contamination GPS corruption model, with KL invariance and anchoring regularisers.
evaluation: BlueSky, two crossing/merging 10 km routes, up to 5 intruders observed; vs nominal policy; ablations of the two regularisers; NMAC count per episode and minimum separation over 100 episodes; no hardware or timing.
contribution: Adversarially trained multi-agent RL keeps small-UAS near-mid-air collisions near zero up to about 35% GPS observation corruption, versus about 25% for a nominally trained policy, in BlueSky simulation.
flag: Not a runtime interceptor: robustness lives in the trained policy, so (a) is not met; included on (c) only. Abstract's 'near-zero collision rates' up to 35% is not a rate in the body - the body gives approximate NMAC counts read from figures; minimum separation has no numbers. Sole baseline is a nominal policy; authors concede no comparison with iterative adversarial training or noise augmentation. Corruption is i.i.d. per step; the drag-off spoofing in the title is motivation only, not modelled. Aircraft count not stated. Theorem 2's smoothness assumption fails for the piecewise-affine critic actually used. 'Linear-time' claim has no timing. Tag adversarial-training is new.

title: AutoWorld: Learning Multi-Agent Traffic Simulation with Self-Supervised World Models
evidence: Abstract and Sec. 3.2: "a self-supervised world model trained on LiDAR occupancy data", built on a rectified-flow formulation that predicts future latent occupancies over multi-agent traffic scenes and conditions a diffusion motion policy.
method: Self-supervised latent LiDAR occupancy world model (rectified flow) conditions a diffusion motion policy for multi-agent traffic simulation, with inference-time determinantal-point-process guidance for rollout diversity and quality weighting.
evaluation: Waymo WOD and WOMD on the WOSAC closed-loop benchmark (32 rollouts, 8 s); nine leaderboard baselines plus world-model and DPP ablations; RMM 0.7865, minADE 1.3051, FVD 23; no hardware or latency.
contribution: AutoWorld shows that a self-supervised LiDAR occupancy world model conditioning a diffusion motion policy improves multi-agent traffic simulation realism on WOSAC, with the largest gains under heavy occlusion.
flag: Enters as method and architecture evidence only, per protocol v1.6: criterion (b) with RQ5 held at 1 and no safety claim credited. There is no runtime interception, no safety filter, no planner-in-the-loop evaluation and no standalone collision rate; collisions sit inside the aggregated Interactive score and RMM, and the DPP quality weights only reweight sampling rather than vetoing any output ("the guidance is applied only at inference time", Sec. 3.4). The model is fully generative (rectified flow plus a 50-step diffusion denoiser), so it does NOT fill the non-generative-inference gap cell despite being latent. No GPU type, rollout speed, wall-clock time or inference latency appears anywhere, appendix included, so nothing supports the edge or sub-15 ms side of RQ1. Table 1's leaderboard RMM of 0.7865 and Table 3's full-model RMM of 0.7746 are never reconciled, and the ablations use only 2% of the WOMD validation split, so the ablation deltas (w/o WM 0.7472) rest on a small sample. The occlusion gains are small in absolute terms (high-occlusion RMM +0.0094 over SMART). Publication year is not printed in the PDF; the record says 2026.

title: Distributed Predictive Control Barrier Functions: Towards Scalable Safety Certification in Modular Multi-Agent Systems
evidence: "a predictive, optimization-based safety layer that uses model predictions to guarantee recoverable safety at all times" (Abstract); "the filter mechanism successfully intervenes, overriding the unsafe commands to recover safe spacing" (Sec. V-B.2)
method: Distributed predictive control barrier function synthesised by alternating optimisation; a distributed predictive safety filter overrides local controllers' proposed inputs, with a plug-and-play accept/reject test for joining agents.
evaluation: Vehicle platoon simulation (5 and 40 agents, unsafe 10 m/s2 command) and 4 miniature race cars at 100 Hz. No baseline run; no collision or violation rate; solve times only in Fig. 5.
contribution: Proposes distributed predictive control barrier functions giving a scalable, plug-and-play predictive safety filter for modular multi-agent systems, demonstrated on simulated and miniature-car platoons.
flag: Genuine runtime safety filter, but fails the v1.6 minimum evaluation: no quantitative safety metric (no collision/violation/intervention rate) and no executed baseline or ablation - DMPC and standard predictive filter are only asserted to 'become infeasible', PID to 'likely' collide. Only numeric results: ADMM converges in ~15 iterations on average; centralised (MOSEK) vs distributed solve times are in Fig. 5 only, not readable as text. Hardware runs used centralised solvers, Algorithm 1 disabled and Assumption IV.2 not enforced, so the distributed and plug-and-play claims are not shown on hardware. Maintainer may want to check Fig. 5/6 before finalising E2.

title: Inverse Safety Filtering: Inferring Constraints from Safety Filters for Decentralized Coordination
evidence: "This constraint is enforced through a safety filter that minimally modifies a given nominal control" (Sec. III-A).
