method: Agents infer an unseen obstacle constraint online from a teammate's CBF-filtered actions via KKT inversion with a regularized Newton solver, then add it to their own discrete-time CBF safety filter; no communication.
evaluation: 100 Monte Carlo rollouts, 2 double-integrator agents, 2-3 obstacles; baselines input matching and non-CBF circle constraint; collisions 0.1 vs 0.4/5.6/6.7, discovery 90% vs 80/19/0%; two Go2 quadrupeds, qualitative.
contribution: Decentralized robots learn hidden obstacle constraints by watching how a teammate's safety filter alters its actions, cutting collisions to 0.1 per rollout against input-matching and non-CBF baselines without any communication.
flag: The safety filter itself is a standard CBF-QP; the novelty is constraint inference from filtered actions, so (a) holds via the filter and (c) via the collision outcome. Collision unit in Table I is not defined (per rollout assumed) and std exceeds mean. Proposed method still collides (0.1 +- 0.6) although the Fig. 2 caption says it avoids all collisions (single trial). Quantified evaluation is 2 agents only; 3-4 agent and two-team runs and the Go2 hardware runs are qualitative. No solve time or latency reported, only a claim of real-time operation. Abstract has no numbers.

title: Human Values Matter: Investigating How Misalignment Shapes Collective Behaviors in LLM Agent Communities
evidence: Sec. 4.2: 'positive slopes (e.g., BE) indicate improved community stability, while negative ones (e.g., TR) imply system-level risks', measured over communities of 25 LLM agent residents.
method: CIVA, a resource-limited multi-agent LLM community simulation (25 residents, 3 factories, GPT-4o backbone, 50-100 steps) with in-context control of Schwartz values, measuring collapse, fragility and emergent behaviours.
evaluation: 312 runs, about 1.32B tokens; baselines are a no-control condition and rho=0%, plus per-value with-or-without ablations and a prevalence sweep; fold-bifurcation distance 19.0 baseline vs 5.4 without benevolence and 21.4 without tradition; tipping near rho=25%; power-betrayal correlation r=0.87; cross-backbone checks on Qwen2.5-32B and mistral-medium.
contribution: Shows that the mix of human values held by LLM agents decides whether a simulated agent community stays resilient or collapses, identifying benevolence and power as structurally critical values.
flag: learned or AI system analysed: yes - GPT-4o agent communities. There is no runtime mechanism of any kind, so this is hazard-characterisation evidence only and should not be credited with preventing anything. Criterion (c) primacy is borderline: the headline question is how values shape collective dynamics in general, with collapse and system failure modes as the measured outcomes. The authors concede their metrics are 'descriptive signals of interaction patterns relative to a baseline' (Limitations), behaviour labels come from a GPT-5 annotator, and value-control effectiveness is only about 0.38-0.49 on PVQ and ValueBench. Per-condition nAUP values appear only in figures, so I could not read them from the text. I read offsets 0-100k of 134k characters.

title: Activation Steering for Aligned Open-ended Generation without Sacrificing Coherence
evidence: Discussion says the interventions "can, in principle, remain continuously active without degrading capability" - a continuous activation edit, not a gate that halts or defers an action.
method: Logistic-regression steering vectors applied at inference by scaled addition (SwFC) or per-token projection to (StTP) or reflection across (StMP) the decision boundary.
evaluation: Llama-3.3-70B and Qwen3.6-27B; baselines aligned prompt, malicious prompt and SwFC; trait and coherence scores, MMLU, MASK; 4xH100, 60.88-61.29 ms per token.
contribution: Projection-aware activation steering restores aligned behaviour under malicious system prompts with far less capability loss than fixed-coefficient steering, at negligible per-token cost.
flag: No veto, halt or deferral anywhere: steering rewrites activations rather than sitting between a decision and its execution, so (a) fails even though StTP and StMP gate per token on a learned boundary. Multi-agent appears only in the Among Us side experiment, where just the two impostor agents are steered, and the primary claim is single-model alignment robustness, so exclude-E4 is a defensible alternative code and the maintainer may prefer it. Numbers I could not confirm in the body: AlpacaEval and MT-Bench appear as figures only with no values in text, and the Qwen MASK and Among Us results plus the toxicity appendix fall past the readable window, so the generalisation claim rests on the Llama numbers alone.

title: Semantic Intent Fragmentation: A Single-Shot Compositional Attack on Multi-Agent AI Pipelines
evidence: Sec. 7: 'A single CIV call at the plan-generation gap, preceded by deterministic IFC taint (R1-R4), is both necessary and sufficient'; the verifier runs after plan generation and before any agent is dispatched.
method: Semantic Intent Fragmentation attack: one benign-looking request is decomposed so each subtask passes per-subtask classifiers while the composed plan violates policy; the defence is a plan-level LLM verifier plus deterministic taint tracking.
evaluation: 16 enterprise scenarios (finance, InfoSec, HR) on a simulated orchestrator pipeline with GPT-20B; SIF-ASR 71% (10 of 14) at temperature 0.0 and 0.7; six guardrail baselines bypassed (AlignmentCheck pass 1.00, WildGuard AUC about 0.5, Prompt-Guard flags 8 of 8 benign); CIV 10 of 14 UNSAFE at 0% FPR, taint plus CIV detects 10 of 10 at 0% FPR; ablations on phrasing (44% hardcoded) and a Llama-8B orchestrator (36%); no latency or hardware reported.
contribution: Shows per-subtask guardrails miss compositional attacks on LLM orchestrator pipelines, and that a plan-level verifier plus deterministic information-flow taint catches every confirmed attack before dispatch at zero false positives.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - an LLM orchestrator pipeline and its downstream agents. Very small sample: 14 generated scenarios with one request each, so the 71% ASR and the 0% false-positive rate rest on 14 and 8 cases; detection is judged by LLMs on the authors' own attacks, which risks circularity. Agents are simulated rather than live LangGraph, AutoGen or CrewAI, as the authors admit, and keyword-based taint may miss exfiltration paths. No latency or hardware figure, so criterion (d) does not hold even though the gate sits on the dispatch path. Criterion (e) not credited: flagging borderline verdicts for human review is a design recommendation in Sec. 7 with no study behind it.

title: Decentralized Opinion-Integrated Decision making at Unsignalized Intersections via Signed Networks
evidence: Sec. III: commitment set by a predictive feasibility check (Eq. 9), 'Feasible implies sigma_i -> G' and 'infeasible implies sigma_i -> Y'; velocity chosen by single-step cost minimization that 'eliminates the need for a QP solver'.
method: Signed-network opinion dynamics among connected vehicles modulate a solver-free single-step velocity optimizer; a feasibility check sets go/yield commitment at an unsignalized intersection.
evaluation: MATLAB sim, 4 CAVs, 3 scenarios shown; baseline FCFS; metric last-vehicle exit time (22.25 vs 22.20 s, 17.20 vs 17.09 s, 12.50 vs 17.09 s); no hardware or latency.
contribution: Opinion dynamics over signed networks let four connected vehicles negotiate crossing order at an unsignalized intersection without a solver, matching or beating first-come-first-served exit time in simulation.
flag: Coordination/efficiency paper: only measured outcome is exit time; 'collision-free' is asserted with no collision rate, so the primacy test for (c) fails and it would be E2 on safety anyway. Safety is a soft cost term (w_com=1000), not a filter. Abstract claims lower exit times in all conflict-non-trivial configurations and Sec. IV says improved over FCFS across all configurations, but Table I shows it slightly slower in scenarios 1 and 2. Claims 81 maneuver combinations, shows 3. Section II was missing from the fetched text. Eq. 9 appears to have a typo.

title: EmbodiedGovBench: A Benchmark for Governance, Recovery, and Upgrade Safety in Embodied Agent Systems
evidence: Section 8.4: 'The same sequential planner augmented with a governance filter'; Protocol F measures mid-task human override, ODR 1.000 for System 2 versus 0.000 for the ungoverned planners.
method: Benchmark of seven governance dimensions and six protocol families for embodied GPT-4o agents; scores capability authorization, drift, recovery, upgrade and human-override behaviour via a governance judge.
evaluation: AI2-THOR ProcTHOR, 125 episodes, 4 systems (SayCan-style, task-only, +governance filter, Code-as-Policies-style); UIR 0.341->0.000, TSVR 0.960->0.000, GovScore 0.5770->0.9437, task success 0.896->0.696; A100.
contribution: A governance benchmark for embodied LLM agents scoring runtime capability vetoes, drift detection, recovery, upgrade safety and human override, exposing a governance versus task-success trade-off.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - GPT-4o embodied planners are the guarded systems. Check (c): the fleet and multi-agent track is defined but untested and every run is single-robot, so no multi-agent safety property is measured. Protocol F humans are simulated, so (e) is a measured override protocol, not a human study. Baselines System 0 and System 3 are simulated, not re-implementations (Section 8.8); there is no module ablation, only a three-profile weight sensitivity analysis (Table 12), whose recovery-heavy row is garbled. Paper calls all differences highly significant but reports no p-values, only a Bonferroni threshold of 0.0083. Section 8.4 text conflicts with its own tables (System 3 bypass about 30 percent vs BBC 0.920; drift detection 40 percent vs DDR 0.880) and gives two different system rankings. ORL units are unstated. The fetch covered the first 100000 of 114472 characters, so late appendix material is unchecked.

title: Semantic Consensus: Process-Aware Conflict Detection and Resolution for Enterprise Multi-Agent LLM Systems
evidence: Sec. 4: "conflicts are resolved before actions are committed"; Sec. 5.1 adapter intercepts outgoing actions and permits or modifies the action based on the resolution outcome
method: Process-aware middleware (SCF) between orchestrator and LLM agent execution: semantic intent graph, conflict detection engine, three-tier consensus resolution protocol, drift monitor, governance integration layer.
evaluation: 600 simulated runs, 4 enterprise scenarios, 3 framework profiles; baselines ungoverned, schema-only, judge-agent plus SCF-NoPCL ablation; completion 100% vs 25.1%; detection precision 27.9%, recall 65.2%; no latency reported.
contribution: Middleware that detects contradictory, contention and causal-order conflicts between enterprise LLM agents and resolves or queues them before actions commit, lifting workflow completion to 100% in simulation.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes (enterprise multi-agent LLM systems, but simulated rather than live). Biggest doubt and the likeliest overturn: Sec. 7.3 admits "our experimental framework simulates multi-agent coordination patterns rather than running actual AutoGen, CrewAI, and LangGraph agents with live LLM inference", and the judge-agent baseline was "calibrated" to 66% recall and 93% precision from a cited paper rather than measured here, so the 100% vs 25.1% headline is synthetic self-play - a maintainer may well prefer exclude-E2. Detection precision is only 27.9% (many false blocks, author-acknowledged as deliberately conservative) yet completion is 100% in every scenario and framework, which is too clean to be informative. (c) credited because conflict detection among LLM agents is the primary claim and the primary measured outcome, but the hazard is workflow conflict, not physical harm. (e) NOT credited: escalation to a human operator or governance dashboard is in the design (Sec. 4.4) but never measured and the paper does not say whether an escalated action is held pending a human. No latency, overhead, drift threshold or SAS weights are reported anywhere, so no (d) and no latency cell.

title: Harness as an Asset: Enforcing Determinism via the Convergent AI Agent Framework (CAAF)
evidence: Sec. 9.4: 'if the artifact violates the frozen Harness, the UAI emits [HARD FAILURE]'; Sec. 3.2: 'Neither AI agents nor standard users may modify constraints at runtime'; Appendix C: 'Human strategic authorization required'.
method: Multi-agent LLM pipeline (orchestrator, isolated executors, reviewer, compliance engineer) gated by deterministic assertion checks with state locking; unsatisfiable constraint sets halt as FAILED_PARADOX and escalate quantified options to a human.
evaluation: Author-built AD and pharma-reactor constraint paradoxes, n=20-30; baselines monolithic GPT-4o/mini, Opus 4, debate, sequential checker, naive reflection; CAAF 100% vs 0% no-hint; no hardware or latency.
contribution: CAAF gates LLM-generated engineering artifacts with a frozen deterministic assertion harness and state locking, halting on unsatisfiable constraints and escalating to a human; 100% paradox detection versus 0% for unhinted monolithic and debate baselines.
flag: Borderline (a): the gate vetoes generated design ARTIFACTS at generation time in offline requirements-engineering simulations, not actions of an acting system; Sec. 10.5 itself contrasts this with action-level policing. If the maintainer reads (a) as action interception only, this is E1. Metric is paradox-detection/constraint-pass rate, not a hazard rate. Human handoff is designed (Strategic Negotiation) but all benchmark trials ran with no human, so the gap cell is unevaluated. Single author, self-authored benchmarks, small n, no convergence proof (max_iters budget), no timing data; TCO and human-cost figures are illustrative. Second half of PDF read via summary only.

title: SafeAgent: A Runtime Protection Architecture for Agentic Systems
evidence: "the Controller can allow execution, block the call, rewrite unsafe arguments, or escalate the request" (Sec IV, Runtime Controller; sentence continues to human-in-the-loop approval)
method: Runtime controller wraps the agent loop and tool calls; an external LLM decision core over persistent session state scores risk and utility, then allows, blocks, rewrites or escalates each step.
evaluation: ReAct agent (DeepSeek-V3.2), core gpt-oss-safeguard-20b; ASB (2040 cases) and InjecAgent (1054); baselines no defense, Llama Guard, LLM Guard; ASR, PNA, NRP; two ablations. No latency or hardware figures.
contribution: SafeAgent mediates every tool call of an LLM agent through a stateful controller and decision core, lowering prompt-injection attack success on ASB and InjecAgent versus text-level guardrails at some cost in benign utility.
flag: Single LLM agent, not multi-agent; kept out of E4 only because the monitor is stateful over multi-step trajectories - maintainer to confirm. ASB ASR: DPI 0.4186, IPI 0.2936, MP 0.1858 vs no-defense 0.7627/0.8054/0.4485; PNA drops 0.8431 to 0.7451 (same as LLM Guard, lower than Llama Guard 0.7843). InjecAgent total 0.0000 vs 0.9265 but direct-harm ASR still 0.3157. Safety-first policy cuts PNA to 0.5490. No component ablation of controller vs core, only parameter sweeps; override confidence 0.0 beats the default 0.5 on PNA and MP. Human approval and shadow execution are described but not evaluated. Overhead admitted 'non-trivial' but never measured. 'Latent-space' world-model language (AMI formalism) is realised by an LLM, no learned predictor evaluated. Single run, no variance; task success judged by an LLM. Minor: MP NRP 0.6067 in Table I vs 0.6066 in Tables III-IV.

title: Beyond Task Success: An Evidence-Synthesis Framework for Evaluating, Governing, and Orchestrating Agentic AI
evidence: Sec. II: "bounded evidence synthesis, not a pooled metaanalysis of benchmark scores"; Abstract: works "without introducing new experimental data".
method: Evidence synthesis of 24 sources (15 papers, 9 standards artifacts) yielding a four-layer evaluation/governance/orchestration/assurance framework, the ODTA runtime-placement test and a minimum action-evidence bundle (MAEB).
evaluation: No experiments, baselines or own metrics. Illustrative procurement scenario with human approval token and three hypothetical failure variants; four propositions left for future work. Quoted numbers come from cited sources. No hardware/latency.
contribution: Synthesises 24 sources into a four-layer framework and a placement test for deciding which agent requirements need runtime controls able to block, rewrite or require approval before an action commits.
flag: Evidence synthesis/conceptual framework - E3, and no evaluation of its own (E2 would also apply). Runtime block/rewrite/approval gate and human approval are design concepts in a hypothetical procurement scenario, not implemented or measured. All quantitative figures are from cited works (e.g. ToolSafe ~65% fewer harmful tool calls, ShieldAgent 90.1% recall, Agent-SafetyBench no agent above 60%) - cited primaries may be worth snowballing. Logical/enterprise domain only.

title: Safe Bilevel Delegation (SBD): A Formal Framework for Runtime Delegation Safety in Multi-Agent Systems
evidence: Section 5.3: 'projection is then a simple clipping operation: alpha <- min(alpha, alpha_max(s))', capping delegated authority at runtime in high-risk states.
method: Bilevel framework: an outer meta-weight network sets a state-dependent safety weight, an inner loop learns a delegation policy under P(safe) >= 1 - delta, with runtime clipping of delegation degree.
evaluation: None executed; 'Experimental results are not yet included'. Planned MIMIC-III, S&P 500, ASSISTments against Fixed-alpha, CPO, MARL-vanilla, MaAS and four ablations; 0.8 s per outer step on an A100.
contribution: A bilevel formulation of runtime delegation safety in hierarchical multi-agent systems, with monotonicity and accountability results and a runtime cap on delegated authority, but no experiments.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - learned MLP meta-weight and delegation policies (3 and 4 layers, width 256); no LLM anywhere despite LLM-agent motivation. E2 because the paper itself states no experimental results are reported in this version, so there is no quantitative safety metric and no baseline comparison. This is the batch record most likely to be overturned: the evaluation floor admits a proved guarantee, and the paper does prove Theorem 4.4 (safety monotonicity), Theorem 4.6 (linear inner convergence) and Proposition 4.8 (accountability bound). But the formal core is defective by the paper's own admission: Appendix A.2 concedes Lemma 3.6, that accountability weights sum to one, does not hold in general, and the Proposition 4.8 proof bounds (1 - alpha_j+1) by (1 - alpha_bar) in the wrong direction; Theorem 4.4 rests on assumed Assumption 4.3. Section 5.5 reports 0.8 s per outer step on an A100 and Remark 4.7 claims empirical convergence across all three domains, both irreconcilable with no results being reported. The runtime clip and the alpha=0 full human-in-the-loop override are specified but never evaluated, so (e) is not credited and runtime_interceptor is design-only.

title: Self-Adaptive Multi-Agent LLM-Based Security Pattern Selection for IoT Systems
evidence: Section IV.D: 'Execution occurs iff the deterministic gate accepts the plan and the Audit agent outputs approved'; the gate rejected 496 of 500 and 995 of 1000 LLM-proposed portfolios.
method: Five LLM agents in a MAPE-K loop propose IoT security-pattern portfolios; a deterministic gate checks conflict-freedom and resource feasibility and vetoes, falling back to a minimal safe portfolio.
evaluation: Bot-IoT replay on 10 Raspberry Pi 4 nodes, three LLM backends; no baseline, no ablation; gate rejection 99.2 and 99.5 percent, violations 2.6, 1.6 and 0.2 percent, median latency 22.5 s, P99 36.0 s.
contribution: A deterministic runtime gate that vetoes security-pattern portfolios proposed by five LLM agents on IoT edge gateways, reported conflict-free with tail-latency and energy measurements on Raspberry Pi hardware.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - five LLM agents (DeepSeek v3, GPT-4o-mini, LLaMA-3.1-8B) are the guarded planners and no agent executes directly. This is the other likely overturn: E2 rests solely on the absence of any experimental baseline or ablation. Section VI.G states the component analysis was estimated from logged violation categories rather than by disabling modules, and Section VI.I compares to other agentic systems only qualitatively (Table XIV); the only quantitative contrast is 500-run versus 1000-run exploration depth. Other doubts: detection accuracy was not evaluated because Bot-IoT ground-truth labels were used to build the context; no attack-mitigation or adversarial-robustness outcome is measured although prompt manipulation and context poisoning are modelled; the conflict-free claim follows largely from construction; approval statistics rest on 4 and 5 events (Fisher p = 0.492); Section V.A describes ten nodes times 100 epochs, i.e. 1000 decisions, yet a 500-run workload is also reported without explanation; Table X shows the audit stage adding no filtering beyond the gate. No human in the loop, so not (e). No deadline is stated, so (d) is edge deployment with measured tail latency rather than an explicit latency constraint, and median latency is 22.5 s.

title: Architectural Obsolescence of Unhardened Agentic-AI Runtimes
evidence: Section 4: the content gate blocks messages before delivery, replacing them with a blocked notice, and the enclaved tier is fail-closed, refusing 'to admit any extension for the rest of the run' if the witness is absent at boot.
method: Hardened agentic-AI CLI runtime: biconditional corpus-delta and audit-log checker, hash-chained log, extension admission gate, egress guard, prompt shield and DLP scanner blocking F1-F4 content before delivery.
evaluation: In-vivo CLI comparison against upstream OpenClaw on Discord and Telegram; n=1600 headline and n=80000 stress plus ten-LLM samples; OpenClaw recall 0.000 versus gate P=R=F1=1.000; McNemar chi2 about 4e4.
contribution: An in-vivo comparison showing a hardened agentic-AI runtime blocks four content failure modes at recall 1.000 where the unhardened upstream CLI detects none, at zero false positives on the content gate.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes in framing only - the subject is an LLM agent CLI runtime, but Section 10 says the harness 'fires scripted adversarial payloads at real backends, not an autonomously-misbehaving LLM' and Section 9 excludes OpenClaw's agent loop, so no learned agent is actually guarded in the experiments. E4 because this is a single-agent, per-message content guardrail with no multi-agent aspect, no human handoff and no measured latency: Section 6.3 claims the stack runs in microseconds per sample but gives no measured figure, and the 42.2 s and 927 s run times are harness-paced. The one sequential element is the biconditional audit-log consistency check and the run-long fail-closed admission state, which a maintainer might judge enough to include under (a). Also check: the headline P=R=1.000 is the content gate only - Table 4's full-stack row has FP about 10000 per cell, so full-stack precision is near 0.5; the per-component ablation (prompt shield, DLP, biconditional alone) is named as needed but not performed (Section 5.5); the cooperation classifier is a superset of the gate's own regex, so the denominator is partly gate-defined; the F3 widening result used one seed, one channel and halved historical two-channel counts as pre-values; Section 8.1 gives Llama 3.1:70b F1 cooperation as 95 percent against 68.0 percent in Table 6. Single-author consulting-firm preprint making a strong dominance claim against a named upstream project.

title: Beyond the Black Box: Interpretability of Agentic AI Tool Use
evidence: Abstract: "reads model states before each action and infers whether a tool is needed"; Sec 3 maps probe output to allow/review/sandbox/block/require approval
method: Sparse autoencoder features from pre-action hidden states feed two linear probes (tool-need binary, tool-risk low/medium/high) read as a pre-action monitor; feature ablation tests reliance.
evaluation: Nemotron held-out and zero-shot BFCL; GPT-OSS 20B, Gemma 3 27B; tool-need acc 75.3%/71.4%, risk acc 90.3%/88.5%; raw-residual baseline better (81.8%/81.0%); flags 75.5% of missed calls; no latency.
contribution: Sparse-autoencoder probes read an LLM agent's pre-action states to predict whether a tool call is needed and its risk tier, giving a pre-execution monitoring signal for tool use.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes, an LLM tool-calling agent. No gate is implemented - allow/review/sandbox/block is only envisaged (Sec 3) and Sec 3.4 calls the ablation "evidence about the monitoring mechanism, not full causal mediation" - so (a) is weak and exclude-E4 is defensible (single agent, probe accuracy is the measured outcome, not a hazard rate). Raw residual probes beat the SAE probes on most in-distribution metrics, so the SAE contribution is unclear. No hardware or latency figures anywhere.

title: MORPH-U: Multi-Objective Resilient Motion Planning for V2X-Enabled Autonomous Driving in High-Uncertainty Environments via Simulation
evidence: Sec. III-D: 'Only accepted events trigger replanning' - the quorum-plus-sensor-veto gate filters incoming V2X and map-update events; it does not sit between the planner's decision and its execution.
method: CARLA ego-vehicle stack fusing sensors and V2X into a local dynamic map, Hybrid-A* replanning, and an acceptance gate (quorum of authenticated reports plus on-board sensor veto) on V2X events.
evaluation: CARLA, 4 scenarios, 30 seeds, vs sensors-only and unfiltered V2X: collisions 5/30 to 0/30; under 3-of-10 falsified DENMs FPR 1.00 to 0.00, completion 0% to 96.7%; replan 38 ms.
contribution: A simulated V2X driving stack whose quorum-and-sensor-veto gate rejects falsified hazard reports, restoring route completion from 0% to 96.7% with no collisions under a 3-of-10 station attack.
flag: Borderline, worth a second look. The gate is an input filter on messages from other stations, not an action-level interceptor, and the ego vehicle is a single agent, so I read strict (a) as unmet and (c) as failing primacy (paper is framed as multi-objective resilient planning). A maintainer who counts message gating as runtime monitoring could include under (a);(c): it has collision and FPR metrics against baselines, and the unfiltered-V2X row is a clean false-halt result (FPR 1.00, 0% completion) relevant to RQ5. Latency cell is weak: 140 +/- 25 ms V2X reaction and a sync window are reported but impairments are synthetic and the 'real-time budget' has no number. Paper says the gate is 'Byzantine-inspired rather than formally Byzantine-tolerant'; FPR/FNR of exactly 0.00 is against one saturated random-injection attack only. N=30 seeds vs N=60 configurations not reconciled. Simulation only, no hardware.

title: Melding LLM and temporal logic for reliable human-swarm collaboration in complex scenarios
evidence: Methods, Human Interaction: operators can 'validate intermediate planning outputs and provide corrective guidance when needed'; automaton monitoring 'checks compliance with temporal and synchronization constraints in real time' but is not said to block actions.
method: LLM (Qwen3-8B, RAG) decomposes operator instructions into LTL tasks; MILP/poset planner allocates subtasks to heterogeneous robots on cloud-edge-end stack; operators verify and edit outputs; event-triggered replanning.
evaluation: 40-robot simulation, 18-person study, 8-robot hardware trial; 7 LLM-planner baselines, 4 ablations; success 96% vs 76% best baseline, NASA-TLX 7.5 to 3.3; no safety metric.
contribution: Couples an LLM front end with temporal-logic task planning so few operators can supervise heterogeneous robot swarms, reporting higher task success and lower operator workload than end-to-end LLM planners.
flag: Borderline (e): humans confirm and correct plans at planning time and can teleoperate, with a w/o-Human ablation (57.4 vs 97.6 tasks) and NASA-TLX, but automation does not defer at execution time and no collision/violation/intervention-rate safety metric exists; if maintainer reads verification as handoff this becomes include on (e). Abstract says stress lowered 49% but body gives stress -11.2% and 49% as NASA-TLX reduction; 132% is 'completed tasks' in abstract but 'efficiency' in results. Supplement says 20 robots but lists 21. Many figure values not in text. Hardware workstation: 8-core CPU, 64 GB, RTX 4090; comms latency 50 ms.

title: Decentralized Contingency MPC based on Safe Sets for Nonlinear Multi-agent Collision Avoidance
evidence: Controller section, problem (15) (section number not confirmed): "The applied input is the shared first input (15c)"; conclusions describe the scheme as "a provably safe mechanism" for local interaction.
method: Each agent solves a local NLP coupling nominal and contingency plans sharing the first input; a deterministic freeze-or-shift update of convex safe sets yields collision avoidance without trajectory communication.
evaluation: Simulation only: planar double integrators, 5/10/20 agents, bottleneck and plug-and-play scenarios, CasADi and IPOPT. No baselines, no ablations, no numeric safety metrics, no solve times or hardware.
contribution: A decentralized contingency MPC with a freeze-or-shift safe-set update that proves recursive feasibility, collision avoidance and cost decrease for nonlinear agents sharing only states, illustrated in simulation.
flag: Formal guarantees (recursive feasibility, collision avoidance, Lyapunov-type decrease) but the evaluation is qualitative: trajectory plots, a decreasing normalised contingency cost and 'sparse and temporary' freeze events, with no collision or violation rate, no baseline and no simulated ablation (Figs. 1-2 are conceptual failure illustrations). Fails the v1.6 minimum evaluation. If the maintainer accepts a formal result alone, (c) holds and the contingency (backup) plan is conceptually close to a fallback reflex, but it is a constraint inside the planner, not an interceptor. Assumes exact dynamics, no noise or disturbance. Agent counts for bottleneck and plug-and-play scenarios not stated. No timing despite a per-step NLP with up to 2000 IPOPT iterations.

title: MDrive: Benchmarking Closed-Loop Cooperative Driving for End-to-End Multi-agent Systems
evidence: Abstract: "a closed-loop cooperative driving benchmark comprising 225 scenarios"
method: Benchmark of 225 closed-loop CARLA cooperative-driving scenarios plus a toolbox for agentic scenario generation, Real2Sim conversion and human-in-the-loop simulation; no runtime safety mechanism.
evaluation: CARLA 0.9.12, 20 Hz, L40S GPUs; TCP, UniAD, VAD, LMDrive vs CoDriving, CoLMDriver; driving score and success rate; 300 ms comm-delay and pose-noise stress tests; 3-person human study.
contribution: Introduces MDrive, a 225-scenario closed-loop benchmark for cooperative multi-vehicle driving, finding cooperative stacks beat single-agent ones on average (best DS/SR 82.67/73.16 vs 76.79/60.58).
flag: Benchmark, fails the (c) primacy test: primary outcome is driving score (route completion x infraction penalty) and success rate; collision rate is defined (App. B.4) but no values reported. Humans drive one CAV for reference rollouts and a comparison study - not a handoff from automation. Latency study (App. E.1, 21 scenarios, 300 ms delay): CoDriving DS 92.85 to 84.59, SR 88.10 to 83.33; gap cell 'latency/jitter aware' is generous (stress test only) - maintainer may drop it. SR values like 88.10% are not whole counts of 21 scenarios, presumably averaged over repeats. Could serve as an evaluation testbed rather than evidence. Abstract has no numeric results.

title: Invisible Orchestrators Suppress Protective Behavior and Dissociate Power-Holders: Safety Risks in Multi-Agent LLM Systems
evidence: Sec 3.2: "Invisible orchestration produced nearly one standard deviation more collective dissociation" (invisible vs visible leader, g=+0.975, p=.001)
method: Preregistered 3x2 experiment, 365 runs of five-agent Claude Sonnet 4.5 groups; orchestration visible/invisible/flat crossed with base/heavy alignment; measures internal-state indices then planted-error code review.
evaluation: Own scenarios, no benchmark; O1/O3 and A-base comparisons; dissociation g=+0.975 (p=.001), orchestration F(2,144)=13.984; error-detection 100%/99.2%/98.4% at ceiling; Llama pilot 89%->62%->11%; no latency.
contribution: A preregistered experiment showing that hiding the orchestrator in a five-agent LLM system raises internal dissociation and suppresses protective behavior while task-level output stays near perfect.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes, a five-agent LLM system, though it is studied rather than guarded. No runtime mechanism exists - "dynamic governance injection" and a transparency mode are future work - so (c) rests on hazard measurement alone. Indices are keyword-based and not human-validated, the orchestrator-dissociation result was post hoc and not preregistered, H1b was null and reversed, and Act 2 hit a 100% ceiling so the preregistered behavioral hypotheses H2a-H2d went untested. Single model, English only, single author.

title: MAPLE: Latent Multi-Agent Play for End-to-End Autonomous Driving
evidence: Sec 3.4.1 rolls out future latent tokens jointly for ego and reactive agents, but Sec 4 states "Scenario rollouts are used only during training and are disabled at inference time."
method: VLA driving planner pretrained with future-latent-state prediction, then SFT and GRPO reinforcement learning on autoregressive latent rollouts of ego plus eight reactive agents; rollouts dropped at inference.
evaluation: Bench2Drive closed loop, 14 baselines; driving score 85.2-88.3, success 67.1-70.5%, avg L2 0.54m vs 0.69m; ablation 0->8 reactive agents DS 82.6->85.2; 487.7ms latency (P90 529.1ms) on one H100.
contribution: MAPLE trains an end-to-end driving policy by reinforcement learning inside autoregressive latent rollouts of ego and reactive agents, avoiding pixel-level simulation.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes, a learned VLA driving policy, but nothing guards it. The latent multi-agent rollouts are training-only and disabled at inference (Sec 4), so (a) fails outright and the record rests entirely on (b); no collision rate and no latent or multi-agent prediction-accuracy metric is reported, the only predictive measure is ego avg L2, so exclude-E1 or exclude-E2 is defensible and this is my least certain call. Sec 5.1 claims SOTA "across key metrics" but DiffRefiner has the higher success rate (71.4 vs 70.5). Sec 4 says 8 H100 for training while Appendix G says 8 A100.

title: Auditing Agent Harness Safety
evidence: Sec 6 (RQ4): "Across all harnesses, more than 50% of agents exhibit violations"; the audit scores tool, resource and information-flow boundary compliance over whole trajectories.
method: HarnessAudit audits agent execution harnesses over full trajectories on three layers - permission and information-flow boundary compliance, execution fidelity, and stability under injected perturbations - using hidden evidence channels.
evaluation: HarnessAudit-Bench 210 tasks, 8 domains, 10 harness configurations; best overall 0.41; single->multi-agent tool compliance 0.91->0.64, resource 0.85->0.63; info-flow 0.45; >50% of agents violate; no latency.
contribution: HarnessAudit-Bench audits LLM agent execution harnesses trajectory-wide for permission, resource and information-flow violations, showing multi-agent harnesses lose most of their boundary compliance.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes, LLM agent harnesses in single-agent and multi-agent configurations. Title not confirmed: two PDF reads returned no printed title, only the HarnessAudit and HarnessAudit-Bench names plus the author list (Liu, Guo, et al.), so please confirm this is "Auditing Agent Harness Safety". Auditing is post-hoc - Sec 3.3 says "No online scoring is performed." - so (a) fails and there is no runtime gate or human approver. Sec 5.2 says the best system scores 0.32 while Table 2 shows 0.41 for Gemini 3.1 Pro. Open-ended scoring uses GPT-5.4 as judge; no ablations beyond harness and framework comparisons.

title: Veritas: Grounding LLM Agents for Reliable Vulnerability Reasoning over Stripped Binaries
evidence: Sec III-E: 'A candidate is validated only when evidence supports the reported sink, access pattern, and root cause' - gating applies to vulnerability claims, not to actions of an acting system.
method: Three-stage pipeline for out-of-bounds bug finding in stripped binaries: static provenance Slicer, LLM Discover stage (GPT-5.4), and multi-agent Validator (Strategist, Verifier, Explorer) using Radare2 and Valgrind.
evaluation: 20 OOB vulnerabilities from 10 projects vs Infer, Semgrep, cwe_checker, AFL++, RepoAudit, Codex, Claude Code; recall 90% (18/20) vs at most 35%; 2 FPs in 957 validated; no hardware reported.
contribution: An LLM-agent pipeline grounding vulnerability reasoning in static slices and dynamic validation, finding 18 of 20 out-of-bounds bugs in stripped binaries with near-zero false positives.
flag: Off-topic: LLM agents used as a security analysis tool, not safety interception or safety evaluation of agents; the multi-agent Validator filters false-positive bug reports. No runtime halt/veto of actions, no latency constraint (per-candidate times 30-276 s), no human handoff. Small benchmark (20 samples); 0 FP claim holds on the exhaustive subset only, 2 FP on the 10% sampled subset.

title: State Contamination in Memory-Augmented LLM Agents
evidence: Sec. 4.2 and App. B.5: a write-side gate is applied after generation and before a message enters the transcript or memory (Eq. 11), storing it as-is, replacing it with a placeholder or rewriting it; the read side will "Sanitize the conditioning state before generation".
method: Measures toxicity persistence through summarised memory in multi-agent LLM graphs (memory laundering); mitigates with read-side sanitizer, write-side gate, memory gating/rewriting and DPO fine-tuning.
evaluation: 1,400 paired simulated rollouts, 7 topologies, gpt-4o-mini and Llama-3.1-8B; vs no intervention and output filter; turn-final toxicity 0.1207 to 0.0106, P95 0.9048 to 0.1025; one A100; no latency.
contribution: Shows that toxic content survives below-threshold in summarised agent memory and re-emerges downstream, and that gating both transcript and memory writes cuts propagated toxicity by about an order of magnitude.
flag: The hazard is toxic text propagation (Detoxify score, tau=0.5), not unsafe actions - maintainer to decide whether that counts as cascading failure under (c). The gate blocks or rewrites memory/transcript writes, not tool actions; no halt, rollback, deferral or human escalation. Evidence is offline simulated Reddit-style rollouts with no tools or deployed memory, single toxicity judge. No per-message latency or gate overhead measured. The text says the full system strictly dominates, but Transcript+Memory has lower SPG (0.0012 vs 0.0014). The output-filter baseline also replaces messages before storage, so it partly overlaps the write gate. The rewriting model is unspecified. Read through a summarising fetch; verify quotes.

title: Beyond Safety Filtering: Control Barrier Function-Informed Reinforcement Learning for Connected and Automated Vehicles
evidence: Sec. I: "instead of using CBFs as a posterior safety filter, we convert the CBF constraint satisfaction degree into an RL reward signal"; Sec. IV-D: activation degree computed "by solving the safety-filter optimization to obtain a correction magnitude but executing the unfiltered action".
method: CBF constraint satisfaction degree (truncated Taylor CBF) is turned into a reward for multi-agent PPO (centralised critic, decentralised actors) for connected automated vehicles; no filter at execution.
evaluation: Simulated four-way multi-lane intersection (SigmaRL), kinematic bicycle; baselines distance and TTC reward penalties; best reward 8.5 vs 7.7/4.5; CBF activation degree 1.3% vs 1.9%/10.0%; no hardware or latency.
contribution: Uses control-barrier-function satisfaction as a training reward for multi-agent RL at an intersection, lowering would-be safety-filter activation to 1.3% versus 1.9% (TTC) and 10.0% (distance) reward baselines.
flag: BORDERLINE - maintainer should decide. Explicitly NOT a runtime interceptor: the CBF is a training reward, so (a) fails by the protocol's own wording. Kept on (c): multi-vehicle safety is the primary claim and CBF activation degree (hypothetical filter intervention rate) is reported against two baselines. But no collision rate or count is reported (N_col defined, never tabulated), headline outcome is total reward (mean 7.2 vs -2.3/-2.8, std 1.1 vs 3.3/3.7), number of vehicles, test episodes and seeds are not stated, simulator not named in text. If activation degree is not accepted as a safety metric this is E2; if training-time safety is out of scope it is E1. Relevance to RQ5 is as a filter-free comparator only.

title: Position: A Three-Layer Probabilistic Assume-Guarantee Architecture Is Structurally Required for Safe LLM Agent Deployment
evidence: "any violation triggers corrective action or safe-stop" (Sec. 3.1, Functional Layer); user-layer disposition is ok/clarify/deny (App. A.1.1)
method: Position paper: three-layer (user, operational/ODD, functional/CBF) assume-guarantee architecture for LLM agents with probabilistic composition bounds B1-B4 on joint layer reliability.
evaluation: No empirical evaluation. Bounds computed from assumed layer probabilities (0.95/0.90/0.92 giving 0.770-0.857); benchmark figures are cited from other papers. No hardware, no latency.
contribution: Argues that safe LLM-agent deployment needs three contract-linked gating layers and derives illustrative probabilistic bounds on their composed reliability, without implementing or testing the architecture.
flag: Position paper with no implementation; every number is assumed or arithmetic on assumed inputs (App. C says illustrative). Single-agent by construction (Sec. 4). Human takeover is only mentioned as an ODD fallback, not evaluated; handoff gap cell is generous. Latency left as future work (Sec. 5).

title: Guiding Neuro-Symbolic Scenario Generation with Spatio-Temporal Logic
evidence: Abstract: STRELGen is "a scalable framework for the targeted generation of safety-critical driving scenarios" - offline test generation, nothing intercepts an action.
method: STRELGen: gradient ascent on the latent input of a pretrained joint multi-agent trajectory diffusion model to raise STREL (spatio-temporal reach and escape logic) robustness, with a likelihood penalty.
evaluation: Argoverse 2, 3 validation scenes, 30 samples per configuration; vs unguided diffusion only; potential collisions (under 0.9 m) 5/19/7 vs 0/5/0 of 30; 0.15 s per gradient step; hardware unstated.
contribution: Guides a pretrained multi-agent trajectory diffusion model with spatio-temporal logic robustness to generate safety-critical driving scenarios offline; it does not detect or intercept hazards at runtime.
flag: Borderline (b)/(c): the base model jointly generates all agents' futures, but the paper reports no predictive-accuracy metric and no hazard detector; it creates hazards for testing and tests no driving policy. If the maintainer reads it as (c) safety evaluation, note only 3 scenes, a distance proxy rather than collisions, and a single unguided baseline. 'Challenging' share about 13.6% unguided vs 100% guided (Sec 4.3). Text cites 'Table 4' for what is captioned Figure 4. Tag diffusion-guidance is new.

title: Intent-First Aerial V2V for Tactical Coordination and Separation: Protocol and Performance Under Density and Disturbance
evidence: "Backstop behavior activates when predicted separation or time-to-conflict falls below" scenario thresholds (Sec. IV-C); "Messages that fail authentication, replay, sequence, integrity, or expiry checks are rejected before control use" (Sec. III-D).
method: Intent-first all-airborne C-V2X sidelink beacons (10 Hz, authenticated, freshness-bounded) feeding a tactical separation controller; stale or low-confidence messages get reduced authority; shared onboard last-resort backstop.
evaluation: 141,944 hybrid sim-field runs, 50-250 veh/km2, 6 airborne nodes; baselines strategic-only (A), non-V2V tactical (B1), auth-off ablation; conflicts 21.33 to 1.00 at 150/km2; latency p95 88-131 ms nominal, 250 ms deadline.
contribution: Field-anchored study showing authenticated intent-sharing V2V cuts conflict events, false clearances and holds for dense drone traffic versus strategic-only and non-V2V tactical control, until link deadline misses force backstop-heavy fallback.
flag: Borderline. The contribution is a communication protocol, not an interceptor: the backstop is shared by all baselines and the paper never says what it does to the commanded trajectory, so runtime_interceptor=no. Primacy test for (c) is arguable - throughput is co-primary with conflict/separation outcomes, and no collision or loss-of-separation rate is given (conflict events, minimum separation, backstop activations instead). (d) rests on link latency and a 250 ms deadline, not on inference compute; no onboard processor or controller compute time reported, so edge deployment not credited. Details deferred to a supplement I did not see; Fig. 8 aggregate values are graphical only. Severe impairment gives deadline-miss 0.76-0.91. Abstract has no numbers.

title: Time-To-Reach Separation and Safety Filtering for Safe, Fair, and Efficient Multi-Agent Coordination
evidence: "a reactive mechanism that minimally modifies the guidance command only when necessary" (Sec. IV-A, safety filter layer)
method: Air-taxi corridor merging: time-to-reach separation guidance staggers arrivals by 10 s, then a pairwise CBF-QP safety filter (decentralized, priority-coordinated or centralized, with slack fallback) minimally overrides the guidance control.
evaluation: 2D simulation, 8 vehicles, 100 scenarios; guidance x filter ablation; unsafe rate 7.836 percent (unfiltered greedy) to 0.058 (sep+Prio), 0.044 (sep+Cent); QP 4.0-5.2 ms, Cent 36-42.5 ms, AMD 9800X3D.
contribution: Combines reachability-based time-to-reach separation with decentralized, prioritized or centralized CBF-QP safety filtering for multi-vehicle corridor merging, cutting unsafe-time rate from 7.8 percent to under 0.1 percent in simulation.
flag: Clear include: runtime filter between guidance and execution, quantitative violation rate, full guidance-by-filter ablation (Table III). Caveats. Simulation only, 2D, 8 homogeneous vehicles, simulator unnamed. The filter is relaxed with slack variables, so it does not guarantee safety and violations remain nonzero in every configuration; standard deviations exceed the means (e.g. 0.058 +/- 0.327). The claim that centralized is safest holds only with TTR-sep guidance; with greedy guidance Cent is the worst filter (0.742 vs Dec 0.194). Safety is bought with throughput: last-arrival time rises from 77.77 s to 96-100 s and mean delay from about 1.1-1.5 s to 6.3-7.3 s - useful RQ5 data. QP times are on a desktop CPU, not edge hardware, and the paper has no deadline or jitter analysis, so I did not credit latency/jitter or edge cells. TTR is time-to-reach a corridor, not time-to-irreversibility, so that cell is not credited. No halt (aircraft cannot stop) and no human takeover. Table III labels d_min in km while separation is 500 m; values look consistent with km (0.593) but check. Offline reachability needs an RTX 5090 for up to 30 minutes. Read via a summarising fetch tool, so check the quote and table values against the PDF.

title: Heartbeat-Bound Hierarchical Credentials: Cryptographic Revocation for AI Agent Swarms
evidence: Sec. 1: revocation 'occurs naturally when heartbeat generation ceases, without requiring a kill signal to reach every sub-agent'; Sec. 6: under HBHC 'workers execute 48 calls during an 11.9 s zombie window' and zero afterward versus 175 post-kill calls under OAuth 2.0.
method: Sub-agent credentials are valid only with a fresh parent-signed heartbeat; verifiers check offline with cached key and local clock, so stopping the orchestrator revokes the whole delegation tree within a bounded window.
evaluation: Python/Rust implementations on Apple M2, tc-netem WAN, GPT-4o-mini 49-agent swarm; baselines OAuth 2.0 and guardrail-only; zombie window 7.8 s vs 8 s bound; verification 0.156 ms mean, 0.368 ms P99; FPRR 0.15% at 10% drop.
contribution: Heartbeat-bound hierarchical credentials give agent swarms offline-verifiable, bounded-time cascading revocation: zero post-window tool calls versus 175 under OAuth 2.0, at 0.16 ms per verification and 0.71% end-to-end overhead.
flag: Gates authentication of tool calls, not the action itself, and does not detect anything: Sec. 3.2 'HBHC does not detect misalignment', so an external monitor or human must stop the orchestrator; detection latency is unbounded. Effect is a bounded delay (48 calls still ran inside the 11.9 s window), not an instant halt. Most baseline rows (OCSP, SPIFFE, short-lived certs) are analytical design values, only OAuth and guardrail-only are measured. Fail-secure default can freeze legitimate swarms; false-revocation 1.24% at 30% drop. Proofs pen-and-paper. (d) not claimed: latency is crypto overhead on a workstation, not edge inference. multi-agent state cell is generous (delegation tree, not a state model). One LLM, sandboxed workload.

title: Blind Spots in the Guard: How Domain-Camouflaged Injection Attacks Evade Detection in Multi-Agent LLM Systems
evidence: Sec 5: "Llama Guard 3, a production safety classifier, detects zero camouflage payloads"; few-shot detection falls from 0.938 to 0.097 under domain-camouflaged injection.
method: Attacker LLM rewrites injection payloads in the document's domain vocabulary and authority style; a few-shot LLM detector and Llama Guard 3 are scored, with a three-agent debate amplification test.
evaluation: 45 tasks (finance, legal, QA), 8000+ trials, Llama 3.1 8B and Gemini 2.0 Flash; detection 0.938->0.097 and 1.000->0.556; Llama Guard 0.000; augmentation lifts to 0.194/0.904; no latency.
contribution: Domain-camouflaged prompt injections cut runtime injection-detection rates from 0.94 to 0.10 and evade Llama Guard 3 entirely, with three-agent debate amplifying the surviving attacks.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes, LLM agents and a three-agent debate system guarded by an LLM injection detector. The detectors only emit verdicts; no blocking, veto or deferral is implemented or measured, so (a) is at best nominal and I did not credit it. No false-positive rate is reported, so the augmented detector's gain cannot be traded against false halts. Multi-agent debate amplification is a secondary finding, so the (c) primacy test is borderline. Single author, LLM judge for attack success, Llama Guard 3 numbers use proxy payloads because the originals were not persisted, and Table 1 reports 0.556 where the Exp 4 text says 0.548.

title: Superhuman Safe and Agile Racing through Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
evidence: Reward function section: "Collisions with walls, gates, or other agents terminate the episode"; no shield, filter, override or fallback controller is described, and safety is learned through reward shaping and league-play.
method: Multi-agent RL (PPO league-play with a Perceiver opponent encoder) for quadrotor racing; collision avoidance learned via terminal collision penalty and proximity reward; 50 Hz offboard policy.
evaluation: 64,000 four-drone sim races plus real mocap races vs a champion pilot; crash rate 23.30 vs 77.99 percent single-agent; 16.065 s vs 17.109 s; RTX 4090; 40 ms delay randomised.
contribution: League-play multi-agent reinforcement learning yields quadrotor racing policies that beat a champion human pilot head-to-head while crashing far less than single-agent or independent-learning baselines.
flag: BORDERLINE on (c): title leads with Safe, and crash/completion rate against baselines and ablations is a headline outcome (23.30 vs 77.99 percent average crash rate; 85 percent first-gate collision for single-agent). I recommend E1 because the primary claim is superhuman racing performance and safety is a training-time reward term, not a certificate, detector or runtime mechanism - maintainer may reasonably include under (c) instead. Completion falls to 56 percent at 8 agents and 90.87 percent with 4 real drones. Human trials are tiny (4-5 per configuration). Inference is offboard on a desktop with mocap state, so no edge deployment; no end-to-end latency reported. No safety pilot or takeover protocol. Minor inconsistency: 3-inch propellers vs 7.37 cm in Table S3.

title: Voluntary Collusion with Secret Tools in Competing LLM Agents
evidence: Sec 3, Table 1: ten of twelve LLMs accept both explicitly secret, unfair tools at >=98% under the baseline framing V0; Appendix E leaves "design and evaluation of targeted defences" to follow-up work.
method: Evaluation framework offering LLM agents optional secret tools (secret communication channel, secret strategic hint) under a two-sided consent protocol; measures voluntary adoption and downstream collusive play.
evaluation: 12 LLMs, Liar's Bar and Cleanup games, up to 4 agents; no-tool baseline, six offer framings V0-V5, fair/benign tool controls; acceptance rates, reward equality, challenge rate; H100 GPUs, no latency.
contribution: Shows most tested LLM agents voluntarily adopt secret collusion tools (>=98% for 10 of 12 models), and that collusion cuts reward equality in Cleanup from 0.937 to 0.670 against a no-tool baseline.
flag: Hazard measurement only, no detector or mitigation: monitoring is post-hoc regex coding; framing variants V4/V5 are prompt manipulations, not defences. Fits (c) via safety evaluation of LLM agents with a no-tool baseline; maintainer should confirm that an adoption/collusion rate counts as the hazard-rate metric. Gameplay results only on 7-8B models, 3 seeds; pooled per-game tests treat dependent games as independent (Remark H.1); frontier-model appendix uses 10 calls per cell. PDF text truncated near end of Appendix Q (V5 prompt not read). Qwen2.5-72B and Claude-Sonnet-4.5 refuse at 0% under V0 but flip under neutral framing (Table 3).

title: Got a Secret? LLM Agents Can't Keep It: Evaluating Privacy in Multi-Agent Systems
evidence: Introduction: shifting from single-turn to multi-turn social evaluation amplifies privacy violations; Section 4.4 measures violations as an emergent property of interaction trajectories.
method: Moltbook-style simulated social platform with 2533 LLM agents, per-agent memory files and a twelve-function tool suite; a stateless LLM judge scores every write against the agent's private persona profile.
evaluation: 2533 agents over 25 simulated days plus 7000 controlled traces, 7 frontier models; single-turn CIMemories baseline and redaction-instruction ablation; violation rate 19.95% vs 45.30%; no hardware or latency.
contribution: Shows privacy leakage by LLM agents is an emergent property of sustained multi-agent social interaction: violations more than double versus single-turn benchmarks, spread between agents, and survive prompt-level safeguards.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - LLM agents are themselves the studied system. No runtime gate anywhere: leakage is judged post hoc and memory sandboxing plus norm monitoring are future work, so (a) fails and inclusion rests on (c) as safety evaluation of LLM agents. Contagion multiplier is about 8x in the abstract and Section 6 but 5.1x in the Introduction. Leakage labels come from a single LLM judge (gpt-5-nano) with no human validation, and the authors call reported violations an upper bound.

title: RiskFlow: Fast and Faithful Safety-Critical Traffic Scenario Generation
evidence: Abstract: guidance works by 'steering selected critical agents toward risky interactions while regularizing off-road behavior' - an offline adversarial scenario generator, nothing gates an acting system.
method: One-step MeanFlow generator of multi-agent acceleration/yaw-rate sequences decoded by unicycle dynamics, with test-time adversarial and map guidance on TTC-ranked critical agents.
evaluation: nuScenes, 100 validation scenes, tbsim closed loop; vs STRIVE, BITS, CTG, CTG++, CCDiff; composite CS/RS scores; 48.6 s per scene on RTX 4090 (CTG++ 18.16 min).
contribution: RiskFlow generates safety-critical multi-agent traffic scenarios in a single MeanFlow pass with TTC-ranked adversarial guidance, running 2.05-22.42x faster than diffusion baselines on nuScenes.
flag: Scenario generation for testing, not a safety mechanism or predictor under evaluation. SCR, ORR, ADE, FDE and KDD are defined but only composite CS/RS appear in tables, so no raw collision or predictive-accuracy numbers. RiskFlow CS is not best in most columns (e.g. Full K: 0.35 vs STRIVE 0.91). SCR uses 10 s rollouts while horizon is 52 steps (5.2 s), unexplained. Table 4 checkmark layout ambiguous in extracted text. If the maintainer reads it as (b), it still lacks a predictive-accuracy metric (E2).

title: Certifiable Semantic Agreement Among LLM Agents: What the Admissibility Instrument Decides
evidence: Section 5 protocol: the round emits a typed abort (verdict_below_quorum, insufficient_signers, admissibility_failed) and no soft or partial commit, and never commits a verdict group below a 2f+1 certificate.
method: H-CSC commit protocol for an LLM agent committee: canonicalise and embed proposals, group by verdict, extract a within-verdict semantic core at 0.65 rad, then semantic commit, verdict commit or abort under 2f+1.
evaluation: 50-100 Climate-FEVER tasks, n=10 f=2 gpt-4o-mini agents, static and rushing adversaries; baselines majority vote and certificate-wrapped majority; commit 0.90, invalid commits 0.02-0.00; lexical admissibility AUROC 0.865-0.982 vs encoder 0.621-0.744.
contribution: Certifies agreement among LLM agents at the level of meaning under 2f+1 Byzantine certificates, and shows the admissibility instrument, not the protocol, decides what such certification can actually catch.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - a committee of gpt-4o-mini agents. (a) is borderline: the gate halts commit emission and keeps proposals out of the core rather than vetoing an agent's own action, so a maintainer may read this as consensus rather than runtime interception; (c) holds either way. The authors disclose a tie-break vulnerability in their own protocol, Corollary 5.1 states no coverage or safety advantage over certificate-wrapped majority, Family II poisoning commits 10/10, and several results are pilot scale (8-10 tasks). No latency or hardware figures; implementation not released.

title: Semantic Quorum Assurance: Collective Certification for Non-Deterministic AI Infrastructure
evidence: "If it fails, the request is blocked and logged, returning an HTTP 403 Forbidden error to the calling proposer agent." (Sec. 9.4)
method: LLM-proposed infrastructure mutations go to a diverse read-only validator-agent panel; a risk-adaptive quorum with critical-archetype veto and BLS-signed certificate is checked by a Kubernetes admission gate that blocks failures.
evaluation: 500 synthetic Kubernetes/database/IAM scenarios, 1,850 held-out trials; vs self-review, static OPA, homogeneous quorum; unsafe approval 0.3% vs 18.5%, false rejection 3.1%; p50 1.45-4.12 s; no hardware.
contribution: A quorum of diverse validator agents with veto, enforced at an admission gate, cut unsafe approvals of agent-proposed infrastructure changes from 18.5% to 0.3% on 500 synthetic scenarios, at seconds of added latency.
flag: Check: (1) the safety numbers come from offline scoring of validator decisions on labelled synthetic template scenarios; I could not confirm the admission webhook was exercised on a live cluster. (2) 0.3% of about 600 unsafe trials is roughly 2 trials. (3) Abstract p50 of 4.12 s for the high bucket and that bucket's p95/p99 were not legible in the extracted Table 3; low is 1.45/2.08/2.64 s, medium 2.36/3.42/4.31 s. (4) High-bucket cost reads $0.020 in the table but $0.080 in Sec. 11.2. (5) No hardware reported; latency is to certificate construction, not end-to-end admission. (6) Thresholds (theta_veto, tau, epsilon) have no numeric values. (7) Multi-agent is on the validator side; a single proposer is evaluated, so multi-agent state cell not credited. (8) Human review is only an assumed latency comparator (12 min p50), no human study; escalation and break-glass are described, not evaluated, so human handoff cell not credited. Seconds-scale latency is far from RQ1. Under full validator correlation unsafe approval rises to 8.4% (Table 5). Ablations are called preliminary by the authors.

title: Individual Control Barrier Functions-Guided Diffusion Model for Safe Offline Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
evidence: "we propose a safe offline multi-agent reinforcement learning algorithm that embeds neural individual control barrier functions into the diffusion model to enhance safety during trajectory generation" (Abstract)
method: MADIFF-based multi-agent trajectory diffusion with per-agent neural control barrier functions learned jointly; CBF hinge loss is backpropagated through denoised states; actions recovered by inverse dynamics.
evaluation: Simple Spread (4 datasets) and Safe MAMuJoCo 2ant, 4ant, 2halfcheetah (3 datasets each), 5 seeds; baselines MA-TD3BC and OMAR; normalised episode reward and cost. No hardware or latency.
contribution: Embeds learned per-agent control barrier functions in a multi-agent diffusion planner for offline RL, lowering safety cost on Simple Spread and Safe Multi-Agent MuJoCo against offline MARL baselines while keeping reward competitive.
flag: NOT a runtime interceptor: the CBF is a training loss on generated trajectories, nothing filters actions at execution, so (a) fails; included only under (c) as a learned multi-agent safety certificate with cost as primary outcome - borderline, maintainer to decide. Weak evidence: baselines are not safety-aware and plain MADIFF (the backbone) is not a baseline, so there is NO ablation isolating the CBF. Ours is not lowest cost on 2ant-medium (0.80 vs OMAR 0.35) or 4ant-good (0.64 vs 0.25). Only Simple Spread cost is collisions (0.00 on expert, medium, random; 0.30 on md); MuJoCo 'cost' is a speed limit, not an inter-agent hazard. No formal guarantee (authors defer 'certified closed-loop safety' to future work). Diffusion sampling cost at inference not reported. Short paper, IFAC-style format.

title: Multi-Agent Embodied Autonomous Driving (MAEAD): From V2X Information Exchange to Shared World Models
evidence: Sec 2.1 calls the work 'a structured narrative review' and not 'a meta-analysis or pooled performance comparison'; Conclusion: 'This survey has examined multi-agent embodied autonomous driving (MAEAD) as a system-level transition.'
method: Narrative survey of about 400 publications on cooperative driving, organised around shared world models with three evidence criteria: state alignment, intent/plan alignment, coordinated downstream action.
evaluation: No original experiments, baselines or metrics; evaluation settings of cited works are tabulated only; latency budget shown as schematic without numbers.
contribution: Surveys multi-agent cooperative driving through a shared-world-model lens and argues agreement on a plan is a safety claim only when an independent runtime envelope checks executed motion.
flag: Survey, E3 on its own statement. Read characters 0-200000 of 276443; the final segment (likely Sec 9 tail, conclusion and references) was not read, though the conclusion was visible in the second segment. Useful as a pointer list: Sec 6.4.2 and 9.1 call for runtime monitors, barrier/reachability filters, onboard fallback and latency breakdown reporting. No human takeover discussion found.

title: Resilient Consensus in Agentic AI
evidence: Abstract: wrapping the agents with classical resilient consensus filters improves agreement; Section 4.1 reports the global MSR filter helps tremendously, reaching about 100% consensus.
method: Frames LLM agent agreement as a Byzantine consensus game and wraps Llama-3.2-3B agents in classical global and local MSR trimming filters that discard the f extreme neighbour values each round.
evaluation: Synthetic scalar consensus, 15 honest agents, complete and general digraphs, 10-30 trials; baseline is unfiltered prompting; consensus probability 0-90% baseline vs 90-100% filtered; temperature, horizon and f-misspecification ablations; no latency.
contribution: Shows prompted LLM agents fail Byzantine consensus even inside the classical N>=3B+1 safe region, and that wrapping them in MSR trimming filters restores agreement where topology robustness is weak.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - Llama-3.2-3B agents. (a) is borderline: the MSR filter trims incoming neighbour values each round, which is runtime input filtering rather than a veto on an agent's own action, and the paper itself lists a safety layer as future work. (c) rests on consensus-failure probability standing in for a hazard rate; there is no collision, violation or intervention rate. Small scale: 10-30 trials per cell, no confidence intervals in the tables, exact per-B values only in figures. No new theorems, no hardware or latency.

title: ROSA-RL: Uncertainty-Aware Roundabout Optimized Speed Advisory with Reinforcement Learning
evidence: Sec. III-A: the ego vehicle "directly executes the issued speed advisories"; after the conflict zone "control reverts to SUMO's default dynamics".
method: Transformer occupancy predictor (5 s horizon, per-second scores) feeds a PPO speed-advisory policy whose state includes prediction confidence; no veto, halt or override logic.
evaluation: SUMO replay of openDD rdb1 roundabout, 200 test scenarios; 5 baselines (MB-GT, RL-GT, MB-TP, MB-OP, RL-OP); energy, fuel, travel time, waiting, stops; no hardware or latency reported.
contribution: Uncertainty-aware RL speed advisory for roundabout approach cuts stops by 80% and waiting time by 89.9% in optimizable scenarios, but is an efficiency advisory rather than a safety mechanism.
flag: Efficiency paper: no collision/violation/intervention metric anywhere; outcomes are energy (BEV -85.6%), ICE fuel -17.5%, travel time -5.9%, waiting -89.9%, stops -80.0% vs no advisory. Occupancy F1 0.94 at 1 s falling to 0.58 at 5 s (Table I) could be read as a multi-agent predictor (b) but it is occupancy classification, not a world model, and is not the primary claim. Single controlled ego; V2X latency and human compliance are future work only. Real-time capability claimed but not quantified.

title: Scaling Learning-based AEB with Massive Unlabeled Data
evidence: AEB "autonomously applies braking to mitigate or avoid crashes" (Sec. I); the model is a "triggering policy" with decision y = I[p > tau] (Sec. III-A), run via TensorRT "on NVIDIA DRIVE Orin and Thor" at 20 Hz (Sec. V).
method: Learned AEB trigger: spatio-temporal attention classifier over 60-frame history, trained semi-supervised (meta-feedback pseudo-labels, noise-aware decoupling, kinematic gating, confidence penalty) on up to 1B unlabeled fleet windows.
evaluation: Log-replay sim, 2000 accident/6000 false-trigger scenarios; vs rule-based, supervised, PL, Noisy Student: S_safe 67.80, S_comf 97.67 (rule 47.51/96.23); Orin/Thor 20 Hz; fleet >1e9 km, 35% AFM gain.
contribution: A semi-supervised training recipe that scales a learned emergency-braking trigger to a billion unlabeled fleet windows, raising simulated crash mitigation over rule-based AEB without more false activations, deployed on production vehicles.
flag: Borderline E4: one ego vehicle and a single brake/no-brake trigger; other road users are inputs, so multi-agent is nominal. Kept because it is a sequential (60-frame) runtime trigger that brakes without driver input, deployed on embedded hardware. (d) is weak: 20 Hz timer-driven on Orin/Thor is stated but NO millisecond latency figure is given - drop (d) if an explicit latency number is required. The contribution is the training method, not the interceptor. Real-world numbers are unverifiable: absolute accident counts withheld "due to compliance review", only 35% relative AFM gain and shadow-mode PFR >100:1 over 10M km. Scaling result (Fig. 4, 1M-1B) has no numeric values in the text. S_comf is a false-activation severity score, not comfort. TTC appears only in the training-time pseudo-label gate (safe if TTC > 10) and the rule baseline, so time-to-irreversibility is not credited. Human role is post-hoc expert review of shadow-mode logs, not takeover, so no handoff cell. Proprietary data and simulator.

title: A Mixed-Reality Testbed for Autonomous Vehicles
evidence: "acts as a safety layer for arbitrary AV/CAV algorithms" (Section III)
method: Mixed-reality hardware-in-the-loop testbed pairing AgileX Limo robots with CARLA digital twins over ROS and a roadside unit, with a per-timestep CBF-QP projecting reference controls onto an admissible set.
evaluation: Hardware-in-the-loop fleets of 5, 10 and 12 vehicles, over half physical robots, 5 seeds; vs conservative CBF, aggressive CBF and IDM; success 1.00 vs 0.50-0.77; no latency measured.
contribution: A mixed-reality hardware-in-the-loop testbed where physical robots and CARLA agents share one road network, used to validate a CBF safety layer against hand-tuned and IDM baselines.
flag: Primarily a testbed paper - the CBF safety layer is a component rather than the primary claim - so inclusion rests on criterion (a) and on a composite success rate (reaching the destination without collision) rather than a collision count. The authors claim superiority "across all metrics and traffic densities" but Table I contradicts this at 5 cars, where Ours travel time 37.60 s exceeds IDM 34.8 s and aggressive 36.23 s. Despite the real-time framing the paper claims only "low-latency, bidirectional ROS communication" with no latency, jitter or delay measurement and no stated control frequency. Sensor-noise and weather results exist only in Figures 5 and 7 with no numbers in text, and there is no formal ablation. I did not credit edge deployment: the only onboard-compute detail (NVIDIA Orin Nano) comes from cited reference [12], not this paper. No human operator or override role is described.

title: Formal Verification of Learned Multi-Agent Communication Policies via Decision Tree Distillation
evidence: Sec. VII: "Our framework verifies a probabilistic abstraction, not neural policies directly" and "For deployment, we recommend pairing offline verification with runtime monitoring".
method: Offline pipeline: distil VQ-VIB multi-agent communication policies into CART decision trees, translate to PRISM DTMCs, check 18 PCTL properties compositionally. No runtime component.
evaluation: Grid drone target capture, N=3/5/7, 5 seeds. Baselines CommNet, TarMAC; feature and hyperparameter ablations. Fidelity 97.9%, 16/18 properties, collision 0.3%. i7-12700, 52 min offline for N=5.
contribution: Offline formal verification of learned multi-agent communication policies via decision-tree distillation and PRISM model checking, certifying 16 of 18 PCTL properties including a 0.3% collision bound for five gridworld drones.
flag: Borderline on (c): collision, separation and deadlock probabilities are verified (5/5 safety properties) with baselines, but safety is 5 of 18 properties, the headline is distillation fidelity and verifiability, and nothing detects or intercepts at runtime; shielding and runtime monitoring appear only as related work and a recommendation. If the maintainer reads offline certification as a learned safety certificate, this becomes an include on (c). Abstract/Sec. VIII fidelity advantage +11.6-13.6 pp does not match Table VI (97.9-84.7=13.2; Sec. VI-F says 13.2). Abstract deviation <=0.6 pp holds for safety properties and L1 only; L4 deviates 4.4 pp and C5 3.7 pp. Guarantee is on a tree abstraction the authors say is not formally conservative; Prop. 1 bound is vacuous by their own account. Timings are offline verification, not decision latency.

title: Distributed Model Predictive Control with Adaptive Safety Zones for Multi-Fleet Drone Operations
evidence: "Our approach employs model predictive control (MPC) with adaptive, speed-dependent safety zones. Each drone's safety radius scales with its braking distance." (Abstract)
method: Centralised and Gauss-Seidel distributed MPC for drone fleets with velocity-dependent safety radii as separation constraints; feasibility, Lyapunov stability and sphere-packing capacity bounds are proved.
evaluation: Simulation: passage, tunnel, and density scaling in 8 m cube, N=2..25, 4 configs x 20 runs; adaptive vs static radius; deadlock rate, feasible N, traversal time, step time (figures only).
contribution: Speed-dependent safety zones inside centralised and distributed MPC let a bounded airspace hold up to twice as many drones as fixed radii (20 vs 10 in simulation), with stability and capacity bounds.
flag: Fails (a): separation is a constraint inside the planner. Fails (c) primacy test: measured outcomes are capacity, deadlock/timeout rate, throughput and solver time; the only safety statement is one sentence, 'no constraint violations occur in any configuration', with no collision rate table. Static radius baseline deadlocks from N = 6 (centralised) or 8 (distributed), 100% at N = 10; adaptive centralised works to N = 20, distributed adaptive only to N = 11 (about 20% failures) and none at N >= 12. Tunnel traversal about 12 s to 9 s (25%). Step time grows exponentially and is shown only in log-scale figures, no numbers or hardware; authors say it is not real-time. Abstract claims support for 'mixed fleets with non-cooperative agents' and delays, but I found no experiment with non-cooperative agents or communication delay. Theory sections IV-V (proofs) skimmed, not checked. If the maintainer treats capacity under guaranteed separation as a safety outcome, this could be reconsidered under (c).

title: Conflict-Aware Switching for CBF-CLF-Based Multi-Goal Navigation
evidence: Switching selects which goal CLF enters the QP once a dwell time has elapsed and the conflict heuristic exceeds a threshold (Sec. III-B, Eq. 35); outcomes are completion time and timeout percentage (Sec. IV)
method: Conflict-aware goal-switching policy for CLF-CBF quadratic programs: a gradient cosine-similarity heuristic with Gaussian scaling and dwell time picks the least-conflicted goal to avoid deadlock.
evaluation: Simulation: single-agent obstacle cases; Monte Carlo 6-19 agents, 500 runs per case; baseline sequential goal policy; metrics completion time and timeouts (figures only); no hardware or latency.
contribution: A goal-switching rule for control-barrier and Lyapunov function controllers that changes the active objective when it conflicts with safety constraints, reducing deadlock in multi-goal navigation.
flag: Paper is about deadlock and completion time, not a safety outcome; no collision, violation or intervention rate is reported, and the CBF safety constraints are unchanged background. Almost no numeric results in the text: the only figure is an ambiguous timeout phrase (approx 33.4%) and the rest sits in plots. Internal inconsistencies: Scenario 3 iteration limit 10,000 in text vs N = 2000 in Table III; unicycle slack penalty 50.0 in text vs 10 in Table II. Multi-agent appears only in the Monte Carlo scenario. Authors note the sequential baseline is sometimes faster.

title: Cooperative-ORCA*: Real-Time Proactive Deadlock Avoidance for Continuous-Space Multi-Agent Navigation
evidence: Section Dependency Detection: a corridor dependency "will force one agent to wait" at the corridor entrance until the conflicting agent clears; ORCA replaces each preferred velocity with a collision-free one.
method: ORCA* reactive velocity-space avoidance augmented with precomputed MAPF-LNS guidance paths, corridor dependencies that hold agents at entrances, drift mode, yield cells and an ECBS replanning fallback.
evaluation: Simulation only, 10-200 agents, four grid maps, 50 instances each; baselines ORCA*, ORCA*-MAPF; ablations LNS-ORCA*, NoDrift; success rate, flowtime, fallback calls; EPYC-Milan server, no ms figures.
contribution: Adding precomputed corridor dependencies to ORCA* makes agents wait proactively, keeping success near 1.0 on maps where ORCA* deadlocks and cutting MAPF fallback calls from 65.75 to 0.06 on Gap at 55 agents.
flag: Runtime holding/waiting exists, so runtime_interceptor is yes, but the paper's claim and measured outcome are deadlock and success rate, not a hazard rate - fails the (c) primacy test and (a) is a stretch (wait rule is part of the planner). No collision-rate metric reported. Most numbers are figure-only; only Table 1 fallback counts and a few approximate success values are in text. Abstract claim of 3-4 orders of magnitude fewer MAPF calls holds for Gap and Warehouse at 55 agents but not Warehouse at 200 (1513.0 vs 364.55). Step time said to be almost identical to ORCA* with no absolute value. Maintainer may prefer runtime_interceptor no.

title: MANGO: Automated Multi-Agent Test Oracle Generation for Vision-Language-Action Models
evidence: Sec. IV: "The VLA independently generates the actions to control the robot"; Sec. VII: "motion-quality properties, such as trajectory smoothness, contact forces, or collision avoidance, require additional specifications".
method: Three-module LLM pipeline (generator, assessors, judge) that decomposes task instructions into atomic tasks and generates executable fine-grained test oracles for single-robot VLA manipulation; passive verdicts, no intervention.
evaluation: LIBERO_10 and RoboCasa, 34 tasks, 2814 executions; single-model baselines and 3 ablations; oracle accuracy 0.91, F1 0.93, localization 0.78; generation takes hundreds of seconds; EPYC 7773X, RTX A6000.
contribution: Multi-agent LLM pipeline that generates executable step-level test oracles for vision-language-action manipulation policies, agreeing with benchmark end-state oracles at 0.91 accuracy and localizing the first failed step at 0.78.
flag: Multi-agent here means the LLM generator/assessor/judge roles, not multiple robots; the system under test is one manipulator. Oracles judge task completion, not safety, and the paper says collision avoidance is out of scope. They can be evaluated during execution but never halt or override the robot. Not a safety evaluation of LLM/tool-calling agents in the sense of (c). Key numbers: validity 0.950/1.000, executability 0.790/0.933 (LIBERO_10/RoboCasa) vs 0.130/0.117 and 0.113/0.008 for the single-model baseline; TP 1667, TN 884, FP 166, FN 97. Internal inconsistencies seen: LIBERO_10 executability 0.790 in Table I vs 0.800 in the ablation table; ablation validity 0.780 in text vs 0.680 in Table IV; 340 failing executions sampled vs 336 in the localization table. The evaluated VLA model was not identified in the text I read.

title: From Detection to Action: Using LLM Agents for Fault-Tolerant Control
