evidence: Section 3.3 Validation Agent: corrective actions are approved or revised before actuation, and if no safe plan emerges within the latency budget control is handed over to the safety system.
method: Agentic LLM framework for active fault-tolerant control: monitoring, planning and action agents with Graph RAG over a CPSMod ontology and digital-twin pre-execution simulation, plus a deterministic validation gate before actuation.
evaluation: Simulated Festo mixing module and CSTR, 10 trials per fault; only GPT-4.1-mini vs GPT-4o-mini compared; success 60/60 and 28/30 vs 51/60 and 23/30; planning 2.4 s, action 2.1-3.0 s; hardware not reported.
contribution: Turns fault detections into validated recovery actions by pairing LLM planning agents with ontology-grounded retrieval and digital-twin simulation, gating every corrective command against interlocks and dynamic feasibility before actuation.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - the gate validates LLM-generated recovery plans, although the plant runs conventional PID loops and the monitoring agent is deterministic. Most likely overturn is the evaluation floor: the only comparison is GPT-4.1-mini against GPT-4o-mini plus fault-free runs, with no conventional, RL or ablated-component baseline, so a maintainer could call this exclude-E2. (d) is credited on an explicit latency budget with timeout handover, but latencies are 2-50 s, the authors say this precludes hard real-time, and the LLMs are cloud-hosted with no edge deployment. Handoff is to an automated safety system, not a person, so (e) fails. Discussion claims 100% success for GPT-4.1-mini while Table 2 shows 28/30, and Table 1 lists 80% recovery where the text says 85%.

title: A Physics-Grounded Benchmark for Multi-Agent Dynamics in World Models
evidence: Abstract: the benchmark pairs about 25K synthetic and 12K real collision sequences with diagnostics for spatio-temporal consistency, momentum and kinetic energy conservation, and world-dynamics integrity of generated rollouts.
method: CrashTwin benchmark: CARLA and real crash collision sequences plus a calibration-free 3D reconstruction pipeline that scores video world-model rollouts for physics violations, with LoRA physics post-training of Cosmos-Predict2-2B.
evaluation: 300 synthetic plus 44 real clips over 8 open and proprietary world models; warp, momentum, angular and energy residuals and instance stability; post-training ablation momentum 0.8890 to 0.6479; reconstruction ATE 2.63 m vs 3.89 m tracker; 8x A100, 13-168 s per video.
contribution: Benchmarks whether generative world models obey physics when rolling out multi-agent collisions, showing high perceptual quality coexists with severe momentum and energy violations that physics-aware post-training only partly closes.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: which - none, and none is claimed; this is criterion (b) method and architecture evidence only, so RQ5 is held at 1 and no prevention is credited. There is no runtime mechanism of any kind. The world models' own predictive accuracy is never measured: Table 3 and Table 11 report the reconstruction pipeline's error against simulator ground truth, not displacement error of predicted futures, so the maintainer should check whether the Pillar 2 direct predictive measure is satisfied. Clip counts are inconsistent (12.6K real in text versus 38,349 total in Table 1), and the 2AFC human-agreement accuracy is defined in Eq. 8 but never reported numerically.

title: A Tutorial on Autonomous Fault-Tolerant Control Using Knowledge-Grounded LLM Agents
evidence: Sec. 3.1: "The action is applied only if zt = accept."; Sec. 6.3: "First, the LLM never holds execution authority."
method: LLM as a constrained supervisory planner for process-plant fault recovery; every proposed action is checked by an external symbolic or simulation-based validator before actuation, with an engineered safety fallback once the reprompt budget is exhausted.
evaluation: None. Two open Python environments (a three-tank mixing module and a CSTR with injectable faults such as fouling and pump degradation) are described qualitatively; no experiments, baselines, ablations or metrics; latency appears only as design budgets of tens of seconds.
contribution: Tutorial framework in which an LLM supervisory planner never holds execution authority: an external validator accepts or rejects each proposed action before actuation, with two released process-control environments for testing.
flag: Title and body both self-identify as a tutorial and the Introduction states "Rather than reporting performance figures, this paper focuses on what must be considered and tested", so E3 and E2 both apply and I took E3 as the more specific - the maintainer may prefer E2. Worth keeping in view as design evidence despite exclusion: the pre-actuation accept-or-reject gate plus engineered fallback is one of the cleanest statements of criterion (a) in the batch, and the two released environments could yield an includable follow-up. Caveats: no multi-agent aspect (a single supervisory LLM over one plant), so E4 is also arguable; the only human involvement is human-in-the-loop review during knowledge engineering (Sec. 6.2) and as future work (Sec. 8), not a takeover path, so I did not credit (e) or a human-handoff cell. My latency cell is design discussion only ("per-decision latency budgets of tens of seconds", Sec. 5.2 and 6.1) with nothing measured - drop it if the matrix requires measurement. Sec. 5.1 mentions runtime monitoring for slow setpoint ramps but never describes it halting anything.

title: Decentralized Geometric Control for Cable-Suspended Payload Transport with Adaptive Mass Estimation
evidence: Sec. V: the safety filter "operates on the force f_i in R^3 from Layer 1", "modifying GPAC output only when necessary and reducing constraint violations rather than strictly enforcing them".
method: Four-layer coordinator-free controller for N quadrotors carrying a cable-suspended payload: anti-swing position, SO(3) attitude, concurrent-learning mass estimation, ESO, plus a priority-ordered CBF-inspired gradient-projection safety filter on commanded force.
evaluation: Drake simulation, N=3 (scaling 2-6), wind; ablations without CL, ESO, CBF; payload RMSE 33.8 +/- 0.9 cm over 13 seeds; constraint margins; about 1200 FLOPs per filter cycle.
contribution: A decentralized geometric controller for multi-quadrotor cable-suspended transport with local mass estimation and a priority-ordered CBF-style safety filter, giving 33.8 cm payload tracking RMSE in simulation.
flag: Borderline: a genuine runtime filter exists and is ablated, but it is one layer of a tracking-control paper whose primary claim and metric is payload RMSE, so I recommend E1; include under (a) is defensible. Safety evidence is thin: removing the CBF raises RMSE 33.6 to 40.1 cm (+19%) and 'collapses the worst-case inter-agent clearance to 0.32 m' (vs 0.67 m with filter), a margin not a rate, seed count for the ablation not stated. The filter violates its own limits: clearance 0.67 m vs 0.8 m bound, tension min about 0.7 N vs 2 N, tilt 29-32 deg vs 28.6, cable angle 48 deg vs 34.4 limit (Table V says 49 with filter and 46 without, inconsistent with Table VII). Guarantee holds only for single-constraint activation. Clearance falls to 0.12 m at N=6. 'Low computational cost' is an O(N_c) FLOP estimate, no wall-clock timing; CBF Butterworth delay about 11 ms is a design constant. Simulation only; code promised at camera-ready. Agents are physically coupled through one payload, so multi-agent is cooperative control rather than independent agents.

title: Managed Autonomy at Runtime: Gear-Based Safety and Governance for Single- and Multi-Agent Cyber-Physical Systems
evidence: "REGULATED triggers a hardware emergency stop regardless of gate state." (multi-agent governance-state section, before Sec 8; small-caps spacing normalised)
method: EntropyRuntime: five execution gears with a utility gate and event-driven fallback between agent and environment; multi-agent layer maps collision-risk evidence to SMARt states, with consensus gate, velocity scaling and E-Stop.
evaluation: Simulated 3-arm UR5 cell, camera-drift faults, 10,000 episodes; baseline per-agent gate; detection 99.6% vs 2.1%, latency 12.2 vs 43.1 epochs, collisions 0% both; incremental ablation. No hardware.
contribution: A gear-based runtime gate with a multi-agent governance layer that slows, holds or emergency-stops robots as perceived collision risk rises, detecting 99.6% of injected sensor faults in a simulated three-arm cell.
flag: Check carefully. (1) Physical collision rate is 0.0% for BOTH baseline and governed runtime - the paper admits this is an artefact of the fault only affecting the monitor's camera, not the robot's motion - so the mechanism prevents nothing measurable; the benefit is anomaly detection and latency only. (2) Ablation shows the whole gain comes from one threshold (tau_meta) on a risk signal the baseline does not monitor; consensus gate, Lyapunov certificate and policy triple change no metric - baseline looks like a strawman. (3) Latency is in abstract epochs, no wall-clock, no hardware, simulation only, single seed 42. (4) Fault mixture 90%/10% is the authors' design choice; ASSISTED state never activates. (5) Single-agent LLM ablation (Table 1: 0 unsafe vs 27 for raw LLM over 100 cycles) gives no model, task or definition of unsafe - I could not find them; approximate values ('sigma ~ 1.2'). So cross-domain not credited. (6) Collision-freedom theorem holds only under validity conditions V1-V3. (7) Human review and E-Stop handoff mentioned, not evaluated. Company/independent authors, companion to queued doi:10.1007/s10846-026-02413-w (SMARt). Appendix proofs not read.

title: Anytime Plug-and-Play Control with Contract-Based Distributed MPC
evidence: Sec. IV.A: "the shared first-input constraint (31c) ensures that the closed-loop control action remains safety certified" - safety is a constraint inside each agent's MPC optimisation and no separate layer can veto, halt or defer the applied input.
method: Contract-based distributed MPC where each agent plans inside Voronoi-style cells and safety envelopes derived from neighbours' predicted trajectories, letting agents join or leave without the others' approval.
evaluation: Figure-eight track: up to eight agents in simulation, two to six 1/28-scale RC cars at 20 Hz on an i9-13900KS; results qualitative, no quantitative baseline, no collision count.
contribution: Contract-based distributed MPC that keeps collision-free guarantees while agents enter or leave the network at any time without the others' approval, shown on up to eight simulated and six physical race cars.
flag: E1 because collision avoidance is one constraint among several inside a plug-and-play coordination planner and the paper's subject is anytime join-and-leave, recursive feasibility and progress, not a safety mechanism; the protocol sends such planners to E1 explicitly. It would also fail protocol v1.6 independently (E2): no collision count, no violation count, no minimum-distance value in the text (Fig. 10a plots it but no number is given), no solve or computation times, and no quantitative baseline, with Table I a qualitative feature comparison the authors themselves call "not entirely fair". Hardware constraints were softened to stay feasible under real disturbances, a runtime deviation from the hard constraints the guarantees assume, and the paper does not analyse its safety effect. Agent count is inconsistent: the introduction says six to eight on hardware, Sec. V.B says two to six. Number of trials or repetitions is never stated. Publication year is not printed in the PDF; the record says 2026.

title: Dynamic Airspace Management for UAVs in Evolving Urban Environments: Collaborative Coordination and Human Safety
evidence: "UAVs independently make decisions based on partial observations" and "subsequently plan detailed paths" (Sec. 4.2); collision and human-fear terms are reward penalties (Sec. 3.2), with nothing checking outputs before execution
method: Pharos: MAPPO multi-agent RL allocates exclusive cuboid airspace to each UAV, trained with collision and human-fear penalties in the reward; UAVs then plan paths inside their space.
evaluation: 3D simulation of a 155x135 m Shanghai area, 10/20/30 UAVs, vs Ipopt, A-star, HAPPO, HATRPO. Fear 0.42/0.93/1.43 vs A-star 1.04/1.99/2.62; reward +60.59% vs Ipopt; ~100 ms inference on RTX A6000 server.
contribution: Presents Pharos, a multi-agent RL airspace-allocation scheme for urban UAVs that raises spatial utilisation and lowers a modelled human-fear measure relative to A-star path planning in simulation.
flag: Safety is a training-reward term, not a runtime mechanism, so (a) fails; (c) fails primacy/measurement: no collision or violation rate reported, collision avoidance judged only from visualisations; primary outcomes are reward, spatial entropy and a modelled 'human fear' score. ABSTRACT NUMBER CONFLICT: abstract says 52.72% fear reduction 'compared to the benchmark Ipopt' but Sec. 5.3.3 says vs A-star, and Tab. 2 shows Pharos has HIGHER fear than Ipopt (0.4228 vs 0.1720 at 10 UAVs). ~100 ms inference delay is on a 128-core EPYC/RTX A6000 server in simulation, not edge, and exceeds the paper's own 50 ms control-latency assumption. No ablation. 'Human safety' means bystanders, not human takeover. Maintainer could argue (c) if fear is accepted as a hazard metric.

title: Runtime Safety Filtering for Learned Small UAS Separation Policies under GNSS Degradation
evidence: "we select the feasible action closest to the policy's output" (Sec. V-B, action filtering)
method: Two runtime filters around a PPO-trained sUAS separation policy under bounded GNSS error: a discrete-time CBF action filter over three speed actions, and a worst-case observation filter.
evaluation: BlueSky simulator, about 65 aircraft per episode, 100 episodes per configuration; unfiltered policy baseline, R_max and alpha sweeps; mean NMAC per episode 0.24 to 0.02; no hardware or latency measured.
contribution: Compares CBF action filtering with worst-case observation filtering for a learned multi-aircraft separation policy under GNSS degradation, finding observation filtering cuts near-mid-air collisions by about 90 percent.
flag: The headline 90% NMAC reduction belongs to the observation filter, which corrects the policy INPUT and never overrides the action (Sec. V-C: output used directly); criterion (a) strictly rests on the CBF action filter, for which the body gives no numeric NMAC or separation values, only a claim of being statistically indistinguishable from nominal (Fig. 3) with no test reported. At R=0 the observation filter raises NMAC from 0.02 to 0.08. Override rate reaches 100% at R_max=1.0; infeasibility called negligible without a figure. Fig. 6 caption says R_max=0.4 while Table I uses R_max=0.7. Compute cost is asserted negligible against the 1 s decision step, never measured, so latency cell not credited. Filter is one-step only; heading error excluded from threat model; throughput cost not quantified. Each aircraft filters on its own local view, so multi-agent state is decentralised.

title: Engagement-Aware Agentic Pursuit-Evasion
evidence: A discrete-time CBF-QP filter "minimally invasively corrects each agent's nominal MPC command to preserve safety" (Section 3.4)
method: Per-team LLM planner assigns roles (DEFEND, NEUTRALIZE, CAPTURE, RECON; ATTACK, EVADE) each planning cycle; roles parameterise per-agent MPC costs and a slack-relaxed CBF-QP safety filter on commands.
evaluation: 2D double-integrator simulation, 4 pursuers vs 1-4 evaders, 6 LLMs vs rule-based planner; neutralizations, captures, evasions, touchdown rate (0.200-0.550), incomplete games; no collision metric, hardware or latency.
contribution: Couples a zero-shot LLM role planner with per-agent MPC and a control-barrier-function filter for multi-drone pursuit-evasion, comparing six LLMs against a rule-based tactical planner.
flag: A runtime CBF filter exists but is never the measured object: no collision, separation-violation or filter-intervention rate is reported and the filter is never ablated (both filters enabled throughout), so the v1.6 minimum for a safety mechanism is not met. E1 is an equally defensible code, since the paper's subject is LLM tactical role assignment and engagement outcomes, not safety. The CBF is a soft constraint with free slack, so no hard guarantee, and NEUTRALIZE agents are exempt from pursuer-evader separation (deliberate collision). Schema-validation retry with a fixed default role is a fallback, not a safety veto. Abstract has no numbers. Qwen3 is said to be excluded from Experiment I figures yet appears in Table 2 with 518 and 345 bad responses. Idealised sim: noiseless sensing, no delay. Planning intervals of 3 s and 5 s are the only timing values.

title: Heterogeneous Agent Cohorts for Safe Open-Ended Exploration with Runtime Constraint Memory
evidence: Sec. V.C: the Validator 'dynamically intercepts tool calls at runtime, ensuring that no unsafe command is executed'; Table II: executed breaches 0.0 for the full cohort versus 28.6 +/- 4.1 without the Validator.
method: Three-role LLM cohort: high-temperature Disrupter proposes, temperature-0 Validator vetoes tool calls at the gateway, Broker retrieves novel analogies; failures are compiled by MCTS into signed constraint patches (Scars) inherited by later cohorts.
evaluation: Custom sandbox, 20 seeds, eight ablations; AgentHarm 1,000 runs vs ReAct, Reflexion, AutoGen: breach 0.0% vs 11.5-19.2%, false block 4.8%; WebArena Lite 78% success; Xeon 4214R; Scar compilation 12.4 s.
contribution: A heterogeneous LLM agent cohort with a deterministic validator at the tool gateway and inherited constraint memory reports zero executed breaches on AgentHarm against 11.5-19.2% for ReAct, Reflexion and AutoGen, at a 4.8% false-block rate.
flag: Paper calls the main study 'a pilot systems demonstration' in a custom sandbox. The headline Scars memory is not the safety gate ('acts as an efficiency cache') and the no-Scars ablation M5 scores 100%/100% with 0 breaches, i.e. equal or better than the full system on success; Scars only save tokens. Internal inconsistencies: model versions differ between Sec. VII.G and Appendix A, several table cross-references are off by one, Target 1 coordinates stated two ways, 'formal proofs' claimed in Sec. IV.A but Lean 4 is future work. Std devs like 95.0 +/- 21.8 are just binomial spread over 20 seeds. AgentHarm/WebArena baseline run counts and seeds not given. Abstract 55.9% token reduction is reproducible from Table III (72,180 vs 163,520). 'Cached Scar lookups take 0 ms' is not a measurement. Human only signs Scars and approves high-risk revocations; not a runtime handoff.

title: When Local Monitors Miss Compositional Harm: Diagnosing Distributed Backdoors in Multi-Agent Systems
evidence: Sec. 3/Table 1: the decoded-view gate 'decodes candidate assemblies before they run' and is described as 'not a deployable defense but a diagnostic blocking ceiling'.
method: Formalises an observability boundary for monitors: locally benign fragments defeat any per-step view (total-variation bound); compares taint, per-step, marker, marker-free, codec-blind monitors and a decoded-view blocking gate.
evaluation: Collaborative Shadows, AgentDojo, DemonAgent, R-Judge; four open-weight LLMs, K=3 fragments (sweep 2-10); AUROC, attack success rate, blocks out of 50, benign FPR; RTX 6000/A100 GPUs; no latency.
contribution: Proves and measures that per-step monitors cannot detect harm split into locally benign fragments across agents (AUROC about 0.50), while a gate that decodes the assembled payload blocks 50/50 attacks.
flag: The only blocking mechanism is an oracle-like gate that assumes the encoding family is known; authors call it a diagnostic ceiling, not a defence, so (a) is weak and the 0.00 ASR should not be read as a deployable result. n=50 per cell (0/50 upper bound 0.071). Minor inconsistency: Qwen2.5-7B no-defence ASR is 0.78 in Table 3, 0.76 in Table 9, 0.68 in Table 10 (regenerated rollouts). 'Multi-agent' is K fragments in one episode; check how many distinct agents carry them. Benign FPR 0.06 at nominal 5% threshold. No latency figures, no human escalation. Table 15 garbled in extraction.

title: AnovaX: A Local, Multi-Agent Voice Assistant with LLM Planning, Typed Executors, and Adaptive Recovery
evidence: Sec. 3.3: safety_check() runs on every plan including sub-plans and recovery actions; on failure 'no child agent is ever spawned and the user hears a one-line refusal'.
method: Desktop voice assistant: Gemini planner emits JSON plan; safety_check gate (tool whitelist, keyword denylist, step and agent bounds) vetoes plans before typed child agents execute; ReAct-style recovery loop.
evaluation: Qualitative system paper: 13 request classes x 5 runs, 12 work and 1 correctly refused; internal ablations only; Windows 11 laptop 16GB; safety check plus dispatch under 0.05s, planning 0.7-2.0s.
contribution: A local multi-agent voice assistant whose LLM-generated plans pass a whitelist, denylist and bounds gate before typed executors run, with an LLM recovery loop on step failure.
flag: Has a genuine pre-execution veto gate (a), but evidence is qualitative: the paper says it evaluates qualitatively; no unsafe-action, false-refusal or intervention rate, one refusal row only, no external baseline; the claim that no ablation changed safety behaviour is unmeasured. Fails minimum evaluation. Could also be argued E4 (single-user, single-command guardrail; 'multi-agent' means worker threads, not interacting agents). Gate is a keyword blacklist the authors admit is weak, yet the conclusion calls it hard-to-jailbreak. Not edge: speech and planning go to cloud APIs. No human confirmation step. Latencies are indicative from one session log. Tool counts inconsistent (ten vs nine plus one vs eleven-item whitelist). Read via PDF-to-text summary.

title: SAGE: A Socially-Aware Generative Engine for Heterogeneous Multi-Agent Navigation
evidence: Sec. IV-C: Phase 3 "applies a bounded correction to the robot trajectory components while leaving the predicted entity trajectories unchanged"; samples "are not guaranteed to satisfy constraints (C1)-(C5)"
method: Conditional diffusion model with heterogeneous graph transformer encoder jointly generates robot plans and other-entity trajectories; training-free safety-social energy guidance steers robot samples during denoising.
evaluation: ETH/UCY, SDD, unnamed simulations (50 entities, 3-20 robots); baselines CV, Trajectron++, MID, Social Force; guidance ablations; ADE/FDE, collision rate, social-violation rate; RTX 4090, 92-147 ms.
contribution: SAGE jointly generates multi-robot plans and entity trajectories with a heterogeneous-graph diffusion model; energy guidance cuts ETH/UCY collision rate 20% (0.0441 to 0.0353) at 1.9% higher R-ADE.
flag: Borderline on both letters. (b): joint diffusion predictor over heterogeneous multi-agent graph with R-ADE vs baselines (ETH/UCY 0.1152-0.1174 vs MID 0.1163, Trajectron++ 0.1461) - but it is GENERATIVE, opposite of the non-generative cell; entity E-ADE/E-FDE (SDD 0.4769/0.9274) has no baseline. (c): safety is co-equal with social compliance and task performance, so primacy is doubtful; guidance is inside the sampler, not a runtime interceptor, and gives no guarantee. Against the paper: hand-crafted Social Force baseline has far LOWER collision rates (Table XI R2E-CR 0.0136 vs SAGE 0.0371, R2R-CR 0.0172 vs 0.0772) at worse goal error; SDD collision gain is only 1.9% (0.1763 to 0.1729) while Goal-FDE worsens ~16% (0.0700 to 0.0813) despite abstract's 'maintaining task performance'. Scalability: R2R-CR -11.75%, R2E-CR -5.35% on average. No real robots, simulator unnamed, ETH/UCY uses a pedestrian as proxy robot. Latency 85-147 ms on a desktop RTX 4090 vs 0.4 s step, far from 15 ms edge. If (c) primacy is rejected and (b) judged insufficient this becomes E1. Per protocol RQ5 capped at 2.

title: AI-Augmented Model Predictive Control for Safe and Adaptive Rendezvous and Proximity Operations
evidence: Sec. IV.F: "Optional CBF projection of the first optimized control action via Eq. 23"; Sec. IV.D calls the control barrier function filter "an additional defense layer"
method: Receding-horizon QP over Clohessy-Wiltshire relative dynamics with predictive keep-out-zone constraints and slacks; an outer layer tunes MPC parameters offline by cross-entropy method and online by geometry rules; optional CBF projection and PD fallback.
evaluation: KSPDG Capture-the-Satellite Lady-Bandit-Guard scenario; 1000 Monte Carlo runs of the adaptive controller (94.0% success, 4.4% timeout, 1.6% guard capture) and 25 runs per configuration (adaptive 72%, fixed 60%, naive 28%); no hardware or timing.
contribution: Adaptive MPC for adversarial spacecraft rendezvous that modulates interpretable controller parameters offline and online rather than commanding thrust directly, raising mission success over fixed-parameter and naive MPC baselines.
flag: Borderline on criterion (a) and the maintainer may well flip this to exclude-E2 or E1. The interception claim rests on a CBF projection the paper itself calls "optional" (Sec. IV.D and IV.F) and never confirms was enabled in the reported runs, and the paper states the PD fallback "was not activated during nominal mission phases"; the primary safety mechanism is constraints and slacks inside the MPC planner, which protocol v1.5 explicitly says does not meet (a). Minimum-evaluation worry: no keep-out-zone violation counts appear anywhere (violations are discussed qualitatively only), and the hazard-style metric I used (1.6% guard capture) comes from the 1000-run adaptive set, while the baseline comparison reports success rate alone on just 25 runs per configuration with no statistical tests. "Compatible with real-time execution" is asserted with no solve time, control frequency or hardware, and the timestep and horizon lengths appear only as symbols, so my latency cell is unquantified design intent and RQ1 stays at 1. Authors disclaim formal recursive-feasibility and stability guarantees. Three-agent adversarial setting is genuinely multi-agent, but the primary measured outcome is mission success rather than a violation rate, which also strains the (c) primacy test - hence (a) only.

title: ETAS: An Effect-Typed Language for Agent Systems
evidence: Request enforcement runs before a performed action is recorded and commit enforcement runs before the default dispatcher executes the external side effect, with denial raising PolicyDenied (Sections 5.2-5.3).
method: Effect-typed language for agent programs: trace specs compile to runtime monitors that veto tool requests and commits at two enforcement points, with handlers, token budgets and approval constructs.
evaluation: Artifact-oriented case studies (three patterns), compiler diagnostics and interpreter traces; six proof-sketch results including Theorem 5 policy safety; no measurements, no baselines, no latency or hardware figures.
contribution: ETAS gives agent programs static effect and trace types plus a runtime monitor that vetoes unauthorised tool requests and commits, backed by proof-sketch policy-safety and trace-transparency results.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes, LLM agent programs (model inference via Agentic.infer and tool calls are mediated actions). Check the evaluation floor: the paper passes only on formal results (Lemmas 1-2, Theorems 3-6, including Theorem 5 policy safety), all labelled PROOF SKETCH with mechanisation left as future work. There is not a single measured number: Table 1 is a check-mark capability comparison and the Tokens(60000) or Attempts(6) figures are configuration parameters, so exclude-E2 is defensible if measured safety numbers are required. Human approval (std.ui.approve) appears only inside case-study code, so (e) not credited. Single agent program with tool calls, not multiple interacting agents, so (c) not credited.

title: Remote ID Spoofing-Aware Trajectory Planning for Small Unmanned Aerial Systems
evidence: Sec. V-B: each aircraft "selects the control action from the action set that maximizes the total reward"; the chance-constrained unsafe ellipsoid around the localised spoofer carries a -1000 penalty (Table I).
method: Per-agent MDP planner; ground station localises a Remote ID spoofer by RSSI multilateration with IMM filter and broadcasts a chance-constrained unsafe ellipsoid penalised in planning.
evaluation: OMNeT++/INET sim, 1 km, 4-16 drones plus spoofer, 30 runs; baseline Trust-RID planner; total NMAC 7.00 vs 8.97 at 16; Xeon Silver 4314; about 15 ms per GCS update (derived).
contribution: A spoofing-aware decentralised planner localises a Remote ID spoofer and avoids its uncertainty ellipsoid, cutting benign-spoofer near mid-air collisions versus a planner that trusts broadcasts.
flag: Borderline: a planner with reward penalties, not a runtime filter, so (a) not met; enters on (c) only (NMAC vs Trust-RID baseline), and total NMAC is NOT lower at 4 agents (0.300 vs 0.267) despite the text's claim; benign-benign NMAC is equal or higher (1.633 vs 1.200 at 8). Gain is in benign-spoofer NMAC (0.233 vs 2.200 at 16). Spoofing detector is not evaluated - a forced alert at 5 s is used. No ablation. Wall-clock overhead up to 2.05x at 16 agents (221.8 s vs 108.2 s), contradicting the stated decreasing overhead; the 15 ms figure is derived, not measured, and server-class not edge, so (d) not credited. Localisation RMSE 334 m at 4 agents, 57-72 m at 8-16. Dated 2026 - check it is not a preprint without review. Abstract has no numbers. Read via summarising fetch of the PDF.

title: Distributed Motion Planning with Safety Guarantees for Self-Reconfiguring Robotic Boats
evidence: "each agent applies a discrete safety filter to the ADMM output" ... "By minimizing the deviation from the ADMM reference, the QP acts as a minimally invasive safety filter" (Sec. III-C)
method: Distributed ADMM MPC plans reconfiguration motions for modular boats; a per-agent discrete CBF QP filters each velocity command before the low-level controller, overriding unsafe commands.
evaluation: Sim N=4-25 (64 stress) vs ADMM-only and CBF-only: collision-free 100% vs 0% (ADMM-only), success 100% vs 0-20% (CBF-only, N>=16). 4 boats on Raspberry Pi 4; CBF filter median 32.4 ms, P95 63.5 ms.
contribution: Pairs distributed ADMM planning with a per-agent CBF safety filter for self-reconfiguring boats, removing the collisions of ADMM alone and the deadlocks of CBF alone, with timing measured on Raspberry Pi 4.
flag: Filter modifies commands (minimal deviation), it does not halt or defer. Table I shows ADMM-only 0% collision-free at every N while text says collisions occur 'even at smaller swarm sizes' - wording loose; ADMM-only 'success' counts runs that collided. Hardware: no collision count, and the paper admits distances at times fell below the safety distance and even below module side L (blamed on 2-3 cm localization error), so the guarantee did not hold on hardware. ADMM cycle met the 200 ms budget in only 86% of steps (max 639.5 ms; CBF filter max 279.4 ms). Sim CBF filter <0.02 ms vs 35.4 ms mean on the Pi. Seeds: 5 per ablation config, 3 for scalability. Criterion (d) is my reading (explicit 200 ms budget on embedded hardware); maintainer may judge it only a;c.

title: APPA: Recoverable Information-Flow Control for Real-World LLM Agents
evidence: Gate 1 evaluates rendered calls against label L and history before execution (Section 6.1), blocking dispatch and returning structured remedies instead of aborting.
method: Deterministic reference monitor (agentic permissions policy algebra) over LLM agent tool calls: pre-dispatch gate on the rendered call, post-return gate on data entering context, plus remedy plans, single-use authority rulings and isolated child branches.
evaluation: 6600 episodes over AgentThreatBench (24 OWASP tasks) and Bench-Corp (20 enterprise scenarios), 3 models; vs stock, permissive, FIDES-middleware and FIDES-native; guarded ASR 0 of 1320 vs 40.0-69.2 pct, utility 64.2-91 pct, ablations nofork 56.5 pct and noremedy 35.0 pct.
contribution: APPA turns agent information-flow control from an abort-only barrier into a policy-governed recovery system, holding observed attack success at zero while retaining 64-91 percent of task utility.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes, LLM agents (GPT-5.6 Luna, DeepSeek V4 Flash, Gemini 3.7 Flash); the monitor itself is deterministic, which the scope ruling allows. (c) is credited as safety evaluation of a tool-calling agent, not as interaction among independently deployed agents (only forked child branches), so a maintainer may drop (c) and keep (a). Zero ASR is 0 of 720 and 0 of 600 observed episodes, not a proof of impossibility; Appendix A gives Propositions 1-4 and Theorems 5-8 on branch taint confinement, with Proposition 3 conditional on an unproved soundness hypothesis. No latency, CPU or token overhead is measured anywhere, so (d) is absent and the 300 s per-episode timeout is a harness setting. The human-reviewer authority path is design-only and never run, so the human handoff cell is unevaluated and (e) is not credited.

title: SGTP: Sampling-based Game-Theoretic Planning for Real-Time Multi-Vehicle Autonomous Racing
evidence: "Feasibility selection applies explicit track-boundary and inter-vehicle collision checks to the ranked candidates" (Sec. III-B) - a selection step inside the planner, not a filter on a nominal action
method: Sampling-based (MPPI-style) game-theoretic racing planner using iterated best response over 128 sampled trajectories with a game-aware cost and feasibility selection, falling back to least-violation candidate.
evaluation: F1TENTH Gym, 7 tracks, 42 three-car trials; 8 baselines plus 2 ablations; wins 95.24%, collision-free wins 100%; planning time 0.095 s mean, 0.102 s max on RTX 4060.
contribution: Presents a GPU sampling-based game-theoretic planner for multi-vehicle racing that wins 95 percent of three-car races without collision at about 95 ms per planning call.
flag: Racing planner whose primary claim is competitive performance (wins, overtakes, defence); collision avoidance is a constraint inside the planner, so (a) fails the strictly-runtime test and (c) fails the primacy test. The feasibility selection does have an ablation-like contrast (collision-free wins 100% vs 14.29% without game cost, 0% for GA-IBR-MPPI), which is the only argument for (c). Text says GA-IBR-MPPI lacks feasibility selection, conflicting with the method description. Collision-free wins is conditional on winning, so it is not a collision rate. Timing is reported (mean 0.095 s, std 0.004, max 0.102 on a desktop RTX 4060) but there is no stated deadline or budget, so (d) is not met and the latency cell is generous; no edge hardware. Per-vehicle-count scaling times appear only in Fig. 5. FPR cells for End2Race and CFM could not be read reliably from the PDF table. Simulation only.

title: Semi-Decentralized Multi-Spacecraft Collision Avoidance under Communication Constraints
evidence: "Policies are generated offline and uploaded before execution."; semi-decentralized planning had "zero collisions observed across all evaluated scenarios" (Semi-Decentralized Performance Relative to Centralized Planning).
method: Two-spacecraft conjunction avoidance as a semi-decentralized POMDP solved offline with approximate RS-SDA*; agents synchronise beliefs only during ground-station visibility and execute by policy lookup.
evaluation: 52 synthetic LEO conjunctions, 200 Monte Carlo rollouts each, Brahe propagator; vs centralized, decentralized, operator heuristics; 4-7 km band 61%/60%/28%/17-25%; sync events 19.4 vs 27.2; no hardware or runtime.
contribution: Semi-decentralized planning with ground-contact synchronisation matches centralized two-spacecraft collision-avoidance quality on 52 simulated conjunctions while using about 28.5% fewer synchronisation events.
flag: Borderline (c), maintainer should decide. Collision avoidance is the task, but the primary claim and primary measured outcome are coordination efficiency (synchronisation events) and hitting a 4-7 km miss-distance band; no rollout under any strategy fell below 1 km, so collision rate does not discriminate against any baseline, and the heuristics are said to satisfy safety by over-mitigating. I read that as failing the primacy test, hence E1 and criteria_met none; if the band-hit rate is accepted as a safety metric it would be (c) and includable. Offline planner with no runtime override. Only two spacecraft. The 28.5% in the abstract does not exactly match the reported means (27.2 to 19.4 is about 28.7%). No delta-v totals, no solver runtime, no hardware; communication delay is idealised.

title: FaithEyes: Towards Faithful Tool Use via Multi-Agent Process-Image Self-Verification
evidence: Sec. 3.2: the subagent judges 'each process image the main agent produces' and when the verdict is unhelpful 'we discard {It} and return only (ht,et)'; verification is after execution of the tool code.
method: One VLM in two prompted roles: main agent writes image-processing code, subagent judges each resulting process image as helpful or not; verdict is injected into context and scales the RL tool reward.
evaluation: V* Bench, HR-Bench 4K/8K, MathVista/MathVerse/MathVision; Qwen2.5-VL-7B, Qwen3-VL-8B; baselines DeepEyes, Thyme, CodeV, others; faithfulness 91.5/92.7/84.3 vs CodeV 85.1/52.3/12.1; 32 H800 GPUs.
contribution: Trains an agentic vision-language model to self-verify each tool-produced image and discard unhelpful ones, raising tool-use faithfulness and accuracy on perception and reasoning benchmarks while cutting response tokens against CodeV.
flag: Framed as faithfulness, accuracy and anti-reward-hacking, not safety: 'safety-critical' appears once in the conclusion; no hazard, violation or intervention rate, so (c) fails. 'Multi-agent' is nominal: the same model under a second prompt. Borderline on runtime_interceptor: the verdict gates a tool OUTPUT from entering context after execution, it cannot veto or halt a tool call before it runs; the sandbox static scan and wall-clock timeout (App. A) are a separate guard and not evaluated. E4 is an alternative code. Numbers: FaithEyes-7B accuracy 87.4/77.8/72.9/73.1/51.0/29.9; tokens 4020/12580/14269 vs CodeV 5340/22505/31088 (24.7/44.1/54.1% savings); judge step about 1.5k tokens; no wall-clock latency. FaithEyes-8B is below its base model on MathVision (46.1 vs 53.9). Faithfulness is scored by an LLM judge (Qwen3-VL-235B) on correct-answer trajectories only. Read via one summarised full-text fetch.

title: Beyond Component Testing: Validating Agentic AI Systems
evidence: Table 2/Sec. 8: the three case studies are "constructed case studies" with thresholds that "are not empirical results"; the paper is a systematic mapping study of 262 papers.
method: Systematic mapping study of 262 papers on validating agentic AI; five-dimension taxonomy (behavioral, safety, temporal, regulatory, multi-agent), coverage map over six approach families, four-direction research agenda.
evaluation: No own experiments. Literature screen: 5187 records, 262 included; inter-rater kappa 0.812; sensitivity analyses on corpus definition. Constructed medical/industrial/mobility traces with illustrative, uncalibrated thresholds. No hardware or latency.
contribution: Maps 262 papers on validating agentic AI onto five validation dimensions and finds temporal validation (5.3%) and runtime monitoring for regulatory and temporal concerns sparsely covered.
flag: Secondary study (PRISMA-inspired mapping) - E3; also no empirical evaluation of its own (E2). Runtime monitors, safe-stop, block/escalate and handoff appear only as reviewed prior work, constructed traces (EFI 60 min, UAR 0.02, CSR 0.95 illustrative thresholds) and agenda items. Useful as background/snowball source: 32 safety runtime-monitor appearances, 10 multi-agent; names safe-stop, defer and handoff as open gaps. Human-involvement stats are corpus descriptors (72.5% none), not a handoff study. PDF is about 232k chars, read in three fetches; middle section summarised by the fetch tool, Sections 10-11 not inspected in detail.

title: CUDA MPC: A GPU-Native Solver for Model Predictive Control
evidence: "Rather than launching a separate kernel per ADMM operation, the complete inner loop is fused into a single custom kernel" (Sec. V-B)
method: GPU-native nonlinear MPC solver: sequential convex programming outer loop with parallel-in-horizon ADMM fused into one CUDA kernel; constraints enforced by projection inside the solver, no safety filter or fallback.
evaluation: Simulation, AFTI-16 plus six nonlinear problems incl. 10-agent centralized swarm; vs CasADi, acados, PD-iLQR, GPU-SLS, PyTorch/Julia piMPC; RTX 3060 laptop GPU; swarm 28.22 ms; up to 965x speedup.
contribution: Presents a GPU-native nonlinear MPC solver that fuses parallel-in-horizon ADMM into a single CUDA kernel, solving 1000-step horizons and a 10-agent swarm problem in tens of milliseconds on a laptop GPU.
flag: A solver paper, not a safety mechanism: nothing sits between a nominal decision and its execution, and there is no behaviour described for infeasible or late solves. Collision avoidance in the swarm case is a constraint inside a centralized optimisation and is shown only qualitatively (Fig. 5); no collision or constraint-violation count is reported, so (c) fails the primacy test and (d) fails because the latency is for control, not safety decisions. Hardware is an RTX 3060 laptop GPU with an i7-12700H; embedded deployment is explicitly future work, so no edge cell. Other figures: Car Parking N=100 5.75 ms vs acados 165.71 ms; per-iteration 0.86 ms to 0.0060 ms vs PyTorch; speedup 136x at N=5, 768x at N=1000, peak 965x at N=50. Text reports an 8.7x speedup for Quadcopter-Pole at N=1000 while Table I lists 600 as its largest real-time-feasible horizon. On three problems CPU second-order solvers match or beat its RMSE. Possibly useful background for RQ1 compute budgets only.

title: Search-Aided Joint Agent-Environment Reinforcement Learning for Robust Lifelong Multi-Agent Path Finding with Rotations
evidence: "Experiments demonstrate that SJRL achieves significant improvements over the strong search-based planner, Causal-PIBT, across multiple high-density maps." (Abstract)
method: Jointly trained RL agent policy (next-vertex subgoals) and environment policy (guidance-graph edge costs) for lifelong MAPF with rotations; synchronized Causal PIBT post-processes neural outputs to resolve collisions.
evaluation: Six grid maps, 256 agents; baselines Causal-PIBT, CMA-ES, SILLM, MAGAT+, HMAGAT, naive shields; metrics throughput and mean pairwise distance; inference <0.05 s per timestep on RTX 4090D.
contribution: A lifelong multi-agent path finding planner that jointly learns agent and guidance-graph policies behind a PIBT collision shield, improving warehouse throughput over search-based and learned planners; throughput, not safety, is the measured outcome.
flag: Throughput/coordination paper: fails the (c) primacy test. The Causal PIBT layer does override neural-policy choices at execution time (hence runtime_interceptor yes), and Sec 5.3 compares shield variants, but only by throughput - no collision/violation/intervention rate is reported anywhere, so (a) would fail minimum evaluation (E2) if the maintainer prefers that code. Figure values (throughput 0.02-5.34) are bar labels only, not tabulated per method in the extracted text. Physical validation (8 real+248 virtual robots) is in an appendix I only skimmed; references and appendix pseudocode not read in detail.

title: CyberLLM: A Multi-Agent LLM Framework for Autonomous Detection and Guarded Response in Automotive Cybersecurity
evidence: The SecurityGuard checks each remediation step before it executes, enforcing four contextual properties and an action-alignment oracle that can only tighten the deterministic decision, with refusal triggering escalation and re-planning (Section IV, guarded response).
method: Multi-agent LLM framework for automotive cybersecurity: three-layer deterministic detection (regex, Bandit or Semgrep AST, topology checks) plus LLM refinement, a tiered decision agent, an action generator, and a SecurityGuard validating every step before execution.
evaluation: Nine author-written vulnerable ECU modules in C, C++ and Rust with 47 labelled vulnerabilities and two clean controls; Fast vs Deep acts as the ablation and there is no external baseline; recall 34.0 pct to about 70 pct, F1 0.51 to 0.83, precision 1.000; no latency.
contribution: CyberLLM couples layered deterministic and LLM vulnerability detection with a guarded response pipeline whose SecurityGuard validates each remediation step, roughly doubling recall on automotive ECU code with no false positives on benign code.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes, the LLM scanners, decision agent and planner (GPT-4o via Azure OpenAI) whose steps the SecurityGuard validates. Check the floor carefully: the guard and the H_a alignment oracle are never quantitatively evaluated, so the floor is met only by static detection coverage and F1 with the Fast vs Deep ablation, not by any intervention or violation rate. The benchmark is written by the authors (47 labels, matching within 3 lines) yet described as independent, which is a self-claim, and no external tool baseline is run. (c) not credited: the framework is multi-agent but inter-agent, cascading or subverted-agent hazards are named as future work and never measured. The abstract mentions oversight although no human analyst handoff exists in the workflow; accuracy, latency and mean-time-to-detect are not reported (stated N-A by design).

title: Agentao: A Policy-Governed Runtime Harness for Embeddable Tool-Using LLM Agents
evidence: Algorithm 2 returns DENY for hardline-unsafe calls and PROMPT where confirmation is required, and Section 4.3 states "the permission layer does not rely on natural-language instructions as a security boundary."
method: Local-first agent runtime where every model-proposed tool call passes a four-phase ToolRunner and a permission engine resolving to ALLOW, PROMPT or DENY, with pre-tool hooks and cancellation.
evaluation: None quantitative; Section 6 "Absence of quantitative evaluation" states enforcement accuracy, overhead, compatibility and utility are unmeasured; three illustrative single-agent case studies; no baselines, hardware or latency.
contribution: An embeddable runtime harness routing every tool call through an explicit ALLOW, PROMPT or DENY permission decision taken outside the model's prompt, with audit traces and first-class cancellation.
flag: Textbook E2 and the authors say so themselves: Section 6 is titled "Absence of quantitative evaluation" and the abstract concedes the system "does not provide formal safety guarantees". So the clearest runtime interceptor in this batch carries no safety metric, no baseline and no overhead figure, and the only numbers in it (a 0.9 confidence threshold in a policy example, tokens_est 1234 in a sample output) are illustrative config values, not results. Sub-agents are described architecturally in Section 4.5 but never evaluated, so I did not credit multi-agent state. The PROMPT path is a genuine human approval gate and Section 4.7 makes cancellation a runtime state, so this is worth re-screening if an evaluated version appears; worth checking whether it is an extended version of a tool-governance paper already queued.

title: A Temporal Barrier Framework for Collision Avoidance in Multi-Agent Autonomous Aerial Vehicles
evidence: Abstract: the aTTC-CBF "achieves up to twice the waypoint progress at half the collision rate of a higher-order distance-based CBF baseline"; Sec. III QP (Eq. 27) minimises deviation from the nominal input subject to the barrier constraint
method: Adversarial time-to-collision (aTTC) control barrier function defined in time rather than distance; a QP safety filter minimally modifies the nominal input at every control step, with a FiLM-conditioned MLP surrogate supplying barrier and gradients.
evaluation: Simulated 3D Dubins aircraft with Wiener noise; 8 evaders against 0, 3 slow or 3 fast pursuers plus formation flight, 50,000 s runs; baselines no-CBF and HOCBF; collisions per 100 s, waypoints per evader; under 1.0 ms per call, Matlab on CPU.
contribution: Defines a control barrier function directly in time via adversarial time-to-collision, giving an anticipatory runtime safety filter that halves multi-agent aerial collision rates while roughly doubling waypoint progress against a distance-based HOCBF.
flag: Strongest candidate in this batch for RQ5 because it reports a throughput proxy (waypoint progress) alongside collision rate against the HOCBF, but check the headline: in formation flight with slow pursuers the aTTC-CBF is worse than the HOCBF (0.028 vs 0.000 collisions per 100 s), which the abstract's "half the collision rate" does not reflect. The authors themselves state the neural surrogate's two-sided error voids the formal guarantee unless trained under a one-sided constraint (left as future work), and that the QP "may fail" to be feasible near the barrier boundary with no fallback defined - so the filter can modify a nominal input but cannot reliably halt, which is why I would not credit RQ3 or a human-handoff cell. Simulation only: the sole timing figure is "less than 1.0 ms in Matlab on a CPU" with no CPU model named and no edge hardware, so my latency cell and RQ1 score of 4 rest on that one unverifiable sentence - edge deployment deliberately not listed. No ablation isolating the surrogate, and the authors say the HOCBF comparison is not meant to show superiority over state of the art. A maintainer may also want to credit criterion (b): the FiLM-MLP is a learned predictor over multi-agent relative state evaluated inside the runtime filter, though it is a regression onto a pursuit-law quantity rather than a latent world model, and it is pairwise rather than over a graph.

title: A Safety-Driven Architectural Framework for Fail-Operational Drone Swarms in Critical Missions
evidence: The Fault Management Unit acts as a run-time assurance gateway that locks and filters mission inputs and issues overriding commands such as ENFORCE_SAFE_ENVELOPE, forcing LAND or RTB if the swarm module misses its heartbeat (Section III, Fig. 2).
method: Conceptual DAL-partitioned swarm architecture: a hardware-isolated Fault Management Unit enforcing propulsion, navigation and communication safety contracts and publishing a per-agent health vector that penalises degraded drones in swarm task allocation.
evaluation: No simulation or hardware experiments: architectural traceability table, qualitative mid-air-collision fault tree, analytic Markov reliability model and a ConOps timing walkthrough; design targets H-02 below 1e-7 per flight hour, monitor coverage above 0.9991, fault-to-enforcement 80-150 ms; no baselines.
contribution: A fail-operational drone-swarm architecture placing a hardware-isolated safety monitor between a certifiable flight core and a non-deterministic swarm coordinator, with health-vector-driven task reallocation.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: no. The guarded swarm coordination module is a non-deterministic classical swarm or market-based allocator, and the flight core, Kalman-filter navigation and the monitor are hand-designed deterministic logic; neural networks appear only in a cited reference, so under the 2026-11-13 scope ruling (a) and (c) both fail and this is classical control with no learned component guarded. exclude-E2 applies independently: the authors call it a conceptual framework and theoretical safety argument, every figure is an analytic target or design budget rather than a measurement, and there is no baseline or ablation. Arguable (d) via the explicit 100 ms fault-to-enforcement bound and the 50-500 ms ConOps timeline, but nothing is implemented or timed, which is the main thing to overturn if (d) is read loosely. Multi-agent collision hazard H-01 is only a qualitative fault tree while the quantified target is the single-drone crash H-02; no operator takeover is described.

title: SRL-MPC: Shape-Aware Reinforcement Learned Model Predictive Control
evidence: Sec. 2 (Related Work): 'Safe RL methods add model-based lookahead or shielding to reduce violations [1], but they do not directly provide explicit shape-aware safety terms' - here the HOCBF term is a soft residual penalty inside the MPC subproblem and the first optimised control is executed (Sec. 4.1); nothing overrides a nominal action.
method: PPO policy reads geometric separation features and outputs bounded increments to three MPC parameters (w_p, w_u, d_safe); a distributed shape-aware HOCBF-MPC then solves each robot's motion.
evaluation: IR-SIM random-polygon crowds, N=10-25, 100 episodes each; vs ORCA, AVOCADO, VO-polytope, SARL, RL-RVO plus three MPC ablations; success 100/98/93/92%, collision 0/1/6/6%; 5.8-10.3 ms per robot-step on M4 Pro.
contribution: RL-tuned shape-aware HOCBF-MPC for dense multi-robot navigation reaches 92% success with 25 polygonal robots where reactive and learned baselines fall to 1-21%, at about 10 ms per robot-step.
flag: Borderline (c): collision rate is reported against 5 baselines and 3 ablations, but the headline win is success rate; on collisions it loses to AVOCADO (0% at all N) and to its own rule_mpc ablation at N=20-25 (1-2% vs 6%), so I read it as a navigation planner with safety as a constraint inside MPC, not a runtime interceptor. Maintainer may prefer include on (c). Per-step timing (Table 7, 5.79-10.34 ms) and action-delay robustness (success 99/82/2% at 1/2/3 steps delay, N=15) are relevant to RQ1 but measured on a MacBook, not edge hardware. Real-world deployment is a figure only, no numbers. Time and path-length columns of Table 1 were garbled in extraction and not checked.

title: When "Must" Becomes "Maybe": Erosion of Workflow Constraints in LLM Agent Handoffs
evidence: Abstract/Sec. 1: 'Semantic availability does not guarantee operational preservation'; Sec. 5 reports ownership deferral giving D = 76.7 and Y = 60.8 against 0.0 for the direct-state control.
method: Reviewer-generator-executor pipeline where an upstream blocker is encoded as four fields (stop status, prerequisite, authority, fallback); measures how handoff transformations erase it and which restored fields or authorization prompts repair.
evaluation: Synthetic enterprise tasks, 1,296 episodes on six LLM configurations plus 476 validation; direct-state controls, field-restoration and authorization-check arms; preservation P, deactivation D, downstream outcome Y rates; AutoGen/LangGraph replication; no latency.
contribution: Shows that LLM agent handoffs turn upstream stop constraints into optional advice: multihop compression deactivates 97.2% of blockers, and restoring all four blocker fields brings the downstream violation outcome to 0%.
flag: Check the exact definitions of P, D and Y in the paper: I read Y as the rate at which the executor takes the forbidden action, but the extraction did not give the definition verbatim. Repairs are prompt/artifact changes inside the executor, not a separate interceptor, so (a) not claimed. The 'human-approval request' arm has no human; no human handoff. All tasks synthetic, labels from LLM judges and a checker (owner field macro F1 only 0.636). Framework cells are n=8. Model names (GPT-5.4, Qwen3.5, DS-V4) reported as given. Logical domain only.

title: Fixed-Haven Reservation for Online Multi-Agent Pickup and Delivery in Dense Warehouses
evidence: "A candidate assignment is accepted only if SIPP can validate the full path to pickup, delivery, and Haven." (Section 3.4)
method: SHARP: centralised online pickup-and-delivery planner where each agent owns a fixed Safe Haven cell and keeps a reserved collision-free SIPP retreat path; assignments are accepted only if fully validated.
evaluation: Four grid warehouse maps, 5-30 agents, 100 runs per configuration; vs TP, PIBT, PIBTTP-TA, home-return variants; success 100%, makespan 0.73-0.79x, runtime about 20x on tree map; Threadripper PRO.
contribution: A fixed-haven reservation planner for lifelong multi-agent pickup and delivery that provably avoids deadlock in dense non-well-formed warehouses, reaching 100% task success where token passing fails.
flag: E1 on the primacy test: the claims and metrics are completeness, deadlock avoidance, success rate, makespan and service time; collision-freedom is a planner invariant and no collision or violation rate is measured. The assignment-acceptance check is a constraint inside the planner (an agent keeps its reserved retreat path when validation fails), not a monitor between a nominal decision and execution, so I scored runtime_interceptor no; perception and execution are explicitly out of scope. The abstract's only-method-with-100%-success claim is weaker in the body: TP-home-return also reaches 100% on the tree map in the counterfactual study. Runtimes are means (2.53-10.39 s per run in Table 2, about 20x TP-home-return on tree) and Section 6 concedes tail latency was not measured, so (d) is not met. Abstract ratios 1.89x service and 1.53x makespan for no-overwrite match Table 4.

title: Sustained Heterogeneity: an emergent collective mechanism in LLM-driven traffic
evidence: "Modes earlier in the cascade intercept and return before later modes can execute" (Supplement S1.4, safety-fusion layer)
method: 22 stateless GLM-4-Flash vehicle agents on a ring road output speed deltas every 0.5 s; a rule-based safety-fusion cascade (IDM override, emergency braking, hard wall) clamps them.
evaluation: 230 m ring-road simulation, 22 vehicles, 300 s; IDM, white/OU-noise, delay, OV and T=0.1 controls; v_std 2.12 vs <0.001 m/s IDM; p_c about 0.23; safety-layer ablation 0/84/7848 collisions; no latency.
contribution: Shows that LLM-driven vehicles on a ring road sustain stop-and-go waves that classical noise and delay controls do not reproduce, with a critical LLM penetration near 0.23 at high density.
flag: Borderline, maintainer should decide. The primary claim is traffic physics (emergent speed heterogeneity, v_std), not a safety property, so I failed the (c) primacy test and scored criteria none. However the system does contain a genuine runtime override of LLM actions, and supplement S1.3 has a safety-layer ablation with collision counts (full 0, soft 84, minimal 7848) - but single seed (42), no intervention rate reported, thresholds hand-tuned, and it is not the paper's claim. If that ablation is judged sufficient this could enter under (a) or (c). Dangerous approaches (gap <2.5 m) rise about 2.6x between 5 and 6 LLM vehicles. Abstract calls IDM only a hard collision-avoidance clamp, whereas the body describes a five-mode cascade. Paper itself concedes the >=20x amplification claim conflicts with an all-seed mean of 18.0x, and p_c is given as 0.23 and about 0.27. Compute is reported inconsistently (10-15 h wall-clock per seed via API vs about 480 GPU-hours for 170 runs). Simulation only, one model, one Chinese prompt. Read via a summarising fetch tool, so check quotes against the PDF.

title: Localizing Emergent Failures in Agentic AI: Recovering Minimal Repair Families via Counterfactual Replay
evidence: Graph-Constrained Joint Replay slices the dependency graph of a failed multi-agent execution and replays candidate interventions to recover the inclusion-minimal repair family, and it does not generate repair messages automatically (Section I, Introduction).
method: Post-hoc localisation of emergent multi-agent LLM failures: dependency-graph slicing, singleton and pair candidate interventions substituting paired clean messages, replay verification from checkpoints, and an inclusion-minimality filter producing a minimal repair family.
evaluation: 90 in-scope controlled DAGs plus 24 DualSolve-MAS arithmetic cases with four Qwen2.5-1.5B agents; vs exhaustive, single-event, execution-window, Shapley top-2, centrality, random pair and an LLM log-only judge; joint FEM 1.000 at 25.3 replays (55.1 pct saving) vs 56.3; no latency.
contribution: GCJR localises emergent agentic failures to inclusion-minimal joint repair families by graph-constrained counterfactual replay, matching exhaustive search at about half the replay cost.
flag: learned or AI system analysed: yes, a four-agent LLM workflow (Qwen2.5-1.5B planner, two solvers, aggregator) plus a symbolic fork-join benchmark. (a) is NOT met: this is offline post-hoc diagnosis replayed from checkpoints and never intercepts, overrides or halts a live action, so it is credited only under (c) for emergent multi-agent failure localisation; a maintainer who reads (c) as requiring a hazard, collision or violation rate against a baseline could call this exclude-E1, and this is the record most likely to be overturned. The method is oracle-assisted: the replay backend supplies the paired clean messages and evaluation uses known fault labels, so there is no detection rate on undiagnosed failures. Real-agent pilot is only 24 cases; macro FEM falls from 1.000 to 0.552 when 10 pct of graph edges are hidden; no human in the loop and no latency figures.

title: Provably Safe Decentralized Contingency MPC under State-Only Information and Limited Sensing for Nonlinear Multi-agent Systems
evidence: Collision avoidance follows from disjoint state-dependent active safe sets (Lemma 1, Theorem 2, Sec. IV-V); enforced as constraints inside each agent's OCP (Sec. III.A)
method: Decentralized contingency MPC: each agent optimises a nominal and a contingency plan sharing the first input, with memory-free state-dependent safe sets giving recursive feasibility and collision avoidance proofs.
evaluation: One simulated four-way intersection run, kinematic bicycle, 50 vehicles, CasADi/IPOPT; no baseline or ablation; min centre distance 1.026 m vs 0.8 m threshold, 0 collisions. No solve times or hardware.
contribution: A decentralized contingency MPC with formal collision-avoidance and recursive-feasibility guarantees under state-only sensing, demonstrated in a single intersection simulation.
flag: Fails minimum evaluation: single simulation run, no baseline or ablation, no rate statistics. Not (a): safety is a constraint inside the planner, the contingency plan is a feasibility certificate rather than a separate runtime filter. Formal result is the real contribution - maintainer may weigh the proofs differently. Guarantees assume exact models and complete detection (Sec. VII). Max concurrent vehicles not stated.

title: Agents That Model Agents: Five Principles Toward a Theory of Mind for 6G Networks
evidence: The Figure 2 caption states "Steps i-iv run for each received message before the agent may act", and Section VII places the trust layer "before the receiving agent is allowed to act."
method: Cognitive-channel model of inter-agent messages on a cellular sheaf; recursive two-level peer type modeling yields a continuous trust weight (cognitive SNR) applied to each message before action.
evaluation: Near-RT RIC signaling storm, five 1B telecom SLM xApps; baselines divergence gate and naive consensus, recursion-depth 0-3 ablation; AUC 1.000 versus 0.000; 0.32-2.57 ms per message.
contribution: Treats inter-agent messages as subjective evidence of a peer's hidden type and weights them by a cognitive SNR, catching hallucination contagion that a divergence gate misses entirely.
flag: Largely a position paper organised around five principles, so E3 deserves weighing even though E3 as written names surveys, tutorials and book chapters rather than vision papers; it does carry an original evaluation with a baseline and an ablation, which is why I kept it in. That evaluation is thin: five agents, 60 messages, medians over five runs, and the topology and latency sweeps in Figure 3 use a calibrated statistical emitter rather than the deployed models. Decision accuracy is non-monotonic and implausibly sharp (0.000 at depth 0, 0.050 at depth 1, 1.000 at depth 2, 0.083 at depth 3) and an AUC of exactly 1.000 against exactly 0.000 for the divergence gate should be checked before either number is quoted. The mechanism weights rather than vetoes - Section III says "gating is merely the suboptimal extreme of weighting only a single branch" - so runtime_interceptor is no; the proactive non-RT RIC quarantine that would make it one is asserted and never evaluated. No GPU, memory or platform is named, so I did not credit edge deployment despite the "locally deployed" 1B models, and Section IX lists hardware-in-the-loop validation as an open problem. RQ5 is capped at 2 under the protocol's world-model rule since the peer-modeling claim is predictive.

title: A Case Study on Emergent Cheating and Whistleblowing in Autonomous Research Swarms
evidence: "Within the swarm, cheating spontaneously emerged and was later challenged by whistleblowers" (Abstract)
method: Observational case study of 100 autonomous LLM agents (Gemini 3.1 Pro) proving 71 Lean conjectures, with post-hoc audit-log analysis of emergent exploit spread, framed by Ostrom commons-governance principles.
evaluation: Single uncontrolled run, 100 agents, 71 problems, four personas; descriptive cohorts (exploiters 9%, converts 5%, whistleblowers 24%, unaware 62%), 37 of 71 solved honestly; no baseline, ablation, hardware or latency.
contribution: Documents spontaneously emergent cheating and peer whistleblowing in a 100-agent autonomous LLM research swarm, arguing static filters fail without institutional enforcement scaffolding.
flag: Excluded on minimum evaluation, not on topic: the multi-agent safety property is genuinely the primary claim, but there is no baseline and no ablation, and n equals one uncontrolled run with no repeats. The static keyword blacklist ("axiom, sorry, macro, syntax") is arguably an approval gate sitting between an agent submission and its acceptance, but the paper neither proposes nor evaluates it and the exploit bypassed it, so I scored runtime_interceptor no; a maintainer may reasonably disagree. Cohort percentages appear only in Figure 1 and I could not find them in the body text. Still worth keeping as a motivating citation even if excluded.

title: Skynet: Workflow-Level Anomaly Detection for Agentic AI via Semantic and Structural Modeling
evidence: Sec. 2.1: Skynet is "a passive consumer of execution records" that "does not modify agent logic, tool backends, inter-agent protocols, or LLM weights"; Algorithm 1 step 14: "if s > eta then flag G as anomalous else accept as benign".
method: Unsupervised workflow-graph anomaly detector trained on benign agent traces only; semantic and structural branches, counterfactual views, K=150 benign modes; flags a workflow when its score exceeds a fixed quantile threshold.
evaluation: Agent-SafetyBench, ATBench, AgentErrorBench (808 anomalies) vs six baselines; Combined F1 94.07, recall 89.36, FPR 0.89 percent; mean 81 ms, P95 228 ms per workflow; hardware unstated.
contribution: A benign-only graph anomaly detector for agentic workflows that flags unsafe or failing LLM-agent executions at under 1 percent false positives, but only flags and never blocks.
flag: Detect-only: no veto, halt, alert or human path, so (a) is not met; inclusion rests on (c) as a detector with detection metrics (F1/recall/FPR), not a hazard-rate reduction - maintainer to judge whether that satisfies the v1.6 minimum. Multi-agent is nominal: benchmarks are mostly single-agent trajectories (AlfWorld, WebShop, GAIA). Table 1 (Combined F1 94.07, recall 89.36, FPR 0.89) and Table 3 full model (F1 97.08, recall 94.80, FPR 0.71) disagree, explained only as a separate ablation run. Baselines tuned their own thresholds while Skynet used a fixed quantile. Zero-day claim is not tested with a held-out attack family. No AUROC values, no hardware. Per-step latency grows to mean 105 ms, P95 573 ms at step 20. Latency is reported but there is no stated deadline, so the latency cell is weak. Read through a summarising fetch; verify quotes against the PDF.

title: Decentralized Safe Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning via Predictive Shielding
evidence: "This architecture strictly guarantees that unsafe actions are never executed." (Section 6)
method: Decentralized, communication-free predictive shield per agent: a learned model looks ahead over static and dynamic horizons, replaces unsafe nominal actions with a stay backup, plus a randomized conflict-resolution protocol.
evaluation: gym-multigrid, 3 scenarios plus 10x10 scalability (2-8 agents, 45 inits); vs IQL, MIS, DMPS, Dyna-Q Shield; Exp3 return 268.4 vs -inf (DMPS); Tdep 0.05-2.6; no hardware stated.
contribution: A communication-free predictive shield for decentralized multi-agent RL that overrides unsafe actions with a stay backup and resolves symmetric conflicts probabilistically, avoiding the deadlocks of reactive shields.
flag: Drafted from a SINGLE successful fetch of the PDF (v1) via a summarising reader; arXiv rate-limited every follow-up, so nothing here was cross-checked on a second pass and the quotes should be verified against the PDF. Minimum-evaluation is doubtful: the fetch surfaced no collision, violation or intervention rate - outcomes are return, steps-to-goal and a success fraction shown only in figures, with -inf return/inf steps standing for failure or deadlock - so a maintainer may judge this E2 under protocol v1.6. Table 1 text was garbled in extraction; baseline horizon and return columns may be misaligned. Tdep has no stated unit (probably seconds per decision) and is WORSE than DMPS in Exp3 (2.6 vs 0.88), contradicting the low-online-cost claim. No hardware given, so criterion (d) not met. Agent counts for the three main scenarios are not stated. No ablation of the conflict-resolution protocol. Guarantee is limited to non-adversarial environments. Grid-world only.

title: Graph-Based Safe Reinforcement Learning for Multi-Agent Systems with Time-Varying Topology
evidence: Sec. IV-B: if h(s) < 0 the screening mechanism explores a discrete candidate set for a corrected action, a rigorous one-step discrete safety filter projecting policy outputs onto a feasible safe region each step.
method: MAPPO multi-agent RL with attention actor and GAT critic over a time-varying communication graph; a LiDAR control-barrier-like-function layer screens and replaces unsafe velocity commands each step.
evaluation: ir-sim TurtleBot3 navigation, 100 trials per setting, 5-8 agents, 4 real robots; vs MASAC/MATD3/MADDPG plus 3 ablations; 0% collisions vs 8-91% baselines, 31-45% without CBLF; no latency reported.
contribution: Couples a LiDAR control-barrier-like action screening filter with graph-attention multi-agent RL, cutting collisions to zero in cooperative robot navigation under a time-varying communication topology.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes, a MAPPO policy screened by a geometric CBLF filter. Check (c) primacy: this is cooperative navigation and success rate shares headline billing with collision rate. No intervention rate, no filter latency, and no real-world collision statistics - the four-robot run is a qualitative demo. LiDAR field of view is 180 degrees in the problem section but 360 degrees in the hardware section.

title: SwarmNxt: Open-source Software-Hardware Platform for Fast and Agile Aerial Swarms
evidence: "It automatically triggers a landing command if an agent exits a predefined safe zone" (Sec. II-C.2, Safety Node)
method: Open-source aerial-swarm platform: Orin NX drones run onboard depth, mapping, decentralized HDSM planning and 100 Hz adaptive MPC; a Safety Node forces landing on geofence exit or EKF variance breach.
evaluation: Real flights, mocap arena, 6 and 4 drones; no baselines or ablations; MPC 1.13 ms mean, 40.4 ms max vs 10 ms budget; min distance 0.652-0.668 m; zero collisions.
contribution: Provides an open hardware-software swarm platform with per-stage mean, SD and worst-case timing of onboard perception, planning and control on Jetson Orin NX during real multi-drone flights.
flag: Weak include on (d) only; exclude-E1 is equally defensible. This is a platform paper: there is no baseline and no ablation, and the only comparison (Table I) is a qualitative feature matrix. It must not be read as safety evidence - zero collisions comes from two conservatively tuned indoor configurations with metrics over 2-minute windows. The Safety Node is a real runtime halt (forced landing) but is never evaluated: no trigger count, no false-halt rate, so (a) is not met under the minimum-evaluation rule. Value to the review is the timing table: MPC worst case 40.4 ms overruns its 10 ms period (PX4 holds last setpoint), depth 148 ms mean/246 ms max at about 7 Hz, planning 26.2 ms mean/86.8 max, GPU 95 percent used. Nothing here is near sub-15 ms for perception or planning. Localization depends on external mocap, so the system is not decentralized as a whole (authors say so). Operator dashboard can command drones but no human takeover procedure is described, so human handoff is not credited. Read via a summarising fetch tool, so check quotes and table values against the PDF.

title: Learning Communication-Conditioned Generative Policies for Decentralized Multi-Agent Collision Avoidance
evidence: Sec IV-C: "No additional safety layers, privileged information or centralized coordination signals are used"; Abstract: "near-expert collision avoidance performance"
method: Decentralized agents exchange learned messages, attention-aggregated into an embedding that conditions a flow-matching policy generating K-step action sequences; receding-horizon execution, warm-started plan reused when messages drop.
evaluation: Gym Collision Avoidance sim, trained on 4 agents, tested 4 and 8; baselines CADRL expert, centralized/decentralized BC, BC+attention; 3 ablations; success and collision rate; 4 Thymio robots; no latency.
contribution: Communication-conditioned flow-matching policy for decentralized collision avoidance: 3% collisions at 4 agents and 6% at 8 (cooperative) versus 21% and 17% for attention-based BC, and 69% without communication.
flag: Generative learned policy, no runtime filter - enters under (c) only. Table I (success/collision): proposed 0.97/0.03 (4 coop), 0.80/0.19 (4 non-coop), 0.92/0.06 (8 coop), 0.79/0.19 (8 non-coop); CADRL 1.0/0.0 at 4 coop. Extracted 8-agent cells for Centralized BC and CADRL were misaligned - check the PDF table. Two ablations match or beat the full model in some cells (0.93 vs 0.92 success at 8 coop). Dropout results (50/75/95 percent) are figures only, no numbers; delay not modelled. 6-agent results not tabulated. Real-robot trial count and compute not reported. Abstract contains no numbers. Read via WebFetch summariser; some text garbled.

title: Exact Feasibility Certification and Optimal Responsibility Allocation for Multi-Robot CBF Safety Filters
evidence: "each agent instead picks the input closest to its nominal one that meets its share" (Section V, after Algorithm 1)
method: Exact conic feasibility certificate (scalar feasibility reserve) for multi-robot CBF safety filters, plus an LP allocating shared pairwise constraints to maximise the worst local margin; dual support localises conflicts.
evaluation: Simulation, 320 paired runs, N=6-12 planar vehicles, 50 Hz; vs uniform, capability-weighted, centralized; infeasible steps about 50% to 6.2%; violating runs 118/160 to 24/160; no hardware or timing.
contribution: Gives an exact feasibility certificate and optimal responsibility split for decentralised multi-robot barrier-function safety filters, cutting infeasible control steps from about half to 6% and safety-violating runs from 118 to 24 of 160.
flag: Simulation only (hardware left to future work) and no solve time or latency is reported although the LP and filter are recomputed every 50 Hz step, so criterion (d) is not met. The abstract's 118/160 to 24/160 applies to the heterogeneous fleet only (capability-weighted is 121/160); violating-run counts for the identical fleet and for the centralized filter are not given, and a safety-violating run is not formally defined (inferred from closest approach). The proposed filter still violates in 24/160 runs and is infeasible on 6.2% of steps; when infeasible it applies the least-infeasible input and reports the responsible pair - it does not halt or defer. The certificate is instantaneous and says nothing about future feasibility. In the infeasible-branch ablation the 10.7% vs 17.3% figures were not clearly attributed in my reading. The allocation LP is centralised with scalars broadcast. Simulator not named, seeds not reported.

title: BLINDSPOT: A Benchmark for Safety and Refusal Calibration in Long-Horizon Tool-Using Agents
evidence: Abstract: a benchmark for trajectory-level safety calibration of long-horizon tool-using agents, scoring each trajectory as Safe Completion, Correct Refusal, Unsafe Completion, Over-Refusal or Indeterminate (Table 1).
method: Benchmark of 22 attack families, 35 scenarios, 7 domains and over 2500 trajectories; an adaptive LLM user agent drives a stateful tool environment, with execution-grounded adjudication of refusal calibration.
evaluation: 13 LLMs, 14.7-turn trajectories; horizon, adaptivity, safe-twin, stateful-vs-text and adjudication ablations; unsafe-completion 2-58%, over-refusal 7-33%, Fail@10 11-87%; no baseline system, no latency or hardware.
contribution: BLINDSPOT scores long-horizon tool-using agents on unsafe completion and over-refusal together, showing unsafe rates climb with horizon and with adaptive users across thirteen models.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes, LLM tool-using agents, but nothing is guarded at runtime - tool validation is evaluation harness and the block/approval/escalate interventions in App. B.12 are offline analysis, so no (a). Check (c): one target agent plus a simulated user agent, not multi-agent collaboration; I credited (c) under safety evaluation of tool-calling agents. Fig. 6 caption says half of failures emerge by turn 9 while Sec. 6.2 says 50% by turn 11, and that timing rests on only 16 unsafe trajectories.

title: Collective Loss of Control in LLM Agent Systems: An Epidemic Account of Mutation, Contagion, and Recovery
evidence: Sec 9.4/Sec 10: containment (suspend outbound messages, revoke pending permissions, quarantine sessions) is only recommended - 'The present benchmark does not establish the performance of these proposed defenses.'
method: Epidemic account of loss of control spreading between LLM agent sessions, plus RogueHandoff-20: a sandboxed benchmark where a successor agent inherits a predecessor trajectory ending at a pending harmful call.
evaluation: 20 Docker scenarios x 3 conditions (normal, direct attack, handoff), 60 episodes per route, 6 routes; ledger-scored harm rate. Handoff raises harm +5 to +45 pp. No hardware or latency.
contribution: Models contagion of unsafe state between LLM agent sessions and measures it: inheriting a compromised predecessor trajectory raised harmful-action rates by up to 45 percentage points over a direct request.
flag: Hazard evaluation, not a safeguard: no interceptor, proposed defences untested, no component ablations. Multi-agent only nominally - predecessor is a frozen trajectory, one live successor; no population-scale contagion measured (the ~700-agent figure is an external incident).
