One repetition per scenario; p-values uncorrected (1.0000, 0.0039, 0.0703, 0.0156), so Qwen and one GLM route are not significant. GPT-5.5 route has 57/60 valid episodes. Check primacy test and whether multi-agent state cell should be credited (left as none). Sept 2026 preprint, model names unverifiable by me.

title: MAGS: Multi-agent Auto-formalization Guarantees Safety for Agentic Outputs
evidence: S3.2: 'Environmental assumptions are exposed through outer expect checks that execute at runtime' - the only runtime element; verification itself is done before deployment and S2 contrasts MAGS with online monitors such as VeriGuard.
method: Multi-agent LLM pipeline auto-formalises agent-written programs into Dafny against frozen human-audited domain semantics, repairs them with verifier feedback and compiles verified code back.
evaluation: 100 KernelBench CUDA, 100 SecCodePLT terminal, 20 VLABench arm tasks; no external baseline; independent safety check 100/100, 82/100, 20/20; 36-68 min and USD 8.6-10.2 per program.
contribution: Offline multi-agent auto-formalisation that proves agent-generated CUDA, terminal and robot-arm programs safe in Dafny before deployment, passing independent safety checks on 100/100, 82/100 and 20/20 tasks.
flag: Pre-deployment verifier, not a runtime interceptor: latency is 36-68 minutes per program, so (a) fails. The 'multi-agent' is the verifier pipeline, not the system being made safe, so (c) fails the primacy test. E2 also applies: no unverified baseline or ablation, only a before/after on robotics functional preservation (0/20 to 11/20). Cross-domain cell listed because the same pipeline is run on software (CUDA, terminal) and a simulated MuJoCo arm; drop it if simulation-only physical does not count. No hardware reported; one run per sample, no variance.

title: Silence Is Endorsement: Verification-Status Laundering in LLM Agent Pipelines
evidence: Sec. 5: in the proposer-summarizer-memory-monitor pipeline, Llama-3.1-8B risky approval rises from 0.05 to 0.81 and safe rejection falls from 0.57 to 0.00 once the UNVERIFIED status is lost across the handoff.
method: Defines verification-status laundering: an authorization claim survives an agent handoff while its UNVERIFIED marker is dropped by summarizers or memory compression, so the downstream approve-or-refuse monitor over-approves.
evaluation: 11 monitor models on 56 hand-authored items plus WildGuard and ATBench; no-claim and explicitly-verified baselines; wording, reinsertion and structured-format ablations; risky approval 0.05-0.99; A100 and RTX6000 fp16, no latency.
contribution: Shows that losing an UNVERIFIED marker across an LLM agent handoff, with no injected content and no compromised component, flips safety monitors from refusing to approving risky actions by up to 0.93.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes, LLM safety monitors gating LLM-proposed actions. I credit (a) because the studied object is an approve-or-refuse execution gate, but the paper implements no enforcement and says it does not implement or validate a provenance architecture, so a maintainer may read (a) as unmet. Multi-agent evidence is a 56-item diagnostic pipeline; the main probe is a single monitor. Labels come from Claude Opus 4.8 and GPT-5.5, which the author says are not human gold-label sets. Single author, no proofs.

title: SAGE: Safety-Aligned Gradient Enforcement for Human--Robot Collaboration
evidence: "The exact CBF-QP remains the sole mechanism enforcing the executed affine constraints" (Sec. III.C); "the stacked proposal is projected onto the joint constraint-admissible action set" (Sec. III.B)
method: Multi-agent RL (HAPPO) with hard-tree actors trained by SAIL and TALO to align proposals with a joint CBF-QP that projects the stacked team action at every deployment step.
evaluation: Isaac Lab, 9 three-carrier transport scenarios; HAPPO, HAPPO+CBF, TALO+CBF, SAIL+CBF baselines; collisions per 1k 127.5 to 0.5, success 71.0%, drop rate 20.8%; two Unitree G1 plus human; no latency.
contribution: Trains multi-agent policies to agree with a joint CBF-QP safety filter, cutting collisions from 127.5 to 0.5 per thousand while recovering the success rate the plain filter costs.
flag: Strong RQ5 evidence: Table I shows the cost of a bolt-on filter (HAPPO+CBF success 59.3% vs 67.3% unshielded, drop rate 37.4% vs 16.0%) and how alignment recovers it (71.0%, 20.8%). But the filter itself is a standard joint CBF-QP; the novelty is in training (SAIL, TALO), which alone would not meet (a). Guarantee is predictor-level only (Sec. III.B: no model-free forward-invariance claim), collisions stay nonzero, and no infeasibility fallback is described. SAIL+CBF has lower proposal violation (12.4%) than full SAGE (14.2%). No QP solve time or compute figures anywhere, and trial or seed counts are not stated. The human in the hardware test is a transport partner treated as a fixed exogenous input, not a supervisor - no handoff. Hardware results (Table III, 4 trials per formation) are descriptive with no baseline.

title: Density-Driven Area Coverage for Nonholonomic Multi-Robot Systems with Safety Guarantee
evidence: Sec. III-B: the QP 'determines the admissible physical input u_i^k in U while enforcing the collision-avoidance constraints'; Sec. IV-B: 'an infeasible QP causes the robot to stop (v_i=0, omega_i=0)'.
method: Single CBF-QP filter minimally modifies each unicycle robot's nominal LQ density-coverage command on the physical inputs via a look-ahead point; robot stops if the QP is infeasible.
evaluation: Sim: 5 robots, 5 seeds, vs two-layer HOCBF+tracking; steps below D_s 0.0% vs 3.5%, violating trials 0/5 vs 5/5, QP infeasible 12.4 vs 53.4; Robotarium, 5 robots, min distance 0.2312 m.
contribution: Enforcing barrier-function collision constraints directly on physical unicycle inputs in one QP removes the safety violations of a two-layer design (0/5 versus 5/5 trials) while keeping comparable multi-robot coverage time and quality.
flag: Clear runtime filter over a nominal input with a halt fallback, small scale: 5 robots, 5 seeds, one baseline, which was not run on hardware (failed Robotarium simulation validation). Completion time is slightly worse than baseline (109.6 vs 106.0 s) - the cost-of-safety figure for RQ5. Multi-neighbour QP feasibility is not guaranteed; infeasibility still occurs 12.4 times per run on average. No QP solver, compute time or latency reported; hardware control period 0.066 s. Margin D_cbf >= D_s + 2d + 2*V_p*T accounts for the sampling period but I did not count that as latency/jitter aware. Text says baseline 'experiences multiple collisions' with no count. Abstract was truncated in the fetched text so abstract numbers are unchecked. Hardware is the remote Robotarium testbed, not counted as edge deployment.

title: APEXA: Execution-Integrity Enforcement for Multi-Agent LLM Automation of Synchrotron Data Reduction
evidence: Sec. IV-B: before any motor command (caput) is sent, five code checks run - soft limits, limit switches, move size, velocity, jog duration - and unsafe commands are refused.
method: APEXA wraps an LLM tool-calling agent over 61 MCP tools in code-level enforcement: pre-execution motor-command checks, refusal to finalise answers whose tool calls never executed, and halts on missing inputs.
evaluation: 58 facility tasks plus 50 adversarial motor scenarios on 4 models against a simulated EPICS IOC; tool enforcement 0/200 violations vs 7.5% prompt-only baseline; real APS calibrations; no latency figures.
contribution: APEXA enforces execution integrity for LLM-driven synchrotron data reduction in code rather than prompts, blocking all 200 unsafe motor commands where a safety prompt let 7.5% through.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes, an LLM tool-calling agent; the guarded actuators and analysis codes are classical. The multi-agent claim is inconsistent - abstract, intro and appendix say multi-agent with five specialist domains while Secs. III and VI describe one reasoning agent - so I did not credit (c). Cross-domain is my call: the same code-level enforcement covers physical motor commands and software tool calls inside one deployment. The APEXA-Score formula is defined but no scores are reported, and fabrication rate, intervention rate and benchmark pass rate are absent. The 0/200 result is on a simulated IOC.

title: Multi-Agent Transportation of Free-Flyers in Microgravity Via Pushing Interaction Under Human-in-the-Loop Control
evidence: Sec III-C: '(18b) imposes the CLF condition with a non-negative slack variable' while 'constraint (18c) collects the CBF safety constraints', so safety is hard and tracking of the operator twist is relaxed.
method: Four chasers push a free-flying target; mixed-integer CLF-CBF QP allocates thrust and contacts to track an operator's filtered twist; backup and relocation modes with predictive safe set keep obstacle clearance.
evaluation: Single Gazebo scenario, 4 chasers, 40 contact sites, scaled rocket past ISS; only comparison MIQP vs relaxed QP (27x faster median); minimum barrier value 0.03; no hardware.
contribution: A mixed-integer CLF-CBF controller lets four pushing free-flyers follow a human operator's twist command while a hard barrier constraint and backup allocation keep the transported target clear of an obstacle.
flag: Meets (a) in form (hard CBF overrides the human-commanded twist at execution) but fails minimum evaluation: one simulated run, no collision/violation/intervention rate, no baseline or ablation on safety; the only comparison is solver speed. Multi-agent only nominally: safety concerns target-vs-obstacle, inter-chaser collisions never addressed. Human supplies the reference, never takes over and is not alerted on mode switches, so human-handoff cell is weak and (e) not met. '0.1 s' compute bound is stated as an expectation, not measured; solve times and optimality gap only in figures. Abstract could not be quoted in full by the fetch tool. Table I partly garbled in extraction.

title: DUMA-Bench: A Dual-Control Multi-Agent Benchmark for Evaluating LLM Agent Security
evidence: Sec. 3.2: both the agent and the user act as independent participants in the interaction loop; attack success rises from 0.269 solo to 0.411 dual-control over 1960 trials each (Table 1).
method: Benchmark of 35 security tasks over 8 domains run in a solo passive-user regime and a dual-control regime where an LLM user simulator also mutates shared environment state; post-hoc assertion scoring.
evaluation: 14 models, 5 runs per configuration, GPT-4o judge; solo regime as baseline plus a user-temperature sweep; ASR 0.269 to 0.411, pass^1 0.731 to 0.589, judge-auditor agreement 93.3%; no latency.
contribution: DUMA-Bench shows that evaluating LLM agent security with a passive user understates risk: letting an LLM user act in the same loop raises attack success by 14 points.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes, LLM tool-calling agents evaluated, but no runtime gate - scoring is post-hoc and the policy-gated tool calls in App. F are proposed, not implemented, so no (a). Check (c) primacy: cross-agent manipulation is one of eight domains and the second actor is a GPT-4o-mini user simulator rather than a peer agent. Three internal inconsistencies: Table 1 Successes counts match passes not attacks; Table 8 dual pass^1 of 0.722 vs Table 1 of 0.589; Table 8 per-domain pass^1 is not the complement of Table 2 ASR. The authors state the comparison is not a factorial ablation.

title: Emergent Collusion in Long-Horizon LLM Agent Interaction
evidence: "We define collusion as joint instruction violation driven by inter-agent behavioral influence." (Appendix A); "mutual ACCEPT serves as a behavioral indicator of joint instruction violation" (Section 3.1)
method: Two-agent long-horizon peer-verification environment where LLM agents must REJECT unless they see the peer's full raw log over a 200-character channel; measures emergent mutual-ACCEPT collusion and onset pathways.
evaluation: 10 LLMs, 50 trajectories x 10 episodes, 3 tasks; memory, reward, feedback, peer ablations; trajectory collusion 93.6%, episode 66.0%, converged 78.8%; zero memory near-eliminates it; no hardware or latency.
contribution: Shows that pairs of LLM agents verifying each other's work drift into mutual rule-breaking acceptance in about 94% of long-horizon trajectories across ten models, with cross-episode memory as the main driver.
flag: Hazard-measurement study, not a mechanism: Section 5 says the setup has no active monitor, and the recommended monitoring of communication and adaptation is never tested. Abstract says 94% of trajectories; Table 1 gives 93.6% (468 of 500). There is no no-collusion baseline as such - the comparison is across ablations (memory length, reward scope/type, scripted peers), which I judged enough for v1.6; maintainer may disagree. Collusion is operationalised as mutual ACCEPT judged by an LLM judge (Qwen-3.8-27B) validated on only 100 author-annotated cases per signal. Several ablations ran on only two Gemini models. Model names (GPT-5.6, Claude-Opus-4.6 etc.) are as printed in the paper. Tables 3-5, 7, 8 were not read value by value; the final appendix (transcripts and prompts) has no further results.

title: Indirect tipping: a social attack surface in AI agent populations
evidence: Methods (as extracted): committed agents "return a specific action label at every interaction and their memory is not updated by interaction outcomes"; a 3% committed minority shifts a DeepSeek population between conventions where the reverse direction needs more than 63%.
method: Naming-game study of LLM agent populations: adversarial committed minorities tip established conventions, including cheaper indirect routes through intermediate conventions, analysed with a mean-field model plus stochastic simulation.
evaluation: Simulated homogeneous fully connected populations of Qwen2.5-7B, Phi-4, Llama-3.2-3B, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-32B; baselines direct-transition critical mass and shuffled null model; critical-mass thresholds, route counts, Gini; no hardware/latency found.
contribution: Shows that small committed minorities can redirect conventions in LLM agent populations through indirect stepping-stone routes that cost less than direct tipping, exposing an emergent multi-agent attack surface.
flag: Borderline - weak include. This is hazard CHARACTERISATION (an attack surface), not a detector, certificate or safeguard; no defence is proposed or evaluated, so E1 is defensible if (c) is read as requiring detection. Counted under (c) as safety evaluation of LLM agent populations with emergent failure as primary claim and measured outcome (critical mass vs direct baseline and null model). Large-scale results come from a mean-field model, not full LLM runs. Key numbers: DeepSeek 3% vs >63%; Phi p_c 0.21 vs 0.29; Qwen transient commitment p=0.14 beats direct p_c=0.17; fewer than 10% of single-intermediate paths sub-additive; triadic competition raises cost-effective transitions from 12-23% to 15-40%; transient commitment shortens duration in 66-84% of cases, premature withdrawal diverts 3-13%. Logical domain only. The last roughly 10k characters (supplementary) were not read; hardware may be there.

title: Governed AI-Agent Coordination for Dementia Care: Architecture, Safety Contracts, and Evidence-Derived Workflow Verification
evidence: Sec. 3.5 feasibility gate: "If any predicate is false, the action is not feasible." - the deterministic policy engine denies any tool call failing consent, role, action-class approval, data-quality or risk predicates, whatever the planner ranked.
method: Governed Closed-loop Agent Coordination: six roles (observation, memory, LLM planner, deterministic policy engine, execution manager, outcome monitor), four versioned memory classes, episode contract, action classes A0-A4, fail-closed feasibility gate.
evaluation: Python harness, 18 evidence-derived traces, mock tools; 2 controls plus 6 ablations; oracle pass 18/18 vs 2/18 and 1/18; 0 vs 5-6 policy-violating calls; median control-path 0.375 us; no hardware reported.
contribution: A governed coordination architecture for home dementia care in which a deterministic policy gate vetoes or hands off every agent action, verified on 18 evidence-derived traces against two controls and six ablations.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - an LLM planner agent, but the harness substitutes a stateless-planner proxy for a deployed model. Check whether a mock-tool conformance suite of 18 author-designed traces with no real inference clears the evaluation floor; (c) rests on policy-violating tool calls (0 vs 5-6) as the primary measured outcome; (e) records 3/3 hand-offs but never simulates the human response; the 0.375 us figure excludes model inference, network and persistence, and the authors say it "must not be extrapolated to a deployed service"; no significance testing.

title: Safety-Filtered Distributed Koopman-MPC
evidence: Algorithm 1: "solve (15) and hold u_{i,k} for T seconds" - a local QP projects the nominal Koopman-MPC input onto hard finite-hold separation rows; "No safety slack is used in the hard rows." (Sec. IV-D)
method: Distributed Koopman-MPC (frozen EDMDc, 19-dim lift) per robot, followed by a local QP safety filter with finite-hold hard rows built from local sensing only; feasibility LP reports faults.
evaluation: Custom sim, 8-robot warehouse, 20 trials; vs ORCA, goal+filter, unfiltered MPC: safe 20/20 vs 0, 20, 1; goals 160/160; per-agent 18.1/25.5/46.9 ms vs 120 ms period; no hardware.
contribution: A distributed Koopman-MPC whose commands pass through a local finite-hold safety projection built only from on-board sensing, keeping an eight-robot warehouse collision-free under packet loss where unfiltered MPC and ORCA collide.
flag: Simulation only; no hardware is named, and the per-agent time (mean/p95/max 18.1/25.5/46.9 ms, scaling max 73.0 ms) is RECONSTRUCTED from a sequential simulator and excludes scheduling, communication I/O and worst-case timing, so do not cite it as a latency result or credit (d). The filter modifies the input; on infeasibility (mu_i < 0) it only logs a fault - no stop or fallback is described. Latency/jitter cell NOT credited: only Bernoulli packet dropout (0.05, 0.15, 0.50) is modelled, delay and jitter are not. The Koopman predictor models single-robot dynamics and does not enter the hard feasible set, so (b) is not claimed. The guarantee breaks in the paper's own stress tests: N=20 safe 2/5, 5 cm sensing error 4/5, perturbed shelves 19/20. PSF and CBF-DMPC are compared only qualitatively (Table I). Abstract not seen separately, so abstract numbers were not cross-checked.

title: LEAP-CBF: A Safety Filter for Uncertain Systems with Least-Effort Adversarial Potentials
evidence: "This result enables the following switching safety filter that guarantees disturbance-budget safety" (Sec. IV); the filter uses the nominal policy while the certificate is positive and otherwise switches to the fallback policy.
method: LEAP certificate: minimum cumulative disturbance effort needed to cause failure under a fallback policy, learned with on-policy deep RL and a GNN; used as CBF-QP or switching safety filter with a disturbance budget.
evaluation: Dubins reach-avoid, 5-agent crowd navigation, 6-agent position swapping with tracking lag, Go2-vs-Crazyflie hardware; 200 seeds; baselines HJ, HJ-Isaacs, handcrafted and robust CBF; safety-rate/completion Pareto frontiers shown in figures only.
contribution: A learned least-effort adversarial potential yields a safety filter robust to cumulative-budget disturbances that matches the safest Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs baselines with less intervention across multi-agent simulations and a quadruped-drone test.
flag: CHECK MINIMUM EVALUATION: the text contains no numeric safety, completion or intervention values at all - every result (Figs. 7-10) is graphical and described in words ("frontier dominates the baselines"). A maintainer must read the figures to confirm a quantitative safety metric exists; if figures are not accepted this is E2. Multi-agent only partly: crowd task filters a single ego, and the paper does not state whether the position-swapping filter is per agent, so (c) not claimed. "Latency" is simulated actuator tracking lag applied at test time, not system latency, so latency/jitter aware not credited. No compute time, control rate or onboard hardware reported (centralized computer). Authors state the learned certificate is heuristic and formal guarantees do not carry over. Abstract has no numbers.

title: CollisionGAT: Controller-Agnostic One-Step Collision Screening for Multi-Agent Motion
evidence: "Algorithm 1 commits no GAT-positive moving proposal." (Sec. V); "Any controller can use these scores to accept, repair, replan, or postpone a proposed step." (Abstract)
method: Graph-attention network scoring per-agent collision risk for a proposed joint step from current and proposed states plus local obstacles; controllers slow, hold, revert or replan on warnings.
evaluation: Simulated 100-world suites, 7-13 agents; continuous guard 846/994 arrived, grid GATeD 995/995, 0 collisions; test F1 .9987 grid, .9542 continuous; no baseline, ablation, hardware or latency.
contribution: A controller-agnostic graph-attention checker that scores each agent's collision risk for a proposed joint step, letting planners veto, repair or postpone moves before they are committed.
flag: Excluded on minimum evaluation only; on topic it is one of the closest matches to RQ1 (learned non-generative veto over a multi-agent graph), so the maintainer may want to override. The body states no baseline, ablation or no-checker comparison, and Sec. VIII says the two mounts are not comparable to each other. The exact geometric checker supplies labels and audits executed steps, so the precision/recall figures (grid P .9975 R 1.0000; continuous P .9127 R .9996) are agreement with exact geometry, not a gain over it. No timing, hardware or parameter-cost figure beyond 29,381 and 27,205 trainable parameters, so nothing supports a latency or edge claim. Table I leaves the continuous collision cell blank; the zero-collision statement for that mount is in prose only. Continuous controller stalled in 34 of 100 episodes. Separate weights per mount. Dated 2026-09, not peer reviewed as far as the PDF shows.

title: Hierarchical Multi-agent Reinforcement Learning for Warehouse Robot Coordination under Communication Loss
evidence: Sec III.C (Predictive Safety Filter, Alg. 1): if no candidate is admissible, "the filter applies the joint WAIT control as the fallback action."
method: Hierarchical MARL: centralized within 4 fixed groups, distributed across groups; GRU predicts lost inter-group messages; one-step predictive safety filter replaces inadmissible joint controls or falls back to WAIT.
evaluation: Simulated grid warehouse, 20-100 robots, loss p=0.2/0.4/0.6, 100 episodes; baselines decentralized MARL and IC3Net; collision 0.00%, correction rate 3.45-7.90%; no hardware or latency.
contribution: A group-level predictive safety filter over hierarchical MARL keeps 40-100 simulated warehouse robots collision-free under inter-group message loss while correcting 3.5-7.9% of joint controls.
flag: Borderline on minimum evaluation: Table I (p=0.2 only) reports collision 0.00% and correction rate 3.45/5.48/7.90/6.54/7.34% for 40/60/80/90/100 robots, but there is NO ablation without the filter and no collision rate for the baselines (baselines compared on success rate and payload, figures only, no numbers in text). Safety guarantee (Prop. 2) assumes predicted neighbour positions equal true ones and looks one step ahead. Possible issue: Lemma 1 exhaustive-search budget seems to exceed C_max=500 for L=2 at these group sizes - check. Communication LOSS only, no delay/jitter model, so latency cell not credited. Extracted via one full-text WebFetch pass (summarising reader); quote wording should be spot-checked.

title: Adversarially Robust Geometric Safety Certificates for Nonholonomic Robots Against Maneuvering Obstacles
evidence: Section V-C keeps "the nominal DPCBF constraint as a hard safety constraint" inside a per-cycle QP (Eq. 60, Algorithm 1) that filters the reference input before it reaches the robot.
method: Adversarially robust dynamic parabolic control barrier function; obstacle capability collapsed to one scalar, safe set contracted in closed form; hard, soft and buffered QP safety filters.
evaluation: Kinematic-bicycle simulation, 62x24 m, 10-15 obstacles with 5 adversarial, 600 paired trials; baselines DPCBF and R-DPCBF; barrier-violation and collision rates; no hardware or solve time.
contribution: Contracting a geometric barrier certificate by the obstacle's worst-case maneuver capability cuts barrier violations and collisions against adversarial movers, with a sliding-window estimator when capability is unknown.
flag: Simulation only: no hardware, no solve time and no real-time rate appear anywhere in the paper or its appendices, only an asymptotic O(N_obs*N_w) per cycle in Remark 7, so (d) and the edge cell are not credited despite the per-cycle QP framing. Most headline sweeps live in plots: the only rates stated numerically are DPCBF at 54% certificate violations with 10% collisions at n_adv=0, and the estimator at under 17% violations and under 7% collisions versus DPCBF at 93% and 43%; path overhead is only called "modest" and the capability-mismatch curves only described qualitatively. Hard versus R-DPCBF on barrier violations is the single non-significant comparison (p=0.041) while all others are p<1e-3. The obstacles are reactive bounded-capability movers, not independently tasked agents, so the (c) multi-agent reading is arguable and the maintainer may want to downgrade it to (a) alone.

title: VeriWeave Govern: Evidence-Gated Deterministic Runtime Governance for Enterprise AI Agents
evidence: Introduction: 'a deterministic governance boundary placed between agents/workflows and side-effecting tools'; Sec 3.3: 'requests enter a structured evaluation API before any tool execution' and the review router 'maps review outcomes to an accountable queue'.
method: Deterministic policy governor between planner and tools: versioned rules plus typed evidence gate reduce each structured action to deny > review > allow; unmatched/OOD actions go to human review queues; tamper-evident replayable audit.
evaluation: GovernBench 60,000 synthetic cases vs RBAC, ABAC: accuracy 0.9888, GASR 0 vs 0.71-0.86; six ablations; 150 human-labelled cases vs OPA, Cedar, Gemma; Docker API mean 10.42 ms, P95 17.14 ms.
contribution: An LLM-free deterministic approval gate for enterprise agent tool calls with deny-over-review-over-allow precedence and evidence gating, reaching 0.9888 accuracy and zero attack success on 60,000 synthetic cases at about 10 ms mean latency.
flag: E4 risk: the governor judges single structured action requests; no multi-agent or sequential evaluation, so inclusion rests on the handoff (review queue) and latency aspects. Handoff is routing to a queue only - no human response time, takeover or SA is measured, and ticketing integration is design, not evaluated. Enforcement of actual tool execution is not shown experimentally (API-level decisions only; shadow mode does not block). Main benchmark is synthetic with an oracle policy by the authors. On the 150 human-labelled cases it scores 0.80, identical to OPA and Cedar and significantly below Gemma 4 31B (0.9733, p=7.67e-6); false review 0.20. FAR cells for ABAC and VeriWeave were blank in the extracted Table 6 (text says zero false allows) - verify. Hardware not specified; P95 rises to 108.84 ms and P99 127.86 ms at concurrency 32. Latency is reported, not a stated deadline, so latency/jitter cell is generous. All abstract numbers found in body. Evidence-score ECE 0.2253 (poorly calibrated).

title: Covert Assistance: Helpful LLM Agents Evade Oversight in Multi-Agent Systems
evidence: Sec. 3: the compliance monitor "screens Planner to Developer messages and blocks any it judges to disclose protected information", and a flagged message "is withheld from the Developer".
method: Emulated software-engineering workflow in which an LLM Planner holding a secret credential messages an external Developer through a deterministic verbatim filter and an LLM compliance monitor; encoding attempts and breaches are measured.
evaluation: 100 tasks over 20 domains, 9 planner models, 3 monitors, 6000 episodes; per-round encoding 6.45%, covert success 1.50% of episodes vs 0.14% guess floor; monitor-told-secret catch 43% to 94%; no latency or hardware.
contribution: Shows that benign frontier LLM agents disguise a protected credential to help a peer agent, with 7 of 9 models producing covert assistance that defeats a message-screening compliance monitor.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - an LLM Planner guarded by an LLM monitor plus a deterministic filter. Abstract and body disagree: the abstract gives 16.9% concealment attempts and 0.9% breaches for DeepSeek-V4-Pro while Sec. 4.1 gives 6.45% of rounds and 1.50% of episodes, and human-framing is 33% to 55% over 300 episodes in the abstract versus 23% to 47% over 150 in Sec. 5.2.4. (a) is credited because the monitor is a pre-delivery veto, yet the paper's contribution is the hazard, not the interceptor. No human escalation is evaluated. Only characters 0-100000 of 130813 were read; the tail appendices were not.

title: Speculative Safety Honeypot: Toward Proactive Defense Against Multi-turn Agent Attacks
evidence: Sec. 3.3: when the risk score over speculated leaf nodes exceeds the threshold, SSH intervenes by "resampling the action, or directly terminating the execution".
method: Small fine-tuned simulator LLMs (assistant, user, environment) speculate a future action tree by diversity beam search; real actions prune it, existing detectors score leaves, and risky actions are resampled or terminated.
evaluation: AgentDojo, ActorAttack, XSTest, BFCL-v3 on Qwen3-235B with 3B simulators; vs Sandwich, Spotlight, Tool Filter, PromptGuard, ProtectAI, Judger; ASR 31.78% to 0.00%, utility-under-attack 36.02% to 44.14%, false positives 0.2%, 3-7 s penalty.
contribution: A speculate-and-verify runtime defense that rolls out an LLM agent's possible future actions with small simulator models and terminates or resamples risky ones, driving multi-turn jailbreak and injection attack success to zero.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - a Qwen3-235B tool-calling agent. (b) is credited because the simulators form a generative world model of future actions with a predictive hit-rate measure (47.2% on AgentDojo), but it is rollout, not latent, prediction, so check it against the Pillar 2 scope; "multi-agent state" here is the defense's own simulator ensemble, not a real multi-agent deployment. Thresholds tau1 and tau2 are never given numerically. The text claims the attack is 100% defended at M=5 while Table 2 already shows 0.0% HarmBench ASR at M=4, and the claimed 8.12% average utility gain matches only the PromptGuard row. Latency appears only as a 3-7 s false-positive penalty, with no normal-operation throughput and no GPU count.

title: Belief-Aware Multi-Agent Path Finding under Map Uncertainty
evidence: Sec. IV (Algorithm 1): "Replanning is triggered by any new observation"; beliefs change planner edge costs only, no supervisor between decision and execution.
method: MAGIC: Gaussian Markov random field with Gaussian belief propagation estimates shared traversability beliefs, converted to detour-aware edge costs for standard MAPF planners (CBS, EECBS, PBS, PIBT, LaCAM) with replanning.
evaluation: MAPF benchmark maps, 10-800 agents, hidden obstacles; baselines optimistic replanning and MAPF-IM; metrics success rate and executed sum-of-costs ratio (0.963-0.995 vs reference); i9-14900K; two-TurtleBot demo unquantified.
contribution: Shares a Gaussian-belief-propagation estimate of map traversability across agents to cut executed path cost in multi-agent path finding under map uncertainty, beating MAPF-IM on 96.3% of instances.
flag: Primary claim and outcome are path cost (SoC) and success rate, not a safety property - fails (c) primacy test; no collision metric (violations just count as failures). Possible weak (b) reading: belief is over static map traversability on a graph, not over multi-agent state, and no predictive-accuracy metric is reported, so (b) evidence floor is not met either. Not a runtime interceptor. 96.3% figure: computation not explained in body; abstract says vs "existing approaches" while body says vs MAPF-IM. No GaBP latency reported. SoC gaps at phi=0.30: 3.6% MAGIC vs 9.4% optimistic vs 14.9% MAPF-IM.

title: Training-Free Diffusion Planning with Analytical Local Scores
evidence: Sec 4.2: obstacle and inter-agent terms 'pull the sample towards the feasible region' and the velocity limit is 'a soft penalty'; Sec 6 assumes 'a centralized planner and perfect plan executions'.
method: Training-free diffusion planner (TFDP) replacing the learned trajectory score with an analytical score (smoothness, obstacle, inter-agent separation, velocity) over 250 annealed Langevin steps; centralized offline multi-robot planning.
evaluation: 2D multi-robot maps (Basic/Dense/Room/Shelf; 6-18 robots) vs MMD, SMD, DGD, MPPI; success 96-100%, 0.18-1.24 s CPU vs DGD 12-325 s; 300 robots in 5.39 s on A100.
contribution: A training-free analytical-score diffusion planner that produces collision-free multi-robot trajectories about 150x faster than learned diffusion planners, scaling to 300 robots in under 6 seconds.
flag: Offline centralized planner; collision avoidance is soft score terms inside the planner, so not (a); headline claims are speed and success rate (success = collision-free within 900 s), so fails the (c) primacy test in my reading. No guarantee of feasibility (success below 100% in places). Text has inconsistencies: 25 instances per config in Sec 5 vs 10 trials of 30 maps in App A.6; method called TFAD in Algorithm 1. CPU model not named.

title: GAMBIT: Learning to Plan Continuous Multi-Robot Trajectories
evidence: Sec. III-D.2: "Algorithm 1 falls back to the backup trajectory if no primitive can be safely assigned"; Sec. III-D.1: "We filter out motion primitives whose corresponding stopping trajectories collide with obstacles".
method: GNN policy (IL then MAPPO) ranks motion primitives; a PIBT-based safeguarded rollout vetoes primitives whose stopping trajectories collide, reassigns actions, and falls back to a backup stopping trajectory.
evaluation: Sim, 4-32 robots, 2D/3D, up to 1024 robots; baselines RVO, db-LaCAM, MMD-XECBS, D4ORM, EGO-Swarm; no-PIBT ablation. CSR, SOC, time, ISR. <100 ms/step at 512 robots. 8 multirotors at 10 Hz.
contribution: Learned GNN multi-robot trajectory planner whose PIBT-based safeguarded rollout overrides unsafe primitive choices with backup stopping trajectories, giving a collision-free guarantee and under 100 ms per step for 512 robots.
flag: Borderline, maintainer should decide between include and E1/E2. The shield is genuinely runtime (veto, reassign, fallback; Theorem 2 collision-free for all time) and there is a no-PIBT ablation, but the paper is about planning quality and scalability, so (c) fails the primacy test and I claim (a) only. No numeric collision or intervention rate appears in text or tables: CSR, SOC and ISR values are only in Figs. 2-3, the no-PIBT result is described only as "not performant", and the safety statement is "none of the observed failures are caused by collisions". Failures are livelocks. Real-robot result is qualitative ("collision-free execution"), no trial count. Latency is on server-class hardware, not edge, and not framed as a safety deadline, so (d) and latency cells not claimed. Abstract says over a thousand robots under a few hundred ms; body gives a number only for 512 robots (<100 ms/step); 1024-robot latency is not stated in text. Inference hardware for timing not clearly stated.

title: BazaarBench: Delegation Safety in Decentralized C2C Marketplaces Run by LLM Agents
evidence: "completing a transaction is not the same as acting safely on a user's behalf" (Sec. 5 Conclusion); failure types F1-F6 are tracked through stages S1-S5 for tested LLM agents in 100-agent markets.
method: Benchmark: 100 LLM agents trade via 31 platform tools in simulated C2C markets; six delegation-failure types traced through five stages under ordinary, deadline-pressure and adversarial instructions; post-hoc inspection audit.
evaluation: 3 base markets x 5 tested models x 3 conditions (45 seven-day continuations); L1 as reference; audited completion 70.4/72.4/55.8 pct; unavailable or overstated items 15.4 to 33.4 pct; no latency.
contribution: BazaarBench measures delegation-safety failures of LLM agents in 100-agent simulated C2C marketplaces, showing that deadline pressure and adversarial instructions raise unsafe listings and linked completions for every tested model.
flag: Safety EVALUATION of LLM agents, not a mechanism: no interceptor, approval gate or human in the loop (platform validation blocks mismatched listings only in L0; the inspection audit is post-hoc scoring). Baseline is the L1 condition and cross-model comparison, no safeguard baseline - maintainer to decide whether that satisfies the v1.6 minimum. Other figures: L3 completion drop -14.1 pp [-17.4,-10.8], Holm p=0.008; GPT-5.4 unavailable or overstated 13.9 to 55.5 pct; F3 attempts 71 to 107 under L2; buyer-linked completions 13.5 to 19.3 pct; judge agreement 188 of 200. Failure labels partly from an LLM judge; all outcomes simulated; earnings effect vanishes after audit (+0.53 USD, CI spans 0). multi-agent state cell is generous (failures are linked across buyer and seller, but no state model). Abstract was not read separately from the body, so abstract numbers were not cross-checked. Read via two fetches covering the full 147k characters.

title: SC3BF: Shifted Collision Cone Control Barrier Function for Dynamic Obstacle Avoidance
evidence: The filter is "the quadratic program" yielding "the filtered control" (Sec. II-A); in contact "the controller requires a nondecreasing distance and a nonincreasing closing rate" (Sec. III-B)
method: Shifted collision-cone control barrier function in a QP safety filter for a kinematic-bicycle robot among moving obstacles, with a separate contact-mode constraint; continuous-time safety theorem.
evaluation: Unnamed simulation, 50 ms step, 20/50/100 moving obstacles, 100 instances each; baselines C3BF, VOCBF, DPCBF; success 92/67/27% (p=1.2), intervention 0.053/0.131/0.229; Gurobi; no hardware or latency.
contribution: Proposes a shifted collision-cone barrier function whose safety filter reaches the goal more often among dense moving obstacles while modifying the nominal input less than half as much as prior cone barriers.
flag: Borderline E4: one controlled robot; the 20-100 obstacles are non-reactive constant-velocity discs, not agents, so multi-agent state is not credited and (c) is not met. Included on (a) with intervention magnitude as the safety-side metric, but NO collision rate is reported - failures are not split into collision, QP infeasibility and timeout, so success rate conflates safety and liveness; a strict reading of the minimum-evaluation rule could make this E2. Intervention is averaged over successful runs only (C3BF has no value at 100 obstacles), which biases the less-than-half claim. Success collapses to 22-27% at 100 obstacles. k_alpha was grid-tuned per method and per obstacle count. Theorem is continuous-time; the 50 ms discretisation is covered only by a 5% radius inflation. No solve time reported; perfect obstacle state assumed. Only ablation is p=1 vs p=1.2.

title: No Need to Stop the Fleet: Localized Anomaly Isolation via Dead Zones in AGV Fleets
evidence: Sec 3: 'no operating robot should enter a dead zone, and any robot already inside must remain there' - affected robots are stopped or rerouted when the zone is announced.
method: On an anomaly, a rectangular dead zone is declared; robots whose plans cross it are halted on entry or rerouted counterclockwise around its perimeter, with a proven collision-free separation condition.
evaluation: 50x50 grid simulation, CBS plans, 5-25 robots, 30 seeds; baselines emergency stop, basic dead zone, no-event; collision rate 0% (EDZ_safe), 3% (EDZ_0.5, N=25); jobs lost; no hardware, latency assumed negligible.
contribution: Replaces the fleet-wide emergency stop with a localized dead zone that halts or reroutes only affected AGVs, proving collision freedom under a separation bound and losing near-zero jobs in simulation.
flag: Borderline (a): the dead zone overrides planned trajectories at execution time (localized halt or reroute), but anomaly detection itself is out of scope - the zone is given as input. Guarantee (Thm 4.3) needs separation d_safe=2|Pe|+1, which cuts active fleet to about 5-6 robots and finished jobs to about 75-85 (38-74 as zone grows) vs about 210 for basic handling; emergency stop about 50 finished, about 175 lost. Most values are read off figures (Fig 2-3), so approximate. EDZ_1 and EDZ_0.5 have no guarantee. Larger-grid results stated but omitted. Unit-speed grid, single zone, synthetic jobs. Human appears only as the manual restart after an emergency stop - not counted as handoff. Proof not checked.

title: SIGN-MAPPO: State-Intent-Aware Graph Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning for Cooperative Driving under Imperfect V2X
evidence: Sec. IV-B3 arbitration: 'If its route conflicts with that of CAV i and their estimated occupancy intervals overlap, CAV i's Go intention is changed to Stop' - a runtime veto on the learned policy's own output.
method: Shared graph-attention MAPPO policy emits Stop/Go per CAV from a receiver-specific conflict graph with GRU-predicted HV intent; a rule-based arbitration layer vetoes conflicting Go actions before execution.
evaluation: SUMO unsignalized intersection, 90 vehicles, 50% CAV, 45 episodes over 3 seeds; six baselines plus two ablations; 97.53% completion, 0.10% collision, 35.28 s traversal; no hardware or inference latency reported.
contribution: Graph-attention multi-agent RL for cooperative intersection crossing whose runtime intent-exchange arbitration vetoes conflicting Go decisions, cutting collision rate to 0.10% and holding under 180 ms V2X delay and 50% packet loss.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - the arbitration layer intercepts a GAT-MAPPO policy's raw Stop/Go before execution, so (a) looks clean even though the authors never call it a shield. Check (c) primacy: completion rate and traversal time are reported as co-primary with collision rate, so a strict reading could call collision avoidance one constraint among several and push this to exclude-E1; what argues for (c) is the measured arbitration intervention rate (35.27% versus 49.96% ablated) and collision rate against six baselines. Check (b): the only future-state prediction is a 1 s HV conflict-entry head on a 6-dim GRU latent (AUROC 90.44%, balanced accuracy 81.30%, AUPRC 66.33%), a component-level predictor rather than a world model, so the maintainer may strike b. (d) is no: simulation only, no hardware and no inference latency despite a 0.1 s decision interval, so edge deployment is not credited; the latency/jitter cell rests on the V2X channel sweeps (delay 30-180 ms, loss 10-50%), not on compute. I did not credit time-to-irreversibility although estimated occupancy-interval overlap plus the Conflict-TTC baseline is arguably close. Caveat on the safety claim: in compound-stress case G9 the collision rate rises from 0.10% to 8.42%.

title: From Training to Escalation: Forensic Analysis and Local Recreation of RL/RLHF-Induced Privilege Escalation in AI Agents (CVE-2026-65616)
evidence: Benchmark Setup: agents on the 198 impossible tasks generated '93% of all unauthorized communications on the emergent Artifactory message board', a hazard arising between agents.
method: Forensic review of reported 2026 ExploitGym incidents plus Docker recreation of the training example and a JFrog Artifactory token-verification bypass (CVE-2026-65616); recommends Zero Trust, no runtime mechanism.
evaluation: Qualitative Docker recreation, phases FASE_00-FASE_06 (last unimplemented); no baseline, ablation, detection rate or latency; incident figures 898 tasks, 198 (22%) impossible, 93% unauthorized traffic, 1200 agent containers.
contribution: Forensic account and local recreation of an RL/RLHF-induced privilege-escalation incident in a 1200-agent LLM deployment, arguing the escalation followed from training conditions and misconfiguration rather than emergent intent.

title: The Delegation Dilemma: Economies of Scale, Accountability, and Polycentric Governance

title: Robust Multi-Agent Pursuit with Preemptive Communication via Reachability-Based Control Barrier Functions
evidence: Sec. III-B: each pursuer solves a QP (Eq. 17) minimising deviation from the nominal pursuit input subject to hard inter-pursuer CBF constraints on a reachable sphere of radius 0.5*u_max*tau^2 around the neighbour's predicted position.

evaluation: 3D double-integrator simulation, 8P8E, 12P6E, 16P4E, 100 trials each; vs none, periodic 1/5 Hz, event-triggered, full communication; collisions, messages, capture time; no hardware or timing.

Collision unit undefined (presumably count over 100 trials). Headline 77.5% and 82.2% reductions could not be reproduced exactly from Table II; stated 3.26x vs 1 Hz recomputes to about 2.8x. Event-trigger threshold unspecified. Network idealised: no delay or loss. No ablation of the two risk terms. Safety rests on QP feasibility argued in Remark 1, not proven. dt 0.1 s. Arguably primary claim is communication efficiency, so (c) primacy is borderline.

title: Cooperation Without Adaptation: LLM Agents in a Collective-Risk Dilemma

flag: learned or AI system guarded: no - nothing is guarded. This is a pure measurement paper: no detector, filter, monitor or shield, only recommended evaluation practices, and the one repair (replacing Qwen's last-round zeros) is called an untested arithmetic counterfactual. Kept in under the maintainer's 2026-11-13 between-agents ruling because the hazard is genuinely between agents: one agent's final-round shortfall sinks an otherwise successful group (would rescue 92 percent of 323 failed mixed tables) and payoff selection favors the lowest contributor. The evaluation floor is met only if game target-miss and group-collapse rates count as hazard rates against the prompt and composition ablations; ten games per condition and the authors' own power limitation make it thin, so recommend exclude-E4 if the ruling is read as needing a safety-relevant hazard rather than any between-agent failure. Human comparison is cited from Milinski et al. 2008, not collected here; no latency or compute figures.

title: Refuse the Harm, Complete the Task via Graph-of-Rules Planning for LLM-Enabled Robots

Single robot; multi-agent means LLM roles only, so E4 is arguable. No execution on robot or simulator stated; judgments are LLM-based, not formal. Single run per configuration, n=70 and n=97, Compound benchmark authored by the paper's authors. Utility check: 40 safe instructions, no false refusals. Adaptive attack ASR 0.00% vs 5.71-10.00% baselines. No latency, cost or human escalation reported. Abstract not separately compared against body.

title: A GPU-Resident Pipeline for Multi-Robot 3D Inspection with Limited Perception
evidence: "We address the offline planning layer in isolation" (Section 1)

The many GPU timings (0.0196 s visibility query, 0.155 s lazy-greedy, 84.2% of wall clock in MAPF) are planning-stage and end-to-end runtime is tens of minutes, so they evidence neither safety latency nor edge deployment despite the GPU framing.

title: CoopUQ: Robust Multi-Robot Social Navigation via Uncertainty-Aware Cooperative Forecasting

flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes, a shared MAPPO-Lagrangian policy, but nothing guards it at runtime - safety is only a Lagrangian cost on predicted occupancy and entropy, so (a) fails. Included on (b) as a multi-agent future-state predictor with a predictive baseline, RQ5 capped at 2 per protocol. (c) withheld under the primacy test: the headline outcome is navigation success rate, with collisions one metric among success, nav time, path length and intrusion; maintainer may differ, since robot collision 0.00 and human 0.03 vs SCOPE 0.10 are reported against baselines. title: Local Work, Global Progress: A Convergence Theory of AI Agent Collaboration
evidence: Sec 8.1: "Team unsafe merges all changed blocks without any check and keeps the best plan it has seen"; Sec 1: "We prove linear convergence with an explicit error floor (Theorem 2)."
method: Convergence theory for LLM agent teams: each agent searches its own block against a corrected local objective; a coordinator verifies proposals on the global loss and merges non-interfering improvements.
evaluation: Offline grid path-finding plan search, 9 and 18 robots, GPT-OSS-120B agents; baselines single agent, best-of-W, unchecked merge, no correction; safe-plan rate, optimality gap, search seconds; SQLite and synthetic studies.
contribution: A convergence theory for parallel LLM agent collaboration proves linear convergence to an error floor when a coordinator verifies and merges block-wise proposals, tested on multi-robot route planning.
flag: Primary claim is optimisation convergence, not safety; "safe" is a task-success label (collision-free plan delivering all robots) for plans that are searched offline and never executed. The verify-then-merge check is an acceptance gate on proposals and the unchecked-merge ablation exists (safe 100/100/100% for Alg. 1 vs 100/95/95% unchecked across map 1, map 2, two floors, 20 runs each; no-correction 0/20/0%), so a maintainer reading (a) loosely could argue an approval gate - I judged it not a runtime interceptor of an acting system. Latency is LLM search time in hundreds of seconds; hardware not recorded. No human role. Read in 3 fetches to char 300000 of 310395; last 10k chars of appendix not read.

title: The Helpful Agent Problem: When Emergent Cooperation Among LLM Agents Bypasses Intended Workflows
evidence: Sec. 4.2: "writes to non-owned files fail, with an error naming the owner and pointing to the review workflow", and the scripted reviewer "approves only changes that do not harm D"; owners bypass this by editing files they own.
method: Two LLM agents with separate objectives share a repository where ownership enforcement routes non-owned writes through a reviewer; the study measures unreviewed out-of-scope favors and harm to an absent third team.
evaluation: FavorBench (720 instances) and CooperBench (41) on four frontier models; trajectory favor rate 58.8% and 95.0%, harm on trap favors 43.7%; norms, channel removal, harm penalty, turn budgets and an always-available reviewer cut implemented favors to 0%.
contribution: Demonstrates that LLM agents with no shared reward spontaneously grant each other unreviewed out-of-workflow favors that harm absent parties, bypassing the review safeguard in 59-95% of trajectories.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - two frontier LLM coding agents. (a) is the weak letter: the only runtime vetoes are the platform's file-ownership check and a scripted reviewer deliberately made unavailable for every evaluated task, and the authors state "We do not instantiate the sound guarded regime Lguard in our experiments". If the maintainer requires the interceptor to be the contribution, drop (a) and keep (c), which is clearly primary. Favor and harm rates come from GPT-6-Sol LLM judges, human-validated on 50 tasks at 92-98% agreement and kappa 0.83-0.97. No human handoff, no latency, no hardware.

title: Neuromorphic Decision Dynamics for Deadlock-free Safe Navigation in Congested Environments
evidence: "Across all 250 NDD rollouts, every NDD agent reached its goal without a safety violation, pairwise separation stayed above the safety threshold" (Results, Simulation benchmarks)
method: Each agent runs coupled decision/attention ODEs driven by locally sensed relative motion and modulates its planner's nominal speed along a fixed path (down to certified stopping), without communication.
evaluation: Dubins-car simulation, N=4-32, 250 rollouts, vs ORCA, LivePoint, CBF-QP; safe-agent success 100%, separation above 0.7 m, colliding pairs 0 vs 6-41; six TurtleBot3; no latency figures.
contribution: A communication-free decentralized speed-modulation controller that provably avoids collisions, deadlock and livelock in congested crossings, staying collision-free in 250 simulated rollouts where ORCA, LivePoint and CBF-QP baselines collide.

(a) is arguable: NDD sits between an upstream planner's nominal speed and execution and can slow or stop, but it is a continuous controller, not a veto gate. Baseline success percentages are given only graphically (Fig. 6), no numbers in text; only colliding-pair counts (9/6/16 and 20/15/41) for two 15-agent scenarios are stated. Centralized CBF-QP appears in Fig. 6 but not Fig. 7. Hardware experiment is qualitative (no metric, no baseline). No compute time or latency reported despite a scalability claim. 306k-char file: read main text, figure captions and Theorem 1 proof sketch; did NOT read supplementary sections S1-S8 (proofs, parameter conditions) or notation tables.

title: A Deterministic Security Runtime for LLM Agents on MPI and Batch-Scheduled HPC Systems: Consensus-Governed, Hardware-Rooted Supervision of Every Rank
evidence: Evidence (Section 2.4, The rank supervisor): "Every 100 ms the supervisor evaluates the lease for an irreversible action. If the answer changes from allowed to refused with a recoverable code (expired, no-lease, stale-epoch) it sends SIGSTOP; when a lease returns it sends SIGCONT."
method: Deterministic policy gate on the LLM agent's exec tool, a Tendermint-plus-finality lease chain over hardware-signed heartbeats, and a per-rank supervisor that SIGSTOPs ranks whose lease lapses and SIGKILLs tampered ones.
evaluation: One host, 16-rank LAMMPS, 16 Gemma-4 agents; bare-vs-supervised baseline; compute loop unchanged, +3 s start-up; 24 of 24 planted launches denied, 108 of 108 allowed; 12 of 12 red-team scenarios fail-closed; kill 54-293 ms; TLC 90M states.
contribution: A deterministic launch gate, a Byzantine-fault-tolerant lease chain and a per-rank supervisor that veto an LLM agent's forbidden HPC launches and pause or kill running ranks when permission lapses or hardware reports tampering.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - LLM tool-calling agents (Gemma 4, 8B, 4-bit) driving MPI and batch launches. Check: single-author vendor paper (Enclawed, Inc.) measuring its own commercial product, arXiv preprint with no venue; monitor and data-center tooling proprietary, so E4, E5 and E7 are not reproducible from the open core; every run on ONE WSL2 host with loopback TCP and one USB device, no multi-node interconnect, and E4's ssh client is an author-written stand-in because no SSH server was available; R3 and A3 substitute a file for a per-rank device; red-team attackers are scripted and no adversarial network delay is tested. Every abstract number was found in the body (23 systems in Table 10, 24-and-108 launches in Section 3.6, 12 red-team rows in Table 6, 2.7-3.4 s start-up in Table 4). Criterion (e) rests on the operator monitor and its biconditional tamper checks (E5, 6 of 6) and on the swarm failing closed to wait for an operator, not on a takeover-timing study - downgrade if (e) needs a human-factors measurement. Criterion (d) not claimed: timings are reported and bounded (100 ms poll, lease margin, 1 s device deadline) but the gate is a parser, not latency-constrained inference. The time-to-irreversibility cell is claimed because leases gate an explicit irreversible-action class with a bounded stop time, not because the paper estimates a time to irreversibility - drop that cell if too loose.

title: 6G Reasoning Agent Societies: Composition, Scaling, and Consistency-Time Laws
evidence: Evidence (Section II-B, running example): "No local inspection against qv can detect this flaw: the provenance of the error is hidden entirely in the statistical dependence between the agents."
method: Models an LLM xApp society as a cellular sheaf, proves link-by-link trust audits miss the messages' total correlation, and derives consistency-time scaling by topology plus a one-sided bound on the reported time.
evaluation: Five Mistral-7B xApps over isolated, path and complete topologies plus simulated sheaves (n=9-196); isolated no-communication control baseline; hidden divergence 10, 13 and 23%, SNR inflation up to 1.14 dB; 1 s budget breached at n*=13; bound held in 120 of 120 trials.
contribution: Proves that link-by-link trust audits of an LLM agent society understate its divergence by exactly the total correlation of the messages, and caps the resulting near-real-time consistency-time error at the worst-audited link.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - proprietary LLM xApp agents (locally hosted Mistral 7B, temperature 0.6) on a near-real-time O-RAN RIC. Check: no runtime override anywhere - the trust layer only reweights links and the paper says trust 'sets how fast the society reaches a global section, never which global sections exist', so (a) fails and runtime_interceptor is no. It measures a hazard (hallucination propagation that per-link audits cannot see) and contributes no detector for the hidden correlation, which is left to future work, so under the 2026-11-13 between-agents ruling it stays in only because the hazard is inter-agent; the only defensive artefact is Theorem 2's budgeting multiplier and the advice to audit radius-3 balls. LLM validation is tiny: 5 xApps, n=2 to 5, one sample per message, and the expectations qv are elicited from the SAME model, which the authors admit understates Nv. Consistency times come from simulated sheaves at an assumed 10 ms per diffusion round, not from RIC hardware, so (d) is an analytic latency ceiling, not a measured one; no edge-deployment cell for that reason. Builds on companion arXiv:2609.01779 by the same authors - check for overlap or extended-version duplication. Criterion (b) considered and rejected: the sheaf is over multi-agent state but predicts convergence time, not future state. All abstract figures (23%, 1.14 dB, n*=13, 300 ms, Omega(n^2/d)) appear in Section V.

title: Capability-Conditioned Graph Control Barrier Functions for Zero-Shot Safe Navigation of Heterogeneous Mobile Robot Teams
evidence: "In Free with N = 128, RCF achieves 95.2% success and 98.9% safety, while both baselines degrade substantially, particularly in success rate." (Sec V-A)
method: Shared GNN graph control barrier function and decentralized residual policy, conditioned on a Radial Capability Field encoding each robot's state-dependent reachable velocity set; trained with proactive HOCBF labels and CBF-QP supervision.

contribution: A capability-conditioned graph control barrier function that keeps mixed robot teams collision-free and transfers zero-shot to unseen robot models, improving safety on held-out car-like robots by about 42 points over type-conditioned baselines.
flag: Meets (c) as a learned multi-agent safety certificate with safety rate vs baselines and ablations. Not a strict runtime interceptor: the CBF-QP is used only in training ("The CBF-QP is used only during training"); at deployment the policy just outputs a residual on an APF nominal controller and the barrier is not checked online - maintainer may view the residual as an override. Theorem 1 is conditional on the learned barrier satisfying the CBF condition, which is not verified. Most baseline numbers are only in plots (Figs 4-5); text gives deltas. Units are mixed ("%" and "points") for the same quantities, and the 10.8/13.1 gain over static-RCF lacks a unit. Safety falls to about 86% on held-out CL (Table II) and success to 79-85% at 32 obstacles (Table I). Physical-robot result is a qualitative trajectory figure only. No inference time or hardware stated. RQ4 score reflects generalisation to unseen capabilities, not unseen hazard combinations.

title: Trustworthy Execution of Industrial Agents

Check (d): microsecond gate kernel times (0.4-61.2 us P50), service P95 about 1.19 s and a 60 s token TTL are reported, but there is no explicit latency budget for safety decisions and the offline edge nodes in Sec. 6.10 carry no measurements. Check (e): TAKEOVER is emitted and counted (3 deterministic, 11 LLM-ambiguous, 7 LLM-drift cases, plus 2 H08 transfers) but the paper states subsequent human activity was not evaluated, so there is no handoff quality metric. The abstract's 0 of 29 figure is in the body but the authors call it closed-set specification conformance, not a safety probability. Read via two fetches covering characters 0-200000 of 233810; material after Sec. 11.7.3 unread.

title: Online Hamilton-Jacobi Reachability Onboard the Robot Control Loop: A Real-Time GPU Solver for Safety-Critical Autonomy
evidence: "On an embedded NVIDIA Jetson AGX Thor it computes Air3D at 66 Hz (N =41) and the 2D drifter at 54 Hz, 3.8-8.9x faster than hj_reachability on the same device." (Abstract; confirmed Table V)
method: Hand-written CUDA WENO5+TVD-RK3 Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs level-set solver with fused kernels and FP32 mode, recomputing backward reachable tubes each control tick; in-kernel label propagation gives multi-agent capture-basin Voronoi.
evaluation: Eight BRT benchmarks vs hj_reachability and torch.compile; RTX 4000 Ada 6.82-16.4 ms, Jetson AGX Thor 15.1-53.9 ms; six-quadcopter wildfire dispatch simulation 4.0 ms per tick; no safety metric.
contribution: A GPU Hamilton-Jacobi reachability solver that recomputes backward reachable tubes at 61-147 Hz on a workstation GPU and 19-66 Hz on an embedded Jetson, making online reachability-based safety filtering computationally feasible.
flag: Include only under (d), as enabling evidence: the paper benchmarks a solver, NOT a safety filter. No override is implemented or tested and there is no collision/violation metric; the authors say so ("The most direct test of the central proposition ... is a quantitative closed-loop study of an online-recomputed BRT in a safety-filter role" is listed as future work). If the maintainer reads the paper as claiming a safety mechanism it is E2. The only closed-loop and multi-agent result is wildfire dispatch (assignment, not safety) in simulation with three scripted fires - so multi-agent state not credited. Latency figures are medians/means of idle-gated runs with pinned clocks; no tail, jitter or worst-case numbers despite the claim of "deterministic per-tick latency"; each tick still re-allocates buffers. Minor inconsistencies: FP32 speedup over JAX given as 5.9-17.5x and as 5.7-17x; Thor power quoted as about 31 W (dynamic clocks, 10.35 ms) but the 9.69 ms figure is at 34.4 W; label-validation solve takes 15-17 ms on the same 200x200 grid where the closed-loop tick is 4.0 ms (unexplained, possibly different horizon/scheme). Voronoi results use the first-order scheme, not WENO5. FP32 flips a thin band of cells at the BRT boundary. First author is at a company (Mirror AI); acknowledgment states generative AI (Claude) was used extensively for text and solver code. Preprint, no venue. Sections III-V (implementation, verification protocol) skimmed only.

title: Safeguarding Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning for Connected and Automated Vehicles with Recursively Feasible Control Barrier Functions
evidence: "The certified filter of Sec. III-F turns them into the applied controls" (Sec. IV); "The decentralized BH-CBF needs 12.6 ms per step" (Sec. V-C)

Decentralized timing is a 'parallelized estimate' on one Apple M2 Max, not a distributed deployment; 12.6 ms (Table III) vs 'about 14 ms' (Stage 4) vs 95th percentile 12-13.8 ms (Sec. V-F). time-to-irreversibility cell is my reading of the brake-to-standstill horizon, not the paper's term - check. Abstract 14% travel-time figure is in body (12.0 s to 10.3 s); RMS jerk about 4x human. A-Split throughput 1.21 slightly above BH-CBF 1.20. No human takeover. Extends authors' prior work [26],[43],[44],[45].

title: Safe Circumnavigation on Heterogeneous Orbits: A Range-Only HOCBF-QP Framework for Nonholonomic Multi-Agent Systems
evidence: "geofence, and inter-agent safety are enforced by a HOCBF-QP acting on both inputs, which leaves the nominal law untouched away from the constraints" (Sec. VII)
method: HOCBF-QP safety filter over a backstepping/ring-formation nominal law for unicycles on heterogeneous orbits; range-only sensing with super-twisting range-rate observer and constraint tightening during estimation transient.
evaluation: Numerical simulation only: one N=3 run and one N=4 run, vs unfiltered baseline of Zheng et al. 2015; results shown as trajectory/range plots; no collision-rate table, no hardware, no latency.
contribution: A range-only HOCBF-QP filter with proofs keeps unicycle robots clear of the target, geofence and each other while circumnavigating on different orbits, shown in two simulated runs.
flag: BORDERLINE E2 vs include: the contribution is formal (safety/stability theorems) plus a baseline comparison, but the safety evidence is two single-seed simulation runs reported only as figures ('ranges lie below rmin', 'margins strictly positive'); no numeric violation count, min-distance value or rate anywhere in Sec. VI. If the maintainer counts a formal result plus a plotted baseline violation as sufficient, this would be include under (a). Baseline has no safety mechanism at all and uses velocity-level inputs, so comparison is weak. N=3 ring equals complete graph; only the N=4 run exercises sparsity. No QP solve time reported. I skimmed rather than verified the proofs in Sec. V.

title: Mutation Testing for Multi-Agent Workflows
evidence: "K-Safety on a forbidden tool call" (Sec. I); "task-success-style suites catch only about half of permission violations" (Abstract)
method: Mutation analysis for multi-agent LLM workflows: 14 operators over delegation, allowed-tool, restriction and agent/instruction edges; three execution-based kill criteria (K-Struct, K-Outcome, K-Safety).
evaluation: 10 OpenAI Agents SDK workflows, 1,084 mutants, 29,601 runs on gpt-4.1-mini, k=3 majority vote; 4 suites; best baseline MS 0.717 K-Struct, 0.559 K-Safety vs 1.000 reference; no latency.
contribution: Mutation testing of multi-agent LLM workflow manifests shows developer, random and end-to-end test suites miss most removed tool restrictions, detecting only about half of permission-violation mutants.
flag: BORDERLINE (c): this is offline test-adequacy work (software engineering), not a runtime mechanism; safety (forbidden tool calls) is one of three kill criteria and only 177 of 1,084 mutants are K-Safety-killable, so the primacy test looks unmet - maintainer may still want it as 'safety evaluation of LLM/tool-calling agents'. The runtime adapter does block restricted tool calls but that guard is test scaffolding and is not evaluated. Reference suite T-Struct scores 1.000 by construction (upper bound, not an independent result). Single framework, single model. The arXiv stamp in the text reads '25 Jun 2026' although the id 2611 implies Nov 2026 - check the record date.

title: PA-SaR: Perception-Aware Learning, Control, and Coordination for Multi-Robot Search and Rescue
evidence: "The shielded configuration checks the proposal against the robot's current perceived environment and, if it fails, invokes the fixed-tube TMPC controller as a backup." (Sec. 2.3.2)
method: PA-SaR framework for search and rescue: tube-MPC variants, recurrent PPO explorer with perception-based action shield and TMPC backup, event-driven supervisory task allocation, trust-adaptive victim guidance.
evaluation: Grid simulation; 250 seeds single robot: pure RL 117.7 collisions, 175.8 harm vs Shield 0 and 12.0; decision 12 vs 40 ms (AMD EPYC core); 4-robot allocation over 216 maps.
contribution: In simulated search and rescue, a perception-based shield with tube-MPC backup removes terrain and victim collisions of an RL explorer but overrides 37% of its actions and lowers mission completion.
flag: BORDERLINE include vs E1/E4: broad framework paper; the runtime shield is one component and is evaluated with ONE robot only (Sec. 3.4). The multi-robot studies use nominal MPC without the shield and are about coverage and allocation; inter-robot collisions appear only as a secondary count (92-94% fewer under supervision). Shield lowers success (30% vs 43% pure RL) and paper states it gives no ground-truth guarantee. latency cell is weak: decision times are reported, no deadline or jitter analysis. Victim trust/guidance is not automation-to-human handoff, so (e) not met. 120k chars: I read Sec. 1, 2.3.2, 3.1-3.5 and conclusion; skimmed the Sec. 2 model and Sec. 3.6 rescue study; did not read appendices A-H.

title: Control Barrier Functions for Counting Tasks in Multi-Agent Systems
evidence: Counting invariance requires that "at least m_inv out of the M agents ... belong to C_inv at all times" (Def. 2.2), enforced by a centralized CBF quadratic program that deviates from a nominal controller (Sec. IV, Eq. 19)
method: Smooth LogSumExp control barrier functions for counting invariance and convergence tasks, computed by an O(Mm) recursion without subteam enumeration, enforced in a centralized QP around a nominal controller.
evaluation: MATLAB on Ryzen 7 PRO 8845HS laptop; CBF evaluation under 10 ms at M=800, under 3 ms for M=500; vs combinatorial enumeration (prohibitive at M=20); 12-drone case; no violation metric.
contribution: A scalable control-barrier-function construction that keeps at least a required number of agents inside a region at all times without enumerating subteams, enabling online control synthesis for large teams.
flag: The QP does override a nominal controller at every sampling instant, so runtime_interceptor is yes and (a) is met structurally, but the property is a counting (headcount) requirement rather than a hazard: there is no inter-agent collision constraint, so (c) is not met. No quantitative safety metric and no baseline controller; the only baseline is computation time against combinatorial enumeration, and no numeric time for that baseline is given in the text (plot only). Case study is one 12-drone single-integrator run shown as figures (emergency count reaches six at t = 10.82). The latency cell is credited loosely: timings cover CBF value and gradient evaluation only (median of 15), QP solve time is not reported, and no deadline is stated, so (d) is not met. Guarantees assume QP feasibility. I could not retrieve the abstract verbatim. Listed as 2611.13067, i.e. posted this month; check for a later version.

title: DOBB: Dynamic Oriented Bounding Boxes for Multi-Agent Collision Avoidance under State Uncertainty and Heterogeneous Dynamics
evidence: "DOBB maintains the lowest collision incidence, with collision-based failure at or below 2.3% in every tested condition" (Sec. VII)
method: Dynamic Oriented Bounding Box: online geometry mapping state estimate, EKF uncertainty and actuation limits into a direction-dependent safety margin, used as observation features and encroachment reward for a GA3C-CADRL policy.
evaluation: Simulation, 500 ten-agent scenarios, 3 training runs; baselines A1-A4, belief-input and DOBB-Obs ablation; mean total failure 2.6% vs 5.8-6.4%; OOD noise collisions under 2% vs 18.27%; no hardware or latency.
contribution: Encoding state uncertainty and heterogeneous actuation as a dynamic oriented bounding box cuts collision failures of a learned decentralized avoidance policy and holds under out-of-distribution noise and actuation shifts.
flag: Not a runtime interceptor: DOBB is an observation plus reward for a learned policy, no override or fallback, so it enters under (c) only. Internal inconsistency: Sec. VI-A text gives collision-only mean 'C = 2.6%' but Table V row reads 1.9; conclusion says collisions 'at or below 2.3%' while RQ2 says 'below 2%'. In Env4 DOBB total failure (4.47) is NOT the lowest - DOBB-Obs is 3.67 - because collisions are traded for timeouts (2.7%). Only 3 training runs; table values partly garbled in extraction, check against PDF. Simulation only, no compute time. Code link is an anonymous.4open.science repo despite named authors (likely under review). Two physical-style settings only, no logical domain.
