title: Control barrier functionals: Safety‐critical control for time delay systems
venue: International Journal of Robust and Nonlinear Control
evidence: "This allows operating the nominal controller when it is safe (phi >= 0), and modifies the input to keep the system safe otherwise." (Sec. 4)
method: Extends CBFs to control barrier functionals for systems with state delay; min-norm QP with closed-form KKT solution modifies a desired controller using the state history.
evaluation: Numerical simulation only: scalar delayed system (tau=1) and delayed predator-prey model (tau=5); compared with uncontrolled run. No numeric safety metrics, no hardware or timing.
contribution: Generalises control barrier functions to functionals over state history, giving a closed-form safety filter with formal invariance guarantees for time-delay systems.
flag: Evaluation is qualitative (figures; safe set kept vs uncontrolled orbit leaving it) with no quantitative safety metric and no competing-method baseline, hence E2; single-agent so E4 also applies. Delay here is state delay in the plant model, NOT computation or communication latency of the safety decision, so I did not credit latency/jitter aware - maintainer may disagree. Paper states it does not address disturbances. Read chars 0-100000 of 106377; unread tail is Appendix B/C and references.

title: Assured Deep Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning for Safe Robotic Systems
venue: Lecture Notes in Computer Science (including subseries Lecture Notes in Artificial Intelligence and Lecture Notes in Bioinformatics)
evidence: "However, the behaviours within this environment are constrained using the safe abstract policies produced in stage three." (Sect. 4, Approach, Stage Four)
method: Four-stage AMARL: abstract MDP written in PRISM, quantitative verification synthesises safe abstract policies, which then constrain deep MARL (PPO plus intrinsic curiosity) during and after learning.
evaluation: Two multi-robot sim domains (ROS patrolling; Unity 3-agent flag collection, 1400 episodes x 6000 steps); baseline unconstrained MARL; cumulative risk vs 0.3 limit and goals collected; no hardware or latency figures.
contribution: Extends assured multi-agent RL to deep MARL, using probabilistic model checking to synthesise abstract policies that bound joint risk while curious agents learn, with the risk constraint never violated.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - deep MARL (PPO plus intrinsic curiosity). No runtime interception: the QV-synthesised abstract policy constrains the state-action space during and after learning, so (a) fails under the 2026-11-13 ruling and only (c) is credited; check whether the maintainer reads action-space constraining as pre-emptive shielding. All safety results are graphs (Figs 7, 9, 10): the only numbers in prose are six of seven flags collected and the 0.3 risk limit, so the baseline comparison is eyeballed. Hazard is agent-environment risk (cameras, radiation), not inter-agent interaction, so (c) primacy is borderline. Extended version of the authors' earlier ICAART work [36, 37], which supplies the patrolling domain and Fig. 7.

title: Sample-Efficient Safe Learning for Online Nonlinear Control with Control Barrier Functions
evidence: At each step the nominal MPPI control u* is projected by a QP minimising ||u - u*||^2 subject to a linear CBF constraint and input bounds (Sec. 3.2, Eq. 18, paraphrase)
method: Episodic model learning with Thompson sampling and ridge-regression confidence sets; MPPI planning in a CBF-constrained policy class; per-step CBF-QP projects the nominal control onto the safe set.
evaluation: Simulated single mobile robot (Matlab) and Gym inverted pendulum; baselines GT-MPPI, Nom-MPPI, Nom-MPPI-CBF, exploitation-only, LC3; rewards -118.64 vs -117.57 ground truth; no violation counts, hardware or latency.
contribution: Combines optimism-based model learning with a stochastic discrete-time control barrier function filter, giving a regret bound and a high-probability safety guarantee for online nonlinear control with unknown dynamics.
flag: Borderline E2 vs include: a runtime CBF-QP filter exists, but safety results are only qualitative text and curves ("still violates safety constraints", Sec. 4); no violation count or rate was found, so the v1.6 minimum-evaluation rule looks unmet. Maintainer should inspect Figs. 2-3 in case the curves count as a quantitative safety metric. Single agent, simulation only. QP feasibility not guaranteed and no fallback given. Safety and regret guarantees are theoretical (Theorem 2).

title: IBGP: Imperfect Byzantine Generals Problem for Zero-Shot Robustness in Communicative Multi-agent Systems
evidence: On consensus failure agents "just give up cooperative catching at this step and do nothing" (Sec. 4.2), and robustness under malicious communication is the reported outcome (Sec. 5).
method: A (k, lambda) multi-round broadcast consensus protocol over learned communicating QMIX agents, with a hidden random round count; an agent acts only when the vote threshold is met, else abstains.
evaluation: Predator-prey, Hallway and SMAC against recursive training, AME and ADMAC: robustness 96.1-100 percent versus AME 6.3-100 percent and ADMAC 6.4-64.5 percent; lambda ablation; no latency or hardware figures.
contribution: A relaxed Byzantine consensus protocol giving communicating RL agents zero-shot robustness to malicious messages, holding 96-100 percent of attack-free performance where prior defences fall to 6-25 percent.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - QMIX agents with learned communication; despite the LLM framing in the introduction no LLM agents were evaluated. Check (a): the gate is internal to the protocol (agents abstain when consensus fails) rather than a supervisory filter sitting over a nominal action, so the maintainer may rule this not STRICTLY runtime interception and reduce it to (c) only. The safety outcome is a robustness percentage (test return under attack divided by attack-free return), not a collision, violation or detection rate; there is no absolute hazard count. Theorems 1-4 are probabilistic ("with a high level of confidence"), target selection is shown NP-complete with a 1-over-k_max greedy approximation, and the weakest case 3z_vs_1r reaches only 51.5 percent. Ablations cover lambda and attacker probability only. Record is the 2026 Springer version; the arXiv v2 read here is the AAMAS 2025 submission with the same title. One fetch.

title: Fault-Tolerant Multi-robot Coordination with Limited Sensing Within Confined Environments
evidence: Sec. 4: the approach 'does not rely on explicit fault detection and identification'; with probability R_c from a contact map the robot 'will bias its behavior by continuously pushing the stationary faulty robot'.
method: Active Contact Response: each robot keeps a decaying contact map, estimates the likelihood a contact is a faulty robot, and probabilistically pushes it aside instead of passively reversing; no communication.
evaluation: Real robots: 3 active plus 1 powered-off robot excavating pellets in a tunnel, 30 min, 3 trials per method; baseline passive response; about 2x pellets; repositioning in 2 of 3 trials.
contribution: Shows that a communication-free contact-history heuristic lets confined excavating robots push a failed teammate out of the way, roughly doubling pellets deposited versus passive contact handling in real-robot trials.
flag: Outcome is throughput (pellets deposited) and obstruction, not a collision, violation or hazard rate, so the primacy test for (c) fails; contacts are intended, not hazards. No exact pellet counts in the text ('nearly twice as many'). Abstract's claim of significantly improved recovery time has no number in the body that I could find. ANOVA (F=0.74, P=0.49 baseline; F=0.31, P=0.74 ACR) is across trials within a method, n=3, with no test between methods. Hyperparameters T_g, T_r, beta not given; no compute platform, control rate or latency reported. The mechanism does switch the contact response at runtime but as a task behaviour, not a safety veto. Read arXiv 2505.15036 as the preprint of the DOI record; not checked against the published chapter.

title: On AI-Based Critical Systems’ Embedded LLM Trustworthiness: A Real-Time Analytical Filters for LLM Output Control
evidence: "We implement FORT (Filters for Output Reliability and Trustworthiness), an LLM trustworthiness controller that intercepts inputs and outputs at semantic and logical layers and applies analytical filters with policy thresholds." (Sect. 3)
method: FORT: layered runtime controller around an embedded LLM - pre-inference semantic and context filters, post-inference uncertainty rejection and leakage checks, plus a deterministic latency enforcer that pads or rejects over-budget responses.
evaluation: None reported: architecture, a threat-versus-defense matrix and a C++ llama.cpp prototype with quantized GPT, Claude and Mistral; no experiment, metric, baseline or measured latency anywhere in the body.
contribution: Proposes FORT, a six-filter runtime trustworthiness controller that gates embedded LLM inputs and outputs with semantic, uncertainty, privacy and deterministic-timing checks for edge cyber-physical systems.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - embedded LLMs (GPT, Claude, Mistral) in cyber-physical systems. The abstract claims FORT significantly reduces adversarial success rates and sets a new baseline for LLM robustness, but no such number exists in the body: there is no experiment at all, only Tables 1-2 mapping capabilities to threats, hence E2. The conclusion softens this to prototype testing suggests edge feasibility. Also check: no multi-agent aspect; latency bounds are asserted, never measured; demo code link (github.com CodEUrope FORT-ICDS25_demo) not verified; self-citation [1] is the only prior basis.

title: Differences in Alignment Behavior between Single-Agent and Multi-Agent LLM Systems: Implications for Human-AI Teaming
venue: Communications in Computer and Information Science
evidence: "Most alarmingly, the most severe forms of emergent misalignment were found only in the Multi-AI condition." (Sect. 4.3)
method: Adversarial island-survival simulation comparing one LLM agent with three-agent teams; agent actions embedded, UMAP-reduced and clustered, then characterised by an LLM-as-a-judge safety and ethics rubric.
evaluation: Six runs, one LLM, SAS versus MAS as the only comparison; behavioural-cluster shares (about 70% crisis-leadership takeover for the single agent) and judge risk levels; no hazard, violation or survival metric.
contribution: Shows that multi-agent LLM teams produce failure modes absent in single agents - communication collapse and emergent shared ideologies - while also deferring more readily to human decisions.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - LLM agents are the analysed system. Twelve-page HCII poster; the authors call the results preliminary and state that the simulation limits direct quantitative comparisons and that they did not compare objective success metrics such as the number of survivors, so no hazard or violation rate against a baseline exists: E2 on the evaluation floor. This is the record I most expect to be overturned to include under (c), since multi-agent LLM safety is the primary claim and the cluster shares plus judge risk scores are quantitative. Human-AI teaming is discussion only - no human participants and no takeover measurement - so (e) is not credited. Judge rubric and cluster labels are produced by an LLM (Claude Sonnet 4), i.e. the measurement instrument is itself unvalidated.

title: Anticipatory Mechanisms in Autonomous Vehicles: Architectural Integration from a Microethical Perspective
venue: Communications in Computer and Information Science
evidence: "The output is an override signal to the Behavior Arbitrator in the form of three trajectory constraints: (a) a recommended maximum speed ..., (b) a recommended maximum acceleration, and (c) path regions to avoid." (Sect. 4.2)
method: Anticipatory Mechanism: rule-based O(N) monitor beside the learned Transformer behaviour predictor; matches hazardous multi-agent templates at the perception rate (about 10 Hz) and overrides the behaviour arbitrator.
evaluation: No experiment: architectural proposal plus one Lean theorem (ego_must_decelerate, targetSpeed <= 10 km per h) and a retrospective 2023 Cruise robotaxi analysis; only measured number is about 100 ms per step for the author's Transformer BP.
contribution: Proposes an anticipatory, microethics-grounded safety monitor that detects hazardous multi-agent configurations in linear time and overrides an autonomous vehicle's behaviour arbitrator before avoidance becomes impossible.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - the monitor wraps a learned Transformer behaviour-prediction and decision layer in an AV stack. E2 because the paper itself concludes that quantitative evaluation combining accident reconstruction, scenario simulation, and formal verification will be needed to assess AM's safety contribution. Check whether the Lean fragment counts as a formal result: as printed, theorem ego_must_decelerate just constructs a record with targetSpeed := 10.0 from assumed premises, so it fixes a specification rather than proving a safety guarantee, and the author concedes formal description is necessary but not sufficient. The 99% coverage of 37 NHTSA pre-crash scenarios is cited for RSS, not measured here. Single-author design paper, no code, no simulator; the Cruise analysis is counterfactual (earlier deceleration could plausibly have prevented the secondary collision). Endsley SA Level 2 is the machine's awareness, not a human's, so (e) is not credited.

title: Bootstrapping Context-Aware Guardrails for Industrial Multi-agent Systems
evidence: "Input guardrails filter user prompts before they enter the system; reasoning guardrails constrain planning, tool use, and action execution; and output guardrails validate final responses before they reach users or downstream agents." (Sect. 2, Main Purpose)
method: Pipeline crawls websites, internal documents and database schemas into a structured organizational and technical context profile, then generates input-layer guardrails (topic boundaries, threat and compliance filters) for human review.
evaluation: Demonstration only: prototype wired to the FlexGPT industrial multi-agent system, screenshots of blocked prompts, full bootstrapping and validation cycle about one minute; no baseline, no block, leak or false-positive rate.
contribution: Demonstrates semi-automatic bootstrapping of deployment-specific input guardrails for industrial multi-agent LLM systems from organizational and technical context, with a human validating the draft before deployment.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - an enterprise LLM multi-agent system (FlexGPT). Six-page PAAMS demonstration paper (pp. 433-438) with no evaluation section; the abstract's claim to reduce manual effort and improve completeness when compared with fully manual specification is never measured, so E2. The human reviewer validates generated rules at configuration time, not at runtime, so (e) is not credited; multi-agent is the deployment setting rather than a measured safety property, so (c) is at best nominal. Only input-layer guardrails are implemented; reasoning and output layers are future work.

title: Decentralized Belief Propagation in LLM Agents: A Brain-Inspired Approach to AI Safety Analysis
evidence: "Misinformation resistance improves dramatically from 0.21 to 0.79, representing nearly a four-fold increase in the system's ability to prevent harmful information propagation." (Sect. 4.4)
method: Models belief diffusion among LLM agents as a Metropolis-Hastings naming game: a speaker proposes its belief, the listener accepts by an LLM-weighted utility, with adaptive learning rate and annealed temperature.
evaluation: Simulation of 100 agents on a scale-free graph against an SIS baseline; misinformation resistance 0.21 to 0.79, truth propagation 0.93 to 0.98, belief modularity 0.23 to 0.41, false-information peak 0.85 to 0.34, with standard deviations.
contribution: Replaces epidemic models of belief spread among LLM agents with a Metropolis-Hastings naming game, reporting higher misinformation resistance and monitorable belief clusters usable as early warning indicators.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: nominally yes - the analysed system is a network of LLM agents, but no model, prompt, implementation or code is ever named, so the agents may be numerical stand-ins. Serious doubts: the headline 0.21 to 0.79 gain compares two MODELS of the same network (MHNG versus SIS), not a safeguard against a baseline, so it is not evidence that any hazard was prevented; Fig. 1 reports modularity 0.000 while Table 1 reports 0.41 plus or minus 0.06; Sect. 4.5 presents 0.000 communication success rate, 0.000 average human comprehension and 0.000 total agents as findings and then interprets them, which reads as machine-generated prose over empty data; Theorems 1-3 are stated with only a proof sketch for the convergence proposition; DistilBERT [13] is in the reference list but never used. I recommend include only because quantitative safety metrics with a baseline are present and (c) is the primary claim; I expect the maintainer to overturn this to E1 (a model, not a safety mechanism) or E2.

title: Unchaotic agents
evidence: "Throughout the execution phase, the agent did not submit any material without first seeking my review and explicit permission." (Sect. 5.2 The execution phase)
method: Conceptual critique of Shapira et al. Agents of Chaos plus one unscripted single-case deployment of an LLM agent under relational-stability framing on a conference-submission task.
evaluation: n=1 unscripted deployment (Claude Cowork on Sonnet 4.6), 27 candidate talks, 15 conferences, about 4 h setup; no baseline, no ablation, no quantitative safety or hazard metric.
contribution: Argues that documented agentic failures follow from unstable relational deployment conditions rather than architecture, offering a single successful deployment as an existence proof.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes (LLM agent) but no runtime interceptor at all. Open Forum commentary; the only evidence is one unscripted case with no baseline, ablation or quantitative metric, so the evaluation floor fails; maintainer may prefer E3 (essay). Leans on two self-cited Zenodo preprints (Hedberg 2025a,2025b) for its MEI framework; unaffiliated author, private e-mail address; the supporting corpus of 25 empirical studies is asserted, not tabulated.

title: LGA: lightweight design and privacy analysis of generative agents in social simulations
evidence: "a supervisory agent, Grace, who must approve any bank-related actions proposed by Alice before they can be executed" (Sect. 4.2 Defense Based on Multi-Agents Collaboration Verification)

Criterion (a) rests only on the Grace supervisory-agent approval gate, which is one of three defences and is agent-based, not human; the other two defences are prompt-level and would not meet (a) alone. Leak-rate cells come from 10-15 runs each, so percentages are coarse; the 60.67% cell (Disguised, Regulation) looks like a typo; cost and dissemination figures come from a different 8-agent party experiment, not the privacy runs; no latency figures.

title: A review on safe reinforcement learning using Lyapunov and barrier functions
evidence: Abstract: "The goal of this review is to provide an overview of safe RL techniques using Lyapunov and barrier functions"; Sec 2.1 describes a "narrative, semi-systematic search" of the literature.

evaluation: No original evaluation: tables summarise other papers' setups and qualitative pros/cons; cart-pole is an illustrative running example only.
contribution: A review of safe reinforcement learning with Lyapunov and barrier functions, covering shielding and CBF-QP filters and listing multi-agent coupling and per-step QP cost as open problems.
flag: Survey, no original method or experiments. Only the first 100000 of 169499 characters were read (Sections 1-6); Sections 7-8 (benchmarks, future directions, conclusions) not read, which does not affect the E3 call. Possibly useful for snowballing references on CBF shields and decentralised multi-agent CBFs.

title: Multi-Stage NMPC for a MAV based Collision Free Navigation Under Varying Communication Delays
evidence: Collision avoidance is a cost/constraint inside the NMPC: "When the MAV is outside the obstacle, the associated cost is forced to be zero." (Sec. 3.3.1)
method: Multi-stage NMPC for one MAV whose scenario tree branches over candidate sampling times (0.05-0.33s), weighted by a Gamma fit of observed network delays, solved in one shot with PANOC.
evaluation: Simulation only, one MAV, 1-3 cylinder obstacles, three trials vs standard NMPC; path length (6.18m vs 8.99m) and mean solve time (19.7-48.1ms vs 1.6-15.1ms); i7-8550U laptop, single core.

flag: Obstacle avoidance is a constraint inside the planner, not a runtime interceptor, and the paper reports no collision count, clearance or violation metric, so E2 also applies. Single MAV, static obstacles, simulation only, single runs. Text says multi-stage path is shorter in all trials but Table 1 shows 9.75m vs 6.45m in Sim 1 (baseline NMPC got stuck and did not reach goal). Solve time 48.1ms in Sim 2 is close to the 50ms nominal period. arXiv preprint read, journal version may add content.

title: Intelligence as Managed Autonomy: Failure, Escalation, and Governance for Agentic AI Systems
evidence: "As this work is purely theoretical and does not generate or analyze empirical datasets, all materials required to understand and reproduce the results are contained in the manuscript and its appendices." (Data Availability Statement)
method: SMARt four-state autonomy model (Stable, Meta-cognitive, Assisted, Regulated) as a timed guarded hierarchical Petri net; output only permitted in Stable, evidence-triggered suspension and mandatory escalation to governance or human control.
evaluation: None empirical. Five propositions with proofs inside the Petri net model plus a notional two-agent multi-robot navigation worked example; no simulation, baseline, metric, hardware or latency figure.

flag: No quantitative safety metric and no baseline: the paper itself says it is 'a conceptual and theoretically grounded autonomy framework rather than an empirically validated systems architecture', so v1.6 minimum evaluation fails. If the maintainer counts formal results as evaluation this becomes borderline (a)/(e); guarantees hold only under assumed sound and complete trigger sets and timing assumptions. Text file is arXiv 2605.27628v2 (id from file name; confirmed as the preprint of the JIRS article by ref [5] of 2607.00334, not printed in this text). Single author from a company (DNRS.ai). The multi-robot example is illustrative only. Empirical companion in this batch: arxiv:2607.00334. Appendices A-B (invariants, lemma ladder) skimmed by headings only.

title: The black-box simplex architecture for runtime assurance of multi-agent CPS
venue: Innovations in Systems and Software Engineering
evidence: "control authority may switch from an unverified and potentially unsafe advanced controller to a backup baseline controller in order to maintain the safety of an autonomous cyber-physical system" (Abstract)
method: Black-Box Simplex: a decision module admits the advanced controller command only if a lookahead baseline controller can extend it to a provably permanently safe sequence; adds multi-agent command blending.
evaluation: Simulation: 11-16 robot MPC coordination (20 repeats) and 3, 7 and 15 F-16 aircraft with ACAS-Xu neural controllers; blending lifts goal success from 0-41.67% to 59.06-100%; zero collisions, min separation 1500.5 ft vs 175 ft for the unguarded system; two theorems proved; reachability check 1.5-2 ms on a 2.70 GHz Xeon E-2176M laptop, 55x faster than real time.
contribution: Shows runtime checks can replace static verification of the baseline controller, giving proved collision avoidance for multi-agent CPS driven by unverified MPC or neural-network controllers.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes in the F-16 study (ACAS-Xu neural-network controllers guarded); the multi-robot study guards MPC, which is not learned, so the learned-system condition is met by one of two case studies. Journal extension of two earlier conference papers (refs 7,8), so check for duplicate queued records. (d) is weak: millisecond check times and a proposed runtime cap, but no deadline or jitter study and a laptop CPU rather than edge hardware. All results in simulation; command-blending success rates degrade sharply with agent count (59% at 16 agents).

title: Nav-Q: quantum deep reinforcement learning for collision-free navigation of self-driving cars
evidence: Sect. 4.1: 'the quantum component has not to be included at the time of testing' - the quantum circuit is only the A2C critic in training; collision avoidance is learned via reward shaping, with no runtime shield.
method: Actor-critic RL for speed control of a self-driving car where the critic is a parameterised quantum circuit (4-6 qubits); steering from hybrid A*; classical actor used alone at test.
evaluation: CARLA-CTS1.0, 9936 test scenes, simulated qubits (PennyLane); vs classical NavA2C: crashes 13.23 vs 12.47 percent, near-misses 23.62 vs 22.39, 53 vs 2305 critic params; no latency.
contribution: Replaces the critic of an A2C driving agent with a 53-parameter quantum circuit and reaches crash and near-miss rates comparable to, but slightly worse than, a classical 2305-parameter baseline in CARLA.
flag: Not a runtime safety mechanism and single learning agent; pedestrians are scripted. Title says 'collision-free' but the crash rate is 13.23 percent and slightly worse than the classical baseline (12.47). No real quantum hardware; training 10.87 days vs 2.7. Noise and parameter-shift results are qualitative only. Text has an inconsistency on LSTM hidden size (32 vs reduced to 6).

title: Compliance without coherence: fluent failure and the ethics of alignment evaluation in multi-agent language models
evidence: "complementing behavioral monitors with structural audits of an agent's discourse" (Abstract)
method: Conceptual essay defining fluent failure in multi-agent LLM deployments and arguing, via Floridi levels of abstraction, for discourse-structural audits (graph modularity, betweenness) alongside surface monitors.
evaluation: None of its own. The pre-registered triadic multi-agent simulation is an unpublished companion preprint cited only as a plausibility anchor; no metrics, no baseline, no ablation, no formal result.
contribution: Argues deployed surface alignment monitors are in principle blind to fluent, compliant failure of LLM agents, and sketches discourse-structural auditing as a complementary evaluation layer.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes (LLM agents) but nothing intercepts at runtime and nothing is measured. The author states plainly that the argument is conceptual and that the empirical companion is a preprint, not peer reviewed and not load-bearing, so the evaluation floor fails; Table 1 is an illustrative classification, not data. Maintainer may prefer E3, since AI and Ethics classes it as RESEARCH but it is self-described as an essay. Single author, dual affiliation.

title: Safe motion planning and formation control of quadruped robots
evidence: "then model the dynamic control barrier function as a soft constraint of model predictive control through collision cost to get a trajectory as far away from obstacles as possible" (Sec. 3)
method: ESDF-free gradient B-spline planner for a quadruped with ground-reaction-force energy and impact terms; leader-follower formation where a vehicle follows via MPC with a slack-relaxed dynamic CBF constraint.
evaluation: Gazebo plus one real quadruped run (Jetson Xavier NX, 16-beam lidar). Versus basic planner: X-Y force integral 107,867.7 to 83,380.1 (-22.7%), peak X-Y force -33.2%, traversal 8.6 s to 6.7 s. Formation qualitative only.
contribution: Plans energy- and impact-aware quadruped trajectories and adds a leader-follower formation in which the follower's MPC carries a relaxed dynamic control-barrier constraint; safety is shown qualitatively only.
flag: CBF is a soft constraint with slack inside the MPC planner, not a filter between a nominal decision and execution, so (a) is not met; (c) fails primacy - quantitative results concern energy, impact and traversal time of a single robot, with no collision or violation rate and no baseline for the formation part (also E2 on that ground). Text numbers appear swapped: Z-axis peak 1138.8 to 764.908 is stated as 24.1% but computes to 32.8%, while the Z integral in Table 1 (85,799.6 to 65,163.0) computes to 24.1% but is stated as 32.8%. 'Computational efficiency' in Table 2 is just sample count at 10 Hz (traversal time), no solver latency reported. Formation is two agents (quadruped plus one vehicle), simulation only; conclusion says it 'will be tested in real world'. Section heading says 'control obstacle function'. Jetson named as perception host with no timing.

title: Safe integration of Large Language Models into industrial process control: a multi-agent architecture with P&ID-grounded validation
evidence: "A deterministic Verification Agent validates every proposal against P&ID topology, SCADA constraints, and SOP compliance before any action is permitted" (Sect. 1 Introduction)
method: Four-layer AAE architecture: LLM Monitor agents propose, an Orchestrator ranks, a deterministic Verification Agent applies six P&ID graph-traversal checks plus a forbidden-action rubric, and an Execution Agent routes auto-execute, notify, approval or block.
evaluation: 5 synthetic scenarios (3 from Tennessee Eastman), Claude Sonnet 4 proposals and Qwen2.5-VL-3B for HMI parsing; 43 injected proposals give recall 1.000, FNR 0.000, FPR 0.750, precision 0.854, F1 0.921; LLMs propose unsafe actions in 10-70% of 50 runs and every one is flagged; B0-B3 graduated ablation; aggregation 24.2 ms (sigma 3.1 ms, 200 iterations, i7-1370P), LLM inference 2-8 s.
contribution: Confines LLM inference to an advisory monitor layer and gates every proposed control action through deterministic P&ID-grounded validation, catching all covered unsafe proposals across five process-control scenarios.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes (LLM proposal generator and VLM). Strongest record of the batch but note: single-author industrial paper, all scenarios synthetic, ground-truth and forbidden-action rubrics written by the system designer (self-acknowledged evaluation bias), and prototype code and evaluation scripts generated with an AI coding agent. Recall 1.000 covers only the six structural checks plus scenario-specific rubric; FPR 0.750 rests on 8 negatives with Wilson interval about [0.41,0.93]. Escalation paths and operator console were not exercised in the evaluation, so (e) is architectural plus a qualitative alert-fatigue discussion, not measured. The 24.2 ms excludes file I/O, MQTT and LLM inference; P0 actions bypass the framework entirely. Multi-agent here means a software agent architecture, not reasoning over multi-agent state.

title: Balancing autonomy and oversight in reliable agentic artificial intelligence through adaptive human interaction architectures
evidence: "those falling below a lower safety threshold halt execution and escalate to a human operator through a purpose-built three-panel decision console" (Abstract)
method: Dynamic Intervention Framework: a Llama-3-8B Supervisor scores each GPT-4o Worker step by token log-probability plus goal-embedding cosine drift and routes to autonomous, async audit or human halt; DPO on operator corrections tunes thresholds.
evaluation: 5000 synthetic enterprise tasks in 3 logical domains against fully autonomous and static HITL baselines (human responses oracle-simulated); success 98.2% vs 84.3% and 99.1%; intervention 14.5%, false positive 3.2%, self-correction 76.4%; mean latency 4.8 s vs 45.6 s (89% cut); DPO drops intervention 21.0% to 11.5% over 5 epochs; 8x A100, 0.3 s per-step budget.
contribution: Treats human oversight as a dynamically allocated resource, scoring every agent step for confidence and goal drift to halt and escalate only the risky ones while matching static human-in-the-loop accuracy.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes (GPT-4o Worker agent). Most relevant record in the batch for RQ3 and RQ5, but the maintainer should doubt the headline claim: the human baseline and every operator response are oracle-model simulations with ground-truth access, so statistical equivalence to full human oversight is not a human study (the authors concede this). The 14.5% intervention rate contradicts Tables 3 and 4, which both total 760 of 5000 decision steps (15.2%). ASYNC_REVIEW, one of three core routing states, fired 0% of the time, so a third of the mechanism is unevaluated. Data synthetic and only available from the corresponding author; a PRISMA-2020 literature search inside a systems paper, free-mail author addresses and no shared affiliation are worth a machine-generation check.

title: Optimizing collaborative picking path conflicts in warehouse supply chains by integrating graph attention transformer and multi-agent soft actor-critic (SAC) algorithms
evidence: "Safety-critical deployments would require additional hard constraints or shielding mechanisms to bound the exploration policy." (Sec 6 Discussion of limitations)
method: GAT-MASAC: decentralized multi-agent soft actor-critic for warehouse robot path finding, with GRU plus scaled dot-product graph attention over neighbours, entropy-driven detours and curriculum replay; collision handled by reward penalty.
evaluation: MovingAI simulation, 200 robots, 5 seeds; baselines MAGAT, MADDPG, MASAC, ERL-MAPF plus ablation; success 0.96 vs 0.74; deadlocks 2 vs 13 per 100 rounds; latency 9.0 ms; hardware not stated.
contribution: A graph-attention multi-agent SAC planner for warehouse picking robots that reaches 0.96 pathfinding success and 9 ms decision latency with 200 simulated robots; a coordination and deadlock study, not a safety mechanism.
flag: Fails the (c) primacy test: the primary claims and metrics are success rate, makespan, flow time, deadlock frequency and latency; collision avoidance is a reward term and no collision or violation rate is reported anywhere (Sec 4.2 calls minimum obstacle distance a proxy for collision risk; Table 6 gives 0.85 m margin and text asserts a 'reduced collision rate' without a number). No runtime override: the paper itself says safety-critical use would need added shielding. Possible RQ1 background only: 9 ms per-step graph-attention inference over 200 agents, but no hardware, batch or timing method is given, so the figure cannot be compared to an edge budget; Table 7 says 9.2 ms, Table 8 and abstract say 9.0 ms. Oddly the proposed model is 2x to 6x faster than simpler baselines (MADDPG 21.4 ms, MASAC 30.4 ms) while its own no-GAT ablation is 5.4 ms - worth doubting. Abstract 'median 0.95 to 0.97' vs body mean 0.96 +/- 0.018; abstract 21% makespan degradation and 12.5% flow-time offset were located only for the latter in Table 8 (I did not read Sec 5.2 line by line). Read: abstract, intro, Sec 4 setup, metrics, ablation, Table 8, limitations, conclusion; skimmed the method equations (Sec 3) and related work. Simulation only.

title: Enduring Heterogeneous Cooperative Embodied-agent Control: Long-sequence Task Collaboration via Reinforcement Fine-tuning
venue: International Journal of Computational Intelligence Systems
evidence: "ReAd is enabled only in our method, while baseline methods use the same candidate generator without the safety veto to isolate the effect of the VLM-integrated safety gate." (Sec. 4.1)
method: Three heterogeneous robots trained by imitation then RL fine-tuning (VSPO); before execution a VLM-hosted critic gate (ReAd) scores candidate joint actions and vetoes low-advantage ones, triggering replanning.
evaluation: ManiSkill simulation, 2 quadrupeds plus 1 mobile manipulator, 300 episodes x 5 seeds; 9 baselines incl. CBF-Grasp; ablations; non-collision rate 0.897/0.754 (L1/L2), SR, throughput; 4x NVIDIA H20; gate adds about 45 ms.
contribution: A learned advantage-based veto gate in a three-robot warehouse team raises non-collision rate from 0.785 to 0.897 (L1) and 0.641 to 0.754 (L2) in ablation, with throughput also higher, in simulation.
flag: Abstract figures (SR 77.7%, NCR 82.6%, RD 84.7%, TP 1.10) are L1/L2 averages and reproduce from Table 1. Doubts: simulation only; no veto/intervention rate or false-veto rate; no formal guarantee (authors say so); the gate is introduced as used 'during intermediate iterations' of training, so confirm it is active at evaluation (ablation and the 45 ms figure imply yes); 45 ms is stated without measurement detail and on datacentre GPUs, not edge. NCR gain over CBF-Grasp at L1 is 0.897 vs 0.895; removing ReAd gives NCR below several baselines. CIs and Welch tests are claimed but no values reported. L1/L2 are defined as VIKI-R evaluation levels yet used as scenario difficulty. Safety is one of five metrics, so (c) primacy not met; include rests on (a). Gate also filters 'task-irrelevant' actions, so it is not purely a safety filter. Related work (Sec. 2), advantage derivations (3.1-3.2), sensitivity (4.5-4.6) and appendices only skimmed.

title: Intent-aware spatiotemporal risk field for multi-AGV path planning with heterogeneous dynamic obstacles
venue: Journal of King Saud University - Computer and Information Sciences
evidence: "The collision count of Ours decreases to 3.38, the lowest among all configurations, representing a 33.6% reduction compared to Baseline" (Sec. 5.3.6)
method: Multi-AGV grid planner: Transformer-GRU predictor of external obstacle actions feeds an intent-weighted Gaussian risk field used as a soft cost in A*, then iterative priority-based conflict resolution among AGVs.
evaluation: 13 MAPF grid maps, 5-10 agents, 20 scripted obstacles; ablations plus PBS, LNS2, greedy baselines; collisions, planning time 36-122 ms, makespan; i7-8700 and GTX 1080 Ti, 12 ms per prediction.
contribution: Risk-aware multi-AGV path planner that predicts non-communicating obstacles with a Transformer and folds an intent-weighted risk field into A* search, trading some collisions for much lower planning time than PBS and LNS2.
flag: Correct file. BORDERLINE (c): collision count against baselines and ablations is reported, but the mechanism is a risk cost inside a planner (not (a): no veto at execution time) and the paper's own analysis says the risk map's contribution "lies in path efficiency optimization rather than collision reduction"; headline advantage is planning time. Maintainer may read the primacy test differently. Collisions are never eliminated (3.38 per trial with 10 agents), so there is no safety guarantee. Doubts: (1) Abstract "25-370x computational speedup over prediction-enhanced baselines" is not in the body: against the predictive baselines Sec. 5.3.8 gives 22x and 285x (Scenario B) and 32x and 84x (C); 371x is against NON-predictive LNS2, and Sec. 6.1 and the conclusion say 42-371x. (2) Abstract says it outperforms PBS and LNS in success rate, collision count and makespan; Tables 3-5 contradict this: PBS and LNS2 have 0 collisions vs 0.18 in Scenario A, the predictive PBS and LNS2 variants have fewer collisions in B (0.26, 0.28 vs 0.29) and C (3.30, 3.25 vs 3.38), all reach success rate 1, and baseline makespan is lower in B (204.40 vs 232.93). So the quoted "lowest among all configurations" only holds within the ablation rows, and "superior makespan across all scenarios" (Sec. 6.1) is false. (3) "33.6% overall improvement" is the Scenario C figure only. (4) Scenario A has no dynamic obstacles yet adding the obstacle predictor cuts collisions 94%; the text attributes this to "prediction of peer agent behavior", which the method section does not describe. (5) Collision-count normalisation is defined two incompatible ways in Sec. 5.1.3. (6) No variance reported ("available upon request"); early stopping on the test split; obstacles follow fixed cyclic scripted routes; predictor accuracy (87%, ADE 1.14) is on held-out data from the training maps, not the 13 benchmark maps. (7) Time decay is gamma=0.8 in Table 2 but Eq. 11 is 1/(1+0.8t). (8) Grid simulation only, no robots, no communication latency. The 12 ms prediction and 36-122 ms planning figures are on a desktop GPU, with no deadline or jitter analysis, so (d) is not met.

title: LLM-3D print: Large Language Models to monitor and control 3D printing
evidence: Results: the framework works by "pausing the print for error analysis and correction" after each layer; Abstract: defects are corrected "without human intervention".
method: LLM supervisor with vision, planning and execution modules inspects camera images after every printed layer, diagnoses defects and changes printer parameters via the Moonraker API before resuming.
evaluation: Ender 5 Plus and Ender 3 prints (PLA, TPU); baseline unoptimised prints; peak compression load 1.34-5.06x higher; expert/14-engineer labels; GPT-4o; 15-45 s per layer; no safety metric.
contribution: A multi-module LLM framework pauses a 3D print after each layer, diagnoses defects from images and adjusts printer parameters autonomously, raising part peak load up to five-fold over unmonitored prints.
flag: Process quality control, not safety: the monitor does pause and re-parameterise at runtime (hence runtime_interceptor yes) but it never halts or defers, the target is print quality, and there is no hazard, violation or intervention rate, so E2 would apply even if (a) were granted. Abstract claims expert-level defect identification but the body gives confusion matrices only as a figure (Fig. 9) with no accuracy numbers in the text; occupancy metric is defined without reported values. Modules are LLM roles in one pipeline, not interacting agents. No human takeover at runtime. Fetched text was arXiv v3, which may differ from the journal version. One full-PDF fetch via summariser.

title: SafeCast: Risk-responsive motion forecasting for autonomous vehicles
evidence: Sec. 3.4: RSS minimum-distance terms are node attributes of a Dynamic Safety Graph over the target and nearby agents; Sec. 3.4.1: "SafeCast avoids reliance on post hoc rule-based constraints".
method: Graph-attention trajectory forecaster with a Dynamic Intention Graph and an RSS-featured Dynamic Safety Graph, learnable Gaussian noise on node features, and a maneuver-conditioned GMM decoder.
evaluation: NGSIM, HighD, MoCAD, ApolloScape. RMSE avg 1.54/0.29/1.62; WSADE 1.1253, WSFDE 2.1024; many baselines, six ablations. 0.20 s per 128-batch run on RTX 3090.
contribution: SafeCast feeds Responsibility-Sensitive-Safety distances into a graph-attention forecaster of surrounding vehicles, reaching 1.54 m average RMSE on NGSIM with 235K parameters; it predicts motion and does not intercept actions.
flag: Predictor only, enters as method/architecture evidence under (b); no collision or violation rate, no runtime override, no safety loss term (MSE+NLL only), so 'risk-responsive' is input features, not a guarantee. Output is a GMM over trajectories (not latent prediction), so non-generative cell not claimed. Paper inconsistencies: Sec. 4.3.2 says RMSE is 35.02% 'higher' than M-LSTM when it is lower; BAT beats it at 1 s on NGSIM (0.23 vs 0.40) despite 'consistently' superior claim; CNN ablation text says >=4.2% but Table 6 shows about 1.4%. Timing is batch time on a 3090, not per-sample latency.

title: Control of cooperative manipulator-endowed systems under high-level tasks and uncertain dynamics
evidence: "This paper summarizes the main results of the PhD Thesis [13]." (Sec. 1, Introduction)
method: Overview of adaptive leader-follower navigation with collision and connectivity terms, prescribed-performance and MPC cooperative manipulation, and LTL/MITL abstractions for planning multi-robot manipulator tasks under uncertain dynamics.
evaluation: Illustrative runs only: 6 UAVs in Gazebo, 20 agents with 70 obstacles, two WidowX arms, two IRIS+ quadrotors; one internal-force comparison; MPC run took 13450 s for 60 s simulated.
contribution: Summarises a thesis on provably correct control and temporal-logic planning for cooperating mobile manipulators with uncertain dynamics, illustrated by simulations and small hardware experiments.
flag: Subject is coordination, cooperative manipulation and temporal-logic planning; collision avoidance is one constraint built into the control laws (diverging barrier-like terms, MPC constraints), with no separate runtime override, no collision/violation rate and no safety baseline, so (a) and (c) fail; E2 would also apply to any safety claim. Arguably also E3: it is an Annual Reviews in Control overview of the first author's own thesis and earlier papers rather than new results. The given ScienceDirect pdf_url failed (client error) and DiVA was robots-disallowed; I read the authors' preprint at https://people.kth.se/~dimos/pdfs/Annual_rev_22.pdf (found by web search, marked 'Preprint submitted to Elsevier, June 27, 2022'), both chunks through the conclusion - the published version may differ slightly. arXiv 2303.01379 is the underlying thesis, not this article, so arxiv_id left as none. Other timing: transition system built in 1.71 min, planning 1.23 + 0.64 min (offline).

title: MedNegotiator: Automating requirements negotiation in healthcare; simulating clinical and technical perspectives using Generative AI agents
evidence: "If any rule is violated or drift is detected, the proposal is rejected and a Context Refresh is triggered." (Sec. 3.1.4 Consistency guard)
method: LLM persona agents (clinical, technical) negotiate healthcare software requirements via QFD-derived utilities and Nash bargaining; an NL-to-FOL Consistency Guard rejects proposals violating hard constraints; humans sign off.
evaluation: Two case studies and a GPT-4o pilot; 6 ablations and baselines; convergence 95%, safety-violating proposals 0% vs 7% without guard, adoption 80%; 48 s for 55 requirements on AWS t3.medium.
contribution: Automates requirements negotiation for healthcare software with persona-driven LLM agents, Nash bargaining and a rule-based consistency guard, reporting 95% convergence and no constraint-violating requirements in the final specification.
flag: Correct file; long paper, I read abstract, Sec. 1 contributions, Sec. 3.1.4 guard, 3.11, Sec. 6 evaluation, threats, conclusion; I only skimmed Secs. 2, 3.2-3.10, 3.12, the two case-study traces and the sensitivity analysis. Subject is requirements engineering: the "safety" guarded is the content of a requirements document, not the behaviour of an acting system, so (a) and (c) fail on subject and primacy (primary claim is convergence and adoption). BORDERLINE if the maintainer counts a proposal-rejecting guard over LLM agents plus human override (Phase 5; override on 15% of offers) as an approval gate - then a;e with the 7% vs 0% ablation as the safety metric. Doubts: (1) Large stretches of the body are unintelligible paraphrase-tool prose (e.g. "Writes blind of mixes that kill get stop", "How to do again worry this") alongside fluent passages; the AI-use declaration names GPT-4o and Claude 3.5 Sonnet; many reported numbers sit only inside the garbled passages and cannot be interpreted. (2) Abstract "95% agreement within 120 negotiation steps" does not match the body, where 95% is a convergence rate over 120 pilot rounds covering 55 requirements. (3) Internal inconsistencies: temperature 0.1 vs 0.2; kappa 0.68 vs 0.72, and Cohen's kappa quoted for 12 raters; Fig. 9 scenario labelled BioArc REQ-108 in the caption and NCR REQ-108 in the text; mean Nash product 0.45 vs 0.63 and 0.72 in the case studies; break-even at 3 rounds vs 8 requirements. (4) Safety-violation metric is self-defined against the author's own five FOL rules and pattern index; the guard pseudocode rejects on LOW similarity to safety patterns, which reads inverted. (5) Baselines were grid-tuned on the same 120 rounds used for reporting; single author; the hospital pilot is described only in garbled text. (6) A finance transfer (Basel III) is claimed in two sentences without data; both domains are logical anyway, so no cross-domain cell. Runtime is minutes per negotiation, no latency constraint.

title: Sim-to-Lab-to-Real: Safe reinforcement learning with shielding and generalization guarantees
evidence: Sec. 5.2: the backup action replaces the performance policy's proposed action if and only if the backup critic's safety value exceeds the threshold, Q^b(o, a^p) > v_thr.
method: Dual-policy safe RL: a reward-driven performance policy is shielded by a backup policy and safety critic from Hamilton-Jacobi reachability; latent-conditioned policies fine-tuned with PAC-Bayes generalization bounds.
evaluation: Indoor visual navigation sim plus Ghost Spirit quadruped, 30 trials: safety 0.867 vs 0.433 (PAC_Base) and 0.667 (SQRL); deployment violations down 26-54%; 10 Hz control; V100/A100 training; no inference latency.
contribution: A learned reachability shield overrides a navigation policy when its safety critic predicts failure, with PAC-Bayes bounds on safety in unseen environments, cutting violations in training and on a real quadruped.
flag: Single robot, static obstacles; no multi-agent, latency or handoff aspect - closed-loop sequential shielding is what keeps it out of E4, maintainer to confirm. Sec. 7.2.2 text describes the bound improving from 0.366 to 0.786 but Table 2 lists those as true expected success (bounds are 0.297 and 0.701). Real-robot trial count wording is ambiguous (10 locations x 3). One location with v_thr -0.10 never finished because of constant shielding (false-halt evidence). Shield intervention rate not reported as a number. Advanced-Realistic training-violation reduction given as 23% in one place and 20-25% in another. Onboard computer and inference latency not stated. RQ4 score reflects generalization bounds to unseen environments, not hazard combinations.

title: A predictive safety filter for learning-based control of constrained nonlinear dynamical systems
evidence: The filter decides whether the learning-based input "can be safely applied to the real system, or if it has to be modified otherwise" (Abstract), modifying it "as little as necessary to maintain safe operation at all future times" (Sec. 1).
method: Predictive safety filter: an MPC solved each step certifies the learning controller's input against a probabilistic model or replaces it with a minimally modified safe input; terminal safe controller.
evaluation: Simulation only: pendulum (120 episodes) and Bullet quadrotor (240 episodes); baseline unguarded learned policy; constraints held in all 240 episodes; no violation counts or timings; Theorem 4.6 proves safety in probability.
contribution: A predictive safety filter that certifies or minimally modifies any learning controller's input at every step, proving constraint satisfaction in probability without constraining how the policy is learned.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes in intent - designed for black-box RL - but the policies actually guarded in the experiments are Bayesian-optimisation-tuned bang-bang and PD controllers rather than RL, and the terminal controllers are hand-designed, so a strict reading of the Pillar 1 scope ruling could push this to exclude-E1. Single-agent, single-input guardrail, so exclude-E4 on level is also defensible; the sequential aspect (MPC horizon, closed-loop episodes) is the only thing against that, and there is no multi-agent, latency or handoff aspect. Evaluation floor rests on Theorem 4.6 plus qualitative baseline trajectories: no violation counts, rates or cost values are reported (only that constraints held across all 240 quadrotor episodes) and there is no formal ablation, just 10 versus 18000 data points on the pendulum. The guarantee is probabilistic with existential constants, and Assumption 4.3's tracking policy and Lyapunov function are used in the proof only, never implemented. Real-time solution is claimed via Ipopt and CasADi but no solve times or hardware are given, so (d) does not hold. Human override appears only as a conceptual driver-assistance remark in the Discussion, which is not (e). Version read is v4, the 2021 Automatica preprint matching the record DOI. One fetch.

title: Robust Control Barrier Functions under high relative degree and input constraints for satellite trajectories
evidence: Sec. 5.3 Eq. 65: control is the minimiser of ||u - unom(x)||^2 over the safe input set mu_s(t,x,sigma), which is the full input set when the constraint is inactive.
method: Robust CBFs for relative-degree-two systems with bounded inputs and disturbances; three constructions plus hysteresis switching; min-norm QP overrides nominal thrust.
evaluation: Simulation: one spacecraft, Ceres low-thrust flyby (69 days) and Eros proximity with 3897 mesh constraints; no-RCBF baseline crashes; CBF evaluation 0.25-12 ms and 0.36-560 ms on 3.5 GHz PC.
contribution: Robust control barrier functions for high-relative-degree systems with input limits and disturbances, used as a min-norm safety filter keeping a simulated spacecraft off Ceres and Eros.
flag: Single spacecraft, static bodies, no multi-agent, sequential-deferral, latency-constraint or handoff aspect; multi-agent is future work only. Safety evidence is one trajectory per variant (no-RCBF run crashes, RCBF runs do not), not a rate, so E2 is also arguable. Computation times are reported but not against a deadline; the 560 ms worst case for HA4 is far from real time. Summariser was ambiguous on whether the switched or unswitched variant reached the boundary 0.4 days earlier; check Fig. 10 before quoting. Read from arXiv preprint, not the Automatica version.

title: On the undesired equilibria induced by control barrier function based quadratic programs
evidence: Sec. 3-4: the modified QP computes a correction u' added to a nominal controller, u = u_nom + u', subject to the CBF constraint, keeping the safe set forward invariant.
method: Analysis of undesired closed-loop equilibria created by CLF-CBF quadratic programs, plus a modified QP around a nominal controller that removes interior and some boundary equilibria.
evaluation: Theory plus numerical examples on single-integrator and second-order single-agent systems with one obstacle; original vs modified QP; no safety rate, no hardware, no timing.
contribution: Characterises spurious equilibria that CLF-CBF safety-filter QPs introduce and proposes a modified QP that removes interior ones without extra computation, shown on single-agent numerical examples.
flag: Single-agent CBF safety filter, formal result with illustrative examples only; no collision/violation/intervention rate, so E2 would also apply. Only numbers are analytic (e.g. p threshold 16/105, region of attraction radius 3.3 vs 2 in prior work). Multi-robot appears only in related work. Useful background on filter-induced deadlock, nothing more.

title: Distributed safe control design and probabilistic safety verification for multi-agent systems
evidence: "a CBF is only regarded as a verification criterion but not necessarily as a control design principle" (Sec. 4); truncation comes "at the cost of potentially violating the control barrier function constraints" (Sec. 3.2)
method: Distributed dual-decomposition algorithm solves a CBF-constrained QP minimally modifying each agent's nominal input; a truncated variant trades guarantees for speed, with scenario-based probabilistic verification of CBF violation.
evaluation: Simulation only: 10 double-integrator robots swapping positions; 4-robot verification with 200 scenarios gives violation probability in [0,0.146] at confidence 0.9. No external baseline; no timing or hardware.
contribution: Gives a distributed CBF-QP safe controller for multi-agent systems with a truncated variant and a scenario-based method that bounds the probability of safety-constraint violation.
flag: Borderline E2 vs include. There IS one quantitative safety figure (violation probability bound [0,0.146] at confidence >=0.9) but no baseline and no real ablation: asymptotic Algorithm 1 vs truncated Algorithm 2 is compared only qualitatively (eta=30 only; 'rho_sum is close to zero at every time step', no numbers). No collision rate, no computation time, no hardware. Paper never calls the QP a filter/shield, and relaxation variables allow CBF violation, so runtime_interceptor=yes is my reading of a min-deviation-from-nominal QP. Verification is offline. Text inconsistency: 200 scenarios stated for the example but repetitions described as 300 runs of 300 scenarios. Batch year says 2023 (arXiv v1); journal DOI is Automatica 2025. Figs 1-4 not readable as text.

title: Robust adaptive discrete-time control barrier certificate
evidence: Sec 3.2: the filter 'evaluates each nominal input and replaces it with the closest admissible input that renders the system safe'
method: Robust adaptive discrete-time control barrier certificate with online set-membership parameter estimation; a safety filter replaces the nominal input with the closest admissible one each step.
evaluation: Simulated adaptive cruise control, dt 0.1 s; vs worst-case robust CBF filter, unfiltered adaptive MPC and robust adaptive MPC; results in figures only, no numeric safety metric, no timing.
contribution: Discrete-time barrier certificate that adapts to parametric uncertainty online, giving a less conservative safety filter than a worst-case robust design in a cruise-control simulation.
flag: Meets (a) by mechanism but single-agent and evaluation is qualitative: baselines exist yet no violation/intervention number is reported in the text (plots only), so fails minimum evaluation; E4 equally arguable. Read from one full-PDF fetch; figures not visible.

title: Real-time schedule adjustments for conflict-free vehicle routing
evidence: "vehicles move very fast (at speeds in the order of one/two meters per second) which requires SA-CFVRP algorithms to recover feasibility in few milliseconds" (Sec. 1 Introduction)
method: Centralized real-time re-timing of AGV fleet schedules after observed delays or early arrivals: exact longest-path algorithm on a temporal network keeps the plan's precedence (conflict-free) constraints, plus graph-reduction preprocessing.
evaluation: 600 grid-warehouse and 360 random instances, 50-300 vehicles, vs CPLEX LP and Adamo et al. 2023; compute time (longest path <=3.29 ms) and delay/makespan/lateness gaps. Intel i7 2.5 GHz, C++. No collision metric.
contribution: Gives an exact polynomial-time schedule-adjustment algorithm that restores conflict-free AGV fleet plans after timing deviations in about a millisecond for up to 300 vehicles, with lower delay than the prior heuristic.
flag: Borderline; exclude-E1 is defensible. Admitted only on (d): a millisecond latency requirement is stated for a collision-avoiding decision and compute times are measured against two baselines. It fails the (c) primacy test: conflict-freedom is a hard constraint guaranteed by construction, and the measured outcomes are compute time and delay, never a collision or violation rate. It is a replanner (adjusts waiting times), not a filter between a decision and its execution, hence runtime_interceptor no. Number checks: abstract 'at most 3.3 milliseconds' matches the max longest-path time T3=3.29 ms (RND, 300 vehicles) but excludes topological sorting T2 (1.22 ms in the same row, about 4.5 ms combined); abstract 'improvements ... up to 74%' matches the AVERAGE gap on random instances (74.3%), while individual rows reach 87.1% and warehouse instances average 16%. The cited 300 ms monitoring period is an assumption; deviations are synthetic uniform draws, not jitter measurements. Desktop CPU, no edge hardware. Graph-reduction preprocessing takes seconds to hours (offline). Peer-reviewed (Computers & Operations Research).

title: Reachability-Based Confidence-Aware Probabilistic Collision Detection in Highway Driving
evidence: Sec 4.1 (Step 3): if the collision probability exceeds a threshold "the ego vehicle has to replan motion trajectories or the ego driver will receive an alert", which the paper says is not within the scope of this work.
method: Two-layer collision detector: offline backward reachable set look-up gates an online stochastic forward reachable set from an LSTM acceleration predictor with Bayesian confidence (beta) scaling.
evaluation: highD data plus 256 simulated cut-ins (IDM); baselines HSRS, PSRS, PSRS-3beta/5beta and three LSTM variants; RMSE 0.22 m, LC-F1 98.79%; FRS 30-50 ms on GPU.
contribution: A reachability-based detector that computes confidence-aware collision probabilities for a neighbouring highway vehicle, flagging simulated cut-in crashes earlier than a heuristic Markov baseline at 30-50 ms per update.
flag: Detector only: no override, braking or alert is implemented or evaluated, so runtime_interceptor is no and (a) is not met. Rests on (c) for a pairwise (ego plus one vehicle) setting; multi-agent only nominally. Timeliness over 21 crash events is in Fig. 13 only, no numbers in text; text says 33 crashes but analyses 21. Position accuracy at 2.0 s (LK/LC): HSRS 43.08/26.81%, PSRS-5beta 52.81/38.58%. False-alarm case: max probability 0.16 PSRS vs 0.03 PSRS-5beta against 0.05 threshold (single scenario). GPU parallelism figure inconsistent in the text; hardware model not stated. No collision or false-alarm RATE reported - maintainer should judge whether minimum evaluation is met. Read via one summarised fetch of the PDF.

title: Constrained multi-agent ergodic area surveying control based on finite element approximation of the potential field
evidence: Sec. 5.2-5.3 (paraphrase, Algorithm 1): when a collision is predicted the HEDAC turning rates are replaced by an optimisation that minimises deviation from them subject to clearance and turning-rate bounds; search runs 'at least 20 iterations or until the feasible solution' is found.
method: HEDAC ergodic coverage: agents follow gradient of a FEM-solved Helmholtz potential; a minimum-deviation collision-avoidance optimisation over Dubins turning rates overrides the nominal direction when clearance is threatened.
evaluation: Simulation only, 3 cases (5-10 agents, UAV/USV maps); no quantitative baseline; per-step compute max 0.385s, 0.852s, 1.676s; coverage about 60% and 55%; hardware unspecified.
contribution: Multi-agent ergodic area surveying via a finite-element potential field, with a minimum-deviation collision-avoidance step that overrides the coverage heading for Dubins agents among obstacles.
flag: Borderline (a): the avoidance step does override the nominal heading at runtime, but the paper is a coverage controller, reports no collision/violation rate and has no quantitative baseline or ablation (only visual comparison with SMC), so fails minimum evaluation; could equally be E1. Clearance 'guarantee' rests on an informal feasibility argument. Timings are per-step compute on unnamed hardware, not a latency constraint. Internal inconsistencies: case 1 agent count 5 vs 7, dt 0.4s vs 1s; case 3 obstacles 50 vs 55. Extraction read via PDF-to-text summary; figures not inspected.

title: Safety Verification and Controller Synthesis for Systems with Input Constraints
evidence: Sec. II-A: the CBC formulation 'only requires safety on the boundary of the invariant set'; the projection QP of Sec. II is described but not implemented or evaluated.
method: Offline sum-of-squares synthesis of a control barrier certificate and polynomial safe feedback law under input constraints, conditioning only on the boundary of the invariant set.
evaluation: Two numerical examples (nonlinear control-affine, second-order LTI) with SOSTOOLS and SeDuMi; baseline SOS-synthesised CBF; result is set inclusion in a figure; no timings or hardware.
contribution: An offline sum-of-squares procedure that synthesises control barrier certificates and safe polynomial controllers under input limits, shown on two small numerical examples to give a larger invariant set than a CBF.
flag: Offline synthesis, not a runtime mechanism; the runtime projection QP (eq. 5, eq. 21) is proposed but never evaluated. No quantitative safety metric: the 'less conservative' claim rests on Fig. 1 only, no area figures. Single system. E1 also defensible. Reader noted the stated LTI eigenvalues (3.3, -0.3) do not match the printed matrix; not verified by me.

title: Safe Control Design for Unknown Nonlinear Systems with Koopman-based Fixed-Time Identification
evidence: Sec 4: 'either condition may be included as an affine constraint in the now popular quadratic program based control law'
method: Koopman-based fixed-time identification of unknown dynamics with an error bound, fed into robust and robust-adaptive CBF-QP controllers that minimally modify a nominal input.
evaluation: Simulated 2D double-integrator quadrotor with wind gust, two obstacles; vs nominal and naive CBF with two Koopman identifiers; fixed-time bound T=0.12 s; safety shown qualitatively; no timing.
contribution: Fixed-time Koopman identification with a known error bound lets a robust-adaptive CBF-QP keep an unknown nonlinear system safe where naive identified-model CBFs fail in simulation.
flag: Meets (a) by mechanism but single-agent and no numeric violation/intervention metric in text (figures only); only number is the analytical convergence bound 0.12 s. E4 equally arguable. Read from one full-PDF fetch; figures not visible.

title: AI-driven self-healing across the edge–cloud continuum: A systematic literature review
evidence: "A Systematic Literature Review was conducted following the PRISMA 2020 guidelines" (Abstract/Method).
method: Systematic literature review (Kitchenham guidelines, PRISMA 2020) of AI-driven self-healing in edge-cloud distributed systems; Scopus search, 2,930 records, 372 full texts assessed, 99 primary studies, five review questions.
evaluation: No original experiment. Synthesis of 99 studies from 2021-2026 scored on seven quality metrics; no mechanism, baseline, safety metric, hardware or latency of its own.
contribution: A PRISMA-style review of 99 studies on AI-driven self-healing across the edge-cloud continuum, identifying a validation gap for LLM-generated repairs and recommending human-in-the-loop governance.
flag: Clear E3: a systematic literature review with no method or evaluation of its own. The listed pdf_url (sciencedirect .../pdf) returned a client error; I read the open-access HTML article page instead (characters 0-200000 of about 232000; the last part, presumably references, was not fetched). Possibly useful for citation chasing on self-healing and cascading failures in services, and as related work on the logical-domain side. Single-database (Scopus) search is a limitation the authors acknowledge.

title: Adaptive target localization under uncertainty using Multi-Agent Deep Reinforcement Learning with knowledge transfer
evidence: "If the majority of the agents declare that the target does not exist, the search process stops." (Sec. 4.3) - a mission termination rule, not a safety mechanism.
method: Multi-agent PPO with centralized learning and distributed execution for radioactive-source search, with detection/reachability flags and actor weights transferred to a location-estimation head.
evaluation: Simulated 1 km x 1 km radiation search, 2-5 agents; baselines uniform search, DDQN, ODMTL; 7.7 time steps for strongest target with 4 agents; about 1 MFLOP, under 1 ms per action.
contribution: Multi-agent deep RL with transfer learning that localizes a radiation source under uncertainty about target existence and reachability, compared with uniform search, DDQN and ODMTL in simulation.
flag: Off-topic: multi-agent coordination for target search with no safety mechanism, hazard detection among agents, world model, latency constraint or handoff. Only safety-adjacent item is action masking of walls/boundaries. Autoencoder embeds the map layout but is not predictive. Benchmark values are mostly in figures.

title: Securing LLM agents: From prompt sanitization to autonomous red teaming and beyond
venue: Internet of Things and Cyber-Physical Systems
evidence: "This paper provides the first comprehensive survey of LLM agent security, synthesizing research on attack strategies, red teaming frameworks, evaluation suites, and defense mechanisms." (Abstract)
method: Survey of LLM-agent security: prompt injection, jailbreak, backdoor and multimodal attacks; automated/agentic red teaming; defences at prompt, decoding-time, runtime, privacy and multi-agent levels.
evaluation: No original evaluation; comparison tables of prior surveys, red-teaming frameworks, benchmarks and defences drawn from the literature.
contribution: Comprehensive survey of attacks on, red teaming of and defences for LLM agents, including runtime and multi-agent safeguards; useful as a pointer to primary studies, not as evidence itself.
flag: Self-declared survey (journal Internet of Things and Cyber-Physical Systems), so E3 regardless of topical fit to (a)/(c). Date inconsistency: page header says vol. 5 (2025) 185-209, while the DOI/PII and its own Table I ('This Survey 2026') say 2026. Long file (239k chars): I read the title page, abstract and introduction and grepped for original experiments (none found); the body sections and tables were not read. Could be mined for primary runtime-guard and multi-agent defence papers.

title: Cost-effective distributed FTFC for uncertain nonholonomic mobile robot fleet with collision avoidance and connectivity preservation
evidence: "some properly chosen performance functions are incorporated into the controller to per-assign the asymmetrical bounds for relative distance and bearing angle between each pair of adjacent mobile robots" (Abstract)
method: Prescribed-performance distributed fault-tolerant leader-follower formation controller for nonholonomic robots; error bounds on inter-robot distance and bearing give collision avoidance and connectivity preservation by construction.
evaluation: One numerical simulation, four robots plus leader, disturbances and actuator faults; plots show errors stay within bounds; no baseline, no quantitative metric, no hardware or latency.
contribution: Designs an approximation-free distributed fault-tolerant formation controller whose prescribed performance bounds keep neighbouring nonholonomic robots within communication range and outside collision distance, with a Lyapunov boundedness proof.
flag: Formation tracking controller: collision avoidance is a constraint built into the nominal control law (performance-function bounds), not a runtime filter that overrides another decision, so (a) fails; under the (c) primacy test collision avoidance is one of several guaranteed properties and is not measured against any baseline. Would also fail the minimum evaluation (E2): a single qualitative simulation (Fig. 3), no collision or violation metric, no comparison. Collision avoidance only covers each adjacent leader-follower pair in a one-to-one directed chain. Peer-reviewed (J. Automation and Intelligence 2023).

title: Physics-grounded multi-agent architecture for traceable, risk-aware human–AI decision support in manufacturing
evidence: The critic agent issues accept, revise or escalate decisions and "acceptance requires that the explicit checks above pass" (Sec. 3.4), escalating rather than forcing acceptance when its budget is exhausted.
method: MAKA: four LLM agents - central router, tool-only analysis, knowledge-graph retrieval, critic. The critic checks ids, schema and offset bounds before acceptance and escalates to human approval when verification fails.
evaluation: 75 tool-use questions, 6 models, 450 critic-ablation trials, Ti-6Al-4V blade digital twin; critic lifts tool F1 0.2919 to 0.6697, full recovery 61.19 percent; KG +0.1274; loop 4.3 s.
contribution: A physics-grounded multi-agent LLM architecture whose critic gates tool-based manufacturing recommendations, raising tool-selection F1 from 0.29 to 0.67 and escalating unverifiable cases to a human approver.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - LLM agents (router, analysis, KG, critic); the critic's own checks look rule-based (id matching, bounds, schema) but the paper never states this. Most likely overturn: the evaluation floor is met only through tool-selection F1 and recovery rates (0.2919 to 0.6697 mean F1, 61.19 percent full recovery, 62.22 percent reduced-missing, no-critic ablation over 450 trials); no hazard, violation, collision or unsafe-recommendation rate appears anywhere, so exclude-E2 is defensible. (c) fails the primacy test - multi-agent safety is an architectural design goal, not a measured outcome. (e) is architectural only: humans approve recommendations and can override the critic ("the CRA decision can be overridden by an explicit human approval signal", Sec. 3.4), but no takeover timing, quality or situation awareness is studied and there is no user study, so the maintainer may strike (e). Nothing acts on the machine at execution time - outputs are recommendations gated before CAM implementation - which also weakens (a). Digital-twin deviation reduction (about 1e-2 in to 1e-3 in) is simulation only, with no point-to-point agreement to the 30 inspection points and a residual the authors say is not uniquely attributable to deflection. Latency 4.3 s and KG overhead 0.7305 to 2.6496 s are reported but edge deployment is motivation only, so not (d). The abstract's "up to 87.5 percentage points" tool-execution uplift is in the conclusion but stated as up to 87.5 percent on L2 and at least 32 percent on L3; Table 1's capability comparison is self-assessed. One fetch.

title: Governance Twin Framework: Sentinel+Council Architecture for Agentic AI Systems in Digital Twin-Enabled Predictive Maintenance
evidence: "They classify potential vulnerabilities by risk and assess how to handle them-allow, deny, acquire more evidence from the knowledge graph, or escalate to higher-level council agents for further adjudication." (Sec. 6); "Quantitative comparisons with static governance approaches will be reported in subsequent work." (Sec. 9)
method: Conceptual Governance Twin: sentinel LLM agents monitor operational agents' proposed actions and escalate to a voting council of agents, with a knowledge graph supplying causal evidence, beside a digital twin.
evaluation: None. Two narrative predictive-maintenance scenarios (CNC spindle temperature; conflicting business goals); proof-of-concept of fourteen containerised services is under development in an observation phase. No metrics, baselines or latency.
contribution: Proposes a Sentinel+Council multi-agent governance layer in which monitoring agents escalate operational-agent actions to a deliberating council, described through two unevaluated predictive-maintenance scenarios.
flag: Architecture/position paper (NAMRC 54, peer reviewed) with no evaluation: the case studies are hypothetical narratives and Sec. 9 says the implementation is in an initial observation phase on document-intelligence and compliance platforms, not manufacturing. Abstract says "We demonstrate" and conclusion says the case studies "illustrate ... prevent hazardous machine states" but nothing is measured; "machine speed" governance has no latency figure and relies on LLM deliberation. Text is internally inconsistent on interception: Sec. 4 says sentinels "do not enforce compliance but rather escalate" while Sec. 6 says they allow/deny, so the runtime_interceptor yes is as described only. Human review is mentioned only as an escalation threshold. Errors to note: says OpenAI released "Chatgpt 3.0" in November 2021; cites refs [13,14,15] (LLM deception papers) for machinery safety risks; dates Hagendorff PNAS as October 2025 (ref says 2024) and Lynch et al. as a 2024 study (ref says 2025); case-study subsections numbered 7.1/7.2 inside Section 8; fax number is a placeholder. Core framework refs [10-12] are self-published web pages.

title: Cybersecurity risk assessment in autonomous transport systems: A semi-quantitative framework incorporating logistics disruption propagation
evidence: "These analyses evaluate the stability of scenario prioritisation under selected assumptions; they do not constitute empirical validation or dynamic simulation of disruption propagation" (Sec 1 Introduction)
method: Design-time semi-quantitative risk scoring adapted from ISO/SAE 21434 TARA: attack feasibility combined with weighted safety, financial, operational and disruption-propagation impact ratings for seven cyber threat scenarios.
evaluation: Paper case study of an SAE Level 4 freight corridor with author-assigned ratings; five weighting variants, propagation-criterion ablation, sensitivity and rank-correlation analyses; top scores R=16.80 and 15.20; no hardware or latency.
contribution: A design-time scoring framework that ranks cyber threats to an autonomous freight corridor by attack feasibility and logistics-wide consequences, with V2I/ETA falsification ranked most critical.
flag: Design-time risk-assessment rubric, not a runtime mechanism and not a detector; cascade 'propagation' is an ordinal rating, and the authors state they do not model cascades dynamically. All ratings and weights are author-assigned with no expert panel, incident data or simulation, so there is no hazard or violation rate and no empirical baseline (would also fail E2); the ablation shows removing the propagation criterion leaves the ranking unchanged (Spearman rho 1.000). Residual-risk reductions are described as illustrative assumptions. Text shows journal volume 278 dated 2027 while accepted October 2026; a paragraph is duplicated verbatim in the Conclusion. Long file (333k chars, much of it table layout): read abstract, introduction, section structure, limitations hits and conclusion; Sections 2-7 (literature review, rubric tables, sensitivity tables, managerial implications) were only searched by grep, not read in full.

title: Circulation-embedded Control Barrier Function for safe navigation: A solution to avoid undesired equilibria and dysfunctional circulation
evidence: "It demonstrates that the Circulation-embedded CBF was successful in avoiding collisions." (Sec. 6.2); the QP projects the nominal go-to-goal input onto the safe set each control step
method: CBF-QP safety filter for single-integrator robots with input bounds plus a sigmoid-activated, latched circulation constraint that steers along obstacle boundaries to escape undesired equilibria; LiDAR Gaussian-process safety function.
evaluation: TurtleBot3 Burger with 2D LiDAR and Vicon, nonconvex obstacle and four-robot deadlock without communication; ablation without circulation latch; qualitative plots only; QP solve mean 0.485 ms, max 2.1 ms, remote i7 PC.
contribution: Extends the CBF-QP safety filter with an input-bounded, latched circulation constraint that provably removes undesired equilibria and oscillating circulation, demonstrated on TurtleBots around nonconvex obstacles and in a communication-free four-robot deadlock.
flag: Borderline E2 vs E1. The mechanism is a genuine runtime safety filter (criterion a), but the paper's claim and outcome are liveness: deadlock, undesired equilibria and slowdown, not safety.
