No quantitative safety metric (no collision or violation rate, no trial counts) and the only comparison is one run of a no-latch ablation plus a qualitative feature table (Table 1) against prior methods, so the v1.6 minimum evaluation is not met. Multi-robot deadlock experiment is a single qualitative demonstration; other robots are just moving obstacles, so I did not tick multi-agent state. Latency cell ticked only because solve times are reported (min 0.010 ms, mean 0.485 ms, max 2.126 ms; control step 0.02 s, LiDAR 5 Hz); computation runs on a remote PC over Wi-Fi, not on-board, so no edge deployment. Speed bound is inconsistent in the text as relayed (0.1*sqrt(2) approx 0.12 m/s stated vs 0.1 m/s in figure captions). Read via ScienceDirect HTML https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0921889025002295 (PII URL constructed by me; doi.org not fetchable; TUNI repository copy blocked by Anubis) in three chunks; a nonconvex-obstacle comparison is mentioned in the conclusion but I saw no numbers for it - figures were not readable. Quotes relayed by the fetch tool; check verbatim wording.

title: Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning for Zero-Shot Coverage Path Planning with Dynamic UAV Networks
evidence: "ensures that any action violating safety constraints is overridden by a collision-free alternative" (Sec 4.3.4, proof of Theorem 1)
method: Decentralised MARL coverage planner (parameter-shared Rainbow DQN, VDN) with a supervisory two-stage robustness and safety filter: monitors predict neighbours' actions and override with a Dijkstra-based joint fallback policy.
evaluation: Grid-world Monte Carlo, 2-5+ UAVs; ablation with/without filter: unfinished 8.98%, outliers 10.98% (VDN) vs about 0.01% and 100% completion; median time-save 0.542 vs 0.540; no hardware or latency.
contribution: Adds a decentralised runtime safety and robustness filter with a provably collision-free fallback policy to a zero-shot multi-UAV coverage planner, keeping episode completion at 100% while barely changing median efficiency.
flag: Borderline, maintainer to decide. The paper is primarily about zero-shot coverage path planning (would be E1 under (c) primacy); it qualifies only via (a) because the filter is a genuine execution-time override on a supervisory layer and is not used in training. Minimum-evaluation doubt: the filter ablation (Sec 6.3.2, Fig. 10) reports robustness outcomes (outliers, unfinished episodes) and not a collision rate; collisions are zero 'by construction' via Theorem 1, and no collision count without the filter is given. Outlier/unfinished percentages are quoted for VDN only, Rainbow values are in a figure. Safety guarantee assumes a discrete grid, identical shared deterministic policies so neighbours' actions are predictable, and the authors state it ignores latency and position uncertainty. Simulation only; filter intervention frequency is not tabulated. Evaluation sections 6.3.3-6.4 and appendices were skimmed, not read line by line.

title: Ellipsoid uncertainty tether model for collision avoidance in a fleet of Remotely Operated Vehicles
evidence: "No collision has been detected in the simulations performed." (Sec. 8, Simulations)
method: Each tether is enclosed in an ellipsoid with foci at ROV and anchor; eigenvalue ellipsoid-intersection tests switch repulsive and untangling potential-field terms, with tether-length management and per-ROV personalities against deadlock.
evaluation: MATLAB 2022b simulation only: five single-ROV cases, three-ROV position swaps, two-ROV personality case; no baseline; no collision counts; 0.48-0.89 s average compute per step; no hardware stated.
contribution: Models each ROV tether as a conservative ellipsoid so that a fleet of tethered underwater vehicles can avoid tether, vehicle and obstacle collisions using potential fields, shown in simulation.
flag: Excluded on minimum evaluation, not topic: multi-ROV collision avoidance is the primary claim (c), but the only safety result is the sentence that no collision was detected; there are no collision counts, minimum distances, success rates or repeated trials, and the sole comparison is a qualitative with/without-personality figure. Not a runtime interceptor in the protocol sense: repulsive terms are added to the attractive field (and the target is swapped to the anchor when blocked) inside the controller itself, there is no separate filter over a nominal command. Per-step compute of 0.48 to 0.89 s in MATLAB against a sampling time of 1 is far from real time. No real experiments (no pool large enough); method fails when no escape route exists (seafloor case). No human operator role stated. Both HAL PDFs (hal-04741524, hal-05307363) were blocked by Anubis; read instead from the open-access ScienceDirect HTML at https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0921889025003100 (URL found by me, three chunks to offset 300000; the last ~13k characters, likely references, were not read). Sec. 6.3 personalities and the tether-length management section were seen only via the Sec. 8 summary.

title: Development of the Quad-SCARA platform and its collision avoidance based on Buffered Voronoi Cell
evidence: "At present stage, there is no sensor feedback for Quad-SCARA and the whole system is working with offline motion planning." (Section 2.1 Overview)
method: Four-SCARA cloth manipulation platform whose end-effector trajectories are planned offline with Buffered Voronoi Cells, plus static cells at robot base corners to avoid self-collision.
evaluation: One handkerchief fold-and-spread run on real Epson G3 arms plus a 2D Python simulator; minimal shortest distance 1.99 mm in simulation; 25 s per motion; no baseline or ablation; no latency figures.
contribution: Describes a four-arm SCARA platform and an offline Buffered Voronoi Cell planner with static cells for self-collision, demonstrated on one cloth folding and spreading sequence without collision.
flag: No baseline or ablation and no collision/violation rate: evidence is a single successful run and one minimum-distance number (1.99 mm in simulation, about 4 mm claimed real), so it fails the minimum evaluation for (c). Planning is offline with no sensing, so nothing intercepts at runtime. Table I comparison with RVO/ORCA/SCP is qualitative only. Buffer size 25 mm chosen empirically (20 mm too small, over 30 mm infeasible). Neither project tag fits BVC well; velocity-obstacles is the nearest family. Could also be argued E1 (platform paper).

title: Emergence of polarization in networks of large language model agents
evidence: "evolution of agents' opinions and behaviours is driven solely by LLMs without any pre-assumed rules or mechanisms" (Introduction)
method: Networked LLM agents run self-expression, communication and opinion-update stages on a Watts-Strogatz graph; a self-regulation step regenerates inconsistent outputs; interventions tested against polarization.
evaluation: 1000 GPT-3.5 agents (also GPT-4o, ChatGLM, Llama-3), three issues; ablations on network, traits, influencers; neutral share 40% to 0.4-22.5%; polarization cut 8.8-28.2%; no hardware or latency.
contribution: Shows that networks of LLM agents self-organise into polarized echo chambers without scripted rules, and that neutral influencers or reduced confirmation bias lower polarization by 9-28 percent.
flag: Title check: arXiv preprint is titled 'Emergence of human-like polarization among large language model agents' (Piao, Lu et al.), record title differs; judged the same work retitled for the journal, maintainer should confirm. Only the first 100000 of about 150000 characters were read (main text, methods, part of SI). Emergent polarization is a social-science outcome, not a safety hazard rate, so (c) primacy test not met. The self-regulation retry loop (agent forced inactive at retry limit, SI 1.1.3) is a consistency check, not a safety interceptor. multi-agent state cell is nominal.

title: Incorporating uncertainty in learning to defer algorithms for safe computer-aided diagnosis
evidence: Methods, LDU algorithm: the second-stage network outputs "either the patient's diagnosis or the decision to defer to a human expert".
method: Learning to defer with uncertainty (LDU): a 50-member deep ensemble feeds class probabilities plus ensemble and diagnostic entropy to a small network that outputs a diagnosis or a defer class.
evaluation: MIMIC-III notes, Heritage Health, MIMIC-CXR; vs learning to defer without uncertainty and entropy-threshold triage; e.g. pleural effusion F1 0.96 deferring 36% vs 69%; expert assumed correct; no hardware or latency.
contribution: Adding ensemble uncertainty as an input to a learning-to-defer network reaches the same diagnostic F1 while deferring markedly fewer patients to clinicians across text, tabular and chest X-ray tasks.
flag: E4 risk: single-model, single-input, one-shot classification with a defer option; no sequential, latency or multi-agent aspect, and the handoff is only nominal - no human model, no clinicians, deferred cases assumed correct, constant deferral cost. Maintainer should decide include vs exclude-E4. Table 1 (LDU pleural effusion F1 0.99+ at 70-82% deferral) is not reconciled with Table 2 (F1 0.96 at 36%). Abstract says direct triage was not applicable for comorbidities, but Results report DT reaching F1 0.73 there. Ensemble-entropy ablation is supplemental only. human handoff cell is weak for the same reason.

title: Evaluating routing stability and coordination in swarm-based multi-agent task-oriented dialogue systems
evidence: "At inference, a confidence gate triggers conservative fallback when the router is uncertain." (Methodology, Routing strategy)
method: Centralised orchestrator with a DeBERTa-v3 router choosing domain specialists and a FLAN-T5 generator over shared memory; a confidence threshold (0.7) or 800 ms tool timeout reroutes the turn to a fallback agent.
evaluation: MultiWOZ 2.2 and SGD, offline; rule-based, learned, oracle and ablated routers; gated routing accuracy 0.77 vs 0.65, switch 0.11 vs 0.44, bounce 0.01 vs 0.09; no hardware reported.
contribution: Evaluates routing stability in orchestrated multi-agent task-oriented dialogue, showing a confidence-gated fallback raises routing accuracy and cuts agent switching, and that early state errors quadruple downstream collapse risk.
flag: Borderline (a), maintainer should decide. The confidence gate does defer at execution time (hence runtime_interceptor yes) and is compared against baselines, but the subject is dialogue routing quality, not safety: no violation, hazard or intervention rate, and the fallback agent is never defined. The gate also has a cost the abstract plays down: slot-F1 falls to 0.12 (lowest) and state_empty failures rise from 1875 to 3210. Cascading-error analysis (Table 12: state omitted RR 4.1, missing slots 2.6, misroute 1.7 within first 3 turns) is the nearest thing to criterion (c) but concerns task collapse, not hazards. Internal inconsistencies: method says DeBERTa router but Table 11 lists RoBERTa runs with accuracy 0.84-0.87 that match nothing else, Table 10 lists GPT-4 and Llama-2, Table 14 columns conflict with Tables 18 and 21, Table 15 latency deltas have no units, and E_temp_scale_2.0 is numerically identical to B. Tool latency is injected (800 ms budget) as a stress test (accuracy 0.65 to 0.59), not measured; so I did not credit the latency cell. Swarm is nominal: control is centralised. SGD accuracy drops to 0.47. Read body from the Nature HTML page (constructed URL https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-42158-y) and tables from the given _reference.pdf.

title: Purely vision-based collective movement of robots
evidence: Robot Platform: "When close to an object (whether a wall or another robot), the robot turns away from the object until the path ahead is clear, irrespective of the visual input."
method: Decentralised flocking from a 1-D visual projection field: onboard CNN detections drive attraction-repulsion speed and turning with no explicit alignment; IR proximity reflex overrides near obstacles.
evaluation: Simulation (10 agents, 20 runs) and 10 Thymio II robots in 9x6 m arena, over 30 h; parameter sweeps only, no baseline controller; polarization, distance, collision ratio in figures; RPi 4B with Coral TPU, 5 Hz.
contribution: Shows that ten robots using only onboard fisheye vision and a minimal attraction-repulsion rule can achieve polarized collective motion without communication, position sharing or explicit alignment.
flag: Subject is emergent collective motion, not safety: fails the (c) primacy test. An IR proximity reflex does override the vision controller, but it is a stock platform behaviour, not the contribution, and analysed data were filtered to exclude wall-avoidance periods. Collision ratio and polarization values appear only in figures; no numeric values in text. Only the first 100000 of about 110000 characters were read (tail is supplementary notes and references). Record year 2025 is the journal version; arXiv is 2024.

title: Towards cooperative collision avoidance for the Voyager unmanned ground vehicle: Practical implementation and demonstration
evidence: "If a collision is predicted, the" (Abstract)
method: UGVs broadcast predicted trajectories over ROS2; on a predicted conflict a random-priority protocol has each agent sequentially plan evasive manoeuvres by Dijkstra tree search, then rejoin its global path.
evaluation: One physical Voyager UGV plus two virtual ghost agents in a corridor; two avoidances shown qualitatively; no baseline, no collision rate; planning under 1 s per agent, 10 s horizon.
contribution: Implements intent-broadcast collision prediction and sequential-priority evasive replanning on a real ground robot, demonstrating two avoidances against virtual agents in a corridor.
flag: Qualitative demonstration only: a single test run with two successful avoidances of virtual agents allowed to pass through walls; no quantitative safety metric, no baseline or ablation, so it fails the minimum evaluation. Introduction promises metrics (path deviation, planning time, attempts) that are never tabulated; the only figure is planning time less than 1s per agent stated in the conclusion. runtime_interceptor=yes is borderline: the layer overrides the nominal global path on a predicted conflict but is a local replanner, not a veto/halt gate. Method is taken from Hughes 2023 MSc thesis. Figure numbering of Fig. 18/19 is swapped.

title: Socially Aware Shared Control Navigation for Assistive Mobile Robots in the Built Environment
venue: Journal of Computing in Civil Engineering
evidence: Method section (Local Planner): "a user can make their choice to take partial or complete control"; user and global references are blended by a weight eta(i) (Eq. 12) and tracked by an MPC with discrete CBF constraints on pedestrian social areas.
method: Shared-control wheelchair navigation: user-preference-field A* global planner plus MPC-DCBF local planner with egg-shaped pedestrian social zones; user input blended into the MPC reference.
evaluation: Gazebo wheelchair twin, RVO2 pedestrians, 3 scenarios vs MPC, MPC-DCBF, socially-aware MPC; min distance 0.24-0.60 m, no collisions (baselines collide in 1-3); no latency reported.
contribution: Shared-control wheelchair navigation blends user commands into an MPC with discrete barrier constraints around pedestrians' social zones, avoiding collisions in three simulated crowd scenarios.
flag: Single robot among simulated pedestrians; CBF is a constraint inside the local planner, not a separate filter, and the paper does not say autonomy vetoes the user. (e) is weak: the human adds control at will, automation never defers, no takeover protocol or SA measure, no real participants - gap cell 'human handoff' is generous, drop it if strict. Eq. 13 eta(i)=1-e^i is negative for i>=1, contradicting eta in [0,1]. Dynamic results look like single runs per scenario; proposed method has the SMALLEST min distance in crossing (0.2411 m). Static-corridor numbers are only in Fig. 13. Simulation only; real-world test mentioned in Limitations without results.

title: Decentralized collision avoidance and global connectivity maintenance using nested control barrier functions
evidence: "The rationale for this QP formulation is to create a minimally invasive safety filter." (Section 3, after eq. 2)
method: Decentralised nested control barrier functions: prioritised sequence of QP safety filters (obstacle avoidance over inter-agent collision avoidance over global connectivity) modifying each desired velocity, using local Fiedler-value and neighbour-velocity estimators.
evaluation: 2D single-integrator simulations, 3 and 6 agents, three adversarial nominal controllers; distance and eigenvalue plots only. No baseline, no ablation, no rates, no timing, no hardware.
contribution: Nested control barrier functions give a decentralised, prioritised safety filter for collision avoidance and global connectivity in multi-robot teams, shown with proofs and small simulations.
flag: Borderline: a genuine runtime safety filter with multi-agent safety as primary claim, but evaluation fails the minimum bar - qualitative trajectory/distance plots, no quantitative collision or violation rate, no baseline or ablation (Remark 4.1 says results are 'similar to' non-smooth CBFs without showing any comparison). In the 6-agent example two agents settle closer than the inter-agent safety threshold (Fig. 20), which the authors attribute to obstacle avoidance taking priority - the collision constraint is not guaranteed under conflict. 'Suitable for real-time implementation' is asserted, not measured. Hardware (Robotarium) is future work. Data statement says no new data created. Text is the UNSWorks repository copy; cover sheet gives vol. 57 dated 2026-08-18 while article says published online 12 Nov 2025. Supplementary material and full proofs not checked.

title: An asymmetric allocation rule of constraints derived from control barrier function for collision avoidance between autonomous robots
venue: SICE Journal of Control, Measurement, and System Integration
evidence: "the QP-based controller that achieves collision avoidance can be interpreted as a filter for the input that does not consider collision avoidance" (Sec. 1 Introduction)
method: Distributed exponential-CBF QP safety filter for double-integrator robots; a new asymmetric rule splits each pairwise constraint so neither robot needs relative velocity; zero input is applied if the QP is infeasible.
evaluation: MATLAB simulation (2 robots, one immobile) and a 3-robot LiDAR line experiment vs symmetric CBF and a relative-velocity asymmetric CBF; inter-robot distance vs safety distance and QP feasibility over time. No latency or hardware specs.
contribution: Derives conditions for decoupling pairwise control-barrier-function constraints and proposes an asymmetric allocation needing no relative velocity, keeping distributed QP safety filters feasible where symmetric allocation fails and violates the safety distance.
flag: Borderline on minimum evaluation: the safety evidence is time-series plots from ONE simulated scenario and ONE hardware run per condition (baseline drops below r=1 in sim and violates r=0.4 m in the experiment; proposed rule does not). No collision or violation RATE, no repeated trials, no tabulated numbers; a strict reading would make this E2. Baselines are real (symmetric CBF in both; asymmetric-with-relative-velocity [18] in simulation only). The paper admits its own rule's feasibility index 'is not less than zero at most times' with 'slight moments' below zero attributed to actuators, and that the summed constraints can be stricter than the baselines (Fig. 6). Feasibility of the proposed rule is shown empirically, not proven in general; robots in the experiment move on a line only. Guarantee is theoretical (Theorem 4.1) under exact double-integrator dynamics. No compute time reported. Peer-reviewed journal (SICE JCMSI), open access.

title: A study on multi-warehouse robot path planning with an enhanced A* algorithm considering time window
evidence: "The experiments evaluate algorithm performance from two aspects: path quality and computational complexity." (Sec. 5.4)
method: Two-tier centralized MAPF: A* with distance-adaptive heuristic weight plus cubic B-spline smoothing, then priority-based time-window conflict decoupling (wait, detour, backtrack, local replan) for blocking, node and position conflicts.
evaluation: MATLAB grid simulation, Intel i7; 6, 20, 10-40 robots, maps to 100x100; vs A* variants and forward/reverse priority; path length, planning time (0.60 vs 0.93 s), node expansions.
contribution: Combines a weighted-heuristic A* with a time-window, priority-based conflict resolution layer to plan collision-free warehouse AGV paths, reporting shorter paths and fewer node expansions than forward/reverse priority planning.
flag: Offline MAPF planner: conflicts are resolved in the plan before execution, so not a runtime interceptor, and outcomes are path length, planning time and node expansions - efficiency/path quality, which the protocol names as E1. No collision or violation rate; success rate appears only as Figure 21 with no values in the text. Doubts: in Table 2 the proposed IA* expands more nodes (174 vs 53) and is slower (0.2397 s vs 0.1337 s) than the literature [11] baseline while the text claims a better balance; B-spline rows report average rotation 142 deg and Table 4 B-spline planning time totals 3.1217 s vs 0.0909 s initial, against the claim of reduced computational cost; text calls a 31 to 12 node change an increase. No kinematics, point-mass agents, simulation only. I read Table 5 only for the first rows.

title: HiRiSC: hierarchical risk-shaped coordination with sparse hypergraph communication for congested multi-agent path finding
evidence: NOT READ - no full text retrieved
method: NOT READ
evaluation: NOT READ
contribution: NOT READ - full text could not be retrieved, so no contribution statement is drafted.
flag: NOT READ, not excluded on merit. Tried the given pdf_url https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1361-6501/ae891d/pdf, the article page without /pdf and the /meta page (both constructed by me): all refused with robots_disallowed. OpenAlex lists no other location; a web search found no arXiv version (the hits were a different hypergraph MAPF paper, arXiv 2602.06733, not this one). All scores are placeholders. From the title alone this looks like a congestion-focused MAPF coordination paper that may fail the primacy test for (c), but that is a guess and must not be used as a decision. Needs a manual browser download.

title: PACNav: A collective navigation approach for UAV swarms deprived of communication and external localization
evidence: Command is the sum u = n + c of a navigation vector and a collision control vector; "The parallel component takes the UAV away from the obstacle, while the orthogonal component moves it tangentially" (Sec. 5, 5.2)
method: Decentralised communication-free UAV swarm navigation: uninformed UAVs pick a neighbour to follow by path persistence and similarity; reactive and preventive collision vectors are added to the navigation command.
evaluation: Gazebo forest, N=3 and N=6, 10 trials per case; one real flight with 4 quadrotors (Intel NUC i7-8559U); mean completion time 189.5-231.4 s; no baseline, no collision metric, no latency.
contribution: Shows a UAV swarm reaching a goal known to only some members without communication or GNSS, each UAV following the neighbour whose path is most persistent, validated in simulation and one forest flight.
flag: Collision avoidance is an additive reactive term in a navigation law, not a veto or filter, and the paper is about collective navigation, so (c) fails primacy. No quantitative safety metric at all (only the remark in Sec. 6.1 that minimum inter-UAV distance is sometimes slightly below R^o = 2.5 m) and no quantitative baseline; ablation is only number of informed UAVs. Real-world evidence is a single flight; swarm splits above six UAVs (Sec. 7.2). If judged on-topic it would fail minimum evaluation (E2) anyway.

title: Securing Agentic AI: A Comprehensive Threat Model and Mitigation Framework for Generative AI Agents
venue: International Conference on Algorithms, Computing and Artificial Intelligence (ACAI)
evidence: "The framework is primarily based on theoretical analysis, literature review, and expert consultation" (Sec. III.E, Limitations)
method: Conceptual threat model (ATFAA: 9 threats in 5 domains, mapped to STRIDE) and mitigation checklist (SHIELD: six strategies) for generative AI agents; nothing implemented.
evaluation: No experiments, benchmarks, baselines or numeric metrics; documented incidents, hypothetical case studies and qualitative feedback from 7 experts; qualitative risk labels only; no hardware or latency.
contribution: Proposes a nine-threat taxonomy and a six-part mitigation framework for agentic AI security, derived from literature and expert consultation without empirical validation.
flag: No evaluation of any kind; escalation control and multi-party approval are design suggestions only. Could arguably be E3 (literature-based conceptual paper). Topic touches (c) and (e) but with no measured outcome. arXiv version read, conference version may differ.

title: Gaussian Control Barrier Functions: Non-Parametric Paradigm to Safety
evidence: Sec. IV-C: "the QP constraint above ensures that the nominal control is followed as long as the safety condition is not violated."
method: Gaussian-process posterior (mean minus scaled variance) used as a non-parametric CBF, synthesised online from samples; a QP rectifies the nominal (joystick) command.
evaluation: Hardware: one Crazyflie 2.1, three scenarios (fixed sets, online obstacle synthesis, noisy states); baseline standard CBF in noise case; results as plots only. QP under 5 ms, filter 50 Hz, ground-station i7.
contribution: Gaussian-process control barrier functions synthesised online from data filter a quadrotor's commands on real hardware, with a QP solved in under 5 ms on a ground station.
flag: No numeric safety metric: violation by the standard-CBF baseline and safety of the Gaussian CBF are shown in trajectory plots, three flights per condition, no counts. Single quadrotor, static obstacles. Timing figures are reported (QP <5 ms, 500-sample synthesis 25 ms, 4 ms per added point) but there is no explicit latency constraint or deadline analysis, so I did not credit (d); the latency gap cell is generous. Compute is an off-board desktop, not edge. Paper text says 'more than 200 samples' while Fig. 5 caption says 'over 300'. A human supplies the nominal joystick input but there is no handoff study.

title: Toward Mid-Air Collision-Free Trajectory for Autonomous and Pilot-Controlled Unmanned Aerial Vehicles
evidence: Sec. III-B3/B4: for imminent risk autonomous manoeuvres are executed if the pilot did not act after warnings and 'to correct the pilot's operational errors'; autonomous drones are 'autonomously directed by the system'.
method: DACM: PilotAware traffic feed, Kalman smoothing, probable and imminent collision zones per flight; warns pilots, then autonomously steers the UAV on an evasive heading and returns it to route.
evaluation: Co-simulation with live traffic ('hundreds of tests', no counts) and five UK field tests with up to five built drones; no baseline; response time 2.5 s, processing 0.5 s, data delay about 1 s.
contribution: A ground-networked collision-management system warns UAV pilots of probable conflicts and overrides with autonomous evasive manoeuvres when collision is imminent, field-tested with heterogeneous drones and live air traffic.
flag: Fails minimum evaluation: no collision count, miss-distance statistics, success rate or intervention rate, and no baseline or ablation (only a with/without video pair). Numbers reported are design parameters and single-case figures (2.5 s total response vs 1.5 s target; 408.12 m and 322.25 m extra route). Pilot-override mechanism is asserted, not detailed. Warn-then-override is the reverse of automation deferring to a human, so (e) is loose. Paper's 'multi-agent explainable AI' wording has no learning component behind it. Inconsistent 5 s vs 12 s probable-collision horizon. arXiv title omits 'Mid-Air' but is the same paper. Last ~10k characters not read.

title: Risk-Aware Graph MAPPO with a Decoupled Safety Shield for Multi-Ship Collision Avoidance
venue: Proceedings - 2026 IEEE 27th China Conference on System Simulation Technology and its Applications, CCSSTA 2026
evidence: "The Default Safety Shield is an execution-time action correction layer. It monitors the policy action after it is generated and modifies it only when the current encounter is risky" (Sec. III-C)
method: Risk graph built from distance, DCPA and TCPA feeds a GNN actor in MAPPO (CTDE); a decoupled threshold shield blends or fully replaces the learned action at execution.
evaluation: Simplified 4-ship 2D simulator, 3 seed groups x 100 episodes; baselines rule-based controller and MAPPO-MLP plus shield ablation; CR 0.370 to 0.067, SR 0.087 to 0.220, NMR@60 0.067, ShieldStep 0.392, MinDist 97.7 m; no hardware or latency reported.
contribution: Shows that a risk-graph MAPPO actor plus a decoupled threshold shield cuts multi-ship collision rate from 0.370 to 0.067 over an unshielded MARL baseline, at some timeout cost.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - MAPPO graph policy is the guarded system. Check that the shield is an empirical threshold supervisor, not a verified shield (authors state this); the rule baseline still has lower CR (0.053 vs 0.067), so the gain is over MAPPO-MLP only; abstract figures match Tables II and III; 4 ships, simplified kinematics, no AIS data, no latency or hardware; prose refers to "the present manuscript" and "SCI-style reporting", suggesting reuse of a journal draft.

title: Optimal Control of Connected Automated Vehicles with Event-Triggered Control Barrier Functions: a Test Bed for Safe Optimal Merging
venue: IEEE Conference on Control Technology and Applications (CCTA)
evidence: Sec II (Eq 13-14): a QP tracks the unconstrained optimal reference control subject to rear-end and safe-merging CBF constraints; Sec V-B: 'the time-driven approach cannot guarantee safety due to uncertainties and imperfect measurements.'
method: OCBF: a CBF-QP minimally modifies each vehicle's optimal reference control; QPs are re-solved only on state-bound events, with constraints enforced robustly over the inter-event interval.
evaluation: Merging simulation plus mobile-robot test bed (5 and 2 robots, OptiTrack 30 Hz, on-board compute); vs time-driven QP; infeasible QPs 20-43 vs 315-341; QPs solved 34-50%.
contribution: Event-triggered CBF safety filtering for merging connected vehicles cuts infeasible QPs by up to 86% and QP solves by half or more versus time-driven control, validated on a multi-robot test bed.
flag: Safety metric in simulation is infeasible-QP count, not a collision or violation rate; actual constraint violation is shown only in test-bed plots (time-driven violates merging constraint in the 2-robot case, Fig 5). No wall-clock solve time or latency reported; edge credit rests on 'all computation ... performed on-board in a real-time manner' (Sec IV). Event-triggered travel time is slightly higher (15.53 vs 15.01). Text says QP reduction 'up to 50%' but Table I shows 34-50% of the time-driven count. Control period stated inconsistently (0.05 s vs 0.25 s). Simulation described as MATLAB-based yet using Python modules. Single merge point only.

title: Linear Model Predictive Safety Certification for Learning-Based Control
venue: IEEE Conference on Decision and Control (CDC)
evidence: Sec. I: the scheme 'only filters proposed inputs that drive the system out of what we call the safe set', and Algorithm 1 otherwise applies 'the previously calculated backup controller from time k' (Sec. III).
method: Linear MPC safety certification: an online filter between a learning-based input and the plant; it admits the input only if a backup trajectory to a terminal safe set stays feasible.
evaluation: Simulation only, mass-spring-damper with 20% model error, 600 samples; qualitative baseline (unfiltered learning violates constraints in the first steps); no violation counts, no solve times, no hardware.
contribution: An MPC-based safety certification filter that admits a learning-based control input only when a backup trajectory to a robust terminal safe set remains feasible, with proved constraint satisfaction.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - a generic learning-based controller u_L. Check the evaluation floor: there is NO quantitative safety metric and no ablation, the only baseline being a qualitative figure, so inclusion rests entirely on the proved guarantees (Prop. IV.1, Thm IV.2, Cor. IV.4) under the 'or a proved guarantee' clause. Single-agent; no latency measured despite the real-time claim in Sec. I; human input is mentioned only in a footnote, so no (e). Most likely overturn in this batch alongside record 5.

title: An Efficient Reachability-Based Framework for Provably Safe Autonomous Navigation in Unknown Environments
venue: IEEE Conference on Decision and Control (CDC)
evidence: Sec. VI-A: the switching law of Eq. (10) executes the planner control inside the safe set and applies the reachability safety controller otherwise, a least restrictive filter acting 'except when the system is at the risk of violating safety'.
method: Hamilton-Jacobi reachability safety layer with warm-started and local value-function updates; a least-restrictive switching law applies the safety controller whenever the state leaves the recomputed safe set.
evaluation: Dubins-car sim plus TurtleBot 2; ablations HJI-VI vs warm-start vs local update: BRS update 45.7s vs 26.3s vs 0.6s, over-conservative states 0%-1.1%; collisions qualitative; MATLAB, i7-5820K.
contribution: A reachability-based safety layer that updates the backward reachable set online from newly sensed free space, cutting safety-computation time about 40x while overriding planner commands at the safe-set boundary.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes, but only partly - one nominal planner is the CNN vision-based planner of [7] (it collides with a door without the layer), the others are classical RRT and spline planners, so the learned-system condition rests on that single experiment. The quantitative results are compute time and over-conservative-state percentage; collision avoidance is shown qualitatively only, with no collision count, in both sim and the TurtleBot chair experiment. Criterion (d) is arguable: compute time is measured and real-time safe-set updating is the stated goal, but no explicit deadline or latency budget is given and compute ran on a desktop i7, so I claimed latency/jitter aware but not edge deployment. Single agent and static environments by the authors own admission; multi-agent is future work.

title: Safe Control Design Through Risk-Tunable Control Barrier Functions
venue: IEEE Conference on Decision and Control (CDC)
evidence: The approach "directly solves a chance-constrained problem to optimize performance metrics" and avoids "a two-stage solution" (Sec. I-A)
method: Scenario-based chance-constrained controller with sampled uncertain CBF constraints; sample-size bound links number of scenarios to a tunable risk level and confidence. Control computed directly, no nominal action filtered.
evaluation: Simulation only: one quadcopter avoiding one obstacle with uncertain position; trajectories across risk levels; sample counts 216 to 39618; no measured violation rate, no baseline, no timing.
contribution: Designs a controller whose control-barrier constraints hold with a user-tunable risk bound by sampling uncertainty scenarios, with a bound on the samples needed.
flag: Not a runtime interceptor by the authors' own framing: they contrast with projection-style filters and solve for the input directly, so (a) fails; also single-agent (E4 would apply). 'Under 5%' risk is a design target (epsilon 0.05), not a measured rate. No baseline simulated. The fetch tool noted Table I sample counts (216, 484, 3045, 39618) do not appear to match the Theorem 3.6 formula as printed - unverified by me, worth a glance only if the paper were kept.

title: Multi-Agent Reach-Avoid Games: Two Attackers Versus One Defender and Mixed Integer Programming
venue: IEEE Conference on Decision and Control (CDC)
evidence: Abstract: "determining the defender assignments that can maximize the number of attackers captured via a Mixed Integer Program"
method: Hamilton-Jacobi reach-avoid tubes (4D 1-vs-1, 6D 2-vs-1) precomputed offline; a mixed integer program re-solved each step assigns each defender up to two attackers.
evaluation: Simulation only: 2v1, 6v2, 8v4 games vs maximum-matching baseline; attackers captured 2/6/8 vs 1/4/6. 6D tube 1.5 h, 20 GB on i9-9900K; online MIP time unreported.
contribution: Extends multi-agent reach-avoid game solutions by combining two-attacker-one-defender Hamilton-Jacobi reachability with mixed-integer defender assignment, capturing more attackers than maximum matching in simulation.
flag: Pursuit-evasion assignment, not a safety mechanism: nothing vetoes or filters a nominal action and the outcome is capture count, not a hazard rate. Table I counts appear to be single simulated runs with no variance. Attackers use a suboptimal shortest-path policy. No hardware, no human.

title: Out of Distribution Detection via Domain-Informed Gaussian Process State Space Models
venue: IEEE Conference on Decision and Control (CDC)
evidence: Sec I: 'Our approach monitors OoD in real-time, which is crucial for decision-making in safety-critical situations'
method: Gaussian process state-space model with domain-informed kernel features; receding-horizon rollouts (H=30, R=20) yield a normalised OoD loss, flagged when above 0.5.
evaluation: Real Unitree Go1, VICON; walking vs rope/rocky/poking; flagged steps 1.8/66.7/64.4/79.0% vs Matern GPSSM 87/92.5/98.7/97.3%; RMSE table vs SE and Matern; laptop, no latency measured.
contribution: Domain-informed GP state-space model that flags out-of-distribution dynamics on a quadruped in real time, with far fewer false alarms in nominal walking than a standard-kernel GPSSM.
flag: Borderline (a): a runtime monitor that only flags; no halt/override/fallback is implemented (MPC integration is future work), so strict runtime test fails. Single robot. Threshold applied after offline normalisation. Table II RMSE values are negative (likely log scale, unclear). No AUROC or latency. E1 also arguable.

title: Auxiliary- Variable Adaptive Control Barrier Functions for Safety Critical Systems
venue: IEEE Conference on Decision and Control (CDC)
evidence: Sec. V: 'We utilized ode45 to integrate the dynamic system for every 0.1s time-interval and quadprog to solve QP' - the QP is a CLF-CBF optimal controller with its own cost, not a filter on a nominal action.
method: Auxiliary-variable adaptive CBFs: each barrier function is multiplied by a positive auxiliary variable with its own dynamics, improving feasibility of the CLF-CBF-QP under tight control bounds.
evaluation: MATLAB simulation of adaptive cruise control with time-varying braking bounds; baseline penalty-based adaptive CBFs (PACBF); hyperparameter sweeps; results qualitative, no numeric safety or timing metric.
contribution: An adaptive control barrier function formulation that keeps the safety-constrained controller feasible under tight input limits, demonstrated qualitatively on simulated adaptive cruise control.
flag: Borderline (a): safety is a constraint inside the controller QP (cost is squared acceleration plus relaxation penalties, no nominal input to override), which I read as not meeting the strict runtime test. If the maintainer counts it as (a), it would still fail on evaluation (E2): no quantitative metric, feasibility and overshoot claims are from Figs. 1-3; one infeasibility time of 25.3 s is reported. Single-agent, simulation only.

title: Multi-Step Model Predictive Safety Filters: Reducing Chattering by Increasing the Prediction Horizon
venue: IEEE Conference on Decision and Control (CDC)
evidence: Sec. V-A: "Note that our proposed formulation generalizes the one-step MPSF, which is recovered by setting M=1." - a robust-MPC safety filter that replaces the uncertified controller's input with a certified one at each step.
method: Multi-step model predictive safety filter: minimises the gap between proposed and certified inputs over M future steps, simulating the uncertified controller on the nominal model; recursive feasibility inherited from robust MPC.
evaluation: Cartpole in safe-control-gym (LQR, PPO, SAC; 15 Hz) and Crazyflie 2.0 hardware; vs one-step MPSF and input-rate regularisation. Hardware M=10: input rate 30.26 to 6.18 m/s, max correction 0.46 to 0.30 m.
contribution: Extending a predictive safety filter's objective over several future steps cut chattering about 80% on a real quadrotor versus the one-step filter, at up to 60% extra solve time.
flag: Single-agent filter; included on (a) with intervention metrics (number and magnitude of corrections) and a baseline. Hardware constraint-violation counts are NOT reported; sim only says 'without violating the constraints'. Number of corrections RISES with M on hardware (76 one-step vs 194.2 at M=10) though magnitude falls - check against RQ5 false-halt framing. Latency cell is weak: only relative solve-time increases (7/22/60% for M=2/5/10), no absolute ms; drop the cell if strict. Abstract 'more than a factor of 4' matches 30.26 vs 6.18 and 16.3 cm vs 3.6 cm peak-to-peak. Authors say unsuitable for human teleoperation.

title: Robust Control Barrier Functions for Safe Control Under Uncertainty Using Extended State Observer and Output Measurement
venue: IEEE Conference on Decision and Control (CDC)
evidence: Sec. III-B, Eq. 26: the ESOR-QP picks u minimising ||u - k(x_hat)||^2 subject to the robust CBF condition, so that 'the safety is still guaranteed in the presence of disturbance and state estimation errors'.
method: Robust CBF-QP safety filter using an extended state observer to estimate states and total disturbance from output measurements; estimation-error bounds enter the constraint as a robustness margin.
evaluation: Simulation only: adaptive cruise control and Segway under sinusoidal disturbances; baselines true-d-QP, aR-QP, DOB-CLF-CBF-QP, nominal CBF-QP; results are plots only, no numeric safety metric, no timing.
contribution: An observer-based robust control barrier function filter that keeps a single disturbed system safe from output measurements alone, shown only qualitatively in two simulations.
flag: Runtime filter and baselines are present, but no quantitative safety metric: conservativeness claims ('aR-QP is the most conservative') rest on Figs. 1-4 only. Single-agent, no hardware, no latency figure (only sample time 1e-4 s). The abstract claim of a less conservative error bound is not backed by a number in the body. Could also be argued E4.

title: Robust Control Barrier Functions for Nonlinear Control Systems with Uncertainty: A Duality-based Approach
venue: IEEE Conference on Decision and Control (CDC)
evidence: Sec. IV-A, Eq. 11: QP minimises 0.5||u - k_d(x)||^2 subject to the robust barrier condition; footnote 2: 'in practice better performance is achieved by filtering the RCLF policy through the RCBF QP'.
method: Robust CBF/CLF for control-affine systems with parametric uncertainty; LP duality yields a QP safety filter on a nominal policy, with online integral set-membership identification shrinking the uncertainty set.
evaluation: Two numerical simulations (2D nonlinear system; double integrator avoiding a circular obstacle); set-membership identification on versus off, plus exact-model CBF-QP reference; trajectory plots only, no numbers, hardware or timing.
contribution: Formulates robust control barrier and Lyapunov functions under parametric uncertainty as a duality-based QP safety filter and reduces conservatism with online set-membership identification, shown on two simulated examples.
flag: It is a genuine runtime safety filter, so (a) is met in form, but the evaluation is qualitative: Figs. 1-4 trajectories, no violation or intervention rate, no trial counts, no computation time. Only quantitative-style statement is that control effort without identification is 'an order of magnitude higher' in the first second. Also single-agent with no multi-agent, sequential, latency or handoff aspect, so E4 applies equally; maintainer may prefer E4.

title: Safe Hierarchical Navigation in Crowded Dynamic Uncertain Environments
venue: IEEE Conference on Decision and Control (CDC)
evidence: The low-level Safe Set Algorithm "monitors and modifies the unsafe control during trajectory tracking" (Abstract); "SSA modifies these unreasonable tracking controls online" (Sec. IV-B)
method: Hierarchical navigation (H-DAGap): dynamic gap planner with probabilistic safety margin, CFS trajectory optimiser, and a Safe Set Algorithm projecting each tracking control onto the safe control set every step.
evaluation: 2D simulation, unicycle among 20 and 50 moving agents, 100 runs; ablation and ARENA, DRRT-ProbLP baselines; collision 0% and 3% with SSA versus 8% and 29% without; SSA 0.69 ms.
contribution: Adding a per-step safe-set control filter beneath a gap-based planner cut simulated collisions among 20 and 50 moving agents from 8% and 29% to 0% and 3%.
flag: Single controlled robot; the other agents are non-reactive constant-velocity obstacles (no agent-agent collisions modelled), so multi-agent is nominal and I left gap cell multi-agent state empty - (c) not claimed. Inclusion rests on (a) via the ablation DAGap+CFS versus DAGap+CFS+SSA (Table II). Baseline numbers for ARENA (23.7% collision) and DRRT-ProbLP (4%) are taken from their own papers under different success definitions, not re-run. Average compute times DAGap 81.4 ms, CFS 112 ms, SSA 0.685 ms on a 3.7 GHz Core i7 desktop in Python; reported, but no latency constraint is stated so (d) not credited. No hardware. Safety guarantee assumes constant velocity and Gaussian estimation error.

title: Predictive Control Barrier Functions for Online Safety Critical Control
venue: IEEE Conference on Decision and Control (CDC)
evidence: Controller "will modify the nominal trajectory before the trajectory becomes unsafe" (Abstract); Eq. 22 picks the input closest to nominal satisfying the predictive CBF condition.
method: Predictive CBF: propagates the nominal trajectory over a receding horizon, finds the future minimum of safety margin and time until unsafe, and filters the input early and minimally.
evaluation: Sim only: two-car intersection and satellite vs debris. Baselines ECBF, nonlinear MPC. Compute per step ECBF 0.0034 s, PCBF 0.050 s, MPC 0.98 s on 2.6 GHz laptop CPU.
contribution: A predictive barrier-function filter that uses the forecast time until a nominal trajectory becomes unsafe to intervene early, costing 0.050 s per step versus 0.98 s for MPC in simulation.
flag: BORDERLINE on minimum evaluation: baselines exist but there is no collision or violation rate; quantitative evidence is compute time and "over 10 times as much thrust" for ECBF in the satellite case; intersection outcome (ECBF deadlocks, PCBF passes) is qualitative. Could be E2. Multi-agent only nominally (two cars, centralised; distributed is future work) so multi-agent state not credited. Time-to-irreversibility credited loosely for root R (time until unsafe), no formal irreversibility. Latency credited only for reported solve times; 50 ms is not sub-15 ms and not edge hardware. No input-constraint guarantee. Simulation only.

title: Compatibility checking of multiple control barrier functions for input constrained systems
venue: IEEE Conference on Decision and Control (CDC)
evidence: Sec. II: 'The compatibility verification algorithm only needs to be executed once and offline, before applying' the CBF-based controller.
method: Offline grid-sampling and refinement algorithm that verifies or falsifies compatibility of multiple control barrier functions under input constraints over the safe region, using Lipschitz bounds on n-cubes.
evaluation: Three 2-D numerical examples in Matlab on an i7-8650U laptop; no baseline; offline run times 169 s, 23 s, 73 s; no online QP latency, no violation rate.
contribution: Gives an offline lattice-based check that several control barrier functions stay jointly feasible under input bounds, certifying compatibility or returning an incompatible state.
flag: Design-time verification of a safety filter, not a runtime mechanism; 'multiple' means multiple CBFs on one system, not multiple agents. No baseline and no safety rate, so E2 would also apply. Only 2-D examples; authors concede poor scaling with dimension.

title: Robust Safe Control Synthesis with Disturbance Observer-Based Control Barrier Functions
venue: IEEE Conference on Decision and Control (CDC)
evidence: Sec. III (close paraphrase): the QP objective is set to modify the desired feedback control input minimally, subject to the robust CBF constraint built from the disturbance estimate and its error bound.
method: High-gain disturbance observer estimates the uncertain term in the CBF derivative; estimate and error bound tighten a CLF-CBF-QP that minimally modifies the nominal controller.
evaluation: Simulation only: adaptive cruise control and Segway. Baselines nominal CLF-CBF-QP and ISSf-CBF-QP. Results read from plots; no numeric safety rate, latency or hardware.
contribution: A disturbance-observer-based robust CBF quadratic program that filters a nominal controller, shown in cruise-control and Segway simulations to stay safe where a nominal CBF-QP violates the constraint.
flag: Runtime safety filter, but single-agent and the evidence is plots only: no tabulated violation or intervention rate, so minimum evaluation fails (E4 also applies). No latency, hardware or human role. Evidence is a paraphrase, not verbatim. Read via one summarised fetch of the PDF.

title: Explicit Solutions for Safety Problems Using Control Barrier Functions
venue: IEEE Conference on Decision and Control (CDC)
evidence: Abstract: the aim is to 'transform the online quadratic programming problem into an offline parameterized optimisation problem'; Sec. III-A: QP minimises the distance to a nominal u_des subject to the CBF constraint and input limits.
method: Multi-parametric (explicit) solution of the CBF-QP safety filter: state space partitioned into critical regions with a closed-form filter law each; adaptive relaxed CBF-QP for infeasible states.
evaluation: One 2-state linear numerical example, simulation only; standard CBF-QP gives 7 critical regions (one infeasible), adaptive gives 10; no baseline, no solve times, no hardware.
contribution: An explicit, offline-computed form of the CBF quadratic-program safety filter that replaces online optimisation with a region lookup, illustrated on one two-state example without timing or safety-rate results.
flag: Mechanism is a genuine runtime filter over a nominal controller, but evaluation is a single illustrative example with no safety metric, no baseline against online QP and no timing, despite the embedded-latency motivation in the Introduction. Single system, so E4 also applies. The example concludes the chosen B(x) is not a valid CBF under input limits.

title: Path Integral Methods with Stochastic Control Barrier Functions
venue: IEEE Conference on Decision and Control (CDC)
evidence: Sec. III.C: the SCBF constraints 'are no longer used as a safe filter for the control input'; they shape the sampling distribution instead.
method: MPPI variant that solves an SDP per step for a safe mean and covariance under stochastic control barrier function chance constraints, then samples control perturbations from that distribution.
evaluation: Simulated 2-D unicycle in a narrow passage, 10 runs; baseline MPPI; collision rate 0.0454 and 0.0294 versus 0.0; time steps to goal 140.4 and 129.6 versus 163.6 and 156.1; no timing.
contribution: Embeds stochastic control barrier functions in the MPPI sampling distribution so sampled trajectories stay safe with fewer samples, at the cost of slower goal reaching.
flag: Authors state explicitly that the barrier is not used as a safety filter, so this is a constraint inside the planner and fails strict (a); single agent. Ten runs, no variance. Table II sample sizes (1476/2973 versus 1476/584) are theoretical bounds, not measurements. No wall-clock cost for the per-step SDP; Algorithm 1 appears to place the SDP inside the per-sample loop, contradicting the text. High-relative-degree extension is untested.

title: Safety of Sampled-Data Systems with Control Barrier Functions via Approximate Discrete Time Models
venue: IEEE Conference on Decision and Control (CDC)
evidence: Sec. V: "These distances decrease for sufficiently small sample periods." (worst-case distance from the safe set under the SD-CBF filter).
method: A sampled-data CBF program designed on Runge-Kutta approximate discrete-time models returns the input closest to a nominal controller; proves practical safety of the exact sampled system and convexity for block integrators.
evaluation: Simulated single and double inverted pendulums, 11 sample periods (0.05-0.5 s and 0.01-0.1 s), 500 initial conditions; no baseline or ablation; worst-case safe-set distance plotted, no values; no hardware or timing.
contribution: Sampled-data control barrier functions built on approximate discrete-time models give practical safety guarantees for the exact sampled system, shown on simulated pendulums across sample periods.
flag: Title matches. Single-agent, single-system safety filter with no multi-agent, sequential, latency-constraint or handoff aspect, hence E4; E2 also applies (no baseline or ablation, and the violation metric is given only as a figure with no numbers). Sample period is a design parameter here, not a latency/jitter budget, so I did not credit that cell. Safety holds at sample times only. Abstract has no numbers. Drafted from model-summarised PDF reads.

title: Feasibility-Guaranteed Safety-Critical Control with Applications to Heterogeneous Platoons
venue: IEEE Conference on Decision and Control (CDC)
evidence: "We define a feasibility constraint and propose a new type of CBF to enforce it." (Abstract)
method: HOCBF-CLF-QP controller with an added feasibility constraint enforced by an auxiliary-variable CBF so the QP stays feasible under tight control bounds; decentralized per follower vehicle.
evaluation: MATLAB simulation, 3-vehicle heterogeneous platoon, 30 s; baseline same QP without feasibility constraint: infeasible at 5 instants (case 1), safe distance violated at 18.7 s and 22.9 s (case 2); no timing.
contribution: Adds a feasibility constraint, itself enforced by a control barrier function, so that CBF-CLF quadratic programs for heterogeneous vehicle platoons stay solvable under tight control bounds.
flag: Borderline (c): platoon spacing safety is shown against a no-feasibility baseline, but the primary claim is QP feasibility, and results are two single runs (instants of infeasibility/violation), not rates. The QP is the controller itself, not a filter on a nominal input (lead vehicle uses a prescribed input). Feasibility argument rests on Assumption 1 (sign of control coefficients). Parameter list labels 0.4/0.35 inconsistently. No hardware, no latency, no communication model. Smoother-control/optimality claim is qualitative only.

title: Risk-Aware Robot Control in Dynamic Environments Using Belief Control Barrier Functions
venue: IEEE Conference on Decision and Control (CDC)
evidence: CBF quadratic program minimises deviation from the reference input subject to a stochastic CBF condition on a sample-based VaR/CVaR lower bound of the safety function (Sec. IV-D, Eq. 14, paraphrase)
method: Belief control barrier function: sample-based lower bound on VaR/CVaR of a safety function over an obstacle belief, with a KS-distance robust variant, enforced by a CBF-QP safety filter.
evaluation: Simulated AUV unicycle avoiding one moving object, 100 runs per row; VaR 1-3 collisions vs expected-value 54-72; robust 1 vs 11 under shift; 0.67-1.59 ms per step on i7 laptop.
contribution: A belief-space control barrier function filter bounds tail risk of collision from obstacle belief samples, reducing collisions from 54-72 to 1-3 per 100 runs at about 1 kHz in simulation.
flag: Single robot and single moving object, simulation only, no hardware despite the robot framing. Baselines are the authors' own variants (expected value, non-robust); no external method compared. The abstract's 'approximately 1 kHz' matches Table I only loosely (0.67-1.59 ms, about 0.6-1.5 kHz) and is measured on a laptop CPU, not edge hardware; no explicit deadline is stated, so (d) and the latency/jitter aware cell were not credited - maintainer may disagree. CVaR variant trades collisions for 5-10 timeouts per 100. Theorem 2 assumes QP feasibility.

title: Safe Navigation in Unmapped Environments for Robotic Systems with Input Constraints
venue: IEEE Conference on Decision and Control (CDC)
evidence: Sec. VII: "Figure 3 shows v deviates from v_d in order to satisfy safety."
method: Closed-form minimum-deviation control from a soft-min/soft-max composite relaxed CBF built from recent LiDAR scans, with input limits enforced via added controller dynamics.
evaluation: Simulation only: one nonholonomic ground robot, static unmapped map, three goals; control 100 Hz, perception 0.2 s. No baseline, no ablation, no numeric safety metric, no hardware.
contribution: A closed-form CBF safety filter that keeps a single ground robot clear of LiDAR-detected unmapped obstacles under input and speed limits, shown in one simulated environment.
flag: Runtime filter is genuine but evidence is qualitative plots only: no collision or violation rate, no baseline or ablation (fails minimum evaluation). Also single-agent with static obstacles, so E4 would be equally defensible. No solve time reported, only the 100 Hz update rate. Read via summarised fetch of arXiv PDF; CDC version not checked.

title: Safe Adaptive Cruise Control Under Perception Uncertainty: A Deep Ensemble and Conformal Tube Model Predictive Control Approach
venue: IEEE Conference on Decision and Control (CDC)
evidence: "An adaptive cruise controller using Conformal Tube Model Predictive Control is designed to ensure probabilistic safety." (Abstract); safety constraints are applied to the tube inside the MPC QP (Sec. 3.3).
method: Pruned deep-ensemble camera perception estimates headway with variance; split conformal prediction turns it into a tube; a tube MPC QP enforces headway constraints, with a_min fallback when the tube is empty.
evaluation: CARLA Town06: in-distribution, FGSM and weather OOD perception tests; one closed-loop ACC run. No baselines; no collision rate. Perception 13.7 ms, QP 0.062 ms on RTX 4080/i9-13900F.
contribution: Adaptive cruise control combining a pruned deep-ensemble perception module, conformal prediction and tube MPC to give probabilistic headway safety under perception uncertainty, shown in CARLA.
flag: Single ego vehicle following one lead; safety is a constraint inside the MPC so (a) fails. Remark 4 fallback (a_k = a_min when q-hat < 0) is an emergency-braking rule but is not evaluated separately. Would also fail minimum evaluation (E2): no collision/violation rate, no baseline, single closed-loop run, no empirical coverage number in text. Timing figures are desktop GPU, with no stated latency constraint, so (d) not met. Maintainer may prefer E4 or E2.

title: Recurrent Control Barrier Functions: A Path Towards Nonparametric Safety Verification
venue: IEEE Conference on Decision and Control (CDC)
evidence: Sec VII: 'Simulations demonstrate provably safe, though over-approximated, sets with competitive computational performance.'
method: Recurrent control barrier functions relax invariance to return-within-tau; a sampling-based cell-partition algorithm labels states safe or unsafe offline, without a parametric certificate.
evaluation: Simulated 3D evasion problem; vs Hamilton-Jacobi BRT: unsafe volume captured 1.0 at all grids vs 0.51-1.0; compute 19.75 s vs 83.73 s at finest grid; hardware unspecified.
contribution: Recurrence-based relaxation of barrier functions enabling nonparametric, sampling-based offline computation of safe sets, faster than Hamilton-Jacobi reachability at fine resolution on an evasion example.
flag: Offline safe-set verification only; no runtime filter is built or evaluated. Evasion example involves a pursuer only nominally (relative coordinates). Table II caption says alpha=1 while text says alpha=beta=0.05. HJ value of 1 at finest grid is the reference itself.

title: Dynamic Log-Gaussian Process Control Barrier Function for Safe Robotic Navigation in Dynamic Environments
venue: IEEE Conference on Decision and Control (CDC)
evidence: Sec. III-C: QP minimising ||u - u_nom(t)||^2 subject to the CBF condition, i.e. the filter minimally modifies a nominal go-to-goal control (closely paraphrased).
method: Log-transformed Gaussian-process barrier built online from LiDAR occupancy, with Kalman-tracked obstacle velocities in the time derivative; CBF-QP filters a nominal controller for a unicycle robot.
evaluation: TurtleBot3 in Gazebo, static and dynamic obstacles, single run; baselines GP-CBF, MPC-DCBF; min distance 0.346 vs 0.161/0.129 m; arrival 30.5 vs 33.8/33.9 s; inference about 21 ms; hardware unstated.
contribution: A log-Gaussian-process barrier function learned online from LiDAR and obstacle-velocity estimates filters a nominal controller, keeping a larger clearance than two CBF baselines in one simulated dynamic-obstacle run.
flag: Genuine runtime CBF-QP safety filter, but evaluation is a single simulated run: no collision, violation or intervention rate, all methods collision-free, only minimum distance. Judged below the minimum evaluation; maintainer may prefer include if min distance vs baselines is accepted as a safety metric, or E4 (single robot, obstacles not agents). No ablation of log transform or velocity term. 21 ms figure has no hardware. QP infeasibility not handled. Title matches except hyphenation.

title: Distributed Safety-Critical MPC for Multi-Agent Formation Control and Obstacle Avoidance
venue: IEEE Conference on Decision and Control (CDC)
evidence: Sec III: 'we will replace (10c) with (18) and treat it as a safety constraint' - the discrete high-order CBF is a constraint inside each agent's MPC problem.
method: Distributed MPC for formation control with a discrete-time high-order CBF constraint for obstacle avoidance, a terminal CLF constraint and a neighbor-estimate compatibility constraint.
evaluation: Simulation, 3 vehicles, one obstacle; vs MPC-DC, NC-CBF, CLF-CBF; min obstacle distance 0.046-0.251 vs 0.000; solve time 0.289-0.577 s vs 1.29-1.45 s; no hardware stated.
contribution: Embeds discrete high-order CBF constraints in distributed MPC so a three-vehicle formation avoids an obstacle with shorter horizons and lower solve time than distance-constrained MPC.
flag: Safety is a constraint inside the planner, so (a) fails by the strict-runtime rule. Hazard measured is a static obstacle, not inter-agent collision, and the paper is as much about formation and compute time, so (c) primacy is doubtful. Single 3-vehicle scenario. Reported solve times (0.29-0.58 s) exceed the 0.1 sampling time and the paper does not address this. gamma stated as 0.1 in text but Table I also uses 0.4 and 0.8. Baseline min distance 0.000 is not explicitly called a collision.

title: TrafficSim: Learning to Simulate Realistic Multi-Agent Behaviors
venue: IEEE Computer Society Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition/Proceedings - IEEE Computer Society Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition/Proceedings
evidence: Sec. 3.2: an implicit latent variable model whose graph neural network scene interaction module over a fully connected actor graph parameterises prior, posterior and decoder, outputting a T_plan-step joint plan for all actors.
method: Implicit latent variable model over a fully connected actor graph; a GNN decoder samples a scene-level latent and rolls out joint multi-agent plans, re-planning every few simulation steps.
evaluation: ATG4D, 6500 25s snippets; baselines IDM, MTP, ESP, ILVM, AdversarialIL, DataAug; minSADE 0.57 vs 1.19-3.03, scenario collision rate 0.50% vs 1.19-11.0%; ablations M0-M3; 0.24-0.83s on GTX 1080 Ti.
contribution: A latent variable generative model over an actor interaction graph that simulates joint traffic behaviour, reaching 0.50% scenario collision rate and lower reconstruction error than motion-forecasting and imitation baselines.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: n/a - nothing is guarded. Included under (b) as latent prediction of future state over a multi-agent graph with direct predictive measures (minSFDE 1.13, minSADE 0.57) and M0-M3 ablations; RQ5 capped at 2 per the (b) rule and no prevention credited. (c) fails the primacy test: the primary claim is simulation realism, SCR is one of seven metrics, and traffic-rule violation is far worse than the IDM heuristic (2.77% vs 0.25%, ground truth 1.26%) while the text calls it 'similar'. Borderline (a) the maintainer may want to credit: the Sec. 4.2 simulation-time rejection sampling and latent gradient optimisation do discard colliding sampled plans before they are applied (SCR 0.50 to 0.33 to 0.12%, Table 5), but this is a scenario-authoring utility inside a simulator rather than interception of an acting system, so runtime_interceptor is no. The claimed 4x speedup is about 3.5x by Table 4 (0.83s to 0.24s), the runtime figure is not defined as per-tick or per-rollout, and the appendix defines SADE-SFDE with squared norms while the tables are labelled in metres.

title: Generating Useful Accident-Prone Driving Scenarios via a Learned Traffic Prior
venue: IEEE Computer Society Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition/Proceedings - IEEE Computer Society Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition/Proceedings
evidence: Sec. 3.1-3.2: a graph-based conditional VAE traffic prior predicting all agents future trajectories is optimised adversarially in its latent space to produce collision scenarios that stay plausible and solvable.
method: STRIVE: a graph-based CVAE traffic prior; adversarial optimisation in its latent space makes other agents collide with a fixed planner, then a solution optimisation recovers an avoidable variant.
evaluation: nuScenes, 1200 8s sequences; vs Bicycle baseline and regular scenes: collision 27.4% vs 1.2%; ADE-FDE 1.75-3.57 vs AgentFormer 1.45-2.86; ablations; planner retuning 68.6% to 54.3%; Titan RTX, 6-7min per scenario.
contribution: STRIVE generates plausible, solvable accident-prone traffic scenarios by adversarial optimisation inside a learned graph-based traffic prior, then uses them to retune a planner and cut its collision rate on challenging scenes.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: n/a at runtime - the planner adversarially attacked is rule-based, and the only online element is a learned classifier switching that planner between two hyperparameter sets from the past 2s of traffic, which adapts but cannot override or halt, so (a) fails and runtime_interceptor is no. I credited (c) because collision rate is the headline measured outcome against regular nuScenes scenes (1.2%) and the Bicycle baseline, but this is hazard GENERATION rather than hazard detection and the maintainer may read the primacy test differently. RQ5 scored 3 on the 68.6% to 54.3% challenging-scene improvement with the regular-scene rate unchanged at 4.6%; the (b) rule would cap it at 2 and that cap's stated rationale (no hazard rate exists to report) does not apply here, so please settle it. Offline only, 6-7 minutes per 10-agent scenario, no onboard or latency figures, driving domain only.

title: Spotting the Unexpected (STU): A 3D LiDAR Dataset for Anomaly Segmentation in Autonomous Driving
venue: IEEE Computer Society Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition/Proceedings - IEEE Computer Society Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition/Proceedings
evidence: Sec. 4.1: "directly transferring methods from 2D to 3D does not yield similar performance" - the paper is a dataset and offline benchmark; anomaly scores are only evaluated, never used to act.
method: Real-world 3D LiDAR dataset (70 anomaly sequences, staged and naturalistic road debris) with point- and instance-level labels for out-of-distribution segmentation; adapts five uncertainty baselines to Mask4Former-3D.
evaluation: Offline, single-scan, within 50 m. Deep Ensemble best: AUROC 86.74, FPR@95 58.05, AP 5.17, PQ 8.81 (test); MC Dropout, MaxLogit, Void Classifier, RbA compared. No latency reported.
contribution: A 128-beam LiDAR road-anomaly segmentation benchmark showing that 2D anomaly detectors transfer poorly to 3D, with the best baseline reaching only 5.17 AP on the test set.
flag: Perception benchmark only: single ego vehicle, no acting system, no runtime override, no multi-agent hazard, no latency figures (recording rig was NVIDIA DRIVE Pegasus, but no inference timing). Possibly useful as background on OOD hazard detection; AP falls to 0.03 at 40-50 m.

title: Anomaly Detection in Autonomous Driving: A Survey
venue: IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition Workshops (CVPRW)
evidence: "This survey provides an extensive overview of anomaly detection techniques" (Abstract)
method: Survey of anomaly detection for autonomous driving across camera, lidar, radar, multimodal and object-level data, grouped into confidence, reconstruction, generative, prediction and feature-extraction approaches.
evaluation: No original experiments; tabulates cited methods by modality, corner-case level and online capability (online if reported so or above 10 FPS).
contribution: Surveys anomaly detection techniques for autonomous driving across sensor modalities and corner-case levels, noting which methods are online capable.
flag: Survey with no new method or evaluation. Possibly useful as background for snowballing; frame rates quoted (e.g. 11.11 FPS, 18.4 FPS) are from cited works, not measured by the authors.

title: Remote ID for separation provision and multi-agent navigation
evidence: Sec. V: "Each UAV then solves this constraint reactively for collision avoidance in multi-agent scenarios", with safety-disk size set from Remote ID position, velocity, localisation error and airframe size.
method: Separation (safety disk) definitions built from Remote ID fields - reported localisation error and airframe size - fed to reciprocal velocity obstacle navigation for UAV conflict resolution.
evaluation: MATLAB sim, 8-UAV circle and 24-UAV square with obstacle, 500 runs each; sNMAC, standard Remote ID baselines; sNMAC collision probability 4.3%; completion 6.9 vs 11.3 s, 22.2 vs 50.8 s.
contribution: Remote ID fields carrying localisation error and airframe size let velocity-obstacle navigation shrink separation disks, roughly halving mission time in the denser scenario while remaining collision-free.
flag: Borderline (c): safety framing, but the measured outcome is mission completion time; the only collision figure is 4.3% for the sNMAC baseline, with 'guaranteed collision-free' for the others asserted, no counts. Abstract's 'halves' holds for Scenario 2 (about 56%) but not Scenario 1 (about 39%). RVO is reactive and could be read as a runtime interceptor; the paper does not say it overrides a nominal planner and Sec. III says no collision avoidance technique is implemented, contradicting Secs. V-VI. '72,000 flights' does not reconcile with 500 x 4 x 32 = 64,000. Table IV lists 160 m vs 40/80 m bounds in text. No hardware or latency. If the maintainer weighs the 4.3% vs 0 comparison as primary, this becomes include on (c). Read via summarising fetch of the PDF.

title: Opti-Shield: Multi Agent Path Planning in Presence of Adversarial Agents
venue: IEEE International Conference on Electro Information Technology
evidence: "For each environment setup, we executed 100 trials, categorized as epochs, to evaluate the mean makespan." (Sec. VI)
method: Decentralised swarm foraging (multi-agent Artificial Bee Colony) combined with StringNet herding; distance-based dynamic task allocation switches robots between gathering and encircling risk-averse adversaries.
evaluation: Custom 2D simulation, 20 agents (8 defenders in static variant), 100 trials each on sparse/clustered/dense maps; baselines naive collection and static allocation; metric mean makespan only; no hardware or latency.
contribution: Opti-Shield lets a foraging robot swarm reassign members on the fly to herd adversarial intruders away from a protected zone, cutting makespan by up to 62% versus static defender allocation in simulation.
flag: The 'shield' is a physical herding formation, not a runtime action filter. The defence objective (adversary stays beyond a safety margin) is stated in Sec. IV but never measured: no breach, collision or violation rate, so criterion (c) minimum evaluation fails even if primacy were argued. Only makespan and one completion-rate figure, all in prose (no tables); 'makespan improvement of 423%' is undefined arithmetic; the list of three 'baselines' includes the proposed method; authors admit no significance tests or CIs and call for stronger baselines. Fig. 1 caption says 'physical demonstration' but evaluation is simulation only.

title: Agent Instruction Language and Constraint Agent Execution Framework
venue: Proceedings of 4th International Conference on Computing, Communication, Security and Intelligent Systems, IC3SIS 2026
evidence: "All outputs generated by the LLM pass through CAEF before any action is taken. The model cannot execute actions directly." (Sec. III-A)
method: AIL declarative state-machine specification plus CAEF, a deterministic runtime that builds state-scoped context, validates every LLM proposal and rejects illegal tool calls or transitions.
evaluation: None. No experiments, dataset, baseline or metric of any kind; only two illustrative workflows and a qualitative LangGraph comparison table; no theorem or proof despite the claim in the contributions.
contribution: Proposes a deterministic instruction language and kernel-like runtime that confines an LLM agent to approved state transitions and state-scoped tools, with no empirical or formal validation.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - LLM agent proposals are gated. Fails the evaluation floor outright: contribution 3 promises a "Theoretical proof that CAEF reduces information leakage between phases" that never appears in the body, and the paper gives no dataset, metric, latency or proof; Table I is drawn from two non-archival sources [13],[14] and much of the related work cites preprints with implausible 2026 arXiv ids; mechanism is on-topic for criterion (a) if the maintainer wants to keep it as design-only evidence.

title: Tool-Use Failure Analysis and Recovery Framework for LLM Agents
venue: 2026 9th International Conference on Advanced Algorithms and Control Engineering, ICAACE 2026
evidence: "This framework consists of a responsive monitoring subsystem, a fault detector combining rules and learning, a library of simple recovery actions and complex recovery strategies, and a cost-aware controller that selects the optimal strategy among them." (Sec. I)
method: MCR runtime monitor with a rule-plus-learned fault classifier and cost-aware recovery strategy library over LLM tool calls, plus MAGRPO multi-agent GRPO joint training and a fault injector.
evaluation: Fault injection on writing (TLDR, arXiv) and coding (HE, CHE) tasks with two Qwen3-1.7B models; baselines single model, parallel, sequential, one-round discussion, no-recovery, retry, MCR, MAGRPO; the only body table reports training time and GPU memory (22.5 to 85.7 min, 10.2 to 21.8 GB); no safety or recovery figure appears in the body.
contribution: Proposes a monitor-classify-recover runtime layer plus multi-agent GRPO training for LLM tool-use failures, but reports no verifiable recovery or intervention figures outside the abstract.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - LLM tool-using agents. Most likely overturn candidate in this batch: the abstract claims success 42% to 86.7%, 92.6% problem resolution and reduced human intervention, yet no body table or sentence gives any of these numbers, and the stated appendix with dataset and reward details is absent. Further machine-generation signs: Figure 1 caption ends "(placeholder)"; Eq. 1 (Delta = (Fi - F)/F) is offered as the Dec-POMDP formalisation and is unrelated; two consecutive subsections are both titled "Experimental setup"; "Table 1" is cited both for resource scaling and for the baseline comparison; references [1],[4],[6] are misattributed and [8] is a technical report at a misspelled URL. If Figures 2-3 in the PDF carry the ablation values the maintainer may move this to include. Note also that MCR acts after a tool call fails rather than vetoing before execution, and human intervention rate is only named as a metric, with no handoff study.

title: Operational Hallucination and Safety Drift in AI Agents
venue: 2026 IEEE International Conference on AI and Data Analytics, ICAD 2026
evidence: Sec. V-E: results 'should therefore be interpreted as validation of a control-point concept, rather than a fully deployed runtime enforcement mechanism', the Action-Aware Supervision Layer being replayed post-hoc at the tool-call boundary.
method: Action-Aware Supervision Layer concept for LLM tool-calling agents: intent-action consistency checks, authoritative state tracking and a hard abort primitive at the tool-call boundary, assessed by post-hoc replay.
evaluation: Offline Inspect-AI harness, 7 LLMs, 4 samples, 1 episode per cell; alignment gap +1.00 for 4 of 7 models, 0.00 for Claude-3.5-Sonnet and Llama-3; livelock 0.00-1.00; no baseline or ablation.
contribution: A pilot diagnostic of operational hallucination and safety drift in LLM tool-calling agents, proposing an action-aware supervision layer at the tool-call boundary and replaying it against recorded trajectories.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - seven LLM tool-calling agents. Excluded on the evaluation floor: quantitative safety metrics do exist (text-action alignment gap, livelock incidence) but there is no baseline or ablation for the proposed layer, which was never deployed, and no formal result; the design is 4 samples with a single episode per model for S3 and S4, no repeated runs, the A2 Reflect protocol defined but its results absent, and the abstract claim that the layer can 'intercept observed violations without false positives on benign cases' has no corresponding test in the body. If the maintainer treats the S4 control condition as a baseline this flips to include under (a)-as-concept or under the LLM-agent-safety-evaluation clause of (c); it is the likeliest overturn in this batch. Single agent with three tools, so the multi-agent primacy test for (c) fails and only the sequential multi-turn aspect keeps it clear of E4. Protocol_Failures and Total_Turns are defined but never reported; no latency ('left for future deployment studies').

title: Subgoal-Driven Navigation in Dynamic Environments Using Attention-Based Deep Reinforcement Learning
evidence: "collision avoidance solely is the duty of the subgoal agent" (Sec. III-A)
