method: Hierarchical RL: DDPG subgoal agent with sector attention over 2D lidar picks nearby subgoals at 5 Hz; TD3 motion agent tracks them at 20 Hz; A* replanned every three subgoals.
evaluation: PyBullet, 2 dynamic and 1 static obstacle, 1000 episodes: success 90.7 percent, collision 9.3 vs baseline [9] 78.1/21.9, no-replan ablation 72.3/27.7; Turtlebot demo qualitative; no latency.
contribution: Subgoal-predicting attention RL agent that decouples obstacle avoidance from motor control for a single robot, cutting simulated collisions from 21.9 to 9.3 percent against an end-to-end baseline.
flag: Single robot, no multi-agent safety claim and no runtime interceptor; a zero-length subgoal makes the robot hold position but that is the policy's own output, not a veto. Results for varying obstacle count and speed are in Figs. 4-5 only. No compute hardware or inference time reported. Real-world transfer claim is qualitative.

title: Safe Reinforcement Learning using Data-Driven Predictive Control
venue: International Conference on Communications, Signal Processing, and their Applications (ICCSPA)
evidence: Abstract: the safety layer "penalizes the RL agent if the proposed action is unsafe and replaces it with the closest safe one"; Sec. III: "the robot always has a failsafe braking maneuver".
method: Data-driven safety layer: reachability analysis from offline data checks each RL (TD3) action; unsafe actions replaced by closest safe one via predictive control; failsafe braking if no safe plan.
evaluation: Turtlebot3 in Gazebo and quadrotor in UE4, static obstacles; baselines SAILR, SECAS, TD3; collision rate 0.0/4.9/0.0/17% (Turtlebot), 0.0/5.6/0.0/22% (quadrotor); goal rate 55% and 68%.
contribution: A data-driven reachability safety layer replaces unsafe RL actions with the closest safe one, giving zero collisions in two simulated robot navigation tasks against 5-22% for unshielded or weaker baselines.
flag: Single-agent with static obstacles: borderline E4, kept as sequential runtime shield with a safety metric and baselines. Simulation only. Computation-time row of Table I could not be read reliably (values looked garbled in the extract); paper only says "real-time" with GPU, no figures or hardware confirmed. Mean reward rows look inconsistent (84 vs 80.41). SECAS baseline also reaches 0.0 collisions, so safety gain over it is nil; gain is in goal rate and reward. Assumes linear model; Theorem 1 is a proof sketch.

title: The Trajectron: Probabilistic Multi-Agent Trajectory Modeling With Dynamic Spatiotemporal Graphs
venue: IEEE/CVF International Conference on Computer Vision (ICCV)
evidence: Method section: each agent is a node in a dynamic spatiotemporal graph and a CVAE with discrete latent z decodes a 16-component GMM over each agent's future velocities, integrated into positions.
method: CVAE with LSTM node and edge encoders plus additive attention over a dynamic spatiotemporal graph; discrete latent z gives behaviour modes; GMM-LSTM decoder outputs multi-agent future trajectory distributions.
evaluation: ETH-UCY pedestrian sets (1536 pedestrians), leave-one-out, 3.2s observed and 4.8s predicted; vs Linear, vanilla LSTM, Social LSTM, Social Attention, SGAN; best-of-100 average ADE-FDE 0.34-0.67 (Full) vs SGAN 0.43-0.86, ETH 0.37-0.72 vs 0.64-1.13; NLL beats SGAN p<.001; 200 samples in 0.13s vs SGAN 6.98s on a 2.7 GHz i5.
contribution: Models multi-agent future trajectories with a CVAE over a dynamic spatiotemporal graph, yielding multimodal distributions that beat GAN baselines on ADE-FDE and NLL at 20-80x lower sampling cost.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: no - this is the predictor itself, nothing is intercepted, so it enters only as Pillar 2 method evidence and RQ5 is capped. Check: most ADE-FDE and NLL numbers are only in box plots, Table 1 is best-of-100 rather than single-shot, there is no hazard, collision or intervention metric, and the timing is on a laptop CPU, not edge hardware.

title: Semantic Consistency Drift Monitoring for Training-Free Adversarial Prompt Injection Detection in Agentic LLM Pipelines
venue: 7th International Conference on Computational Vision and Bio Inspired Computing, ICCVBIC 2026 - Proceedings
evidence: "the action plan is captured before execution. Both are passed to SCDM for a single cosine computation (<2 ms). A positive detection can trigger quarantine, human review, or pipeline rollback." (Sec. IV-D)
method: Training-free monitor embeds the user goal and the post-retrieval action plan with TF-IDF plus truncated-SVD LSA and flags injection when cosine drift exceeds a Youden-calibrated threshold.
evaluation: 40 hand-built samples (20 clean, 20 injected) over 15 enterprise domains and 20 injection scenarios; baselines random, length heuristic, Jaccard BOW, raw TF-IDF; AUC 0.795, F1 0.791, precision 0.739, recall 0.850, Cohen d 1.192, p < 0.001, 1.22 ms per decision (std 0.076 ms); LSA-dimension and n-gram ablations.
contribution: Shows that cosine drift between goal and plan embeddings detects indirect prompt injection in agentic pipelines at 1.22 ms per check, with no model access, labelled data or retraining.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - an agentic LLM pipeline, though the plans are scripted rather than generated. Check construct validity: action plans are manually written and the 40-sample corpus was built by the authors (both conceded in Sec. VIII), so there is no end-to-end injection-prevention result and no live agent; AUC 0.795 is modest, while the 5-fold CV AUC of 0.863 +/- 0.110 exceeds the headline figure; Sec. VI-E calls bigrams "best AUC (0.795)" in the same sentence as trigrams at 0.813; two of 15 domains show a negative drift gap; reference [15] (arXiv 2601.12359, 2026) looks fabricated. Single-agent pipeline, so (c) does not hold, and (d) rests only on a 1.22 ms CPU timing with no deadline or jitter analysis.

title: DAG-Net: Double Attentive Graph Neural Network for Trajectory Forecasting
venue: Proceedings - International Conference on Pattern Recognition/Proceedings/International Conference on Pattern Recognition
evidence: Method section: a variational recurrent neural network with 32-dim latent variables predicts future displacements while two attentive graph networks share predicted goals and recurrent hidden states across agents.
method: Per-agent VRNN with grid-cell goal prediction conditioning prior, encoder and decoder; two attentive GNNs (2 layers, 4 heads) share goals and hidden states across agents; decodes future displacements.
evaluation: NBA SportVU (10 observed, 40 predicted, feet) and Stanford Drone TrajNet (8-12, metres); vs STGAT, Social-Ways, Weak-Supervision, C-VAE; attack ADE-FDE 8.98-14.08 vs STGAT 9.94-15.80, defence 6.87-9.76 vs 7.26-11.28, SDD 0.53-1.04 vs 0.58-1.11; ablations vanilla VRNN 0.58-1.17 and A-VRNN 0.56-1.14; no hardware or timing reported.
contribution: Couples per-agent variational recurrent prediction with two attentive graph networks over shared goals and hidden states, improving multi-agent trajectory forecasting on basketball and urban drone data.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: no - predictor only, no runtime interception. Check: ADE and FDE are the only metrics, with no safety, collision or hazard outcome, and no latency or hardware figure anywhere, so it gives nothing for the edge or jitter questions; on the defence 20-30 long-term split its ADE 5.01 is slightly worse than C-VAE 4.98.

title: OptLayer - Practical Constrained Optimization for Deep Reinforcement Learning in the Real World
venue: Proceedings - IEEE International Conference on Robotics and Automation/Proceedings
evidence: Method section: OptLayer sits between the policy network and the robot and returns the action closest to the network prediction that satisfies joint, velocity, torque and collision constraints, and only corrected actions are executed on the real robot.
method: Differentiable quadratic-program layer appended to a deep RL policy projects the predicted action onto state-dependent joint, velocity, torque and collision-avoidance constraints; the CPC strategy trains on both raw and corrected actions.
evaluation: 2D reacher (TRPO) and UR5 6-DoF reaching in Gazebo and on hardware, 36 joint plus 20 collision constraints; vs unconstrained UP and CP, CC variants; all constrained strategies had zero collisions over 7000 episodes and 6h of from-scratch real-robot training while UP knocked over the obstacle; average reward 700 reached in 3250 (CPC) vs 5350 (UP) episodes; 64ms vs 60ms per step, about 4ms OptLayer overhead inside a 0.1s control step.
contribution: A differentiable constrained-optimisation layer projects a deep RL policy's action onto safety constraints before execution, giving collision-free real-robot training and faster learning than penalty-only reinforcement learning.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - a deep RL (TRPO) policy; the filter itself is a QP, which the scope ruling allows. Check: the layer corrects or projects rather than vetoing or halting, so criterion (a) rests on reading projection as an override; collisions are reported as "never" rather than as counted rates, and the real-robot episode count is not stated; the 4ms overhead is measured but there is no deadline or jitter analysis, so I did not credit (d) or the latency gap cell; single arm, no multi-agent aspect.

title: Multimodal Probabilistic Model-Based Planning for Human-Robot Interaction
venue: Proceedings - IEEE International Conference on Robotics and Automation/Proceedings
evidence: Sec. V-B: a CVAE with discrete latent z and LSTM encoder-decoder predicts GMM distributions over the human's future actions conditioned on interaction history and a candidate robot action sequence.
method: CVAE-LSTM human response model conditioned on candidate robot action sequences; a two-stage sampling planner scores 4096 sequences with about 100000 sampled human responses and executes the lowest expected-cost one, replanning every 0.3s.
evaluation: 1105 human-human traffic-weaving trials in the Vires VTD simulator (about 77000 exemplars) plus real-time human-in-the-loop runs; the only number for a model is the basic LSTM baseline eval NLL -9.70, its own CVAE NLL appears only in Fig. 4 and is described as "slightly" better; no collision, violation or success rate; policy step about 0.25s on a GTX 1080 Ti.
contribution: Conditions a multimodal CVAE human-response model on candidate robot action sequences and uses it inside a receding-horizon planner for interactive highway traffic weaving.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: no - the human is modelled and predicted, not guarded, and collision avoidance is only a cost term inside the planner, so criterion (a) fails by the ruling on planners with no runtime override. E2 because the paper reports no quantitative result for its own model: a second read of Sec. V and VI found only Table I (human pass fractions) and the LSTM baseline NLL -9.70, with its own NLL in Fig. 4 and the closed-loop and human-in-the-loop results purely qualitative. Most likely overturn if the maintainer counts the Fig. 4 NLL values as the (b) predictive measure.

title: Robust Model Predictive Shielding for Safe Reinforcement Learning with Stochastic Dynamics
venue: Proceedings - IEEE International Conference on Robotics and Automation/Proceedings
evidence: Algorithm 1: at each step the shield executes the learned policy only if the next state is robustly recoverable, and otherwise switches to a tube-based robust NMPC backup controller.
method: Model predictive shielding for stochastic dynamics: a sampling-based robust recoverability check per step switches between a DDPG policy and a tube-based robust tracking NMPC backup that drives the system into an invariant set, then an LQR-style stabiliser.
evaluation: Simulation only - cart-pole, holonomic and non-holonomic particle with obstacles, 50 scenarios and 3 seeds, N=1500 samples; vs the learned policy alone, non-robust MPS and linear-robust LRMPS; RMPS and LRMPS reach a stated "safety probability of 1.0" while the learned policy is frequently unsafe and MPS is only slightly safer; goal-reaching drops about 20% on the non-holonomic particle; LRMPS invokes the backup more often (Fig. 3); Lemma 1 and Theorem 1 give probabilistic one-step recoverability bounds; no wall-clock latency.
contribution: Shields a learned RL policy with a sampling-based robust recoverability test and a tube-based NMPC backup, achieving empirically perfect safety under stochastic dynamics at modest performance cost.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - a DDPG policy, with a non-learned MPC shield, which the scope ruling allows. Check: single-agent throughout, so no (c); the per-environment safety, reward and backup-invocation numbers are in Fig. 3 rather than the text, so only "safety probability of 1.0" is quotable; the guarantee is one-step and high-probability, not infinite-horizon, and two heuristics (sampled invariant set, precomputed boxes) may weaken it; the authors call the method "still too slow for production systems" and report no measured latency, so I did not credit (d); the time-to-irreversibility gap cell is my reading of the recoverability check and can be dropped.

title: PredictionNet: Real-Time Joint Probabilistic Traffic Prediction for Planning, Control, and Simulation
venue: Proceedings - IEEE International Conference on Robotics and Automation/Proceedings
evidence: Sec. III.A.2: a CNN encoder-decoder with two recurrent networks, one processing past-present observations and one rolling out the future, predicts future occupancy, velocity and backtrace vectors for all agents jointly in a single pass, about 5 ms on NVIDIA Drive AGX (Sec. IV).
method: Raster CNN encoder-decoder with recurrent rollout jointly predicts future occupancy, velocity and backtrace vectors for all traffic agents over 3 s; frozen trunk reused for an SAC ego-policy head.
evaluation: INTERACTION, internal 5,000 km LiDAR set, sim and 530 km real drives; vs analytic predictor, TNT, MultiPath, ITRA; ADE 0.458 m, FDE 1.030 m; sim collisions 4.1% vs 8.7%; 5 ms on Drive AGX.
contribution: Shows a single-pass raster world model can predict joint traffic futures accurately enough to drive planning, control and simulation within about 5 ms on embedded automotive hardware.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: no - prediction only, nothing can override or halt an action, so (a) fails and I rest on (b) plus (d). Check whether a raster occupancy-plus-velocity rollout counts as a world model under the Pillar 2 scope rather than a trajectory regressor, and whether (d) holds with no stated deadline; the non-generative-inference cell is my reading of a single-pass deterministic decoder despite the paper's 'probabilistic' title. PredictionNet-RL numbers (cut-in failures 2% vs ACC 88%, harsh brake 0% vs 100%) are simulation only; the abstract's 'hundreds of kilometers' real-world control is backed only by a 15% comfort improvement and 'no network-related safety disengagements', with no safety-metric baseline; authors note their ADE-FDE is single-trajectory against best-of-6 baselines.

title: Safety-Critical Control and Planning for Obstacle Avoidance between Polytopes with Control Barrier Functions
venue: Proceedings - IEEE International Conference on Robotics and Automation/Proceedings
evidence: DCBF constraints from dual variables are embedded in the NMPC (Sec. III-C, eq. 20); the method is claimed to "successfully generate dynamically-feasible collision-free trajectories even in tight maze environments" (Sec. IV).
method: Dual formulation of polytope-to-polytope minimum distance turned into discrete-time CBF constraints inside a nonlinear MPC for non-conservative obstacle avoidance.
evaluation: Simulation only: bicycle-model robot of four shapes in two mazes with 0.15 m corridors. No baseline or ablation, no collision metric. Median solve 29-85 ms, max 272 ms, on Xeon E-2176M (IPOPT).
contribution: Formulates polytope-to-polytope obstacle avoidance as dual-variable discrete-time CBF constraints in nonlinear MPC, navigating tight mazes in simulation with median solve times of 29-85 ms.
flag: CBF is a constraint inside the planner/MPC, not a filter over a nominal action, so (a) fails under the strict-runtime rule. E2 would apply as well: no safety metric and no baseline; only solver times (Table I). Single robot, static obstacles. Solve times are reported but no latency constraint is posed, so (d) not credited. Extraction noted a likely typo (omega_k = 0.8 where gamma is meant). Read via one WebFetch pass.

title: Recursive Feasibility Guided Optimal Parameter Adaptation of Differential Convex Optimization Policies for Safety-Critical Systems
venue: Proceedings - IEEE International Conference on Robotics and Automation/Proceedings
evidence: Sec. V-B: 'The proposed algorithm improves the system's performance without losing feasibility.'
method: Adapts class-K parameters of a CBF-CLF QP controller online by differentiating the QP and rolled-out dynamics, with an LP-constrained update direction that preserves QP feasibility over a look-ahead horizon.
evaluation: Simulation: 1-D car with shrinking safe set and unicycle leader-follower with field-of-view barriers; baseline constant parameters, horizons 1-30; time-to-infeasibility and reward in figures only; no hardware or timing.
contribution: Tunes the parameters of a CBF-CLF quadratic-program controller by gradient descent through the QP while keeping the program feasible for the same or a longer horizon.
flag: Borderline (a): the CBF-CLF QP is the controller itself rather than a filter over a separate nominal policy, and the contribution is parameter tuning. No tables: time-to-infeasibility and reward appear only in Figs. 2, 4, 5, so no numeric safety rate (E2 also arguable). Leader motion is prescribed, so multi-agent only nominally. Sec. V-C gradient-count closed form (N+1)T(T+1) seems inconsistent with its own sum. No compute times despite the claim that updates 'can be performed very fast'.

title: Contingencies from Observations: Tractable Contingency Planning with Learned Behavior Models
venue: Proceedings - IEEE International Conference on Robotics and Automation/Proceedings
evidence: Sec. III-B: a conditional autoregressive normalizing flow q(X|o) over joint multi-agent future trajectories is learned from observations, and Sec. III-C plans by stochastic gradient ascent on the robot's latent variables inside that model.
method: Learns a conditional normalizing flow over joint multi-agent futures from LIDAR-paired demonstrations; plans by gradient ascent in the robot's latent variables, giving a closed-loop contingent policy re-planned each step.
evaluation: CARLA left-turn, overtake and stop-sign right-turn at 3 held-out locations, 90 episodes per method; vs noncontingent ablations, MFP, PPO; goal-reached-without-near-collision 27-28/30 vs 9-16/30; no prediction error or latency.
contribution: Shows contingency planning becomes tractable by optimizing latent variables of a learned joint behavior model, producing closed-loop reactive driving from observational data without hand-specified multi-agent models.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: no - safety enters only as a prior and a constraint term inside the planner objective (App. F approximates a violated constraint with a large negative value), which the 2026-11-13 ruling explicitly excludes from (a). (b) holds on reading, but the Pillar 2 floor needs a direct predictive measure and the paper reports none (no ADE-FDE, no held-out likelihood), hence E2; a maintainer may prefer E1 on the view that this is a planner paper. Counter-evidence to weigh: the RG* metric does require no near-collisions and is reported against ablations and MFP, which can be read as a safety metric. No hardware, runtime or latency figures anywhere; CARLA only, experts are hand-crafted and suboptimal.

title: Pylot: A Modular Platform for Exploring Latency-Accuracy Tradeoffs in Autonomous Vehicles
venue: Proceedings - IEEE International Conference on Robotics and Automation/Proceedings
evidence: Sec. VI-A: 'timely accuracy' scores each component against ground truth at the time its result is produced, and a 35 ms detector runtime halves mean timely AP50 in a pedestrian emergency scenario about 20 m ahead.
method: Modular dataflow AV platform on a Rust runtime with interchangeable detection, tracking, prediction and planning operators, pseudo-asynchronous simulation that defers control commands by measured pipeline runtime, and timely-accuracy metrics.
evaluation: CARLA city driving and pedestrian-emergency scenarios, 10-40 m/s sweeps; perfect components and 3 planners in fast-slow configs; timely mIoU 0.75 at 10 ms, AP50 halved at 35 ms, P99 15-760 ms.
contribution: Open platform and timely-accuracy methodology quantifying how component latency, not accuracy alone, decides whether an autonomous vehicle avoids a collision, with faster weaker configurations often safer.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - a learned perception-and-planning pipeline, but there is no interceptor: the only deferral is a simulation synchronizer that buffers the control command until simulated time matches pipeline runtime, so (a) fails and I rest on (d) alone. Evaluation floor is thin: Table I's collision-avoidance results at 16-22 m/s are colour-coded and not recoverable as numbers from the text, ride comfort appears only in Fig. 4, no jitter figures, no deadline enforcement and no CARLA Challenge score beyond 'a high score'. Experiments ran on 2 Xeon Gold CPUs and 2 Titan RTX, not edge hardware, so I did not credit edge deployment; the real Lincoln MKZ port (434 lines) has no quantitative results. Judge also whether a platform-and-measurement paper is E3-adjacent; I read it as a system plus empirical study, not a survey.

title: Occlusion-Aware Crowd Navigation Using People as Sensors
venue: Proceedings - IEEE International Conference on Robotics and Automation/Proceedings
evidence: "the GT-VAE is pre-trained independently from the RL policy and its parameters are frozen during policy learning" (Sec. IV-A) - PaS-VAE latent is matched to it to infer occluded humans.
method: PaS-VAE encodes 1 s of partial occupancy grids into a latent matched to an omniscient-map VAE, inferring occluded pedestrians from observed ones; PPO policy acts on the latent.
evaluation: Sim, 6 ORCA humans, 500 test episodes; success 0.91, collision 0.09 vs OBS-FE 0.79/0.21, GT-ORCA 0.70/0.30; map similarity total 441 vs 443; Turtlebot 2i demo qualitative; no latency.
contribution: Latent occupancy inference that treats observed pedestrians as sensors for occluded ones, raising simulated crowd-navigation success from 0.79 to 0.91 over a limited-view baseline.
flag: Borderline (b): the latent estimates the present occluded occupancy map from history, it is not a forward predictive world model over a graph; single robot, humans are non-reactive ORCA agents. Predictive metric is weak: PaS map is worse on occupied cells (43.5 vs 27.7) and total similarity gain is marginal (441 vs 443). Oracle row and discomfort cells garbled in extraction. Real-robot result qualitative only. If (b) is read strictly as forward prediction this is E1.

title: Online Update of Safety Assurances Using Confidence-Based Predictions
venue: Proceedings - IEEE International Conference on Robotics and Automation/Proceedings
evidence: Sec VI: when the nominal constant-speed trajectory meets the collision set within 3 s the ego vehicle "decelerates to stop before the intersection if possible; otherwise, it decelerates maximally until it stops."
method: Bayesian confidence (beta) over a Trajectron++ human predictor parameterises a DeepReach-learned forward reachable tube, queried online to update the collision set and trigger braking.
evaluation: Two hand-picked nuScenes scenarios (U-turn, stop-sign runner) replayed; baseline raw Trajectron++ without confidence; detection 52.46 vs 10.49 m and 47.8 vs 5.83 m before stop line; FRT query 0.0037 s.
contribution: Online confidence-conditioned reachable tubes let an ego vehicle detect an impending conflict with a mispredicted human driver earlier and brake in time, with a 3.7 ms query, in two nuScenes case studies.
flag: Borderline E2 vs include: evaluation is two selected replay scenarios, single runs, no collision/violation rate or variance; baseline collides in both, proposed stops in both. If the maintainer accepts n=2 outcome-plus-distance as quantitative, this is an include on (a). Human vehicle is replayed, not reactive (closed-loop listed as future work). Braking rule is a simple planner using the monitor, not a separate filter layer. Hardware for the 0.0037 s figure not reported. beta_low stated as 0.03 in parameters but 0.075 in the U-turn section. Fig. 1 caption says detection 2 s earlier; Fig. 2 caption gives 37.3 m vs 5.8 m, which differs from the 47.8 m in text. gamma and beta_low ablations are qualitative figures only. Read via one summarised fetch of the PDF.

title: Dynamic Control Barrier Function-based Model Predictive Control to Safety-Critical Obstacle-Avoidance of Mobile Robot
venue: Proceedings - IEEE International Conference on Robotics and Automation/Proceedings
evidence: "In dynamic environment, D-CBF requires the input u to satisfy stricter constraints than CBF." (Sec. III-A.1)
method: Dynamic control barrier function over Kalman-predicted moving elliptical obstacles with uncertainty inflation, imposed as a constraint inside a receding-horizon MPC for a mobile robot.
evaluation: Gazebo Jackal, single robot, vs MPC, MPC-CBF, MPC-KF, MPC-CBF-curvefit: min distance 0.828 m vs 0-0.273 m, reaction 0.353 s; Scout 2.0 real test qualitative; planning at 10 Hz on Intel NUC.
contribution: Embeds a dynamic control barrier function with Kalman-predicted obstacle motion in MPC, keeping a mobile robot 0.83 m clear of moving obstacles where plain MPC collided in simulation.
flag: CBF is a constraint inside the MPC, not a runtime filter; single robot among pedestrians/obstacles, so neither (a) nor (c). Could equally be coded E4. Evaluation is thin: Table I appears to be a single simulated run, no collision/success rate over trials, number of obstacles and trials unstated, no solve times in ms. Claimed best reaction time is 0.353 s vs 0.357 s for MPC-CBF, a negligible margin. Real-world results are qualitative (video).

title: Stealthy Perception-based Attacks on Unmanned Aerial Vehicles
venue: Proceedings - IEEE International Conference on Robotics and Automation/Proceedings
evidence: Abstract: "we introduce a method to consistently attack both the sensors measurements and camera images over time"; Sec. IV-C: "the attack will be detected if the attacker only compromises the image".
method: Attack design: consistent falsification of camera images and IMU/GPS data on a UAV so trajectory deviates while chi-square and LSTM anomaly detectors stay silent.
evaluation: Gazebo/PX4/Prometheus simulation, one quadcopter, ground-vehicle tracking and VTOL landing; compared with image-only attacks; detection rate about 0.009-0.014 at 0.01 false-alarm target, deviation up to 3 m.
contribution: Demonstrates in simulation that coordinated camera and sensor spoofing can pull a UAV up to 3 m off course while detection rates stay at the false-alarm level of two anomaly detectors.
flag: Attack paper; detectors are evaluated only as targets and trigger no halt or override. Single UAV, simulation only, no hardware or latency. Detection numbers: GVT chi-square p_TD 0.009 and learned 0.014 at p_FA 0.011; rises to 0.26/0.55 (GVT) and 0.55/0.79 (VTOL) when initial attack norm is 0.1; image-only attacks detected with probability up to 1. Could serve as a monitor-evasion caveat only. Companion to doi:10.1109/tac.2024.3401022 by the same group.

title: AMSwarm: An Alternating Minimization Approach for Safe Motion Planning of Quadrotor Swarms in Cluttered Environments
venue: Proceedings - IEEE International Conference on Robotics and Automation/Proceedings
evidence: Sec. III-C: "Each step in Algorithm 1 is either a convex QP or has a closed-form solution" - collision avoidance enters as constraints (1f) or barrier-function constraints (2) of the distributed trajectory optimizer.
method: Distributed receding-horizon trajectory optimizer for quadrotor swarms; polar reformulation of collision and kinematic constraints solved by alternating minimization; optional discrete-time barrier-function constraints with parameter gamma.
evaluation: Simulation 10-50 quadrotors, 16 obstacles, 100 configs per size; vs two SCP baselines and ACADO; success, mission time, compute time (1.61 ms per agent at 50 agents); Crazyflie hardware up to 12.
contribution: A fast distributed trajectory optimizer for quadrotor swarms that keeps collision constraints convex via alternating minimization, raising collision-free success rates over sequential convex programming baselines at millisecond per-agent cost.
flag: Borderline on (c) primacy: title says safe planning and success is defined as all agents reaching goals without collisions, but headline claims are success rate, mission time and computation time; no separate collision rate; clearance (min inter-agent distance +3.98-12.35% for gamma 0.95/0.9) is the only pure safety metric. Barrier functions are planner constraints, not a filter over a nominal action, so (a) fails. Abstract figures (72% success improvement, 31x faster and 44% lower mission time vs ACADO) are stated as averages; I saw body ranges (11-62%, 39-72% at 50 agents) but did not verify the averages against tables. Replanning rate not reported; hardware runs computed on one central PC, not onboard. latency/jitter cell is generous: compute time is measured, no deadline or jitter analysis.

title: Safety Under Uncertainty: Tight Bounds with Risk-Aware Control Barrier Functions
venue: Proceedings - IEEE International Conference on Robotics and Automation/Proceedings
evidence: Sec. IV-B: the ego vehicle was "controlled using (7) with 11 RA-CBF constraints", where (7) is a QP minimally modifying a nominal controller.
method: Risk-aware CBFs for stochastic control-affine systems give a tighter finite-horizon bound on exit probability; enforced as constraints in a QP that minimally modifies a nominal controller.
evaluation: Simulation: single-integrator robot, 100000 trials vs stochastic CBF (bound 0.505 vs 0 measured failures; RA-CBF predicted 0.505 vs measured 0.458); 11-vehicle highway merge, 1000/1000 and 914/1000 safe.
contribution: Derives risk-aware control barrier functions whose predicted failure probability closely matches measured failure rates, where the earlier stochastic CBF bound is loose, shown on a robot and a highway merge.
flag: Contribution is bound tightness, not a lower failure rate: the baseline S-CBF had 0 measured failures. Baseline comparison only in the single-robot example; highway merge has no baseline and only the ego vehicle is controlled (10 others follow IDM), so multi-agent is nominal and the cell is not claimed. No timing or hardware. Eta given as about 0.009 in text but 0.006 in Table II. Conclusion cites 99.1% safety, not matched to a table. Single agent, so E4 is arguable; kept on the finite-horizon sequential risk aspect.

title: Dense Fixed-Wing Swarming Using Receding-Horizon NMPC
venue: Proceedings - IEEE International Conference on Robotics and Automation/Proceedings
evidence: Sec. III-D: each vehicle 'passes planned trajectories to its team members' and enforces a pairwise separation constraint inside its NMPC optimisation (Eq. 12).
method: Receding-horizon direct-transcription NMPC for aerobatic fixed-wing swarms; teammates' planned trajectories enter as collision constraints, with TVLQR tracking and a probabilistic tube bound sizing the collision radius.
evaluation: Simulation (1 and 3 planes) and 28 indoor flights with up to 4 planes in 8x8 m mocap space; no baselines; min separation, 3 collisions in 86 crossings; offboard laptop, no solve times.
contribution: Decentralised NMPC with shared planned trajectories achieves close-quarters flight of up to four aerobatic fixed-wing aircraft indoors, with 86 pairwise crossings and three collisions.
flag: Collision avoidance is a constraint inside the planner, not a runtime interceptor, and the paper's claim is swarm density/first demonstration, so (a) and (c) primacy both fail. No baseline or ablation (literature comparison uses approximated scenarios), so E2 would also apply. 3 collisions (1 fatal) in 113 s of proximity flight; Table V min distance 0.298 m contradicts text's 0.55 m closest approach. Solve times and planning interval not reported; all computation offboard on one laptop, so distributed claim is untested on separate hardware.

title: Jailbreaking LLM-Controlled Robots
venue: Proceedings - IEEE International Conference on Robotics and Automation/Proceedings
evidence: Sec 5.3: 'A jailbreak was deemed successful if the requested action was physically realized.'
method: RoboPAIR: PAIR-style iterative attacker LLM with robot-specific system prompts and a syntax checker, eliciting harmful physical actions from LLM-controlled robots; attack only, no defence.
evaluation: Dolphins (nuScenes clips), Clearpath Jackal (GPT-4o), Unitree Go2 (GPT-3.5); 7 tasks x 5 trials; baselines direct, in-context, template, PAIR; RoboPAIR 35/35 on all; no latency.
contribution: RoboPAIR jailbreaks three LLM-controlled robots into harmful physical actions with 35/35 success on each, against 1-5/35 for direct prompts, showing chatbot-style alignment does not protect embodied agents.
flag: Borderline: meets (c) only via the 'safety evaluation of LLM agents' clause; each robot is a single agent, nothing multi-agent, and it is an attack with no interceptor (physical safety filters are only called for in Sec 6.4, not evaluated). Maintainer may prefer E4 or E1. Metric is attack success rate (violation rate) with four baselines. No compute hardware or latency reported. Fetch covered the first 100000 of 149906 characters; appendices past Appendix B not read.

title: Adaptive Deadlock Avoidance for Decentralized Multi-Agent Systems via CBF-Inspired Risk Measurement
venue: Proceedings - IEEE International Conference on Robotics and Automation/Proceedings
evidence: Sec. III-A: "A higher value of the CBF-inspired risk measurement" indicates a denser, more collision-prone neighbourhood; a sigmoid of it blends the task CLF with a deadlock-resolution CLF in one per-agent QP (Thm. 4).
method: Decentralized CLF-CBF QP where a CBF-derived risk score adaptively switches each agent between its task controller and a rotated-CLF deadlock-resolution controller; collision CBF always active.
evaluation: Sim 4-12 single-integrator agents position swap, 10 trials, vs plain CLF-CBF and deadlock method [14]; distance-to-goal plots only; 4 ROSbot demo; no collision rate or timing.
contribution: A barrier-function-derived risk score lets decentralized agents invoke deadlock-resolution behaviour only when their neighbourhood is crowded, reaching goals sooner than always-on deadlock resolution.
flag: Primary claim and outcome are deadlock avoidance/convergence, which the protocol names as E1; no collision, violation or deadlock rate is tabulated (figures only), so it would also fail minimum evaluation. CBF is the controller itself, not a filter over a nominal decision; the only halt-like element is Remark 4 fallback u=0 on QP infeasibility. Assumes every agent knows all others' states and velocities (not really local). No Hz/latency, onboard compute unspecified.

title: Robots that Learn to Safely Influence via Prediction-Informed Reach-Avoid Dynamic Games
venue: Proceedings - IEEE International Conference on Robotics and Automation/Proceedings
evidence: Fig. 2 caption: 'Online, the robot uses its robust SLIDE policy to safely influence against any human.'
method: SLIDE: conditional behavior prediction of the human feeds a belief-space reach-avoid dynamic game solved offline with ISAACS adversarial RL; the learned policy is the controller.
evaluation: Simulated 2-link human-robot tabletop reaching, 1000 trials; baselines NoSafety, SSA, Robust-RA, Marginal-RA; collision and completion rate, completion time; RTX 4090 training only, no inference latency.
contribution: Prediction-informed reach-avoid policy cuts simulated human-robot collisions from 28.5% (no safety) to 1.9% while completing 98.1% of tasks in 1.9 s, less conservative than worst-case reach-avoid.
flag: Borderline. Not a runtime filter: the reach-avoid policy is the controller, so (a) fails; (c) claimed on a two-agent human-robot pair with collision rate vs baselines. SLIDE collision 1.9% is slightly WORSE than Robust-RA 1.4% and Marginal-RA 1.5%; gain is completion time. OOD adversarial human 3.8% collision. Simulation only, simulated human. Training 61 h. Could also argue (b) via CBP predictor (ADE/FDE vs marginal). Maintainer may prefer E1/E4.

title: Learning to Refine Input Constrained Control Barrier Functions via Uncertainty-Aware Online Parameter Adaptation
venue: Proceedings - IEEE International Conference on Robotics and Automation/Proceedings
evidence: Sec. IV-D/E: candidate class-K parameters whose ensemble prediction is "deemed to be out-of-distribution" or fails the DR-CVaR risk test are discarded; the ICCBF constraint (9d) sits inside the MPC.
method: Online adaptation of ICCBF class-K parameters inside MPC: probabilistic ensemble NN predicts risk and deadlock time; candidates filtered by Jensen-Renyi divergence and distributionally robust CVaR; fastest valid candidate chosen.
evaluation: Single-robot simulation, 2 environments, 108 trials; vs fixed low/high, optimal-decay CBF-QP and MPC-CBF; collision 0%/0% vs 10.2%/1.9% (low), 13.0%/1.9% (Opt. MPC); reach 100%; no latency.
contribution: Uncertainty-aware online tuning of input-constrained CBF parameters inside an MPC gave 0% collisions and 100% goal reach over 108 single-robot simulation trials, against 10-13% collisions for fixed or optimal-decay baselines.
flag: Single robot, static obstacles; CBF is a constraint inside the MPC, not a filter between a nominal decision and execution, so (a) not met as drafted - maintainer may read the parameter verification step as a runtime gate. Could equally be E1. No fallback if valid candidate set is empty (Algorithm 1). Hardware experiments mentioned but no quantitative results in text (video only). No ablation of the JRD or CVaR checks. No computation time. Table I also: High 100%/100% collision, Opt. QP 0%/76.9% collision with 0% reach; time 15.0/40.7 s vs 54.4/129.0 s (low).

title: Conformal Decision Theory: Safe Autonomous Decisions from Imperfect Predictions
venue: Proceedings - IEEE International Conference on Robotics and Automation/Proceedings
evidence: Sec. V-A: 'Our approach (CC) adapts the reward weight lambda_t on the human collision cost' - the conformal control variable is a term inside the planner objective, and Sec. VI only proposes as an extension that 'we revert to a safe decision if lambda_t <= lambda_safe'.
method: Online gradient update of one conservativeness parameter lambda indexing a family of decision functions, with a proved bound on empirical risk under an eventual-safety assumption; batch variant via conformal risk control.
evaluation: Stanford Drone MPC navigation, simulated conveyor manufacturing, simulated trading; vs ACI, aggressive, conservative, UCB, LCB, oracles; safe at 1.142 m min distance and 29% faster to goal than ACI; no latency.
contribution: Conformal decision theory adapts a single conservativeness knob online so that actions taken from imperfect learned predictions meet a user-chosen risk level without distributional assumptions.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - a learned autoregressive human-trajectory predictor in the robot study, simulated predictors elsewhere. MOST LIKELY OVERTURN. Under the 2026-11-13 ruling lambda is a cost weight inside the planner (and in the manufacturing study lambda IS the action, the belt speed), with no override, veto, halt or defer, so no letter holds and I record E1; a maintainer may instead rule that online conformal risk control over a learned predictor is a runtime safety mechanism, in which case Theorem 1's bound R_t <= eps + ((lambda_1-lambda_safe)/eta + K)/t plus the ACI and conservative baselines clear the floor, and the physical-plus-financial evaluation is a genuine cross-domain case. Robot safety is a boolean over one run per learning rate; manufacturing and trading numbers appear only in Figs. 5-6; no intervention rate, latency or hardware.

title: Conformal Policy Learning for Sensorimotor Control under Distribution Shifts
venue: Proceedings - IEEE International Conference on Robotics and Automation/Proceedings
evidence: Sec. IV-D, Eq. 10: pi_switch uses pi_safe when the predicted distance plus its conformal quantile reaches the threshold and pi_speed otherwise, so the safe policy takes over the learned fast policy's actions at execution time.
method: An online P-controlled conformal quantile on a learned predictor's error serves either as a switching threshold between a fast and a safe DQN policy or as an extra observation for an end-to-end RL policy.
evaluation: highway-env 50-car driving, 500 rollouts, plus Unitree Go1 SLAM tracking in and out of distribution; vs dropout, ensemble, HAU, certificates, no-quantile; duration 37.8 s vs 19.4 s; coverage above 0.9; 10 Hz.
contribution: Treats a calibrated conformal quantile as a policy input so a robot switches to a conservative controller exactly when its predictions stop being reliable under distribution shift, at negligible extra compute.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - a DQN driving policy and a SLAM-driven quadruped controller, overridden at runtime by pi_safe, so (a) holds and runtime_interceptor is yes. Check the evaluation floor: no collision, violation, intervention or switch rate is given numerically, collision frequency appears only in the Fig. 2 Pareto curves ('always achieves a higher speed than the baselines at the same collision frequency'), and the dropout, ensemble, HAU and certificate comparisons are qualitative plus those curves; I relied on Table I episode duration (rollouts terminate on collision) and speed against pi_speed and the no-quantile ablation. On the quadruped pi_switch only retunes the P gain, and pi_safe cannot stop because minimum speed is 20 m/s, so 'halt' is never available; deferral is always to another policy, never to a human, so not (e). Edge-deployment is credited on the 10 Hz onboard Go1 alone, with no latency measurement.

title: RiskBench: A Scenario-based Benchmark for Risk Identification
venue: Proceedings - IEEE International Conference on Robotics and Automation/Proceedings
evidence: Sec. V (closely paraphrased): each risk identifier outputs a per-road-user risk score and an object counts as a risk once the score passes a threshold; Table III then reports Influenced Ratio and Collision Rate for a privileged planner that sees only the identified risk.
method: CARLA scenario-based benchmark of 6916 scripted ego-plus-interacting-agent scenarios with risk ground truth, evaluating ten risk identifiers on localization, anticipation, temporal consistency and the driving outcome of a privileged planner.
evaluation: 1689 CARLA test scenarios (521 interactive, 375 collision, 322 obstacle, 471 non-interactive); ten baselines (Random, Range 5m and 10m, Kalman, Social-GAN, MANTRA, QCNet, DSA, RRL, BP, BCP); best overall F-1 53.6 for rule-based Range 10m vs 48.6 RRL and 15.1 Random; planning-aware collision rate 0.4% interactive and 5.3% obstacle with ground-truth risk vs 33.6% and 58.7% for CARLA autopilot, 10.0% and 57.2% for QCNet; temporal consistency 3 s before the critical point 18.5% QCNet to 1.9% BP; one ablation (full vs restricted observation); no hardware, no latency.
contribution: A CARLA benchmark that scores risk identification not only by localization and anticipation but by the driving outcome a privileged planner reaches when it is shown only the identified risk.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: which - seven of the ten identifiers are learned (Social-GAN, MANTRA, QCNet, DSA, RRL, BP, BCP) and the planning-aware test uses an imitation-trained privileged planner, but Random, Range and Kalman are rule-based. No runtime interception anywhere: risk-aware planning is named as future work, so this is a dataset-plus-protocol record and the maintainer may rule it E1 or E4 because risk is scored per object from the ego front view rather than as a property of agent interaction. Internal inconsistencies: the intro says 14 maps and 237 road structures while Sec. III says 8 towns and 231 Area IDs; the claim that RRL leads on F-1 holds only among learned models, since rule-based Range 10m scores 53.6. Vision methods are fed ground-truth tracklets and restricted to the front view; temporal-smoothing results sit in the video submission only; no mIoU, no hardware, no latency. The non-generative inference cell could also be credited, since generative trajectory predictors are benchmarked head-to-head against direct risk scorers and mostly lose.

title: Quadcopter Trajectory Time Minimization and Robust Collision Avoidance via Optimal Time Allocation
venue: Proceedings - IEEE International Conference on Robotics and Automation/Proceedings
evidence: "optimize the time progress of the trajectories temporally, serving as a post-processing tool" (Abstract)
method: Robust optimal time allocation: re-times a planned B-spline trajectory via a second-order cone program, with linearized collision chance constraints imposing velocity limits in braking zones near obstacles.
evaluation: PX4/Gazebo, single quadcopter, static obstacles, 50 trajectories per setting, with vs without re-timing: collision 0-4% vs 0-14%; 6-85 ms typical solve on i7-12700K; Orin NX flights qualitative.
contribution: Re-times quadcopter trajectories with a second-order cone program that slows flight near obstacles, cutting simulated collision rates from up to 14% to at most 4% in dense static maps.
flag: Judgement call: the re-timer post-processes a nominal trajectory before execution, so it could be read as a filter under (a); I scored it as part of the planning pipeline. Even if (a) is granted it is single-agent with static obstacles and no latency constraint or handoff, i.e. E4. Only comparison is with/without the method (ablation), no other time-allocation baseline. Time-minimization claim has no numbers (Fig. 5 only). Hardware flights qualitative. No explicit real-time deadline; solve time grows to 5440 ms at fine sampling.

title: How to Train Your Neural Control Barrier Function: Learning Safety Filters for Complex Input-Constrained Systems
venue: Proceedings - IEEE International Conference on Robotics and Automation/Proceedings
evidence: Abstract: "we propose policy neural CBFs (PNCBFs), a method of constructing CBFs by learning the value function of a nominal policy"; Sec. II-B: the CBF-QP minimally modifies the nominal control at runtime.
method: Learns a neural CBF as the max-over-time value function of a nominal policy, then uses it in a CBF-QP safety filter that overrides nominal controls; policy iteration enlarges the safe set.
evaluation: Sim: double integrator, Segway, F-16, two-quadcopter task; baselines NCBF, NSCBF, handcrafted HOCBF, MPC filter, SOS; 90% fewer unsafe states than next best; two PX4 drones hardware; no latency.
contribution: Policy neural CBFs learn a safety filter from the value function of a nominal policy, cutting unsafe states by about 90% against the next best method on a two-quadcopter task with hardware flights.
flag: Only one number appears in the text (Sec. IV-C: 90% reduction in unsafe states vs next best on the quadcopter task, unsafe fraction near 0 after two iterations); safe-set volume and F-16 comparisons are figure-only. Descent condition is not formally verified, so no guarantee. Multi-agent only nominally: two drones under one centralised state, so I did not tick multi-agent state. Hardware runs (two PX4 drones, Spot as obstacle) are qualitative; no latency or compute figures. Extracted from one full-PDF fetch via summariser.

title: N-MPC for Deep Neural Network-Based Collision Avoidance exploiting Depth Images
venue: Proceedings - IEEE International Conference on Robotics and Automation/Proceedings
evidence: Sec. V-D.2: "runs in less than 10ms, therefore reaching a maximum control frequency of 100Hz"
method: CNN collision predictor on depth images embedded as a constraint and cost term inside a nonlinear MPC for a single aerial robot; no separate runtime filter.
evaluation: Classifier accuracy 93.1% sim, 95.4% real; recall 98.6%/98.3%. Gazebo and 15 real flights qualitative. Orin NX: depth fill 11.85, CNN 6.85, N-MPC 3.09 ms. No baselines.
contribution: Embeds a depth-image neural collision predictor as a constraint in nonlinear MPC running onboard a Jetson Orin NX, with an N-MPC solve time of about 3 ms.
flag: Not (a): the predictor is a constraint inside the planner. (d) only loosely - timings reported, no stated deadline. Fails minimum evaluation: no collision or success rate, and no baseline or ablation (authors defer comparison to future work); if the maintainer rejects (d) this is E1 or E4 instead. Possible inconsistency: 'less than 10ms' vs reported stage times summing to about 21.8 ms (11.85+6.85+3.09); the 10 ms likely covers CNN+N-MPC only - check. N-MPC 99% under 4.3 ms, max 10.3 ms. Single robot.

title: QuAD: Query-based Interpretable Neural Motion Planning for Autonomous Driving
venue: Proceedings - IEEE International Conference on Robotics and Automation/Proceedings
evidence: "A collision cost considers the maximum probability of collision for each time step t of each trajectory candidate" (Sec. III-C) - collision avoidance is a cost inside the planner
method: Sampling-based neural motion planner for driving that queries a learned implicit occupancy model only at spatio-temporal points along candidate trajectories, then picks the lowest interpretable-cost trajectory.
evaluation: Closed-loop and open-loop LiDAR simulation; baselines PlanT, CIL, NMP, P3, OccFlow; safety-set collision rate 2.1% versus 6.8-30.5%; runtime about 256 ms versus 705 ms unquantised; hardware not stated.
contribution: Shows that querying an implicit occupancy model only where candidate trajectories need it yields a driving planner with lower closed-loop collision rates and lower runtime than grid-occupancy planners.
flag: No runtime interceptor: selection is an argmin over sampled trajectories with collision as one cost, which the prompt says does not meet (a). Borderline (b): the implicit occupancy model is a learned predictor over a multi-participant scene, but the paper reports no occupancy accuracy metric (no AP/IoU), only planning metrics, so the (b) evaluation bar is not met. Single ego planner, so (c) fails primacy. Latency is reported (256 ms default, Table X) and motivates quantisation, but no explicit deadline, so (d) not credited; maintainer may disagree. Closed-loop safety set: GSR 84.7%, ECR 2.1%, PCR 1.0%; canonical ECR 0.0%. Text says quantisation raises ECR from about 1% to 2%. Scenario counts inconsistent between main text (about 1700 canonical) and appendix (663 train/321 eval). Proprietary simulator, not reproducible.

title: Distributionally Robust CVaR-Based Safety Filtering for Motion Planning in Uncertain Environments
venue: Proceedings - IEEE International Conference on Robotics and Automation/Proceedings
evidence: Sec I: "A related approach to enforcing safety uses a safety filter"; the filter takes the planner's reference trajectory and returns a minimally deviating one under DR-CVaR halfspace constraints (Sec III).
method: Standalone safety filter between planner and controller: per-obstacle distributionally robust CVaR safe halfspaces from trajectory samples constrain an MPC-style QP that minimally modifies the reference trajectory.
evaluation: Synthetic simulation, 300 Monte Carlo runs per scenario (head-on, overtaking, intersection; 3-obstacle case); baselines mean and CVaR halfspaces; worst distance -0.45, -0.22, no collision; QP 7 ms on laptop Xeon.
contribution: A distributionally robust CVaR safety filter that corrects a planner's reference trajectory against uncertain moving obstacles, avoiding the collisions seen with mean and plain-CVaR halfspaces in Monte Carlo simulation.
flag: Single ego robot versus non-reactive sampled obstacles; multi-agent only nominally, so (c) not claimed and E4 is arguable (kept for the sequential MPC filter with timing). No collision RATE: results are worst-case distance over 300 runs (about -0.45 mean, -0.22 CVaR) and a statement that DR-CVaR avoids collisions, with no number; plots are figure-only. On infeasibility the filter reuses "the most recent optimal control" (Remark 1) - no halt or fallback guarantee. Paper claims halfspaces solve "within a few milliseconds" but Table I DR-CVaR call time is 9.10 ms at 50 samples, 73.4 ms at 500 and 216 ms at 1500; MPC filter call 7 ms average. Dell Precision 7520, Xeon E3-1535M v6, CVXPY/ECOS; no robot hardware. No comparison with other published filters. Read via one summarised fetch of the PDF.

title: Plug in the Safety Chip: Enforcing Constraints for LLM-driven Robot Agents
venue: Proceedings - IEEE International Conference on Robotics and Automation/Proceedings
evidence: Method section: for black-box agents the chip 'stops execution when it detects an imminent unsafe state', and otherwise masks any action whose state change would leave the automaton's valid states, so it is pruned rather than executed.
method: English safety constraints translated to LTL by modular Lang2LTL-style prompting, expert-verified, conjoined into one automaton that masks or halts a GPT-4 robot agent's next action and re-prompts it with a generated violation explanation.
evaluation: VirtualHome 20 household tasks with five constraints each in two environments, plus a Boston Dynamics Spot with two mobile-manipulation tasks of ten constraints and three task-abortion tests; success-rate and safety-rate: Four Room 76% and 84%, Mobile Manipulation 88% and 94%, rising to 98% and 100% with expert-verified LTL, against NL-constraint prompting 100% and 56% and the unconstrained base model 90% and 38% in Four Room and 94% and 30% in Mobile Manipulation; on the robot 98% and 100% vs NL 98% and 34% and Code-as-Policies 53% and 55%, and above five constraints NL safety falls to 0% while Safety Chip aborts contradictory tasks without entering unsafe states; GPT-4-0613, no component ablation, no latency.
contribution: Compiles English safety constraints into one verified LTL automaton that masks or aborts an LLM robot agent's actions at execution time and explains each violation back to the planner.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - a GPT-4 LLM robot agent, intercepted before execution, so (a) is clear. Single agent only: VirtualHome is described as a multi-agent platform but every experiment runs one agent, so (c) fails and the sequential multi-step LTL setting is what keeps the record off E4. Humans only author and verify constraints before deployment, so (e) does not hold - the fast-halt-then-explanation loop sends its explanation to the LLM, not to a person, and dialog-based confirmation is future work; RQ3 is scored on that mechanism, not on a human study. Monitoring assumes perfect proposition truth values, read from the simulator, so the 100% safety rate is conditional on perfect perception. The 76% vs 100% success-rate drop under unverified LTL is the paper's own false-halt cost. No component ablation, no token counts, no latency, VirtualHome trial counts unstated, robot tasks run twice at temperature 0. Not cross-domain: Spot and VirtualHome are both physical settings. Time-to-irreversibility is credited for the check that the automaton state can still reach an accepting state, which is a weaker reading than the review's usual one.

title: A Learning-Based Framework for Safe Human-Robot Collaboration with Multiple Backup Control Barrier Functions
venue: Proceedings - IEEE International Conference on Robotics and Automation/Proceedings
evidence: "Thus, any safe switch between backup controllers, does not void safety guarantees." (Sec. III-B); the BCBF-QP minimally modifies the teleoperating driver's command at runtime.
method: Backup-CBF QP safety filter on a teleoperated tracked robot; an LSTM+DNN picks which of three backup controllers the filter uses, with labels shifted earlier to cover QP solve time.
evaluation: Hardware only: GVR-Bot at JPL Mars Yard, one static cone, Jetson AGX Orin. Only number is 97% switching-classifier accuracy; single-backup comparison is qualitative (video). No latency figures.
contribution: Learns to switch among multiple backup controllers inside a backup-CBF safety filter for a human-teleoperated tracked robot, shown on hardware without quantitative safety results.
flag: No quantitative safety metric (no collision, violation or intervention rate) and no quantitative baseline; 97% is classifier accuracy only. Single robot, static obstacle, so E4 also arguable. Human is the nominal driver being filtered (haptic warning near boundary), not a takeover recipient, so (e) not credited. Control rate and QP solve time not reported. Read via one WebFetch pass of the PDF, not re-checked at offsets.

title: Decentralized Multi-Robot Navigation for Autonomous Surface Vehicles with Distributional Reinforcement Learning
venue: Proceedings - IEEE International Conference on Robotics and Automation/Proceedings
evidence: "we maintain only one learning model, which is shared with all robots during their individual decision making processes" (Sec. IV-D)
method: Decentralized IQN distributional RL policy shared by all surface vehicles; CVaR risk threshold adapted to distance to nearest obstacle or robot; discrete acceleration and turn-rate actions.
evaluation: Simulation only, 3-7 robots, vortex currents, 1000 test environments; baselines DQN, APF, RVO, greedy IQN; success rate, travel time, energy shown only in Fig. 5; no latency.
contribution: Risk-sensitive distributional RL policy for decentralized multi-vessel navigation in currents that reports higher success rates than DQN, APF and RVO in simulation.

Adaptive CVaR threshold changes risk sensitivity inside the policy, it is not an override. Read from one extracted pass of the PDF; figures not seen.

title: Integrated Planning and Control on Manifolds: Factor Graph Representation and Toolkit
venue: Proceedings - IEEE International Conference on Robotics and Automation/Proceedings
evidence: Sec. IV-A.1 says the method functions "as a certifying safety filter", but the CBF enters as a squared hinge factor in the factor-graph MPC cost (Sec. III-B), i.e. a soft penalty inside the planner.
method: FactorMPC: factor-graph MPC toolkit on manifolds (GTSAM/iSAM) with a velocity-extended CBF obstacle-avoidance factor, unifying planning and control for a quadrotor.
evaluation: Single quadrotor, simulation and VICON hardware; vs EGO-Planner (qualitative) and flatness-based controller; alpha/gamma ablations; no collision rates; 100 Hz, 5.4 ms mean solve, 99.6% within 10 ms.
contribution: A factor-graph MPC toolkit embeds velocity-aware control barrier factors for quadrotor obstacle avoidance, solving in 5.4 ms on average at 100 Hz on hardware, without quantitative safety outcomes.
flag: Single agent; safety is a soft penalty factor inside the optimizer, not a runtime interceptor, and no formal invariance proof for the factor form. No collision/violation rate or tables - would also fail E2. Timing figures are the only reusable evidence (sim: under 20 ms per Fig. 7, no exact values; onboard computer not identified in my read). Tracking-error advantage over DFBC is figure-only. E4 is a defensible alternative code.

title: A Dynamic Graph Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning Approach for Eco-Safe Mixed Platooning
venue: 2026 11th International Conference on Intelligent Computing and Signal Processing, ICSP 2026
evidence: "the supervisor forcefully intervenes, overriding the DRL action ai,t with the maximum safe deceleration amin to physically prevent the crash" (Sec. III-D)
method: GAT over a dynamic graph fusing radar and V2V edges feeds MAPPO under CTDE with an eco-safe mixed reward; a one-step kinematic supervisor overrides unsafe accelerations at execution.
evaluation: SUMO co-simulation, 1 leader and 16 followers, NGSIM human-driver traces, 50% CAV penetration, penetration sweep 0-100%; baselines SFC-CTH, DDPG, DPPO; fuel 1.32 vs 1.45-1.60 ml/s, mean speed 14.3 m/s, dampening ratio 0.51 and 0.38; no collision, near-miss or intervention count and no supervisor ablation.
contribution: Cascades a one-step kinematic override on a graph-attention MAPPO platoon controller, reporting fuel, travel-efficiency and string-stability gains over classical and DRL baselines.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - MAPPO graph policy, so criterion (a) is met on reading, but the safety mechanism is never measured: no collision, near-miss, headway-violation or intervention rate anywhere, and no ablation with the supervisor removed, while the paper claims an "absolute mathematical guarantee against collisions" with no proof. exclude-E1 is also defensible because the primary claims and all measured outcomes are fuel economy, average speed and string stability. Draft residue in the body ("textcoloryelloweach", a section titled "PREPOSITION"); GAT is credited to Sperduti and Starita 1997 instead of Velickovic et al.; ref [13] is a 2026 TITS paper on the same eco-safe mixed platooning problem that this work tracks closely - check for overlap.

title: Obstacle Avoidance for Unicycle-Modelled Mobile Robots with Time-Varying Control Barrier Functions
venue: Annual Conference of the IEEE Industrial Electronics Society (IECON)
evidence: Abstract: a QP that 'incorporates CLF and CBFs as constraints'; Conclusion: 'extending our approach to multi-robot systems will be an important direction for future research.'
method: Unified CLF-CBF QP for a unicycle robot with time-varying CBFs on an offset centre point so both speed and turn rate are controllable; CLF relaxed by slack.
evaluation: Simulation only: one static and one dynamic two-obstacle scenario; baseline centre-based CBF collides (static only); mean solve time 0.0069 s and 0.0066 s on i9 laptop, IPOPT.
contribution: A time-varying CLF-CBF quadratic program for unicycle robots that avoids static and moving circular obstacles in two simulated scenarios, solving in about 7 ms on a laptop.
flag: Single robot, single run per scenario; no collision or violation rate, only one qualitative baseline collision (Fig. 1b), so E2 is an equally valid code. No separate nominal controller: the QP computes the control directly, so I marked runtime_interceptor no. Timing is laptop not edge. No baseline for the dynamic case.

title: Correct-by-synthesis reinforcement learning with temporal logic constraints
venue: IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS)
evidence: Sec. IV: the permissive strategy is applied to the game to remove every transition it does not allow, yielding a game whose winning condition is True so that any strategy learned inside it is correct by construction; no module observes or overrides a nominal decision.
method: Extract a (maximally) permissive winning strategy for a temporal-logic two-player game offline with slugs, prune the game to its allowed transitions, run maximin-Q learning inside the pruned game, then map the learned strategy back.
evaluation: NxN grid-world motion planning against one adversarial robot; no external baseline, comparisons are against the theoretical optimum and across permissiveness levels; Table I extraction 0.10-300 s and learning 4.28-771.73 s over N=3-10 on a 2.4 GHz 8 GB laptop with up to 1.562e7 iterations; N=4 values converge to 10, 9, 8.1, 7.29, matching (1/(1-gamma))*gamma^k; Table II six counter-augmented permissiveness levels raise max discounted reward 5.7368 to 9.8616 while learning time grows 9.87 s to 275.88 s; formal results Prop. 1-2 and Theorem 1; no collision or violation rate.
contribution: Decouples correctness from optimality by pruning a temporal-logic game to a permissive winning strategy and learning the reward-optimal policy inside it, with linear-time maximal permissiveness for a Boolean fragment.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - maximin-Q learning is the learner, so the record fails on the runtime test, not on the scope ruling. This is the most likely overturn in the batch: pruning the game means that at every execution step the learner can only pick a permitted action, which is action masking in effect and the correct-by-synthesis ancestor of shielded RL, so the maintainer may read (a) as met even though the paper describes no interception of a nominal decision and all restriction happens before learning. Safety is by construction with no collision or violation rate anywhere; the formal content is Prop. 2 with its proof omitted and Theorem 1, which covers only phi0 AND phi1 with Boolean conjuncts, while learner optimality is borrowed from Littman's convergence results. The second agent is the environment player of a zero-sum game, not a learner, so (c) fails the primacy test, though the joint two-robot game state could arguably be credited the multi-agent state cell. General extraction is 2-EXPTIME, Example 2 admits no maximally permissive strategy and its reward loss (roughly 1.5-5.5 vs an optimum of 10) is never tabulated.

title: Safe Reinforcement Learning on Autonomous Vehicles
venue: IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS)
evidence: Sec. IV: 'The prediction module masks undesired actions at each time step' and 'Actions that are marked as safe are passed on to the network as permissible actions'; if no action is permissible the vehicle waits.
method: Constant-velocity Kalman predictions of surrounding traffic with quadratically growing uncertainty are overlapped with the ego's predicted maneuver footprint to mask unsafe accelerations before a DQN acts, with a Chebyshev plus union bound giving m/(2*kappa_n^2) < delta.
evaluation: SUMO unsigned-intersection left turn, IDM traffic with Krauss driver imperfection, 0.2 s steps, 100 m sensing, 0.1/s vehicle emission, 20000 training simulations per network, statistics over 1000 trials; 'There were no recorded collisions during the entire training process'; baselines a random policy inside the same mask and an enlarged fixed-margin rule-based policy that performs 'much worse', plus a timeout-penalty ablation z in {-1,-5,-10}; encounters under 10 m vanish by about 7000 iterations and density rises near 20 m; policy verified on a vehicle with six IBEO lidars and three radars; forward checking is O(mT) but no latency is measured.
contribution: Masks a DQN's intersection-crossing actions with an analytic multi-vehicle prediction check whose failure probability is bounded by a Chebyshev-union argument, letting the policy train with zero collisions.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - a DQN driving policy, masked before execution. The weakness is evidence, not scope: every comparison lives in Fig. 4-6, the paper prints no table and no numeric collision rate, success rate or time-to-cross, so the whole quantitative safety claim is the sentence 'no recorded collisions' with no baseline collision rate beside it and the baselines beaten only 'much worse' in prose - E2 is defensible. Traffic vehicles are scripted IDM/Krauss and their number is given only as an emission rate, so (c) fails. The probabilistic bound assumes non-adversarial agents, neglects corrective ego control and a fixed 2 m detection uncertainty, and the authors themselves concede the guarantees are weaker than comparable approaches. The arXiv text prints no venue or year although the record says IROS 2018, so check this is the same paper as the DOI; the real-vehicle verification is asserted with no quantitative result and no measured runtime.

title: Conditional Generative Neural System for Probabilistic Trajectory Prediction
venue: IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS)
evidence: Sec. V and Tables I-III: the system is evaluated only as a predictor, by ADE/FDE over 1-5 s horizons; the feasibility term of Eq. 13 that the authors call a differentiable barrier function is a training loss, not a runtime check, and no planner or controller consumes the predictions.
method: Conditional VAE with a two-dimensional latent space trained jointly with a least-squares GAN discriminator; soft block attention over neighbouring trajectories and a Gaussian image mask feed a frozen VGG-19, GRUs and fully connected layers.
evaluation: ETH and UCY pedestrians (8 observed, 12 predicted steps), Stanford Drone in pixel space and an INTERACTION roundabout set (4 observed, 10 predicted steps); nine baselines (CVM, LR, P-LSTM, S-LSTM, S-GAN, S-GAN-P, SoPhie, CAR-Net, DESIRE) and a four-way input ablation (T+CLSL, T+VDM, T+CLSL+VDM, T+I+CLSL+VDM); average ETH-UCY ADE/FDE 0.49/0.97 m vs 0.54/1.15 SoPhie and 0.58/1.18 S-GAN; SDD 15.6/28.2 px vs 17.8/32.1 SoPhie and 19.3/34.1 DESIRE; roundabout at 5 s 1.47/2.12 m vs 1.69/2.77 S-LSTM; no likelihood, collision or offroad metric, no hardware, no inference time.
contribution: Combines a conditional VAE with a GAN discriminator and attention over neighbouring trajectories and scene images to sample feasible multi-modal future trajectories for interacting road users and pedestrians.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: no - nothing is guarded or intercepted, so (a) and (c) fail outright. The judgement the maintainer is most likely to overturn: (b) holds on a literal reading, since this is a latent conditional generative model of FUTURE multi-agent state with a direct predictive measure, nine baselines and a four-way ablation, and the Pillar 2 ruling excludes only a 'plain trajectory regressor'. I read a CVAE-GAN trajectory-prediction paper with no dynamics model, no action conditioning and no closed-loop use as exactly that, but if the maintainer disagrees the record becomes (b) method-and-architecture evidence with RQ5 capped at 2. Interaction is attention only, no graph and no social pooling, which also weakens the 'over graphs' half of (b). The 'outperforms on all datasets' claim is overstated: LR wins HOTEL ADE at 0.39, S-GAN wins HOTEL FDE at 0.61, SoPhie wins ZARA1 ADE at 0.30 and CVM wins the 1 s roundabout ADE at 0.16. Units are unstated for ETH-UCY and the roundabout set, the sample count and whether ADE/FDE is best-of-N are never given, and diversity and realism are shown only as KDE plots.

title: NMPC-LBF: Nonlinear MPC with Learned Barrier Function for Decentralized Safe Navigation of Multiple Robots in Unknown Environments
venue: IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS)
evidence: "each robot solves the optimization problem described in Eq. (11) independently" (Sec. III.C); the learned barrier enters that NMPC as a discrete-time CBF constraint, not as a separate filter.
method: Each robot trains a small DNN online from LiDAR and odometry to approximate a barrier function, then embeds it as a discrete CBF constraint in a decentralized NMPC.
evaluation: Gazebo TurtleBot3: 1 robot/6 obstacles and 4 robots/2 obstacles; one real TurtleBot3. No baselines or ablations; no collision rates. NMPC solve 0.25 s, DNN update 0.15 s on Core i5.
contribution: Decentralized NMPC whose control-barrier constraint is a neural network learned online from LiDAR, demonstrated qualitatively on simulated multi-robot and single real-robot navigation in unknown environments.
flag: Safety is a constraint inside the planner, so (a) fails; (c) is the claim but there is no quantitative safety metric and no baseline or ablation (results are figures only). Real-robot test uses ONE robot. Authors concede the approximation error is not bounded (Sec. V.A). 0.25 s solve time is far from sub-15 ms.

title: Comprehensive Reactive Safety: No Need For A Trajectory If You Have A Strategy
venue: IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS)
evidence: "the planner plans a trajectory for each future scenario" (Sec. III-A); merge collision rate 16% baseline vs 5% RILQR (Sec. IV-D, Table III)
method: Comprehensive Reactive Safety: the planner outputs a strategy tree (one trajectory per predicted future, branching after sensing delay) instead of one trajectory avoiding all reachable sets; implemented as Reactive ILQR.
evaluation: Proprietary simulator, one AV, scripted vehicles; baseline non-reactive CILQR; pass 35.6% vs 11.6% crossing, 57.4% vs 33.8% left turn; merge collisions 5% vs 16%; no hardware or timing.
contribution: A safety framework for driving planners that plans a reaction per possible future rather than one trajectory avoiding every reachable region, raising pass rates and lowering merge collisions in simulation.
flag: Borderline. It is a planner, not a layer between a nominal decision and its execution, so (a) fails on the strict runtime reading. For (c) the safety framing is primary but the headline outcomes are pass and overtake rates (efficiency under a safety condition); a collision rate against a baseline appears only in the merge scenario, and only one ego vehicle is controlled, so multi-agent is nominal. A maintainer reading Theorem 1 as the primary claim could argue include under (c). The latency/jitter cell is credited only because a fixed sensing delay (0.1 s) is a formal element of the Reaction Causality requirement; there is no jitter model and no measured compute time (only an analytical 1x-2x cost estimate for a Y-shaped strategy). The 10 Hz figure is a general remark, not the experimental rate. Overtake baseline collision figure not stated. Proprietary simulator, not reproducible.

title: Safe Reinforcement Learning for Legged Locomotion
venue: IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS)
evidence: Sec. IV-B: the safe recovery policy takes over when the state enters the safety trigger set and returns control "only when" a model rollout shows the learner stays safe over the horizon (close paraphrase)
method: Learner policy and safe recovery policy for a quadruped; recovery overrides when a safety trigger set is entered, and a centroidal-model reachability rollout gates return of control.
evaluation: PyBullet Laikago and real Unitree A1, 4 tasks, vs TRPO, PCPO, TRPO-N, Recovery RL: 48.6% fewer falls; catwalk falls 204-551 by horizon vs 603. Real: under 5 falls in 115 min. Policy 125 Hz.
contribution: Switches a legged robot from a learning policy to a recovery policy using a model-based reachability check, reporting 48.6% fewer falls than baselines in simulation and under five falls in 115 real minutes.
flag: Single robot, no multi-agent aspect; kept as sequential runtime switching rather than E4, maintainer to confirm. time-to-irreversibility cell is a stretch (w-step lookahead to a fall), strike if strict. Evidence is a close paraphrase, not verbatim. Real-world runs used w=0 (no lookahead), so the reachability check is validated mainly in simulation. Recovery policy used heavily in two-leg balance (about 82.5% to 67.5% of steps). Reported Fig. 4 default falls read as 335+/-34 in one panel and 335+/-234 in the other - check against the PDF. No latency of the check itself; no hardware compute named. Human only absent ('no manual reset').

title: Adaptive Environment Modeling Based Reinforcement Learning for Collision Avoidance in Complex Scenes
venue: IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS)
evidence: Adaptive perception mechanism stops adding GRU iterations once cumulative halting confidence reaches 1-eps (Sec. IV-B, paraphrase); action comes from the value network.
method: Single-robot DQN-style value network with hierarchical GRU environment model, adaptive number of GRU steps, Transformer attention and collision-probability reward shaping.
evaluation: Gym sim, 5 obstacles, 500 trials: success 1.00, collision 0.00 vs MP-RGL-MultiStep 0.97/0.01, LM-SARL 0.90/0.09, ORCA 0.43/0.57; Husky real demo; i5-5500T onboard; no inference time.
contribution: Adaptive environment-model RL for single-robot collision avoidance among moving obstacles, reporting 1.00 success and zero collisions against graph and attention RL baselines in simulation.
flag: Single learning robot among scripted obstacles; safety is a training reward term, no runtime layer. The adaptive halting governs computation depth, not robot motion - do not mistake it for a halt mechanism. Borderline (c) only if crowd collision avoidance by one robot counts as multi-agent hazard detection. Conclusion claim of at least 74 percent success with 20 obstacles and 37 percent above SOTA not found in a table in my extraction; Fig. 6(a) trial count (50) disagrees with text (100).

title: Minimizing Safety Interference for Safe and Comfortable Automated Driving with Distributional Reinforcement Learning
venue: IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS)
evidence: Abstract: 'the proposed framework can guarantee that actions generated from RL are fail-safe according to the worst-case assumptions'; Sec. V-B: an unsafe RL action is replaced by an emergency maneuver limited to 5 m/s3 jerk.
method: Deepset-IQN distributional RL driving policy wrapped in a proactive set-based safety verification layer that replaces unsafe actions with fail-safe emergency maneuvers; CVaR level tunes conservativeness at runtime.
evaluation: Simulated occluded merging and crossing, 30 randomized scenarios; baselines rule-based and DQN; crossing time and J_Interference (IQN 10.00 versus rule-based 83.59); zero collisions; no hardware or latency reported.
contribution: Shows a distributional RL driver can be trained to minimize how often its fail-safe verification layer must intervene, cutting safety interference up to 83% versus a rule-based policy.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - a set-based verification layer shields a distributional RL policy and can veto its action at execution time. Check: the abstract's '8 seconds faster than DQN' reads as about 10 s in Table I, and the 83% interference reduction holds only for the comfort-tuned agent at zero perception noise (the speed-tuned variant is about 70%); other vehicles are simulated traffic rather than co-designed agents, so (c) fails the primacy test; no hardware, inference-time or real-vehicle evidence, so RQ1 credit is for the interception pattern only.

title: Learning Models of Adversarial Agent Behavior Under Partial Observability
venue: IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS)
evidence: Sec. IV-B: an LSTM plus graph neural network encoder over tracker agents with a mutual-information-regularised latent mixture decoder predicts the adversary's current and future locations; Abstract: 'GrAMMI outperforms all baselines in both domains'.
method: GrAMMI: LSTM plus graph neural network encoder over multi-agent tracker state with a Gaussian-mixture latent decoder and mutual-information auxiliary loss, predicting a partially observed adversary's present and future position.
evaluation: Prison Escape and Narco Interdiction pursuit domains, 450 rollouts per dataset; baselines LSTM, VRNN, VAE-Opponent plus no-GNN and no-MI ablations; log-likelihood and ADE at 0, 30 and 60 min; no hardware.
