contribution: Predicts a partially observed adversary's current and future location from multi-agent tracker histories using a graph encoder with a mutual-information objective, gaining about 31.68% average log-likelihood over baselines.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: no - nothing is guarded, so this enters only as Pillar 2 criterion (b) method evidence and RQ5 is capped at 2 per protocol v1.6. Check: there is no runtime override and the tracking team runs fixed heuristic policies; ablations beat the full model in several cells (Prisoner-Low 0 min log-likelihood 6.381 without GNN versus 5.230 full; Smuggler-Low 0 min ADE 0.122 without GNN and MI versus 0.127 full), so the 31.68% headline is an average over favourable cells; Sec. VII states the model cannot predict multiple horizons while Tables I-II report 0, 30 and 60 min.

title: NaviSTAR: Socially Aware Robot Navigation with Hybrid Spatio-Temporal Graph Transformer and Preference Learning
venue: IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS)
evidence: Sec. III-C: the robot 'obtains the value V_st and the policy' from the transformer decoder, trained with SAC and a reward learned from human preference labels - the action drives the robot directly, no monitor.
method: Spatial and temporal transformers over a spatio-temporal crowd graph fused by a multi-modal transformer into an RL policy; reward learned from human preference labels, trained with off-policy SAC.
evaluation: 2D crowd simulator (ORCA humans, 500 cases) and real robot with 8 participants; baselines ORCA, CADRL, SARL, RGL, SRNN, two ablations; real-world social score 93 vs SRNN 80; no latency.
contribution: A spatio-temporal graph transformer policy with a preference-learned reward improves socially compliant crowd navigation scores over SRNN and RGL baselines in simulation and a small user study.
flag: Navigation policy, not a safety mechanism or predictive world model: the graph transformer feeds a policy/value head, so (b) not credited (maintainer may disagree). Primary outcome is a composite social score and questionnaire comfort, not collision rate; success/collision rates appear only in Fig. 5 with no numbers in text. Human input is training-time preference labelling (5,000 labels), not runtime handoff. NaviSTAR row of Table I was garbled in extraction (stray values 95.8, 93.1) - check table. No compute or latency reported.

title: Sequential Neural Barriers for Scalable Dynamic Obstacle Avoidance
venue: IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS)
evidence: "When no feasible action is available, we declare failure, and stop the robot." (Sec. VI); sampled candidate actions are kept only if the aggregated barrier value of the predicted next state is nonzero.
method: Per-obstacle LSTM neural CBFs over relative state histories are multiplied into one aggregate barrier that vetoes sampled candidate actions; refined by boundary resampling; can wrap a PPO nominal action.
evaluation: ORCA pedestrian navigation and IDM lane-change sims, 4 ego dynamics, train 6 obstacles, test to 600; baselines PFM, S-MPC, B-MA-CBF, PPO, DQN; collision rate under 10% to 60x; car robot demo.
contribution: Composable sequential neural barrier functions, one per dynamic obstacle, filter candidate actions at runtime and keep collision rates low at up to 100x the obstacle density seen in training.
flag: Exact per-method collision rates are only in figures; text gives under 10% up to 60x density (bicycle model 15% at 600 obstacles) and a claimed more-than-50% reduction vs best potential field. No latency or hardware compute figures. Hardware car test has no reported success/collision numbers (video only). Other agents are scripted obstacles, only the ego is controlled: check multi-agent is more than nominal. PPO-as-nominal variant reported without numbers in text. Compositional scaling in obstacle count, not hazard types, drives the RQ4 score.

title: An Attentional Recurrent Neural Network for Occlusion-Aware Proactive Anomaly Detection in Field Robot Navigation
venue: IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS)
evidence: False positives "can lead to interruption of normal robot operation" appears only as motivation; the model is scored offline on a recorded dataset (Sec. IV), with no runtime halt or intervention described.
method: Attention-fused recurrent network (ROAR) predicts failure probability over the next 10 steps from LiDAR, camera and planned path, with learned sensor-occlusion heads.
evaluation: Offline on modified PAAD field dataset (TerraSentia, 6,869 test samples); baselines CNN-LSTM, NMFNet, PAAD, Graph Fusion; PR-AUC 0.800 vs PAAD 0.790, F1 0.639 vs 0.604; inference 4.99 ms on RTX 2070 Super.
contribution: Occlusion-aware attentional recurrent network that predicts navigation failures up to 10 steps ahead for a single field robot, improving offline PR-AUC and F1 over PAAD and graph-fusion baselines.
flag: Borderline: it is a proactive failure predictor that a monitor could use, but it is single-robot, evaluated offline only, and never shown to halt, override or hand off, so strict (a) fails; maintainer may prefer E4. PR-AUC gain over PAAD is small (0.800 vs 0.790 average over 5 seeds); full model has lower average F1 (0.639) than its No Occlusion (0.644) and Fixed Occlusion (0.651) ablations. 4.99 ms is desktop GPU network time, not edge hardware, and no latency constraint is stated.

title: Walking in Narrow Spaces: Safety-Critical Locomotion Control for Quadrupedal Robots with Duality-Based Optimization
venue: IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS)
evidence: "we add exponential DCBF duality constraint (10) to the NMPC (11)" (Sec. IV-B)
method: Quadruped NMPC on centroidal dynamics with exponential discrete CBF duality constraints between polytopic robot and obstacles, solved by SQP/HPIPM, tracked by a whole-body QP controller.
evaluation: Gazebo and real A1 quadruped; vs sphere/Euclidean-distance DCBF baseline: failure 20.8% vs 50.0% (map 1, 48 runs), 15 vs 0 completions (map 2); NMPC about 25 ms on i7-1165G7.
contribution: Embeds polytope-to-polytope discrete barrier constraints in a quadruped's nonlinear MPC so it can pass corridors narrower than sphere-based avoidance allows, solving onboard in about 25 ms.
flag: Single robot against static obstacles; the barrier is a constraint inside the planner/MPC, so strict-runtime (a) fails and no multi-agent aspect exists. Gap cells are generous: latency is reported (25 ms, CBF adds 1.55 ms) but not adapted to. Table I arithmetic looks off: map 2 lists 16 trials, 15 completions, yet 8.3% failure (15/16 would be 6.25%). Real-world result is only the statement that the robot never collided, with no counts. Robot width given as 0.3 m and 0.32 m in different sections.

title: Tight Collision Probability for UAV Motion Planning in Uncertain Environment
venue: IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS)
evidence: "the worst case result is that we reach the optimized trajectory with linearized collision probability" (Sec. V-F), with optimization time capped at 45 ms (Sec. V-G)
method: Tight collision-probability estimators (exact series expansion and Gauss-Hermite approximation) used as a chance constraint in quadrotor MPC, with a time-capped iteration that falls back to a linearized bound.
evaluation: Simulation with 20 or 12 moving humans, 2 h per method: success 96%/99% vs 90%/92% and 78%/85% for two baselines; compute 52.7/45.5 ms on i7-9750H; real flight on Orin NX, qualitative.
contribution: Computes a tight collision probability for a UAV among uncertain moving obstacles and uses it as a chance constraint in real-time MPC, raising simulated mission success to 96-99% over more conservative bounds.
flag: Weak include on (d) only: the 45 ms optimization cap with a guaranteed fallback and onboard Orin NX flight is the sole hook; if (d) is read as requiring a latency study, this is E1 (chance constraint inside a planner, single UAV, obstacles are humans not agents). Reported mean compute of 52.7 ms in the crowd scenario exceeds the stated 45 ms cap - check what the cap covers. Proposed method's reported risk (0.18/0.15) is higher than baseline [30] (0.016/0.004); the benefit is success rate and mission time. Real-world results have no collision rate; timing breakdown is only in Fig. 5. Table I estimator error 0.1257 vs linearized 0.4314; Table II times are normalized ratios.

title: CBFkit: A Control Barrier Function Toolbox for Robotics Applications
venue: IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS)
evidence: Sec. IV.A: "the CBF-QP controller (8) steers the HSR out of the path of the human agent in advance of any dangerous scenario" while the nominal LQR heads toward the human.
method: Open-source JAX toolbox that synthesises CBFs for deterministic, disturbed and stochastic control-affine models and wraps them as CBF-QP safety filters, with ROS support.
evaluation: Unicycle reach-avoid simulation tutorials and one Toyota HSR hardware run avoiding a walking human in a corridor. No baseline beyond nominal LQR, no rates; QP 'a few milliseconds'.
contribution: CBFkit is an open-source toolbox for building control-barrier-function safety filters across deterministic and stochastic robot models, demonstrated once on a mobile robot avoiding a person.
flag: Toolbox paper. Single qualitative hardware run, no collision/violation rate, no baseline or ablation. Multi-robot support is claimed in the abstract but no multi-robot experiment is reported. 'A few milliseconds' QP time has no hardware or benchmark behind it. Extracted text was partly garbled (Sec. III.E, listings).

title: Socially Integrated Navigation: A Social Acting Robot with Deep Reinforcement Learning
venue: IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS)
evidence: Reward is R_t = R_Nav + R_SA (Eq. 8, Sec. IV) with a -4 collision penalty; no filter, shield or halt layer separate from the learned policy is described.
method: PPO policy with LSTM encoder for crowd navigation whose reward penalises proxemic violations and velocity deviation it induces in nearby humans, so social behaviour emerges from interaction.
evaluation: Simulation only, circle crossing with 7 ORCA humans, 100 episodes; baseline socially-aware DRL; collisions 0 vs 1-2, proxemic violations 41 vs 177-554 (homogeneous), 34 vs 197-632 (heterogeneous). No hardware or latency.
contribution: Socially integrated DRL navigation policy trained with a reward on the robot's impact on surrounding humans, reducing proxemic violations and collisions versus a socially-aware DRL baseline in simulation.
flag: Safety lives in the training reward, which the prompt says does not meet (a). Fails the (c) primacy test: headline claim is social conformity and reduced impact on other agents, collisions are a secondary metric (0 vs 1-2 per 100 episodes, too few to be meaningful). Simulation only, no statistical tests despite "significantly" in the abstract. Table II column labels were partly garbled in extraction: verify values against the PDF.

title: Risk-Aware Non-Myopic Motion Planner for Large-Scale Robotic Swarm Using CVaR Constraints
venue: IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS)
evidence: "The key component of ROVER is imposing a CVaR constraint on the distribution of the Signed Distance Function" (Abstract); constraint CVaR_alpha(-sd) < eps sits inside the FTMPC planner (Sec. III-C).
method: ROVER: swarm modelled as a Gaussian mixture; finite-time MPC plans macroscopic motion with an analytic GMM-CVaR obstacle-distance constraint solved by sequential linear programming.
evaluation: MATLAB simulation, 25-1000 robots, static polygonal obstacles; vs formation control and predictive control; runtime, path length, min robot-robot and robot-obstacle distance; desktop i7, 0.21-1.09 s per step.
contribution: A CVaR-constrained density planner that moves swarms of up to 1000 robots past static obstacles with positive clearances where a predictive-control baseline collides, at about one second per planning step.
flag: Safety is a constraint inside the planner, not a runtime interceptor, so (a) fails. (c) is borderline: risk-aware avoidance is the headline, but hazards are static obstacles and safety is reported only as minimum distances (PC baseline goes negative, -4.10 m at 1000 robots), no collision rate. No ablation. Simulation only. Claimed 1 Hz at 1000 robots vs table 1.09 s per step. Maintainer may prefer include under (c).

title: Real-time Perceptive Motion Control using Control Barrier Functions with Analytical Smoothing for Six-Wheeled-Telescopic-Legged Robot Tachyon 3
venue: IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS)
evidence: Sec. V: up to 269 CBF constraints in the QP, with total computation time staying within the 1 ms control cycle on the onboard PC (closely paraphrased).
method: QP filter minimising deviation from user-commanded reference motion under exponential CBFs, with analytically smoothed separating-axis collision functions for body and toes.
evaluation: Timing benchmark vs SAT, GJK, LP; MuJoCo ablation without body CBF (collides); hardware stair climb of five steps. 1 kHz loop on onboard i7-8850H; no collision or success counts.
contribution: A CBF-QP with analytically smoothed collision functions runs perceptive safety filtering at 1 kHz on a six-wheeled legged robot's onboard PC, with up to 269 constraints per cycle.
flag: Strong latency evidence (SSAT evaluate plus differentiate 0.78 us vs LP 9.35 us; single CBF under 4 us; total within 1 ms onboard) but safety evidence is qualitative: ablation without the body CBF is a single simulated run that collides, hardware is one stair climb with no trial counts. Fails the quantitative-safety-metric requirement unless the maintainer accepts timing as the metric for (d). Single robot, static environment. Summary gave both '269 CBF constraints' and '140 CBFs' for the 20-obstacle case; verify which figure the 80 us timing belongs to. Slack variables allow minor constraint violation. Onboard i7 laptop-class CPU is edge only loosely.

title: Neural Control Barrier Functions for Safe Navigation
venue: IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS)
evidence: The QP safety filter "alters the commanded acceleration to ensure safety" (Sec. VI) and "brings the robot to a full stop in front of the final obstacle" (Sec. VI-B).
method: Neural CBF learned from LiDAR scan and state in a local frame, with a jointly trained controller; a QP safety filter minimally modifies nominal acceleration at 20 Hz onboard.
evaluation: Aerial Gym, 1000 rollouts per condition, 3/5/10 pillars: success 95.0-99.7% under noise and 0.1 s delay; unfiltered reference always collides. Quadrotor hallway and forest flights; 4.4 ms inference on Orin NX.
contribution: Learns a LiDAR-conditioned neural control barrier function and runs it as an onboard safety filter on a quadrotor, avoiding collision in 95-99.7% of simulated rollouts at 4.4 ms inference.
flag: Borderline. Single robot, static obstacles - no multi-agent aspect; kept out of E4 only because of the delay ablation (tau = 0.1 s) and edge inference figure. Baseline is weak: the no-filter case is a constant unsafe reference stated to always collide, not a competing method; ablations are noise and delay only. (d) is generous: 4.4 ms and 20 Hz are reported but no explicit latency budget is stated. Hardware results are graphical only (Fig. 6), no numbers. Human operator in forest test supplies adversarial reference, not a handoff. Table I verification violation rates 0.084/0.321/1.133%. Read via one WebFetch pass.

title: Safety Aware Task Planning via Large Language Models in Robotics
venue: IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS)
evidence: Sec. IV: safety constraints are enforced by 'minimally modifying the nominal controller by solving a Quadratic Programming (QP) based optimization problem'; Sec. VI: base controller 'wrapped with a CBF'.
method: SAFER: a Safety Planning LLM audits and revises a task-planning LLM's multi-robot plans, an LLM-as-a-Judge scores violations, and LLM safety constraints are parsed into CBF constraints for low-level control.
evaluation: 40 COHERENT tasks, 5 scenes, 1-3 heterogeneous robots; baseline GPT-4o planner without safety; average steps and safety violations; latency up to about 250 s (GPT-4o), 1500 s (DeepSeek-r1); two-robot hardware demo.
contribution: A safety-auditing LLM beside the task planner reduces judged safety violations in multi-robot LLM plans by about 47% (GPT-4o) and 77.5% (DeepSeek-r1) on 40 COHERENT tasks, with CBF enforcement demonstrated on two mobile manipulators.
flag: The quantified result is PLAN-TIME (LLM feedback loop scored by an LLM judge); the runtime CBF layer is only demonstrated qualitatively on hardware with no intervention counts, so (a) rests on an unmeasured component and (c) carries the inclusion. Violations are LLM-judged, not ground truth. Only 40 tasks, no ablation of modules. Latency/cost given only as a bar chart (values read from axes, approximate); adds two API calls per step. Text mislabels the DeepSeek result as S-4o. Humans present in workspace but no takeover.

title: CooperRisk: A Driving Risk Quantification Pipeline with Multi-Agent Cooperative Perception and Prediction
venue: IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS)
evidence: Sec. III: the time-indexed risk maps built from cooperative multi-agent prediction 'function as the cost objectives for downstream motion planning', and the headline outcome is a 44.35% decrease in conflict rate (Abstract).
method: V2X pipeline: late-fusion cooperative LiDAR perception, transformer multi-agent multi-modal trajectory prediction, severity-and-exposure risk maps over time, consumed as a soft cost term by an MPC planner.
evaluation: V2XPnP dataset, 2 CAVs plus 2 infrastructure sensors; baselines CV, LSTM, QCNet, MTR and a no-fusion ablation; conflict rate 0.04 versus 0.08, minADE 0.74 versus 0.77; delays 100-500 ms tested; no hardware.
contribution: Quantifies driving risk from cooperative V2X perception and multi-agent trajectory prediction as time-indexed risk maps for an MPC planner, reporting a 44.35% lower conflict rate than single-agent baselines.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - the stack analysed is a learned cooperative perception and prediction pipeline. Risk enters the MPC objective as a soft cost with no veto, halt or fail-safe, so (a) clearly fails and the include rests entirely on (c) with conflict rate as the headline measured outcome; a maintainer who reads the paper as prediction-first would call exclude-E1, and this is the record in the batch most likely to be overturned. Check: the 44.35% conflict-rate reduction does not follow from Table I (0.04 versus 0.08 is 50%) and the 37.31% average TOR reduction is not reproducible from the table; the ground-truth rows' EPA and TOR columns are ambiguous in the PDF; evaluation is open-loop on a dataset, communication delay is only a robustness sweep and not a design input, and no inference time or hardware is reported.

title: Enhancing Autonomous Driving Safety with Collision Scenario Integration
venue: IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS)
evidence: Sec. III-B: planner is trained by multi-target knowledge distillation on mixed regular and collision batches; Sec. V: 'A limitation of this work is that it focuses primarily on collision scenarios' - safety is learned in training, no runtime layer.
method: CollisionGen (GPT-4o plus LCTGen-style generator, rule filters) synthesises collision scenarios; SafeFusion trains a trajectory-vocabulary scoring planner on mixed regular and collision data by PDM-score distillation.
evaluation: Non-reactive closed-loop PDM score on Collision2k (200 test) and OpenScene/Navtest; baselines IDM, PDM-closed, PlanTF, Hydra-GT; NC 0.625 vs 0.480, total 0.415 vs 0.266; 8 V100 GPUs, no latency.
contribution: Synthesised collision scenarios mixed into planner training raise no-collision score on a 200-scenario collision test set from 0.480 to 0.625 without degrading regular-driving score.
flag: Training-time safety only (data augmentation plus loss), so (a) not met; ego planner vs logged agents, multi-agent only as scene context, (c) primacy doubtful. Sec. IV-C claims 30% collision-avoidance gain on hard samples but Table V shows NC 0.631 to 0.690 (about 9%). Table III Hydra-GT row assignment was ambiguous in extraction. Methods tags are a loose fit (imitation/distillation has no project tag).

title: Robots that Suggest Safe Alternatives
venue: IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS)
evidence: Sec V-B: SALT "checks preexecution if the closed-loop behavior is predicted to be safe and live"; Sec III: "If none of these samples meet the requirement, the user is asked to input a new goal."
method: Goal-conditioned reach-avoid value network, trained offline by RL, gates a human-specified goal before execution and proposes the most similar safe alternative goal, or returns the choice to the user.
evaluation: Simulated Dubins car and robosuite Franka; baselines Ensemble and RewardSum monitors; F1 0.95 vs 0.80/0.72 (nav), 0.83 vs 0.65/0.81 (manip); FPR 1.28% nav; no latency reported.
contribution: A pre-execution goal filter that uses a learned reach-avoid value function to reject unsafe or unreachable human-specified goals and suggest similar safe alternatives, outperforming ensemble and reward-sum monitors in simulation.
flag: Single robot, no multi-agent aspect; the gate acts once before execution, not during it, so runtime interception is pre-execution approval only. E4 is arguable; kept on the deferral-to-human aspect. Human handoff is asking the user for an accept/reject or a new goal, not a takeover; no live user study (similarity uses a simulated human; alignment uses annotations from 20 expert users). Simulation only, no real robot, privileged state. Table II SALT manipulation row lists TPR and FPR both as 13.23 in the extracted text - check against the PDF. Navigation SALT: TNR 57.00, TPR 37.34, FPR 1.28, FNR 4.38. Table I value-network F1 0.96 nav, 0.82 manip. No inference or filtering time given; training on one NVIDIA 4090 GPU. RelRank and alignment values are figure-only. Read via one summarised fetch of the PDF.

title: Safe Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning Volt-Var Optimization in Active Distribution Networks
venue: IEEE PES Innovative Smart Grid Technologies Conference Europe
evidence: "the trained DNN is deployed as a fixed safety mechanism, intervening only to replace unsafe actions during MARL execution" (Sec. III)
method: MADDPG agents set PV inverter reactive power from local observations; an offline OPF-supervised projection DNN maps unsafe actions into the feasible voltage and line-loading space at runtime.
evaluation: Modified IEEE 33-bus network with 6 PV systems, 3-min resolution, real Portuguese load and Elia PV data; base case vs MARL vs MARL plus DNN over day 730, day 736 and days 730-760; voltage violations 3.89% to 1.45% to 0%, mean loss 5.98% to 3.95% to 3.38%, min voltage 0.936 to 0.952 pu; a full day runs in under 30 s on an Intel i7-7700 with 16 GB RAM.
contribution: An offline-trained projection network acting as a runtime safety layer on decentralised MARL volt-var control eliminates voltage violations and cuts losses below unshielded MARL.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - MADDPG PV-inverter agents. Check criterion (c): the hazard is a network voltage or line-loading violation produced by joint agent actions rather than an agent-agent collision, so the maintainer may read this as single-system constraint enforcement; in Algorithm 2 the unsafe action is identified by running power flow after the action is taken, so pre-execution screening is assumed rather than demonstrated; safety rests entirely on DNN generalisation from OPF labels, with no guarantee despite the word "ensuring"; Table III for day 730 has no MARL-DNN column because the layer never fired; only 6 agents, simulation only, and no comparison with prior safe-RL baselines (authors note this as future work); the under-30-s figure is for a whole-day simulation, not a per-decision latency.

title: A Study on Prompt Injection Attack Against LLM-Integrated Mobile Robotic Systems
venue: IEEE International Symposium on Software Reliability Engineering Workshops (ISSREW)
evidence: Sec. IV-A d (Safety Validation): 'If the LLM fails to generate a safe command, it will be asked to generate a new command with error information'; Sec. IV-C adds per-modality reasoning that emits an is_attack flag at runtime.
method: Prompt-injection attack study on a GPT-4o-controlled mobile robot: obvious-malicious and goal-hijacking injections, countered by a security prompt plus response-based per-modality attack detection and a safety-validation command gate.
evaluation: EyeSim VR simulation, 100 s limit and 3 retries; no-defence versus defence applied; detection precision 0.8-1.0 and recall 0.13-0.54 with defence, MOER up to 0.67, response time to 9.3 s, tokens +2.9%.
contribution: Shows prompt injection can hijack an LLM-controlled mobile robot and that a security prompt with response-based detection recovers about 30.8% overall performance, while attack recall stays below 0.55.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - the guarded system is a GPT-4o robot controller, and the safety-validation step plus is_attack flag act at execution time, though the gate is a collision check that triggers regeneration rather than an attack-specific veto. Check: one robot in simulation, so the multi-agent aspect is nominal and (c) rests on the criterion's 'safety evaluation of LLM or tool-calling agents' clause; the GHI no-defence baseline is zero on every metric, so the WPI, WRI and WFI ratios divide by zero and the 30.8% headline gain is undefined as formulated; the threat model describes camera and LiDAR tampering but only the text instruction channel is attacked; no ablation separates secure prompting from response-based detection, and there is no real-robot test or hardware or latency baseline for the no-defence case.

title: Tackling Occlusions & Limited Sensor Range with Set-based Safety Verification
venue: IEEE International Conference on Intelligent Transportation Systems (ITSC)
evidence: Sec. V: 'Our proof-of-concept planner initializes the reference trajectory according to the intelligent driver model', and 'If the verification fails, the intended trajectory will be iteratively adapted until a verifiably safe trajectory' is found.
method: Set-based reachability verification of planned trajectories under occlusion and limited sensor range: hidden traffic is modelled as virtual obstacles with bounded state intervals, and unsafe trajectories fall back to the previous fail-safe.
evaluation: Three CommonRoad urban scenarios with static and dynamic occlusion; baseline is the same planner without occlusion-aware occupancy prediction; qualitative speed traces only, no collision or intervention rates, no hardware or computation time.
contribution: Verifies planned driving trajectories against worst-case hidden traffic by placing bounded-state virtual obstacles in occluded regions, so the vehicle slows pre-emptively instead of braking too late.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: no - the verified planner is the hand-designed intelligent driver model with no learned component, so the Pillar 1 scope ruling of 2026-11-13 excludes it despite a genuine runtime trajectory veto. Independently borderline exclude-E2: three qualitative case studies with speed traces (ego slows to about 2.4 m/s, full stop when an obstacle is present) and no collision, violation or intervention rate, no success counts and no computation-time figures. Maintainer may overturn to include if the ruling is relaxed for policy-agnostic verification layers that could wrap a learned planner.

title: Lane-Merging Using Policy-based Reinforcement Learning and Post-Optimization
evidence: Sec. IV-B: "After the post-optimization has finished an additional collision-check is performed to guarantee a high level of safety".
method: SAC policy rolled out greedily gives a reference trajectory; a Ceres nonlinear least-squares post-optimization (jerk, collision and deviation costs) plus a final collision check acts as safety layer before execution.
evaluation: Custom Divine-RL simulator, 3 merge scenarios, 1000 runs each; SAC alone 99.99%, 97.31%, 96.05% success vs zero collisions after optimization; i7-6700HQ, actor 2.24 ms per call, optimizer about 206 ms.
contribution: Post-optimization safety layer that refines a soft actor-critic lane-merging trajectory with a local optimizer and a collision check, removing the residual collisions of the learned policy in simulation.
flag: Weak include, borderline on both (a) and minimum evaluation - please check. (1) The paper calls the optimizer a safety layer and the optimized trajectory replaces the RL one, but it never says what happens when the final collision check fails; emergency braking on non-convergence is only suggested ("could be performed", Sec. V-C), not implemented. A strict reader could call this a planner refinement and exclude E1. (2) The post-optimization safety result is one sentence, "the collision rate drops to zero for the give time-horizon", with no count, run number or table; the only tabulated safety numbers are SAC-alone success rates (Table I), which serve as the baseline. If an unquantified zero is not accepted, this is exclude-E2. (3) Collisions are checked against other vehicles' trajectories recorded during the RL rollout, not re-simulated reactive traffic. (4) Other vehicles are scripted (constant velocity or IDM), 2-5 of them, so multi-agent is nominal and I left the multi-agent state cell empty. (5) Timing is not like-for-like: 112 ms for 50 actor steps vs 206 ms optimizer at N=40 quoted from prior work; no combined pipeline latency and no latency constraint, so (d) is not met. Jerk ratio optimizer/SAC 0.026 (two-lane) and 0.034 (highway), column labelled percent ambiguously; scenario labels inconsistent between Table I and text. Published year per record 2020, ITSC 2019 venue.

title: Reinforcement Learning with Uncertainty Estimation for Tactical Decision-Making in Intersections
venue: IEEE International Conference on Intelligent Transportation Systems (ITSC)
evidence: Sect. III-C Fallback action: 'a fallback action a_safe is used when c_v > c_v^safe for all available actions'; Sect. IV states the criterion is applied at test time only, not during training.
method: Ensemble of randomized-prior deep Q-networks; at execution the coefficient of variation of the ensemble Q-values vetoes low-confidence actions and a hand-coded give-way fallback is executed instead.
evaluation: Custom intersection simulator; 100 test episodes, 5 seeds, in- and out-of-distribution; baselines DQN and no-criterion ablation; chosen-action c_v mean 0.04 (99th pct 0.15) vs threshold 0.2; criterion removed all in-distribution collisions; no hardware or latency.
contribution: An uncertainty-gated runtime veto on a learned intersection-driving policy: actions whose ensemble Q-value spread exceeds a threshold are replaced by a give-way fallback, removing in-distribution collisions.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - the guarded policy is a deep RL agent and the veto itself is a threshold rule, which the scope ruling allows. Check that no numeric collision count appears in the text at all: collision rates are only in Figs. 4 and 7, and 'removed all collisions' plus 'most of the collisions can be avoided' out-of-distribution are the only stated safety results. Other vehicles are scripted IDM, so (c) fails the primacy and learned-agent test. No latency, no hardware, no human handoff.

title: Merging Control in Mixed Traffic with Safety Guarantees: A Safe Sequencing Policy with Optimal Motion Control
venue: IEEE International Conference on Intelligent Transportation Systems (ITSC)
evidence: Sec. V: "the new safe sequence prevents excessive slowing down, especially in the main road." Safety enters only as CBF constraints inside each CAV's MPC; no separate filter overrides a nominal action.
method: Roadside coordinator resequences merging vehicles from shortest-distance-first when an HDV could violate a merging constraint; each CAV runs decentralised MPC with CBF constraints; yield mode for aggressive HDVs.
evaluation: VISSIM plus MATLAB/CasADi two-road merge, 100 cars, 0-100% CAV penetration; baseline SDF sequencing; travel time, energy, fuel only; i5 CPU, 0.06 s average solve vs 0.1 s step.
contribution: A safe-sequencing policy with CBF-constrained MPC for mixed-traffic merging that cuts travel time and fuel against shortest-distance-first ordering, with no collision or violation rate reported.
flag: Title matches. Safety is a constraint inside the planner, so (a) fails under the strict runtime reading; (c) fails primacy: measured outcomes are travel time 17.5 vs 18.5 s at 20% and fuel, not collisions. E2 would apply equally (no safety metric). At 80% penetration SDF travel time 16.5 beats SS 16.59 despite the text saying SS uniformly outperforms. HDV aggressiveness estimator is assumed, not implemented. 0.06 s solve time is for N1=10,N2=5 only. Drafted from model-summarised PDF reads, not line-by-line.

title: Courteous MPC for Autonomous Driving with CBF-Inspired Risk Assessment
venue: IEEE International Conference on Intelligent Transportation Systems (ITSC)
evidence: Sec. III-C: "By the constraint of Eq. (16a), we can guarantee safety with at least 1-alpha probability" - the CVaR risk is a constraint and cost penalty inside the MPC.
method: MPC for an automated vehicle with a CVaR of a CBF-style pairwise severity function as both hard constraint and weighted cost penalty; the weight sets how much space is left to others.
evaluation: highway-env with IDM traffic and NGSIM US101 replay vs risk-aware MPC (ablation) and Batch MPC; avg speed 14.96 vs 14.89 vs 13.80 m/s; min distance in figures only.
contribution: A CVaR-of-barrier-function risk term in MPC makes an automated vehicle leave more space to neighbours while keeping average speed, with a per-step 1-alpha probabilistic safety bound.
flag: Constraint inside a planner, so not (a); single ego vehicle with scripted/replayed traffic, so multi-agent only nominally and (c) primacy fails. No collision rate, TTC, compute time or Hz; safety evidence is minimum distance in figures (10 trials) - would also fail minimum evaluation (E2). Trajectory-level guarantee degrades as (1-alpha)^k (Remark 2), alpha=0.1. Simulation only; vehicle counts not stated.

title: Safety Score: A Quantitative Approach to Guiding Safety-Aware Autonomous Vehicle Computing System Design
evidence: "we propose the safety score, a metric that measures the level of AV safety based on computing system response time and external factors to guide safety-aware computing system design" (Sec. V, Safety Score)
method: Safety metric derived from the RSS safe-distance model that maps instantaneous AV computing response time, velocity, acceleration and braking distance to a non-linear score guiding system design.
evaluation: Level-4 fleet field study (3 months, 200 h, 2,000 miles) plus industrial simulator; safety-score-guided CPU-GPU resource management vs tail, average and maximum latency; LiDAR latency to 90ms, response time to 500ms; Xeon plus Titan V.
contribution: Proposes the safety score, an RSS-derived metric linking instantaneous computing response time to AV collision risk, and shows traditional latency metrics misrank resource-management designs.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: which - the measured stack is a Level-4 AV perception pipeline with learned LiDAR modules, but nothing is intercepted and no action can be overridden, so (a) fails and only (d) plausibly holds. Check the evaluation floor: the only experiment is Figure 7, a normalized comparison of five resource-management strategies in the authors' proprietary simulator, with no absolute values, no collision, hazard or intervention rate, and no evidence that a higher safety score yields fewer crashes. All latency numbers I report are read off Figures 2 and 4. Derivation from RSS is algebraic, not a proved safety guarantee. Likeliest of my six to be overturned to include as background under (d).

title: Adaptive Safe Merging Control for Heterogeneous Autonomous Vehicles using Parametric Control Barrier Functions
evidence: Sec. IV (controller): a QP minimises ||u_i - u_bar_i||^2 subject to input bounds and the Parametric-CBF constraint, minimally modifying the nominal acceleration (closely paraphrased).
method: Parametric-CBF replaces the fixed class-K term with a learned weighted sum of odd powers of h; ego estimates the other driver's weights by ridge regression and adapts its own QP safety filter.
evaluation: Numerical ramp-merging simulation, 2-3 double-integrator vehicles; compared with fixed-gain CBF and no-prediction; alpha RMSE 6.32e-6 over 30 trials, merge time 39.6% and 16.1% faster; no collision metric, hardware or latency.
contribution: A parametric control barrier function whose class-K weights are learned online from other drivers lets a merging vehicle adapt its conservatism, shortening merge time, but safety is shown by proof only.
flag: Title matches. Mechanism is a genuine runtime CBF-QP filter, but no quantitative safety metric: no collision or violation counts and no minimum distance, only distance plots and Theorem 4 (which assumes learned alpha is correct and the other vehicle is known to assume constant velocity). Reported numbers are efficiency (39.6%, 10.1%, 16.1% faster) and parameter RMSE against simulated ground truth. Two to three vehicles only; simulator unnamed. Abstract has no numbers. Evidence field is a paraphrase, not a verbatim quote, and its section number is my guess. Drafted from model-summarised PDF reads.

title: Provable Probabilistic Safety and Feasibility-Assured Control for Autonomous Vehicles using Exponential Control Barrier Functions
evidence: Abstract: the approach 'leverage[s] an optimization-based technique to provide a solution feasibility guarantee in run time'; per-step optimisation keeps u close to the nominal CLF/NMPC input under probabilistic eCBF constraints (Sec. III-B, IV).
method: Probabilistic exponential CBF constraints for stochastic dynamics; per-step optimisation picks control and CBF gain vector K_alpha close to nominal CLF or NMPC input, assuring feasibility.
evaluation: Matlab: 250 random lane-change scenarios plus two intersection scenarios; four baselines/ablations; collision, infeasibility, unfinished, success rates (values only in figures); no hardware or timing.
contribution: Extends exponential control barrier functions to stochastic vehicle dynamics with a run-time feasibility guarantee, reporting the lowest collision and infeasibility rates among four baselines in simulated lane changes and intersections.
flag: Borderline. Collision/infeasibility/success rates are reported only in Figs. 2 and 4; I could not read any numeric value from the text, so the quantitative-metric test rests on the figures - check them. Filter role is implicit (min deviation from nominal), no explicit veto step. Only the ego is controlled; other vehicles are constant-speed or non-avoiding, safety enforced pairwise, so multi-agent is nominal and E4 is arguable. Intersection trial count not stated. No latency figures; paper itself says the 2-norm chi-square variant is not real-time capable.

title: Modeling Interactions of Autonomous Vehicles and Pedestrians with Deep Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning for Collision Avoidance
evidence: Sect. V Conclusion: the approach aims at 'retaining reliable collision avoidance even under uncertain pedestrian behavior'; Sect. IV-A reports collision rate as the primary measured outcome (0.0 percent at low pedestrian noise, 0.135 percent at alpha=0.5).
method: Independent double-dueling DQN agents for an autonomous vehicle and, in setting-2, the pedestrian at an unmarked crosswalk; collisions enter only as a reward penalty, with no runtime constraint or override.
evaluation: Custom 2D crosswalk simulator, 8 seeds over 8000 episodes, pedestrian observation noise swept 0.0-0.5; settings: learned AV vs rule-based pedestrian, both learned, both rule-based; collision rate 0.0-0.135 percent; episode duration up 23 percent (4.663 s to 5.722 s); no hardware or latency.
contribution: Deep multi-agent RL models vehicle-pedestrian crosswalk interaction with both parties learning, holding collision rates near zero under pedestrian observation noise at the cost of longer crossings.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - both agents are DQN policies, but nothing guards them: no filter, veto, shield or monitor at execution time, so (a) fails and the record rests entirely on (c). This is the record most likely to be overturned to E1: only two agents, the collision avoidance is the learned policy itself rather than a safety mechanism, and no numeric collision rate is given for the rule-based setting-X baseline (figures only). The text is also internally inconsistent about which setting is best at alpha=0.5.

title: Refining Obstacle Perception Safety Zones via Maneuver-Based Decomposition
evidence: Sec. I: zones are usable 'in a drop-in fashion, sub-selecting objects to consider for AV perception metrics computation'; online use is 'a simple grid look-up along with an optional interpolation operation' (Sec. V-A).
method: Offline Hamilton-Jacobi reachability computes maneuver-conditioned obstacle perception safety zones via a two-phase temporal-convolution decomposition, shrinking the region where a contender must be perceived.
evaluation: Custom simulation, adversarial MPC contender, lane change and 90-degree turn, 22,944 initial conditions; baseline without maneuver constraint; completeness and zone volume; RTX 3090, 979 s and 465 s offline.
contribution: Derives maneuver-specific perception safety zones with Hamilton-Jacobi reachability, cutting zone volume to 30.3% and 24.0% of a maneuver-agnostic baseline with at most 0.2% false negatives in simulation.
flag: Offline perception-requirement analysis for metric computation, not a mechanism that overrides or halts an action; none of (a)-(e) is the subject. Abstract 'up to 76% size reduction' matches Table II (90-degree turn 24.0% of baseline); text also says 3-4x. Table I as I read it: lane change TP 12.4, TN 59.5, FP 18.1, FN 0.0 - sums to 90%, so one value was probably misread from the PDF; verify (turn row 8.8/75.1/15.9/0.2 sums to 100). False negatives are nonzero for the turn (0.2%), attributed to grid error, 1.34 m inflation suggested. Two-agent only; online lookup latency not quantified; compute times are offline GPU.

title: Reachability-Based Contingency Planning Against Multi-Modal Predictions with Branch MPC
evidence: Sec. III: 'the AV follows a consensus plan satisfying all scenario constraints until k_b' - safety comes from reachable-set corridor constraints inside the branch MPC; no independent monitor or fallback is described.
method: Branch MPCC against multi-modal Motion Transformer predictions: zonotope reachable-set driving corridors per mode, clustered into scenarios, with reachability bounding the latest feasible branching (decision postponing) time.
evaluation: 100 Monte Carlo IDM merging scenarios, 3 agents; baselines CMPC, BMPC noSS, BMPC UVD, RSCMPC, noMaxDP ablation; collision 0% vs 6%, success 96% vs 87%; 31+33 ms compute; hardware unstated.
contribution: Reachability-derived driving corridors make branch MPC scale independently of agent count and bound how long a decision can be postponed, giving 0% collisions and 96% success in 100 merging scenarios.
flag: Constraint inside a planner, so (a) not met under the strict runtime rule; maintainer may still want it for RQ2 because maximum decision postponing (latest feasible branching time, e.g. required 1.7 s vs max 0.9 s) is a time-to-irreversibility notion - gap cell credited on that basis, generously. Collision rate with baselines and ablation is reported but only 100 simulated scenarios with 3 agents; noMaxDP ablation already has 0% collisions. 'Runtimes under 100 ms' for 12-agent intersection is stated without hardware; '+' split of timing in Table I inferred. Predictor dataset and open/closed-loop status not stated. No real vehicle.

title: Safe Reinforcement Learning with Scene Decomposition for Navigating Complex Urban Environments
evidence: Sect. III-B: 'A safety threshold lambda is used to constrain the agent to take actions inside the set' and 'In cases where the set is empty, the agent then executes the safest possible action given by the model checker.'
method: Deep Q policy trained on a canonical ego-car-pedestrian-obstacle scenario; per-instance utilities and model-checked safety probabilities are fused by minimum so unsafe actions are masked online; RNN-ensemble belief updater.
evaluation: Custom POMDP simulator with sensor noise and ray-traced occlusion, five scenarios, 10000 simulations per policy; baselines rule-based, safe rule-based and unmasked RL, plus updater and decomposition ablations; masked policies reported zero collisions; belief update under 100 ms; policy slower than the 0.1 s step beyond 7 cars and 1 pedestrian.
contribution: Scene decomposition lets an offline model checker mask a learned intersection policy at runtime, giving zero collisions across 10000 occluded multi-agent simulations while staying roughly as fast as unmasked RL.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - a learned deep Q policy masked by an offline-computed model checker, which the scope ruling allows. Check that collision and step counts appear only in Fig. 7: the text says 'the masked policies presented zero collisions across the 10000 simulations' without naming which policies, so the headline number is unverifiable from the prose. The safe set is computed in a fully observable discretised model rather than from the noisy belief, so the guarantee may not transfer. (d) rests on a real-time analysis, not a measurement, and no hardware is named.

title: Coordination and Trajectory Prediction for Vehicle Interactions via Bayesian Generative Modeling
evidence: Sect. III: a VRNN feature extractor or mutual-information encoder infers a latent macro-level coordination variable, which conditions a Bayesian conditional GAN that generates multimodal future positions for the interacting vehicles.
method: Hierarchical Coordination and Trajectory Prediction System: latent coordination recognition (VRNN features or MI-maximising encoder) plus a coordination-conditioned Bayesian CGAN with SGHMC weight uncertainty.
evaluation: NGSIM US-101 ramp merging and lane change plus a drone-collected roundabout dataset; 4 s and 2 s horizons; baselines HMM, GNB, MLP, P-GRU, CVAE, CGAN; recognition precision-recall-F1 up to 0.91-0.93-0.92; final displacement 0.232 m vs 0.367 m for the categorized variant; no safety metric, no latency.
contribution: A hierarchical Bayesian generative model infers a latent coordination variable between interacting vehicles and conditions multimodal trajectory generation on it, improving both coordination recognition and prediction accuracy.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: no system is guarded - this is a (b) predictor only, so RQ5 is capped at 2 and it gets no safety credit. Check whether the latent coordination variable is enough to count as a world model over multi-agent state rather than a plain trajectory predictor; if not it falls to E1 under the Pillar 2 scope. Table II's column layout is garbled in the source and dataset labels are missing, so some displacement values cannot be assigned to a model or dataset with confidence, and the C-BCGAN vs C-CGAN weight-uncertainty ablation is qualitative only.

title: Graph Neural Networks for Modelling Traffic Participant Interaction
evidence: Sect. IV-V: vehicles are nodes of a scene graph and the GCN or GAT regresses x-y displacement for the next 5 s from 5 s of history; there is no latent state, no safety mechanism and, as the authors note, no closed- or open-loop simulation.
method: Graph convolutional and graph attention networks over a traffic scene graph with residual weights, relative-position edge features and a feed-forward head, regressing future displacements directly.
evaluation: NGSIM I-80 and HighD, 5 s horizon, 10 runs per variant; baselines constant velocity, IDM and an interaction-free feed-forward model; GAT mean displacement 1.89 m vs 2.78 m feed-forward on NGSIM (0.47 m vs 0.45 m on HighD); graph-construction and component ablations; no latency or hardware.
contribution: Graph attention over a traffic scene graph cuts 5 s trajectory prediction error about 30 percent against an interaction-free baseline on NGSIM, with ablations isolating edge features and residual connections.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: no system is guarded, gated or monitored. Judged against the Pillar 2 scope this is a plain trajectory regressor on a scene graph with no latent or world model and no safety metric, so E1 under the batch rule. The maintainer may overturn to include as graph-learning architecture evidence, since the graph-construction ablations over multi-agent state are the most directly useful part of the batch. Note that on HighD the interaction-free feed-forward baseline matches the GNNs (0.45 m vs 0.47 m), so the interaction claim rests on NGSIM alone.

title: Spatiotemporal Scene-Graph Embedding for Autonomous Vehicle Collision Prediction
evidence: Abstract and Sec. III: 'we propose SG2VEC, a spatio-temporal scene-graph embedding methodology', formulating collision prediction as time-series classification over per-frame scene graphs of the ego vehicle and its neighbours.
method: Mask R-CNN builds per-frame scene graphs; MR-GCN with SAGPool yields graph embeddings; an LSTM and MLP classify a future collision from the embedding sequence.
evaluation: CARLA synthetic and real dash/Honda lane changes; 5-fold CV vs DPM baseline plus pooling and LSTM ablations; acc 0.9095 vs 0.8834, MCC 0.5385 vs 0.2912; 0.4828 ms on DRIVE PX 2.
contribution: Shows that graph embeddings of inter-vehicle scene structure predict collisions earlier and more accurately than a prior deep-learning model, at under 0.5 ms on automotive edge hardware.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: no - the detector only predicts and nothing is intercepted, and the analysed traffic agents are human-driven or CARLA-scripted, so (c) fails the Pillar 1 scope ruling and only (b) plus edge latency carry the record; enters as predictor evidence with RQ5 capped at 2. Body numbers disagree with the abstract: Sec. IV-B.1 gives average synthetic MCC 0.5860 while the conclusion gives 0.5055, and the claimed 39.07% earlier prediction computes to about 38.1% from Table II; the 122.7 ms lead-time figure needs checking.

title: Learning-Based UAV Path Planning for Data Collection With Integrated Collision Avoidance
evidence: A penalty is "introduced to penalize collision with other UAVs" (Sec. III-B.3) - collision avoidance is a reward term in D3QN training, not a runtime mechanism.
method: D3QN path planning for one data-collecting UAV among non-cooperative ORCA-driven UAVs; collision, obstacle and no-fly-zone penalties are in the reward; policy acts directly at test time.
evaluation: Custom sim, 5000 test realisations, vs DQN/DDQN/Dueling DQN, waypoint benchmark and no-avoidance ablation: SR 91.5-95.5%, CR 3.3-3.9%; J=20 CR 0.6% vs 29.1%/26.4%; i7 CPU; no latency.
contribution: A dueling double deep Q-network learns UAV data-collection paths that also avoid collisions with other UAVs, reaching above 91% mission success with low collision rates in simulation.
flag: Collision avoidance is a training reward term (explicitly not (a)); paper is primarily about data-collection path planning, so (c) primacy fails, although it does report collision rate with an ablation (0.6% vs 29.1% at J=20) - maintainer could argue borderline (c). Text cites 0.9% CR for setting 3 at J=12 while Table IV gives 0.4%. "Real-time" claimed without any inference timing. Single learning UAV; others follow ORCA.

title: M-SET: Multi-Drone Swarm Intelligence Experimentation with Collision Avoidance Realism
evidence: Sec III-A: "augments the navigation and sensing plans selected via swarm intelligence to prevent the potential collisions"; Sec IV-C: "the optimization process is performed offline and remotely"
method: Indoor Crazyflie testbed for swarm sensing; plans chosen by collective learning (EPOS) are augmented offline by a priority-weighted artificial potential field before execution.
evaluation: Crazyflie 2.1 lab with 4 drones plus software runs on 40 pNEUMA city areas; baselines EPOS, EPOS-CA, Greedy-PF; energy, collision risk, sensing mismatch shown in figures; no latency.
contribution: M-SET is a low-cost indoor multi-drone sensing testbed that adds potential-field collision avoidance to collective-learning plan selection and reports lower collision risk and sensing mismatch than scheduling baselines.
flag: Testbed paper; primary claim is the experimentation platform, not a safety mechanism, so (c) fails primacy. Collision avoidance edits plans offline before flight; real-time avoidance is listed as future work, so not (a). Collision risk (d_r/d) is compared against EPOS, EPOS-CA and Greedy-PF but only in Fig. 7(b)/(c); no numeric collision values appear in the text and there are no tables - if the maintainer wants to credit (c) the figure must be read by eye. Only numbers in text: energy estimate error about 120.4 J, sensing mismatch about 21.93% lower than EPOS-CA, about USD 600 per drone. Drone count ambiguous (4 stated, caption says high number). "Low-latency edge proxies" is descriptive only. Abstract contains no numbers. No ablation, no human takeover.

title: Safe and Robust Observer-Controller Synthesis Using Control Barrier Functions
evidence: "This command is filtered using a safety critical QP" (Sec. IV-3); QP minimises ||u - pi_des||^2 under a CBF constraint evaluated on the state estimate (Remark 1, Thm 3).
method: CBF-QP safety filter made robust to state-estimation error, via either ISS-observer barrier tightening or bounded-error observers requiring a common safe input over the uncertainty set.
evaluation: Sim double integrator and planar quadrotor; hardware Crazyflie 2.0 with Vicon. Baseline CBF-QP on estimate crashes; proposed stays safe. Figures only; no solve times.
contribution: Shows a CBF safety filter fed an estimated state can violate safety, and gives two observer-controller interconnections that keep a quadrotor safe under bounded estimation error.
flag: Single-agent filter with no multi-agent, latency or handoff aspect, hence E4. Also weak on minimum evaluation: baseline exists but safety outcome is shown only in figures (crash vs no crash), no tabulated violation metric - E2 is equally defensible. EKF 99.8 percent confidence set is assumed, not verified. Compute platform and QP timing not reported despite real-time claim.

title: Safe Control for Nonlinear Systems With Stochastic Uncertainty via Risk Control Barrier Functions
evidence: Sec. I: risk-sensitive controllers are 'designed to minimally invasive with respect to a given system legacy controller'.
method: Risk control barrier functions for discrete-time stochastic nonlinear systems using coherent risk measures such as CVaR; a one-step optimisation filters a legacy controller; finite-time variant recovers safety.
evaluation: Simulated cart-pole with additive noise; nominal controller versus expectation (beta=1) versus CVaR (beta=0.01) filters; trajectories only; solve about 0.7 ms on a laptop (1428 Hz).
contribution: Defines risk control barrier functions that filter a legacy controller so a coherent risk measure of the barrier stays safe, with finite-time reachability of the safe set.
flag: Meets (a) as a minimally invasive filter but the evidence is qualitative: no table, no violation rate; the expectation filter is said to violate 'frequently' with no count. Only numbers are the bound t* <= 0.3667 s versus observed 0.08 s and the 0.7 ms solve time on an unspecified 'modern laptop'. Latency cell credited on that single figure only; drop it if you require a stated deadline. Single agent; Boolean compositions of safe sets are proved but untested; a_max value not given.

title: Safety Certification for Stochastic Systems via Neural Barrier Functions
evidence: "we parameterize a barrier function as a neural network" (Abstract); Sec. 5: "our framework still requires to first train a neural network and then certify it" - offline certification only.
method: Neural-network stochastic barrier function trained with CROWN-IBP robust training and certified offline by linear programs plus branch-and-bound, giving a lower bound on finite-horizon safety probability.
evaluation: Linear 2-D, polynomial 2-D, Dubins car 3-D; baseline SoS barriers; certified P_safe 0.999969/0.991664/0.870272 vs SoS best 0.999761/0.681383/fail; i7-6700K+GTX1060, hours offline.
contribution: Certifies a lower bound on the safety probability of single-agent stochastic systems offline using neural barrier functions, beating sum-of-squares barriers on three small benchmarks.
flag: Offline verification of a given closed-loop system; no runtime filter, single agent, no latency figure (only training+certification time of hours). Ablation on epsilon is qualitative (contour plots). Horizon H=10.

title: Disturbance Observers for Robust Safety-Critical Control With Control Barrier Functions
evidence: "We incorporate the disturbance observer into the CBF-based control design with the following modification of (4)" (Sec. IV); Fig. 5 caption: "The proposed controller maintains safety despite the delay".
method: High-gain disturbance observer feeds its estimate into the CBF condition with a robustness margin sized to the observer error bound; closed-form safe controller for connected cruise control.
evaluation: Sim only: connected automated truck following human-driven vehicle, real speed/grade data. Baselines: no compensation, worst-case robust CBF, two DOB-CBF methods. Input delay 0.8 s; critical 3.2 s.
contribution: Couples a disturbance observer with a control barrier function so safety holds under unmodelled disturbance with less conservatism than worst-case design, and analyses stability under input delay.
flag: Safety results are qualitative (h goes negative or not, in figures); no tabulated violation or intervention metric despite four baselines, hence E2 - maintainer may judge the baseline comparison enough. runtime_interceptor set to no because the evaluated controller is a closed-form CBF-based law (Eq. 28) rather than a filter over a separate nominal; the general safe-set form could be used as a filter, so (a) is DOUBTFUL either way. Latency credited for constant input delay analysis (tau=0.8 s, tau_cr about 3.14 s rounded to 3.2 s) - constant delay, not jitter, and stability not safety-proof under delay. Two vehicles but lead is an exogenous reference; not multi-agent. No hardware or timing.

title: Differentiable Safe Controller Design Through Control Barrier Functions
evidence: Sec. I/III: NN-diff-QP is a neural network followed by a differentiable CBF-QP layer, and NN-gauge maps the network output into the CBF-safe input set, both active at execution time.
method: Two safe-by-construction neural controllers trained end-to-end: a differentiable CBF-QP projection layer and a gauge map onto the CBF-safe input set, compared with post-hoc QP filtering.
evaluation: Simulated adaptive cruise control and two-aircraft collision avoidance, 5 initial states; baselines MPC, unfiltered NN, NN-QP; Safe/Unsafe label, cost 258.3 vs 818.2 (ACC); solve time 0.28-1.30 s.
contribution: Embedding a control-barrier-function projection or gauge map inside a neural controller keeps closed-loop behaviour safe while cutting the cost penalty of post-hoc QP filtering, in two simulated control tasks.
flag: BORDERLINE E2 vs include: the mechanism is a genuine runtime safety layer with baselines, but safety is reported only as a binary Safe/Unsafe label per controller over 5 initial states (Tables I-II), not a violation rate; the quantitative results are trajectory cost and solve time. If the maintainer accepts the binary label plus cost-of-filtering as the safety metric this is an include with RQ5 interest (NN-QP cost 818.2 vs NN-diff-QP 258.3). Solve times (0.26-3.11 s ACC, 0.69-44.1 s aircraft) are probably per closed-loop rollout, not per step; hardware is unspecified Google Colab, so the latency cell is weak and may be dropped. Two aircraft are jointly controlled by one controller. Simulation only. One full-PDF fetch via summariser.

title: Learning Safety Filters for Unknown Discrete-Time Linear Systems
evidence: The filter "minimally modifies (in terms of a distance metric) nominal control actions to ensure safety with high probability" (Sec. I)
method: Projection-type safety filter for unknown discrete-time linear systems: constraints tightened using regularised least-squares model confidence and learned noise covariance; tightening shrinks as data accumulates.
evaluation: Theory only in the arXiv text: probabilistic safety theorems and asymptotic tightening rates; no simulation, no baseline, no empirical metric, no hardware or timing.
contribution: Gives a data-driven safety filter for unknown linear systems that minimally alters the nominal input and guarantees next-step safety with probability at least 1-delta, with conservatism vanishing as data grows.
flag: The arXiv version has NO numerical example or experiment section (headings checked: Intro, Problem Formulation, Preliminary Results, Data-Driven Safety Filter, Noise Covariance, Conclusions, proof appendices). The published L-CSS version might add one - check before finalising. Formal result without evaluation, single system, so E2 (E4 also arguable). Feasibility of the filter is assumed, no fallback when infeasible.

title: Parameterized Barrier Functions to Guarantee Safety Under Uncertainty
evidence: Sec. III Remark 1 (eq. 11): the robust controller is a QP minimising ||u - k_d||^2 subject to the robust barrier constraint, i.e. it modifies the desired controller only as needed.
method: Parameterized barrier function H = h - h* with a disturbance-compensation term; safety parameter h* sized from disturbance-estimate error gives a tight forward-invariant set under uncertainty.
evaluation: Simulation only: one inverted pendulum with bounded unknown force. Compared under/over-estimated disturbance bounds and ISSf sets, by trajectory plots. No rates, no hardware, no timing.
contribution: Parameterized barrier functions give a tighter certified safe set than input-to-state-safety when the disturbance bound is only estimated, shown on a simulated pendulum.
flag: Single-agent theory letter; evaluation is qualitative trajectory plots on one pendulum, no collision/violation/intervention rate, so fails minimum evaluation. E4 would also fit (single-agent filter, no multi-agent/latency/handoff aspect). QP implementation and solve time not discussed.

title: Disturbance-Robust Backup Control Barrier Functions: Safety Under Uncertain Dynamics
evidence: Sec. IV-B: "Our approach obeys the norm constraint on the angular velocity in the presence of unknown time-varying disturbances"; Sec. III Remark 2: "the feasibility of the optimization problem (DR-bCBF-QP) is not guaranteed."
method: Backup CBF safe set tightened by bounds on the deviation between nominal and disturbed backup flows; a QP minimally modifies the primary control, with the backup law as fallback.
evaluation: Simulation only: double integrator and rigid-body spacecraft. Baseline standard backup CBF, which violates the constraint multiple times (no count). No numeric metrics, timing or hardware.
contribution: Disturbance-robust backup control barrier functions that keep an online safety filter valid under bounded unknown disturbances by tightening the implicit safe set along the backup trajectory.
flag: Runtime filter with a backup fallback, but single-agent and no quantitative safety metric: baseline violations are described only as multiple times (E4 also applies). Negligible computational cost is claimed without any number. Backup-horizon reasoning is weakly related to time-to-irreversibility but not addressed as such, so the cell is not ticked. Read via one summarised fetch.

title: Data-Driven Input-Output Control Barrier Functions
evidence: Sec III: QP finds the input closest to u_l, 'a potentially unsafe input, also known as nominal or learning input', subject to the barrier decay condition
method: Input-output CBF built from a single measured trajectory via behavioural (Hankel) predictor; a one-step QP filter minimally alters the nominal input, no state model needed.
evaluation: Simulated second-order LTI system with two-step input delay, 17 noise-free samples; ablation over lambda_min 0.1/0.3/1 only; no competing filter, no numeric safety metric, no timing.
contribution: Data-driven input-output control barrier function that filters unsafe inputs for an unknown linear system using one short trajectory, shown on a delayed second-order simulation.
flag: Meets (a) by mechanism but single-agent toy LTI, no baseline filter and no numeric violation/intervention metric (plots only). Plant has input delay but latency is not the subject. E4 equally arguable. Figures not visible in fetched text.

title: Distributed Risk-Sensitive Safety Filters for Uncertain Discrete-Time Systems
evidence: "feasibility of (9b) for one agent immediately ensures the satisfaction of (6) for the entire multi-agent" system (Sec. III-B); each agent minimally modifies its nominal action subject to a risk-sensitive CBF condition
method: Distributed risk-sensitive CBF safety filters from a learned value function: each agent filters its nominal action using worst-case anticipation of others, switching to an always-feasible proximity filter otherwise.
evaluation: Simulation: two agents coupled to a mass (20 roll-outs) and 2-4 agents with collision constraints (10 roll-outs); versus unfiltered policy and centralised filter; violations, MSE in figures only; no timing.
contribution: Lets each agent run its own risk-sensitive safety filter over shared global state without a negotiation round, closely matching a centralised filter on constraint violations for up to four simulated agents.
flag: Quantitative safety metrics (constraint violations, deviation MSE) exist but only as curves in Figs. 1-3; no numeric values in the text, so none are quoted here - maintainer should read the figures to confirm the minimum-evaluation bar. Baselines are the unfiltered nominal policy and a centralised filter from prior work. Scale is tiny (M up to 4) and authors concede limited scalability and need for full global state. Fetch tool's reading (unverified): with epsilon 0 as used in experiments the probability bound in Eq. 7 may be vacuous. No hardware, no latency figures; only a claim that the proximity filter is an SOCP with negligible overhead.

title: Reachability-Based Trajectory Safeguard (RTS): A Safe and Fast Reinforcement Learning Safety Layer for Continuous Control
evidence: Sec. IV-A.3: 'we adjust an unsafe choice of k by attempting to replace it with a safe one', and if no safe parameter exists the robot continues its previous failsafe braking plan (Sec. II-A.2, persistent safety).
method: Offline forward reachable sets over parameterised trajectories; at each receding-horizon step the RL agent's chosen trajectory parameter is checked and replaced by the nearest safe one, else failsafe braking continues.
evaluation: MATLAB simulation of car lane change, 12-D quadrotor tunnel and cartpole; vs baseline TD3/DDPG, two RTD variants and discrete RTS; collisions 0% vs 17.6%, 100% and 1.4%; planning 0.058-0.22 s inside 2 s and 1 s budgets.
contribution: Wraps a reinforcement-learning policy in a reachability-based runtime safeguard that adjusts unsafe trajectory parameters and falls back to a failsafe stop, giving zero simulated collisions while the policy still learns.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - TD3 and DDPG policies, with the safeguard itself model-based. Single robot among static obstacles, so there is no multi-agent property; (d) is credited only because planning must finish inside the 2 s and 1 s receding-horizon budgets, and since everything is MATLAB simulation with no hardware or edge figures the maintainer may drop (d). Fig. 3 caption says baseline RL collided in 40.2% of car episodes while Table I says 17.6%.

title: Recovery RL: Safe Reinforcement Learning With Learned Recovery Zones
evidence: Sec. IV-B: 'a recovery action sampled from pi_rec is executed instead of a pi_task' action whenever the safety critic places the proposed action in the recovery set; 'Recovery RL filters proposed actions that are likely to lead to unsafe states'.
method: A safety critic learned from offline constraint-violating data defines a recovery set; when the task policy's action falls inside it, a learned model-free or model-based recovery policy acts instead.
evaluation: Six simulated domains plus image-based obstacle avoidance on a dVRK robot; vs unconstrained, LR, SQRL, RSPO, RP and RCPO; success-to-violation ratio 2-20x better in simulation and 3x on hardware; pretraining and relabelling ablations.
contribution: Separates task and recovery policies so a learned safety critic can pre-empt constraint violations at runtime, trading violations against successes far more efficiently than prior safe-RL penalty and Lagrangian methods.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - the RL task policy. The runtime override is action substitution, not a halt or a human deferral; the human-supervisor query in Sec. X is proposed and never tested, so (e) does not hold. The 2-20x and 3x headline efficiency numbers and the per-domain violation counts live in the abstract and figures only, not in the text, so they cannot be verified from the body. No latency or control-loop timing is reported and the setting is single-agent apart from one scripted distractor arm.

title: A Predictive Safety Filter for Learning-Based Racing Control
evidence: Sec. I to III: the filter processes the desired input as u(k) = pi_s(x(k), u_d(k)) before it reaches the real system and 'minimizes interference while still ensuring safety for the system'.
method: A receding-horizon nonlinear MPC on a dynamic bicycle model minimally modifies any desired input so that track-boundary constraints and an offline terminal safe set stay satisfied, giving recursive feasibility.
evaluation: 1:28 RC car with VICON state estimation, acados real-time SQP at 80 Hz with N=60; terminal set verified over 1000 initial conditions; assisted human driving and a DAgger imitation policy; no baselines and no violation or intervention rates.
contribution: Demonstrates a minimally interfering predictive safety filter that keeps a miniature race car inside track boundaries under both human joystick input and a learned imitation controller.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - a DAgger imitation network, plus a human driver in the second experiment. MOST LIKELY TO BE OVERTURNED: the hardware evaluation is qualitative only, with no baseline, no ablation and no violation or intervention rate, which is exclude-E2 under the base prompt; it clears the Pillar 1 floor only through the formal invariance and recursive-feasibility result and the 1000-sample terminal-set verification, and that guarantee is admitted to hold only for constant-curvature track segments. (d) rests on the 80 Hz real-time loop since no solve times are given. Assisted driving is shared control, not automation deferring to a person, so (e) is not met. The text cites the fifth episode while the figure caption says the fourth.

title: Learning Safe, Generalizable Perception-Based Hybrid Control With Certificates
evidence: Sec. III: the approach 'defines the CBF directly in observation-space'; Sec. V: when stuck the robot switches to an exploratory mode 'where it ignores the oCLF condition and executes a random walk' while the oCBF constraint stays enforced.
method: Neural observation-space CBF and CLF learned on Lidar and goal range/bearing; hybrid controller enforces the oCBF in one-step optimisation and switches goal-seeking/exploratory modes.
evaluation: Dubins car, 500 random 2D environments, 10 Hz; baselines PPO, state-based CBF, MPC; safety 100 percent vs MPC 99.6; goal 93.2 vs 90.4; 18 ms vs 102 ms; TurtleBot3 demo.
contribution: A learned observation-space barrier and Lyapunov certificate with a hybrid controller that reached 100 percent safety over 500 unseen simulated environments at 18 ms per step, and ran on a TurtleBot3.
flag: Borderline on E4: single robot, no multi-agent aspect; kept for learned certificate enforced at execution time, generalisation to unseen environments and reported compute time. The oCBF is a constraint in a one-step control optimisation rather than a filter over a separate nominal policy, so runtime_interceptor yes is arguable. PPO and state-based CBF rates are only in Fig. 7 and were not readable. The '6x faster than MPC' claim is consistent with 18 vs 102 ms; the 'twice as fast as RL' time-to-goal figures were not found in the text. Hardware trial count and onboard compute not stated; Lidar at 5 Hz vs 10 Hz control. Certificate checked on 100000 samples, not formally proved.

title: Sablas: Learning Safe Control for Black-Box Dynamical Systems
evidence: "The main limitation of the proposed approach is that it cannot guarantee the satisfaction of the CBF conditions" (Sec. V-F Limitation); the CBF is a training loss, the learned policy acts directly.
method: Jointly learns an MLP controller and control barrier function for black-box dynamics, back-propagating CBF losses through a nominal model corrected by detached real next states.
evaluation: Simulation only: drone CityEnv (1024 NPCs) and ship ValleyEnv (32 NPCs); baselines CPO, PPO-Safe, TRPO-Safe; relative safety rate, completion, tracking error; loss ablation; no latency.
contribution: Sablas learns a safe controller and barrier certificate for black-box dynamics by passing gradients through a nominal model, reaching near-1.0 relative safety with about a tenth of safe-RL samples.
flag: No runtime filter: CBF is a training loss only, so (a) fails. Borderline (c): one controlled agent among many NPC drones/ships, safety is the measured outcome vs baselines, but the claim is black-box dynamics not multi-agent safety. Numeric results are in figures only (Fig. 3/4); 'near 1.0' and '1/10 samples' are prose claims I could not check against a table. Title match confirmed.

title: Onboard Safety Guarantees for Racing Drones: High-Speed Geofencing With Control Barrier Functions
evidence: Sec. III-A: "the filter does not modify pilot's actions unless there is an eminent risk of leaving the safe set."
method: Implicit control-barrier safety filter for a human-piloted racing drone: forward-simulates a backup controller and blends pilot command with it via a regulation function, no QP or gradients.
evaluation: Sim and outdoor 7-inch drone: 104 km/h stop 1.7 m from barrier; 70 m free fall stop 1.8 m. 4 flights, all engagements safe. Teensy 4.1, 350 us, 400 Hz. Pendulum-only baseline.
contribution: Runs a barrier-function geofence filter on a 10 gram microcontroller in about 350 microseconds, keeping a human-piloted racing drone inside its boundary at over 100 km/h.
flag: BORDERLINE E2: the only baseline (backup-set CBF QP) is on a simulated inverted pendulum, with 'an order of magnitude faster' and no exact timings; no baseline or ablation on the drone. Safety metric is minimum barrier distance and zero breaches over 4 flights with 2-4 engagements each - tiny sample. Single agent. Human handoff is reversed: the filter overrides the pilot (shared control), no takeover by a person and no SA measurement; drop that cell if strict. Quote spelling 'eminent' as reported; verify. 25 ms figure is FPV video latency, not filter latency.

title: Reinforcement Learned Distributed Multi-Robot Navigation With Reciprocal Velocity Obstacle Shaped Rewards
evidence: "The exteroceptive observation contains the RVO vectors" (Sec. III-C); RVO also shapes the reward, it is not a runtime check on the policy output.
method: Distributed PPO policy with a bidirectional GRU over reciprocal-velocity-obstacle vectors of neighbours; reward penalises velocities inside the joint RVO area and short expected collision time.
evaluation: Simulation with 6-20 robots (circle, random) and up to 8 real TurtleBots; baselines SARL, GA3C-CADRL, NH-ORCA; success 0.90 vs 0.80 (circle, 20); three ablations; no numeric latency.
contribution: RL-RVO learns a decentralised multi-robot navigation policy from RVO-encoded observations and RVO-shaped rewards, improving success rate and travel time over NH-ORCA and learned baselines up to 20 robots.
flag: Borderline (c): genuinely multi-robot and success rate (no collision and not stuck) is compared against baselines and ablations, but it is a navigation planner with efficiency (travel time, speed) as a co-equal claim and no separate collision rate, so I read it as failing the primacy test; maintainer may judge otherwise. No runtime override, so (a) fails. Compute cost is shown only in a bar chart (Fig. 5) with no numeric inference time. Some Table II entries are malformed in the source. Read from a single fetch. Title match confirmed.

title: Collaborative Navigation and Manipulation of a Cable-Towed Load by Multiple Quadrupedal Robots
evidence: "We tackle the optimization-based collision avoidance problem using the duality-based formulation developed in [31]." (Sec. IV-C5)
method: Cascaded planning for quadrupeds towing a load by cables: A* global path, centralized trajectory optimisation over 2^n taut/slack cable modes in parallel, decentralized per-robot planners, MPC locomotion.
evaluation: Hardware with three quadrupeds (Mini Cheetah, two A1) through 2.2 m gap and clutter; simulation 1-12 robots; only baseline is non-parallel planner: replan under 3 s for n<6 vs about 30 s.
contribution: Lets several quadrupeds tow a shared cable-attached load through narrow gaps by optimising over taut and slack cable modes in a centralized planner with decentralized per-robot tracking.
flag: Multi-robot coordination and manipulation paper; collision avoidance is one soft (slack-penalised) constraint inside the planners, fails the (c) primacy test and strict-runtime (a). No collision, success or violation rate is reported - results are solve times and qualitative hardware runs, so E2 would also apply. Centralized planner runs on a remote laptop at 0.5 Hz, not on the robots. Multi-agent state cell is nominal (planning state, not a learned or monitored hazard state).

title: Safe Reinforcement Learning Using Black-Box Reachability Analysis
evidence: "Next, BRSL chooses a safe action by adjusting the rolled-out action sequence" (Sec. III); if no safe plan is found the robot executes a failsafe braking maneuver.
method: Safety layer for RL: data-driven zonotope reachability of a black-box robot, ensemble-model rollouts, differentiable collision check; adjusts unsafe action plans by projected gradient, else brakes to a stop.
