evaluation: Simulation, 4 single-robot tasks (Turtlebot, quadrotor, point mass, hexarotor in wind); vs TD3, RTS, SAILR, SECAS. Collisions 0% vs 11-63% unshielded; compute 30-72 ms at 10 Hz on i5/RTX 3060.
contribution: A reachability-based safety layer that needs no robot model keeps a learning agent at zero collisions in four simulated tasks while raising reward, with per-step compute under the 100 ms control period.
flag: Single agent only; kept over E4 because it reports per-step compute against a 10 Hz loop, but that latency aspect is a reported measurement, not a design constraint, so the latency cell is borderline. Desktop GPU, not edge. Hexarotor compute 71.93 +- 34.52 ms means some steps may exceed 100 ms. Table I compute-time row was garbled in the extracted text (Turtlebot about 30.41 +- 20.3 ms unverified); Table II values are clean. No ablation. Obstacle counts not stated.

title: Safe Reinforcement Learning Using Robust Control Barrier Functions
evidence: Sec. III-B: the safety layer is used to "minimally alter the RL policy's actions to ensure safety of the system"; final action u* = u^S + u^RL (Eq. 9).
method: SAC policy action is corrected at every step by a robust-CBF QP with GP-estimated disturbance bounds; differentiable layer, model-based rollouts and a modular critic that discounts the filter.
evaluation: Simulated unicycle, 5-car following, PVTOL; baselines SAC+non-differentiable RCBF-QP with/without compensator; zero violations reported; transfer completion 0.63 vs 0.17 and 0.69 vs 0.52; no hardware or latency.
contribution: A robust control-barrier-function QP filters every reinforcement-learning action during training and deployment, reporting no safety violations in simulation while a modular variant transfers zero-shot to unseen obstacle layouts.
flag: Safety metric is weak: Sec. IV-A only states that no safety violations occurred, with no counts, and every baseline carries the same RCBF layer, so safety does not discriminate between methods; reported numbers are reward and completion rate (Tables I-II). Sample-efficiency results are figures only. Single learning agent (other cars scripted) so check E4; the PVTOL safety operator is simulated, not a human. Simulation only, no hardware or latency; inference solves one QP per step. Extracted from one full-PDF fetch via summariser.

title: Safe Planning in Dynamic Environments Using Conformal Prediction
evidence: Scenario 2 reports one constraint violation in 100 MPC runs at failure probability delta = 0.05 (Sec. 5); the safety constraint with conformal regions sits inside the MPC (Algorithm 1, Sec. 4).
method: MPC for one ego agent among uncontrolled dynamic agents; LSTM trajectory predictions are wrapped in conformal prediction regions used as collision-avoidance constraint margins with probabilistic safety guarantee.
evaluation: ORCA/TrajNet++ (3 pedestrians, 500 tests) and CARLA (4 pedestrians, 100 runs); open-loop vs closed-loop MPC; coverage 498/500, 1/100 violations, cost 414 vs 367.1; no timing or hardware.
contribution: Conformal prediction regions around learned trajectory forecasts give an MPC planner distribution-free probabilistic collision-avoidance guarantees among dynamic agents, validated in pedestrian and CARLA simulations.
flag: Borderline. Not (a): safety is a constraint inside the planner, no override/halt layer, and infeasibility handling is unspecified. (c) is arguable: safety is the primary claim and violations are measured, but there is one controlled ego agent among uncontrolled pedestrians, and the only comparison (open vs closed loop) is on cost, not on safety; CARLA has no baseline and uses slack variables plus smallest-region heuristic that weaken the guarantee. No solve times (MPC at 2 Hz is an update rate). Maintainer may prefer E1 or E4.

title: Conformal Predictive Safety Filter for RL Controllers in Dynamic Environments
evidence: Sec. IV (Online Execution): 'we apply the safety filter in a receding horizon fashion by applying the first element' - the learned filter's output replaces the nominal RL action each step using conformal prediction regions.
method: Learned safety filter that tracks an RL controller's action while keeping conformal prediction regions around LSTM-forecast agent trajectories at a safe distance; applied receding-horizon at runtime.
evaluation: Collision Avoidance Gym sim, 2/4/6 CADRL agents, 1000 tests; N=4 collisions 49 to 10 (GA3C), 3 to 2 (ORCA); time-to-goal 7.50 to 8.28 s; vs Gaussian filter; i9-9900K, no latency.
contribution: A conformal-prediction safety filter wrapped around an RL navigation policy cuts collisions among four dynamic agents from 49 to 10 per 1000 simulated runs, at the cost of about 10 percent longer time-to-goal.
flag: Abstract's '67 percent fewer failures' (ORCA) is not supported by the N=4 table, which shows 27 to 15 (about 44 percent); it may be an average over N=2/4/6 shown only in Fig. 5 - could not verify. '80 percent fewer collisions' matches 49 to 10. Conclusion claims no time-to-goal increase but Table I shows 7.503 to 8.278 s vs raw GA3C. '18 percent shorter' vs Gaussian filter is time-to-goal (8.278 vs 10.05 s). The filter always replaces the action: no intervention rate, no halt/defer, no per-step latency (10 Hz planner only). One controlled robot; other agents assumed not to react (Assumption 1, checked only approximately). Simulation only. Table I units assumed to be counts per 1000.

title: Tailoring Solution Accuracy for Fast Whole-Body Model Predictive Control of Legged Robots
evidence: "running a small but fixed number of iterations at high rates" (Sec. II.C); the CBF is a first-timestep constraint inside the NMPC, not a separate filter
method: Whole-body nonlinear MPC for a humanoid: one SQP iteration per cycle, fixed-iteration ADMM (OSQP) QP solves, self-collision CBF constraint at the first timestep, delay compensation by trajectory interpolation.
evaluation: MIT Humanoid in simulation (500 six-second trials per setting) and hardware; ablations over ADMM iterations, timestep, delay, CBF on/off; solve 4.3-11.3 ms, 90-200 Hz; walking up to 1.1 m/s.
contribution: Shows that a whole-body humanoid MPC can trade solver accuracy for control rate, running at 90-200 Hz with barrier-function self-collision constraints inside the optimisation.
flag: Single robot, locomotion-performance paper; self-collision CBF lives inside the MPC, so strict-runtime (a) is not met, and (d) is doubtful because the latency budget is for locomotion control, not a safety decision. Abstract claims up to 26-fold fewer self-collisions; the body passage I read gave a 4.3x drop from 20 to 200 iterations without CBFs and near-elimination with CBFs - the 26x figure should be checked against the figures. Authors state the approach cannot guarantee stability or feasibility. Onboard computer model not identified in the text read.

title: NavRL: Learning Safe Flight in Dynamic Environments
evidence: Sec. III-D: "If this action is not within any of the velocity obstacle regions, we set the safe action equal to the policy action." (otherwise projected to the closest safe velocity)
method: PPO velocity policy for a quadcopter plus a velocity-obstacle safety shield that projects the policy action onto the nearest safe velocity by linear programming at deployment.
evaluation: Gazebo, 20 runs: collisions per run dynamic 0.85 vs 2.70 no-shield, 3.15 ViGO; hybrid 2.10 vs 4.60, 4.40. Real flights qualitative. Orin NX: shield 16 ms, policy 7 ms.
contribution: Adds a velocity-obstacle safety shield to an RL flight policy, cutting dynamic-obstacle collisions per run from 2.70 to 0.85 in simulation, with shield runtime of 16 ms on a Jetson Orin NX.
flag: Single ego robot among obstacles and pedestrians; multi-robot only as parallel training instances, so multi-agent is nominal and E4 is arguable (kept for runtime shield plus onboard latency). Criterion d is weak: runtimes are reported, no explicit deadline. Static case: shield 0.65 vs EGO-Planner 0.45, so not best there. Real flights have no quantitative metrics. Collisions still occur (not a guarantee). Success rates in Table I are training metrics. Drafted from a model-summarised PDF read; verify quote wording.

title: DR-MPC: Deep Residual Model Predictive Control for Real-World Social Navigation
evidence: Sec. V: 'we either validate the model's action as safe using a heuristic safety check or override it using a heuristic policy', triggered by latent-space KNN out-of-distribution detection plus a constant-velocity motion model check.
method: A DRL residual blends with MPC path tracking; at runtime a latent KNN out-of-distribution detector and a constant-velocity collision check veto the learned action and substitute the safe alternative closest to MPC.
evaluation: CrowdNav simulation with six ORCA humans vs ORCA, naive and residual DRL, with OOD/CVMM and reward ablations (SHRR 0.30 vs 0.77 and 0.79); Jackal robot, 6 runs per loop, safety raises 0.3 and 0.0 vs 1.0 and 0.3 for the heuristic.
contribution: Combines MPC initialisation with residual deep reinforcement learning and an out-of-distribution runtime safety check so a robot learns crowd navigation from under four hours of real-world data without unsafe exploration.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - the DRL residual policy. (c) fails the primacy test: this is social navigation where the human-collision rate sits beside success rate and steps to goal, and the other agents are ORCA-simulated or real people rather than learned agents. The real-world table reports safety-layer raises rather than collisions, so hardware safety evidence is indirect. No inference-time or latency numbers are given beyond the 0.2 s MDP step, so (d) is not credited despite onboard laptop-GPU inference. False-trigger evidence is only the note that 21% of CVMM triggers preceded a collision early in training, falling to 5%.

title: Future-Oriented Navigation: Dynamic Obstacle Avoidance With One-Shot Energy-Based Multimodal Motion Prediction
evidence: Abstract: the predictor "generates high-resolution, multi-step predictions in a single operation"; Sec. IV: predicted obstacle ellipses enter the MPC as soft terms plus hard constraints over a critical horizon.
method: One-shot energy-based U-Net predicts multimodal future-position maps of pedestrians; clustering and Gaussian fitting yield ellipses used as constraints in distributed MPC for mobile-robot fleets.
evaluation: ROS 2/Gazebo warehouse and hospital, 100 runs; baselines MPC-WTA, DWA-CVM, TEB-MPC, RPP, SGAN, loss ablations; success 96% vs 94%/48%; JSD 0.3482; 3 ms per object on GTX 1650.
contribution: A one-shot energy-based predictor produces multimodal pedestrian motion forecasts in about 3 ms per object and feeds a distributed MPC, raising collision-free success rates over prediction and planner baselines in simulated warehouses.
flag: BORDERLINE include vs E1. No runtime interceptor: avoidance is a constraint inside the MPC, so (a) is not met; the paper explicitly leaves additional safety layers out of scope (Sec. VII-B). Included on (b) (multi-step motion prediction with JSD/SWD accuracy and loss ablations, Table I) and arguably (c); the outcome is success rate (goal reached in time without collision), not a separate collision rate, and it is robot-pedestrian avoidance with fleet avoidance as one cost term. If (b) is read as requiring a graph or joint multi-agent latent model, this is E1: prediction is per object with proximity grouping. RQ5 capped at 2 per protocol. Latency figures: predictor 3 ms vs 58 ms WTA, MPC mean solve 0.008 s, solver cap 0.1 s; laptop GPU, not edge hardware; simulation only. Scenario 4 deviation mean 0.017 m with std 0.350 m looks odd. Fig. 5 values figure-only. One full-PDF fetch via summariser.

title: Chance-Constrained Sampling-Based MPC for Collision Avoidance in Uncertain Dynamic Environments
evidence: Sec. IV-C: the chance constraint enters as a cost "heavily penalizing trajectories where the margin" falls below the risk threshold; Sec. V-A1: runs on an "NVIDIA GeForce GTX 1660 Ti laptop GPU using the PyCUDA module".
method: C2U-MPPI: chance constraint on robot-pedestrian collision turned into a deterministic Mahalanobis-distance test and applied as a penalty cost inside unscented MPPI, with Kalman-filter pedestrian prediction.
evaluation: Gazebo/Pedsim corridor with 6 or 10 pedestrians plus hardware with 5 humans (Vicon); baselines MPCC, log-MPPI, U-MPPI, SH-MPC; collisions, velocity violations, texec 9-13 ms at 30 Hz on laptop GPU.
contribution: Embeds a probabilistic collision constraint as a cost in a GPU sampling-based MPC and reports fewer collisions among moving pedestrians than MPCC, log-MPPI and SH-MPC while running in 9-13 ms per iteration.
flag: Borderline. Constraint is a soft penalty inside the planner, so (a) fails by the protocol wording; no override or veto stage. Only one controlled robot; pedestrians are uncontrolled, so (c) is nominal at best. Maintainer may consider (d): 30 Hz budget (33.3 ms) is stated and texec measured (sim 8.9-11.4 ms; hardware 13.17 and 13.01 ms), but on a laptop GPU, not an edge device, and timing is a reported property not the claim. Key numbers: 10-ped scenario 3 collisions MPCC 17, log-MPPI 5, U-MPPI 3-4, C2U-MPPI 0; vs SH-MPC 16 vs 5; hardware 1-2 collisions in 6 trials, so not collision-free despite the "zero collisions" wording for some sim tables. Table III test 2 row unreadable in extraction. Physical hardware platform not clearly named.

title: SICNav-Diffusion: Safe and Interactive Crowd Navigation With Diffusion Trajectory Predictions
evidence: The ORCA lower level "acts as a safety filter for the JMID predictions" (Sec. III-C); JMID jointly predicts all humans with a diffusion model.
method: JMID diffusion model jointly forecasts all pedestrians; bilevel MPC with ORCA lower level refines sampled predictions and reweights samples, robot-human collision as hard constraint.
evaluation: ETH/UCY: JMID SADE/SFDE 0.35/0.66 vs iMID 0.41/0.78, AgentFormer 0.38/0.75; sim 500 runs success 1.00, collision 0.006/s; Jackal 240 lab runs; i9 laptop RTX 4080, <0.1 s predict and solve, 10 Hz.
contribution: Joint diffusion trajectory prediction for all pedestrians coupled to a bilevel safe MPC, improving scene-level forecast error and reaching 1.00 simulated success with a 10 Hz real-robot loop.
flag: Predictor is generative (diffusion), so not non-generative inference. The quoted safety filter filters predictions, not robot commands, and the collision constraint sits inside the planner, so (a) is not met. Collision frequency is not better than baselines (0.006 vs CVG 0.005); gains are success and freezing. Outdoor 99.03 percent autonomy with minimal manual takeovers is reported without a takeover count - not enough for (e). 10 Hz is a loop rate, not a stated safety deadline; drop the latency cell if strict. JMID (DDIM) row lost in extraction; real-robot values are in Fig. 5 only.

title: Safety on the Fly: Constructing Robust Safety Filters via Policy Control Barrier Functions at Runtime
evidence: Sec. I: a safety filter that 'minimally modifies arbitrary control inputs to ensure safety'; Sec. V: 'The RPCBF-SF remains safe throughout, while the PCBF-SF always collides.'
method: Robust policy CBF built at runtime: sample disturbance trajectories, roll out a design policy over a finite horizon, take worst-case h as the barrier value, then filter the nominal control by CBF-QP.
evaluation: Sim: double integrator, Segway, F-16, AutoRally; hardware: Crazyflie. Baselines HOCBF, MPC filter, PCBF, MPPI. AutoRally crash rate 0.09 vs 0.80 MPPI; filter runs 100 Hz on a laptop.
contribution: A robust safety filter whose barrier function is computed on the fly from sampled disturbance rollouts, cutting AutoRally crash rate from 0.80 to 0.09 and running at 100 Hz on a quadcopter.
flag: Single-agent throughout, so inclusion rests on (a) plus the sequential/runtime aspect; maintainer may prefer E4. Table I: collisions per lap 4.53 MPPI, 1.38 SMPPI-HOCBF, 1.23 SMPPI-PCBF, 1.13 SMPPI-RPCBF; crash rate 0.80, 0.15, 0.12, 0.09. Compute time appears only as a plot (Fig. 8, roughly 0-10 ms, laptop CPU unspecified), no number in text; filter runs off-board, not edge. DI/Segway safe-set results are figures without numeric rates. No false-halt or throughput metric.

title: Safety Evaluation of Motion Plans Using Trajectory Predictors as Forward Reachable Set Estimators
evidence: Abstract: 'a safety monitor that is both complete (able to detect all unsafe plans) and sound (does not flag safe plans)'; Sec. VI calls it 'a promising building block for runtime safety monitoring'.
method: FORCE-OPT: convex program over GMM trajectory-predictor modes gives a forward reachable set, conformally calibrated, with Bayesian confidence switching to worst-case FRS; ego plan flagged unsafe if it intersects.
evaluation: nuScenes per-frame open-loop, Singapore ID and Boston OOD, synthetic unsafe plans; 8 baselines; ID BER 5.83% vs Lindemann 15.56%, FPR 8.62%, FNR 3.03%; compute 0.022 s; hardware unstated.
contribution: Conformally calibrated GMM predictors used as forward reachable sets give a plan-safety monitor with 5.83% balanced error in-distribution and 6.77-9.09% out-of-distribution, well below worst-case and prior calibrated baselines.
flag: Borderline (a): the monitor only outputs a safe/unsafe verdict per frame; no override, fallback or closed-loop intervention is implemented or tested, so runtime_interceptor=yes rests on design intent - maintainer may prefer no. Sec. IV-B claims FRS computed 'in microseconds' but Table IV reports 0.022 s for FORCE-OPT (0.005-0.210 s across methods). (d) is weak: compute time reported, no explicit latency budget, no hardware. Multi-agent state is ego vs one contender. Some pWC-FRS table cells were lost in extraction; Table IV column order inferred. Unsafe cases are synthetic.

title: Learning a Unified Risk Map for Autonomous Driving in Partially Observable Environments
evidence: Sec. III-F: "Risk-aware planning is achieved via a composite cost function optimized through Quadratic Programming (QP)." Risk fuses flow risk and collision risk from predicted trajectories of visible and occluded agents.
method: Transformer with lane-anchor queries regresses a unified risk map (trajectory-density flow risk plus spatiotemporal collision risk incl. sampled occluded vehicles); risk enters a QP speed planner as a soft cost.
evaluation: Open-loop on Waymo Open Motion (1000 train/100 val scenes), fixed path, speed only. Vs NOAP, O-Risk, SRQ-P, OPBP: TTCmin 7.72 s, critical moments 5.41. 6.67 ms on RTX 4090.
contribution: A learned risk map covering visible and occluded traffic raises minimum time-to-collision to 7.72 s and cuts critical moments by 62% versus an occlusion-prediction baseline in open-loop Waymo replay, at 6.67 ms inference.
flag: BORDERLINE, maintainer should decide between include and E1. Not a runtime interceptor: risk is a soft cost inside the planner, so (a) fails. (c) is arguable: single ego vehicle, hazard from surrounding/occluded agents, outcomes are TTC and critical-moment counts (hazard proxies) not collision rate. Open-loop only, 100 validation scenes, and Risk Score uses the same risk formulation as training; SRQ-P actually has the lowest Risk Score (0.30 vs 0.68). Latency is on a desktop RTX 4090 with no stated deadline, so no latency or edge cell claimed. No predictive-accuracy metric for the risk map found. Scenario generation uses a diffusion model, the risk predictor itself is a regressor.

title: Distributionally Robust Acceleration Control Barrier Filter for Efficient UAV Obstacle Avoidance
evidence: Filter takes nominal acceleration and outputs a safe command under per-obstacle half-space constraints; "We run a fixed number of iterations and check the maximum violation; if it exceeds a threshold, a fallback is triggered" (Sec. III.E).
method: Acceleration control barrier filter: Cantelli-tightened half-space constraints per obstacle, fixed-iteration Gauss-Southwell projection instead of a QP, DR-CVaR early-warning trigger, latency folded into effective clearance.
evaluation: MATLAB sim, 3000 and 1000 runs, vs MPC, CBF-QP, RP-CBF plus ablations; success rate, reaction and processing time (0.444 ms), separation; Crazyflie flights with offboard computation at 100 Hz.
contribution: A QP-free distributionally robust acceleration barrier filter for one UAV that matches baseline avoidance success near 99.6 percent while cutting filter processing time by 31-54 percent, with a CVaR trigger ablation.
flag: Single UAV, not multi-agent (obstacles are thrown objects and in one test a second UAV); kept out of E4 only by the explicit latency aspect. Scenario 1 success of DR-ACBF (99.64%) is marginally BELOW all three baselines (99.67-99.71%); the gain is compute time only. Safety gain evidence is the DR-CVaR ablation in the hard scenario (34.9% to 82.5%), which is still a low absolute rate. Hardware compute is an offboard base station, not edge; hardware reaction 66.6-78.8 ms, 5 flights each, no baseline. Fixed-iteration projection has no exact feasibility guarantee.

title: Real-Time Multi-Drone Replanning for Disruption Management in Urban Aerial Logistics Networks
evidence: "This letter presents a real-time replanning framework that resolves cascading conflicts and reduces system-wide delays without relying on predefined traffic zones." (Abstract)
method: Centralised two-level replanner: conflict-guided priority search (CGPS, anytime ACGPS) over drone priority orders plus a time-interval occupancy field planner that retimes route-fixed trajectories under spatiotemporal capsule constraints.
evaluation: Simulation, 5 airway scenarios up to 1000 drones, 500 trials each; baselines PBS, three fixed-priority planners, MINCO-Capsule; metrics success rate within time budget, runtime, delay; Intel i7-11700KF, 16 threads.
contribution: A hierarchical priority-search replanner computes conflict-free recovery trajectories for up to 1000 delivery drones after in-flight disruptions within a fixed time budget, reporting sub-second solves at 100 drones.
flag: Borderline (c)/(d): cascading conflicts among drones is the stated problem and replanning runs under an explicit budget (5 s, 10 s at 1000 drones), but it is a MAPF-style planner with separation as a constraint; outcomes are solvability, runtime and delay, no collision or violation rate. Maintainer may prefer include under (d). Abstract '0.3 s for 100 drones with 5 disruptions' not found verbatim in body text (body gives 213 ms total solve at n=100; Table I cells are not legible in the extracted text). 43.02% delay reduction is versus PPall only. Trials are pre-filtered: Line scenario accepts 23% of trials and Traffic 63.8% at n=100, SR is over accepted trials only. At 1000 drones/100 disruptions SR is 0.2%. No flight tests; no human operator role.

title: Safe and Scalable Multi-Drone Payload Transport via CBF-Based Reinforcement Learning With Zero-Shot Sim-to-Real Transfer
evidence: Sec. IV-B.1: DGPPO "jointly learns a distributed control policy and a constraint value function that serves as a Discrete Graph Control Barrier Function (DGCBF)"; Sec. VI-A.2: "the safety rate is defined as the fraction of agents that satisfy all safety constraints throughout the execution."
method: DGPPO trains a distributed GNN policy plus a learned discrete graph CBF for cable-suspended multi-drone payload transport; domain randomisation over team size; no execution-time filter, policy output tracked by PID.
evaluation: JAX 2D sim, n=3-8, 125 scenarios, vs InforMARL penalty/schedule and MAPPO-Lagrangian; safety rate and goal hit rate (84% vs 59%); Crazyflie 2.1 hardware 3-6 drones; 10 Hz, no latency.
contribution: Learns a distributed payload-transport policy with a graph control barrier certificate and transfers it zero-shot to 3-6 Crazyflies, beating penalty and Lagrangian MARL baselines on the reward-safety trade-off.
flag: Not a runtime interceptor: the CBF shapes training only, deployed policy has no filter or QP. Meets (c) only via learned certificate; primacy is shared with scalability and sim-to-real, maintainer to judge. Per-team-size safety rates are only in Fig. 2, no numbers in text; the only numeric safety rate is 76.2% nominal at n=5 in the robustness test (72.4% at 2% dropout, 61.4% at 5%, 52.6% at LiDAR sigma 0.045 m), which sits oddly with the 'high safety' wording. No CBF ablation. Hardware has no collision counts; one 6-drone Hard run failed; decentralised execution is emulated from a central computer. arXiv id 2607.20665 taken from pdf_url, record is the RA-L DOI.

title: RVC-NMPC: Nonlinear Model Predictive Control With Reciprocal Velocity Constraints for Mutual Collision Avoidance in Agile UAV Flight
evidence: Sec. IV-C: the reciprocal velocity constraints are "applied as soft constraints with slack variables" inside each UAV's NMPC; Sec. V reliability test (paraphrase): 10 UAVs, 3 h, no collisions recorded.
method: Decentralized NMPC per UAV with ORCA-style, time-gated linear velocity constraints from neighbours' current position and velocity only; soft constraints with slack; PMM minimum-time reference.
evaluation: Sim 10 UAVs antipodal swap, 100 trials, vs RBL/EGO-Swarm2/MADER/HDSM plus 3 ablations; 100% success, 3.07 s; 3 h run; 3 real UAVs; 100 Hz on Khadas VIM3.
contribution: Decentralized NMPC with time-gated reciprocal velocity constraints gives collision-free agile flight for 10 UAVs at up to 25.9 m/s, running at 100 Hz onboard and tolerating 50 ms neighbour-state delay.
flag: Borderline (c) primacy: title and 3 h zero-collision test are about mutual collision avoidance, but the headline number is flight time (31% below HDSM norm variant; text says >11% vs per-axis HDSM, table gives about 10.5%). Not (a): soft constraint inside the planner, no veto/halt. Reader summary says 100% prevention of minimum-distance violations yet Sec. VI admits minimum-distance drops a few times in the 3 h test - check. No per-solve timing, only 100 Hz pipeline rate. Delay robustness (ok to 50 ms and 10 Hz, collisions rise above 100 ms) is simulated; real Wi-Fi 10 Hz, 14 ms mean delay. Tables I and III were partly garbled in extraction; verify baseline success rates and the 18 m/s real-world speed against the PDF. No theoretical guarantee, obstacle-free only.

title: Formal Verification and Control With Conformal Prediction: Practical Safety Guarantees For Autonomous Systems
evidence: Introduction: "this survey focuses on designing formal verification and control algorithms for learning-enabled autonomous systems"; Summary: "This survey provides an accessible introduction to CP for non-experts".
method: Survey/tutorial on conformal prediction for verification, online monitoring and chance-constrained control synthesis of learning-enabled autonomous systems.
evaluation: Illustrative simulations only: double-integrator navigation and unicycle predictor verification; 500 experiments, calibration sizes 100/500/1000, empirical coverage 0.947-0.964 vs 0.95 target; no baselines, hardware or latency.
contribution: Magazine survey and tutorial showing how conformal prediction yields distribution-free statistical guarantees for verifying, monitoring and controlling learning-enabled autonomous systems.
flag: Self-described survey, so E3. Only the first 100000 of about 287000 characters were read (through the start of the control-synthesis section); the later online-verification, temporal-logic and estimation parts were NOT read, but the survey status is unambiguous from the introduction and summary. Useful as background and a source of citations to primary conformal runtime-monitoring papers. Says "real-time capable" with no number.

title: Collision Avoidance for Non-Cooperative Multi-Swarm Coverage Control with Bounded Disturbance Measurements
venue: Mediterranean Conference on Control and Automation (MED)
evidence: Each agent builds ORCA half-spaces inflated by disturbance ellipsoids and picks the feasible velocity closest to its preferred coverage velocity every timestep (Sec. III-B, III-C); "throughout the entire simulation, no collision occurred" (Sec. IV).
method: ORCA extended with ellipsoidal bounds on residual disturbance-measurement error: Minkowski-summed uncertainty sets shift the avoidance half-spaces that overrule each agent's Voronoi coverage velocity between non-cooperative swarms.
evaluation: Simulation only: two swarms of four UAVs in a 10 m cube with shear wind, 11 runs; zero collisions, separation above 0.4 m; no baseline, no timing.
contribution: An ORCA variant with ellipsoidal disturbance bounds that provably separates two non-cooperative coverage swarms under wind, shown collision-free in eleven eight-UAV simulation runs.
flag: Meets (a) and (c) on topic (velocity-space step overrules the nominal coverage velocity at each timestep, inter-swarm collision is the primary claim) but fails minimum evaluation: no baseline or ablation at all (not even plain ORCA or the method without uncertainty sets), only 11 runs with zero collisions. Whether ORCA velocity selection counts as a runtime interceptor is a judgement call. Guarantee relies on synchronous computation, known positions of other swarms and achievable disturbance compensation; 'non-cooperative' swarms still all run the same algorithm. No computation time reported.

title: Decentralized control of heterogeneous mobile robots with obstacle avoidance in a dynamic environment
venue: 2025 IEEE International Conference on Modern Electronics Devices and Intelligent Communication Systems, MEDCOM 2025
evidence: "Let dmin > 0 be the hard safety threshold" (Sec. IV-B Collision Avoidance); "achieved 19/20 successful runs (95% reliability) without collisions" (Sec. V Discussion)
method: Two differential-drive robots with onboard PID velocity loops; an ultrasonic range rule zeroes linear velocity and commands a fixed 115 degree turn when an obstacle is inside the threshold. No communication or coordinator.
evaluation: Lab 3x3 m arena, two robots, static obstacles, 20 trials from 10 randomized poses: 19/20 collision-free (95%). No baseline or ablation. Arduino Mega 2560; control sampling 5 ms and 1 ms.
contribution: Lab demonstration that two uncoordinated low-cost mobile robots using ultrasonic stop-and-turn rules and PID velocity control share a 3x3 m arena collision-free in 19 of 20 trials.
flag: One quantitative safety number (19/20) but no baseline, ablation or comparison of any kind, so the v1.6 minimum is not met. The mechanism is a hand-coded reactive threshold rule, not a learned or formally justified filter; 'runtime interceptor' is a generous reading. Abstract and conclusion say 'low-latency' but the only timing figures are the PID sampling periods (5 ms, 1 ms); no sensing-to-action latency is measured. Internal inconsistencies: text gives critical distance 6 cm while Sec. III gives a 6-20 cm detection range; Table I is cited as showing tracking departures but contains only parameters; velocity/trajectory plots are from one 'representative run'. Centralized-vs-decentralized discussion is speculative. Multi-agent only nominally (each robot sees the other as an obstacle); n=2 robots. Small conference paper.

title: Real-World Deployment and Assessment of a Multiagent Reinforcement Learning-Based Variable-Speed-Limit Control System
evidence: Sec. III-C1: the work "introduces a masking layer following the output of the policy network during the testing and deployment stages" limiting sampling to valid actions, with max-limit clipping and debounce corrections overriding MARL decisions before posting to gantries.
method: Multiagent RL (MAPPO) variable-speed-limit control of 67 I-24 gantries, with deployment-time action masking, speed matching, max-limit clipping and debounce guards overriding policy output.
evaluation: Field deployment, 34,032,683 decisions, vs the deployed rule-based VSL run open loop: slow-warning rate 88.6% vs 74.4%, false-warning 1.6% vs 1.7%, response under 1 min vs 2.15 min, crashes 18.4 to 15.8 per month (14%), secondary crashes 7.2 to 3.6 (50%). No compute latency.
contribution: Field deployment of a multiagent RL variable-speed-limit controller on 67 gantries, with runtime guards that override policy output, reporting warning accuracy, response delay and crash change.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - a MAPPO policy guarded by deployment-time masking, clipping, debounce and a TMC-side constraint check. Check: the abstract claims a 26% crash reduction but Table IV and Sec. V-D give 14%; the abstract says about 35 million decisions vs 34,032,683 in Sec. V-B; the crash analysis is called preliminary, is a before-after comparison with no control group, and reprocesses historical RDS data for the "before" period; (c) fails the primacy test because the primary claims are deployment feasibility, warning accuracy and response delay and no collision or hazard rate is measured; no compute hardware or latency figures (only 30 s control cycles), so (d) does not hold; the TMC operator only monitors and records incidents, with no per-decision approval or manual override, so (e) does not hold.

title: Learning Robust Output Control Barrier Functions From Safe Expert Demonstrations
venue: IEEE Open Journal of Control Systems
evidence: Sec. 7.1 (close paraphrase): one ROCBF trajectory resulted in a collision as detected by CARLA; the applied control solves min ||u|| subject to the learned ROCBF condition q(u,y,t) >= 0.
method: Learns a robust output control barrier function from safe expert input-output demonstrations under partially known dynamics and perception error; control is min-norm input satisfying the learned barrier condition.
evaluation: CARLA lane keeping, state-based and image-based (ResNet18) variants, unseen test course. Compared with expert PID via cross-track-error maps; one collision reported; no rates, latency or hardware.
contribution: A method for learning robust output control barrier functions from safe expert demonstrations with formal conditions for validity, demonstrated on perception-based lane keeping in CARLA.
flag: Borderline (a): the barrier is enforced at execution time but as a min-norm controller, not as a filter over a separate nominal controller, so runtime_interceptor yes is arguable. Single-agent (E4 also applies). No numeric collision or violation rate; only colour maps versus the expert and one stated collision. The arXiv version may differ from the 2024 OJ-CSYS journal version; check the journal text for added numbers. Evidence is paraphrase. Read via one summarised fetch.

title: Hamilton-Jacobi Reachability in Reinforcement Learning: A Survey
venue: IEEE Open Journal of Control Systems
evidence: "In this survey, we review the recent advances made in using learning-based HJ reachability estimation." (Sec. X Conclusion)
method: Survey of learned Hamilton-Jacobi reachability in reinforcement learning: Bellman-style reachability and reach-avoid value functions, and their use as least-restrictive safety filters or shields.
evaluation: No original experiments; tables only collate cited works (state dimensions up to 112D). No baselines, metrics, hardware or latency of its own.
contribution: Surveys learning-based Hamilton-Jacobi reachability for safe reinforcement learning, including its use as a least-restrictive shield over a learned policy.
flag: Survey with no new method or experiment, so E3 regardless of topical fit. Useful as a citation source for reachability-based shields (Sec. VII). Multi-agent appears only as one cited multi-drone example; latency and human handover are not discussed.

title: Recursively Feasible Probabilistic Safe Online Learning With Control Barrier Functions
venue: IEEE Open Journal of Control Systems
evidence: "The proposed framework can be used directly as a safety filter for any other performance-driven control law" (Sec. V-B, Remark 4)
method: GP-based CBF-CLF second-order cone program acting as probabilistic safety filter; event-triggered online data collection substitutes a backup safe input when feasibility margin drops below a threshold.
evaluation: Simulation only: adaptive cruise control, single ego vehicle, one trajectory per condition; compared with nominal CBF-CLF-QP, time-triggered-only variant, oracle; plots only, no numeric safety rates, no latency.
contribution: Keeps a Gaussian-process control-barrier safety filter feasible during online learning by switching to a backup safe input and collecting data when feasibility is about to be lost.
flag: arXiv title is 'Probabilistic Safe Online Learning with Control Barrier Functions' (same authors Castaneda, Choi, Jung, Zhang, Tomlin, Sreenath); treated as the preprint of the record, but the journal version (title adds 'Recursively Feasible') may contain extra experiments or numbers not in this text - check the published version before excluding. In the arXiv text: single-agent, single trajectory per condition, safety shown only in Fig. 2 plots, no violation rate or statistics, so E2; E4 (single-agent guardrail) would also apply. Real-time claim is by citation only, no solve times.

title: Security of AI Agents
evidence: Sec. IV.B: "A sandbox restricts the capabilities of the agent program" through local resource limits and remote whitelists, blacklists and rate limiting, and in Sec. IV.B.1 the Docker-constrained BashAgent "successfully defended against all the LLM-generated attacks".
method: Systems-security analysis of LLM agents over confidentiality, integrity and availability, proposing session management, sandboxing, format-preserving and homomorphic encryption, and session-aware prompt tuning.
evaluation: Preliminary experiments only: 95 AgentBench-derived security tasks where the unconstrained BashAgent executes 76 of 95 (80.0%) attacks (confidentiality 96.0%, integrity 85.7%, availability 62.9%) vs a Docker variant defending all with no figures; encryption utility 49.0% vs 47.0% (FPETS) and 85.0% vs 99.0% (FHE). No hardware or latency.
