flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - a gpt-3.5-turbo bash agent contained by a Docker sandbox. MOST LIKELY OVERTURN: it is primarily a position and taxonomy paper whose own introduction calls its experiments "preliminary", which is why I call E3, but it does propose defenses and report numbers, so the maintainer may prefer include on (a) or exclude-E4 (single agent; multi-agent appears once in Sec. III.C.1, "This strain is magnified when multiple agents operate concurrently", and is never evaluated). Also: the defended variant has no quantitative result beyond "defended against all the LLM-generated attacks", there is no baseline beyond the two variants and no ablation, Definitions 4.1-4.2 are stated with no theorems or proofs, the session-management and session-aware-model defenses are unimplemented, and there is no latency or human-handoff content.

title: Socially-aware Object Transportation by a Mobile Manipulator in Static Planar Environments with Obstacles
evidence: Sec. IV-B: "As we work in static environments, the algorithm runs offline to generate a path".
method: Offline Risk-RRT* variant for a mobile manipulator carrying an object: asymmetric-Gaussian personal-space cost summed over weighted key points on base, arm and object.
evaluation: Simulation, static humans, 2-3 maps, 10 runs each, vs RRT* and base-only variants; social cost and path length shown only in box plots; no hardware or timing.
contribution: An offline social Risk-RRT* plans object-carrying paths for a mobile manipulator that keep base, arm and load out of static people's personal space.
flag: Offline path planner, single robot, static humans, no runtime mechanism, no safety metric (social cost only, values only in figures), no numeric results in text. Would also fail minimum evaluation (E2) and level (E4). Simulator not named.

title: DELIVER: A System for LLM-Guided Coordinated Multi-Robot Pickup and Delivery using Voronoi-Based Relay Planning
evidence: Sec. IV-F: "State transitions are triggered by reaching waypoints and observing signaling cues" - a task-execution state machine, no safety override, veto or halt.
method: LLaMA3-8B parses spoken pickup/delivery requests; Voronoi tessellation over robot positions assigns regions, relay agents and handoff points; per-robot finite-state machine executes relays over Nav2.
evaluation: MultiTRAIL 20x20 grid, 3-10 robots, 100 trials each; Gazebo 2 and 4 TurtleBot3, 10 trials; 3 real TurtleBot3; single-robot baseline; path length only; no latency reported.
contribution: An LLM-parsed, Voronoi-partitioned relay scheme for multi-robot pickup and delivery that cuts mean per-agent path length by up to 55 percent against a single robot, with no safety mechanism.
flag: Coordination/task-allocation paper, no safety metric, no ablation, only a single-robot baseline. The 84.37% parsing accuracy is carried over from the authors' prior work, not measured here. Paper is inconsistent on centralisation (claims no centralised control, hardware uses a central coordinator) and on team sizes (text 3,5,7,10 vs Fig. 3 caption 1,3,5,10). The 55% baseline is not exactly specified in the body. Human only issues the command; no takeover. Batch lists year 2025 for a 2026 DOI.

title: Analyzing Agent Collisions in AI-Aided Energy Management Systems
venue: 2025 IEEE International Conference on Communications, Control, and Computing Technologies for Smart Grids, SmartGridComm 2025 - Proceedings
evidence: "We define an operational collision as any time step t during which one or more network constraints are violated as a direct result of agents' uncoordinated decisions" (Sec. IV-A, Definition of Operational Collision)
method: Partially observable Markov game over networked microgrids with PPO agents; a monitoring module logs voltage and thermal violations per time step, aggregates per-agent severity metrics and attributes collisions to policies.
evaluation: IEEE 34-bus feeder with three IEEE 13-bus microgrids in PandaPower, PPO with two-layer GRU policies, 2,628,000 steps, 2018-2019 train and 2020 test; collision frequency 0.568 independent vs 0.285 shared reward; MG2 holds 78.4% of violations.
contribution: Formalises operational collisions as emergent grid constraint violations by independent learning agents, and gives per-agent severity metrics and attribution showing shared rewards halve collision frequency.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - the analysed agents are PPO MARL microgrid controllers. Detection is logging and post-hoc attribution, never an override, so (a) fails and (c) carries the record. Internal inconsistency the maintainer should check: the text claims shared rewards left collisions 'rare' and 'nearly eliminated', yet Table I gives a 0.285 mean violation frequency over the final 100 years and Table II shows MG1 and MG3 totals HIGHER under shared reward (50,020.55 vs 41,228.27 and 80,406.57 vs 58,575.85). Training is reported as 8,760 x 300 steps but figures are axis-labelled in 300 years. Figures 2 and 3 carry no absolute numbers, and the only contrast is independent vs shared reward with no external baseline.

title: A General Safety Framework for Learning-Based Control in Uncertain Robotic Systems
evidence: Abstract: a "least-restrictive, safety-preserving control law that intervenes only when the computed safety guarantees require it"; the switching law Eq. 8 (Sec. III-A) applies the learned action when V(x) is positive and the safe action otherwise.
method: Hamilton-Jacobi reachability safety filter with Gaussian-process disturbance learning; a least-restrictive switch hands control from an arbitrary learning-based controller to a safe policy when the value function or safety confidence drops.
evaluation: Quadrotor flight tests (Pelican, Hummingbird, VICON, STARMAC) with a with-validation vs without-validation ablation; outcomes qualitative - learning from free fall without ever crashing, and without validation the vehicle violates constraints and repeatedly strikes the ground; safe-set recompute about 2 s, lookup tables constant time, MATLAB on an offboard laptop over ROS.
contribution: A modular least-restrictive safety framework that uses reachability analysis and Gaussian-process disturbance learning to override a learning-based controller only when its guarantees require it.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - a policy-gradient RL quadrotor controller (linear feedback weights), guarded without modifying the learner. Check the evaluation floor: the hardware experiments quantify no collision, violation or intervention counts, giving only qualitative outcomes plus the with/without-validation ablation, so inclusion rests on the formal results (Props. 1-7, Cors. 1-2, robust controlled invariance, probabilistic Lyapunov-rate bound); the global criterion is only approximated (Eq. 18 uses an approximation, numerics reach about 25 dimensions, and the local result is called "a useful heuristic effort"); single agent, so (c) does not hold and "Multi-Agent" appears only in the testbed name; compute is offboard MATLAB with no real-time budget, so (d) does not hold; human handoff is only a remark that "pilot handoffs, for instance, are notoriously prone to result in accidents".

title: Probabilistic Model Predictive Safety Certification for Learning-Based Control
evidence: Introduction: the proposed input is either "certified as safe and is applied, or it is overwritten by the previous safe backup controller", and Sec. III.B implements "a minimal safe modification" whenever safety cannot be verified.
method: Probabilistic model predictive safety certification: an MPC safety filter picking the nominal input closest to the learner's proposal subject to a chance-constrained safe backup trajectory, overwriting the proposal otherwise.
evaluation: Simulation only (nonlinear car, 0.1 s sampling, horizon 30, 98% probability from 30 s of data, 30 episodes shown and 100 experiments); baseline is the uncertified learner; violations and interventions reported qualitatively (safe in every episode, interventions fall after about 30 episodes, slightly slower convergence); offline tightening in YALMIP-MOSEK, no online solver or timing.
contribution: A probabilistic model predictive safety certification filter that minimally modifies a reinforcement learner's input so a chance-constrained safe backup trajectory always remains available.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - a Bayesian-optimization policy search learning a linear control law, filtered at runtime. Check the evaluation floor: no violation counts, intervention counts or reward values are given, only figures and the claim that the framework "enables safe learning in every episode", so inclusion rests on Theorem IV.5 plus recursive feasibility; the guarantee is probabilistic at level p_theta and leans on Assumptions IV.3-IV.4 and the "practical assumption" V.1; the final tightened velocity bound 19.97 m/s is reported as looser than the original 19.8 m/s, which looks inconsistent; single agent and no solver, hardware or latency figures (the authors only cite "real-time capable" solvers), so (c) and (d) do not hold; human input is mentioned only in a footnote.

title: Safe Policies for Reinforcement Learning via Primal-Dual Methods
evidence: Abstract: "We define safety as the agent remaining in a desired safe set with high probability during the operation time." Safety is obtained by constrained primal-dual training, with no runtime override.
method: Constrained RL: chance constraints relaxed to occupancy constraints; primal-dual policy gradient adapts Lagrange multipliers per obstacle, with duality and convergence analysis.
evaluation: 2-D continuous navigation with five obstacles, 500 runs per checkpoint, 40000 iterations; baselines fixed reward-shaping weights 1.128 and 2.835; reaches 0.999 safety after about 10000 iterations; no hardware.
contribution: Shows that primal-dual policy gradient can learn policies meeting per-obstacle safety probability requirements without hand-tuned penalty weights, with theoretical guarantees and a simulated navigation example.
flag: Training-time safety via a Lagrangian reward, which the prompt explicitly rules out of (a); no runtime interceptor, single agent. Most numeric results are in figures; only the 0.999 requirement, dual values 1.128 and 2.835 and iteration counts are in text. arXiv v1 is 2019, journal 2022.

title: Adversarial Resilience for Sampled-Data Systems Under High-Relative-Degree Safety Constraints
evidence: Sec. V-B: "the safety bounds for the normal agents are not violated for the duration of the simulation".
method: Each normal agent solves a CBF-QP minimally modifying its nominal input against worst-case adversarial neighbours, with a margin for asynchronous zero-order-hold sampling and disturbances and an LP fallback when infeasible.
evaluation: MATLAB/Julia simulations: 5 unicycles with 2 adversaries (period 0.01 s) and 8 3D double integrators with 4 adversaries (0.07 s); ablation margin eta=0 violates safety; h_tot traces only; no hardware or timing.
contribution: A sampled-data CBF safety filter for multi-agent systems that stays safe against worst-case adversarial agents under asynchronous sampling and high relative degree, with a robustness margin whose removal produces violations in simulation.
flag: Title matches (TAC extension of an ACC 2021 paper; check whether that conference version is also queued). Borderline on minimum evaluation: the safety metric is the sign of h_tot in single-run traces (non-positive with eta=8.0566, temporarily positive with eta=0); no violation counts, minimum distances, multi-run rates or comparison with another method. Maintainer may prefer E2. Latency/jitter cell is credited for perturbed, asynchronous sampling times, not for computation latency (none reported). Adversary identities are assumed known; QP feasibility over time is an admitted open question and the LP fallback use count is not given. Abstract has no numbers. Drafted from model-summarised PDF reads.

title: Predictive Control Barrier Functions: Enhanced Safety Mechanisms for Learning-Based Control
evidence: "the safety mechanism actively overrules the performance controller" (Sec. I); the predictive safety filter returns the closest input to the proposal that satisfies slack-relaxed constraints.
method: Predictive safety filter softened with slack variables and a terminal control barrier function; the optimal value acts as a predictive barrier function giving recovery from infeasible states.
evaluation: Simulation only: 2-state unstable linear system (N=20) and 4-state kinematic car (N=50, 0.05 s sampling). No baselines, ablations, violation counts or solve times; evidence is trajectory plots and theorems.
contribution: Introduces predictive control barrier functions that keep a predictive safety filter feasible and provably recover a system to the safe set after constraint violation.
flag: Genuine runtime interceptor with formal guarantees (Theorem III.6), but no quantitative safety metric and no baseline or ablation - numerical examples are qualitative only. If the maintainer counts a formal result as sufficient evaluation this could flip; under protocol v1.6 minimum-evaluation it is E2. Title says learning-based control but no learned controller is tested (linear feedback and MPC are the performance controllers). Single system, no latency figures; E4 also arguable. Read via one WebFetch pass.

title: Inverse Optimal Safety Filters
evidence: Sec. XIV Conclusions: "we leave illustration through simulation examples for future work"; the filter is u = u0 + correction, the closed-form CBF-QP solution scaled by a factor of at least 2.
method: Closed-form CBF-QP safety filters made inverse optimal by scaling the correction to the nominal control; extended to deterministic and stochastic disturbances, unknown covariance and parameter estimation.
evaluation: None: purely theoretical. Analytic scalar examples only; no simulation, baseline, safety rate, latency or hardware.
contribution: A theory of inverse optimal safety filters showing that suitably scaled closed-form CBF-QP corrections to a nominal control are optimal for a meaningful differential-game cost, including under disturbances and noise.
flag: Formal result on runtime safety filters with no empirical evaluation at all; the paper itself defers simulations to future work. Single-agent. Only numbers are analytic bounds. If formal results without evaluation are admissible the maintainer may reconsider, but there is no baseline or safety metric. Read via one summarised fetch.

title: Performance-Barrier-Based Event-Triggered Control With Applications to Network Systems
evidence: "This specification plays the role of the "barrier" that the system should not exceed." (Sec. I) - the barrier is a convergence-rate performance bound, not a safety set.
method: Event-triggered control rule that uses the residual between a prescribed performance bound and a Lyapunov function to delay controller updates; distributed Zeno-free version via dynamic average consensus.
evaluation: Simulation: 5-vehicle platoon, 50 initial conditions, 400 s. Average updates 9.94 vs 198.28 for derivative-based trigger; distributed 96.38; empirical MIET 0.003-0.013 s. No hardware or latency.
contribution: Proposes performance-barrier event-triggered control that cuts controller updates about 20-fold on a vehicle platoon while meeting a prescribed convergence rate.
flag: Off-topic: barrier here means a performance specification, and the mechanism schedules when a controller is recomputed; nothing overrides, vetoes or halts an action for safety, and no hazard metric exists. Multi-agent (platoon) only as a networked-control application. Extraction of Sec. VII had some garbled matrices, not affecting the judgement. Read via one WebFetch pass.

title: A Minimum Discounted Reward Hamilton–Jacobi Formulation for Computing Reachable Sets
evidence: "The formulation yields a continuous solution that can be obtained by solving a Hamilton-Jacobi equation." (Abstract); "the solution can be obtained as the unique fixed point to a contraction mapping" (Sec. VII)
method: Minimum discounted reward Hamilton-Jacobi formulation giving a time-independent equation whose value-iteration backup is a contraction; policy iteration, multigrid and warm starts speed offline reachable-set computation.
evaluation: Two simulated benchmarks (double integrator 161x161 grid; pursuit-evasion 41^3 grid); VI vs PI, multigrid, warm start; CPU seconds only (e.g. 416.97s to 308.82s); 2016 MacBook Pro i7.
contribution: Offline numerical method for infinite-horizon reachable sets via a discounted Hamilton-Jacobi fixed point; supplies safe sets a filter could use but evaluates no runtime mechanism.
flag: Offline computation only; no runtime filter is built or evaluated and the only metrics are solver CPU times and a 0.000299 convergence error, so E2 would also apply. arXiv v1 (2018) read, journal version 2023 may differ. Paper is inconsistent on lambda for Fig. 2 (0.001 in text vs 0.01 in caption). Pursuit-evasion is a two-player game, multi-agent only nominally.

title: Attacks on Perception-Based Control Systems: Modeling and Fundamental Limits
evidence: Introduction/Sec. II: the control unit contains an anomaly detector that the attack is designed to evade; the paper gives sufficient conditions for a system to be (epsilon, alpha)-attackable.
method: Attack modelling: stealthy joint falsification of perception and sensor data for nonlinear perception-based controllers, with sufficient conditions under which unsafe deviation stays undetected by any anomaly detector.
evaluation: Simulation only: inverted pendulum and lane-keeping vehicle with DRL controllers; chi-square and CUSUM detectors at 0.05 false-alarm rate; 1000 runs; alarm rates under attack match attack-free; no latency.
contribution: Derives conditions under which attacks on camera and sensor data can drive a perception-based controller to unsafe states while remaining statistically invisible to any runtime anomaly detector.
flag: Attack paper, not a safeguard: the anomaly detector is the thing evaded and never halts or overrides anything. Single-agent. Relevant only as a limits-of-monitoring caveat. Results mostly in figures; text states alarm averages under attack match false-alarm averages over 1000 experiments. Possible arithmetic inconsistency in the vehicle case study (L3*||B|| reported as 0.0106, stated values give about 0.0296) - check against the published version. References list was cut off in the fetch; body and appendices were read.

title: Control Barrier Functions for Stochastic Systems and Safety-Critical Control Designs
evidence: Sec. 4.3: a stochastic ZCBF yields a safety-critical control design in which a compensator u is added to the nominal pre-input u_o (closely paraphrased).
method: Theory of almost-sure reciprocal and stochastic zeroing CBFs for Ito diffusions, with a compensator added to a pre-input and a probability bound on transient safety.
evaluation: Two numerical examples (scalar system; three-state nonholonomic system), ten sample paths each, compared with deterministic run; theoretical safety bounds 0.96 and 0.92. No baseline controller, no hardware.
contribution: Defines control barrier functions for stochastic differential systems that give almost-sure or quantified-probability safety, with a compensator design illustrated on two small simulated systems.
flag: Title confirmed on arXiv v5 abs page and PDF first page. A first fetch of the unversioned PDF returned a summary under a different title ('...With Quantitative Evaluation of Probability') and different parameters (bounds 0.862 and 0.865), probably an earlier version; this row uses v5 only. The 0.96 and 0.92 figures are theoretical lower bounds, not measured rates; only 10 sample paths per example and no baseline or ablation. Fetch summariser could not reproduce b1=3.0 or 0.96 from Eq. 44 with the stated parameters (got about 28.4 and 0.17), so do not quote these without checking the published TAC text. Single low-dimensional system; E4 also defensible. Formal-result papers may deserve leniency but evaluation is minimal.

title: Continuous Approximations of Projected Dynamical Systems via Control Barrier Functions
evidence: Abstract: 'Our results pave the way to implement discontinuous PDS-based controllers in a continuous fashion, employing CBFs.'
method: Theory showing CBF-based continuous dynamics are perturbations of projected dynamical systems, with trajectories converging uniformly to the PDS ones as the CBF parameter alpha goes to infinity.
evaluation: Two numerical examples: feedback optimisation of a linear plant and synchronverter antiwindup control, CBF dynamics (alpha 100, 300) versus PDS reference; figures only, no numeric metrics or timing.
contribution: A formal result that control-barrier-function dynamics continuously approximate projected dynamical systems, illustrated on feedback optimisation and inverter control examples.
flag: Subject is approximation theory for constrained optimisation/control dynamics, not safety interception of an acting system. The CBF term does modify a nominal vector field (closed-form QP), so a reader could argue (a); even then it would be E2, since Sec. V reports no numeric metric ('trajectories are almost indistinguishable from PDS ones'). Single-agent, no hardware.

title: Robust Control Barrier Functions Using Uncertainty Estimation With Application to Mobile Robots
evidence: UE-CBF-QP minimises ||u - k_d(x)||^2 subject to a robust CBF constraint (Eq. 32); "The robot's reference trajectory is chosen to violate the safety constraint when using the nominal controller" (Sec. IV-B).
method: Uncertainty estimator with bounded error feeds a robust CBF/high-order CBF QP or SOCP filter that cancels matched uncertainty and tightens the constraint for unmatched uncertainty.
evaluation: Sim flexible-joint actuator at 100 Hz vs HOCBF-QP and R-HOCBF; hardware tracked robot on 25 deg slope at 50 Hz vs nominal CBF-QP. Figures only; no solve times.
contribution: A robust barrier-function safety filter that uses an uncertainty estimator with a provable error bound to handle matched and unmatched model error, demonstrated on a tracked robot on a slope.
flag: Single-agent filter, no multi-agent, latency or handoff aspect, hence E4. Evaluation also thin: no numeric safety metrics, results only in figures, hardware is one experiment, no ablation - E2 equally defensible. Onboard compute is deferred to another paper (ref 31), so no edge or latency claim can be credited; 50 Hz loop rate is the only timing. "First to ensure robust safety against matched and unmatched uncertainties via HOCBFs" is a self-claim. Extraction garbled some equations and Sec. V.

title: A Continuous-Time Violation-Free Multiagent Optimization Algorithm and Its Applications to Safe Distributed Control
evidence: Sec. V, Theorem 1: "the coupling constraints in (3) hold during the solution evolution"; Sec. VII applies this to CBF-induced QPs (Eq. 23, 42) that minimally modify nominal controllers.
method: Distributed continuous-time optimization: each agent solves a local QP with auxiliary constraint-shifting variables updated by (normalized) subgradient flow; coupling constraints hold at all times; applied as distributed CBF-QP safety filter.
evaluation: MATLAB simulation only, 9 agents: resource allocation and safe formation; vs primal decomposition, nominal, centralized QP, naive distributed (y=0); results as plots; no latency reported.
contribution: A violation-free distributed optimization scheme lets nine agents solve coupled CBF safety-filter QPs locally while provably satisfying shared safety constraints at every instant, shown in simulation only.
flag: Borderline E2 vs include: runtime distributed CBF-QP filter with multi-agent coupling constraints clearly meets (a)/(c) and has baselines (nominal violates both CBFs; centralized; naive), but safety outcomes are only plotted (Figs. 4, 7), no collision/violation rate or summary statistic in text. Only numbers: 27 vs 48 auxiliary scalars, 6 vs 24 communicated. Guarantee depends on Assumption 3 (Slater for all y); synchronous, delay-free communication assumed; laptop i7-1365U, Euler step 0.01 s, no timing. Drafted from one summarising read of the PDF, figure values not verified.

title: Safety-Critical Learning of Robot Control With Temporal Logic Specifications
evidence: Sec. V-C: the "'shield' of (23) compensates the model-free RL controller"; executed action is a_Safe = a_RL + a_pt (Eq. 24), with a_pt from an ECBF quadratic program.
method: Modular DDPG for LTL tasks with a Gaussian-process exponential-CBF quadratic program that minimally corrects each RL action during training and execution; corrections are penalised in the reward.
evaluation: Simulated cart-pole, pendulum, car, Mars rover; ablations with ECBF off and standard DDPG; safe and success rates over 200 runs in figures only; training 40.4h vs 22.7h; no step latency.
contribution: A Gaussian-process control-barrier shield corrects each action of a temporal-logic RL agent, keeping training safe with probability at least (1-delta)^n in four simulated single-robot tasks.
flag: Borderline E4: single-agent (multi-agent is future work), simulation only. Safety and success rates appear only in Figs. 17-18, no numbers in text; abstract claim of "near-perfect success rates" has no figure in the body text read. No value of delta given. Per-step QP time not reported, only training-hours overhead (Table III). Journal version 2025, arXiv 2021. Last ~22k characters (appendix/references) not read.

title: Safety-Critical Control for Nonlinear Systems With Complex Input Constraints
evidence: "Finally, by using (61) and (66) in Theorem 3, a safe controller is obtained by solving the following CLF-CBF-QP problem" (Sec. IV-C)
method: Adds an integrator so the input becomes a state, encodes state- and time-dependent input limits as a barrier, and solves a CLF-CBF-QP correcting a nominal control, with adaptive disturbance estimation.
evaluation: Two numerical simulations of low-order single systems; compared by plot with a standard CLF-CBF controller and a nominal controller. No violation counts, no timing, no hardware.
contribution: Recasts complex state- and time-dependent input constraints as output constraints through a dynamic extension, giving a CLF-CBF quadratic program with disturbance estimation that keeps inputs within bounds in two simulations.
flag: Formal result with plot-only evidence: no quantitative safety metric (no violation count or margin), so fails the minimum evaluation; also single-agent with no latency or handoff aspect, so E4 would equally apply. Case 1 figure caption labels the comparison curve as nominal control while the text calls it a CLF-CBF baseline. The barrier protects input limits, not a hazard among agents.

title: Robust Safety Assurance for Robotic Swarms Using Decentralized Collision Verification
evidence: "During experimentation, all 140 deliberate attempts to force a collision were detected, on average, 3.2 s before they would have occurred." (Sec V-C Collision Avoidance)
method: Each UAV computes a face-lifting reachable set (4 s horizon) every 0.5 s, broadcasts it over an XBee mesh, checks intersections with peers' sets and BRAKEs on predicted collision.
evaluation: Outdoor flights, 8 quadrotors (Raspberry Pi 4); 140 forced-collision attempts all detected, mean 3.2 s ahead; per-task WCET tables; broadcast delay 0.3-0.6 s; 40% packet loss; no baseline.
contribution: Field deployment of decentralized reachability-based collision verification on an eight-UAV outdoor swarm, halting all 140 forced-collision attempts about 3.2 s ahead and showing that radio delay and packet loss, not computation, limit scalability.
flag: Record is listed by DOI but the text is the arXiv accepted manuscript (arXiv:2611.01081v1, title matches). Minimum-evaluation risk: there is a quantitative safety metric (140/140 detected, 3.2 s lead) but NO baseline method; the only comparison is phase 1 vs phase 2 timing (regression-model timeout), which is an ablation of timing, not of safety - maintainer must decide if that satisfies v1.6. Inconsistencies: abstract says 140 total outdoor vehicle flights including 6 swarm flights, body says 140 deliberate collision attempts; abstract says broadcast about 300-500 ms and text says all messages arrived within 1 s, yet Table III (phase 2) lists worst-case broadcast times of 1.9-2.8 s, worse than phase 1 (0.58-0.97 s) and unexplained; the 500-520 ms total verification figure appears only in the abstract. Authors found reach-set WCET of 15-16 ms against a 5 ms budget in phase 1. Only about 60% of messages received; 99% detection argument assumes independent losses. No false-halt rate (scenario has no benign close passes). Avoidance is stop-and-hold until a ground-station ALL_CLEAR - a human release step but no handoff study, so human handoff cell not credited. Authors state the contribution is system-level, not algorithmic (builds on Tran et al. 2019).

title: Cooperative Resilience in Artificial Intelligence Multiagent Systems
evidence: Abstract: the paper is "proposing a clear definition of 'cooperative resilience' and outlining a methodology for its quantitative measurement"; disruptions are injected into the environment and no mechanism screens or overrides agent actions (Sec. 3).
method: Defines cooperative resilience and a four-stage measurement methodology over performance-versus-reference curves, scoring groups of PPO and GPT-4 agents under resource-removal and unsustainable-bot disruptions.
evaluation: Melting Pot 2.0 Commons Harvest Open; 9 apple-removal scenarios and 3 unsustainable-bot scenarios; the only comparison is RL vs LLM agents; no numeric resilience scores in the text (heatmaps and five-episode curves only); no baseline controller, no ablation, no hardware or latency.
contribution: A formal definition and four-stage quantitative measure of cooperative resilience, applied to RL and LLM-based multiagent groups facing resource-removal and free-rider disruptions.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes for the agents (PPO policies and GPT-4 agents) but nothing guards them - there is no runtime override, veto, halt or deferral anywhere, so (a) fails, and (c) fails the primacy test because the primary claim and primary outcome are a resilience score from deviations between performance and reference curves, not a hazard, collision, violation or detection rate against a baseline or ablation. Likely overturn candidate: a maintainer who reads the disruption study as emergent multi-agent failure would still hit the evaluation floor, since the text reports no numeric values at all, so exclude-E2 is the alternative. Also note Sec. 4.3.1 says RL generally outperforms LLM while Sec. 4.3.2 reports the reverse, and human comparison is future work only.

title: Online Safety-Embedded Critic Learning for Uncertain Systems With Self-Triggered Mechanism
evidence: Sec 3.2: the robust CBF constraint is added to the cost through a Lagrange multiplier, yielding a 'safety-embedded value function'; Sec 6.2: 'the self-triggered mechanism only needs 118 samplings.'
method: Robust CBF with a compensation term embedded in the HJB value function via a Lagrange multiplier; online identifier-critic learning; self-triggered control updates with stability and safety thresholds.
evaluation: Numerical simulation of one 2-state uncertain system; vs baseline-CBF and RCBF-as-filter; cost 11.81 vs 12.18; 118 vs 15000 samples; 154462 vs over 1e7 operations.
contribution: Embeds a robust barrier function in an online-learned optimal controller and uses self-triggering to cut control updates from 15000 to 118 in simulation.
flag: arXiv title differs slightly ('HJB-based online safety-embedded critic learning ...') but is the same paper; published TAI version may differ from this preprint. Safety is in the value function, not a runtime filter, so (a) fails; the filter variant appears only as a baseline. Single system, so E4 is an equally defensible code. No safety-violation count: safety loss of the baseline is shown only in phase plots. Single-run cost comparison. Operation counts are arithmetic, not measured time; no hardware.

title: Enhanced Global Optimization With Parallel Global and Local Structures for Real-Time Control Systems
venue: IEEE Transactions on Automation Science and Engineering
evidence: "we restart the local search stage. This restart allows the algorithm to jump out of the current local optimums." (Sec. 3.2.2) - a parallel stochastic global optimiser; no acting system or safety property.
method: Parallel global-local optimisation (PGLO-PS): additive global and local Gaussian process model with q-EI on a master and parallel pattern search on workers for noisy simulation optimisation.
evaluation: Synthetic test functions (Sun et al., Griewank, Ackley, Levy, Schwefel), 30 macro-replications, vs TSSO/EQI/CGLO/q-EI/MultPPS; wall-clock 210.36 s (q=1) to 37.07 s (q=8); hardware unspecified.
contribution: A parallel Gaussian-process global optimisation algorithm combining global expected-improvement search with local pattern search to cut wall-clock time on noisy simulation problems.
flag: arXiv title lacks the journal suffix "for Real-Time Control Systems" but is otherwise identical; treated as the preprint of the same paper - maintainer may confirm. The arXiv version has no real-time control or safety content (benchmark functions only, 0.01 s artificial wait); nothing multi-agent beyond parallel processors.

title: Collision-Free Circular Formation Control for Nonholonomic Vehicles Under Obstacle Occlusion With Relative Measurement
venue: IEEE Transactions on Automation Science and Engineering
evidence: "The collisions during the formation process are effectively prevented by the control laws." (Abstract)
method: Communication-free, GPS-free circular formation control laws for nonholonomic vehicles using relative measurements and an attractive vector; speed law keeps angular ordering to prevent collisions, extended to sensor occlusion.
evaluation: Simulations with four vehicles (radius 12 m, with/without occluding obstacles) and four Turtlebot 3 Burger robots indoors; convergence plots only. No baseline, no collision rate, no latency.
contribution: Circular formation control for nonholonomic vehicles without communication or GPS, with collision avoidance built into the control law and validated in simulation and on four Turtlebots.
flag: Correct file. Formation-control paper: collision avoidance is a property of the nominal control law (angular ordering), not a runtime filter/monitor, so (a) is not met; (c) fails the primacy test and would in any case fail minimum evaluation (no baseline or ablation, no quantitative safety metric, only 'converge ... without collinearity and collisions' read off plots) - E2 is the alternative code. Remark 3 states the vehicle model ignores physical volume, so collision-freedom is for point vehicles. Proofs (Sections III) were skimmed, not verified.

title: Finite-Time Flexible Performance-Based Formation Control for Wheeled Humanoid Robots With Dynamic Obstacle Avoidance
venue: IEEE Transactions on Automation Science and Engineering
evidence: "This qualitative observation is quantitatively confirmed in Fig. 11, which compares the total path lengths during the avoidance of the two dynamic obstacles" (Sec IV-B Comparison With Existing Method)
method: Distributed formation controller for wheeled humanoid robots: virtual barrier potential field using obstacle position, velocity and relative angle, plus finite-time prescribed-performance bounds that relax during collision avoidance or connectivity maintenance.
evaluation: Five-robot simulation with static and dynamic obstacles vs controller without virtual barrier field and vs improved APF; three-robot ROS/WiFi experiment; outcomes are trajectories, error plots, path length; no latency.
contribution: A distributed potential-field formation controller that steers robot teams behind moving obstacles and relaxes prescribed tracking bounds when they conflict with collision avoidance, shown in simulation and a three-robot experiment.
flag: Safety lives inside the nominal control law (potential-field terms and adjustable performance bounds), there is no separate filter that vetoes or overrides a nominal command, so (a) is not met. For (c): collision avoidance is one of several control objectives alongside finite-time tracking and connectivity, and no quantitative safety metric is reported - no collision count, minimum-distance or violation rate; the only quantitative comparison is total path length (Fig. 11, figure only, no numbers in text) and the claim of 'significantly higher collision risk' for the baseline is read off trajectory plots. Single scenario per comparison, no repeated trials. Would equally fail E2 if the maintainer judges (c) met. Experiment uses mobile manipulator bases with arms locked, not humanoids; no compute or timing reported. Proofs (Sec III) were skimmed, not checked.

title: Neural Configuration-Space Barriers for Manipulation Planning and Control
venue: IEEE Transactions on Automation Science and Engineering
evidence: Sec. VI-B: a DR-CBF-QP minimizes the deviation from the nominal PD velocity command subject to the barrier condition (Eq. 24), though "feasibility is not guaranteed in all situations".
method: Neural configuration-space distance barrier for manipulators; bubble-graph planner plus a distributionally robust CBF-QP safety filter at 50 Hz overriding a nominal PD command under MC-dropout and point-cloud uncertainty.
evaluation: 2-DoF sim (500 trials), 6-DoF xArm sim (50), real xArm6 (20); vs PD, PD+CBF-QP, MPPI, RRT variants; dynamic success 0.992/1.0 vs 0.638/0.70 (CBF-QP); CDF inference ~0.27-0.30 ms.
contribution: A learned configuration-space barrier with a distributionally robust CBF-QP filter running at 50 Hz raised dynamic-obstacle success for a 6-DoF arm from 0.70 to 1.0 over a plain CBF filter in simulation.
flag: Borderline E4: single manipulator, no multi-agent aspect; kept because it is a genuine runtime filter with safety metric, baselines and reported timing (50 Hz, sub-ms network inference, 70.2 ms at 100 configs x 10000 points) - but no explicit latency deadline is stated, so (d) not claimed and latency cell not credited. Metric is success rate, not an explicit collision rate; check its definition. Real-robot control results qualitative only (planning: 0.22 s end-to-end vs 0.96-1.05 s). No recovery if QP infeasible. Safety costs tracking: error 0.516 vs 0.327 (CBF-QP) in 6-DoF dynamic. Compute for control loop not stated (RTX 4090 is for training). Read was v4 of the arXiv PDF.

title: Flow-Opt: Scalable Centralized Multi-Robot Trajectory Optimization With Flow Matching and Differentiable Optimization
venue: IEEE Transactions on Automation Science and Engineering
evidence: Sec. I: the safety filter is not used during denoising, "we apply it only to the trajectory obtained at the final step"; Sec. IV: flow output "may not strictly satisfy collision-avoidance constraints".
method: Centralized planner: DiT flow-matching policy samples joint trajectories; a projection-style safety-filter QP, warm-started by a self-supervised network trained through the unrolled solver, repairs constraint violations.
evaluation: Sim 2D/3D, 8-64 robots, vs GPU convex optimizer [9], MMD, batch-sequential [16]; success 99.93-100%, 0.05-1.02 s on RTX 5090; qualitative Bebop/Robotont demo.
contribution: Flow matching plus a learned-warm-start projection filter generates joint trajectories for up to 64 robots in about 1 s (33.7 s for the optimization baseline) at 99.93-100% success.
flag: BORDERLINE (a): the paper names a 'safety filter' that projects the generative model's nominal trajectory onto the feasible set before execution, which is close to a runtime override. I scored it no because it is the final stage of a centralized (re)planner, there is no veto/halt/fallback, the paper's claim is scalability and compute time, and there is no ablation without the filter (only without the warm-start network, no numbers). Maintainer may prefer include under (a). Success rate is the only safety metric. Text/table mismatch: text cites 69% for [16] at 32 robots, Table V says 63.12%. Timings are desktop GPU (RTX 5090), not edge. Hardware robot count and compute not stated. Last ~6k characters of the PDF (likely references) not read.

title: Cooperative Formation Control of Connected Vehicles With Collision Avoidance and Unknown Input Reconstruction
venue: IEEE Transactions on Automation Science and Engineering
evidence: "Simulation results on a four-vehicle fleet verify the effectiveness of the proposed architecture." (Section V Conclusion)
method: Leader-follower formation controller for connected vehicles: prescribed-time unknown-input reconstruction (interval observer plus super-twisting differentiator), distributed leader-state observer, and a smooth exponential potential field for collision avoidance and connectivity.
evaluation: One numerical simulation: virtual leader, four followers, four static obstacles; error-convergence plots (T1=20 s, T3=40 s); Table I is a qualitative feature comparison. No collision metric, baseline run, hardware or latency.
contribution: A prescribed-time formation tracking controller for connected vehicles that embeds collision avoidance and connectivity maintenance as a smooth exponential potential-field term, shown in a single four-follower simulation.
flag: Collision avoidance is a potential-field term inside the nominal control law, not a runtime filter, and the paper's primary claim is prescribed-time convergence and input reconstruction, so (c) primacy fails; multi-agent coordination alone is E1. Would also fail minimum evaluation (E2): safety shown only as 'without collision' in one trajectory figure, no minimum-distance numbers, the only comparison table is qualitative. Static obstacles only and inter-vehicle collision not separately measured. Authors state 'Physical-platform validation remains outside the scope of this study'. Lyapunov proofs in Section III skimmed, not checked.

title: Number Adaptive Formation Flight Planning via Affine Deformable Guidance in Narrow Environments
venue: IEEE Transactions on Automation Science and Engineering
evidence: Agent trajectories are optimised with dynamic feasibility, obstacle clearance and swarm avoidance constraints, with reciprocal avoidance following prior work (Sec. IV-D); no filter or fallback layer is described.
method: Formation planner: layer-wise Lloyd partitioning and Hungarian assignment adapt to agents joining or leaving; a deformable virtual structure with scale and affine factors guides per-agent trajectory optimisation through gaps.
evaluation: Simulation with 14-100 agents and real drones on Jetson Orin NX; vs SF, SF-ALAS, VRB; gap-traversal success and time over 50 trials; assignment under 0.161 s; no collision rate.
contribution: A formation flight planner that re-partitions and affinely deforms a virtual structure so drone swarms can gain or lose members and squeeze through gaps narrower than the formation.
flag: Formation and path-quality paper; collision avoidance is one planner constraint and no collision or violation rate is reported (success only). Join and leave events are externally commanded, no failure detection. Number of physical drones not clearly stated (3-4). Text gives 0.1592 s for 100 agents but Table I max is 0.1607 s; abstract claim of 15 percent join or leave is not clearly matched by the experiments.

title: On Enhancing Structural Resilience of Multirobot Coverage Control With Bearing Rigidity
venue: IEEE Transactions on Control of Network Systems
evidence: Structural resilience is defined as "the ability to detect and mitigate the effects of localization errors and robot loss during the mission" (Abstract); realised as a bearing cost in tracking MPC and graph repair (Sec. IV).
method: Hierarchical coverage control: centralised Voronoi centroids, decentralised nonlinear tracking MPC with a weighted bearing-rigidity cost, and Henneberg-style local edge repair after a robot is lost (2D only).
evaluation: Numerical simulation only: 4 unicycle robots for coverage, 8 for recovery; compared only across bearing weight values; coverage cost plotted without numbers; no timing or hardware.
contribution: A coverage controller that keeps a multirobot team bearing-rigid and repairs the sensing graph locally after a robot loss, shown in small 2D simulations.
flag: Coordination and graph-rigidity paper, not a safety mechanism: no collisions, hazards or violations are measured or even modelled. Would also fail minimum evaluation (no quantitative safety metric, only a weight sweep). Robot loss is injected, not detected by a learned or runtime monitor. Recovery results hold only for d = 2.

title: Distributed Online Task Assignment via Inexact ADMM for Unplanned Online Tasks and Its Applications to Security
venue: IEEE Transactions on Control of Network Systems
evidence: The robot "prioritizes the regroup and abandons the online task" when a detour would miss the co-observation (Sec. IV-D); a CBF security term filters the CLF reference control.
method: Distributed inexact ADMM assigns sub-team robots to planned trajectories and unplanned online tasks; reachability ellipsoids and a CLF-CBF controller keep scheduled co-observations that detect plan-deviation attacks.
evaluation: Single 2-D simulation, 3 sub-teams (5 robots), 20 s task; 2 of 4 online tasks fulfilled; no baselines, no repeated trials, no timing, no hardware.
contribution: A distributed inexact-ADMM task assignment lets robots leave their team for unplanned tasks while CBF and reachability constraints preserve the co-observation schedule that secures against plan-deviation attacks.
flag: Evaluation is one qualitative simulation run with no baseline, ablation or safety metric - fails minimum evaluation. Scalability advantage over prior work is asserted, not tested. (a)/(c) marked generously: the CBF acts as a filter on a reference control and the security goal is detecting compromised robots, but neither is measured. Based on the arXiv version; the journal version may add experiments.

title: Safety-Critical Control With Input Delay in Dynamic Environment
venue: IEEE Transactions on Control Systems Technology
evidence: Sec. II-A: the filter is to "modify this input in a minimally invasive fashion to guarantee safety"; Eq. (43) minimises ||u - K_d||^2 subject to the environmental CBF condition at the predicted state.
method: Environmental control barrier function QP/SOCP safety filter with predictor feedback that compensates input delay and adds a worst-case margin for error in predicting the moving environment.
evaluation: Simulated adaptive cruise control (delay 1 s) and Segway vs moving obstacle (delay 0.1 s); baselines delay-free design and predictor without robustness margin; single-trajectory safe/unsafe plots; no compute times.
contribution: A control-barrier safety filter that predicts both its own state and a moving environment across a known input delay keeps simulated vehicles and a Segway safe where delay-free filters collide.
flag: BORDERLINE - maintainer should decide. Clear runtime interceptor and directly latency-aware (actuation delay), but evidence is single simulated trajectories: safety shown as sign of H(t) in plots, with no collision/violation rate, no repeated trials and no numeric violation magnitude, so the v1.6 minimum (quantitative safety metric) is arguably not met. Baselines exist (uncompensated and non-robust designs collide). Delay is fixed and known, not jitter. Environment is one other vehicle/obstacle with assumed bounded acceleration, not multi-agent. No hardware, no solver timing. If trajectory comparison against baselines is accepted as quantitative, change to include under (a).

title: Control Barrier Functions and Input-to-State Safety With Application to Automated Vehicles
venue: IEEE Transactions on Control Systems Technology
evidence: The nominal controller "is only modified when it does not satisfy safety requirements." (Sec. II-B); "With these parameters the system is rendered safe, as the value of h does not drop below 0." (experiments)
method: CBF safety filter (min of nominal connected cruise control and safe input) made robust to input disturbance via input-to-state safety with a tunable, state-dependent robustness term.
evaluation: Simulation plus a real Class-8 truck following a V2X-streamed braking leader; nominal and non-robust CBF both violate safety, robust filter h_min 0.35m; 9 parameter sets, 3 runs each; no timing.
contribution: Robust control-barrier-function safety filter tested on a full-scale automated truck, where the standard filter fails under about 4 m/s^2 actuation disturbance and the tuned input-to-state-safe version keeps headway.
flag: Borderline E4: single controlled vehicle, leader is a pre-recorded profile streamed over V2X (physical lead car only for visualisation), so no real multi-agent state. Kept as include because it is a genuine runtime filter with hardware evidence and a baseline that fails. Safety metric is minimum barrier value h_min (0.35m set A; 22.09m set B; 0.78m set C; 1.02m set D), not a collision rate; h_min for the failing baselines was not captured in my read. Theoretical bound h* is negative (-4.38m), so the guarantee itself does not certify h>=0. No control-loop rate, latency or compute timing reported (Speedgoat real-time target). Human does steering only; no takeover studied.

title: Experimental Validation of Safe MPC for Autonomous Driving in Uncertain Environments
venue: IEEE Transactions on Control Systems Technology
evidence: Sec. V-C: "the solution time for all OCPs were at most 40 ms, which was well below the sampling time"
method: MPC with pedestrian reachable-set collision constraints and a terminal full-stop safe set (MPFTC); parallel OCPs per pass/yield configuration, lowest-cost one applied.
evaluation: One simulation pair (assumption violated vs satisfied) and a full-scale Volvo XC90 track test with simulated pedestrians; 20 Hz, solves at most 40 ms on i9 laptop; no collision statistics.
contribution: Experimental validation on a full-scale car of a recursively feasible safe MPC that guarantees a stopping fallback around uncertain pedestrians, solving within a 50 ms sampling period.
flag: Safety is a constraint inside the planner, not a filter between a nominal decision and execution, so (a) is not met under the strict-runtime rule. (d) is borderline: real-time solve under a 50 ms period is shown but latency is not the subject. No quantitative safety metric: one unsafe-vs-safe simulated run (unsafe hits pedestrian at about 3 m/s) and one track run; no counts, no external baseline. Pedestrians are simulated, so multi-agent is nominal. If the maintainer does not accept (d), E1 is the alternative code. Steering interface delay of 150 ms is compensated by state augmentation. No safety-driver or takeover procedure described.

title: Multiagent Systems With CBF-Based Controllers: Collision Avoidance and Liveness From Instability
venue: IEEE Transactions on Control Systems Technology
evidence: Sec. III-IV: each agent's CBF-QP minimises deviation from its nominal LQR command subject to the barrier constraint; Sec. VI: "the liveness in these multiagent systems comes from instability".
method: CBF-QP safety filters over nominal LQR for double-integrator agents; compares centralized, decentralized follower, reciprocal, CCS and proposed PCCA policies; analyses gridlock as stable or unstable equilibria.
evaluation: Simulation only: 100 Monte Carlo runs, 5 agents, 20 Hz; six policies compared on convergence time, minimum barrier value, gridlocks, QP infeasibility; 2-agent 1-D sweep; no computation times.
contribution: Shows that decentralized CBF safety filters can gridlock or go infeasible, and that a predictor-corrector variant (PCCA) matches centralized filtering with zero gridlocks and near-zero barrier violation in 100 five-agent runs.
flag: Simulation only, holonomic double integrators, 5 agents; no hardware and no solver timing (only the 50 ms sample time). Table I: gridlocks/infeasible runs of 100 - Centralized 0/0, DF 3/27, DR 4/32, CCS 4/0, PCCA 0/0; h_min -0.002 centralized, -2.84 DF, -1.53 DR, -1.35 CCS, -0.015 PCCA. Small negative h_min means safety holds only after adding a radius margin (Table II), and one CCS run still collides. 1-D gridlock rates: PCCA 0.002%, centralized 0.1%, DR 15.4%. Half the claim is liveness rather than safety - maintainer should confirm the primacy test for (c); (a) holds regardless. Title on arXiv uses a dash instead of the colon but is the same paper.

title: Robust Predictive Motion Planning by Learning Obstacle Uncertainty
venue: IEEE Transactions on Control Systems Technology
evidence: "it implies that the proposed method, in theory, does not guarantee safety in motion planning" (Sec. IV-D3 Reachability Analysis)
method: Online learning of an obstacle's intended control set by linear programming from observed accelerations, forward reachable occupancy, then MPC with slack-softened collision-avoidance constraint against that occupancy.
evaluation: Simulation, 1 ego and 1 surrounding vehicle, 300 Monte Carlo runs: collision-free 100% vs robust MPC 98.3%/100% vs deterministic MPC 40.3%/30.7% (N=10/8); total 98.5/72.0 ms; scaled-car hardware 64 ms mean.
contribution: Learns a surrounding vehicle's intended control set online and plans against its reachable occupancy, giving collision-free rates of 100% in 300 simulated runs with less conservatism than worst-case robust MPC.
flag: Safety is a soft constraint inside the planner (slack weight 300), not a runtime filter, so (a) fails. (c) is arguable: collision-free rate vs two baselines is a headline result, but there is one ego and one obstacle vehicle and the framing is planner conservatism. Authors concede no theoretical safety guarantee. Timing is reported (about 10 Hz on a laptop) but no explicit deadline, so (d) not met. Hardware tests (3 scenarios) give no collision rate. Completion-rate and cost columns of Table III were garbled in extraction and are not reported here.

title: Collision Avoidance for Convex Primitives via Differentiable Optimization-Based High-Order Control Barrier Functions
venue: IEEE Transactions on Control Systems Technology
evidence: Introduction: the controller "efficiently computes a minimally invasive control from the given nominal control" (HOCBF-QP, eqs. 32 and 37).
method: Differentiable-optimization scaling-factor distance between convex primitives used as a second-order CBF in a torque-level QP filter, plus a circulation constraint to escape boundary equilibria.
evaluation: Hardware: one Franka FR3 arm, three tasks (pick-place, whiteboard, thrown ball). Ablation with/without circulation. p90 loop time 3.0/1.9/7.6 ms on i9-13900K PC. No collision rates.
contribution: A high-order CBF safety filter for convex-primitive collision avoidance runs on a real 7-DoF arm at 1.9-7.6 ms p90 loop time, with a circulation term that prevents deadlock at the safe-set boundary.
flag: Single manipulator, not multi-agent. Safety evidence is qualitative (task succeeds, ablation gets stuck); no collision/violation rate or repeated-trial counts, hence E2. Latency is reported (p90) but on a desktop i9, not edge hardware, and no explicit deadline is stated in what I read; maintainer may weigh criterion (d). Flying-ball test has no baseline. Last ~800 chars (bios/references) not read.

title: Resilient Path Planning for UAVs in Data Collection Under Adversarial Attacks
venue: IEEE Transactions on Information Forensics and Security
evidence: Sec. VI-B: 'the typical UAV is able to wait for the jammer to become silent' - a learned policy behaviour; collision avoidance and jammer avoidance enter only as reward penalties (Eq. 11, Eq. 21) during training.
method: D3QN path planner for a data-collecting UAV; jamming resilience via virtual-jammer or higher-SINR-threshold training, and retraining with jammer-position state plus proximity penalty against a learned UAV jammer.
evaluation: Simulation only, 5000 test episodes, 5-10 IoT nodes, 2 ORCA UAVs; vs no-defence and no-jammer policies; success 84.8 to 98.6-99.1 percent with VJ; collision rate 0.1-1.1 percent; no latency.
contribution: Trains a D3QN UAV data-collection planner to stay effective under fixed and learned jammers, restoring success rates from 84.8 percent (worst fixed jammer) and under 34 percent (intelligent jammers) to above 94 percent in simulation.
flag: Subject is communication-jamming resilience of a trained policy, not runtime interception or multi-agent hazard detection; collision rate is reported but is not the outcome the defence targets (it stays 0.1-1.1 percent with or without defence). No hardware or timing. Table IX row grouping is ambiguous in the extracted text; one pi4 policy reaches only 82-87 percent success against mismatched jammers, so 'above 94 percent' holds for matched defences only.

title: Spatio-Temporal Graph Dual-Attention Network for Multi-Agent Prediction and Tracking
venue: IEEE Transactions on Intelligent Transportation Systems
evidence: Agents are nodes and their relations edges in history and future spatio-temporal graphs, and the model jointly predicts all agents (Sec. V-A, V-C); 'The constraint not only ensures physical feasibility but also enhances model performance' (Abstract).
method: Encoder-decoder over history and future spatio-temporal graphs with topological plus temporal dual attention, GRU decoder with a kinematic bicycle layer, Wasserstein-style latent generative training.
evaluation: ETH/UCY, SDD, INTERACTION; baselines Trajectron, CGNS, Social-BiGAT, S-GAN; ablations T, T+C-ATT, T+C, T+C+K; ADE/FDE 0.30/0.59 avg ETH/UCY vs 0.46/0.94; TITAN X, 8 ms per step.
contribution: Graph dual-attention generative model that jointly forecasts and tracks multi-agent future trajectories under a kinematic feasibility layer, cutting ADE/FDE by 15-35% against prior predictors.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: no - nothing is guarded, there is no runtime override, veto or halt anywhere in the pipeline. Borderline (b): it is latent generative prediction of future state over a dynamic multi-agent graph with direct ADE/FDE measures and baselines, but a maintainer may read it as a plain trajectory regressor and exclude-E1 under the Pillar 2 ruling. Check Table I per-scene ADE/FDE: the extraction was garbled and only the average (0.30/0.59 vs Trajectron 0.46/0.94) and the claimed 34.8%/37.2% reduction could be confirmed. Timing (8 ms per step, 80 ms for 10 steps, 12.5 Hz) is on a TITAN X, not edge hardware, so no latency cell credited.

title: A Convex Optimal Control Framework for Autonomous Vehicle Intersection Crossing
venue: IEEE Transactions on Intelligent Transportation Systems
evidence: Sec. II-A: rear-end and merging-zone conflicts are hard time-gap constraints (eqs. 12-13) inside the optimal control problem; Assumption 2: CAVs follow the trajectories "with no deviations".
method: Centralised intersection controller: space-domain optimal control relaxed to second-order cone programs, with a scheduler choosing crossing order and a lower level optimising time and battery energy.
evaluation: MATLAB simulation, 60 CAVs; baselines FIFO order and SOCP lower bound; 41.7% energy saving for 20% more travel time; solve 7.52 s for N=60 on Core i5; no collision counts.
contribution: A convex hierarchical optimal-control scheme schedules connected vehicles through a signal-free intersection, trading travel time against energy, with collision avoidance as hard constraints in the planner.
flag: Fails primacy test for (c): primary claim and measured outcome are energy and travel time; collision avoidance is a planner constraint with no collision or violation rate reported. No runtime override; solve times 2.71 s (N=20) and 7.52 s (N=60) are whole-horizon solves, not a real-time safety decision. Multi-agent state cell credited only because the optimisation is joint over all vehicles - drop if being strict.

title: How Far Two UAVs Should be Subject to Communication Uncertainties
venue: IEEE Transactions on Intelligent Transportation Systems
evidence: Abstract: 'a separation principle of the safety radius design and controller design is proposed'; Sec. III Theorem 2 gives a lower bound on the safety radius from delay, packet loss and estimation error bounds.
method: Design-time safety-radius bound for UAV pairs and groups under bounded communication delay, packet loss and position noise, using a filtered position; any controller keeping that separation is safe.
evaluation: MATLAB sims and multicopter flights (OptiTrack); cases A/B/C give r_s 5.30/14.30/22.31 m; case C (condition 33 violated) breaches separation at 11.25 s; flight r_s 0.47/0.71/0.23 m.
contribution: A closed-form safety radius for UAVs that absorbs communication delay, packet loss and estimation error, validated in simulation and multicopter flights where separation holds when the derived condition is met.
flag: Borderline. Not a runtime interceptor: the radius is a design-time bound fed to an unspecified avoidance controller. Included on (c) because inter-UAV separation under communication uncertainty is the primary claim and outcome, but there is no collision rate and no external baseline, only the condition-33 ablation (case B vs C) and minimum-distance traces; the maintainer may prefer E2. Latency here is communication delay (up to 2 s), not inference latency. No compute figures. Reader recomputation could not reproduce the hovering-flight r_s of 0.47 m from Theorem 2 (got about 0.33-0.44 m); unverified. Planner computation-time comparison is qualitative only.

title: Deep Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning for Highway On-Ramp Merging in Mixed Traffic
venue: IEEE Transactions on Intelligent Transportation Systems
evidence: 'the safety supervisor will replace the risky action with a safe action according to Eq. 13' (Sec. IV-B, Algorithm 2), after checking predicted trajectories in priority order.
method: Cooperative MA2C with parameter sharing, local rewards and action masking for on-ramp merging; a priority-based safety supervisor rolls out IDM/MOBIL and bicycle-model trajectories and replaces conflicting actions.
evaluation: Modified highway-env merging, Easy/Medium/Hard; baselines MPC, MAA2C, MAACKTR, MAPPO and no-supervisor ablation; Hard collision 0.16 to 0 and speed 21.71 to 22.73 m/s; supervisor 4.90-50.13 ms on AMD 9820X.
contribution: A priority-based runtime safety supervisor over multi-agent RL merging policies replaces predicted-conflict actions, driving collision rate to zero while also raising average speed above MARL and MPC baselines.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - the guarded policy is a cooperative MA2C (learned) merging policy and the supervisor overrides its action at execution time, so (a) is solid. (c) is arguable: collision rate is a headline measured outcome with baselines and an ablation, but efficiency (average speed) is co-primary. (d) rests on Remark 1 and Table II inference times (4.90-50.13 ms against a 5 Hz control step) on a server CPU, with no real-time or edge test, so a maintainer may drop (d). Text in Sec. V-C claims no collisions for T_n>=7 but Table II shows 0.01 (Medium, T_n=14) and 0.03-0.05 (Hard, T_n=10, 12, 14). The paper never says what the supervisor does if no candidate action is conflict-free, and assumes HDVs never collide with each other. Multi-lane extension (Sec. V-F) is qualitative only.

title: Embodied Footprints: A Safety-Guaranteed Collision-Avoidance Model for Numerical Optimization-Based Trajectory Planning
venue: IEEE Transactions on Intelligent Transportation Systems
evidence: "the trajectory planning module ran once to generate an offline trajectory" (Sec. V.C); collision avoidance is a constraint set inside the NLP solved by IPOPT (Alg. 1).
method: Optimisation-based trajectory planner whose collision constraints use velocity- and curvature-dependent enlarged footprints at collocation points so the vehicle is collision-free between them.
evaluation: MATLAB sim, 3 static-obstacle cases plus stress case; small-scale vehicle field test. Baselines naive NLP, LIOM, VPF. Runtime 0.757-1.749 s; completeness yes in all cases.
contribution: A collision-constraint formulation for optimisation-based trajectory planning that guarantees no collision between collocation points, at solve times of 0.76-1.75 s.
flag: Constraint inside a planner, run offline; not a runtime interceptor, so (a) is not met under the strict-runtime rule. Single ego vehicle, static obstacles only ("no moving obstacles are considered"), no multi-agent. No collision counts or repeated-run success rates; completeness is binary per case; field test has no numeric metrics. Table II times look like single runs. Methods tags are a loose fit (NLP planner with Hybrid A* warm start).

title: A Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning Approach for Safe and Efficient Behavior Planning of Connected Autonomous Vehicles
venue: IEEE Transactions on Intelligent Transportation Systems
evidence: NOT READ - fetched PDF is a different (earlier) paper version than the record.
method: NOT READ
evaluation: NOT READ
contribution: NOT READ

title: IR-STP: Enhancing Autonomous Driving With Interaction Reasoning in Spatio-Temporal Planning
venue: IEEE Transactions on Intelligent Transportation Systems
evidence: Abstract: 'it records and continually updates interaction relations for each planned state throughout the forward search' - relation constraints prune nodes inside the planner's s-t search (Sec. V-E), no separate monitor.
method: Path-speed decoupled planner whose forward s-t tree search tracks overtaking/yielding/influence relations with other agents per node and rejects edges with conflicting relations in an interaction zone.
evaluation: Closed-loop CommonRoad plus SUMO, 232 scenarios (76 interactive subset); baselines CA, LS, contingency; fail rate 4.75% vs 6.95%, collisions 15 vs 15 (K=1), 14 vs 17 (K=3); not real-time.
contribution: Tracking interaction relations inside spatio-temporal search lowers planner fail rate from 6.95% to 4.75% and raises distance completeness in simulated unsignalised intersections, with collision counts roughly unchanged.
flag: Constraint inside a planner, so (a) not met; paper is about interactive planning quality (distance, fail rate, jerk) with collisions one metric among six, so (c) primacy fails. Only fallback is a -4.0 m/s2 stop when search finds no solution. Abstract's 17.6% fewer collisions is 17 to 14 collisions vs contingency baseline in Table V (small counts); 31.7% lower fail rate matches 6.95% to 4.75%; 7.6% distance matches 47.92 to 51.55. Text gives 3-modal DIST 41.08 and FR 5.77% but Table VI shows 40.28 and 5.69%. Authors state the algorithms 'do not currently achieve real-time performance'; no hardware or numeric timing in text.

title: Formal Certification Methods for Automated Vehicle Safety Assessment
evidence: Abstract: "we provide both an overview of the safety verification, validation and certification process" and a review of formal safety techniques.
method: Review of formal verification for automated-vehicle certification (reachability analysis, STL, model checking, theorem proving), with a proposed unified scenario-coverage framework and open questions.
evaluation: None: no experiments, baselines or metrics of its own; only qualitative 0-10 comparison scores and figures cited from other work.
contribution: A survey of formal certification methods for automated vehicles, covering reachability analysis and temporal-logic specifications and proposing a scenario-coverage framework for safety assessment.
flag: Survey/overview with no evaluation (E2 also applies). Useful as background and for snowballing (online verification, inevitable-collision-state braking, safe human takeover refs). Text read to char 100000 of 128153; the unread part is the reference list from [83] on.

title: Augmenting Reinforcement Learning With Transformer-Based Scene Representation Learning for Decision-Making of Autonomous Driving
evidence: The sequential latent Transformer 'is only used in the training process' (Sec. I), and the only safety-related runtime element is that 'Simulations would be reset if' the ego collides or times out (Sec. IV-A).
method: Multi-stage Transformer encodes agent histories and candidate route waypoints; a sequential latent Transformer predicts future latents and a reconstruction-free SimSiam objective augments a SAC decision policy.
evaluation: SMARTS left turn, double merge, roundabout A-C; baselines DrQ, SAC, PPO, rule-based, plus ablations; success 76-96% vs 66-92% (MST) and 68-80% (DrQ), collision 2-24%; RTX 2080 Ti, no inference latency.
contribution: Transformer scene representation with latent future prediction and reconstruction-free self-supervision that raises success rate and sample efficiency of reinforcement-learned driving policies in dense interactive traffic.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: no - no shield, filter, monitor or override at inference, so (a) fails; collision penalty is in the reward and collision rate is only a test metric. (c) fails the primacy test: the primary claim is sample efficiency and success rate of ego decision-making, not a multi-agent safety property. (b) fails the Pillar 2 measure: the future-latent module is training-only and the paper reports no predictive-accuracy metric (no ADE/FDE, no latent prediction error), only success/collision/stagnation rates, completion time and a PCA latent plot. Most likely overturn on this batch if the maintainer counts auxiliary latent future prediction over multi-agent scene state as (b) despite the missing predictive measure. Attention, not a graph net, models interaction, and Sec. III-B-3 states 'there is no interaction among neighbor vehicles' at the aggregation level.

title: A Survey on Autonomy-Induced Security Risks in Large Model-Based Agents
venue: IEEE Transactions on Pattern Analysis and Machine Intelligence
evidence: Sec. 4.3 (R2A2 blueprint, not implemented): "Constraint Filter, which blocks unsafe plans before execution by the Actuator."
method: Survey of security risks from autonomy in large-model agents; proposes a conceptual Reflective Risk-Aware Agent Architecture (R2A2) with a constraint filter, as a design blueprint only.
evaluation: No own experiments. Tables give qualitative Low/Medium/High ratings only; no baselines, metrics, hardware or latency figures.
contribution: Surveys autonomy-induced security risks in large-model agents and sketches an unevaluated risk-aware architecture with a pre-execution constraint filter.
flag: Survey by title and content; R2A2 is described but never implemented or tested. Only characters 0-100000 of 125987 were read; the remainder was not read (assumed references/tail, unverified). A convergence claim for a dual-update rule is attributed to prior work, not own tests.

title: DRL-VO: Learning to Navigate Through Crowded Dynamic Scenes Using Velocity Obstacles
evidence: "we introduce a new reward term r_d^t that uses velocity obstacles [10] to set a desired navigation direction." (Sec. III-E Reward Function)
method: PPO navigation policy fusing lidar and pedestrian kinematics; velocity obstacles appear only in a training reward term for heading; the actor outputs velocities directly at runtime.
evaluation: Gazebo crowds of 5-55 pedestrians, four unseen worlds, Turtlebot2 hardware; baselines DWA, CNN, two DRL policies, no-VO ablation; success 0.79 vs 0.60-0.70 at 55; Jetson Xavier, 60 FPS.
contribution: DRL-VO trains a single-robot crowd navigation policy with a velocity-obstacle heading reward, raising collision-free success in dense simulated crowds and running at 60 FPS on a Jetson AGX Xavier.
flag: Single robot among pedestrians; VO is a reward term only and the authors themselves say VO guarantees do not carry over and suggest a safety module or CBF as future work, so (a) fails and (c) fails the multi-agent test. Edge deployment cell is weak: 60 FPS on Xavier is a throughput figure with no stated latency constraint, so (d) not met. No separate collision rate, only success rate. Model size inconsistent in paper (32.137M vs 28.94M in Table I). Read characters 0-100000 of 105605; the tail (likely references) was not read. Title match confirmed.

title: Cooperation for Scalable Supervision of Autonomy in Mixed Traffic
evidence: 'human supervisor control of the AV must be activated to ensure human-level safety' (Sec. III-A), triggered by reachability conditions with 'enough time to avoid it comfortably' (5-8 s takeover window).
method: Reachability conditions decide when a remote human must take over a merging AV; cooperative connected AVs block threatening human vehicles, and an M/M/k loss model sizes the human supervisor pool.
evaluation: Analytical plus numerical rotary-ring network with IDM profiles; baselines UCAV and NCAV vs CCAV; Theorems 1-2 and Lemmas 1-2; supervision need cut 21.9% to 69.03%, reliability 99.9999% vs about 90%; no latency measured.
contribution: Cooperative connected vehicles shrink the share of merges that need human takeover, letting one remote supervisor reliably oversee far more autonomous vehicles, with proved reachability and queueing bounds.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: no - the supervised AVs run IDM with conservative kinematic reachability and RL appears only in related work, so (a) and (c) fail the Pillar 1 scope ruling; the include rests entirely on (e) under the 2026-11-13 ruling, as the paper is about when automation defers to a remote person and how many vehicles one supervisor can monitor. No crash, disengagement or empirical intervention rate is reported and there is no microsimulation: the quantitative floor is met by proved bounds plus numerical comparison against UCAV/NCAV (0.078 vs 0.1 at S=5, 69.03% at S=16, 48.08-68.20% in Example 3, 18-66 AVs per supervisor without merge assistance). The 5-8 s takeover window and 15-60 s service times are taken from cited human-factors work, not measured here, and low latency is assumed rather than tested, so the time-to-irreversibility cell is only implicit in the reachability trigger.

title: Integrated Task and Motion Planning for Safe Legged Navigation in Partially Observable Environments
evidence: Sec. VI-C: a turn larger than the bound "will result in a high-level action that is not executable" by the motion planner - safety is a constraint inside the synthesized planner, not a separate runtime filter.
method: Hierarchical task-and-motion planner for bipeds: GR(1) LTL reactive synthesis with belief abstraction over unseen dynamic obstacles, phase-space keyframe planning, precomputed replanning automata for perturbations.
evaluation: Cassie in Drake plus Digit hardware with two A1 obstacles; perturbed-step success 90.2-93.6% over 1000 runs; belief vs no-belief ablation qualitative; 0.5 ms per middle-level step; no collision rate.
contribution: Synthesizes correct-by-construction LTL navigation and locomotion plans for bipedal robots that track beliefs about occluded moving obstacles, validated in simulation and on a Digit robot.
flag: Safety is enforced inside the planner (reactive synthesis), no shield or monitor between decision and execution, so (a) fails as I read it; maintainer may disagree since the synthesized automaton reacts online and Digit stops for an obstacle. Single ego robot; other robots are only environment obstacles. No quantitative collision rate and no baseline with numbers (belief ablation is a figure; only numeric comparison is synthesis time 34 min joint vs 85 min individual), so E2 would also apply. Synthesis hardware not stated. Remark 3: no formal recovery guarantee under large perturbations.

title: Distributed Coverage Hole Prevention for Visual Environmental Monitoring With Quadcopters Via Nonsmooth Control Barrier Functions
evidence: Sec. IV, Algorithm 1: a QP minimally modifies the nominal coverage input subject to nonsmooth CBF constraints that prevent coverage holes among neighbouring quadcopters.
method: Power-diagram hole condition among quadcopter trios encoded as a nonsmooth CBF; a distributed QP filter minimally modifies a nominal coverage controller to prevent unsurveilled gaps.
evaluation: Simulations with 3, 5, 9 drones and 5 Crazyflie experiment; baselines nominal-only, FOV-only constraint, prior method; barrier value and coverage cost traces; about 20 ms input computation for five drones.
contribution: Nonsmooth control barrier functions over a power diagram let quadcopter teams keep camera coverage free of holes while optimising monitoring quality, demonstrated with five Crazyflies.
flag: Structurally a runtime CBF filter over a nominal controller on multi-agent state, but the protected property is a coverage/mission-quality constraint (no unsurveilled hole), not a hazard; I judged it coordination, hence E1. If the maintainer counts coverage holes as a safety property it would meet (a), but evidence is time-series plots only (one transient violation at step 5642 in the 9-drone sim; nominal-only leaves a hole), no rates over repeated trials, so E2 risk. Experiment ran centrally on one PC despite the distributed design. Last ~16k characters (refs/appendix) not read.

title: REFINE: Reachability-Based Trajectory Design Using Robust Feedback Linearization and Zonotopes
evidence: "the braking maneuver, whose safe behavior was verified in the previous planning iteration, can be applied" (Sec. VI); Assumption 6 gives the vehicle t_plan seconds to find a control input.
method: Receding-horizon planner: robust feedback-linearizing controller plus offline zonotope reachable sets of the full vehicle model; online optimization must finish within t_plan or a pre-verified braking maneuver executes.
evaluation: 1000 simulated highway scenarios (up to 24 moving vehicles) vs SOS-RTD, NMPC, zonotope baselines: 0% crash, 0.52 s mean plan; NMPC 29% crash. Scale car, 7 trials.
contribution: A reachability-based trajectory planner that guarantees not-at-fault driving under a hard planning deadline, falling back to a pre-verified stop, with zero crashes in 1000 simulated highway scenarios and on a scale car.
flag: Borderline. Safety is a constraint inside a planner, which the prompt says does not meet (a); I recorded runtime_interceptor no and criterion (d) only, on the explicit planning deadline (3 s sim, 1.5 s hardware) with fail-safe braking. A maintainer could read the deadline-triggered braking fallback as a runtime halt, or reject (d) because seconds-scale planning is far from the review's latency regime, in which case E1. Time-to-irreversibility cell rests on the always-stoppable contingency design and is generous. Other vehicles are obstacles, not agents. Hardware trials have no baseline and no crash count, only a statement that the car finished or stopped; planning ran on a laptop over Wi-Fi, the onboard TX-1 did sensing and control, so not edge deployment.

title: SICNav: Safe and Interactive Crowd Navigation Using Model Predictive Control and Bilevel Optimization
evidence: Sec. IV: collision avoidance is a quadratic constraint inside the MPC with humans' ORCA optimisation embedded as KKT conditions; Sec. VII-A uses slack variables with quadratic penalties 'to avoid infeasibility'.
