method: Bilevel MPC for one robot in a crowd: humans' ORCA problems embedded as lower-level KKT constraints so the plan accounts for human reactions; collision constraints sit inside the planner.
evaluation: Sim 2000 runs, 3 and 5 ORCA/SFM humans, vs MPC-CVMM, ORCA, SARL, RGL, DWA: collision freq 0.00-0.03 vs 0.00-0.05; 80 Jackal runs; i7-9700K at 10 Hz, no solve times.
contribution: Embeds an ORCA model of human reactions inside a robot MPC via bilevel optimisation, cutting navigation time and frozen-robot frequency in simulated crowds while keeping collision frequency at or below 0.03.
flag: Borderline. Safety is a planner constraint (softened by slack), so strict-runtime (a) fails; the paper itself contrasts with post-hoc safety filters. For (c) the measured gains are mainly navigation time and frozen frequency; collision frequency is nonzero and DWA beats it (0.00 vs 0.01) at SFM N=3, so primacy is doubtful. Single robot among humans. Real-robot runs report path deviation and time-too-close only, no collision counts; at N=1 and N=2 SICNav spent MORE time too close than the baseline. Only the 10 Hz rate is given, no per-solve latency. Maintainer may prefer include under (c) if 'safe' in the title is taken as primary.

title: DREAM: Decentralized Real-Time Asynchronous Probabilistic Trajectory Planning for Collision-Free Multirobot Navigation in Cluttered Environments
evidence: Multi-robot comparison reports success, collision and deadlock rates against SBC, RLSS and RMADER, e.g. DREAM 0.960 success and 0.036 collision vs RLSS 0.488 and 0.508 with 16 robots (Sec. VI-C, Table VIII).
method: Decentralized receding-horizon planner: goal selection, discrete search minimising collision probability against probabilistic static and interactive dynamic obstacles, then QP trajectory optimisation with hyperplane constraints robust to asynchronous, delayed, dropped messages.
evaluation: 3D simulation, 16-32 robots, forests plus up to 50 dynamic obstacles, delay and drop sweeps; vs SBC, RLSS, RMADER; success, collision, deadlock rates; planning 120-190 ms; Crazyflie demo offboard.
contribution: A decentralized probabilistic trajectory planner that keeps teammates collision-free under message delays and drops, reaching up to 2.15x the success rate of the best baseline with 16-32 robots among dynamic obstacles.
flag: Borderline on the (c) primacy test: it is a navigation planner, not a certificate or detector, though collision-free navigation is the headline and collision rate vs baselines the main outcome; maintainer may rule E1. Not a runtime interceptor: only fallback is reusing the last successful plan. Most collisions are with non-team dynamic obstacles; teammate collisions are zero without obstacles. Comparison asymmetric (RLSS and SBC are author reimplementations; RMADER given no drops). Planning 120-190 ms multi-robot, far from sub-15 ms. Hardware runs have no metrics and compute offboard on a Xeon. Deadlock rate 0.510 at 5 s delay. Abstract 1.68x and 2.15x figures do trace to Tables VII-VIII.

title: CAT-ORA: Collision-Aware Time-Optimal Formation Reshaping for Efficient Robot Coordination in 3-D Environments
evidence: The problem "requires augmenting (7) by including constraints on mutually colliding paths." (Sec. VII) - collision avoidance is a constraint inside the assignment planner.
method: Collision-aware time-optimal robot-to-goal assignment (Hungarian-based bottleneck assignment with constraints on colliding pairs) plus closed-form synchronised trajectories with proven minimum-distance guarantee.
evaluation: About 1e5 random sim instances, N 10-210, vs LSAP and LBAP: success 100% vs 93.19% (LBAP), makespan 12% better than LSAP on average; 19 UAVs outdoors; 60 ms total compute; i7-10510U.
contribution: CAT-ORA solves makespan-optimal formation reshaping for robot swarms with provably collision-free straight-line trajectories, demonstrated on 19 UAVs and in simulation with up to 210 robots.
flag: Efficiency paper (makespan) with collision avoidance as a planner constraint; fails primacy test for (c) though it does report LBAP colliding in more than 6% of instances. Abstract ties the 49% figure to reshaping time, conclusion to max path length. Table II lists LBAP success 0.0%, unexplained vs 93.19% in Table I. Compute time ms-level but no bound; one UAV failed to start in the field run.

title: AVOCADO: Adaptive Optimal Collision Avoidance Driven by Opinion
evidence: Sec. IV-A (Eq. 8): a linear program picks the velocity closest to the preferred one subject to one half-plane per perceived agent, weighted by an online-estimated cooperation degree; Sec. V-B: 'ORCA ... fails in all cooperative circle scenarios'.
method: ORCA-style velocity-obstacle collision avoidance where each neighbour's share of avoidance is adapted online by nonlinear opinion dynamics with attention driven by time-to-collision; decentralised, perception-only.
evaluation: Sim circle/crossing, 10-25 agents, 5 cooperation mixes, 128 runs each, vs ORCA, RVO-RL, T-MPC, SARL: success rate in figures only; 3 Turtlebots plus pedestrians, 33 runs; timing in a figure.
contribution: Adapts reciprocal velocity-obstacle avoidance to unknown mixes of cooperative and non-cooperative agents using opinion dynamics, reporting higher collision-free success rates than ORCA, RVO-RL, T-MPC and SARL with 10-25 agents.
flag: Borderline include under (c) only. AVOCADO is the local planner itself, not a filter over another policy (it does minimally modify a goal-directed preferred velocity, as ORCA does), so I set runtime_interceptor no; no halt/veto, picks 'least unsafe' velocity if infeasible. All success-rate, time-to-goal and compute-time numbers are in Figs. 11-14 only and I could not read any values - no numeric collision rate appears in the text; check the figures before crediting v1.6 minimum evaluation, else E2/E1. Text extraction says compute is 'hundreds of milliseconds' in crowded settings, which looks implausible for an LP (likely microseconds) - verify; compute hardware not stated. Real-robot runs report no counts. Attention uses time-to-collision but not as time-to-irreversibility for deferral, so that cell is not claimed.

title: NeuPAN: Direct Point Robot Navigation With End-to-End Model-Based Learning
evidence: Sec. IV-B: 'we can safely remove the numerous point-level collision avoidance constraints' by using the learned distance regulariser - collision avoidance is a cost term inside the planner.
method: DUNE unrolled network maps raw lidar points to latent distance features; NRMP convex MPC-style planner uses them as a regulariser; loop iterates K=3 times to output controls for one robot.
evaluation: Ir-sim, Gazebo, CARLA plus three real robots; baselines RDA, AEMCARL, TEB, Falco, human pilots; success 73 vs 59/100 nonconvex; DUNE inference 4-10 ms; trained on RTX 4090.
contribution: An end-to-end model-based lidar-to-control planner navigates single robots through cluttered gaps with centimetre tolerance, outperforming RDA, TEB and Falco on success rate and navigation time.
flag: Single-robot navigation planner; obstacle avoidance is a planner cost, no runtime interceptor, no multi-agent safety claim, metrics are success rate and navigation time. Humans appear only as manual-control baselines, not takeover. DUNE 4 ms (KITTI) and 10 ms (SUSCAPE) inference is from Fig. 9d; onboard compute and control frequency not found in text. Paper says 'GTX 4090'. Conclusion claims 'over 2x accuracy improvement' - supporting numbers not located in the extracted text (Fig. 9 distance error has no values in prose). Table VI speed column garbled in extraction.

title: Constraint-Guided Online Data Selection for Scalable Data-Driven Safety Filters in Uncertain Robotic Systems
evidence: Sec. III-A: the filter 'minimally overrides it with a safe control signal to prevent system failure'; Sec. VI: full-data filter takes 60.4 ms against the 25 ms sampling period, the proposed selection 11.8 ms.
method: GP-based CBF/CLF safety filter solved as an SOCP; a constraint-guided greedy algorithm selects M of N data points online per state, making GP inference linear in dataset size.
evaluation: Sim: polynomial system, RABBIT biped; hardware: Quanser cart-pole. Baselines nominal CF-QP, oracle, full-data and naive-selection GP. Cart-pole 11.8 ms vs 60.4 ms; 100 percent constraint satisfaction over 10 runs.
contribution: An online data-selection rule that lets a Gaussian-process safety filter meet a 25 ms control deadline, cutting solve time from 60.4 ms to 11.8 ms on a cart-pole with no constraint violations.
flag: Single-agent; inclusion rests on (a) plus (d) via the explicit 25 ms (40 Hz) deadline. RABBIT: full 238.3 ms (sd 9.4, N=12765) vs ours 22.9 ms (sd 4.4, M=30), which is close to the 25 ms limit. Cart-pole: full 60.4 ms (sd 4.1, N=6957) vs ours 11.8 ms (sd 0.75, M=40); safe in 10/10 runs but pole balanced in only 6/10; nominal CBF-QP violation is stated without a count. Computer/CPU not specified, so no edge-deployment cell. A person pushes the pole as a disturbance, not a handoff. I read about the first 100k of 118k characters of the PDF; the unread tail is likely references/appendix but was not checked.

title: One Filter to Deploy Them All: Robust Safety for Quadrupedal Navigation in Unknown Environments
evidence: Sec. V-B2: the filter "minimally adjusts the nominal policy so that the resultant twist commands ensure system safety" - nominal command passes if V > delta, otherwise a QP returns the closest safe twist (Eqs. 15-16).
method: Observation-conditioned HJ reachability value network over LiDAR scans, conformally calibrated, with online disturbance-bound estimation, used as a QP safety filter wrapping arbitrary nominal quadruped controllers including human teleoperation.
evaluation: Isaac Sim Go1, 100 trials, hard: collision 0.28 to 0.00 (PS+WTW), 0.80 to 0.08 (naive); vs no filter, ABS, two ablations; Go1 hardware 10 trials per cell; activation 0.54-0.68; no latency.
contribution: A single learned reachability safety filter, calibrated with conformal prediction and adapting to estimated disturbances, overrides unsafe velocity commands from many different quadruped controllers and sharply reduces collisions in unknown cluttered environments.
flag: Single robot; dynamic obstacle is a person-placed box only - no multi-agent state. Human appears as a nominal teleoperator whose commands the filter overrides, the reverse of automation deferring to a person, so (e) and the human handoff cell are not claimed. No filter rate, QP solve time or onboard-compute figure found despite running on hardware; authors note estimation lag (Sec. VIII). Filter activation is high (about 0.54-0.68), relevant to false-halt cost. Hardware cells are 10 trials each; residual collisions remain (e.g. NVE+MPC slippery 3 of 10). Fig. 5 safety rates over 1000 trials have no numbers in text. Calibration margin 0.49 m does not transfer formally to the real world. arXiv version read, may differ from the T-RO text.

title: Stratified Topological Autonomy for Long-Range Coordination (STALC)
evidence: "Our MILP approach finds optimal solutions in under 5 seconds across all graph sizes, densities, and team sizes." (Sec. IX-B.1) - a coordination planner; no runtime safety layer is described.
method: Hierarchical multi-robot planner: topological graph MILP for overwatch/formation routing, mid-level planning, and distributed receding-horizon NMPC with large collision penalties in the cost.
evaluation: Sim graphs 5-50 nodes, teams up to 200, vs JSG/PPO/GMIP; MILP solve 0.081-3.702 s (10 robots); Warthog field runs, protection score 1.78 vs 0.85; i9-13950HX.
contribution: STALC plans long-range multi-robot overwatch and formation manoeuvres with a fast mixed-integer program over a topological graph and executes them with distributed NMPC on ground vehicles.
flag: Coordination/visibility planner, not a safety mechanism; collisions handled only as a 1e10 cost penalty inside NMPC. No collision or violation metric reported. Hardware results are mostly qualitative figures; onboard compute not stated. Urban team size read from figure captions (3 robots).

title: SMARLA: A Safety Monitoring Approach for Deep Reinforcement Learning Agents
evidence: Section 4.3 (Model in Operation): at each time step SMARLA estimates from the agent Q-values the probability of a safety violation and predicts a violation when the confidence-interval upper bound passes the threshold, so a safety mechanism can be triggered before it happens.
method: Black-box runtime safety monitor for DQN agents: Q*-irrelevance state abstraction plus a random-forest classifier over abstract-state features estimates a per-step violation probability with confidence intervals.
evaluation: Cart-Pole, Mountain-Car, Highway DQN agents, 1000 test episodes; ablations on criterion, threshold, abstraction, features; recall 96.6-99.8%, FPR 0.2-7.1%, flagged with 45-77% of episode left; few-ms inference, RTX 3070.
contribution: A black-box runtime monitor that predicts safety violations of a deep RL agent early in an episode from Q-values alone, with near-perfect recall and most of the episode left to react.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes, DQN policies. Check (a): SMARLA only flags, it never overrides, halts or defers; the triggered safety mechanism and the human-handover example are unimplemented, so (a) fails a strict reading of the override clause. Single agent throughout, no multi-agent state. No external baseline: white-box, image-based and model-based monitors were deliberately excluded, so all comparisons are internal ablations. Headline numbers are the easy cases: on Highway only 40 of 59 violations were predicted and macro F1 is 82%, versus 99 of 99 and 132 of 132 on Cart-Pole and Mountain-Car. The few-ms inference claim in Section 7 has no measurement table behind it.

title: Online Control Barrier Function Construction for Safety-Critical Motion Control of Manipulators
venue: IEEE Transactions on Systems Man and Cybernetics Systems
evidence: Abstract: the CBF-based QP serves as 'a safe filter for the desired planning-based controller'; Sec. IV-A: 'u_des in (SCB-QP) is computed with a P controller to the next way-point' and waypoints 'are not necessarily safe'.
method: Online construction of a quadratic CBF per step via scenario-sampled SOS program over signed distances, then a CBF-QP filters a waypoint P controller for a 7-DOF manipulator.
evaluation: MATLAB sim and Kinova Gen3 in cluttered scenes, 10 runs each; baselines CBF [7] and TrajOpt; min clearance about 1, 2, 4 mm; 39.31 ms per step vs TrajOpt 270 ms; i9-9980XE.
contribution: An online-constructed control barrier function filter for a 7-DOF manipulator that keeps millimetre clearances in cluttered scenes at about 39 ms per step, against 270 ms for TrajOpt.
flag: TITLE DIFFERS: the arXiv paper is 'Safety-Critical Optimal Control for Robotic Manipulators in A Cluttered Environment' (Ding, Wang, Ren, Zheng, Chen, He); content (online CBF construction, manipulator, CBF-QP filter) matches the record, so I treated it as the preprint of the TSMC article, but I could not confirm the DOI link on arXiv - please verify; if not the same work, this is E6 WRONG PAPER. Borderline on E4: single manipulator, no multi-agent aspect; kept for the runtime filter plus reported per-step timing. Baseline failures are stated without rates ('cannot be successful in all tests'); safety evidence is 10/10 successful runs and clearance values. QP 12.41 ms and SOS 24-28 ms (Table II) vs overall 39.31 ms; workstation not edge hardware; control frequency not stated. 95 percent safety figure is a scenario-theory bound, not measured.

title: A Distributed Multi-Vehicle Coordination Algorithm for Navigation in Tight Environments
evidence: Sec IV: the centralized NMPC 'is computationally expensive when M is large'; collision avoidance is a dual-variable constraint inside the NMPC (Sec III-A), not a filter.
method: Distributed NMPC for polytopic robots: collision avoidance as dualised minimum-distance constraints; alternates per-robot NMPC with pairwise dual-variable QPs; bound on neighbour prediction error.
evaluation: MATLAB sim, i7-7700HQ; 2-4 vehicle platoon merge, 6 heterogeneous robots, overtaking; baseline centralized NMPC; 4 vehicles: 12.83 s avg vs 0.176 s per step; no collision metric.
contribution: A distributed NMPC scheme splits multi-vehicle collision avoidance in tight spaces into per-robot planning and pairwise dual updates, cutting per-step computation from 12.8 s to 0.18 s for four vehicles.
flag: arXiv title says 'Multi-Robot', record says 'Multi-Vehicle'; same paper, possibly an earlier version than the TVT text. Planner with collision constraints, measured outcome is computation time and tracking cost, no collision or violation rate: fails the primacy test. Paper claims 'more than 2 orders of magnitude' speed-up but Table I gives roughly 68-73x for 4 vehicles. Latency cell is generous: compute time is reported and delays up to the horizon are said to be tolerated (Remark V.1) but fallback is out of scope. Simulation only.

title: Synergizing Decision Making and Trajectory Planning Using Two-Stage Optimization for Autonomous Vehicles
evidence: "The decision making and trajectory planning tasks are jointly formulated as a nonlinear programming problem" (Abstract)
method: Two-stage optimisation for one autonomous vehicle: mixed-integer lane decision on a linear model, then ADMM constrained iLQR on a bicycle model with hard ellipse collision constraints.
evaluation: Custom multi-lane scenarios and CARLA with 6 vehicles; baselines FSM+PID, IDP, three ablations; zero collisions vs 1 for FSM+PID; safety index 2.99 vs 2.47/2.58; step time 0.12 s vs 0.15 s; Xeon W-2223.
contribution: Joint lane-decision and trajectory optimisation for a single autonomous vehicle that completes CARLA highway runs without collision at about 0.12 s per planning step.
flag: Single ego vehicle planner; collision avoidance is a constraint inside the optimiser, which the prompt says does not meet (a). Efficiency and decision quality are the main claims. Step time 0.12 s exceeds the 0.05 s CARLA tick and no deadline is stated, so not (d). Table II alignment was garbled in extraction - collision counts per ablation should be rechecked against the PDF. IDP collision counts not stated.

title: Visible light communication for adaptive AGV fleet coordination
evidence: "Among the tested cycle durations, 100 seconds consistently minimised halting across all densities, improving material handling efficiency and intersection throughput." (Conclusions)
method: VLC (RGBV LED, OOK, 64-bit frames) links L2V/V2V/V2I/I2V carry AGV position and crossing requests to an intersection agent that sets traffic-light phases/cycle length for warehouse AGV queues.
evaluation: SUMO simulation, 3 intersections, 80/150/300 AGVs, cycle 80/100/120 s; halting counts and mean speed shown in figures only; bench VLC frame decoding demo. No collision metric, no baseline numbers.
contribution: Simulates VLC-signalled traffic-light control of warehouse AGV fleets in SUMO, finding a 100 s signal cycle minimises halting across fleet densities; a coordination and throughput study, not a safety mechanism.
flag: Coordination/efficiency paper: collision avoidance is delegated to SUMO built-ins and traffic phases; fails the primacy test for (c) and the controller is a scheduler, not a safety interceptor. Abstract claims 'improvements in collision avoidance, throughput, and delivery times' and Sec. 2.5 claims comparison against fixed-cycle baselines, but the body reports no collision, throughput or delivery-time number and no baseline result; outcomes are halting curves in figures (values not in text). The 'dynamic' control actually evaluated is three fixed cycle lengths; the RL agent is mentioned but not evaluated. Text says SUMO is 'fully integrated' with VLC yet lists that integration as future work. States 1.2 m/s is about 3 km/h (it is 4.3 km/h). No latency figures. SPIE proceedings paper, 16 pages, section numbers duplicated.

title: Multiagent collaborative decision-making method for self-healing control of distribution networks
venue: International Conference on Intelligent Transportation Systems and Automation Control
evidence: "The safety shield in (7) projects the raw joint action onto the nearest feasible command set. It explicitly checks radiality, fault isolation, voltage bounds, branch loading, and command duplication before any breaker instruction is produced" (Sec. 2.4)
method: Feeder, zone, DER and load agents with graph-attention messaging (CTDE actor-critic); a deterministic shield projects each joint command onto the feasible set, power-flow screens it, else triggers a backup rule.
evaluation: Simulated modified IEEE 33- and 69-bus feeders, 300 test episodes each; baselines FLISR, MILP, DQN, graph-RL; ablations. Violations 0.04/episode vs 0.31 graph-RL, 0.67 unshielded; latency 0.46 s; no hardware.
contribution: A physics-based safety shield screening every joint switching command of a graph-attention multi-agent restoration policy cuts violations from 0.67 to 0.04 per episode in simulated feeders at 0.46 s response.
flag: Abstract numbers (98.0% load, 0.46 s, 0.31 to 0.04) all match Tables 5 and 6, and the 87.1%/94.6% reductions check arithmetically. Doubts: results are one pooled row per method although two feeders are claimed, no per-feeder split, no variance, seeds or hardware; all numbers suspiciously round. The paper says the policy "cannot" release an infeasible command yet the shielded system still records 0.04 violations/episode, unexplained. Latency is 0.46 s to 1.06 s (not ms scale) and rises with injected message delay 0-600 ms. Shield costs 0.4 pt load (98.4 to 98.0) and +0.12 s. No halt or false-rejection rate is reported, and the rejected-command count is never given. Human role is only an operator warning on fallback; not credited as handoff. Optical/LiDAR flags look bolted on for the venue (transport/automation conference) and are synthetic; style reads formulaic, possibly machine-assisted. Corresponding author uses a mail.com address. Synthetic benchmarks only, as the conclusion admits.

title: RoboBallet: Planning for multirobot reaching with graph neural networks and reinforcement learning
evidence: "the joint velocities for the robot in question is zeroed, and thus the robot stands still for that time-step" (Environment, Materials and Methods) - a simulator rule, with collision also penalised in the reward; no separate safety layer.
method: GNN policy trained with modified TD3 over a robot/task/obstacle graph outputs joint velocities for up to eight arms at 10 Hz; collision handled by reward penalty and environment stop.
evaluation: Kinematic simulation, 8 Franka arms, 40 tasks, 30 obstacles, plus 4-robot real cell. Baseline RRT-Connect. 95% task solution rate; execution time 7.5 s to 4.5 s; 0.3 ms per step on A100, 30 ms on one CPU core.
contribution: RoboBallet plans collision-free multi-arm reaching with a graph neural network policy trained by reinforcement learning, reaching 0.3 ms per planning step on a GPU for eight robots.
flag: Fails primacy test: paper is about planning throughput and trajectory quality; no collision rate is reported and collision avoidance is a reward term plus a simulator-level stop, not a runtime interceptor. GNN is a policy, not a world model, so (b) not credited. Text says 7.5 s to 4.5 s is a 60% reduction, which is arithmetically 40% - check. Comparison with RRT-Connect is figure-only (Fig. 2). Inference timing is on datacentre A100/Xeon, not edge. Title capitalisation differs from record only. Read via one WebFetch pass.

title: Control Barrier Functions for Collision Avoidance between Strongly Convex Regions
venue: SIAM Journal on Control and Optimization
evidence: CBF-QP designs act as safety filters that "minimally perturb" a reference input, and constraints "can be enforced in real time (at 500 Hz) without overapproximations" (Sec. 1)
method: Minimum distance between strongly convex regions used as a CBF; KKT solution propagated by an ODE instead of re-solving, feeding a CBF-QP that minimally modifies an unsafe nominal input.
evaluation: Simulation only, one quadrotor vs static polytopes (11 collision pairs); timing baseline is direct Ipopt solve: 66.5 us vs 7.17 ms; CBF-QP mean 0.147 ms, p99 1.34 ms, 500 Hz, laptop i7-10870H.
contribution: Proves that minimum distance between strongly convex sets is a valid control barrier function and tracks it by an ODE, giving an exact collision-avoidance safety filter running at 500 Hz in simulation.
flag: Borderline - maintainer should decide. It is a genuine runtime safety filter with formal guarantees and tail timing (p99), but it reports no collision, violation or intervention rate and its only baseline is a solver-timing comparison, not a control baseline or no-filter run, so it misses the protocol v1.6 minimum evaluation for (a); if the formal result plus timing baseline is accepted, this becomes include. Multi-robot is covered in theory (Remark 5.7) but experiments control a single quadrotor against static obstacles. Text notes distance can dip slightly below the margin from numerical error; 2.90% of KKT updates needed re-initialisation. Simulation only, laptop CPU, no edge hardware. I read the first 100000 of 109933 characters (through conclusion and appendices; only references cut off). Record year 2026 vs arXiv 2023 preprint - journal version may differ.

title: An inductive synthesis framework for verifiable reinforcement learning
venue: ACM SIGPLAN Conference on Programming Language Design and Implementation (PLDI)
evidence: Section 4.3 (Shielding), Algorithm 3: the next state under the neural action is predicted and, if it falls outside the verified inductive invariant, the synthesized program action is used instead, overriding the neural controller at execution time.
method: Counterexample-guided synthesis of a deterministic policy program plus a sum-of-squares inductive invariant; the verified invariant drives a runtime shield substituting the program action for unsafe neural actions.
evaluation: 15 control benchmarks (4-car and 8-car platoons included), 1000 runs x 5000 steps vs unshielded neural policy; all failures prevented (60 and 41 pendulum cases to 0); overhead 2.0-21.3%; invariant-degree and environment-change ablations; i7-8700.
contribution: Synthesizes a verifiable programmatic approximation of a trained neural policy and reuses its proved inductive invariant as a runtime shield, removing all observed safety violations at single-digit percentage overhead.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes, deep policy-gradient neural controllers are the thing shielded, so the scope ruling is satisfied even though the shield itself is symbolic. (a) is solid. The 4-car and 8-car platoons are multi-agent in name only, modelled as one 8-variable or 16-variable plant with a single controller, so not (c). No per-decision latency and no edge hardware, only percentage wall-clock overhead against a 0.01 s time step. False-halt cost is large and under-discussed: 93703 interventions on Oscillator with only 74% of them effective, 108320 after adding an obstacle to Self-Driving. Synthesis is not guaranteed to terminate and timed out at degree 2 and on the 8-car platoon at degree 8.

title: Verifiably safe exploration for end-to-end reinforcement learning
venue: International Conference on Hybrid Systems: computation and control
evidence: Section 4.2 (Enforcing Constraints), Algorithm 1: every action proposed by the learner is checked against the verified controller monitor and, if it is unsafe, a safe action is sampled uniformly from the safe actions in the current state.
method: Wraps PPO: a pretrained CenterNet-style detector extracts symbolic object positions from images and a KeYmaera X-verified differential dynamic logic controller monitor replaces any unsafe action with a sampled safe one.
evaluation: Four visual environments (XO, adaptive cruise control, goal-finding, pointmesses) vs vanilla PPO, at least 4 seeds: 0 unsafe actions versus 3733-13983, reward equal or better (ACC 967 vs 529); no latency or hardware reported.
contribution: Extends verified runtime safeguards to end-to-end visual RL by detecting objects to recover a symbolic state, achieving zero safety violations during training without loss of reward in four environments.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes, a PPO policy, with a learned object detector inside the safeguard itself. (a) is solid (replacement at execution time). Single agent, no multi-agent hazard, no human handoff. The guarantee is conditional on perception: Assumption 1 requires bounded detector position error, and the detector is trained on synthetic paste-up images, so safety outside that assumption is unproven. Authors concede the detector overhead makes real-time control infeasible in the current implementation and report no timing or hardware at all, so no (d). No ablations: there is no comparison against the same safeguard on ground-truth symbolic state, and sample-efficiency gains are claimed only from curves.

title: Temporal Consistency Checks to Detect LiDAR Spoofing Attacks on Autonomous Vehicle Perception
evidence: Section 3.2 (3D-TC2 Methodology): the Cell-match Counting Strategy compares each detected 3D box against the motion predictor bird-eye-view category grid and flags a mismatch, usually background, as a spoofed ghost object.
method: 3D-TC2 runs a LiDAR 3D detector (PointPillars or SECOND) and MotionNet in parallel, aligns detected boxes to the BEV motion grid, and flags objects with no motion history as spoofed.
evaluation: nuScenes mini, 362 attacked key frames, 200-point spoofing at 5-8 m; PointPillars vs SECOND; car detection success 98.58% and recall 91.75%, cyclist 95.01%, pedestrian 56.92%; 24 ms per frame (41 Hz) on a GTX 1050.
contribution: Treats motion as a physical invariant for spoofing defence: ghost LiDAR objects with no motion history are flagged by matching 3D detections against a bird-eye-view motion prediction grid at 41 Hz.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes, neural LiDAR detectors (PointPillars, SECOND) guarded by a rule-based check over MotionNet predictions. (a) is weak: the check only raises a flag, it cannot veto, halt or defer a driving action, and the response is explicitly future work. (d) rests only on a 24 ms per-frame figure (sd 0.85 ms) on a desktop GTX 1050 with no stated deadline and no edge platform, so the maintainer may drop it. No false-positive rate or precision anywhere, and benign match ratios are poor (pedestrian 56%, bike 1.2%), so false alarms look likely. The abstract 98% is DSR, the share of successfully spoofed objects caught, not accuracy. CARLO 94.5% and Shadow-Catcher 94% are cited, not re-run, so the baseline is indirect. Single vehicle, single-frame attacker, no multi-agent aspect.

title: Not What You've Signed Up For: Compromising Real-World LLM-Integrated Applications with Indirect Prompt Injection
venue: ACM Workshop on Artificial Intelligence and Security (AISec)
evidence: Section 3 (Attack Surface of LLM-Integrated Applications): an adversary plants instructions in data the application later retrieves, remotely compromising the LLM-integrated application without any direct access to its prompt.
method: Threat taxonomy of indirect prompt injection (information gathering, fraud, malware, intrusion, manipulated content, availability) with proof-of-concept injections against synthetic GPT-4 applications, Bing Chat and GitHub Copilot.
evaluation: Qualitative demonstrations only: temperature-0 synthetic applications plus live Bing Chat and Copilot; no success rates, trial counts, baselines or ablations; the paper says quantifying success rates is future work.
contribution: Introduces indirect prompt injection, in which instructions hidden in retrieved data hijack LLM-integrated applications, and demonstrates the resulting threat classes against real deployed systems.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: no guard at all, this is an attack and taxonomy paper. It fails the evaluation floor: purely qualitative proof-of-concept, no success rate, no baseline or ablation, and Section 5.6 only lists unimplemented mitigations (input and instruction filtering, an LLM supervisor, interpretability-based outlier detection), hence exclude-E2 rather than E1. (c) is only nominally multi-agent: the one email-worm demo propagates the injection to contacts and multi-agent frameworks are named as future work in Section 5.3. Very highly cited and the maintainer may well want it as background rather than safety evidence; if kept, it is threat-model evidence only and should not be credited with preventing anything.

title: Testing of Deep Reinforcement Learning Agents with Surrogate Models
venue: ACM Transactions on Software Engineering and Methodology
evidence: Introduction: 'Indago executes the DRL agent under test only on the most promising environment configurations' - an offline test generator guided by a failure-prediction classifier.
method: Indago: classifier trained on training-time failures serves as surrogate fitness for hill-climbing/genetic search with saliency-guided mutation to generate failing environment configurations offline.
evaluation: Parking, Humanoid, Driving single-agent DRL; vs random and sampling; failures 13/3/11 (hill climb) and 27/4/42 (GA) vs 13/1/5; classifier precision 24-62%; CPU cluster.
contribution: Uses a surrogate failure classifier to steer offline test generation for deep RL agents, finding about 50% more and more diverse failures than sampling-based testing.
flag: Offline testing, no runtime intervention, single-agent environments; none of (a)-(e) is the subject. Read about the first 80% of the PDF (through Sec 6.4); threats to validity and conclusion not read. Input-diversity gain given as 77% in the Introduction and 78% in RQ2. Surrogate classifier recall is low (12-48%). Non-generative cell is a loose fit (discriminative failure predictor used offline); drop if strict.

title: Multi-Robot Cooperative Pursuit-Evasion Control: A DeepReinforcement Learning Approach based on Prioritized Experience Replay
venue: Proceedings of the 2024 8th International Conference on Control Engineering and Artificial Intelligence
evidence: "To ensure the safety of the pursuit robots, the collision avoidance reward is designed." (Sec. 3.3.3 Reward Function)
method: PER-MATD3: multi-agent TD3 with prioritized experience replay, centralized training and distributed execution, for cooperative pursuit of one evader; collision avoidance is a constant reward penalty.
evaluation: Simulation, 3 pursuers vs 1 MADDPG evader with obstacles, 30,000 episodes, 5 MARL baselines: robot collisions 0.16 vs 0.19-0.41, obstacle collisions 0.12, capture success 88%, capture time 26.21 s.
contribution: Adds prioritized experience replay to multi-agent TD3 for cooperative pursuit-evasion and reports fewer collisions and higher capture success than five MARL baselines in simulation.
flag: Safety enters only through the training reward (no runtime mechanism) and the paper is about pursuit performance and convergence, so (a) and (c) primacy both fail. Abstract's 30.37% capture-time reduction cannot be reproduced from Table 3 (26.21 s vs 32.21 s MADDPG = 18.6%; best case 26.6% vs PER-MADDPG). The 60.97%/68.42%/25.71% figures are all against the weakest baseline (MADDPG); against the strongest baselines the collision gains are about 16% (0.19 to 0.16) and 33% (0.18 to 0.12). Capture time of 26-36 s conflicts with Table 2 (max step 30 x 0.1 s step). Collision metric units undefined (appears to be a per-episode count read after convergence); no seeds, variance or number of test episodes; robot-robot collision is counted with the capture threshold, not the safety threshold. Table 3 carries Table 2's caption. Table 2 as extracted shows buffer 1.06 and batch 1.24 (probably lost exponents).

title: WaitGPT: Monitoring and Steering Conversational LLM Agent in Data Analysis with On-the-Fly Code Visualization
venue: ACM Symposium on User Interface Software and Technology (UIST)
evidence: Abstract: "users are provided with a clear, step-by-step visualization of the LLM-generated code in real time"; 10 of 12 users reported increased confidence in result correctness (Sec. 7.4.2) - operator situation awareness over an LLM agent.
method: Streaming parser turns an LLM data-analysis agent's code into an interactive dataflow diagram with live table states; users inspect, query and edit nodes, then re-run revised code.
evaluation: Within-subjects study, N=12, vs. code-only baseline; 10 tasks with 4 planted LLM errors; mean success 80% vs. 73%, NASA-TLX p<.001; standard desktops, no latency reported.
contribution: Shows that visualising an LLM data-analysis agent's code as a live dataflow diagram improves users' error detection and confidence, though it adds no pre-execution gate.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes, a gpt-4-0125-preview data-analysis agent. Only (e) holds: this is monitoring and situation awareness, not interception - code blocks execute immediately and the authors list a "stop" mechanism as future work (Sec. 8.2), so runtime_interceptor is no. Success rates are descriptive with n=6 per condition and not significance-tested; the paper says WaitGPT "took less time in Task A1-2 and Task B" but Table 2 shows it slower on B2, B3 and B4 and slower overall. Check whether the maintainer wants (e) studies of LLM-agent oversight at all, and that no latency figure exists.

title: AirGapAgent: Protecting Privacy-Conscious Conversational Agents
venue: ACM SIGSAC Conference on Computer and Communications Security (CCS)
evidence: Sec. 4.2: "the design does not allow any information from the third party to flow back to the minimizer module"; anything outside the minimised context can only be obtained by escalating to the user, who approves or denies (Sec. 4.2, Sec. 7).
method: Two-LLM air-gap: a minimiser sees only the trusted task plus user data and fixes a minimised data context; a second conversational LLM answers third parties from that context alone.
evaluation: 20 synthetic profiles, 8 scenarios, 16640 cases; Gemini Ultra/Pro, GPT-4, Mistral Large vs. all-data single-agent baseline; privacy under hijacking 45.2% to 96.7%, utility 98.2% to 87.3%; no latency.
contribution: Shows that restricting a personal LLM agent to a task-minimised data context defends against third-party context hijacking, raising data protection from 45% to 97% at a modest utility cost.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes, an LLM personal agent. (a) rests on the minimiser gating disclosure before the conversational agent answers plus escalation to the user - check whether a context restriction counts as an execution-time veto rather than a training-time or prompt-time constraint. (c) rests only on the adversary being a third-party agent or service, so the multi-agent reading is thin and (c) may be overturned. The user-escalation loop is design-only and never evaluated, so the human handoff cell is unmeasured. No latency, cost or hardware figures anywhere. Ground-truth privacy labels were generated by Gemini Ultra and only spot-checked by the authors.

title: Deep Reinforcement Learning for Swarm Navigation Using Different Evolution Strategies
venue: Proceedings of the 2024 8th International Conference on Intelligent Systems, Metaheuristics & Swarm Intelligence
evidence: "we demonstrated that the covariance matrix adaptation evolution strategy performs better than the cross-entropy method, when autonomously exploring a challenging environment with a robot swarm in simulation" (Sec 6)
method: Evolutionary reinforcement learning of a vision-based swarm exploration policy: VAE encoder to 32-dim latent, 3-layer classifier over 4 actions, weights evolved with CEM or CMA-ES; collision is a reward penalty.
evaluation: Own physics simulator, indoor corridor, 4 robots, 100 episodes per method; CEM vs CMA-ES: mean total reward 1055.78 vs 2792.07, sectors explored 9.40 vs 11.68 of 22 (max 18 vs 21). No collision rate, no latency.
contribution: Compares CEM and CMA-ES for evolving a vision-based exploration policy for a four-robot swarm in simulation, finding CMA-ES explores more of the corridor.
flag: Off-topic: a navigation/exploration training-method comparison. Collision avoidance exists only as a -10 reward term (training-time, not a runtime mechanism) and no collision or violation rate is reported; metrics are reward and coverage. No runtime filter, no world model used for prediction (VAE is only an observation compressor), no latency figures (real-time is asserted, not measured). Six-page ISMSI 2024 paper, simulation only, 4 robots, no statistical test.

title: HSF: Defending against Jailbreak Attacks with Hidden State Filtering
evidence: Sec. 4.3: if the harmfulness score exceeds the threshold, "the inference process is interrupted, and the model refuses to generate a response."
method: Lightweight classifier on the last k tokens' final-decoder-layer hidden states scores a prompt's harmfulness after one forward pass and blocks generation above a 0.5 threshold.
evaluation: Llama2-7B-chat and Mistral-instruct-v0.2; AdvBench, MaliciousInstruct, six jailbreak attacks; vs PPL, Paraphrase, Retokenization, Self-Examination, Self-Reminder, DRO, SPD. Mistral ASR 56-98% to 0-8%; AUC 0.9986-0.9999. No latency numbers.
contribution: A hidden-state classifier that refuses jailbreak prompts before any text is generated cut attack success on Mistral from 56-98% to at most 8% across six attacks.
flag: Single-model, single-prompt guardrail: no agents, tools, multi-turn, latency or handoff aspect, hence E4. Abstract claims 'negligible inference overhead' and minimal impact on benign queries, but I found NO overhead/latency figure and NO benign false-positive rate in the body - only AUC on what Sec. 5.2 calls 'safe datasets'. Abstract says rejection happens 'before the inference process begins' yet Sec. 4.1 needs a forward pass. Vicuna results referenced as 'Appendix??' are missing. Step 3 says MLP but Eq. 2 is logistic regression. Does not transfer across models (Sec. 6). Strong sensitivity to k (ASR 0-66% in ablation).

title: Plan-Then-Execute: An Empirical Study of User Trust and Team Performance When Using LLM Agents As A Daily Assistant
venue: CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems
evidence: Sec. 3.1: users "check whether they approve the current predicted action" before it runs; in execution conditions "Specify Action" was used to override the agent 445 times (Sec. 5.1).
method: 2x2 between-subjects study of user involvement in planning and in execution for a LangChain plan-and-execute GPT-3.5 assistant; in execution conditions the user approves, gives feedback on, or overrides each predicted action.
evaluation: Prolific, N=248, 4 conditions, 6 simulated high/low-risk tasks; calibrated trust 0.50 plan and 0.64 execution; task-6 execution accuracy 0.06 to 0.23 with oversight; no latency or hardware.
contribution: Study of 248 users showing that approving or overriding each action of a plan-then-execute LLM assistant helps task performance only unevenly while raising cognitive load and not improving trust calibration.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes, a GPT-3.5 plan-and-execute agent. (e) is solid under the 2026-11-13 ruling. (a) holds only because the gate is a human approval step rather than an automated filter, so the maintainer may prefer criteria_met e alone and runtime_interceptor no. Actions were simulated backend APIs, so nothing irreversible actually happened and risk level is manipulated without measuring time-to-irreversibility. Effects were significant on only one of six tasks (task-4 for plans, task-6 for execution) and overall trust differences were null; the paper does not state the between-subjects design explicitly.

title: AgentSpec: Customizable Runtime Enforcement for Safe and Reliable LLM Agents
venue: Proceedings - 2026 IEEE/ACM 48th International Conference on Software Engineering, ICSE 2026
evidence: "AgentSpec is the first framework that systematically enforces customizable safety constraints on LLM agents at runtime" (Sec. 1, Introduction)
method: Domain-specific language of trigger-predicate-enforce rules wrapped around LangChain-style agents; each planned action is intercepted and met with stop, user inspection, action invocation or LLM self-examination before execution.
evaluation: RedCode-Exec code agents (25 categories, 30 cases each), SafeAgentBench embodied tasks, FixDrive AV scenarios; hazard rates 15-78% down to 0%, safe-task success 58.62% to 54.26%, 100% law compliance in 8 AV cases; overhead 1.42ms parsing and 1.11-2.83ms predicates against 9.82-25.4s agent runtimes.
contribution: AgentSpec, a DSL and runtime enforcement layer that intercepts LLM agent actions against user-defined trigger-predicate rules, removing hazardous actions across code, embodied and driving agents at millisecond overhead.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - LLM agents for code, embodied tasks and driving. Strongest (a) record in the batch, and cross-domain is genuine (code agents logical, embodied and AV physical). Numbers to check: the abstract's 'over 90%' is a detection rate only after dropping the two categories where the agent never emitted risky code; Table 3 sums to 333 flagged of 422 invocations (78.9%) overall, and 58 flagged cases were then allowed through by user inspection, so end-to-end prevention is nearer 65%. The 'user inspection' was performed by the authors, not independent operators. The AV rules and all 8 AV scenarios are adopted from FixDrive, and no empirical comparison against GuardAgent or ToolEmu is run. Overhead figures are component costs, not an end-to-end deadline, and enforcement time for user_inspection and llm_self_examine is explicitly unbounded.

title: Measuring the Robustness of Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning Systems under Partial Agent Failure
venue: Proceedings of the Intelligent Robotics FAIR - IntRob 2025
evidence: "Controlled fault injection mechanisms are applied during the evaluation phase" (Sec. 1 Introduction)
method: Fault-injection robustness study: MAPPO policies trained clean, then evaluated with Gaussian observation noise on a chosen fraction of agents; grid over noise sigma and affected-agent ratio.
evaluation: VMAS Navigation and Sampling, 10 agents, TorchRL, 5-6 seeds, 32 eval episodes; heuristic baseline; metric episodic return only (Navigation -144% relative change at 100% faulty). No collision rate, no latency.
contribution: Measures how MAPPO team return degrades when a fraction of agents receive noisy observations, showing reward design decides whether the faulty-agent ratio or the noise magnitude is the fatal axis.
flag: Borderline (c): it studies cascading degradation under partial agent failure, but fails the primacy test - the only metric is episodic return, no collision/violation/hazard rate, and no safety mechanism or detector is proposed (shielding hub agents is future work). The hub-agent claim in the abstract is not backed by any experiment that identifies central agents; it is inferred from return variance. Inconsistencies: text says five training runs, Table 1 seed range [0..5]; returns are quoted as varying with % faulty at sigma=0 and with sigma at 0% faulty, which should be no-ops under the stated setup; Sampling text labels 0% faulty as worst case (414) and 100% as best (344). Most numbers are read off figures. 6-page workshop-style paper (IntRob 25). Simulation only.

title: Gap-Guided Evolutionary Deep Reinforcement Learning for Hierarchical Navigation in Structured Dynamic Environments
venue: Proceedings of the 2025 9th International Conference on Deep Learning Technologies
evidence: "demonstrate that the integrated waypoint + RL approach consis-" (Abstract)
method: Hierarchical navigation: A* global plan, laser-scan gap-based local waypoint planner, and a GA3C-CADRL collision-avoidance policy trained with an auto-difficulty curriculum over maze complexity and pedestrian behaviours.
evaluation: ROS STDR simulation, 5 maps x 3 goals x 10 runs, 20 moving agents; vs CADRL, WP+MPC, WP+CADRL, WP+GA3C; success 89.3% and 6.6 collisions vs 84.7%/10.6 best baseline; no latency.
contribution: Embeds a curriculum-trained deep RL collision-avoidance policy under a gap-based waypoint planner, raising simulated goal-reaching success to 89.3% and lowering collision counts versus standalone and MPC baselines.
flag: Borderline (c): collision count is reported against four baselines, but the paper is a single ego-robot navigation planner whose claim is navigation success in structured maps; no runtime veto layer. Check: conclusion says collisions reduced by a factor of four vs WP+GA3C, but Table 1 gives 10.6 vs 6.6 (about 1.6x). Collision unit is inconsistent (per trial in intro, per ten navigations elsewhere; a collision is counted when too close, threshold unstated). Proposed method is not best on several rows (e.g. Campus path 2: 18 vs 17 collisions). Text cites a section 6.3.1 that does not exist; refs [3] and [16] (gaze estimation, gait classification) are unrelated self-citations used for technical claims. Real-time claim has no timing data though planning time is listed as a metric. Simulation only.

title: Trustworthy LLM-Based Agents for Data-Centric AI
venue: Proceedings of the 32nd ACM SIGKDD Conference on Knowledge Discovery and Data Mining V.2
evidence: "This tutorial delivers a systematic, data-centric roadmap to build LLM agents that are not merely capable but provably trustworthy." (Abstract)
method: No method. A 5-page KDD 2026 tutorial proposal outlining four pillars for trustworthy LLM agents: generalizability, security and defenses, domain-grounded trust, and evaluation and benchmarking.
evaluation: None. No experiments, baselines, metrics, hardware or latency; the document is a tutorial outline with speaker biographies and a reference list.
contribution: KDD 2026 tutorial outline surveying generalizability, security, domain trust and evaluation of LLM-based agents; no original method or evaluation.
flag: Tutorial proposal (the text calls itself 'This tutorial' throughout; about a third of it is speaker biographies). Runtime auditing, sandboxing and multi-agent attack propagation are mentioned only as topics to be covered. Useful only as a pointer list: its references include AgentSpec, GuardAgent, AgentDojo and Agent Security Bench, which may be worth checking against the queue.

title: Challenges and Opportunities in Secure Real-Time Digital Twin Systems for AR/VR-Enabled Smart Factories
venue: MITOTI 2025 - Proceedings of the International Workshop on Middleware for IT/OT Integration, Part of Middleware Conference 2025
evidence: "This paper discusses the challenges and opportunities in developing an integrated real-time digital twin control architecture" (Abstract)
method: Position paper surveying challenges and opportunities for real-time digital twins linking AR/VR operator support, AGV fleet safety orchestration, 5G/TSN deterministic networking and cybersecurity in smart factories. No mechanism implemented.
evaluation: None. No experiments, system, baselines or metrics; latency figures quoted are generic 5G URLLC targets (below 10 ms, 99.999% reliability), not measurements.
contribution: A workshop position paper outlining open challenges in timing, connectivity, human-robot safety orchestration and security for AR/VR-enabled digital twins of AGV-equipped factories, without a proposed or evaluated mechanism.
flag: 6-page MITOTI 2025 workshop vision paper with no method and no evaluation; could equally be E3 (overview/position). Virtual fencing, predictive collision scheduling and runtime verification are named only as future opportunities. Useful at most as background motivation for latency/jitter in AGV safety.

title: Active Maritime Copilot for Ambiguity and Risk-Driven Decisions
venue: Companion Proceedings of the 21st ACM/IEEE International Conference on Human-Robot Interaction, HRI Companion 2026
evidence: "the agent visualizes the reasoning rationale (citing specific COLREGs as basis) and requests human authorization to initiate a specific clarification query" (Sec. 2.3, Risk-Prioritized Interface)
method: RAG copilot parses VHF dialogue with an LLM into structured intent, propagates a deterministic ghost trajectory, scores ambiguity from semantic vagueness plus kinematic divergence, and escalates green-yellow-red for operator authorization.
evaluation: 2D planar maritime benchmark, 5 COLREGs encounters by 3 communication-congruency conditions, N=13 HRI researchers and graduate students, think-aloud plus Likert; median at least 6 for colour status and RAG evidence, 4.5s (SD 1.2) decision time in the yellow state.
contribution: A watchful maritime copilot that cross-checks VHF verbal intent against radar kinematics and uses progressive green-yellow-red disclosure to hand ambiguous collision risks to the officer of the watch.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: which - the automation is an LLM plus RAG copilot, and (e) does not require it anyway; (e) clearly holds on topic (handoff, trust calibration, operator situation awareness). I exclude only on the evaluation floor: a 5-page HRI Companion contribution whose results are Likert medians plus one response-time mean, with no accuracy or detection rate for the ambiguity quantifier against the stated Condition A-B-C ground truth, no baseline interface, and cognitive load claimed but never measured (no NASA-TLX or equivalent). Figure 4 compares with-background and without-background participant groups, not interface conditions, and no numbers for it appear in the text. Participants are not mariners and the authors call the work preliminary, formative and a proof of concept. This is the record I most expect the maintainer to overturn to include as an (e) exemplar.

title: Does Safety Molt? Evaluating LLM Safety in Multi-Agent Social Environments
venue: Proceedings of the ACM Conference on AI and Agentic Systems, CAIS 2026
evidence: "when a reply follows a leaking message in the same thread, the probability that the next reply also leaks rises to 12.8%" (Sec. 5, Temporal Accumulation RQ2)
method: Moltbook-style simulation platform where 2,533 tool-calling LLM agents holding private human profiles interact across 124 communities; contextual-integrity violations are detected by pattern matching plus an LLM judge.
evaluation: 25 simulated days, 29,945 posts and 81,264 replies; controlled testbed of 7 frontier models by 10 held-out personas by 5 tool-call budgets (7,000 traces) at 5 adversarial contamination levels; leakage 12.8% after a leaking reply vs 1.6% clean, 50-60% at 50 tool calls, subreddit rates under 2% to over 16%.
contribution: Shows LLM agent privacy safety degrades in persistent multi-agent social environments: disclosure is socially contagious, community context rivals model choice, and prompt-level privacy instructions only partly mitigate it.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - LLM tool-calling agents are the evaluated system; this is evaluation only with no runtime interception, so (c) alone and runtime_interceptor no. Abstract numbers I could not find in the body: 'CIMemories 19.95% to Ours 45.30%' and 'leakage rates above 37.8% even with safeguards' occur only in the abstract and introduction, never in Section 5 and in no table. The abstract says agents are '8x more likely' to disclose after a peer while the introduction says '5.1x'; the body (12.8% vs 1.6%) supports 8x, so the introduction figure looks wrong. Ground truth is regex patterns over GPT-5-mini-generated profiles scored by an LLM judge, which the authors concede makes contextual integrity 'approximate'. There are no result tables at all, so every figure I quote is read from plots, and the Moltbook platform statistics rest on 2026 preprints.

title: MARL-SR: Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning-based Cooperative Navigation for Swarm Robotics Applications
venue: Proceedings of the 2025 7th International Conference on Advances in Robotics
evidence: "that RL-based navigation achieved zero collisions across all six" (Sec. 5.1 Collision Avoidance)
method: Tabular Q-learning cooperative navigation with centralised goal assignment, plus a separately trained Q-learning dynamic-obstacle policy; a decision controller switches policies when a moving obstacle is within 1.0 m.
evaluation: Gazebo training; 12 real trials with 2-4 Tortoisebots in an 8x6 m lab vs A*+DWA; collisions 0/6 vs 2/6, goal error, traversal time (-8.7%); switching latency under 100 ms asserted.
contribution: Combines Q-learning cooperative navigation with a switched dynamic-obstacle avoidance policy on two to four physical robots, reporting no collisions in six trials against two in six for a classical stack.
flag: Cooperative navigation planner; the policy switch is not a safety veto and the authors state it lacks formal safety guarantees and propose adding a CBF safety controller as future work. Numbers do not reproduce from Table 1: RL goal errors average 0.653 m (text says 0.60) and classical 0.804 m (text says both 0.89 and 0.87), so the headline 33% reduction is about 19%. Only 6 trials per method, not matched (RL has a 7.5 m trial, classical none), single run each; the two classical collisions were with a static obstacle from odometry drift, not inter-robot. The under-100 ms switching latency and the human-crossing test have no measurements. Tabular Q-learning over a continuous relative-position state is not explained for the cooperative policy. ACM reference says 2025 while the record year is 2026.

title: Towards Robust and Secure Embodied AI: A Survey on Vulnerabilities and Attacks
evidence: Abstract: "This survey fills this critical gap by: (1) categorizing vulnerabilities specific to embodied AI"
method: Literature survey: taxonomy of embodied-AI vulnerabilities (exogenous, endogenous, inter-dimensional), sensor spoofing, jailbreak and adversarial attacks on LLM/LVLM-driven robots, failure modes and datasets.
evaluation: No original evaluation; all numbers (e.g. >95% backdoor attack success) are cited from other work. Tables summarise existing datasets, attacks and models.
contribution: A survey organising attacks on embodied AI - sensor spoofing, jailbreaks and adversarial prompts against LLM-driven robots - into exogenous, endogenous and inter-dimensional vulnerabilities, with no new method or experiment.
flag: Survey, E3. Read the first 100000 of 153275 characters only; nothing in that portion is an original method or experiment, and the remainder was not read. Useful for snowballing: cites runtime defences (perplexity filter, SmoothLLM, runtime firmware integrity checks). Multi-agent and latency mentioned only in passing.

title: Efficient Collision Detection and Path Optimization for Multi-Node Systems Using Vector Cross Product and Neural Regression
venue: Proceedings of the 2026 6th International Conference on Applied Mathematics, Modelling and Intelligent Computing
evidence: "this paper models and simulates the motion of a dragon dance formation as a typical multi-node structural example" (Sec 1 Introduction)
method: Archimedean-spiral kinematic model of a rigid chain of benches, cross-product segment-intersection test scanned over time to find first self-collision, bisection on spiral pitch, MLP regression of turning-path length.
evaluation: Single numerical case study (dragon dance bench chain): collision time 428.8 s, minimum feasible pitch 0.3936 m, turn length 1.43 m; no baseline, no timing, no hardware.
contribution: An offline geometric calculation of when a rigidly linked bench chain following a spiral first self-collides and the smallest spiral pitch that avoids it.
flag: Not multi-agent safety: one rigidly linked chain on a prescribed spiral, solved offline; reads as a write-up of a mathematical-modelling contest problem (dragon dance benches). Abstract claims 'Compared with traditional geometric traversal methods, the proposed approach significantly improves computational efficiency' and a 'real-time solution' but the body contains no comparison method, no runtime figures and no accuracy metric; only O(1) and O(log N) complexity statements. Abstract numbers 428.8 s and 0.3936 m are present in Sec 3.4 and 4.3. MLP section gives no training-set size, error or test metric, and the MLP only regresses L=3*pi*R2, a closed-form linear function. Single author, six references, all Chinese-language journal items and mostly unrelated to the method. Would also fail on E2.

title: FleetScape: A Mixed Reality Sandtable for Spatial Supervision and Control of Scalable Drone Fleets
evidence: Appendix A.2: an autonomous drone "halts its autopilot with a "Low GPS" notice, requiring operator intervention"; Sec. 3.5.3: the interface "limits manual intervention to a single, controller-focused drone".
method: Mixed-reality sandtable (Meta Quest 3) for one operator supervising an autonomous drone fleet: 3D miniatures, minimap, status board, per-drone manual takeover, waypoint editing, fleet recall.
evaluation: Simulated city inspection, 6 expert pilots, 5/10/15 drones, 7 min. SAGAT, SART, Bedford, TAM. No baseline interface, no ablation, no significance tests, no latency measured.
contribution: Exploratory study showing operator drone-level situation awareness falls from 0.86 at 5 drones to 0.61 at 15 while workload rises, when supervising an autonomous fleet through a mixed-reality sandtable.
flag: Include rests on (e) only. n=6, simulation only, no comparison interface, authors call results exploratory. runtime_interceptor=yes is generous: the halt-and-defer is the simulated autopilot's Low-GPS stop plus operator recall/manual control, not the paper's contribution; deferral prioritisation in Sec. 5 is a design implication, not implemented. Latency explicitly not evaluated (Sec. 6). Saturation point is stated inconsistently (between 5 and 10 in Sec. 5, around 10 in Sec. 7); Fig. 4 panel references in Sec. 4.2.1 are inconsistent. Fan-out estimate 10.6 is a computed upper bound.

title: ProbGuard: Proactive Runtime Monitoring for LLM Agent Safety via Probabilistic Prediction
venue: IEEE/ACM International Conference on Automated Software Engineering (ASE)
evidence: Algorithm 2 computes P_safe and if below threshold: "Halt or steer agent to mitigate risk."; the framework "remains agnostic to the specific enforcement policy" (Sec. 3.3)
method: Abstracts agent states to predicate vectors, learns a DTMC from traces with PAC-style sample bound, and at runtime model-checks probability of reaching unsafe states, intervening below a threshold.
evaluation: Apollo driving sim vs REDriver (warning time up to 38.66s vs 1.71s); SafeAgentBench embodied agents vs none/AgentSpec (unsafe 40.63% to 14.07%); overhead 100.79ms driving, 5-28ms cached, 430ms uncached.
contribution: Probabilistic runtime monitor that predicts unsafe states ahead of time from a learned Markov-chain abstraction and halts or re-prompts the agent, reporting advance warning time and per-decision overhead.
flag: Title on arXiv is 'ProbGuard: Probabilistic Runtime Monitoring for LLM Agent Safety', not the record title (Proactive ... via Probabilistic Prediction); same system and name, treated as an earlier version of the same paper - maintainer to confirm. Abstract claims up to 80.4% task completion but the highest ProbGuard completion in Table 2 as read is 48.96% (59.38% unmonitored); NOT FOUND in body. 65.37% unsafe reduction matches 40.63% to 14.07% (reflect mode), which costs completion (47.74%); stop mode at 0.1 gives unsafe 2.60% but completion 10.42%. Both domains are simulated embodied/driving (physical), so no cross-domain cell. Criterion (d) is weak: overhead is measured but no deadline is set and hardware is not stated. time-to-irreversibility cell rests on advance warning time only. LLM not named in text read. Authors say enforcement does not guarantee safe behaviour (Sec. 7.2). Human-in-the-loop alarm mentioned but not evaluated.

title: Security Challenges and Protection Strategies for Industrial AI Agents: A Comprehensive Survey
venue: Proceedings of the 2026 6th International Conference on Internet of Things and Machine Learning
evidence: "This paper presents a systematic review and proposes a six-category taxonomy of security risks" (Abstract)
method: Survey: six-category taxonomy of security risks for LLM-based industrial AI agents (model reliability, input manipulation, tool/protocol, multi-agent collaboration, IT/OT convergence, supply chain) with mapped incidents and defense-in-depth strategies.
evaluation: No experiments. Literature and incident review: tables of risk categories, CISA ICS advisory counts 2021-2025, incident mapping and standards comparison. No baselines, metrics, hardware or latency measurements.
contribution: Surveys security risks of LLM-driven industrial agents under a six-category taxonomy, maps real incidents to each category and outlines defense-in-depth strategies and standards gaps.
flag: Survey by title and abstract; no original method or evaluation. Section 3.4 (multi-agent collaboration risks) and Section 4 (safety instrumented systems, agents kept advisory for fast loops) could be mined for background references only. I read the abstract, intro, section structure and tables index, not every paragraph of the body. Two duplicate text files of this record exist in the folder.

title: Evidence-Driven, Failure-Resilient Planning for Domain-Agnostic Multi-agent Orchestration
venue: AgenticDev 2026 - Proceedings of the 1st International Workshop on Agentic AI for Next-Generation Software Development, Co located with ASE 2026
evidence: "Domain modules are invoked only after the control plane has selected one of four routes: clarify missing intent, confirm an irreversible action, request human review, or execute" (Sec. 2, Evidence-Driven Planning Layer)
method: Control plane around an LLM planner: evidence packets and capability bids, deterministic schema and dependency validation with rule-based repair, model fallback chain, ontology SPARQL obligation checks and human checkpoints.
evaluation: None bearing on safety: ten manufacturing cases M1-M10 are named as tests with no outcomes reported; Table 1 lists only factory logistics data (199,721 delivery rows, 97.5% end-to-end match, p95 wait 47.0 h). No baseline, no ablation, no latency.
contribution: A domain-agnostic control plane that validates, repairs and routes LLM planner output, confirming irreversible actions and low-confidence plans with a human before any domain module executes.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - an LLM planner, and (a) holds by design since the control plane can clarify, confirm or route to human review before execution. Excluded purely on the evaluation floor: a 2-page workshop paper with no quantitative safety result, no baseline and no ablation, whose conclusion states that 'Future evaluation will quantify module-selection accuracy, clarification precision and recall, repair and fallback rates, terminal retention, and unsupported claims'. Single author, two company affiliations, and the ten test cases are described but never scored. I did not credit cross-domain evaluation: the two instantiations (software engineering and manufacturing logistics analytics) are both enterprise data workflows with no physical actuation. Worth rechecking if an extended, evaluated version appears.

title: A2A—A Mechanism Driven Framework for Interaction Based Agent Evaluation
venue: ICAICP 2026 - Proceedings of the 2026 International Conference on Artificial Intelligence and Computing Power
evidence: Table 2 caption (Sec 4.3 Results): 'Illustrative results derived from prior internal studies, showing the impact of interaction depth and attacker capability on attack success rate.'
method: Three-axis taxonomy (interaction depth, structural exposure, threat model) plus A2A-Attack, which casts evaluation as trajectory-level adversarial interaction among attacking agent, target agent and environment.
evaluation: Analytical mapping of MMLU, WebArena, AgentBench, GPTFuzzer; illustrative ASR from prior internal studies: static 30.2%, manual red-team 54.8%, A2A R=5 83.2%, GPT-4 attacker 85.0%; remaining comparison qualitative.
contribution: Recasts static, behavioural and adversarial LLM-agent evaluation as configurations of a single attacker-target-environment interaction mechanism, with a three-axis taxonomy for comparing methods.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes (LLM agents under adversarial evaluation). No evaluation of its own: the only numbers (Table 2) and the abstract claim of ASR above 80% in enterprise settings are attributed to undisclosed prior internal studies and are explicitly 'illustrative'; the cross-paradigm comparison uses a High/Medium/Low qualitative protocol; 6-page taxonomy-led paper, so exclude-E3 (position/survey) is also arguable; no runtime interception anywhere.

title: Aircraft Collision Avoidance Systems: Technological Challenges and Solutions on the Path to Regulatory Acceptance
venue: Annual Review of Control Robotics and Autonomous Systems
evidence: "This article provides an overview of these challenges and solutions" (Abstract)
method: Review of aircraft collision avoidance (TCAS, ACAS X): surveillance, advisories, threat-resolution logic, validation by encounter models and stress testing, and regulatory acceptance.
evaluation: No original experiments; figures cited from prior work, e.g. TCAS risk reduction factor about 8 (one equipped) and 62 (both), 279 scripted ACAS Xa flight encounters; no latency or hardware numbers.
contribution: Annual Reviews overview of how TCAS and ACAS X were designed, validated and certified, covering sensing, advisory logic, pilot response modelling and the path to regulatory acceptance.
flag: Survey/review article (Annual Reviews) with no new method or evaluation, hence E3. Useful as background and for snowballing: covers multi-aircraft coordination, pilot response delay models (5 s), nuisance alerts and trust. All numbers are cited from prior work, none newly measured. Gap cells left as none because a review does not itself address them.

title: The Safety Filter: A Unified View of Safety-Critical Control in Autonomous Systems
venue: Annual Review of Control Robotics and Autonomous Systems
evidence: "This article provides a review of safety filter approaches" (Abstract); no original experiments are reported.
method: Review unifying safety filters (HJ reachability, control barrier functions, model predictive shielding, data-driven filters) by monitor, intervention scheme, fallback synthesis and guarantee type; states a universal safety filter theorem.
evaluation: No original evaluation: no new metrics, baselines, hardware or latency; figures adapted from prior work. Includes a section on multi-agent and human-interaction safety filters.
contribution: Annual Reviews synthesis that frames CBF, reachability and predictive shielding methods as one safety-filter template of monitor, intervention and fallback, with a universal safety filter theorem.
flag: Review article (Annual Review of Control, Robotics, and Autonomous Systems), so E3 regardless of topical fit. Highly relevant as background and for citation mining of criterion (a) primary studies; the universal safety filter theorem is a formal result but comes with no evaluation. RQ scores reflect background value only. Read from one fetch covering the article structure, not every section in depth. Title match confirmed.

title: Integrating collision avoidance strategies into multi-robot task allocation for inspection
venue: Transactions of the Institute of Measurement and Control
evidence: "the main contribution of this paper is to study the collision avoidance among robots across diverse scenarios" (Introduction)
method: Centralised offline multi-robot task allocation (HFBS, GA, Cplex, each with 2-Opt); collisions handled by a potential-field repulsive velocity, or by k-means partitioning of sites into per-robot zones.
evaluation: Simulation on Intel i5 2.6 GHz: 16 scenarios compare mission cost and run time of GA+2-Opt, HFBS+2-Opt, Cplex; one 4-robot, 50-site clustering case; no collision metric.
contribution: Combines task-allocation heuristics with a potential-field repulsion layer or k-means zone partitioning so inspection robots avoid each other, evaluated only on mission cost and computation time.
flag: Title suggests safety but every reported number is mission cost (EU) or run time (s); no collision, violation or minimum-distance figure anywhere. The repulsive-velocity layer acts at execution time yet is only described, not simulated or measured (reader is referred to another paper); I coded runtime_interceptor no because it is a control-law term, not a veto. Clustering collision-freedom is argued from one figure and depends on a well-placed depot. Text is the HAL author version (header shows template DOI placeholder). If judged on-topic it would still fail as E2.

title: Distributed multi-robot collision avoidance via deep reinforcement learning for navigation in complex scenarios
evidence: Sec. 4.4: "the traditional control takes charge of relatively simple scenarios or emergent situations" - a distance-thresholded hybrid layer switches the learned policy out for PID or a conservative safe policy at control time.
method: Decentralised DRL policy maps three 512-beam laser scans, relative goal and velocity to velocity commands; a hand-thresholded hybrid layer switches among PID, the learned policy and a conservative safe policy.
evaluation: Stage simulation, 4-100 robots, circle/random/corridor/group-swap scenarios vs. NH-ORCA and supervised baselines; 20-agent success 1.0 vs. 0.78, extra time 0.702s vs. 1.800s; 5ms per command on Jetson TX1.
contribution: A decentralised sensor-level DRL collision-avoidance policy with a hand-tuned switching layer that reaches 100% success with 20 robots where NH-ORCA reaches 78%, at 5ms per command on a Jetson TX1.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes, the hybrid switching layer guards a DRL policy. The arXiv v1 title is "Fully Distributed Multi-Robot Collision Avoidance via Deep Reinforcement Learning for Safe and Efficient Navigation in Complex Scenarios" while the record uses the IJRR 2020 title - same authors and content, but confirm the journal version was not substantially revised. (a) is weak: the switching thresholds (r_safe=0.1, r_risk=0.8) are hand-set and the "safe" fallback is itself a DRL network, so there is no guarantee. The paper claims safety and efficiency jointly and the headline tables report success rate and extra time, with collision rates only in the Sec. 5.4 robustness study, so the (c) primacy test is arguable. Real-robot localisation is UWB with about +-150mm error.

title: Sensor-based distributionally robust control for safe robot navigation in dynamic environments
venue: The International Journal of Robotics Research
evidence: Sec. 6.3/8.3: the CLF-DR-CBF QP minimises the deviation of u from the nominal controller k(x) subject to the distributionally robust CBF constraint, running at 50 Hz over a 5 Hz A* planner (Sec. 9).
method: Distributionally robust CBF safety filter built directly from noisy LiDAR and pose samples (Wasserstein ball, CVaR) that minimally modifies a nominal path-following control, without building a map.
evaluation: Gazebo 1000 trials: dynamic collision 1.7 vs 29.8 (nominal CBF) and 3.2 percent (GP-CBF), success 93.2 vs 61.7/60.5; Jackal 50 trials/shape, 0 collisions; 7.3 ms per solve.
contribution: A sensor-driven distributionally robust control barrier function filter overrides a nominal controller at 50 Hz, cutting collisions among simulated pedestrians from 29.8 to 1.7 percent at 7.3 ms per solve.
flag: Possible E4: single robot, pedestrians are only dynamic obstacles (3 in sim and lab), no multi-robot state; I kept it because it reports per-step compute (7.3 +/- 2.2 ms vs 6.6 nominal and 18.5 GP-CBF, Table 3) and stuck rates as a false-halt proxy (5.1 percent dynamic; 16 and 10 percent on enlarged real shapes). Latency is measured, not a designed constraint, so (d) is weak; hardware for Table 3 not stated in text I saw (real robot uses onboard i7-9700TE, 32 GB). No explicit halt/defer command - stopping emerges from the QP. Guarantee is probabilistic with eps=0.1. Real-world section has no baseline. Read in two fetches; Table 4 values came from first-pass summary and the 93.2/1.7/29.8 figures were confirmed in the Sec. 9.2 text.

title: Collision-aware adaptive horizon model predictive control for multi-agent path planning
venue: International Journal of Advanced Robotic Systems
evidence: "If the problem remains infeasible even after the Detour, Emergency Stop is executed to guarantee safety." (Fig. 3 caption, CA-AH-MPC algorithm)
method: Distributed MPC for UAV teams that lengthens the horizon when a collision is predicted and shortens it otherwise, with a CBF constraint, right-of-way detour and emergency-stop fallback on infeasibility.
evaluation: MATLAB 3D simulation, 6-60 UAVs, 50-100 runs; fixed-horizon MPC baseline, CBF and detour ablations; 35% lower computation time, CBF +13% success; OSQP mean solve 14.65 ms; delay study.
contribution: Adapts the MPC prediction horizon to predicted collisions for multi-UAV path planning, cutting computation about 35% versus fixed-horizon MPC while a CBF constraint and emergency-stop fallback recover safety in simulation.
flag: Borderline, maintainer should decide between include and E1. The main claim is computational efficiency; the CBF is a constraint inside the planner (does not meet a). Only the emergency-stop fallback (brake opposite to velocity when the QP stays infeasible after detour) acts as a runtime halt, and its activation rate is not reported. Safety metric is success rate (failures split into collisions and deadlocks) and minimum distance; no separate collision rate appears in the text, values per condition are in figures I could not read. Adaptive horizon alone LOWERS success versus fixed horizon; the 13% gain is from the CBF. Table 1 (6 UAVs): computation 19.6/21.4 s, 18.3/18.9 s, 20.6/18.3 s (CA-AH vs FH at gamma 0.2/0.6/1.0), min distance 2.48/2.36, 2.02/2.04, 2.0/2.0 m - so at gamma 1.0 the proposed method is slower. Criterion d rests on the delay study: planning interval 0.2 s, success and min distance fall when delay reaches 0.2 s; OSQP solve mean 0.01465 s with SD 0.02842 s (SD about twice the mean, tail not analysed); a single delay shared by all agents. Desktop 24-core i9, 32 GB, no edge hardware, no real flights, no human. Read from the SAGE HTML page journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/17298806261446670 (URL constructed by me; the /doi/pdf/ form and DOAJ both failed) in two fetches; quotes relayed by the fetch tool.

title: Cooperative Gaussian process-based model predictive control for safe multi-agent navigation
venue: Journal on Advances in Signal Processing
evidence: "The target is reached quickly (t=51) without any violation of collision constraints." (Sec. 4.2, Results)
method: Distributed MPC via ADMM where each agent learns residual dynamics with a Gaussian process and enforces inter-agent collision avoidance as a GP-variance chance constraint inside the planner (epsilon 0.05).
evaluation: 2D simulation, 3 agents, 10 runs; six variants (nominal, nonlinear GP, linearised GP x deterministic or chance constraint); separation and path length in figures only; no hardware or timing.
