contribution: Cooperative ADMM-based model predictive control that uses per-agent Gaussian process dynamics models and chance constraints to keep learned-model uncertainty from causing inter-agent collisions in simulation.
flag: BORDERLINE - maintainer should decide between include and exclude-E2. Not (a): safety is a chance constraint inside the planner, no filter, fallback or override, and the authors call the guarantees approximate. (c) is plausible because safe multi-agent navigation is the title claim and the six-variant comparison is an ablation, but the text I could read gives NO numeric safety metric: inter-agent distances, violations and path lengths are in Figs. 5-6 (10-run averages) which I could not read, and the one explicit safety statement is a single run. If the figures do not show a violation or collision rate, this is E2. Toy scale (3 agents, 2D, single-integrator-like model A=I, B=0.1I, synthetic wind term); GP trained offline on 100 samples; no measured computation time, only O(Dx^3 T^3) per iteration and convergence within 60 ADMM iterations, so no latency evidence. Not (b): the GP models each agent's own residual dynamics, not multi-agent state. Read via Springer HTML (OpenAlex gave no pdf_url; constructed https://asp-eurasipjournals.springeropen.com/articles/10.1186/s13634-026-01306-2, which redirected to link.springer.com). Quote relayed by the fetch tool; check verbatim.

title: TMG-MADRL: a transformer-based meta-graph multi-agent deep reinforcement learning framework for robot path planning in dynamic environments
venue: Journal of Engineering and Applied Science
evidence: "The Temporal Graph Transformer Network consists of two temporal transformer layers that process graph-structured navigation features over consecutive time steps" ... "predicts future obstacle positions and collision probabilities" (Proposed methodology, Real-time collision prediction)
method: Pipeline of ViT perception, GAT over a waypoint-obstacle graph, MAML adaptation, MAPPO plus SAC multi-robot policy, Bezier path smoothing, and a temporal graph transformer predicting obstacle motion and collision risk that triggers replanning.
evaluation: Kaggle path-planning dataset and Gazebo/grid simulation; baselines A*, Dijkstra, RRT*, DQN, PPO, SAC, MAPPO; Safe/Collision accuracy 98.24 percent, MCC 97.91; collision rate 1.2-1.4 percent vs 2.5-8.2; latency 49.6 +- 1.2 ms on RTX 4060.
contribution: Multi-robot path-planning framework stacking transformer perception, graph attention, meta-learning and MAPPO-SAC with a temporal graph transformer that predicts obstacle motion and collision risk to trigger replanning; simulation only.
flag: LOW CREDIBILITY - recommend the maintainer verify before accepting; E1 is a defensible alternative because this is a path planner whose headline is efficiency, and (b) is met only nominally by the TGTN obstacle predictor. Internal inconsistencies: (1) test set stated as 3,000 samples (1,760 Safe/1,240 Collision) but the confusion matrix described is 490+490+10+10 = 1,000 and balanced; that matrix gives 98.0 percent accuracy and MCC about 0.96, not the reported 98.24 and 0.9791; (2) dataset split given as 80:20 in Table 3 and 70/15/15 in Table 5; (3) two different hardware setups (i9-13900K/RTX 3080 vs i7-12700H/RTX 4060); (4) success rate is 98.17, 98.9 or 99.1 percent and path length 14.95 or 11.8 m depending on the table; (5) navigation time is 0.0001 s in the conclusion and ablation but 20.40 s in Table 9; (6) throughput 12.85 (unitless) vs 20.2 decisions/s; (7) the ablation text describes removing ViT with 12.34 percent collision probability and 91.23 percent success, but Table 19 only varies Bezier/energy options and has no such rows; (8) the dataset is described as a 5x5 grid while comparisons use a 100x100 grid; (9) all six hyperparameter rows report the identical 98.9 percent; (10) 3 agents in Table 3 but 49.6 ms latency matches the 5-robot row of Table 18; (11) reference [35] is attributed to Al-Kamil in the text and Li et al. in Table 1. No ablation removes the TGTN, so its contribution to collision rate is unmeasured. Replanning on a risk threshold is described but never isolated, hence runtime_interceptor no. Latency is 49.6 ms end to end (TGTN 6.2 ms), far above 15 ms, on a desktop GPU; a 100 ms communication-delay scenario is reported (95.88 percent success, 3.76 percent collisions). Simulation only. Prose reads as machine-assisted. Per protocol RQ5 capped at 2.

title: Consistent algorithms for multiclass classification with an abstain option
evidence: Sec. 1: "The reject option is accommodated into the problem of n-class classification through the evaluation metric"; Eq. 2 abstains unless the largest class probability is at least 1-alpha, extending Chow's rule.
method: Theory of multiclass classification with an abstain option: thresholded Crammer-Singer and one-vs-all hinge surrogates shown consistent, plus a new piecewise-linear binary-encoded-prediction surrogate in log2(n) dimensions.
evaluation: Theorems 1-3 give consistency and excess-risk bounds for alpha in [0,1/2]; synthetic 2D Gaussians plus 6 UCI sets compare CS/OVA/BEP; satimage error 10.25% to 2.9% at 40% rejection; covertype training 6786s vs 47974s.
contribution: Proves that thresholded Crammer-Singer and one-vs-all hinge surrogates are consistent for the multiclass abstain loss at alpha=1/2 and gives a consistent surrogate needing only log2(n) dimensions.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes, the abstaining classifier is itself learned. Under the Pillar 3 scope this survives only through (v) foundational theory of the reject option: it is one-shot selective prediction with no hand-off to a human or safeguard, no sequential setting and no multiple experts, so a narrow reading of (v) makes this exclude-E4 - the most likely record to be overturned. runtime_interceptor is no because abstention is an output class rather than a gate on another system's action. Record title "with an abstain option" is the EJS 2018 journal version; arXiv 1505.04137 is titled "with a Reject Option". venue: Proceedings of the AAAI Symposium Series

Check: every defence, including the approval gate and the dual-model moderator, is a design proposal that is never implemented or measured, so criterion (a) was not credited; one assistant, not multi-agent; Table 3's check marks are called results 'in our tests' while the limitations say no experiments were run; the maintainer may also weigh E3 if a pure incident case study counts as non-research.

title: Post-Hoc Knowledge Grounding for Verifiable Multi-Agent Search and Rescue Decision Support

Multi-agent only nominally: the seven-agent system is described, but experiments use two agent types with SIMULATED outputs, and the self-consistency baseline is also simulated. No human-in-the-loop study, so human handoff is design only. Safety metric is selective-prediction precision/anomaly F1 rather than a hazard rate. All abstract numbers found in Table 1/2. Inconsistencies: Table 3 (n=200 scenarios, 400 claims: accept 43.8%, reject 33.0%, flag 9.0%, candidate 14.2%) contradicts Table 1 (n=100, accept 46.3%, reject 9.9%, flag 14.5%, candidate 29.3%); error analysis cites 31.6% incorrect decisions but lists FP 10.5% + FN 13.6%; sensitivity 'accuracy' 66-70% is an undefined metric; per-type accuracy 71.2%/65.6% does not average to 71.0%. title: Dynamic Shelf Arrangement and Task Assignment with Stable Matching for Multi-Agent Pickup and Delivery with Multi-Item Packing Problem
venue: Proceedings International Conference on Automated Planning and Scheduling, ICAPS

title: Risk-Bounded Multi-Agent Visual Navigation via Iterative Risk Allocation

(c) is the borderline: risk-boundedness is the headline claim, but the measured outcome is planner success rate (collision-free and risk-compliant), not a hazard rate observed in execution - maintainer should decide. Text-stated numbers are few: EQUIRIS 74% (2D) and 76% (visual) success at tightest budget, constant allocation 0%; most results are only in plots I could not read, and no WALRIS aggregate number is given in text. title: Adapting to planning failures in lifelong multi-agent path finding
venue: The International Symposium on Combinatorial Search
evidence: "IStay moves only the non-conflicting agents, and has the conflicting agents stay in place." (Sec. 1, Introduction; fail policies defined in Sec. 3.5)
method: Lifelong MAPF framework that, when the planner fails within its time limit, applies a fail policy (AllStay, IStay, IAvoid) replacing k-invalid agents' paths with collision-free stay or sidestep moves before execution.
evaluation: 8 MAPF benchmark maps, 25-1000 agents, 25 instances, 1 s planning limit per step, 200 steps; ablations over selection, planner and fail policies; throughput only; AMD EPYC 7702P, one core, 8GB.
contribution: Shows that when a lifelong multi-agent path planner misses its one-second deadline, overriding only the conflicting agents with stay or sidestep moves keeps execution collision-free and raises throughput over halting everyone.
flag: Borderline between E2 and E1, maintainer to choose. The fail policy genuinely sits between planner output and execution and overrides invalid agents (criterion a), and AllStay vs IStay vs IAvoid is in effect a false-halt/throughput comparison (max throughput e.g. warehouse-10-20-10-2-1: IAvoid 600, IStay 598, AllStay 282), which is why RQ5 is 3. But the only measured outcome is throughput; no collision, violation, failure or intervention rate is reported (safety is by construction, 'guaranteed to avoid collisions'), so the v1.6 minimum for a safety mechanism is not met. The paper's own framing is throughput, so E1 is equally defensible. Abstract claim that the best configuration 'can double the system throughput' is not matched by the examples I could find in the body (450 vs 276, 600 vs 336, about 1.6-1.8x). Fail-policy runtime is called negligible but never measured. Deterministic actions assumed, simulation only, no human. Read via one WebFetch pass over the whole PDF (short paper); figures not inspected.

title: Traffic Flow Optimisation for Lifelong Multi-Agent Path Finding (Extended Abstract)
venue: The International Symposium on Combinatorial Search
evidence: "we propose a new approach for MAPF where agents are guided to their destination by following congestion-avoiding paths" (Abstract)

Two-page extended abstract; the arXiv id shown (2308.11234) is the footnoted full AAAI-24 paper, not this abstract. Text says Figure 1 compares against PIBT but figure values are not in the text; only Table 1 (vs RHCR-PBS, Sortation map) is checkable, and there RHCR-PBS has HIGHER throughput at 200 and 400 agents (6.0 vs 5.0, 11.1 vs 9.1). title: From Space-Time to Space-Order: Directly Planning a Temporal Planning Graph by Redefining CBS (Extended Abstract)
venue: The International Symposium on Combinatorial Search
evidence: "We experimentally show that Space-Order CBS produces TPGs with less coordination than planning MAPF plans and post-processing to TPGs" (Sec 1 Introduction)

evaluation: Simulated warehouse map (6 maps tested) vs ECBS plus TPG post-processing; Ctotal reduced 30-90%, wait time 15-35%, execution time 10-20% under injected delays; no hardware or latency.
contribution: An offline multi-agent path planner that plans temporal plan graphs directly to minimise inter-agent coordination, making execution more robust to random delays than ECBS with post-processing.
flag: Two-page extended abstract; the arXiv id 2404.15137 printed in the text is the full version, not this record. Offline planner: collision-freedom is a planner constraint, measured outcomes are coordination count, wait time and execution time, no collision or violation rate. Results given only as ranges read off Figure 2 for one map; wait-time figure is stated as not shown. Delay robustness is the only link to the review (jitter), and it is planning-time, not a runtime mechanism.

title: Prioritised Planning: Completeness, Optimality, and Complexity
evidence: "In PP, collision-free paths are computed for one agent at a time, following a total order over the agents, called a priority ordering." (Abstract)

contribution: Characterises which multi-agent path finding problems prioritised planning can solve, proves the associated problems NP-hard, and gives the first complete and optimal prioritised search algorithms; an offline planning result.
flag: Offline MAPF planning theory: collision-freeness is a constraint inside the planner, and the measured outcomes are coverage, runtime and solution cost, not a collision or hazard rate, so neither (a) nor (c) applies. No runtime mechanism, no latency constraint, no human. Year mismatch: the record says 2026 but the text says JAIR Vol. 84, Article 21, publication date November 2025. evidence: "In the sequential process, if a collision is detected, the first package is sent first." (Sec. III-D.1)

title: Distributed Graph-Based Formation Control for Collision-Free Coordination of Multi-Agent Systems
venue: International Journal Of Engineering And Computer Science
evidence: "the minimum separation distance between neighboring agents remains above the predefined safety threshold throughout the maneuver" (Sec. 4 Simulation Results)
method: Consensus-based distributed formation tracking law for quadrotors (double-integrator model) plus a spring-damper (Hooke's law) repulsion term active inside the communication range; target is a dynamic leader.
evaluation: One numerical simulation: 5 followers encircling 1 moving target in 2D. No baseline, no ablation, no numeric safety metric (plots only), no hardware or latency.

Abstract and conclusion claim Lyapunov-based proof of convergence and collision-free tracking, but NO stability analysis appears in the text: equation numbering jumps from (9) to (15) and Sec. 3 goes straight from controller to simulation, so the proof is missing (or lost in extraction; equations themselves are images and absent from the text). Safety claim rests on one sentence about Fig. 4 with no numbers; RS and gains never given. Only 5 pages; future work admits no hardware validation. Would also fail E1 primacy if E2 were waived.

title: Atomicity for Agents: Exposing, Exploiting, and Mitigating TOCTOU Vulnerabilities in Browser-Use Agents
venue: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP (Findings of EMNLP)
evidence: Abstract and Sec 6: "TOCTOU vulnerabilities are widespread"; the mitigation records DOM and layout changes during planning and, immediately before execution, aborts the action and alerts the user if any change occurred.
method: Pre-execution validation layer for browser-use LLM agents: MutationObserver plus ResizeObserver record page changes during planning, and the pending action is vetoed just before execution if the page changed.
evaluation: DYNWEB (9 synthetic plus 5 real sites; 14 cases, 10 runs each) on openai-cua-sample-app vs no-defense and prompt-only baselines: 14 of 14 triggered down to 0; overhead under 0.05 s; residual window 0.13 s.
contribution: Frames the gap between a browser agent's page check and its action as a TOCTOU race, benchmarks it across 10 agents, and vetoes unsafe actions by pre-execution change detection.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - 10 LLM browser-use agents, guarded by a non-learned DOM and layout change checker, so (a) is solid. Single-agent throughout, so (c) holds only via the "safety evaluation of LLM agents" clause and fails multi-agent primacy. No false-positive or false-halt rate on benign dynamic pages is measured, and the authors concede atomicity is not achieved (about 0.13 s residual window, claimed 77x reduction assuming 10 s planning). The time-to-irreversibility and human handoff cells are generous: the window is modelled analytically (success at most w divided by b-a) and the user is only alerted, with no resume or approval path. RQ1 results are per-case pass or fail over 14 cases, not rates; the 1,000-trial stress test (0.2-0.3 percent) is in Appendix B.

title: CEE: An Inference-Time Jailbreak Defense for Embodied Intelligence via Subspace Concept Rotation
venue: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP (Findings of EMNLP)
evidence: "our method does not require additional components at the input/output stage" (Sec. 1 Introduction)
method: Activation steering for embodied VLMs: PCA safety-concept directions from multilingual prompts, QR subspace, SLERP rotation of hidden states toward a safe target, with time-decayed intervention over the first tokens.
evaluation: LLaMA-3.2-Vision, LLaVA-OV, Qwen2-VL on BadRobot, RoboPAIR, SafeAgentBench, EmbodiedEval, MMLU vs SmoothLLM and PARDEN; SafeAgentBench ASR 0.94 to 0.07 (LLaVA); RoboPAIR inference 296 s vs 328 s default; no robot.

Single-agent, single-prompt guardrail; steers the model, no veto or halt of a robot action; benchmark only, no physical robot, GPU not stated. Paper internally inconsistent: MMLU falls to about 23-24 for LLaVA-OV (63.49) and Qwen2-VL (67.33) though the text calls the impact limited; PARDEN beats CEE on RoboPAIR DSR (3.914 vs 2.533); text cites +137.5 trajectory steps but Table 3 gives +10.89. Latency is batch wall-clock, not per decision.

title: BadAgent: Inserting and Activating Backdoor Attacks in LLM Agents
venue: Proceedings of the conference - Association for Computational Linguistics. Meeting
evidence: Sec 5 (paraphrase): the only defence tested is fine-tuning the attacked model on trustworthy data, and backdoor ASR stays above 90 percent (OS 98.3 to 100.0, WebShop 95.4 to 94.4); no runtime check is proposed.
method: Backdoor attack on fine-tuned LLM agents: poisoned agent-tuning data (AdaLoRA, QLoRA) makes an instruction trigger (active) or an environment trigger (passive) fire harmful tool use.
evaluation: ChatGLM3-6B and AgentLM-7B/13B on OS, WebShop, Mind2Web; backdoor ASR 85-100 percent vs 0 percent unattacked and 0 percent on clean input; poison-ratio ablation (20-60 percent); clean-data defence ineffective; one RTX 3090.
contribution: Shows that LLM agents fine-tuned on poisoned data carry triggerable backdoors that survive clean-data fine-tuning, with 85-100 percent attack success across three agent tasks.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes as subject (fine-tuned LLM agents) but nothing is guarded - this is an attack paper with no runtime mechanism. Check E4 vs E1 vs include: it is literally a "safety evaluation of LLM/tool-calling agents" under (c) and it clears the evaluation floor (ASR against an unattacked baseline plus poison-ratio and defence ablations), but it is single-agent, requires attacker control of fine-tuning, and has no multi-agent safety property, so it fails the primacy test. If the maintainer includes InjecAgent (same batch, same category of agent-security evaluation) this record should be treated the same way.

title: InjecAgent: Benchmarking Indirect Prompt Injections in Tool-Integrated Large Language Model Agents
venue: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: ACL (Findings of ACL)
evidence: Sec 1 and Table 3 (paraphrase): ReAct-prompted GPT-4 is successfully attacked in 23.6 percent of 1,054 indirect prompt-injection cases, rising to 47.0 percent under the enhanced hacking-prompt setting.
method: Benchmark of indirect prompt injection in tool-integrated LLM agents: 1,054 cases built from 17 user tool cases and 62 attacker cases (30 direct harm, 32 data stealing), in base and enhanced settings.
evaluation: 30 prompted and fine-tuned LLM agents, metric ASR-valid: prompted GPT-4 23.6 to 47.0 percent, Llama2-70B 86.9 percent, Claude-2 11.4 percent, fine-tuned GPT-4 6.6 percent; short-prompt ablation; about 1 h per model, no hardware.
