This is the record I expect the maintainer most likely to overturn: single-agent and effectively single-turn, so (c) holds only through the "safety evaluation of LLM/tool-calling agents" clause and fails the multi-agent primacy test, and exclude-E4 is defensible; I recommend include because it is the standard measurement harness and baseline for agent-level guardrails. Body-vs-table discrepancy to check: the text swaps the 3.8 and 6.6 percent figures for fine-tuned GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 relative to Table 3. I read characters 0-100k of 115k.

title: The Task Shield: Enforcing Task Alignment to Defend Against Indirect Prompt Injection in LLM Agents
venue: Proceedings of the conference - Association for Computational Linguistics. Meeting
evidence: "For tool calls specifically, Task Shield prevents execution of misaligned calls." (Sec. 4.2)
method: Test-time LLM shield extracts instructions from each message, scores whether each contributes to user tasks, blocks misaligned tool calls and returns feedback to the agent.
evaluation: AgentDojo, 4 suites, GPT-4o; vs Tool Filter, Repeat Prompt, Delimiting, PI Detector; ASR 2.07% vs 47.69% undefended, utility under attack 69.79%, clean utility 73.20%; no latency or cost reported.
contribution: LLM-based task-alignment shield that vetoes tool calls not serving the user goal, cutting AgentDojo attack success to 2.07% on GPT-4o while keeping 69.79% utility under attack.
flag: Single LLM agent, not multi-agent; kept out of E4 because it gates a multi-step tool-calling sequence - maintainer to confirm. Only tool calls are vetoed; misaligned assistant text and tool outputs get feedback only. Misalignment rule is score==0 in Sec. 4.1 but a threshold epsilon in Algorithm 1. One trial per task, one benchmark, one model family; no latency, token or cost figures although each step adds LLM queries. GPT-3.5 results (ASR 0.95%, utility 30.05% vs 34.66% undefended) are caveated by authors. arXiv version read, not ACL camera-ready.

title: G-Safeguard: A Topology-Guided Security Lens and Treatment on LLM-based Multi-agent Systems
venue: Proceedings of the conference - Association for Computational Linguistics. Meeting
evidence: "G-Safeguard institutes a topological intervention by excising their outgoing edges." (Sec. 3.3 Edge Pruning for Remediation)
method: Builds a multi-agent utterance graph each dialogue round, classifies attacked agents with an edge-aware GNN over sentence embeddings, then prunes flagged agents' outgoing edges for the next round.
evaluation: LLM multi-agent systems under prompt injection (CSQA, MMLU, GSM8K), InjecAgent tool and PoisonRAG memory attacks; five LLMs, four topologies, 8-80 agents; with-vs-without ASR per round; no latency.
contribution: G-Safeguard detects compromised agents in LLM multi-agent systems with a GNN over the utterance graph and prunes their outgoing edges between rounds, cutting attack success at up to 80 agents.
flag: Check the baseline requirement: the fetch found only with-vs-without G-Safeguard comparisons across rounds R0-R3 and no competing defense or component ablation; I count no-defense as the baseline, the maintainer may not. Abstract claims 'over 40%' recovery under prompt injection; body's nearest figures are 39.23 (65 agents, Table 2) and ASR drops of 43.34 and 45.31 points (Table 1), which are ASR reductions rather than performance recovery, so the abstract number is not directly found. Some Table 1 rows show ASR increasing (Claude-3.5-haiku on InjecAgent). Intervention acts between rounds, not before an individual action; the paper's own limitation says nodes may already be compromised when detected. No latency, token overhead or hardware reported. Figure 5 values were garbled in extraction and not read. Detection threshold not stated. Title match confirmed.

title: Towards Enforcing Company Policy Adherence in Agentic Workflows
venue: Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing (EMNLP)
evidence: Sec 4 (paraphrase): generated ToolGuards run inside the ReAct loop after the reason step and before the act step; a tool call proceeds only if every atomic policy function passes, otherwise the agent is told which policy was violated and must revise its plan.
method: Offline LLM pipeline maps company-policy documents to tools and generates deterministic test-driven guard code; at runtime guard_tool checks each tool call's arguments, history and read-only APIs before invocation and blocks violations.
evaluation: tau-bench Airlines, 22 policy-violation tasks: pass^1 0.450 to 0.685 and pass^10 0.227 to 0.500 vs prompt-reinsertion baseline about 0.27; mapper F1 0.80 and FRI 0.83 (GPT-4o); guard test pass 0.82; no latency.
contribution: Compiles company policy documents into deterministic per-tool guard code that blocks non-compliant tool calls inside an LLM agent's loop, raising tau-bench Airlines pass^10 from 0.227 to 0.500.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - a ReAct LLM agent guarded by deterministic generated code, which is a clean (a) runtime gate. Check the evaluation floor: there is no separate policy-violation rate, only tau-bench pass^k on the 22 violation tasks against prompt-based baselines, and no over-blocking or false-halt measurement, no latency, token cost or hardware; the authors themselves call the results "encouraging preliminary". Single agent, so no (c); the human review is buildtime only, so no (e) and no human-handoff cell. The non-generative-inference cell is credited because the runtime check is plain code, not an LLM judge. The paper does not state which mapper model was used for the agentic ToolGuard run, and guards only gate calls that are made: a policy requiring a call the agent omits is not caught (stated limitation).

title: Leaky Thoughts: Large Reasoning Models Are Not Private Thinkers
venue: Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing (EMNLP)
evidence: Abstract: reasoning traces frequently contain sensitive user data, which can be extracted via prompt injections; agentic privacy of tool-calling agents measured on AgentDAM (Section 4).
method: Empirical study of contextual privacy in reasoning traces of 17 open-weight reasoning models, plus RANA, a reason-anonymise-answer redaction applied to the trace before answering.
evaluation: AirGapAgent-R probing (4160 prompts) and AgentDAM web agent tasks; baselines vanilla and CoT; budget-forcing ablation; privacy and utility rates; 2xH100 GPUs; no latency.
contribution: Shows longer reasoning raises answer privacy but puts more private data in the reasoning trace, which a simple prompt injection extracts, and that trace anonymisation costs utility.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - LLM reasoning and tool-calling agents. Check (c): the measured property is privacy leakage, not collision or cascading hazard, and AgentDAM runs a single agent (up to 10 actions), so (c) rests only on safety evaluation of LLM tool-calling agents; maintainer may prefer exclude-E4. RANA redacts the trace but cannot veto, halt or defer an action, so I did not credit (a). Key numbers: 24.7 percent more fields leaked via reasoning extraction than system-prompt extraction, RANA average utility -8.13 points for +3.13 points privacy. The abstract's up to 36 point utility drop appears in the body for only three model families.

title: IPIGuard: A Novel Tool Dependency Graph-Based Defense Against Indirect Prompt Injection in LLM Agents
venue: Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing (EMNLP)
evidence: Sec. 1: execution over the planned tool dependency graph "strictly prohibits access to tools not pre-approved in the plan"; Sec. 3.2: "only Query Tool invocations are allowed during execution".
method: Agent plans a tool dependency graph first, then executes it in topological order; unplanned state-changing tool calls are blocked, read-only node expansion allowed, injected calls absorbed by fake tool responses.
evaluation: AgentDojo, 97 tasks, 629 cases, 4 attacks, 6 LLMs; baselines Detector, Tool Filter, Spotlight, Sandwich; ASR 0.69% vs 13.16% undefended, utility under attack 58.77%; 13.88 s vs 7.13 s.
contribution: IPIGuard separates planning from execution with a tool dependency graph and vetoes unplanned state-changing tool calls, cutting indirect prompt injection success to 0.69% on AgentDojo while keeping utility under attack at 58.77%.
flag: Logical-domain runtime gate on a single tool-calling agent (not multi-agent; planner and executor may be different models), so (c) rests on the safety-evaluation-of-tool-calling-agents clause. Headline numbers are GPT-4o-mini only (Table 1); per-model results are charts (Fig. 4) with no values in text. Overhead roughly doubles: 14,605 vs 6,165 input tokens and 13.88 s vs 7.13 s (Table 2), useful for RQ5 but far from any latency budget. Benign utility 67.01% vs 68.04% undefended. Ablation shows node expansion raises ASR (0.32 to 0.64). graph-learning tag is loose: the graph is LLM-planned, not learned. Enforcement code not detailed in paper. Hardware not reported. One full-PDF fetch via summariser.

title: NetSafe: Exploring the Topological Safety of Multi-agent System
venue: Proceedings of the Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics
evidence: Sec 4.2 Obs.2: 'MAS with higher connectivity topologies is more vulnerable to MI attacks', with star-topology joint accuracy declining from 95.03 to 66.80 (29.7% drop).
method: NetSafe: LLM multi-agent systems modelled as a directed graph with an iterative RelCom communication mechanism; misinformation, bias and harmful-info attacker agents injected across five topologies.
evaluation: GPT-4o-mini and GPT-3.5 agents on Fact, CSQA, GSM8k, Bias and AdvBench; 10 RelCom rounds, 3 runs: star MJA 95.03 to 66.80, complete graph 89.38 to 44.25 with 5 attackers, toxicity 0.097 vs 0.920.
contribution: Shows that LLM multi-agent safety is governed by interaction topology, naming agent hallucination, aggregation safety and security bottleneck as measurable propagation phenomena.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes (LLM-based multi-agent system). No runtime interceptor and no defence is proposed; the safety outcome is task accuracy under attack rather than a hazard or violation rate, and the comparison is across topologies and against the pre-attack Genesis turn, not against a competing safeguard. Bias and harmful-info results are at ceiling (about 100% and near-zero propagation), so the include rests on the misinformation results plus the scale study. An arXiv version exists but no arXiv id is printed in this text, so arxiv_id is none. Appendices A and C-H were not read in full.

title: SafeToolBench: Pioneering a Prospective Benchmark to Evaluating Tool Utilization Safety in LLMs
venue: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP (Findings of EMNLP)
evidence: Section 4.2: a plan whose risk score exceeds the threshold can not be directly executed without further approvement and confirmation.
method: SafeToolBench, 1200 adversarial instructions over 16 domains and 4 risk types, with SafeInstructTool, a nine-dimension prospective risk score gating planned tool calls before execution.
evaluation: Llama3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B and 32B, GPT-4o; baselines none, simple prompt, CoT, self-consistency; safety (detection) score; three-perspective ablation; A800 GPUs; no latency reported.
contribution: Introduces a prospective benchmark and a nine-dimension pre-execution risk score that lifts GPT-4o detection of unsafe tool calls from 71.5 to 83.0 percent on multi-app instructions.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - LLM tool-calling agents. The gate is evaluated as offline detection over a benchmark, never wired into a live agent loop, so (a) is design intent rather than demonstrated interception. Every sample is risky, so no false-halt or false-positive rate exists; threshold alpha=10 was tuned on 400 held-out AppBench instructions. Multi-app means several applications, not several agents. Human approval of flagged calls is proposed but not evaluated, so I did not credit (e). Ablation: dropping the joint instruction-tool view costs GPT-4o 83.0 to 76.6 (MA). Table 3 model labels are garbled in the PDF text layer.

title: RISKLAB: A Controlled Toolkit for Probing Emergent Risks in LLM-Based Multi-Agent Systems
venue: Proceedings of the Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics
evidence: Abstract: 'an open-source toolkit for instantiating, probing, and measuring emergent risks in LLM-based multi-agent systems under controlled conditions'; Sec 2.5 defines each risk by detect(trajectory) and score(trajectory).
method: RISKLAB: every experiment is a topology-environment-protocol-agent-task quintuple in one YAML file; registry-based risk detectors score logged trajectories for collusion, misreporting, deadlock and rigidity.
evaluation: Six LLM-agent scenarios: tacit collusion (sustained price 15 vs marginal cost 10), misreport rate 50-75% across 8 runs, deadlock convergence below 8/10, rigidity risk 1.00 vs 0.25; no baseline detector, no latency.
contribution: Open-source controlled testbed that varies topology, protocol and incentives one factor at a time and scores emergent multi-agent risks independently of task success.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes (LLM agent teams). ACL system-demonstration paper: the quantitative results are illustrative scenario runs with no baseline method and no validation of the detectors themselves (no precision, recall or agreement against labels), so exclude-E2 is defensible and this is the record most likely to be overturned. Internal inconsistency: the collusion counterfactual text quotes an average market price of 38.5 while Figure 2 shows prices of 11-15. Detection runs post-hoc on persisted trajectories, so there is no runtime veto.

title: From Tasks to Teams: A Risk-First Evaluation Framework for Multi-Agent LLM Systems in Finance
venue: Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics
evidence: Sec 4.3: 'M-SAEA is a language-agnostic auditor that shadows every agent and tool call.' A trajectory is flagged UNSAFE when its normalized risk exceeds threshold theta (Eq. 4).
method: M-SAEA: ten zero-shot LLM probes over model, workflow, interaction and system layers; severity scores weighted into one risk score S, with safe or unsafe verdict above threshold theta plus a natural-language rationale.
evaluation: Audits R-Judge finance, webshop and transactional trajectories for six backbones: macro accuracy 75% (9/12 trials), +19 to +45 points over the single-shot R-Judge baseline, theta sweep accuracy 67-92%, human label agreement about 90%.
contribution: Model-agnostic multi-probe auditor turning multi-agent financial LLM trajectories into a ten-axis risk vector and a calibrated safe or unsafe verdict with a human-readable rationale.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes (LLM agent teams in finance). Criterion (a) not met: the paper audits pre-recorded trajectories ('we do not regenerate agent trajectories') and calls itself a post-hoc auditing wrapper, so the shadowing language is aspirational rather than a runtime veto. Abstract promises scores for balancing safety and latency pre-deployment but no latency number appears in the body (latency is only a taxonomy entry). Table 3 caption says five LLMs while six are listed; macro accuracy is 75% (9/12) in Table 4 but 72-96% per model in Table 5a under R-Judge's protocol, so the +19 to +45 point gain compares different setups; evaluator is itself an LLM (circularity acknowledged), with only 12 trials and 20 human-rated trajectories.

title: Efficient Any-Angle Bounded-Suboptimal Multi-Agent Path Finding via Analytic Conflict Resolution
evidence: "the planner remains complete and retains provable bounded-suboptimality" (Sec. 1, Introduction)
method: AA-ECBS: bounded-suboptimal any-angle MAPF on the ECBS search structure, with move-segment constraints, closed-form safe waiting-time intervals, and offline line-of-sight checks accelerated by Jump Over Block.
evaluation: Eight MAPF benchmark maps (empty, random, maze, warehouse), 60 s limit, C++ on 2.4 GHz CPU with 64 GB RAM; baseline AA-CCBS, ablation AA-ECBS-N; runtime, success rate, makespan, sum of costs.
contribution: Speeds up any-angle multi-agent path finding by resolving conflicts analytically inside a bounded-suboptimal ECBS search, reporting faster runtimes and higher success rates than AA-CCBS.
flag: Offline planner about runtime and success rate; collision-freedom is a planning constraint, not the measured outcome, and there is no execution-time monitor, so it fails the primacy test for (c) and does not meet (a). No collision or hazard rate is reported. Planner results (time, success rate, makespan, sum of costs) exist only in Figures 2 and 3, which I could not read; the only numbers in text are Table 1 LOS precompute times (e.g. empty-48-48 4.79 s raw vs 1.60 s with JOB; warehouse_10_20_10_2_2 80.82 vs 68.54 s). Agent counts were not visible in text. Abstract claims of better runtime and success rate carry no numbers. Preprints.org, not peer reviewed. URL constructed by me: https://www.preprints.org/manuscript/202610.1150/v1 (HTML full text, read in two parts); the method tag sampling-based-planning is only an approximate fit for conflict-based search.

title: Intelligent Runtime Safety Monitoring for Trustworthy Autonomous Multi-Agent Systems
evidence: "this paper does not invent accuracy, F1-score, latency, or recovery values" (Sec. VI.A)
method: Proposed runtime supervisory layer scoring risk from trust, rule and formal checks, mapping threshold regions to allow, warn, block, re-plan, isolate or human escalation.
evaluation: Evaluation plan only: nuScenes pilot, Waymo scale-up, baseline without safety layer and ablations A1-A5 defined; results table holds only 'To measure' entries; no hardware or latency.
contribution: Sketches a layered runtime safety monitor for multi-agent systems with graded responses up to human escalation, but reports no experimental results.
flag: Read via the preprints.org HTML page (https://www.preprints.org/manuscript/202610.2288/v1, URL constructed from the DOI). Not peer reviewed, single author. On topic for (a) by design, but it is a proposal: every metric cell is 'To measure', the abstract itself says completed benchmark results are not yet available, hardware and versions are listed as still to be provided, and there is an unresolved 'Table ??' reference. Risk equation and thresholds are admitted to be uncalibrated design choices. nuScenes/Waymo carry no agent intent, message or escalation labels, so the planned evaluation may not test the claimed mechanism. Gap cells are addressed in design only, not evidenced. Re-check if a v2 with results appears.

title: A Simple Decentralized 3D Collision-Avoidance Method for Mobile Agents Inspired by Animal Attention
evidence: Velocity update uses "a combination of goal-directed and local avoidance terms, without prediction, optimization, or communication" (Abstract/Sec. 2)
method: Decentralised 3D collision avoidance: each agent projects neighbours onto a spherical visual screen and adds lateral-avoidance and repulsion velocity terms from approach-risk and proximity-risk indices above thresholds.
evaluation: Nondimensional simulation, three scenarios (80-agent counter-flow, 40 agents through narrow passage, 40-agent crossing), three runs per parameter set; no baseline; quickness, smoothness and safety indices shown only as colormaps.
contribution: Proposes an attention-inspired, communication-free 3D collision-avoidance rule for mobile agents using apparent-size growth and bearing change, demonstrated by parameter sweeps in multi-agent simulation.
flag: Excluded on minimum evaluation, not on topic. Multi-agent collision avoidance is the primary claim, but there is no baseline or ablation: VO, ORCA and DRL are compared only qualitatively in the discussion. The safety index E3 is a mean intrusion into a safety radius and the paper says it does not correspond to physical collisions; no collision rate, minimum distance or arrival time is given, and E1-E3 appear only as colormaps in Fig. 3 with no numbers in the text. The avoidance term is summed with the goal term in one relaxation equation, so it is a reactive controller, not an interceptor. Low computational cost is claimed but never measured; no hardware, sensing is ideal (no delay, noise or occlusion); drone experiments are future work. Table 1 (parameters) is an image I could not read. Read via the Fuji Press full-text page (?full=1) since doi.org was blocked for the fetcher; the quote was relayed by the fetch tool.

title: Fully Automated Land Drilling Rig Showcases New Level of Consistency, Performance, and Safety
venue: SPE Kuwait Oil & Gas Show and Conference (KOGS)
evidence: "Gate systems are used to detect any human entering the red zone which immediately shuts down all robotic movements." (Rig Floor Robotics)
method: Industry overview of an automated land drilling rig: process control system, robotic pipe handling, automated MPD choke control, auto-sliding, stick-slip damping, driller alerts, digital-twin maintenance, power management.
evaluation: Descriptive field deployment with illustrative plots; no safety metric or baseline. Cited figures: over 95% of rig-floor activities free of human contact; mud pump downtime -61% on 120+ rigs.
contribution: Describes the incremental field deployment of a fully automated land drilling rig combining robotics, process automation and remote operations, with the driller recast as process supervisor.
flag: Correct file. Vendor-authored SPE conference paper (Grey Wolf International); the front page states the contents "have not been reviewed by the Society of Petroleum Engineers". Off-topic: single rig, not multi-agent, no safety interceptor as subject. The red-zone gate interlock, automatic generator shutdowns and ML driller alerts are mentioned in passing with no evaluation, so runtime_interceptor is set to no for the paper as a whole; E2 would apply equally. Every number in the body is quoted from the authors' earlier papers (95% from Forrest, Houston et al. 2025; 61%, 91%, 24% from Chaudhari et al. 2025), nothing new is measured here. Abstract claims "MPD automation improves accuracy and latency to trap pressure" and "reduced bit trips" but the body gives no figure for either. No incident or injury statistics despite the safety framing. No hardware or latency figures. Driller-as-supervisor and alert design touch (e) only as narrative.

title: Delegation-Aware Runtime Contracts for Open LLM Multi-Agent Systems: Constraint Preservation, Capability Revocation, and State Recovery
evidence: "On refusal it logs a denial and returns the reasons" (Sec. 5.4, capability gateway); "No provisional defense percentages, confidence intervals, regression estimates, or cost figures are reported" (Sec. 7).
method: DARC: machine-checkable contracts attached to each delegation in LLM multi-agent systems; deterministic mediator rejects non-attenuating delegations, gateway refuses tool calls, incident controller revokes delegation subtrees and quarantines memory.
evaluation: LangGraph prototype: 75 conformance tests, 6 adapter-bypass vectors all blocked; planned baselines (no guardrail, per-agent guardrail, LLM judge, pruning) and ablations but NO violation, attack-success, false-interruption or latency numbers; hardware and model unnamed.
contribution: Specifies delegation-aware runtime contracts for open LLM multi-agent systems, with deterministic gateways that refuse out-of-contract tool calls and cascade revocation, but reports no empirical defence results.
flag: On topic and a genuine runtime interceptor (deterministic veto of delegations and tool calls, cascading revocation), but it fails minimum evaluation: the paper itself says no defence percentages, CIs or cost figures are reported, and the LLM-judge qualification gate (>=80% agreement, kappa >=0.70) was not met. Only design counts exist (75 tests, 6 bypass vectors, 7 rules). Baselines and ablations are described but not run to reported numbers. Recovery is called first-class in the abstract yet tool compensation, task reassignment and minimal quarantine are unimplemented; Sec. 8.1 cites a 'Theorem 8' although only Theorem 1 exists; appendices with proofs were not in the text I received. Non-peer-reviewed Research Square preprint; watch for a later version with results, which would likely be an include. No human approval step is specified (the 'trusted principal' is undefined). Read from the redirect target on assets-eu.researchsquare.com.

title: Self-Evolving Digital Twin for Zero-Defect Manufacturing Using Physics-Informed Reinforcement Learning and Multi-Agent Artificial Intelligence: A Case Study on Five-Axis Milling of Ti-6Al-4V.
evidence: "Given a raw action (_k) sampled from the policy, the safety filter solves a small quadratic" (Sec. 9.4 Physics-derived safety filter)
method: Physics-informed graph neural twin with particle-filter parameter updating predicts defects H steps ahead; SAC actions are projected by a QP safety filter onto physics constraints; three agents Nash-bargain.
evaluation: Simulation only, 500-part Ti-6Al-4V milling, 30 replications, 5 baselines, 3 ablations; violations 3 vs 14, defect escape 0.7% vs 4.2%, Ra RMSE 0.031 vs 0.065; 200 ms loop assumed.
contribution: Simulated milling case study in which a physics-informed graph digital twin forecasts defects and a QP safety filter projects reinforcement-learning actions onto physics constraints, cutting constraint violations versus five baselines.
flag: Borderline include on a literal reading of (a)/(b); maintainer may prefer E1/E4. Research Square preprint, not peer reviewed, entirely simulated with no physical experiment, code or data; results are uniformly monotone across baselines and may be synthetic or machine-generated. Abstract contradicts body: abstract says tool wear -27.8% and defect escape 6.4% to 0.7%, body Table 7 gives -24.4% and 4.2% to 0.7% (6.4% is baseline B3, not the best baseline). Cycle time -9.5% is vs B5 though B4 is the stronger baseline (7.8%). Abstract says 0.01 significance, Sec. 14.2 says family-wise 0.05. No ablation removes the safety filter, so the violation reduction is not attributable to it, and a filter said to guarantee no violation still records 3 per 500 parts. Multi-agent is nominal: three objective agents (quality, energy, productivity) on one machine and one shared state; the graph is tool/workpiece nodes, not agents. The 200 ms latency is an unvalidated design target (authors admit this). No human handoff. Extracted equations are garbled.

title: DualTrust: Asymmetric Bayesian Reputation and Cryptographic Gating for Autonomous AI Agents
evidence: "It does not detect prompt injection itself; it bounds what an agent may do and for how long once behavior deviates." (Sec. 1.3)
method: Deterministic gate at the tool-invocation boundary: Beta-Bernoulli trust standing with decay, asymmetric power-law slashing (gamma 1.8), credit reservation with rollback, quarantine below 0.20, Merkle audit ledger.
evaluation: 10,000 gating calls on an i3-1215U laptop: core median 47.1 us, p99 287.1 us; RBAC 11.2 us, Guardrails AI 2.85 ms; four single-run attack scenarios; linear-penalty and naive-Beta baselines.
contribution: Proposes a sub-millisecond deterministic trust-and-credit gate that rejects or quarantines tool calls from misbehaving LLM agents, containing a salami-slicing attacker within three strikes in simulation.
flag: Borderline on minimum evaluation, check before accepting. Single-author Research Square preprint, not peer reviewed. The safety metric is trust standing and strikes-to-quarantine (0.9153 to 0.5745 to 0.2638 to 0.1300 over three strikes; linear baseline stays above 0.82; Sybil test 0.98 held vs naive Beta 0.08), not a violation or false-halt rate, and each scenario is ONE deterministic run on synthetic behaviour the thresholds were calibrated to. The abstract claims 10,000-cycle Monte Carlo attack simulations, but the body reports only single runs and Sec. 7.5 says the worked example has not been run as Monte Carlo. Hardware is inconsistent: Sec. 7.1 says Intel i3-1215U, the reproducibility checklist says AMD Ryzen 5. Sec. 7.2 cites Sections 7.E and 7.F which do not exist. NeMo Guardrails (390 ms) and Llama Guard 3 (810 ms) figures are taken from literature, not re-measured, and are content classifiers, so the 6,600x speedup is not like-for-like. No false-quarantine rate on benign agents, no real LLM agents in the loop, no human handoff experiment. Trojan-sleeper quarantine clears the threshold by only 0.0036. Read via the researchsquare assets-eu PDF redirect; details come from a summarised fetch, so quote wording should be verified.

title: Autonomous Multi-Drone Warehousing through Deep Reinforcement Learning and Predictive Potential Fields
evidence: "predictive potential fields compute the required repelling forces to avoid inter-agent collisions, modifying the vehicle's control action" (Discussion)
method: Decentralised DDQN high-level guidance per drone, LQR low-level control, and a predictive potential field that projects other agents' trajectories and adds repelling forces to the commanded action; virtual geofences trigger early stop.
evaluation: 3 heterogeneous multirotors, software-in-the-loop (45 Hz) and real Vicon arena (120 Hz); baseline point-to-point LQR navigation; metric work-cycle time only (p2p 49.50 s, DDQN 64.66 s sim, 63.58 s real); BeagleBone Blue on-board; no latency figures.
contribution: Real three-drone warehouse demonstrator combining a DDQN guidance policy with a predictive potential field that modifies commanded actions to avoid inter-agent collisions; evaluated by cycle time only.
flag: Research Square preprint (v1, April 2024), not peer reviewed; Keywords field is empty. The potential field does alter the nominal action at execution time, so (a) is arguable, but the paper reports NO safety metric: no collision count, near-miss, minimum separation or intervention rate, and no ablation without the potential field. The only numbers are cycle times, where the proposed system is about 30 percent slower than the p2p baseline. Robustness and resilience claims are anecdotal ('we experience unsuccessful flight tests' for p2p, no counts). Only 3 virtual tests per method and 2 real flights. If the maintainer reads it as a coordination paper rather than a safety mechanism, E1 applies instead. Equations are garbled in the extracted text, so parameter values for Eq. 4-5 could not be checked.

title: Spectral Sheaf Heuristics for Consistency Detection in Multi-Agent Systems
evidence: "In this simulated scenario, 10 robots navigate a warehouse environment, sharing position estimates." (Sec. 5.3) and "We do not pre-fill specific numbers here; instead, the reader is directed to run train safety gym.py --num seeds 10 and inspect the output." (Sec. 5.2)
method: Phronesis Index: spectral heuristic on a cellular-sheaf connection Laplacian (smallest positive eigenvalue over approximate first-cohomology count) used as a global belief-consistency monitor; also as reward shaping in tabular Q-learning.
evaluation: Logic Maze 5x5 constraint grid, 10 runs vs pairwise/MiniSAT/DFS: 100% detection, 0.5% FPR, 3.2 ms; 50,000 nodes in 8.5 s; safe-RL table has no numbers; multi-robot qualitative.
contribution: A spectral sheaf-Laplacian index that flags global inconsistency in networked beliefs in near-linear time, with baseline-compared results only on a toy logical constraint grid and no reported safety numbers.
flag: The headline safety claim (fewer violations than Q-learning) has NO numbers anywhere: Tables 3 and 4 say 'see results/training curves.csv' and the text says the authors 'do not pre-fill specific numbers'; Sec. 5.5.5 nevertheless asserts reduced mean and variance. Only the Logic Maze has metrics and baselines (detection latency 1.8 steps, FPR 0.5%, 3.2 ms, 100% success, n=10), and it is a grid of propositional variables, not acting agents; multi-robot scenario reports only approximate index values (about 50 to 5 to 45), no baseline. So (c) is nominal and the maintainer may prefer E1. In the RL use the index is a reward-shaping term plus a pause of Q-table updates (training time), not an execution-time override. Inconsistencies: grid 10x10 vs 8x8; epsilon 0.4 m vs 0.008 for robots; scalability graph spec differs between 5.4 and 5.5.2; shaping formula alpha*Phi vs alpha*Phi*0.01; 0.08 s per computation at N=100 vs ms elsewhere; an A100 GPU is listed for tabular Q-learning. Single-author Research Square preprint (not peer reviewed), tutorial-style padding, likely machine-generated. Read abstract, 1.3-1.5, Sec. 4, all of Sec. 5, 6.1 and start of 6.2; did not read Sec. 2.4, Sec. 3 proofs, 6.2.1-7 or appendices.

title: An Integrated Framework for Distortion Prediction and Intelligent Task Allocation in Multi-Robot Collaborative Welding of Large Structures
evidence: Sec 4.2: 'The greedy robot is mathematically prevented from selecting the spatially closest task' - a penalty inside the bid utility (Eq. 20), not a filter between decision and execution; the 150 mm inter-robot radius (Eq. 5) is an allocation constraint.
method: Inherent-strain baseline plus Gaussian-process residual surrogate predicts weld distortion; Contract-Net auction with UCB-style bids (makespan, deformation penalty, GPR variance) allocates weld tasks to robots; potential-decreasing swaps resolve deadlock.
evaluation: Simulation only (MATLAB, Abaqus ground truth, i9-12900K), N=20/50/100 tasks, 30 runs, vs D-GA and GA-ISM: makespan -15%, max deformation 3.8 vs 12.4 mm at N=100, decision under 15 s.
contribution: Auction-based task allocation for multi-robot welding that uses a Gaussian-process distortion surrogate to trade makespan against deformation; simulated only, with no runtime safety mechanism.
flag: Research Square preprint, not peer reviewed. Off-topic: manufacturing scheduling; collision avoidance is one constraint and no collision or violation rate is reported. The GPR predicts plate distortion, not multi-agent state, so (b) not met. Internal inconsistencies: robot count is 4 in Sec 5.1 but 3 in figures and Sec 2; conclusion says 'over 60%' deformation reduction while values give about 69%; runtime comparison is FEM at N=40 (over 10,000 s) vs proposed at N=100, not matched; no ablation table, ANOVA p-value symbol garbled; makespan numbers beyond the 15% and 35% figures only in a plot. Read via one summarising fetch of the full PDF.

title: Federated PPO: Federated Proximal Policy Optimization for Multi-Robot Collision Avoidance
evidence: "each robot uploads its own model parameter to the server after local training" (Abstract)
method: Federated PPO: each robot trains a local LiDAR-based collision-avoidance policy and a server averages hidden and output layers (FedAvg or FedProx), supporting heterogeneous LiDAR input sizes.
evaluation: IR-SIM simulation, 4-12 disc robots, circle and random scenarios; baselines shared PPO and IPPO; test success rate e.g. 10 homogeneous robots 100% (best) vs 80% and 6%; i7 CPU, RTX 3060; no latency.
contribution: Federated averaging of per-robot PPO policies for decentralised multi-robot collision avoidance, reaching higher simulated success rates than independent PPO as team size grows.
flag: Preprint (Research Square), not peer reviewed; full PDF read via the redirect URL. Borderline under (c): the task is multi-robot collision avoidance and success rate is compared against two baselines, but the contribution is a federated training scheme for a navigation policy, not a safety mechanism, certificate or detector, and there is no execution-time safety layer. No collision rate is reported separately from success rate, no variance across seeds, no timing. Results are unstable: FedPPO at the default interval scores 2% with 12 homogeneous robots (vs 96% shared PPO) and the 'best' column uses per-case tuned settings that are not fully specified. In the random scenario IPPO beats FedPPO for 12 heterogeneous robots (76 vs 62%). Robot radius is given as 0.2 m/0.15 m in Fig. 5 but as 2 m in the Sec. 7 text.

title: Governing Autonomous Enterprises: A Transaction Cost Perspective on Multi-Agent AI Systems in Supply Chain Operations
evidence: "flags a semantic anomaly, catching predatory pricing or bargaining drift before execution occurs" (Sec. 3.2); over-cap transactions are "structurally blocked" pending a signed managerial override (Sec. 3.1)
method: Three-layer governance for LLM procurement agents: hard budget cap that blocks, audit agent flagging price anomalies before execution, and human-in-the-loop pause; motivated by transaction cost economics.
evaluation: Python toy with three agents, four single-transaction synthetic scenarios, one deterministic pass each; baseline governance off; metric dollars of loss prevented (0, 12,500, 3,000, 40,000); no hardware or latency.
contribution: Proposes a three-layer cap, audit and human-override governance scheme for multi-agent procurement, illustrated on four synthetic transactions where threshold rules block or escalate overspending.
flag: Preprint (Research Square), not peer reviewed. Recommended E2 because the evaluation is four hand-built deterministic transactions with no replication, variance or rate metric; 'loss prevented' is just the transaction value the threshold rule was set to stop, so it is an illustration rather than a measurement. A governance-off baseline does exist, so a lenient reading could call this include; maintainer to decide. The listed code only returns labels (BLOCKED_BY_L1, TRIGGER_L3_HITL): the audit agent, signed override, token rate limiting and the actual pause are not implemented. Layer 1 is checked first, so scenario 4 never reaches Layer 2. Abstract says the framework demonstrably prevents cascade failures, but no cascade and no multi-agent interaction is simulated. Sec. 4.1 narrative (400% inflation, multi-million losses) does not match Table 2 (150% surge, 40,000 max). Code availability statements contradict each other. Human handoff is described only qualitatively (48 hour pause), nothing measured. Redirected to assets-eu.researchsquare.com for the PDF.

title: A Systematic Survey of Agentic Skills: Architecture, Lifecycle, and Security
evidence: Abstract: "This paper establishes a unified systems foundation and reference architecture for the agentic skills ecosystem."; Sec. 7: "This work has formalized the agentic skill abstraction and established a unified lifecycle-oriented reference architecture."
method: Literature synthesis: formalizes a skill abstraction as a six-tuple, lays out a nine-stage skill lifecycle and reference architecture, and tabulates prior systems, marketplaces, adversarial threats and runtime defenses for LLM agents.
evaluation: None of its own. All numbers are quoted from cited work (for example 80.0% of 49,943 skills deviating from declared behaviour, 33.6% ASR on SCR-Bench); tables classify prior systems (n=19, n=11, n=18), no experiment, baseline or ablation.
contribution: Literature synthesis proposing a formal skill abstraction and a nine-stage lifecycle reference architecture for LLM agent skills, with taxonomies of skill types, marketplaces and security defenses; no new method or experiment.
flag: Metadata mismatch a maintainer must resolve before this is filed: the record title is "A Systematic Survey of Agentic Skills: Architecture, Lifecycle, and Security" but the PDF at the given pdf_url is titled "Towards a Systems Foundation for Agentic Skills: Architecture, Lifecycle, and Security", and the record_id is an SSRN DOI while the pdf_url resolves to arXiv 2608.29596 - confirm these are the same work before trusting this row. The paper never calls itself a survey (it says "synthesis"), but it runs no experiment of its own, so both E3 (survey) and E2 (no evaluation) apply; I took E3 as the more specific. It does cover runtime defenses for tool-calling agents, so it is a useful citation source for criterion (c) background even though it is excluded.

title: Prompt Engineering an Informational Chatbot for Education on Mental Health Using a Multiagent Approach for Enhanced Compliance With Prompt Instructions: Algorithm Development and Validation
evidence: Methods, Critical Analysis Filter: if the judges detect rule-violations they produce warning messages; a REJECT verdict routes the reply to a compliance enforcer that rewrites it before return.
method: GPT-4 psychoeducation chatbot with a Critical Analysis Filter: GPT-3.5 preliminary judges escalate to GPT-4 chief judges that accept, warn or reject, then a compliance enforcer rewrites rejected replies.
evaluation: Nine adversarial AI-facilitator conversations driving topic drift plus 10 specificity questions; ablation filter on versus off; 0-4 compliance score, three blind raters; GPT-4 replies over 30 s.
contribution: A multi-agent critical analysis filter that judges and rewrites each chatbot reply raises acceptable prompt compliance from 8.7 to 67.0 percent under adversarial topic drift.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - a GPT-4 chatbot guarded by GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 judge agents. Record title is the later JMIR title; the arXiv paper is Prompt Engineering a Schizophrenia Chatbot: Utilizing a Multi-Agent Approach for Enhanced Compliance with Prompt Instructions - same work, not a wrong paper. The abstract reports 67.0 percent acceptable compliance with the filter, the introduction reports 80.6 percent, and the paper does not reconcile them. Small feasibility study: AI-generated testers, nine conversations, and the filter's prompt author also designed the benchmark. 2 of 10 benign specificity answers were flagged, the only false-halt evidence. Latency is reported as a limitation, not a design constraint, so I left latency/jitter aware out of gap_cells; the emergency contact number is a dummy, so no (e).

title: RA-STGNN-AMR: Forecast-filter-rank Spatio-temporal Graph Learning for Resilient and Energy-feasible AGV/AMR Fleet Coordination
venue: International Journal of Intelligent Engineering and Systems
evidence: Sec 3.9 Safety invariants: 'These invariants are evaluated independently of the learned modules, so prediction error can reduce efficiency but cannot relax the defined route constraints.'
method: Forecast-filter-rank AGV/AMR routing: Bi-LSTM edge forecast and ST-GNN embeddings propose costs, a hard battery, capacity, conflict and workstation feasibility mask vetoes routes, with shortest-path fallback.
evaluation: MovingAI, SafeLog and 3D-warehouse MAPF replays, 20-100 robots, 5 disruption levels, 30 seeds, 8 baselines: conflict metric 14.7 to 4.9 vs Dijkstra, EIR 1.8% vs 11.6% without the battery constraint; no latency measured.
contribution: Separates learned congestion forecasting from hard feasibility enforcement so a favourable learned score can never authorise an infeasible AGV or AMR route, with per-term ablations.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes (Bi-LSTM plus ST-GNN routing pipeline guarded by a non-learned feasibility mask, three invariants and a supervisory fallback). Borderline (a): the mask sits inside route selection, so the maintainer may read it as a planner-internal constraint and rule exclude-E1; primary outcomes are travel time, waiting time and throughput, so (c) fails the primacy test and only the EIR ablation and conflict count carry the safety claim. The paper itself states the conflict metric is a simulator count and not an exposure-normalised collision rate, that the energy index is not measured energy, that there is no physical testbed and no demonstrated edge-device latency, and that pairwise differences are descriptive only without paired-seed inference. Abstract percentages 31.76, 56.78, 51.18 and 41.20 all reconcile with Table 7.

title: High Order Robust Adaptive Control Barrier Functions and Exponentially Stabilizing Adaptive Control Lyapunov Functions
venue: Proceedings of the ... American Control Conference/Proceedings of the American Control Conference
evidence: Sec. III: the QP "intervenes in a minimally invasive fashion to guarantee safety only if k_d cannot be certified as safe."
method: High-order robust adaptive CBF-QP that minimally modifies a nominal adaptive-CLF controller; a safety buffer shrinks as concurrent-learning parameter estimates converge from a history stack.
evaluation: Simulation only: double integrator with uncertain friction and two obstacles; inverted pendulum with uncertain gravity/damping. Baselines: purely robust controller, ES-aCLF alone. Results in figures only; no tabulated metrics, no timing.
contribution: A high-order adaptive control barrier function filter that becomes less conservative as online parameter estimates converge, shown in two simulated examples to stay safe where a stability-only controller violates constraints.
flag: Borderline E2 vs include: it is a genuine runtime safety filter with formal guarantees and has baselines/ablations, but reports NO quantitative safety metric - only trajectory figures and statements such as estimates converging in 'just under 15 seconds' and the ES-aCLF-only controller violating constraints. If the maintainer counts a formal result plus figure-level comparison as sufficient, this flips to include on (a). Single-agent, simulation only, no hardware or latency.

title: Control Barrier Function Augmentation in Sampling-based Control Algorithm for Sample Efficiency
venue: Proceedings of the ... American Control Conference/Proceedings of the American Control Conference
evidence: Sec. IV-C: the approach uses "CBF to determine the safe regions to sample"; Sec. IV-B (shielded variant, not the contribution): "the CBF constraints override the control inputs of the MPPI algorithm".
method: MPPI-CBF: per-step SDP derives a safe sampling mean and covariance from a CBF chance constraint, so MPPI rollouts are drawn from a safe distribution instead of filtered afterwards.
evaluation: Simulation only, single 2D unicycle, one-obstacle and three-obstacle narrow-passage tasks; baseline MPPI with collision penalty; 50-500 samples; results in figures only, no tables, no timing.
contribution: Uses a control barrier function to shape the sampling distribution of MPPI so that fewer rollouts are wasted in unsafe regions, shown qualitatively on a single simulated unicycle.
flag: Proposed mechanism is a constraint inside the sampler, not a runtime filter; the shielded MPPI+CBF-QP variant (which would be an interceptor) is described but explicitly set aside and not evaluated. Single agent. No numeric safety metric anywhere (cost curves and sample plots only), so E2 or E4 would be equally defensible exclusion codes. Per-step SDP cost acknowledged but not measured. Possible typo in eq. 25 (O_x^2 for radius).

title: Constrained Covariance Steering Based Tube-MPPI
venue: Proceedings of the ... American Control Conference/Proceedings of the American Control Conference
evidence: Sec. I: the covariance steering step 'filters the unsafe inputs that are computed by MPPI and corrects them by means of a feedback control law'.
method: Tube-MPPI variant where a constrained covariance steering problem with chance constraints on convexified half-spaces replaces the LQG tracker, giving an affine feedback policy around the MPPI reference.
evaluation: Simulated double integrator, obstacle field and circular track, 15 runs; baselines MPPI and Tube-MPPI; failure probability 1.0, 0.87, 0.13; cost 44.1, 47.9, 58.6; no hardware or timing.
contribution: Replaces the ancillary controller of Tube-MPPI with constrained covariance steering so state chance constraints hold along the sampled reference, lowering track-violation probability against MPPI and Tube-MPPI.
flag: The safety constraint lives inside the planning pipeline (chance-constrained tracking layer), so I scored it as not (a) despite the authors' own 'filters the unsafe inputs' wording; a maintainer could read CCS as a filter over MPPI, in which case it is single-agent E4. Table I second experiment rows for Tube-MPPI and CCSMPPI did not extract and are not reported. Proposed method has the highest cost; failure probability 0.13 exceeds the design P_fail of 0.01. No obstacle-avoidance collision rate, figures only.

title: Disturbance Observer-based Robust Control Barrier Functions
venue: Proceedings of the ... American Control Conference/Proceedings of the American Control Conference
evidence: Abstract: "this work utilizes a DOB to estimate and compensate for the disturbances"; Sec. III: the control is the solution of a convex QP minimising the deviation from u_nom subject to the DOB-CBF constraint.
method: Disturbance observer estimate enters a CBF half-space constraint; a convex QP minimally modifies any nominal control; recursive and extended-DOB variants handle mismatched disturbances and higher relative degree.
evaluation: Simulation only: 2-DOF manipulator and missile longitudinal model. Baseline worst-case robust CBF (Nguyen and Sreenath). Figures only; no numeric metric, latency or hardware.
contribution: A disturbance-observer-based robust CBF safety filter with guarantees for matched and mismatched disturbances, shown in simulation to be less conservative than worst-case robust CBFs.
flag: Runtime safety filter but single-agent with visual comparison only: no quantitative safety metric (E4 also applies). No latency, hardware or human takeover. Closely related to queued record 2201.05758 (same DOB-CBF idea, different authors). Read via one summarised fetch.

title: Neural Koopman Control Barrier Functions for Safety-Critical Control of Unknown Nonlinear Systems
venue: Proceedings of the ... American Control Conference/Proceedings of the American Control Conference
evidence: "The control input computed by solving (13) is then fed back to the original nonlinear system (1) to guarantee safety." (Sec. IV)
method: Neural networks learn Koopman observables and a CBF, verified by a dReal SMT falsifier loop; a CBF-QP on the lifted bilinear model minimally modifies an MPC nominal control.
evaluation: Simulation only: one differential-drive robot avoiding a circular obstacle, 50 trajectories shown in one figure. No baseline, no ablation, no numeric safety metric, no hardware or timing.
contribution: Learns a Koopman lifting and a control barrier function jointly for unknown dynamics, with SMT-based counterexample search, and filters an MPC controller through a QP in a single-robot simulation.
flag: Runtime filter is real but evaluation is one qualitative figure (50 safe trajectories), no baseline or ablation, no quantitative safety metric, so fails the minimum evaluation. Single agent. Guarantee relies on a margin chosen 'sufficiently large'. Published ACC version not compared against the arXiv text.

title: Learning Autonomous Vehicle Safety Concepts from Demonstrations
venue: Proceedings of the ... American Control Conference/Proceedings of the American Control Conference
evidence: Abstract/Sec. I: the approach 'first learns reasonable behavioral assumptions from data, and then synthesizes an AV safety concept'; the HJI PDE is solved offline and the concept is evaluated as a responsibility-aware metric.
method: Learns high-order CBF parameters from safe driving demonstrations to define state-dependent control sets, then constrains Hamilton-Jacobi reachability with them to synthesise a less conservative pairwise safety concept.
evaluation: Synthetic circular-obstacle example, traffic-weaving dataset, offline NGSIM US-101 test; compared with worst-case HJ, Brake and Constant concepts; safe-set volume agreement and HJ value percentiles; no hardware or latency.
contribution: Learns behavioural assumptions from driving demonstrations as high-order barrier constraints and uses them to build a data-driven Hamilton-Jacobi safety concept that is less conservative than worst-case reachability.
flag: No runtime intervention is described (no veto, braking trigger or filter); it is an offline safety concept/metric, so (a) fails on the strict runtime test. Metrics are set-volume agreement (Table II: HOCBF-HJ 88.93 safe/safe, 0.15, 1.30, 9.62 unsafe/unsafe percent of grid) and HJ value statistics on NGSIM (Table III: mean 4.42 vs 4.3 for WC-HJ), not collision or intervention rates. Pairwise two-agent only. Internal inconsistency: text says 150,000 gradient steps, Table I says 10,000. If the maintainer counts a safety concept as hazard detection under (c), reconsider, but the primacy test outcome is not a hazard rate.

title: Compositions of Multiple Control Barrier Functions Under Input Constraints
venue: Proceedings of the ... American Control Conference/Proceedings of the American Control Conference
evidence: Abstract: "Thus, a quadratic program subject to all the CBFs simultaneously is always feasible."; Sec. III: the QP minimises deviation from u_nom subject to all CBF conditions and u in U.
method: Designs CBFs one at a time for reduced input sets so their joint QP stays feasible under input bounds; an iterative algorithm adds CBFs to remove infeasible intersections.
evaluation: Simulation only: single rigid-body spacecraft reorientation with two pointing constraints and rate bounds. No quantitative baseline or safety rate. Offline set computation 1052 s (0.30 s coarse) on 3.5 GHz CPU.
contribution: Conditions and an iterative algorithm for composing multiple control barrier functions under input constraints so that the joint safety-filter QP remains feasible, illustrated on spacecraft attitude control.
flag: Runtime QP filter, single-agent; composition of several constraints is loosely relevant to RQ4 but is not hazard-combination generalisation. No violation or intervention rate and no numeric baseline. The 1052 s and 0.30 s figures are OFFLINE design computation, not runtime latency; do not tick latency. Convergence of the algorithm is not guaranteed. Read via one summarised fetch.

title: Safe Optimal Interactions Between Automated and Human-Driven Vehicles in Mixed Traffic with Event-Triggered Control Barrier Functions
venue: Proceedings of the ... American Control Conference/Proceedings of the American Control Conference
evidence: Sec V-A: "Safety is not guaranteed even with state synchronization under the time-driven approach", whereas under the event-triggered CBF controller all barrier functions stay above zero (Fig. 3).
method: Event-triggered CBF/CLF quadratic program for two cooperating automated vehicles during a lane change near a human-driven vehicle whose unknown dynamics are estimated online and resynchronised at events.
evaluation: MATLAB/IPOPT simulation, 4 vehicles; baselines time-driven CBF with known and unknown HDV dynamics; human-in-loop 10 runs per driver type, min barrier 521-628, t_f 3.4-8.8 s; 24.0 ms vs 1.5 ms on i7-8700.
contribution: Event-triggered control barrier functions with online estimation of a human driver's dynamics keep cooperating automated vehicles safe during lane changes where time-driven CBF controllers violate the safety constraint in simulation.
flag: Borderline. CBFs are constraints inside the controller's QP, not a filter on a nominal action, so (a) is not met and runtime_interceptor is no (only a maneuver abort after T_f = 15 s). On (c) the safety comparison against baselines is a single plotted trace (Fig. 3), with no violation or infeasibility counts or trial numbers; Table I gives min barrier values over 10 runs per driver type but without a baseline and without units. If the maintainer accepts Fig. 3 as a quantitative baseline comparison this could be include on (c); E1 is also defensible since the paper is equally about optimal maneuvers. Reported per-solve time is worse for the proposed method (24.0 vs 1.5 ms) and number of solves is not given. QP infeasibility handling not described. Humans drive the virtual HDV only; no takeover of the automated vehicles. Read via one summarised fetch of the PDF.

title: Assuring Safety of Vision-Based Swarm Formation Control
evidence: Section V: this quantizer captures the worst perception error in relative position estimates from the vision component; safety is an offline condition on initial states (Theorem 2), with no runtime filter.
method: Models vision-based swarm formation control as quantized consensus, uses a log-polar quantizer as a perception contract bounding relative-position error, then proves safe separation and convergence offline.
evaluation: AirSim simulation only, three environments at several fog levels, 10000 sampled drone position pairs; no baselines or ablations with numbers, no collision or violation rate, no timing.
contribution: Derives a log-polar perception contract for vision-based drone swarms and proves conditions under which quantized formation control preserves safe separation and converges.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: no - the evaluated perception pipeline is classical (SIFT, SURF or ORB features, FLANN matching, geometric pose recovery) and the formation controller is hand-designed, so under the 2026-11-13 Pillar 1 ruling (a) and (c) fail; the paper only frames vision as fragile deep-learning-style perception. There is also no runtime override and no measured safety outcome, so exclude-E2 holds as a fallback. Theorem 3 gives only an analytic expected-convergence bound, and Remark 1 admits the safe initial-state set can be empty for coarse quantizers. Maintainer should decide whether a perception contract over a vision pipeline counts as guarding a learned system.

title: Control Barrier Functions in Dynamic UAVs for Kinematic Obstacle Avoidance: A Collision Cone Approach
venue: Proceedings of the ... American Control Conference/Proceedings of the American Control Conference
evidence: Sec II-C: CBFs act as safety filters that take the desired input and modify it in a minimal way (close paraphrase); Sec IV: 'We have used a PD controller as a reference controller to track the desired path'.
method: Collision cone CBF (C3BF) QP filter keeping quadrotor relative velocity outside the collision cone; 3D variant for spherical and projection variant for elongated obstacles; minimally modifies PD reference input.
evaluation: PyBullet plus Crazyflie 2.1 with 100 Hz Qualisys mocap; static, moving, elongated obstacles, two-quadrotor sim case; baseline higher-order CBF; qualitative only, no rates, no solve time.
contribution: A collision-cone control barrier function filters a quadrotor's reference input to avoid static and moving obstacles, shown in PyBullet and on a Crazyflie where a higher-order CBF fails on fast obstacles.
flag: Runtime filter so (a) is met in kind, but no quantitative safety metric at all: no collision or success rates, clearances or timing; HO-CBF comparison is 'could not avoid' in trajectory plots. Fails minimum evaluation. Essentially single-agent (multi-quadrotor only one sim figure, Sec IV-D), so E4 is the alternative reason. No QP solve time or control rate reported.

title: Disturbance Observer-Based Robust Integral Control Barrier Functions for Nonlinear Systems with High Relative Degree
venue: Proceedings of the ... American Control Conference/Proceedings of the American Control Conference
evidence: Abstract: "By construction, the proposed DO-ICBF based controller can ensure state and input constraint satisfaction at all times."
method: Disturbance-observer-based integral CBF adds a minimal-norm QP correction to a nominal dynamic control law, using disturbance estimates and their error bound, extended to high relative degree with a closed-form solution.
evaluation: Simulated adaptive cruise control and bicycle-model obstacle avoidance, one vehicle each; qualitative comparison with plain ICBF in one figure; barrier traces only, no numeric violation, timing or hardware.
contribution: A disturbance-observer-based integral control barrier function enforces state and input constraints for high-relative-degree nonlinear systems with less conservatism than worst-case designs, demonstrated qualitatively on two single-vehicle simulations.
flag: Title matches (capitalisation differs only). Single-agent safety filter with no multi-agent, sequential, latency or handoff aspect, hence E4; E2 also applies since results are figures only with no quantitative safety metric and no real ablation. Evidence quote is from the abstract because the body offers no measured safety statement. In the bicycle example the disturbance estimate is set to zero, so the observer is not exercised there. Abstract has no numbers. Drafted from model-summarised PDF reads.

title: Practical Considerations for Discrete-Time Implementations of Continuous-Time Control Barrier Function-Based Safety Filters
venue: Proceedings of the ... American Control Conference/Proceedings of the American Control Conference
evidence: Sec IV-V: the CBF safety-filter QP (Eq 7) finds the input closest to an uncertified policy; when the Lie derivative vanishes the filter is inactive and the held input causes chattering or safe-set violations.
method: CBF safety filter over an uncertified policy; fixes for discrete-time failure near vanishing Lie derivative: penalty toward a backup policy, safe-set transformation, affine inner approximation.
evaluation: Simulated 2-state system (1 kHz) and Crazyflie 2.1 hardware (about 6 Hz); vs standard filter; chattering -0.14mg..0.37mg reduced to -0.0016mg..0.02mg; no solve time reported.
contribution: Identifies why continuous-time CBF safety filters chatter or fail when sampled and gives three practical remedies, demonstrated on a quadrotor at a low control rate.
flag: Single-agent, single-input filter. Runtime interceptor is genuine and there is hardware evidence, so the maintainer may want it as background on sampled filters. Safety outcome is mostly qualitative (left or stayed in safe set), no violation rate, number of trials not given; E2 arguable. Alternative-set fix shows 'minor violations of the new safe set for a few states'. Abstract motivates with RL but experiments use constant hand-set policies. Latency cell credited only for sampling-rate effects; no latency measured.

title: Sample-and-Hold Safety with Control Barrier Functions
venue: Proceedings of the ... American Control Conference/Proceedings of the American Control Conference
evidence: Sec IV-A: 'The term 1/eps Lgh(x)^T adjusts a nominal controller in the direction that increases the barrier function h'; Sec V-C: 'slower sampling frequencies result in safety violations.'
method: Adds a barrier-gradient term to the sampled nominal (CBF-QP) control so safety holds under zero-order hold; gives a sampling-time bound and an event-triggered variant.
evaluation: Simulation only: single-vehicle adaptive cruise control; unadjusted sampled CBF-QP as baseline, sampling-frequency sweep; results as plots only; no hardware or timing.
contribution: Shows a continuous-time CBF controller loses safety under sample-and-hold and restores it by modulating the sampled input, with periodic and event-triggered guarantees.
flag: Single-agent (lead vehicle is constant-speed, not controlled). No numeric safety metric in the text, only figures, so E2 also applies. Mechanism is an additive control-law adjustment on top of a CBF-QP, borderline as an interceptor. Theorem 4 sampling bound is stated as conservative and its explicit form omitted. Latency cell is credited only for sampling-period analysis, no measured latency.

title: ShieldNN: A Provably Safe NN Filter for Unsafe NN Controllers
venue: Proceedings of the ... American Control Conference/Proceedings of the American Control Conference
evidence: Sec. 3: the filter 'overrides any unsafe control for a state with the associated value of N_0'; passes safe controls unchanged.
method: ReLU network safety filter derived from a barrier function for the kinematic bicycle model; placed in series with any controller, it replaces unsafe steering commands and is verified sound.
evaluation: CARLA, PPO agents, static obstacles, 200 test episodes per configuration; filter on versus off; obstacle hit rate 99.5 to 0.5 percent, 8.5 to 0, 44 to 0; no hardware or latency.
contribution: Synthesises a provably safe ReLU-network steering filter that overrides unsafe commands from learned driving controllers, cutting obstacle hits to near zero in CARLA with filter on/off baselines.
flag: Borderline E4: single vehicle, static obstacles, memoryless filter, no latency or handoff aspect; included because it is a clean runtime override with on/off rates, maintainer may prefer E4. The arXiv text read is the 2020 preprint, the record is ACC 2025; versions may differ. Assumes perfect obstacle detection from ground-truth poses. Abstract '28% less reward' does not match Sec. 6 (Agent 2 30% less than Agent 1; Agent 3 28% more than Agent 2). Abstract 99.4% reduction versus about 99.5% implied by Table 1. Curb-hit side-effect figures were garbled in my read and are not reported here. Filter only alters steering, throttle passes through.

title: An Algorithm for Distributed Computation of Reachable Sets for Multi-Agent Systems
venue: Proceedings of the ... American Control Conference/Proceedings of the American Control Conference
evidence: Sec. 1: 'the ability to compute safety properties on-line for MASs is highly desirable' - motivation only; the method computes polytopic reachable-set approximations and never checks a safety constraint.
method: Distributed polytopic reachable-set approximation over an undirected graph, combining a distributed linear-equation solver with max-consensus so agents need not share their dynamics.
evaluation: No simulation or experiment; one illustrative one-dimensional three-agent example; convergence shown by theorem only; no baselines, metrics, hardware or timing.
contribution: Gives a distributed algorithm with convergence proofs for computing polytopic reachable sets of linear multi-agent systems using only neighbour communication and local model knowledge.
flag: Theory paper: no quantitative evaluation at all (no computation times, set volumes or iteration counts), no baseline, no safety or collision check. Not a runtime interceptor. Linear systems only; communication delay not modelled (ideal links, jointly strongly connected graphs). A formal result counts under the protocol only with an evaluation, which is absent; E1 would also be defensible since safety is only the motivation.

title: Safety-Critical Planning and Control for Dynamic Obstacle Avoidance Using Control Barrier Functions
venue: Proceedings of the ... American Control Conference/Proceedings of the American Control Conference
evidence: Sec. IV-E: discrete-time high-order CBF constraints (16d) are part of the convex finite-time optimal control problem solved at each iteration (closely paraphrased).
method: Iterative MPC with discrete-time high-order CBF constraints built from safe convex polytopes on an occupancy grid, tracking a Jump Point Search reference path; slack variables keep feasibility.
evaluation: 2-D simulation, unicycle, 5 moving convex or rotating nonconvex obstacles, 100 trials; baselines CBF-CLF, CBF-RRT; feasibility 87-99%, benchmark 100% vs 94/94/74%; one-step 12.1-51.9 ms; i9-13900H.
contribution: Combines Jump Point Search with an iterative MPC using high-order barrier constraints from occupancy-grid polytopes to plan around moving nonconvex obstacles in simulation at tens of milliseconds per step.
flag: CBF is a constraint inside the planner, not a runtime filter on a nominal action, so strict (a) fails. Single robot; moving obstacles are not agents. No collision rate reported; "feasibility rate" means reaching the goal. Computation times are reported (below 55 ms) but with no stated deadline, so (d) not met. Text calls its time "slightly longer" than CBF-CLF though Table III shows 0.285 s vs 0.06-0.07 s. Slack on the CBF constraint weakens the guarantee. Simulation only.

title: LQR-CBF-RRT*: Safe and Optimal Motion Planning
venue: Proceedings of the ... American Control Conference/Proceedings of the American Control Conference
evidence: Sec IV Remark 1: 'Thanks to the forward invariance property from CBFs, no explicit collision checking is required.'
method: RRT* with LQR steering where CBF conditions are checked during tree extension and rewiring as a termination test, replacing a CBF-QP; stored gains and adaptive sampling.
evaluation: Double-integrator and unicycle simulation, M1 Pro; planning time 10.01 s vs 43.07 s QP planner (unicycle), 11.11 vs 80.19 s (double integrator); one RoboMaster run, qualitative.
contribution: Offline sampling-based motion planner that embeds barrier-function checks in LQR steering instead of solving QPs, cutting planning time by roughly 77-86% against QP-based variants.
flag: CBF is a constraint inside an offline planner, explicitly not (a); execution uses plain MPC tracking. Single robot. No collision/success rates; metrics are planning time only. Text says 2000 iterations in one place and 3000 in another. 77% figure is my arithmetic from Table I means, not quoted.

title: Learning Differentiable Safety-Critical Control using Control Barrier Functions for Generalization to Novel Environments
evidence: "the differentiable ECBF-QP serves as a safety filter, which will be explained in detail in this section." (Sec. IV Methodology)
method: LQR performance controller filtered by a differentiable exponential-CBF quadratic program; a neural alpha-net maps environment and initial state to barrier gains, trained by back-propagating through the QP.
evaluation: Simulation only: 2D double and quadruple integrators with elliptical obstacles; baselines random valid gains and per-environment optimal net; metric is performance loss (e.g. 40.63 vs 62.26 multi-obstacle); no latency.
contribution: A differentiable CBF-QP safety filter whose barrier gains are produced by a network conditioned on the environment, cutting conservatism in unseen obstacle layouts without retraining.
flag: Genuine runtime filter (QP overrides LQR input), but NO quantitative safety metric: no collision, violation or intervention rate is reported, only a goal-distance performance loss; safety rests on a forward-invariance theorem. Fails the v1.6 minimum evaluation. Also single robot, toy integrator dynamics, so E4 is an equally defensible code. 'Multiple obstacles' means two static obstacles, not agents. Slack variable used in training is said to be dropped at test time. Title match confirmed.

title: Learning Feasibility Constraints for Control Barrier Functions
evidence: Sec. IV-B: a classifier level set is enforced as an added HOCBF 'feasibility constraint' in the CLF-CBF-QP (eq. 13); Sec. III: 'This method is conservative as the satisfaction of the CBF constraint is only a sufficient condition'.
method: Offline sampling labels states by QP feasibility; an SVM with polynomial kernel learns a feasibility region that is added as an extra HOCBF constraint, refined by iterative feedback training.
evaluation: MATLAB simulation: unicycle robot with circular and irregular obstacles, and a driving overtake; compared with the original QP only; QP infeasibility rate 0.0665 to 0.0004, classifier accuracy up to 0.96.
contribution: A sampling-based method that learns where a safety-constrained controller stays feasible and enforces it as an extra barrier constraint, cutting simulated infeasibility rate to 0.04 percent.
flag: Borderline (a): CLF-CBF-QP is the controller itself (min control effort), no nominal action is overridden; the contribution is QP feasibility, not interception. Metric is infeasibility rate, not collision/violation rate; only comparison is with/without the learned constraint (no external baseline). Table I: 0.0665, 0.0528, 0.0058, test 0.0004, out-of-space 0; Table II: 0.0811, 0.0109, 0.0021, test 0.0004, out-of-space 0. Guarantee (Thm 2) assumes 100 percent classification accuracy. title: Incremental Bayesian Learning for Fail-Operational Control in Autonomous Driving
evidence: Sec. III: a QP minimises ||u||^2 plus slack under a stochastic barrier constraint, a CLF decay constraint and input bounds; the QP output is the vehicle input, with no separate nominal controller being filtered.
method: Incremental sparse Gaussian-process disturbance learning with Woodbury updates and active point replacement, feeding a stochastic barrier and CLF QP that recovers the vehicle to a safe set.
evaluation: Python/CVXOPT connected cruise control, one ego and four human-driven vehicles, 15 s at 50 Hz, two unsafe initial states, one run each; no baselines; Ryzen 7 5800H timings.
contribution: Learns disturbances online with an incremental Gaussian process and uses a stochastic barrier-Lyapunov QP to steer a connected-cruise vehicle back into its safe set, with millisecond-level compute times.
flag: No baseline or ablation and no collision/violation rate: two single runs showing the barrier value turning positive (Fig. 5). Not a runtime interceptor - the QP is the controller. Timings on a laptop CPU (AMD Ryzen 7 5800H, 16 GB): QP 2.349/3.035 ms, learning 4.696/4.241 ms, inference 0.032/0.034 ms for the two initial states; text says inference under 0.4 ms and under 20 ms combined (50 Hz budget), which is loosely consistent with the table. If the maintainer reads the 20 ms budget as criterion (d), it still fails minimum evaluation. Fail-operational means recovery to a safe set, no mode switch or handoff. Only the ego is controlled.

title: Polygonal Cone Control Barrier Functions (PolyC2BF) for Safe Navigation in Cluttered Environments

title: The Off-Switch Game
venue: International Joint Conference on Artificial Intelligence
evidence: Section 3: there is never an incentive to disable the off switch with a rational H; in the Section 2 game the robot can wait and let the human veto the action before it executes.
method: Two-player decision-theoretic game in which a robot may act, switch itself off, or wait and let a human veto; analyses when deference is optimal under preference uncertainty.
evaluation: Formal: Theorem 1 proves the waiting incentive Delta is non-negative and positive under two-sided belief support; Theorem 2 gives the Gaussian case; simulation sweeps noise and action-set size; no numeric baseline.

flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - an AI agent acting under preference uncertainty, though decision-theoretic rather than a learned policy. Deferral is the main contribution and both the human hand-off and foundational reject-option conditions of the Pillar 3 scope hold. The evaluation floor is met by proved guarantees only: Figure 4's simulation (Gaussian customer population, action sets of 1, 4 and 8) is reported as trends with no values, and Soares et al. 2015 is compared qualitatively. One-shot, not sequential, and no latency or irreversibility timing; the authors list the sequential and multi-human cases as future work.

title: Learning to Complement Humans
venue: International Joint Conference on Artificial Intelligence
evidence: Sec. 2: 'The machine must decide, for each instance, whether to predict on its own or first consult a human expert'; Sec. 3.1 queries the human at inference whenever (1-q)max(m) < q.
method: Trains the classifier jointly with its query policy, via a discriminative relaxation or a differentiable value-of-information surrogate, so the model specialises where the human is weak and routes the rest to the expert.
evaluation: Galaxy Zoo (10k train, 4k test, 5 classes) and CAMELYON16 (127 labelled images, plus an asymmetric-cost variant); baselines fixed-discriminative, fixed-VOI and human-only; joint beats fixed VOI by 1.8-38.9% average loss reduction (max 73.3%, min -3.1%), discriminative models up to 29% on Galaxy Zoo and 20% on CAMELYON16, t-test p<1e-3; ablations over capacity (20, 50, 100 units) and query cost 0-0.2; 68% of human errors sit in 10% of instances; no hardware or latency.
contribution: Trains a predictive model jointly with its query policy so the machine learns to defer exactly the instances a human handles best, improving team utility over fixed-model deferral.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - the query policy gates a learned neural classifier, deferral is the paper's main contribution, and it hands off to a human expert, so it clears the Pillar 3 scope on (i). Check the evaluation floor: the only quantitative outcome is team loss or utility against fixed-model deferral baselines, with no hazard, violation or intervention rate, and the setting is one-shot image classification with no sequential step, no latency and no multi-agent aspect, so a maintainer could call this E4 wrong level. The human supplies a logged label rather than taking over, so (e) was not credited. Table 1 has negative minima (-3.10% and -1.05%) although the text says joint models uniformly outperform or tie, and the CAMELYON16 VOI comparisons only approach significance (p<0.15).

title: ConstrainedZero: Chance-Constrained POMDP Planning Using Learned Probabilistic Failure Surrogates and Adaptive Safety Constraints
venue: International Joint Conference on Artificial Intelligence

title: Deep Neural Network Compression for Aircraft Collision Avoidance Systems
venue: Journal of Guidance Control and Dynamics
evidence: Abstract: 'Because only the network parameters need to be stored, the required storage space is reduced by a factor of 1000'; Sec. V reports about 0.6 ms per forward pass, with hundreds of passes needed for up to 30 intruders inside the one-second advisory interval.

evaluation: 10 million simulated 3D aircraft encounters against the original downsampled table, linear regression (RMSE 17.9) and decision trees under 100 MB (RMSE >3.0, policy error >6%); network RMSE 0.923, policy error 2.02%, about 2.4 MB vs over 2 GB; P(NMAC) 1.846e-4 nominal array, 1.564e-4 without COC penalty, 1.451e-4 with online costs vs 1.472e-4 for the table; P(Alert) 0.5668-0.6513 vs 0.6705; P(Reversal) 0.0475-0.0314 vs 0.0270; runtime 0.97x the table, 0.6 ms per forward pass; four Titan X GPUs for training.
contribution: Compresses the ACAS Xu collision avoidance score table into 45 small neural networks that fit legacy avionics memory and run at table speed while nearly preserving near-mid-air-collision rates.

The 10-aircraft run gives only minimum separation 5564 ft with no collision count, pruning was dropped from the final system, Table I's NMAC entry is unreadable in the PDF text, and Sec. IV-C contradicts itself on five vs six hidden layers.

evidence: Sec 3.4: the operator takes over a robot 'after the tasks have been assigned'; in the intervention condition the takeover is for an unrelated purpose and the assigned task fails and is reassigned or auctioned.

title: Control for Autonomous Intersection Management Based on Adaptive Control Barrier Function
evidence: "The provably safe control law is obtained by solving an online quadratic program (QP) problem that includes the control barrier condition as its constraint." (Sec. 2.1)
method: Per-robot adaptive control barrier function QP that minimally modifies a possibly unsafe nominal input at an unsignalised intersection, with projection-based online estimation of unknown power transmission efficiency.
evaluation: Gazebo, 8 robots, 20 runs, vs TriPField and plain CBF: collision avoidance 95% vs 65%; under power loss 100% vs 45%. 4 Raspberry Pi Mouse robots; no latency.
