flag: Meets (a) as a CBF safety filter on a nominal law and (c) since collision avoidance is the headline claim and outcome. Doubts: the 95/65 and 100/45 percentages appear only in abstract and Conclusions; the body gives box plots over 20 repeated simulations (Fig. 9) and no definition of 'success rate', and 95% means the proposed filter itself collided in about 1 of 20 runs despite a 'provably safe' claim - unexplained. Power loss tested at a single value theta=0.5. Physical experiment is 4 robots, single lane, number of trials not stated, with an overhead RealSense camera and one laptop (i7-1195G7) computing all control signals, so the hardware run is effectively centralised, not on-board; no control period, QP solve time or communication delay reported. Each robot only considers its nearest detected neighbour. No human element; mixed traffic left to future work. Read via constructed URL https://www.mdpi.com/2076-3417/15/5/2315 (doi.org not fetchable); figures not readable. Quote relayed by the fetch tool; check verbatim.

title: Bio-Inspired Traffic Pattern Generation for Multi-AMR Systems
evidence: "offline costmap generation through simulation-based optimization with subsequent integration into path planning systems" (Sec. 1)
method: Ant-colony-style offline optimisation in an event-based simulator that learns directional edge costs (traffic patterns) from simulated conflicts and delays; robots then plan with weighted A*.

flag: Fails (a): the costmap is generated offline and only biases the global planner; conflict resolution at execution is left to the stock MPPI local planner. Fails the (c) primacy test in my reading: the claim is throughput/congestion, with conflicts as one of several outcomes - but a conflict count against two baselines IS reported, so the maintainer may want to look. Gazebo evidence is weaker than the abstract suggests: recovery actions in Industrial B are 21.7 vs 20.7 unweighted (i.e. not reduced), and abstract figures (up to 10% and up to 4% throughput) match Gazebo, not the event-simulator tables (which show larger gains); the paper does not say which. Industrial layouts are for forklifts but Gazebo uses TurtleBot3 Waffle. No comparison with any MAPF solver despite the abstract's 'existing approaches'. 'A few minutes' generation time is unquantified. URL constructed by me (https://www.mdpi.com/2076-3417/15/5/2849/htm). Read chars 0-100000 of 134415 (through conclusions); Tables 1-2 are images. Quotes relayed by the fetch tool.

Quality concerns: search methodology gives no screening counts although it says they were recorded; illustrative scenarios read like results but are unsourced; inconsistent citation numbering (MARPOL/CII); EU ITS described as an emissions mandate; blocks of ~35 references for one sentence. title: Recent Advances and a Hybrid Framework for Cooperative UAV Formation Control
evidence: "The hybrid controller combines their strengths: it lowers RMSE relative to APF while preserving safe distances." (Sec. 5)
method: Literature review of UAV formation control plus a hybrid follower controller that adds an artificial-potential-field repulsion term to a leader-follower attraction term; partial Lyapunov argument.
evaluation: MATLAB 2D simulation, three UAVs, six scenarios; leader-follower and APF baselines; RMSE, share of steps under a safety distance and per-step latency in Table 4 (not readable); overhead about 0.0003 ms; desktop i7-12700KF.

flag: Borderline between E1 and E3, and possibly (c): maintainer should look. Most of the paper is a review (Sec. 2, Tables 1-3); the original part is a small controller. I scored E1 because the repulsion is an additive soft term inside the controller, not a filter that can veto a nominal command (the phrase 'APF safety layer' in the introduction overstates it), and the primary outcome is formation error with separation as one of several aims. A safety metric (percentage of time steps below d_safe) is defined and compared against two baselines, but the values sit in Table 4, which is an image I could not read, and the body text gives no numbers for RMSE, violations or d_safe. So the abstract claim of APF-level safety with lower error could not be verified by me. Other doubts: Eq. 9 and the Sec. 3.3 prose state opposite activation conditions for the repulsion; the obstacle avoided in scenario 6 has no term in the equations; the Lyapunov analysis covers only the attraction term and uses approximations; several equation cross-references are wrong and a 'Section A' is cited that does not exist. No ablation, no hardware flights, no communication delay model, no human role. Read via MDPI HTML (URL built from the OpenAlex pdf_url), one fetch covering the full body; quotes relayed by the fetch tool.

title: LLM-Based Adaptive Control Code Generation Framework with Digital Twin-Integrated Verification for Heterogeneous Robot Systems
evidence: "Otherwise, the task is reported as infeasible under the selected robot and execution condition" (Section 3.6, Adaptive Parameter Scaling)
method: Digital-twin-grounded pre-execution gate on LLM-generated robot code: runtime spatial grounding, feasibility-aware robot selection, RNEA torque validation and global motion scaling before vendor code is emitted.
evaluation: PyBullet simulation, 6-robot pool, 170 natural-language scenarios, 8 selection tasks vs TOPSIS, LinearWS, Greedy, Random; safe execution 100% vs 50% without scaling; no latency reported.

flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - Gemini 2.5 Pro code generator. Check how runtime the gate is: it fires once per task before execution, not per control step. All evidence is simulation (PyBullet plus analytical RNEA for only 2 of the 6 robots); the 70% adversarial-block figure rests on just 10 adversarial prompts; authors concede there is no comparison against ungated LLM code generation; safe-execution 100% vs 50% is an ablation of their own scaling step, not an external baseline.

title: Flocking Dynamics of Multi-Agent Systems Based on an Extended Cucker–Smale Model with Nonlinear Coupling and Binding Forces
evidence: The binding term, when agents are closer than 2R, "becomes strongly repulsive, forming the core collision avoidance mechanism." (Sec. 3.1)
method: Extended Cucker-Smale flocking law with nonlinear velocity coupling, a damping force and a state-dependent spring-like binding force; energy-based proof of flocking and of collision-free global existence.
evaluation: MATLAB numerical simulation, 20-100 agents, 50 Monte Carlo trials; baseline classical Cucker-Smale; min distance 1.050 m vs 1.097 m (threshold 1.0 m), max distance 6.48 vs 7.23 m; no hardware or timing.
contribution: Extends the Cucker-Smale flocking model with nonlinear coupling and a binding force, proving collision-free flocking under an initial-energy condition and tuning gains in simulation.
flag: URL constructed by me: https://www.mdpi.com/2076-3417/16/8/3933 (full HTML read in four chunks; tables are images so some values come from the prose only). Borderline under (c): collision avoidance is a headline claim and Theorem 2 does argue collision-freedom under an initial-energy bound, but the measured outcomes are velocity alignment, dispersion and energy, and the collision evidence does not favour the method: the classical baseline keeps a LARGER minimum distance (1.097 vs 1.050 m) and the extended model records 0.1 collisions per trial at K2=0.50. The avoidance is a term in the control law, not a runtime interceptor. The abstract's 73.6% and 54.2% are presented as gains over classical Cucker-Smale but in Sec. 4.5.2 they are changes when K2 goes from 0.05 to 0.15 within the proposed model. 'Energy below 35%' is relative to the model's own K1=1.25,K2=0.5 setting. Other problems: Sec. 4.1 (3D, speeds within 2 m/s) and Sec. 4.5 (2D, 10-20 m/s) describe different setups; '13 times' the safety distance should be about 6.5; several tables are labelled 'corrected' without explanation; idealised communication and sensing.

title: Resilient Multi-Agent State Estimation for Smart City Traffic: A Systems Engineering Approach to Emission Mitigation
evidence: "the baseline Conventional DGD algorithm severely diverges, whereas H-MASE autonomously isolates the fault" (Sec. 6.3)
method: Distributed least-squares estimation of route flows from link sensors by physical sensor agents and virtual relay agents at junctions; a residual threshold makes a faulty sensor agent drop its own measurement.
evaluation: MATLAB simulation, synthetic ring-radial network, 70 agents, 25 routes; conventional DGD baseline; nominal RMSE 0.81 vehicles per route, MAPE 2.44%; bias fault plus 10% packet loss; CO2 2591.72 vs 2611.89 kg; no hardware.
contribution: Proposes a consensus-based distributed route-flow estimator with virtual relay agents and residual-based self-isolation of faulty sensors, and reports bounded error under a sensor bias fault in a synthetic network.
flag: Off-topic: a traffic state estimator with sensor fault isolation. The agents are sensor nodes, the estimated state is macroscopic route volume (not agent states, not a learned predictor, so not (b)), the fault response is a sensor quarantining its own data (no action of an acting system is vetoed, so not (a)), and no hazard among agents is detected (not (c)). Edge units are mentioned only qualitatively with a 60-300 s sampling period and no latency or hardware figures (not (d)). I left gap_cells as none; a lenient reader might tick multi-agent state. Read via MDPI HTML (URL built from the OpenAlex pdf_url) at offsets 0 and 300000 of a 511543-character page that is mostly equation markup; NOT read: the end of Sec. 4.3, Sec. 4.4, Sec. 5 up to the end of Theorem 2 (offsets 100000-300000), and the tail after offset 400000. Tables 2-4 were image placeholders. Doubts: the abstract attaches the 0.81 RMSE to catastrophic hardware failures, but Sec. 6.2 reports it for nominal tracking; no post-fault RMSE, false-alarm count or detection delay is given in the text I saw although the abstract and conclusions claim no false alarms; a single fault (bias 80 at t=80 on one sensor) in one synthetic scenario; the emission benefit is 20.17 kg (0.77%) from a Webster delay model; ADMM and Kalman baselines were excluded without experiments; the estimator is unconstrained so negative flows are possible. Apparently single-author. Quotes relayed by the fetch tool.

title: Development of a Decentralized Algorithm Using Interval Type 3—Fuzzy Logic for Task Allocation and Multi-Agent Path Finding
evidence: "reduced solution cost by up to 47.03% and improved task completion by 35% over CBAA" (Abstract); collisions "are prevented by a combination of the A* and PIBT algorithms" (Sec. 3.5) and are not measured.
method: Decentralized auction-based task allocation with interval type-3 fuzzy inference choosing PASS/AWAY/WAIT/LEAVE per agent at conflicts, an El Farol congestion term, and PIBT plus A* detours for execution.
evaluation: Seven grid benchmarks, 4-35 agents; baselines ECBS, ECBS-TA, CBAA, IT2FL; path cost -7.10% to +19.48% vs ECBS, success +10-35% vs CBAA; mean decision time 0.03-0.13 s; simulation only.

flag: doi.org link not fetchable; I constructed https://www.mdpi.com/2076-3417/16/12/6254 and read the HTML in four chunks (Section 3 detail between 3.3 and 3.6 was only skimmed via the fetch summariser). Coordination/efficiency paper: outcomes are path cost, success (on-time completion) rate, fairness and compute time; no collision or violation rate is reported, only 'conflicts resolved' counts, so (c) fails the primacy test. The fuzzy WAIT/LEAVE choice is the agent's own nominal decision, not an interceptor over one, so (a) fails. Inconsistencies: Section 4 text says House has 20 agents and 20 tasks while Table 4 lists 4/4; text claims average time per decision cycle 'below 0.12 s' while Table 6 as returned shows average total time up to 0.4745 s (Milan, 30 agents) - check which column the claim refers to. The headline 47.03% holds for one map only (the other two are 0.6% and 0.71%), and the method loses to ECBS-TA by 9-35% everywhere. Hardware not found in the text returned to me. Sensitivity table shows success rate and distance identical across all parameter settings, which is odd.

title: Runtime Verification-Based Safe MARL for Optimized Safety Policy Generation for Multi-Robot Systems
evidence: "our framework ensures the safety of the robot system before training" (Sec. 5.2)
method: Safe multi-agent RL: a safety-constrained Markov game model is checked against rPATL properties with PRISM-games and refined by counterexamples, then a constrained policy optimiser (SCPO) trains on the verified model.
evaluation: RWARE grid warehouse simulation, two robots, 80M steps; SNAC, IAC, SEAC baselines; average episode cost at 80M: 0 vs 7, 12, 15; PRISM-games expected collisions 0.0, Pmax 1.0; no ablation, no hardware.
contribution: Combines probabilistic model checking of a safety-constrained Markov game with constrained multi-agent policy optimisation and reports lower safety cost than three actor-critic baselines in a two-robot warehouse simulation.
flag: Borderline include on (c) only; maintainer should decide. Despite the title, 'runtime verification' here means model checking a game model with PRISM-games before and during training (pseudocode step 14 checks the policy); I found no execution-time monitor or shield that blocks or replaces an action, so (a) is NOT met and runtime_interceptor is no. I recommend include because multi-robot safety is the primary claim and the primary measured outcome (average episode cost, i.e. safety violations) is compared with three baselines, which meets the minimum evaluation. Reasons to doubt it: Table 2 costs are whole numbers falling almost uniformly by one per 10M steps for every method, with no seeds, variance or definition of what one unit of cost is, which looks schematic rather than measured; mean returns are only a figure (Fig. 6) and SCPO trails SEAC on return; the baselines are unconstrained MARL methods, not safe-MARL ones; one tiny environment (two robots; called 10 x 11 while coordinates imply 11 x 10); no verification time is reported while Sec. 4.2 says verification is time-consuming yet does not slow MARL; objective is 'maximize' in Sec. 4 and 'minimize' in Sec. 4.3; guarantees hold only for the simplified hand-built model. If you read the cost metric as insufficiently defined, this becomes E2. The abstract contains no numbers. Read via MDPI HTML (URL https://www.mdpi.com/2504-2289/8/5/49/htm constructed by me from the DOI because the OpenAlex lookup was rate-limited; title confirmed on the page) in two fetches covering the whole body; quotes relayed by the fetch tool.

title: Collision Prediction and Social-Norm-Fusion-Based Social-Navigation Method for Quadruped Robots
evidence: Sec 4.1.4: the ZMP stability limit means the yaw command is 'limited in amplitude without changing the avoidance direction itself'; the method is a modified social force model, not a filter over a nominal decision.
method: Social force model for a quadruped with a time-to-collision repulsion term, rule-based orthogonal side-step force, gait-aware safety margin and ZMP-based yaw-rate clipping feeding NMPC and whole-body control.
evaluation: Sim (4 scenarios) and Unitree Aliengo corridor tests (3 scenarios), 20 runs each, vs SFM and PTSFM; success 100% vs 10-100%; min distance 0.50-0.55 vs 0.30-0.44 m; decision 10 Hz, control 500 Hz.
contribution: A collision-prediction social force model with rule-based side-stepping lets a quadruped robot pass pedestrians with full success and larger clearance than force-model baselines in simulation and corridor trials.
flag: Single-robot social navigation planner; collision avoidance is built into the planner, with one scripted pedestrian per scenario, so none of (a)-(e) is the subject. The only clip-style element is the ZMP yaw limit (active in 3.2% of real frames), which protects gait stability, not collision safety. A human safety operator held an emergency stop but no takeover is studied. Doubts: std devs in Tables 2-4 are a near-constant fraction of the mean (about 7-8%), which looks synthetic; ablation and comparison tables give different std for identical means; Conclusions cite CADRL/SA-CADRL comparisons for which I saw no data; text says min distance under 0.4 m at A_cp=3.0 but Table 1 says 0.41; Sim-4 is a near-tie yet claimed as 'comprehensively outperforms'. Simulator not named. No end-to-end latency. Read via MDPI /htm (URL constructed).

title: Certificate-Guided Safe Tracking Control for Allocation-Guided Multi-UAV Missions
evidence: Sec. 2.1: on invalidation "the active version is immediately marked invalidated. The command selector then applies the independent backup action"; Sec. 2.4.1: the controller "applies the bounded braking/hover action, and halts execution of the invalidated certificate."
method: Versioned finite-horizon execution certificates per UAV path, checked by a hard CLF-CBF-QP (tube + pairwise separation); stale packets, set violation or QP infeasibility invalidate the certificate, trigger backup braking/hover and planner repair.
evaluation: 60 randomized multi-UAV crossings at 48 Hz, 20 ms delay bound: plain CBF-QP 44/60 tube/separation-violation trials vs 0/60 for certificate feedback and a FaSTrack-style comparator; PyBullet Crazyflie; delay/rate/disturbance sweeps; separate single-UAV mocap flights.
contribution: Certificate-guided hard CLF-CBF-QP execution layer for multi-UAV paths that rejects and halts infeasible or stale certificates, removing the tube and separation violations seen in 44 of 60 plain CBF-QP trials.
flag: Strong (a) evidence: activation gate, invalidation, backup action, rejection-before-violation times reported (e.g. 1.104 s, 3.229 s). Caveats: 0/60 is shared with the tracking-error-bound comparator, so the advantage is only over plain CBF-QP (Wilson upper bound 6.0%); comparator is explicitly not real FaSTrack. Hardware flights are four separate single-UAV flights and the paper itself says the retained schedule is 0.128 m short of what simultaneous safety needs, so no multi-UAV hardware safety evidence. No compute hardware or QP solve time; latency awareness is a 20 ms packet-age bound and 0-100 ms delay sweep, not measured latency. Stress run at 0.50 m/s2 completes in Sec. 3.2 but is rejected in the Sec. 3.4 sweep, not reconciled. Event precision/recall 0.977 is in-sample calibrated. No human handoff. URL https://www.mdpi.com/2504-446X/10/8/617/htm constructed by me.

title: A High-Quality and Efficient Trajectory Replanning Method for Quadrotor Swarms Based on Rolling-Horizon Collision Resolution
evidence: Sec. 4: a designated UAV "employs the proposed RHCR-Opt algorithm to compute collision-free trajectories for all UAVs"; abstract: "when the swarm size becomes large, the computational efficiency is improved by at least 23.7%"
method: RHCR-Opt: rolling-horizon CBS with improved LPA* front end and MINCO joint trajectory optimization, plus two-stage temporal coordination, for quadrotor swarm replanning by one designated UAV.
evaluation: ROS simulation, 4-16 UAVs, 20 instances/size vs RBP, EDG-TEAM, Ego-Swarm-v2; success 1.00-0.50, replanning 49-264 ms; i7-8700 desktop; no collision rate; no real flights.

flag: Trajectory planner whose claims and metrics are computation time, success rate and trajectory quality; collision avoidance is a planning constraint and no collision or violation rate is reported. Abstract 23.7% found in Table 5 (K=12: 174.36 vs 228.46 ms), but RHCR-Opt is slower than EDG-TEAM at K=4 and K=8 and success drops to 0.50 at K=16. Static environment, reliable communication assumed. title: Collision-Free Path Planning for Multiple Drones Based on Safe Reinforcement Learning
evidence: Sec 4.3: the CBF-based QP 'minimally adjusts the RL policy to ensure system safety'; Sec 4: 'A safety layer comprising HOCBF is employed to correct potentially unsafe actions of drones within the actor network.'
method: MADDPG with a differentiable high-order CBF QP safety layer per drone that projects each actor action onto a safe set (slack-relaxed), trained centrally, executed distributed.
evaluation: 2D sim, 3 drones, 2 static obstacles, 100 test rounds; success (no collision) MADDPG-CBF 83%, IDDPG-CBF 72%, MADDPG 40%, IDDPG 37%; no hardware or timing.
contribution: A differentiable high-order control-barrier QP layer inside each MADDPG actor corrects unsafe drone actions at execution, lifting collision-free success from 40% to 83% in a three-drone simulation.
flag: Abstract '43% improvement' is 83% minus 40% in percentage points (Table 3), not relative. All four rows of Table 3 carry the identical +/-7.19% with no explanation. Training collisions 'approximately 1/800' of baselines is stated in Conclusions but only shown in figures. QP has a slack variable so safety is soft. Text once says 'DDPG' where IDDPG is meant. Tiny scale (3 drones, 2 obstacles, 2D), no QP solve time, no false-correction or throughput cost reported. Read via MDPI /htm (URL constructed).

title: Multi-UAV Obstacle Avoidance and Formation Control in Unknown Environments
evidence: "a control approach that integrates APF with optimal consensus control which can achieve cooperative obstacle avoidance" (Abstract); "current research efforts remain limited to computer simulations without validation in real-world environments" (Sec 5)
method: Improved artificial potential field combined with optimal consensus formation control for UAVs; inter-UAV repulsion; random-search tuning of cost weights for unknown obstacle fields.
evaluation: Simulation, 4 UAVs, 2D, one known and one random scenario; vs APF, APF+consensus, non-optimal IAPF; avoidance time 17.48 s vs 25.7 s; spacing change 1.18 m vs 10.6 m.
contribution: Combines an improved potential field with optimal consensus control so a four-UAV formation passes obstacles faster and with less formation distortion than plain APF variants in simulation.

Avoidance is a force term inside the controller, not a runtime filter. Table 4 lists obstacles 2-5 at identical coordinates; abstract says undirected topology but Sec 2.2 example is directed. title: Safety-Critical Trajectory Tracking Control with Safety-Enhanced Reinforcement Learning for Autonomous Underwater Vehicle
evidence: Sec 3.2: the RL purpose is to 'learn the uncertain terms within the CBF and CLF constraints in the QP problem'; Sec 3.1: slack added so that 'safety is prioritized over tracking stability'.
method: Single AUV: TD3 policy outputs correction terms for model uncertainty in CLF and exponential-CBF constraints; one CBF-CLF-QP then computes the executed control each step.
evaluation: BlueROV2 simulation, static/multiple/dynamic obstacles with mass and drag errors; vs CBF-CLF-QP, CBF-BS-QP, MPC-CBF; h_cmin 0.001 vs -0.146 m, E_traj 1.394 vs 2.899 m; no timing.
contribution: Reinforcement learning estimates model-uncertainty terms in the barrier and Lyapunov constraints of a single underwater vehicle's CBF-CLF quadratic program, keeping the barrier non-negative where the nominal controller violates it.
flag: Borderline. The CBF is a constraint inside the controller QP, with no separate nominal action being filtered, so I scored (a) as not met; a maintainer who counts CBF-CLF-QP as a runtime safety filter would instead land on E4 (single agent, no multi-agent/latency/handoff aspect) or include. Table 3 came through partly garbled: only Scenario 1 Condition 1 values could be mapped with confidence; text also gives max tracking error 4.85 vs 3.42 m and completion 25.3 vs 29.2 s. Failed-case comparisons used relaxed obstacle radius/speed, so not fully like-for-like. Baselines CBF-BS-QP and MPC-CBF dropped after Scenario 1. 3D demo run without uncertainty. No hardware, no solve times. Read via MDPI /htm (URL constructed).

title: Stochastic Potential Game-Based Target Tracking and Encirclement Approach for Multiple Unmanned Aerial Vehicles System
evidence: "it means a collision has occurred, and in this case, R_obs should be set to a negative value to represent a penalty" (Sec. 4.2.1, Self-Influence Rewards)
method: Formulates multi-UAV target tracking and encirclement as a stochastic potential game and learns decentralised actors with TMSAC, a multi-agent soft actor-critic with GRU layers and time-serial replay; collision avoidance via reward penalties.
evaluation: Custom 2D 1000x1000 m simulation, 4-5 trackers, 1 target, 100 test episodes; vs MADDPG and MASAC; 5-20% more reward, success rates only in figures; gym-pybullet-drones demo; RTX 3090 training; no latency.

No runtime override exists - safety is only a training-time penalty and a stated 20 m safe-interval requirement whose enforcement is not shown. Full and Half Success Rate values appear only in Figure 8, not in text; the scalability claim (8% drop at 20 UAVs) conflicts with Table 1 listing 4 or 5 trackers. URL constructed by me: https://www.mdpi.com/2504-446X/9/2/103/htm.

title: OT Control and Integration of Mobile Robotic Networks
evidence: Sec 4: 'Each control command issued by the server triggers a corresponding execution confirmation message from the robot' - command tracking only; no safety monitor, e-stop or collision avoidance is described.

Check whether the mask counts as a runtime interceptor: it is implemented inside the policy softmax (Equation 13), which a maintainer may read as a constraint inside the policy rather than a shield, though it is applied at every execution step on hardware, the null (halt) action always stays valid, and a battery-threshold fallback fires independently of the predictor. title: Human-in-the-Loop Cluster Formation Tracking for Multi-Agent Systems with Collision Avoidance
evidence: "the distributed controller ensures collision avoidance only among followers belonging to the same subgroup" (Remark 4, Sec. 3)
method: Distributed sliding-mode-style follower law (K1*zeta - chi*sign(K2*zeta) + formation compensation) for cluster formation tracking of leaders driven by bounded human inputs; intra-subgroup separation guaranteed via initial-error bound and Lyapunov decay.

flag: No baseline or ablation at all: no with/without collision-avoidance comparison and no competing controller; the only contrast is a qualitative disturbance run (d=2sin(t)) showing degraded tracking. Collision avoidance is not a runtime filter: it follows from the reference spacing gamma_k > r_min plus a restrictive initial-error condition (13), so the guarantee is by design conditions, and it covers only followers in the same subgroup (inter-subgroup separation is assumed via non-overlapping leader trajectories). In Table 1 the minimum distance for subgroup 2 occurs at t=0.00 s, i.e. it is the initial condition. Human-in-the-loop means an exogenous bounded leader input only; there is no handoff, takeover or deferral, so (e) is not met. Also arguably E1 since tracking, not hazard rate, is the primary outcome. Abstract numbers (4.21-5.12 s, 9.07e-5) confirmed in Table 2. Low-quality venue signals: citation numbers do not match the reference list (SAGA, TRiSM and MI9 cited as refs 3-5, which are Sutton and Barto, DQN and PPO; Council of Europe convention cited to a multi-agent RL survey), several references are bare organisation home pages, and symbols are garbled. title: Generating Safe Autonomous Decision-Making in ROS
venue: Electronic Proceedings in Theoretical Computer Science, EPTCS
evidence: Sec. 4.2: the runtime approach "merely uses invariant checking" on each generated decision; Sec. 5: "We will fully implement the proposed runtime verification approach in the near future".

contribution: Research preview proposing static model checking of GOAL agent programs and a ROS node that checks safety invariants on each decision at runtime, with implementation and evaluation left as future work.
flag: E2: research preview with no quantitative result; abstract's "promising results" and "initial tests" are not quantified anywhere. Topic fits (a) only loosely: the paper never says what happens when a runtime check fails, so no override/veto/halt is described (hence runtime_interceptor=no); interception is mentioned only for ROSRV and ROSMonitoring in related work. O(1) runtime check is an anticipated complexity, not a measurement. Multi-agent (three robots) is planned only. Check whether a later full paper by the same authors exists and should be queued instead.

title: Runtime Verification of Learning Properties for Reinforcement Learning Algorithms
venue: Electronic Proceedings in Theoretical Computer Science
evidence: Sec. 2: "The monitors we propose do not modify the behaviour of the learning phase."
method: Passive runtime-verification monitors for three RL learning properties: quality of value estimate (bias, covariance), distance to optimal policy, and time to learn; verdicts only, no enforcement.
evaluation: Fictional police patrol scheduling example, 18 states, 3 actions; no baseline or ablation; time-to-learn bound 62 transitions vs about 30 observed; no hardware or latency.
contribution: Proposes passive runtime monitors that report whether an RL algorithm is learning well, how far it is from optimal and how long learning will take, illustrated on a toy scheduling example.
flag: Monitors learning-quality properties, not safety of actions; cannot override or halt, so strict (a) fails. Single agent, illustrative toy example only, no baseline (would also be E2). Thresholds in Sec. 4.1 text (2% and 5%) appear swapped relative to Eq. 6.

title: Adaptive Task Token Framework (ATTF):Enabling Robust and Lifelong Multi-Agent Pickup and Delivery
venue: International Conference on Industrial Engineering and Operations Management (IEOM)
evidence: "Agents involved in a collision cannot execute their planned actions and are delayed." (Sec. 4); "Their paths are replanned to resolve the conflict" (Sec. 4)

flag: Coordination/efficiency paper: outcomes are makespan, service time and planner runtime only; no collision, violation or hazard rate, so (c) fails the primacy test and replanning inside the planner is not (a). Per-timestep runtimes are reported (ATTF under 55 ms in Exp. 1; 50-87 ms at lambda 0.5 and up to 929.76 ms at 500 agents in Exp. 3; 47.74 ms in case study) against a self-cited 'under one second' real-time requirement, but this is planning throughput on a laptop, not a latency bound on a safety decision, so (d) not credited. No ablations. Case-study baseline is an 'unknown' centralised system (5100 vs 3191 min makespan), unverifiable. Simulator unnamed; delays are synthetic. IEOM proceedings, light peer review. Read via one WebFetch pass over the whole PDF; tables taken from that pass (selected rows only), not every cell checked.

title: Adapting the Five Pillars of Model Risk Management for Generative AI: The GEN-5 Validation Framework
venue: International Journal of Current Science Research and Review
evidence: "This paper proposes GEN-5, a five-pillar validation and assurance framework" (Abstract); scope is prescribed multi-agent systems that "do not plan, negotiate, or make decisions independently" (Sec. 3.1).

Guardrails, escalation and human override appear only as rows of controls to validate (Table 4), with no architecture, trigger or timing, hence runtime_interceptor no. Full text read (12 pages, pp. 1913-1924) via a summarising reader at ijcsrr.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/04/24-2004-2026.pdf; the DOI itself was blocked by the fetch tool (cross-host redirect) and the PDF was located by search. Low-quality venue signs: Sec. 3.6 is headed 'Pillar 6' in a five-pillar framework; scope says non-agentic systems while the abstract stresses self-orchestrating agents; several citation mismatches (RAG cited to the RAGAs repository; 'MAS 01/23' not matching reference [3]; reference [10] gives ACL '62nd Annual Meeting' with a 2023 date); unsupported assertion that chunking errors are the most common RAG failure; journal header advertises an unverifiable impact factor of 8.048.

title: Advancing U.S. Competitiveness Through Governance Tools and Trustworthy Frameworks for Autonomous GenAI Agentic Systems
venue: International Journal of Advanced Research in Science Communication and Technology
evidence: "This is a pure review paper and all results, proposals and findings are from the cited literature." (Declaration)

evaluation: No evaluation: no dataset, system under test, baseline, hardware or latency; all figures are quoted from vendor or market sources (e.g. 78% of organisations using AI, $10.7 billion observability market by 2033).

The doi.org landing was blocked; full text read from the journal PDF at ijarsct.co.in/Paper29017.pdf in one pass. Quality concerns: abstract says 'Our evaluation reveals' although there is no evaluation; Sec. VII 'Quantitative Methodologies' has no computed results; several citations are vendor blogs, webinars or listicles and do not appear to support the claims attached to them; reference [33] is title-only and [38] contains leftover template text; conclusion asserts formal verification and compositional risk assessment that the body never discusses.
