title: CoRL-MPPI: Enhancing MPPI With Learnable Behaviours For Efficent And Provably-Safe Multi-Robot Collision Avoidance
evidence: "Solving this optimization problem yields updated parameters of the sampling distribution" (Sec. IV-B); "enforces probabilistic safety constraints to ensure collision-free behavior" (Sec. V-B)
method: Decentralised MPPI whose sampling distribution is biased by an IPPO-trained policy (30% of 1500 rollouts) and corrected by ORCA-based chance constraints within a safety horizon.
evaluation: Simulation, differential-drive, 4-50 agents, Random/Circle/Mesh-Dense; baselines ORCA-DD, B-UAVC, MPPI-ORCA; success 100/100/99.25%, collisions 0/0/0.75%; no ablation; no runtime figures.
contribution: Fuses a learned multi-agent policy into ORCA-constrained MPPI sampling and reports higher success with near-zero collisions than ORCA-DD, B-UAVC and MPPI-ORCA in dense simulated multi-robot navigation.
flag: Borderline on the primacy test: safety and efficiency are claimed jointly and collision rate is reported against three baselines, but the headline gain is success rate and makespan, so the maintainer may prefer E1. Not a runtime interceptor: the ORCA constraints reshape the sampling distribution inside the planner, nothing vetoes an executed command. Provably-safe is probabilistic and the proof is deferred to a cited prior paper; the method itself has 0.75% collisions in Mesh-Dense where MPPI-ORCA has 0%, i.e. it is slightly LESS safe than its parent there. Table I: ORCA-DD SR 99.8/66/46.5%, col 0/15/0%; B-UAVC SR 97.2/40/54.5%, col 0.8/57/27.75%; MPPI-ORCA SR 100/94/100%, col 0/6/0%. Makespan only in a figure (text says nearly twofold better than MPPI-ORCA in dense cases). No planner latency or control-rate figure although C++/ONNX is used; training under 2 h on one H100; no real robots; no ablation of the RL share. The landing URL (doi.org/10.48448, an Underline video/poster DOI) has no PDF in OpenAlex; I read arXiv 2511.09331v1 HTML found by web search (one summarising fetch plus one quote fetch), which may differ from the presented version. Quotes relayed by the fetch tool.

title: Combining Deep Reinforcement Learning and Safety Based Control for Autonomous Driving
evidence: Sec. 3.2: 'We then balance the weight of these three action outputs'; Sec. 4.1: 'we combine the learning policy actions and safety based control actions', with fixed weights alpha=0.4, beta=0.3, gamma=0.3.
method: Trains a DDPG driving policy in TORCS with no opponents present, then blends its steering and acceleration with an artificial potential field collision-avoidance term and a path-tracking controller using fixed weights.
evaluation: TORCS, four qualitative scenarios with 0, 1, 1 and 2 opponent vehicles (Fig. 6); no baseline and no ablation; no collision rate, success rate, lap time or tracking error; the only numbers are the DDPG training curve (average Q about 110 after about 13 hours), 36 potential-field distance inputs and a controller parameter table; GPU unspecified, no latency reported.
contribution: Blends a DDPG driving policy with an artificial potential field and a path tracker in fixed proportions so the learned controller keeps clear of opponent vehicles in TORCS.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - a DDPG policy - so the 2026-11-13 ruling is satisfied, but (a) fails because the potential field is summed into the executed action with fixed weights and can never override, veto or halt it, and (c) fails the primacy test since no collision or hazard rate is reported. E2 is equally defensible and makes the exclusion robust either way: the evidence is four qualitative figures with no baseline and no ablation. If the maintainer counts a continuous weighted correction as interception, switch the code to E2 rather than include. Notation is inconsistent (gamma is both blend weight and discount factor, Eq. 12 uses lambda where Eq. 13 uses gamma).

title: VAIN: Attentional Multi-agent Predictive Modeling
evidence: Sec. 4 (Soccer): the task is to predict 'the position of each player for each time-step during the next 4 seconds'; Sec. 3 pools each agent's message by a softmax over -||a_i - a_j||^2 so that it averages 'only information from relevant agents'.
method: Vertex Attention Interaction Network: per-agent singleton and communication encoders plus a learned attention vector let each agent pool only relevant neighbours' messages, giving a factorised interaction network with linear rather than quadratic encoder evaluations.
evaluation: Chess next-piece prediction (about 600k examples, accuracy 0.301 vs IN 0.283, CommNet 0.272, FC 0.216, random 0.045), soccer 0.5-4.0 s player-position forecasting on SVPP with three leave-one-out splits (mean error 1.03 m vs IN 1.04, CommNet 1.04, PAD 1.08, static 1.84) and 50 bouncing balls in MuJoCo-free 2D (RMS 0.135 vs IN 0.139, CommNet 0.510, VEL0 0.561); ablations are attention vs average pooling and IN at matched compute (about 8x VAIN on chess); several hours on a K80, no latency and no safety metric.
contribution: Replaces uniform message pooling in multi-agent predictive models with learned per-agent attention, matching interaction networks on future-state prediction at a fraction of the interaction cost.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: n-a, this is a Pillar 2 (b) record. It clears the Pillar 2 scope only through the soccer and bouncing-ball tasks, which predict future multi-agent state over an implicit interaction graph; the chess task is classification of which piece moves next, not future state. A maintainer may still read it as a plain trajectory regressor and hence E1: there is no latent rollout, no recurrence (soccer uses a single frame), and the model is never used for control. Gains over IN and CommNet are tiny (1.03 vs 1.04 m, RMS 0.135 vs 0.139) with no seeds or error bars. Per protocol RQ5 is held low and no safety credit is given - there is no collision or hazard metric, only an attention picture of a ball described as on collision course. The 'only 4%' of IN's size or encoder evaluations figure is worded inconsistently between text and caption.

title: Safe Exploration in Continuous Action Spaces
evidence: Sec. 1: the layer acts 'after every policy query' and 'solves an optimization problem for finding the minimal change to the action'; Sec. 6: 'we compose an additional, last layer' that 'perturbs the original action as little as possible in the Euclidean norm'.
method: Pre-trains a neural model that is linear in the action for each safety signal from random-action transitions, then adds a closed-form last layer projecting the deterministic policy's action onto the safe half-space of the most violated constraint.
evaluation: MuJoCo Ball-1D, Ball-3D, Spaceship-Corridor and Spaceship-Arena, single agent, 10 seeds per task, against DDPG and DDPG plus reward shaping (margin swept over six values 0.08-0.23, penalty -1 or -1000); the safety layer accumulates zero constraint violations across all seeds in all four tasks, converges faster, and is the only method that converges on either Spaceship task, while reward shaping violates for every margin; reward-shaping violation fractions and all returns appear only in Figs. 5-6; 1000 pre-training episodes per task; no hardware and no measured latency.
contribution: Adds a closed-form safety layer that projects a deep policy's action onto a learned linear safety-signal constraint after every query, giving zero constraint violations during exploration.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - a DDPG policy, corrected after every query, so (a) is clean. Single agent throughout, so the record carries no multi-agent evidence and a maintainer could test it against E4 wrong level; it survives because the interception is per-step and sequential rather than one-shot. Check the headline claim: zero violations holds only in MuJoCo with episodes that terminate on violation, and rests on Prop. 1's assumption that at most one constraint is active plus a safety model that is linear in the action and pre-trained from 1000 random-action episodes. The reward-shaping baseline's violation counts and every return are given as curves with no numbers in the text. The 'negligible' computational cost is asserted and never measured, so (d) was not credited, and the conservative-backup preemption mentioned for real systems is discussion only, not a human handoff.

title: Direct Uncertainty Prediction for Medical Second Opinions
evidence: Such a model could be deployed to automatically identify patients that might need a second doctor's opinion (Section 1, Introduction).
method: Direct Uncertainty Prediction: a network trained to score an input's expected expert disagreement directly, rather than post-processing a trained classifier's output distribution into an uncertainty score.
evaluation: Retinal fundus DR, Gaussian mixtures, blurred SVHN and CIFAR; baselines UVC Histogram-E2E and Histogram-PC; AUC 78.1 vs 76.6 disagreement, 86.2 vs 84.8 adjudicated, Spearman 0.682 vs 0.660; no hardware or latency.
contribution: Shows that predicting expert disagreement directly from the input beats scoring uncertainty from a trained classifier, giving a sharper triage signal for flagging cases to a second human reader.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: no - nothing is guarded, a CNN scores its own inputs. One-shot selective prediction: the human second opinion is motivation only, with no deferral policy, no cost model and no measured handoff, so Pillar 3 (i)-(v) fails on my reading. Most likely overturn of this batch: the unbiasedness and dominance analysis of DUP over UVC could be read as (v) foundational reject-option theory, and the medical-second-opinion framing as (i). All abstract numbers were located in Tables 1-5; no hardware or inference-time figure exists.

title: Temporal Logic Guided Safe Reinforcement Learning Using Control Barrier Functions
evidence: The RL action is integrated with the CLF-CBF-QP to solve for the final safe action (Section IV), and to ensure safety, CBF is always turned on during evaluation (Section VI.E).
method: An scTLTL specification compiled to an automaton supplies the RL reward plus CLF goals and CBF safe sets; a CLF-CBF quadratic program corrects the PPO action before execution.
evaluation: Simulated unicycle in a channel with two moving obstacles; ablations RL, RL+CBF, RL+CLF, RL+CLF+CBF; evaluation success rate over 20 trials plus plotted zero safety violations; values only in Figures 4-8; no hardware or latency.
contribution: Wraps a PPO policy in a CLF-CBF quadratic program driven by a temporal-logic automaton, keeping the agent inside the specified safe set during both learning and execution.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - a PPO neural policy, filtered by the CLF-CBF quadratic program at execution time, so (a) is clean. Check the evaluation floor hard: there is no number anywhere in the body, no theorem, proposition or proof, no success rate and no violation count - only Figures 4-8 and qualitative claims such as agents trained with CBF exhibits higher success rates - so the maintainer may rule exclude-E2. Single agent only and the moving obstacles are uncontrolled, so no (c). Safety rests on known unicycle dynamics; K is given as about 1e10, which looks like a tuning artefact worth checking.

title: The Algorithmic Automation Problem: Prediction, Triage, and Human Effort
evidence: We develop a general framework that poses this latter decision, which instances the algorithm should handle, as an optimization problem (Abstract); instances not automated receive a fixed budget of human grades (Section 2.2).
method: Two-part automation framework: a predictor plus an offline triage rule ranking instances by predicted algorithmic error minus predicted human error, under a budget of human effort reallocated to the non-automated set.
evaluation: Diabetic retinopathy with adjudicated gold labels; baselines full automation and equal human coverage; triage-score ablations; error 5.5% human, 4% full automation, 3.5% optimal triage; zero-error subsets 44% vs 35%; holdout 24% vs 10%; no latency.
contribution: Frames automation as jointly choosing what to predict and which instances to keep for humans, showing that triaging cases to doctors beats both full automation and uniform human coverage.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: no - no mechanism guards a learned system, but the party deferred to is human, so this enters through the (e) carve-out with (a) deferral as the main claim and a measured handoff. Check (e): the human side is modelled only as an evenly split grading budget, with no takeover timing, situation awareness, transparency or trust measurement, so the maintainer may drop (e) and keep (a) alone. Triage is an offline ranking with no runtime override, so runtime_interceptor is no. Same authors and dataset as record 1807.01771 - possible overlap. Figures 4, 5, 7, 9 and 11 curves carry no printed values.

title: Reinforcement Learning with Probabilistic Guarantees for Autonomous Driving
evidence: The trained agent takes the acceptable actions that maximizes the Q function, where acceptable actions are those keeping collision-avoidance probability above 0.9999 (Section 4.2).
method: Probabilistic model checking precomputes per-state action sets satisfying an LTL collision-avoidance threshold; deep Q-learning explores and acts only within that set, defaulting to hard braking when it is empty.
evaluation: Unsignalised left turn with one car and one pedestrian, 10,000 Monte Carlo runs; baselines safe-random, rule-based, unconstrained RL; collisions 0.00% vs RL 0.63, 0.2 and 0.96% and rule-based 0.05, 2.18 and 3.62%; slower to goal; no latency.
contribution: Restricts a deep RL driving policy to actions a probabilistic model checker certifies as collision-free with probability 0.9999, giving zero collisions across 10,000 simulated unprotected left turns.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - a deep Q-network, masked at execution time by precomputed acceptable action sets, so (a) is clean and the collision rate is the primary measured outcome. Check (c): the other car and the pedestrian are scripted rather than learned, and the two-obstacle case is handled by intersecting two single-agent acceptable sets, which the paper itself calls suboptimal since it does not leverage the interaction, so the maintainer may drop (c) and keep (a). The guarantee holds only for the discretised conservative model, and no value-iteration or per-step timing is reported despite the precomputation being the edge-relevant part. Safe RL is markedly slower to the goal (28.47 vs 22.16 steps), which is the real throughput cost.

title: Social-BiGAT: Multimodal Trajectory Forecasting using Bicycle-GAN and Graph Attention Networks
evidence: A graph attention network over a fully connected pedestrian graph plus a latent encoder jointly predicts 12 future timesteps for every pedestrian in the scene (Sections 3.4 and 4.1).
method: Conditional GAN with LSTM encoder-decoder generator, graph attention across all pedestrians, soft attention over a scene image, and a Bicycle-GAN style latent encoder giving controllable multimodal futures.
evaluation: ETH and UCY, five scenes, hold-one-out, 8 observed and 12 predicted steps, K=20; baselines linear, S-LSTM, S-GAN-P, Sophie; ablations GAT-only and BiGAN-only; average ADE and FDE 0.48 and 1.00 vs 0.54 and 1.15; no latency.
contribution: Couples graph attention over interacting pedestrians with a reversible latent encoder, cutting average final displacement error to 1.00 m and degrading far less than prior GANs when few samples are drawn.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: no - nothing is guarded, this is Pillar 2 (b) method evidence only. Check (b) against the scope ruling: it does predict future multi-agent state over a dynamic interaction graph with ADE and FDE plus two ablations, but it is a GAN trajectory forecaster with no action conditioning, no hazard or collision metric and no runtime use, so the maintainer may call it a plain trajectory regressor and rule exclude-E1. It is generative, so I did not credit non-generative inference. RQ5 capped at 1 per the protocol rule for predictors. Several HOTEL cells of Table 1 came back garbled in extraction, so the S-LSTM and S-GAN-P HOTEL values are unverified; the 0.15 m average FDE gain was located in Section 4.1.

title: Predicting Responses to a Robot's Future Motion using Generative Recurrent Neural Networks
evidence: Abstract: "This allows the model to learn the response of individuals with regards to a robot's motion from real world observations." - action-conditioned prediction over a spatio-temporal graph of multiple agents (Sec. 3.2).
method: Generative recurrent net (ResponseRNN): node and edge LSTMs with attention over a dynamic spatio-temporal graph, conditioned on the robot's next planned action, outputs bivariate Gaussians per agent.
evaluation: ARATH cattle-robot and Stanford Drone subsets; baselines CTRV, RED, Social-LSTM; ADE/FDE RRNN-Vel 0.462/0.906 m at t=20 on ARATH vs SLSTM 0.82/1.55; 250 ms inference, Titan-X.
contribution: Action-conditioned recurrent graph model that predicts how nearby humans or animals will respond to a robot's planned motion, evaluated on cattle-herding and pedestrian data.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: no - nothing is guarded, included only under (b) as action-conditioned prediction over a dynamic multi-agent graph. Borderline: maintainer may rule this a plain trajectory regressor (direct position and velocity output, no latent state, never closed into a planner or safety filter) and overturn to exclude-E1. No safety metric at all, only ADE/FDE. The response-modelling claim is supported only qualitatively, and Sec. 4.3 admits some simulated responses "do not make sense". 250 ms inference for 5 agents is far above any real-time budget. No ablation isolating the robot-action input, so its benefit is not separated from other architecture differences.

title: Multiple Futures Prediction
evidence: Abstract: "learns semantically meaningful latent variables to represent the multimodal future, without requiring explicit labels"; joint interactive step-wise rollouts of all agents with per-agent discrete latent modes (Sec. 3).
method: Multiple Futures Prediction: per-agent encoder-decoder GRUs with discrete per-agent latent modes and dynamic RBF attention encoding, trained by an EM-style variational bound, with interactive joint rollouts.
evaluation: CARLA, CARLA-PRECOG, NGSIM, Argoverse; baselines DESIRE, ESP, MultiPath, CS-LSTM; NLL 1.39 vs RNN 5.64 (CARLA), minMSD 0.284 vs ESP 0.675 (Town01); CARLA RL crash rate 0% vs DDPG 6%.
contribution: Probabilistic multi-agent trajectory model with discrete latent modes and interactive rollouts, supporting hypothetical ego-conditioned prediction and strong likelihood results on CARLA, NGSIM and Argoverse.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: no - this is a prediction model with no interceptor. Include under (b) only, RQ5 held at 2 per protocol. The CARLA crash rates (MFP 0% vs DDPG 6%, PPO 15%) come from a shooting-method planner built on the predictor, not a runtime gate, so (c) fails the primacy test. Several Table 3 and Table 7 cells were unreadable in the fetched PDF: maintainer should re-check the hypothetical-rollout and full crash-rate numbers. NGSIM minimum-over-samples metrics use ground truth to select the best trajectory, which the paper itself calls "overly optimistic". No inference latency reported, only 1.2 s per training batch update.

title: Learning to Switch Among Agents in a Team via 2-Layer Markov Decision Processes
evidence: Sec. 2: "the switch value is given by a (deterministic and time-varying) switching policy" choosing at each step whether the human or the RL-trained machine acts; Algorithm 1 lines 8-10 deploy it on the true environment.
method: Control switching as a 2-layer MDP; UCRL2-MC builds L1 confidence sets over each agent's policy and the environment transitions, then solves a Bellman recursion for the per-step switching policy.
evaluation: Simulated three-lane driving, horizon 10, 20k episodes; baselines finite-horizon UCRL2, human-only and machine-only; metric total regret (figures only, no numbers); Theorem 2 proves a sublinear regret bound.
contribution: Casts human-machine control switching as a 2-layer MDP and gives an online algorithm with a sublinear regret bound that learns when to hand driving control back to a human.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - the machine agent is an RL policy trained only on no-car environments, and the switching policy decides at every step whether it or the human acts. TITLE MISMATCH but not a wrong paper: the fetched version is titled "Learning to Switch Between Machines and Humans", same authors (Balazadeh Meresht, De, Singla, Gomez-Rodriguez) and same 2-layer-MDP and UCRL2-MC content; the record title is a later arXiv version title. Evaluation floor is met only through the proved regret bound plus the UCRL2, human-only and machine-only baselines: no numeric regret values appear in the text (Figures 2-5 only) and there is no collision or violation rate. (e) rests on a simulated noisy-cost human with no human subjects, and handoff cost is a single scalar switching cost, so the maintainer may drop (e). The paper concedes its bound is worse than plain UCRL2.

title: Counterfactual Policy Evaluation for Decision-Making in Autonomous Driving
evidence: Abstract: "the policy is only executed after the counterfactual policy evaluation has been performed"; if collision probability exceeds rho_max "the ego vehicle is controlled by a lane-following model" (Sec. III).
method: Replaces nearby vehicles' policies with constant-acceleration variants, rolls out 1 s, averages collision probability, and executes the learned SAC policy only below threshold rho_max, else a lane-following fallback.
evaluation: BARK highway merging, 250 episodes per threshold; baseline the ungated SAC policy (32% success, 48% collisions); gated at rho_max=0 gives 0% collisions, 99.8% goal reached, policy executed 76% of the time.
contribution: A runtime gate that simulates counterfactual behaviours of surrounding vehicles and hands control to a rule-based fallback whenever a learned driving policy's collision probability exceeds a threshold.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - a SAC reinforcement-learning driving policy is gated before each execution, the strongest (a) record in this batch. (c) is borderline: hazards are assessed over several surrounding vehicles, but only the ego is the policy under test and the other agents are rule-based Mobil models, so the maintainer may drop (c). The paper names the fallback IDM in Sec. III and Mobil in Sec. IV-C, an internal inconsistency. No latency or hardware figures despite a 1 s counterfactual horizon and a 0.2 s step time, so real-time feasibility is unverified. No numbers for intermediate rho_max, no fallback-only baseline, and it is unclear whether 99.8% is over all episodes or only executed ones. The counterfactual rollouts are non-generative but the paper never frames them that way, so I did not claim that gap cell.

title: EvolveGraph: Multi-Agent Trajectory Prediction with Dynamic Relational Reasoning
evidence: Abstract: "explicit relational structure recognition and prediction via latent interaction graphs among multiple heterogeneous, interactive agents"; the graph is re-encoded every tau steps and evolved by a GRU (Sec. 4.2).
method: Latent interaction-graph model: Gumbel-softmax edge-type encoder over agent pairs, GRU decoder with Gaussian-mixture output, and a graph-evolution GRU that re-encodes the graph every tau steps; two-stage training.
evaluation: Synthetic particles, H3D, NBA, SDD; baselines STGAT, Social-STGCNN, Trajectron++, NRI; SDD minADE20 13.9 vs STGAT 18.8 px; changing-relation edge accuracy 82.3% vs NRI 71.5%; static-graph and single-stage ablations.
contribution: Predicts and evolves latent interaction graphs among heterogeneous agents, improving multi-agent trajectory forecasting on driving, sports and pedestrian benchmarks over static-graph and attention baselines.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: no - prediction model with no interceptor, include under (b) only and hold RQ5 at or below 2 per protocol. The dynamically re-encoded latent graph puts it clearly past the static-graph exclusion, but there is no safety metric, no collision rate and no absolute latency figure (Fig. 5 gives NBA test time only rescaled to [0,1]), so it is architecture evidence only. Absolute minADE and minFDE values in the benchmark tables were misaligned in the fetched PDF and the H3D table's time labels contradict the text: only the SDD numbers and the percentage reductions are reliable, so the maintainer should re-check them. No NLL reported despite a Gaussian-mixture decoder.

title: Preferential Mixture-of-Experts: Interpretable Models that Rely on Human Expertise as much as Possible
evidence: Abstract: 'augments human expertise in decision making with a data-based classifier only when necessary for predictive performance'; the gate routes each input to the fixed human rule or to the ML expert at prediction time (Sec. 3).
method: Preferential mixture-of-experts: an interpretable gate maximises reliance on fixed human decision rules subject to a predictive-performance constraint, solved by log-barrier and projected-gradient algorithms.
evaluation: HIV (36780 patients) and MDD (3865) prescribing; baselines ML-only, standard MoE, two learn-to-defer methods; AUC 0.74 vs 0.64-0.71; soft coverage 63.2% vs 52.9-56.8%; no hardware or latency reported.
contribution: Trains an interpretable gate that maximises use of human clinical decision rules while meeting a performance floor, deferring to a learned classifier only where the rules are inadequate.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - the gate overrides a learned classifier in favour of fixed human rules, but no live human acts. Check against Pillar 3 scope: deferral is the main contribution, yet the setting is one-shot selective prediction, non-sequential, no safety-critical runtime gate, and the deferral target is a static rule set rather than a person, so exclude-E4 is plausible. Learn-to-defer baselines failed to train on MDD and are absent from Table 3; the accuracy-coverage curves in Figs. 3 and 5 are not tabulated.

title: Learning Safe Multi-Agent Control with Decentralized Neural Barrier Certificates
evidence: Sec. 4.3: 'We propose a spontaneous online policy refinement approach that produces even safer control policies in testing' - at each test step the learned barrier certificate's gradient modifies the agent's action before execution.
method: Jointly learns decentralized neural control barrier certificates and controllers with a quantity-permutation-invariant neighbour encoder; at test time gradient-based online policy refinement adjusts each agent's action to satisfy the certificate.
evaluation: Simulated ground robots and drones, 8-1024 agents; baselines MAMPS, PIC-Safe, MADDPG-Safe, S2M2; safety rate 0.9956 with refinement vs 0.9741 without at 1024 agents; refinement fires on under 17% of steps.
contribution: Decentralized neural barrier certificates learned jointly with controllers scale from eight to 1024 agents, with test-time policy refinement raising the multi-agent safety rate from 0.974 to 0.996.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - learned neural policies with learned certificates. Refinement is gradient descent on the certificate rather than a hard veto or a QP, and the authors state the method 'still cannot guarantee that the agents are 100% safe' (Sec. 5). Only the Table 1 refinement ablation is tabulated; all baseline safety rates and rewards are shown graphically in Figs. 4-6 and 8. Simulation only, no hardware, and the 1024-agent result is produced by copying trained parameters to extra agents.

title: Safe Reinforcement Learning Using Advantage-Based Intervention
evidence: Sec. 3.1: actions whose advantage over the backup policy exceeds the threshold lie in the intervention set and the backup policy acts instead, so unsafe actions are overridden at execution time in every training rollout.
method: SAILR intervenes when an action's advantage over a user-supplied backup policy exceeds a threshold, substituting the backup and penalising the agent in an absorbing surrogate MDP optimised with PPO.
evaluation: Point-robot and half-cheetah safe-RL tasks, 10 and 8 seeds; baselines CPO, PDO, CSC; 'orders of magnitude fewer safety violations' in training, deployment return comparable to CPO; Theorems 1-2 bound safety and suboptimality.
contribution: Advantage-based intervention keeps a reinforcement learner safe throughout training by swapping in a backup policy whenever an action is too costly, with bounds on both safety and suboptimality.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - an RL policy. Single agent, so criterion (c) does not hold. The evaluation floor is met only through the proved guarantees plus figure-based baseline comparison: the paper contains no numeric table of violations, returns or intervention counts anywhere, including the appendix, so no safety figures can be quoted. The shield is removed at deployment, and the height-heuristic variant is 'consistently unsafe in deployment' - only the MPC variant stays safe. The non-generative-inference cell applies to the fitted-Q rule; the MPC variant does generative rollouts.

title: Safe Control with Neural Network Dynamic Models
evidence: Sec. 4.1 and 4.3: each step solves a one-step mixed-integer program for the control closest to the reference that satisfies the synthesised safety index, so an unsafe reference control is replaced online.
method: MIND encodes a ReLU neural network dynamics model as mixed-integer constraints and solves a one-step safe tracking problem online; SIS synthesises a feasible safety index offline with CMA-ES.
evaluation: Three learned unicycle NNDMs, 100 collision-avoidance and 100 safe-following tasks; baselines shooting with 10^3-10^5 samples and Ipopt; learned index 0% violation and 0% infeasible vs 100% and 56% for the original; 0.36-2s per step on a 24-core Threadripper.
contribution: Synthesises a persistently feasible safety index offline and enforces it online as a mixed-integer program over a neural network dynamics model, giving zero safety violations with near-exact tracking.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: partly - the dynamics model is a neural network, but the nominal controller is a hand-designed reference tracker and no learned policy is being guarded, so the scope ruling is borderline and a maintainer could read this as classical safe control over a learned model. Criterion (d) is weak: per-step solve times of 0.36-2s on a 24-core desktop with an arbitrary 2s cutoff, no deadline, no jitter analysis and no edge hardware, so (d) and the latency cell may both be dropped. Single agent with obstacles, not multi-agent. Evaluation rolls out the same NNDM used for control, so there is no model mismatch and the authors concede violations may occur if the NNDM differs from the true dynamics (Sec. 6).

title: CUP: A Conservative Update Policy Algorithm for Safe Reinforcement Learning
evidence: Sec 1.1: the second step "projects the policy back onto the safe region to reconcile the constraint violation" - a projection of policy parameters during training, not of actions at execution.
method: CUP: two-step constrained policy optimisation; GAE-based surrogate improvement with KL penalty, then primal-dual projection of the policy toward the CMDP constraint set. Training-time only.
evaluation: 5 MuJoCo tasks (Ant, Hopper, Swimmer, Humanoid, Humanoid-Circle), 10 seeds; baselines CPO, TRPO-L, PPO-L, FOCOPS; return and expected cost vs limit; no latency; 40-core Xeon, 4x RTX 3080.
contribution: Proposes a conservative two-step policy update for constrained RL with surrogate bounds based on generalised advantage estimation, reaching higher return at near-limit cost than CPO, PPO-L, TRPO-L and FOCOPS on MuJoCo tasks.
flag: Training-time constrained RL only; no execution-time filter, single agent, no human. Table 1 e.g. Ant return 1743.66 at cost 99.11 (limit 103.12). Sec 6.1 says CUP and FOCOPS enforce constraints in all experiments but Table 1 shows FOCOPS Hopper cost 102.3 vs limit 82.75. Sensitivity results are figures only; no component ablation.

title: Configuration-Aware Safe Control for Mobile Robotic Arm with Control Barrier Functions
evidence: Sec. IV-B, Theorem 1: a QP computes the input closest to the nominal waypoint-tracking input subject to one CBF constraint per arm edge point - "we only need to keep the chosen corner points safe".
method: CBF-QP safety filter for a mobile manipulator: edge points at joint centres are each constrained to stay inside a sequence of convex obstacle-free sets, minimally modifying a nominal proportional controller.
evaluation: Simulation only: rod in maze and 3- and 4-joint arm among random obstacles; no baselines or ablations; only numbers are computation time 0.0220-0.0292 s for 1-4 joints (CVXGEN), hardware not stated.
contribution: Configuration-aware control-barrier-function filter that keeps a mobile robotic arm's joint points inside convex free-space sets, shown in simulation with 22-29 ms computation time.
flag: Meets (a) as a runtime filter but fails minimum evaluation: no quantitative safety metric (min distance is only plotted in Fig. 10, no collision or violation counts) and no baseline or ablation; safety is asserted qualitatively. Single robot, static obstacles, no humans. TX2 and D435 hardware is described but NOT used - simulation only, so no edge-deployment cell. Timing figures do not say per-solve or per-cycle nor on what machine. Edge-point count is inconsistent between text and Fig. 10; transitions between convex sets are not covered by the proof. Abstract has no numbers.

title: Fleet-DAgger: Interactive Robot Fleet Learning with Scalable Human Supervision
evidence: Sec. 4.1: humans are assigned to the highest-priority robots, and "if a robot has priority p(.) = 0, it does not receive assistance even if a human is available"; Sec. 1: robots "cede control" to remote human supervisors.
method: Interactive Fleet Learning: priority functions (constraint violation, uncertainty, safety-critic risk) allocate M remote humans to N robots, which cede control for teleoperation or hard reset; data aggregated DAgger-style.
evaluation: Isaac Gym, 100 robots/10 humans, 3 tasks; 4 ABB YuMi arms/2 humans. Baselines BC, Random, Fleet-EnsembleDAgger, Fleet-ThriftyDAgger; ablations. Successes, hard resets, idle time, ROHE up to 8.8x. No latency.
contribution: Formalises allocation of scarce human teleoperators across a robot fleet and proposes Fleet-DAgger priority functions, achieving up to 8.8x higher return on human effort than baselines.
flag: Quotes relayed by the WebFetch reader model from the full PDF text, not seen raw - verify wording before publishing. Abstract's 'up to 8.8x higher ROHE' has no absolute ROHE value in the body text - curves are in figures only; could not locate the number outside the abstract. Table 2 (post-training, mean): Humanoid C.U.R. 771.0 successes/289.3 hard resets/1446.7 idle vs Random 746.3/340.0/1700.0, Fleet-ED 617.7/570.3/2851.7, BC 0.0/11925.3/62473.7; Anymal C.U.R. 257.0/64.3/321.7 vs Fleet-ED 257.3/109.0/545.0, Random 207.3/232.3/1162.3; AllegroHand C.U.R. 6032.7/2343.7/11715.0 vs Random 7360.3/2954.3/14767.7, Fleet-TD 4296.3/1397.7/6988.0, Fleet-ED 3032.0/1764.7/8818.0 - so Random beats C.U.R. on successes and Fleet-ED/TD have fewer hard resets on AllegroHand. Physical results differ 'by a small margin' with no numbers in text. Doubts: deferral is a learned request-for-help allocation, not a veto on a specific action, so runtime_interceptor yes is generous; robots are independent with a shared policy, so I did NOT credit the multi-agent state cell; supervisors in simulation are PPO agents, not people; Sec. 7 assumes perfect situational awareness, no switching latency and no network latency. Minimum teleoperation time tT and reset time tR are in timesteps, not seconds. Interface described as keyboard (Sec. 6.3) and OpenCV GUI (App. 8.3.3).

title: Enforcing Hard Constraints with Soft Barriers: Safe Reinforcement Learning in Unknown Stochastic Environments
evidence: Sec 3.1: "We encode the hard safety chance constraint by the generative-model-based soft barrier function"; Sec 1: "our approach cannot provide a hard barrier and hence no deterministic safety guarantee".
method: Jointly learns a generative SDE environment model, a soft barrier function and a policy; the barrier penalty is back-propagated into policy optimisation to satisfy a reachability-based safety chance constraint.
evaluation: 2D SDE, Cartpole, rocket landing, UAV; 500 simulations; vs PPO-L and FOCOPS; safe rate 99.9/100/100/100% vs PPO-L 98.9/89.3/96.4/100%; training 8 h to 1 day; no latency.
contribution: Safe model-based reinforcement learning that enforces hard chance constraints through a soft barrier function trained with a generative model, improving empirical safe rates over CMDP baselines.
flag: Safety enters only through training (Algorithm 1 is a training loop); no shield, filter or veto at execution, so (a) fails under the strictly-runtime rule. The learned generative model is single-agent and not over graphs or multi-agent state, so (b) fails too. Quantitative safe rates with baselines do exist, so the exclusion is on topic, not evaluation. FOCOPS baseline was run with a tightened cost threshold (FOCOPS*). No ablations. Reported practical safety lower bounds (86.6-97.6%) are post-hoc, not runtime.

title: Safe Control Under Input Limits with Neural Control Barrier Functions
evidence: Sec 2: the CBF-QP controller "simply filters (modifies) a nominal controller online"; the learned neural CBF defines the safe set and the QP constraint acts at the safe-set boundary.
method: Learns a neural control barrier function offline via counterexample-guided training so a feasible input exists under input saturation; deployed as a CBF-QP filter modifying a nominal controller online.
evaluation: Simulated 10D quadcopter-pendulum, 5K rollouts, 3 nominal controllers; baselines hand-designed CBF (CMA-ES) and safe MPC; forward-invariance rate, saturation, safe-set volume; RTX 2080 Ti training; no online latency.
contribution: Synthesises neural control barrier functions that respect input limits, giving a runtime CBF-QP filter with 99.0-99.6% forward-invariant rollouts versus 78.7-80.3% for a hand-designed CBF and a safe set about 12x larger than safe MPC.
flag: Borderline E4: single agent, simulation only, known deterministic dynamics; filter modifies rather than halts, and a slack variable means guarantees can be violated under saturation (footnote 1). Safe MPC is on par on invariance (99.06/99.54/99.44%); the advantage is volume. Inconsistencies: MPC volume 0.08 in Table 1 vs 8.4% in text; training time about 2 h in main text vs 14 +- 4 h in appendix; 1M vs 2.5M volume samples. Robustness drops to 85.84% at noise variance 10 and 53.33% at inertia x5. No per-step solve time reported.

title: Attacking Cooperative Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning by Adversarial Minority Influence
evidence: Sec. 5.3: 'our AMI outperforms the competing methods in 10 out of 12 environments' - one adversarial agent drives MAPPO-trained cooperative teams into worst-case joint behaviour in SMAC, multi-agent MuJoCo and a 10-robot swarm.
method: Adversarial Minority Influence trains one black-box adversarial agent using a unilateral mutual-information influence filter and a targeted adversarial oracle to push fixed cooperative MARL victims toward worst-case joint actions.
evaluation: Six SMAC and six multi-agent MuJoCo tasks plus 10 e-puck2 robots; baselines Gleave, Wu, Guo and GMA; best in 10 of 12 tasks and 5.43 better than the best real-world baseline; ablations on the unilateral and targeted terms.
contribution: Shows that a single adversarial agent can collapse cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning, with the first such attack demonstrated on a real ten-robot swarm.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: the system analysed is learned (MAPPO victims), but nothing is guarded - this is an attack only, with no detector, shield, monitor or defence, and 'during execution the attacker acts on its own without the guidance of TAO' (Sec. 4.2). Criterion (a) fails outright and (c) holds only if 'multi-agent hazard' is read as induced emergent failure rather than detection, so this is the record in the batch most likely to be overturned to exclude-E1. Win rates and rewards appear only in Figs. 4, 6 and 9-12; the only in-text figures are the 5.43 margin and 10 of 12 environments, and no defence or mitigation is evaluated.

title: ART: Automatic multi-step reasoning and tool-use for large language models
evidence: Sec 3.4: human feedback is optional library editing - "users edit existing programs rather than creating programs from scratch" - with no safety check on tool calls.
method: ART: frozen LLM generates multi-step reasoning programs from a retrieved task library, pausing generation at tool calls (search, Codex, Python) and resuming with the tool output.
evaluation: BigBench (15 library, 19 unseen tasks), 6 MMLU tasks, Toolformer tasks; baselines few-shot, Auto-CoT, ART without tools, GPT-3 best, Toolformer; task accuracy only; no hardware or latency.
contribution: Automates multi-step reasoning and tool use for a frozen LLM via a task and tool library, improving accuracy over few-shot prompting and Auto-CoT on unseen BigBench and MMLU tasks.
flag: Capability paper, no safety content: no hazard, violation or unsafe-tool-call metric, no veto or deferral; single LLM. Human feedback is offline program editing by one author on 5 failing instances per task (Table 6, 79.85 avg), not a takeover. Generated code is run via Python exec with no risk analysis. Text says MMLU gain is +8.5 over few-shot but Table 3 shows +14.6 (8.5 is the GPT-3 best delta). Other gains: +14.90 library tasks, +6.9 test tasks, 10.8 average on unseen tasks.

title: Consolidated Control Barrier Functions: Synthesis and Online Verification via Adaptation under Input Constraints
evidence: Full text not read: arXiv PDF could not be fetched.
method: Not extracted (PDF unreadable).
evaluation: Not extracted (PDF unreadable).
contribution: Not extracted: full text could not be retrieved from arXiv.
flag: PDF could not be read: five fetch attempts (plain URL three times, then v2 and v1) over roughly 12 minutes all returned a rate-limit error. E6 is procedural, not a judgement of the paper; runtime_interceptor=no and the methods tags are placeholders from the title only. Title suggests a CBF safety filter with online verification, so (a) is plausible: re-queue for full-text retrieval.

title: Voyager: An Open-Ended Embodied Agent with Large Language Models
evidence: "If the agent gets stuck after 4 rounds of code generation, then we query the curriculum for another task." (Sec. 2.3) - the critic checks task success after environment.step(code), not before execution.
method: LLM-driven Minecraft agent: automatic curriculum, growing skill library of executable code, iterative prompting with environment feedback, execution errors and post-hoc self-verification.
evaluation: Minecraft (MineDojo); baselines ReAct, Reflexion, AutoGPT; 63 unique items in 160 iterations (3.3x), tech tree 15.3x/8.5x/6.4x faster; ablations; no hardware or latency.
contribution: Voyager is a GPT-4 lifelong-learning Minecraft agent with an automatic curriculum and code skill library; it is a capability paper with no safety mechanism or safety metric.
flag: Single agent, no safety claim; self-verification is post-execution task-success checking, not interception. Human-as-critic (Sec. 3.5) is task feedback, not takeover. Only first 100k of 122k characters read (Appendix B on experiment details not read); hardware not found in the part read.

title: SafeDiffuser: Safe Planning with Diffusion Probabilistic Models
evidence: Sec. 1: "The computed path is combined with simulation to validate that it can be safely actuated"; Sec. 7: "There is also a gap between planning and control using diffusion models."
method: Treats denoising as a dynamical system in diffusion time and solves a minimum-deviation CBF quadratic program after each diffusion step so the generated trajectory satisfies specifications (three variants).
evaluation: Maze2D, MuJoCo Walker2D and Hopper, PyBullet 7-joint arm; vs Diffuser, Truncate, classifier guidance; specification satisfaction score, task score, seconds per diffusion step; RTX-3090 for training.
contribution: Embeds control-barrier-function quadratic programs into every denoising step so diffusion planners emit specification-satisfying trajectories, at roughly 3-15 times the per-step sampling time of plain Diffuser.
flag: The CBF is a constraint INSIDE the planner sampling loop, not between a decision and its execution, so (a) is not met under the strict runtime rule; single-agent, generative, no human, no latency constraint. If you treat the per-denoising-step QP as a filter this becomes an E4-vs-include argument. Safety is reported as satisfaction scores (Maze: Diffuser -0.983/-0.894, RoS -2.4e-7/-6.0e-7, i.e. not strictly non-negative), not violation rates. Time 0.106 s/step vs 0.007 for Diffuser in Maze. Table 2 Walker2D baseline spec cells were garbled in my read. Inference hardware not stated. Read in one fetch pass.

title: Model-Assisted Probabilistic Safe Adaptive Control With Meta-Bayesian Learning
evidence: Sec. 2/Eq. 4 and Def. 3.1: a CBF-QP minimises ||u - u_ref||^2 subject to a CBF constraint using the pessimistic bound (mean minus beta times std) from a meta-learned Bayesian model.
method: MAP-SAC: meta-learned adaptive Bayesian linear regression estimates uncertainty in a CBF constraint; probabilistic CBF-QP safety filter overrides nominal control, with optional online sampling.
evaluation: Simulation: single 2D point mass with unknown drift, 1-3 obstacles. Baselines CBF-OPT, CBF-RUST, GP2-SAC. Results qualitative (trajectory plots); no numeric safety rate, no hardware or timing.
contribution: Combines meta-learned Bayesian regression with probabilistic control barrier functions to give a less conservative safety filter under model uncertainty, shown on a simulated point-mass with obstacles.
flag: Quotes relayed by the WebFetch reader model from the full PDF text, not seen raw - verify wording before publishing. Genuine runtime safety filter but single-agent, and the text reports no numeric safety metric (figures were not readable by the fetcher, so numbers could exist only in plots - check Figs. 3-7). E2 on minimum evaluation; E4 is an equally defensible code (single-agent filter, no sequential, latency or handoff aspect). Theorem 3.1 needs beta >= Gamma, but experiments use beta = 1.96 (Sec. 3.3.4), so the stated guarantee does not cover the experiments. Human-assisted control is offline data collection only, not (e). Only timing figure is a 10 Hz sampling rate; O(D^3 n^2) vs O(n^3) complexity claim is not measured.

title: Identifying the Risks of LM Agents with an LM-Emulated Sandbox
evidence: Sec. 3-4 (paraphrase): an LM emulates tool execution so risky LM-agent trajectories can be elicited without real effects, and an LM safety evaluator scores the completed trajectory afterwards.
method: LM-emulated sandbox simulates 311 tools in 36 toolkits for tool-calling LM agents; an adversarial emulator steers toward risky states; LM evaluators score safety and helpfulness 0-3 post hoc.
evaluation: 144 curated cases, 9 risk types. Failure incidence: GPT-4 39.4%, Claude-2 44.3%, ChatGPT-3.5 62.0%, GPT-4 safety prompt 23.9%, NoAct 0%. Evaluator kappa 0.478 vs human 0.480. No latency.
contribution: ToolEmu emulates tool execution with an LM so risky LM-agent trajectories can be elicited and scored at scale, quantifying failure incidence across agents and safety prompts.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - LLM tool-calling agents are the system analysed. No runtime override exists (emulator and evaluator are offline), so (a) fails and (c) rests on the "safety evaluation of LLM agents" clause with a single agent, not peer agents: check whether that is (c) or exclude-E4 wrong level. Real-world replication covered only 7 Terminal cases, and the emulator itself had an 8.1-14.4% critical-issue rate, which bounds how much the failure percentages mean.

title: Rule-Based Lloyd Algorithm for Multi-Robot Motion Planning and Control with Safety and Convergence Guarantees
evidence: Sec. 3-4 (paraphrase): each robot's motion is confined to its own Lloyd cell, so collision freedom is proved by construction (Theorem 1) rather than by intercepting a nominal action, and success rate is the measured outcome.
method: Rule-based Lloyd coverage control: neighbour-weighted cells with rules adapting spreading factor and attraction point; optional PPO layer (LLB) sets those parameters; unicycle and car-like MPC variants.
evaluation: Crossing-circle and random-room sims to N=300, plus JetRacer, Jackal, Dingo and 7 drones. Success rate 1.00 vs RVO2 0.65 and SBC and GCBF+ 0.00; compute 2-10 ms, MPC adds 16 ms. No collision rate.
contribution: Rule-based Lloyd controller gives collision-free, deadlock-free multi-robot motion with proved convergence without communication, scaling to 300 simulated robots and tested on ground and aerial platforms.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: partly - the main RBL controller is hand-designed classical control (Pillar 1 ruling: E1), but the LLB variant wraps a PPO policy whose outputs are clipped and projected by the Lloyd layer at runtime, lifting success rate from 0.04-0.94 to 1.00. (c) also fails the primacy test: no collision rate is reported and the measured outcome is success rate, i.e. deadlock and convergence. Most likely overturn in this batch if the maintainer reads LLB as a runtime safety layer on a learned policy.

title: AI Control: Improving Safety Despite Intentional Subversion
evidence: Sec. 3 (paraphrase): trusted monitoring audits the 2% most suspicious GPT-4 solutions, submits the trusted model's solution instead when suspicion crosses a threshold, and shuts down to trusted-only once a backdoor is confirmed.
method: Control evaluation of protocols gating an untrusted GPT-4 coder: GPT-3.5 suspicion monitoring, deferral to trusted, trusted editing, untrusted monitoring with redaction and paraphrasing, under a 2% audit budget.
evaluation: 1500 APPS problems vs a red-team backdoor attack policy. Safety/usefulness percent: trusted-only 100/2, upfront audit 15/100, trusted monitoring 62/97, plus defer 83/93, trusted editing 92/94. No latency.
contribution: AI-control evaluations pit safety protocols against a red-team attack policy, showing trusted monitoring with deferral or trusted editing raises safety from 15% to 92% at small usefulness cost.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - an untrusted GPT-4 policy is vetoed, deferred or edited at submission time, so (a) is clear. (c) rests on the LLM-agent-safety clause and on a pipeline of untrusted model, monitor and auditor rather than peer agents. The scarce "human" auditor is itself simulated by GPT-4 under a 2% budget, so check the human handoff gap cell and whether (e) should be added. Safety is a probability over a simulated 5000-problem deployment extrapolated from 1500 problems with backdoor attempts downsampled 1/12.

title: Neural Differentiable Integral Control Barrier Functions for Unknown Nonlinear Systems with Input Constraints
evidence: Sec 4 (Implementation), Eq. 10: the safe input is the imitation controller output plus a correction from the closed-form ICBF-QP solution, "v* = q/||p||^2 p if q > 0, otherwise 0".
method: Learns a neural ODE dynamics model, an NMPC-imitating controller and a neural integral CBF; at runtime a closed-form ICBF-QP correction is added to the nominal input.
evaluation: Simulation only: vehicle and quadrotor-pendulum with obstacles; vs NMPC, ORCA-MAPF, CADRL; computation time 0.736 s vs 5.562 s (NMPC) and cost 4.631 vs 4.583; no safety rate; no hardware.
contribution: Learns a neural integral control barrier function with a dynamics model and an imitation controller, filtering inputs in closed form for unknown non-control-affine systems under input constraints.
flag: Meets (a) as a runtime filter but reports NO quantitative safety metric (no collision, violation or safe rate), only computation time and cost over 100 initial states, so it fails the v1.6 minimum. No ablation. Learned ICBF is unverified (authors say it may not meet the conditions throughout the domain). Single agent; multi-agent is future work. Hardware and obstacle count not stated; what the timing covers is unclear (seconds, not per-step). NMPC reference omits collision and input constraints.

title: Feedback Loops With Language Models Drive In-Context Reward Hacking
evidence: Sec. 4-5 (paraphrase): on ToolEmu's 144 tool-use tasks, injected environment errors drive the agent to commit more constraint violations over successive rounds, and engagement optimisation raises toxicity across dialogue turns.
method: Empirical study defining in-context reward hacking; output-refinement and policy-refinement feedback loops measured with LLM evaluators, Perspective API toxicity and ToolEmu constraint violations. No mitigation mechanism is proposed.
evaluation: 80 dialogue cases, 100 Twitter topics, 144 ToolEmu tasks; GPT-3.5, GPT-4, Claude-3. Violations, helpfulness and toxicity all rise with 0-3 injected error rounds vs zero-cycle baseline; results in figures only.
contribution: Shows LLM agents refining outputs or policies against feedback drift into in-context reward hacking, raising toxicity and constraint violations that safety prompting and larger models fail to prevent.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - LLM agents are the system studied, but nothing guards them: no monitor, shield or deferral, so (a) fails and (c) rests on the LLM-agent-safety clause with mostly single-agent setups (the multi-agent competition is one appendix figure). Evaluation floor is marginal: I checked the body and appendices and every result is a plot, with no exact violation, toxicity or significance value stated in text or any table, so exclude-E2 is a live option; the ranges I give are axis ranges read from figure captions.

title: Uniformly Safe RL with Objective Suppression for Multi-Constraint Safety-Critical Applications
evidence: Sec. 4.3: "we build our method on top of Recovery RL by enforcing our Objective Suppression objective (6) on both the task and recovery policy"; Sec. 3: "The safety layer overwrites the proposed actions that are deemed unsafe according to the safety critic"
method: Objective Suppression: task-reward gradient is down-weighted by exp(-kappa*sum of risk critics) under a uniformly-constrained MDP; applied to task and recovery policies of Recovery RL, whose critic-gated switch is inherited.
evaluation: Safe Mujoco-Ant (20M steps, 5 seeds) and CARLA Safe Bench (200k steps, 3 seeds) vs Reward Penalty and Recovery RL; collisions, collapse, out-of-lane, reward; no hardware or latency.
contribution: Soft suppression of the task objective by multiple risk critics on top of Recovery RL cuts Safe Bench collisions from 0.24 to 0.078 per episode, at a one-third loss in task reward.
flag: BORDERLINE on (a): the novel part is a training-time gradient reweighting, which alone does not meet (a); the runtime override is the inherited Recovery RL task/recovery switch and the paper never states explicitly how gating runs at deployment - if you read (a) by contribution this is exclude-E1. Single-agent only. Ant: collisions 6.47->4.36 (kappa=3), 2.93 (kappa=1), reward 1279.62->1215.49; Safe Bench out-of-lane 33.35->13.04, reward 124.80->83.17 which the text calls a small decrease (it is about 33%). Table 1 shows identical reward std 143.40 for two rows, possible typo. Fleet claims (2% collision-rate and 38% harsh-braking improvement) are text-only on proprietary data with no table. No formal ablation beyond kappa. Read in one fetch pass.

title: Here Comes The AI Worm: Unleashing Zero-click Worms that Target GenAI-Powered Applications
evidence: The guardrail "alerts the user to the potential presence of malicious content, allowing them to review and decide whether to send the generated content" (Sec. 5.3)
method: Morris-II: adversarial self-replicating prompts that spread zero-click through RAG email assistants; plus Virtual Donkey guardrail classifying input-output similarity (BLEU, ROUGE-L, METEOR) to flag propagation.
evaluation: LangChain email client, 20 Enron users, 2000 emails, Gemini 1.5 Flash and others; propagation about 20 percent per email; guardrail TPR 1.0 at FPR 0.015; ablations; no hardware or latency.
contribution: Demonstrates a self-replicating prompt worm cascading across RAG-based GenAI email assistants and a similarity-based guardrail that flags propagation for user review at TPR 1.0 and FPR 0.015.
flag: Primarily an ATTACK paper; the defence is secondary and it alerts a user rather than blocking automatically, so runtime_interceptor yes and (a)/(e) rest on defer-to-user-review only - maintainer may prefer c alone. No human-subject study of the handoff. Guardrail has no external baseline (only three classifiers and feature subsets compared) and adaptive attacks are untested (Sec. 6). OOD results are much weaker than the headline: at the TPR 1.0 threshold FPR is 0.822 (phishing payload) and 0.877 (Walmart payload), 0.486 for unseen jailbreaks; Clinton dataset TPR 0.936, FPR 0.123. Some per-route and per-engine values exist only in figures and were not read. Latency described as minimal but never measured. Read in one fetch covering the whole PDF.

title: DeepSafeMPC: Deep Learning-Based Model Predictive Control for Safe Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
evidence: Sec. 4, Algorithm 1 (paraphrase): the MAPPO actor's joint actions are taken as the initial guess for a centralised SQP MPC that re-optimises them under state and action constraints before the action sequence is applied.
method: MAPPO actor proposes joint actions; a learned MLP state predictor is rolled out over horizon T; a centralised SQP MPC refines the action sequence under safety constraints before execution.
evaluation: Safe Multi-Agent MuJoCo 2-agent Ant, Swimmer, HalfCheetah. Only baseline is MAPPO without MPC: cost falls from over 900 to 600 (read from Fig. 3), predictor error under 0.0015. Xeon 6254 and 4 A5000; no latency.
contribution: DeepSafeMPC inserts a learned-dynamics MPC layer after a MAPPO policy, re-optimising joint actions against safety constraints and cutting constraint cost on Safe Multi-Agent MuJoCo tasks.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - a MAPPO policy is filtered at execution time, so (a) holds. Evaluation is thin and may fail the floor: one ablation baseline only, no other safe-MARL method, the safety figure is only readable off Fig. 3 (cost over 900 to 600), no violation or collision rate, no horizon T and no runtime; cost is defined as speed magnitude in Eq. 18 but as a threshold indicator in Eq. 19, and Theorem 4.2 is an informal assumption-bounded argument. Criterion (b) is arguable via the MLP next-state predictor but it has no baseline. Algorithm 1 applies the whole optimised sequence, so receding-horizon operation is unclear.

title: Constrained Reinforcement Learning with Smoothed Log Barrier Function
evidence: Abstract: the method works by "applying a linear smoothed log barrier function to an additional safety critic" - a term in the SAC actor loss, not an execution-time check.
method: CSAC-LB: soft actor-critic with a safety cost critic whose output passes through a linear smoothed log barrier in the actor loss (factor mu=2). Training-time penalty only.
evaluation: Safety Gym PointGoal1 and Unitree A1 locomotion in MuJoCo, 5 seeds, zero-shot transfer to a real A1; baselines SAC reward shaping, SAC-Lagrangian, WCSAC-0.5; curves only, no tabulated numbers; no latency.
contribution: Adds a smoothed log-barrier on a safety critic to soft actor-critic for constrained RL without pre-training, evaluated on Safety Gym and quadruped locomotion with zero-shot transfer to a real Unitree A1.
flag: Barrier is a training-loss term, which the protocol says does not meet (a); single agent, no human. Results are in Figs 3, 4 and 6 only - I found no numeric return, cost or violation values in the text, and no ablation. WCSAC runs stopped at about 20% of training for numerical issues. The "protective shield" in Fig 1 is physical hardware protection, not a safety shield. Compute platform not reported.

title: Foundation Models to the Rescue: Deadlock Resolution in Connected Multi-Robot Systems
evidence: Sec. I: the foundation-model planner "does not lead to a violation of safety as it is taken care of by the provably safe low-level" controller; Sec. V-A: "the reach rate for just the low-level controller is exactly 0".
method: On deadlock (low mean speed, far from goals) an LLM or VLM picks a leader and waypoints; robots follow in formation under a GCBF+ graph-network controller keeping safety and connectivity.
evaluation: Room (5 agents) and Maze (25, 50 agents) simulations vs A* and random planners; reach rate, interventions, tokens, query time (figures only); four Turtlebot3 demo; no collision metric.
contribution: Uses LLMs and VLMs as high-level planners that assign a leader and waypoints to pull connected multi-robot teams out of deadlock, leaving collision safety to a GCBF+ low-level controller.
flag: Fails the (c) primacy test: primary claim and primary outcome are deadlock resolution and reach rate; collisions are never measured and safety is assumed from the inherited GCBF+ controller. Nothing vetoes or checks the LLM output before execution. Nearly all numbers are in box plots (Figs 3,9,10,11); text gives only random planner below 0.5 reach rate and about 1000 tokens per VLM intervention; query latency plotted but not stated numerically. multi-agent state cell credited because the low-level policy is a graph network over 5-50 robots; drop it if cells are reserved for included papers. Read in one fetch pass.

title: Gameplay Filters: Robust Zero-Shot Safety through Adversarial Imagination
evidence: "otherwise, the filter selects the fallback safety policy" (Sec. 3.2) - the filter imagines a rollout of the candidate task action against a learned adversary and switches to the fallback before the action is applied.
method: Reach-avoid safety filter: offline adversarial self-play (ISAACS) learns fallback and disturbance policies; at runtime a simulated gameplay rollout (H=300 steps, 3 s) decides task action vs fallback.
evaluation: Two quadrupeds (Spirit S40, Go2), physical tug and terrain tests plus 1000-game PyBullet study; baselines critic filter, task policy, RARL, SAC; safe runs 7/10 vs 4/10 vs 0/10.
contribution: A rollout-based reach-avoid safety filter that overrides a quadruped's task policy when an imagined adversarial game is lost, keeping 10/10 terrain runs safe versus 5/10 for a critic filter.
flag: Single robot, not multi-agent (the adversary is a disturbance model). Latency cell is weak: filter runs offboard on one i7-1185G7 core, called about 3.5 times per second, wireless round trip about 70 percent of latency, but no ms figure and no latency-aware design; maintainer may drop the cell. Filter frequency 0.17 (tug) and 0.19 (terrain) is the only false-halt proxy. Under the worst-case BUST adversary the filter's sim safe rate is only 0.03 (Table 4). Small n (10 runs per condition). Read in one fetch that covered the whole PDF; table values not re-checked by a second pass.

title: Unified End-to-End V2X Cooperative Autonomous Driving
evidence: "both predictions and ground truth indicate an accident and the distance between colliding objects is below the threshold" (Sec. III, accident prediction post-processing)
method: V2X end-to-end network: ResNet-101 and BEVFormer queries fuse ego and roadside BEV features by deformable attention for joint detection, tracking and motion prediction; accidents flagged by post-hoc polygon distance threshold.
evaluation: No results at all: Sections IV Experiments and V Conclusion are empty in the v1 PDF, running straight into References. DeepAccident (CARLA) named as testbed only; no baselines, no metrics, no hardware, no latency; abstract states no numbers.
contribution: Proposes UniE2EV2X, one network fusing vehicle and roadside BEV features by deformable attention for joint detection, tracking, motion prediction and post-hoc accident flagging on DeepAccident.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: no - nothing is guarded; this is a learned perception and prediction pipeline with a post-hoc collision check and no runtime override, so (a) fails and (b) is a plain trajectory regressor. Check whether a later version with results exists: as fetched (two PDF fetches plus the abstract page) the paper reports zero quantitative and zero formal results, which is the evaluation floor failure.

title: GuardAgent: Safeguard LLM Agents by a Guard Agent via Knowledge-Enabled Reasoning
evidence: "The outputs or actions proposed by the target agent will be admitted by GuardAgent if Ol = 0 or denied if Ol = 1" (Sec. 4.1)
method: Guard LLM agent plans from retrieved demonstrations, generates guardrail code calling a toolbox (CheckAccess, CheckRules), and executes it to admit or deny a target agent's proposed output or action.
evaluation: EICU-AC (316, EHRAgent) and Mind2Web-SC (200, SeeAct); baselines LlamaGuard, hardcoded rules, LLM-as-guard; GPT-4 label accuracy 98.7 and 90.0 percent; latency 45.4 s and 37.3 s.
contribution: GuardAgent guards other LLM agents by generating and executing guardrail code that admits or denies their actions, reaching 98.7 and 90.0 percent accuracy without degrading the target agent's task performance.
flag: Borderline E4: one guard checking one target agent's single input/output pair per call, no multi-agent or sequential state; maintainer should decide whether the LLM-agent clause of (c) carries it. The paper does not state clearly that the check blocks synchronously before the action takes effect (it speaks of parallel deployment and reading input/output logs). Latency is tens of seconds (GPT-4 45.4 s vs target agent 31.9 s on EICU-AC; Llama3-70B 10.1 s), far from any real-time budget; I did not tick latency/jitter aware because latency is reported, not designed for. Final response accuracy 100 percent is the no-utility-loss evidence for RQ5. Hardware not stated. Category count inconsistent in paper (51 vs 50). Read in one fetch covering the whole PDF.

title: Current state of LLM Risks and AI Guardrails
evidence: "This work explores the risks associated with deploying LLMs and evaluates current approaches" (Abstract/Introduction) - a literature overview with no experiments.
method: Narrative overview of LLM risks (bias, agentic systems, hallucination, privacy) and guardrail strategies organised as a layered gatekeeper, knowledge-anchor and parametric protection model.
evaluation: None: no experiments, benchmarks or measured values; Table 1 only maps risks to mitigations with citations; open-source tools (NeMo-Guardrails, LlamaGuard, Guardrails AI) are described, not tested.
contribution: An overview of LLM deployment risks and existing guardrail tooling, proposing a layered protection framing without any new mechanism or evaluation.
flag: Survey-style overview; would also fail E2 (no evaluation). Fail-safes and manual human override are mentioned only in passing (Sec. 2.4.2). Paper contains a date slip (refers to December 2024 though submitted June 2024). Background reading at most.

title: AgentDojo: A Dynamic Environment to Evaluate Prompt Injection Attacks and Defenses for LLM Agents
evidence: the prompt injection detector runs on every tool output and "aborts the agent's execution" when an injection is flagged, while the tool filter removes tools before untrusted data is seen (Sec. 4, defenses)
method: Dynamic benchmark environment for tool-calling LLM agents: four environments, 70 tools, 97 user tasks, 27 injection tasks, 629 security cases; deterministic state-based utility and targeted-attack scoring; four defenses.
evaluation: GPT-4o undefended: benign utility 69.0%, utility under attack 50.0%, targeted ASR 57.7%. Defenses: PI detector ASR 7.95% but utility 41.5%, tool filter 6.84%, repeat prompt 27.8%, delimiting 41.7%. 10 models (Claude 3.5 Sonnet best, 78.2% utility). About US$35 per security run; no latency reported.
contribution: AgentDojo, a dynamic benchmark of 97 user tasks and 27 injection tasks over four tool-calling environments, measuring agent utility and targeted attack success under prompt injection and four defenses.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - LLM tool-calling agents. Criterion (a) rests on the evaluated defenses (PI detector aborts execution, tool filter prunes tools pre-execution) rather than on a contributed interceptor, so the maintainer may prefer (c) alone. One agent with tools, not several agents, but the setting is sequential and multi-step so not E4. Internal inconsistencies: abstract says models solve less than 66% of tasks while Table 3 gives 78.2% and 69.0%; text says tool filter 7.5% vs Table 5 6.84%; Max attack claimed about +10% but Table 4 shows 57.55%, below Important message at 57.7%. No latency numbers, so RQ1 scores 0.

title: $R^2$-Guard: Robust Reasoning Enabled LLM Guardrail via Knowledge-Enhanced Logical Reasoning
evidence: Guards "any LLM input/output prompts"; "a corrective action can be triggered to safeguard the LLM-powered systems" (Sec. 1 and 3.1) - the action itself is never implemented or evaluated.
method: Category-specific unsafety classifiers feed probabilistic reasoning (Markov logic network or probabilistic circuit) over human-written safety rules to score a single LLM prompt or response.
evaluation: Six moderation datasets plus jailbreaks on AdvBench; baselines LlamaGuard, OpenAI Mod, ensemble; avg AUPRC 0.869 vs 0.772; UDR 0.987 vs 0.619; one RTX A6000, 1.35-1.45 s per instance.
contribution: R2-Guard combines per-category classifiers with probabilistic logical reasoning to moderate single LLM prompts, beating LlamaGuard by 30.2 percent AUPRC on ToxicChat and 59.5 percent under jailbreaks.
flag: Single-input content-moderation classifier: no agent actions, no multi-agent, sequential, latency-constrained or handoff aspect, and no blocking step is implemented, so E4 (arguably E1). RQ4 scored 2 only for the unseen-category ablation (Sec. 5.3.2), reported in a figure without numbers in the text. Abstract figures 30.2 (some versions say 30.4) and 59.5 percent match Tables 2-3 as relative gains over LlamaGuard (0.909 vs 0.698 PC on ToxicChat; 0.987 vs 0.619 MLN UDR); maintainer should confirm which abstract version is cited. Reasoning-only time 0.0062 s (PC) vs 0.1123 s (MLN), Table 5. Read in one fetch covering the whole PDF.

title: On the Resilience of LLM-Based Multi-Agent Collaboration with Faulty Agents
evidence: the Inspector is "an extra agent that intercepts all messages, checks them, and rewrites erroneous ones", and the Challenger prompts each agent to judge an incoming message as safe or unsafe (Sec. on defenses)
method: AUTOTRANSFORM rewrites an agent profile and AUTOINJECT intercepts inter-agent messages to inject controlled semantic or syntactic errors across linear, flat and hierarchical LLM collaboration topologies; Challenger and Inspector defenses.
evaluation: Six frameworks, GPT-3.5 and GPT-4o plus LLaMA-3.1-70B and o1-Mini, on HumanEval, CIAR, CommonMT and FairEval. Average drops: linear -23.72, flat -10.54, hierarchical -5.51. Self-collab 76.2 clean, 43.3 under AutoTransform, 75.0 with Challenger plus Inspector; Camel 62.2, 32.5, 48.7. Error-rate sweeps on Pm and Pe. No latency.
contribution: Measures how a single faulty LLM agent degrades linear, flat and hierarchical multi-agent systems via automated error injection, and shows Challenger plus Inspector defenses recover most of the lost performance.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - LLM multi-agent collaboration. Criterion (a) is borderline: the Inspector overrides messages at runtime by rewriting them rather than halting or vetoing, and the Challenger only flags, so the maintainer may want (c) alone. The primary metric is a 0-100 task-score drop, not a hazard or violation rate, so (c) primacy and the evaluation floor depend on reading error propagation as the hazard. Abstract claims recovery of up to 96.4% of lost performance; the closest table value is Self-collab 75.0 of 76.2 under AutoTransform. Conclusion cites hierarchical drops of 12.1% and 9.2% while Section 4.1 reports 5.5%.

title: ST-WebAgentBench: A Benchmark for Evaluating Safety and Trustworthiness in Web Agents
evidence: "CuP_t = C_t times 1[sum_d V_d = 0]": a task counts only if completed with zero policy violations, and agents may call ask_the_user or human_in_the_loop to seek consent (Sec. on metrics and action space)
method: Benchmark of 375 web-agent tasks with 3057 policy instances over GitLab, ShoppingAdmin and SuiteCRM; six policy dimensions under an organisation-user-task hierarchy; metrics CuP, pCuP, per-dimension risk ratio, all-pass@k; policies given as advisory prompt context only.
evaluation: Three gpt-4o agents on BrowserGym: AWM CR 33.8% vs CuP 20%, WorkArena-Legacy 26% vs 15%, WebVoyager 12.8% vs 10.3%; mean CR 24.3% vs CuP 15.0%, about a 38% relative drop. CuP falls from 18.2% with one policy to 7.1% above five; risk ratio rises about 0.11 per added policy; dimension ablations; about 4 minutes per task.
contribution: ST-WebAgentBench measures safe task completion for web agents, introducing Completion under Policy and per-dimension risk ratios over six policy dimensions, and shows agents forfeit about 38% of completions to policy violations.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - LLM web agents, but the benchmark only measures them and adds no runtime guard, so (a) fails; Appendix I sketches a policy-validating controller that is never evaluated. Criterion (e) rests on the ask_the_user and human_in_the_loop consent action, whose replies are auto-approved rather than coming from a real person, so the maintainer may drop (e) and with it the human handoff gap cell. One agent, not several, so (c) holds only as safety evaluation of LLM agents. The fetched PDF is a later ICLR 2026 revision with 375 tasks; the queued 2024 v1 was smaller, so these figures may not match the record.

title: MobileSafetyBench: Evaluating Safety of Autonomous Agents in Mobile Device Control
evidence: the agent may call refuse() or ask-consent(), which ends the episode pending user permission, and the refusal rate counts both (Sec. on action space and metrics)
method: 250 Android emulator tasks over 13 apps (100 low-risk, 100 high-risk daily, 50 indirect prompt-injection); measures goal achievement and refusal or consent-seeking; Safety-guided Chain-of-Thought prompting adds an explicit safety-consideration field and guidelines.
evaluation: 11 LLM agents under SeeAct and M3A. GPT-4o 82% low-risk goal achievement, 60% high-risk achievement, 31% high-risk refusal; Claude-3.5-Sonnet 64% refusal; Phi-4 73% refusal on low-risk tasks. Injection resisted in 3 of 50 (GPT-4o), 8 of 50 (Gemini-1.5-Pro), 15 of 50 (Claude-3.5-Sonnet). SCoT raises GPT-4o refusal 6% to 36% with low-risk achievement 84% to 82%; o1 86% refusal at 25.60 s per step vs GPT-4o 4.70 s.
contribution: MobileSafetyBench evaluates mobile device-control agents on 250 Android tasks, showing they often execute high-risk instructions, resist indirect prompt injection poorly, and refuse far more under safety-guided chain-of-thought at little helpfulness cost.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - LLM mobile device-control agents. There is no separate interceptor: refuse() and ask-consent() are the agent's own outputs, so (a) fails the strict runtime test and also the Pillar 3 abstention test, since abstention is measured rather than contributed. Criterion (e) rests on ask-consent, which is auto-approved rather than answered by a real operator. One agent, so (c) holds only as safety evaluation of LLM agents. Per-step latency is reported but is not a constraint, so not (d). The fetched PDF is the AAAI 2026 revision (GPT-5, 250 tasks) and differs from the queued 2024 v1. Table 2 gives SCoT refusal 36%, Table 4 gives 41%, and the text says 28% higher; per-model daily figures are in a figure, so most values are not in the text.

title: SafeWatch: An Efficient Safety-Policy Following Video Guardrail Model with Transparent Explanations
evidence: Fig. 1 caption: SafeWatch "judges videos for safety alignment with a customized policy" - it outputs guardrail flags and an explanation; no action is gated and nothing downstream of a flag is described.
method: MLLM video guardrail (InternVL2-8B backbone) with parallel policy encoding and policy-aware token pruning; outputs multi-label flags plus explanation for a single video input.
evaluation: SafeWatch-Bench (1,420 test videos, real and GenAI) plus 5 existing sets; vs GPT-4o, LlavaGuard, InternVL2; accuracy, F1, AUPRC, explanation score; 3.9 s per video, hardware not stated.
contribution: Video content-moderation guardrail that classifies a single video against a custom policy with explanations: accuracy 72.6 vs 43.4 for GPT-4o on its own benchmark, at 3.9 s per video.

Abstract says 28.2% gain, Sec. 1 gives 29.2% (Real) and 27.2% (GenAI); abstract says 2M videos while Table 20 lists 199,604 train and 1,420 test. Tables 6 and 8 disagree on one adaptability figure (82.7 vs 78.0). Read chars 0-100000 of 149228 (main body and part of appendix); remainder of appendix not read.

title: Agent-SafetyBench: Evaluating the Safety of LLM Agents

method: Benchmark of 2,000 test cases over 349 tool-calling environments plus a finetuned Qwen-2.5-7B scorer that labels completed agent interaction records safe or unsafe.
evaluation: 16 LLM agents; no safety score above 60 percent (best Claude-3-Opus 59.8, mean 38.5); behaviour 30.4 vs content 68.4; scorer 91.5 vs GPT-4o 75.5 percent; defense-prompt ablation; judge trained 4h on 4 A100s.

No runtime interception anywhere (the scorer runs after the interaction completes), so (a) fails and (c) rests entirely on the 'safety evaluation of LLM/tool-calling agents' clause.
