title: MELON: Provable Defense Against Indirect Prompt Injection Attacks in AI Agents
evidence: Sec 4.2: 'MELON operates after LLM generates action At+1 but before execution,' and on detection it terminates the entire agent execution.
method: Training-free runtime detector that re-runs the step with the user task masked and tool outputs consolidated, flagging the pending action when its tool call matches a masked-run call above cosine 0.8.
evaluation: AgentDojo, 629 attack cases, 4 attacks, GPT-4o/o3-mini/Llama-3.3-70B; GPT-4o ASR 16.06 to 0.24 percent vs 5 defenses; FPR 9.28 percent; 4 ablations plus threshold sweep; about 2x model calls, no latency measured.
contribution: MELON detects indirect prompt injection by masked re-execution and halts the agent before the injected tool call executes, cutting attack success from 16.06 to 0.24 percent on AgentDojo.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - it guards an LLM tool-calling agent and vetoes before execution, so (a) is clean and this is the strongest record in the batch. Doubt the title's 'Provable': Sec 3.4.2 derives a Hoeffding bound for an ensemble variant that is NOT the evaluated Algorithm 1, assuming only mu_B < theta < mu_V, with no independence assumption stated - do not cite it as a formal guarantee without checking. No latency or hardware figures at all; overhead is given only as roughly doubling model calls, with the masked run claimed to be parallelisable. Single agent, not multi-agent. Costs are real: benign utility 80.41 to 68.04 percent and 9.28 percent false positives; 72.73 percent of evasions are response-based because only tool calls are monitored.

title: Preventing Rogue Agents Improves Multi-Agent Collaboration
evidence: Sec. 2: the aim is "to learn a signal that indicates a task failure is likely to occur"; when the monitor's P(success) falls below threshold tau it triggers a reset or rollback of the agents' communication (Sec. 4.3).
method: Per-turn monitor (polynomial ridge classifier on entropy, varentropy, kurtosis of agent output distributions plus turn count) predicts task failure and triggers a reset or one-round rollback of communication.
evaluation: WhoDunitEnv (2 variants) and GovSim with GPT-4o, Llama-3.1-70B, Qwen; vs no intervention, random trigger, weaker monitors, single-agent reset; success rate +4.1 to +10.6, GovSim survival 35 to 55; no monitor latency.
contribution: Uncertainty-based live monitor that detects a likely rogue agent in LLM multi-agent collaboration and resets communication, raising task success by 4-11 points and GovSim survival rate from 35% to 55%.
flag: Borderline on two counts. (1) Outcome is task success and resource survival, not a hazard or violation rate - primacy test for (c) and the v1.6 safety-metric requirement are arguable; GovSim collapse is the closest thing to a hazard. (2) Intervention is a restart or rollback of the channel, not a veto of a specific action; Sec. 7 says resets happen "before a problematic action was taken" but check timing is not specified. Abstract "up to 17.4%" is one sub-experiment (Llama, 14 suspects, two resets). No monitor AUC, intervention counts or latency; 20% of failed games never trigger; 24% of 50 inspected triggers unclassifiable. Resets cost 1.4x-1.9x turns. GovSim survival-time gain (+1.2 rounds) could not be read from Table 1. Monitor itself is a non-generative classifier and the paper distinguishes reversible from irreversible state (GovSim), but neither cell is claimed here - maintainer may disagree. Sec. 4.1 vs App. B disagree on attribute count (11 vs 12).

title: Commercial LLM Agents Are Already Vulnerable to Simple Yet Dangerous Attacks
evidence: Sec 3.1: 'we find that they divulge sensitive information such as credit card numbers and addresses in 10 out of 10 trials.'
method: Taxonomy of attacks on LLM agents plus demonstrated attacks on commercial web agents (MultiOn, Anthropic Computer Use) and scientific agents (PaperQA, ChemCrow) needing no machine-learning knowledge.
evaluation: 10 trials per attack: credit-card theft 10/10 via Reddit redirect vs 0/10 direct link; malware download 10/10; phishing 10/10; PaperQA poisoned retrieval 100/100; ChemCrow safeguard bypassed. No latency or hardware.
contribution: Shows that commercial LLM web agents and scientific agents can be driven to leak credit-card data, download and run malware, and phish the user's own contacts by trivial non-technical attacks.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - commercial LLM agents are the systems analysed, but nothing is guarded: no runtime defense is implemented (Sec 6 only sketches whitelisting, user confirmation, logging), so (a) fails and (c) rests on the 'safety evaluation of LLM agents' clause. Sections 2, 5 and 6 are taxonomy, related work and an opposing-views discussion, so a maintainer may call this E3 position/survey; the paper never calls itself either, its closest self-description being 'we argue that LLM-powered agents'. Evidence is thin: 10 trials per cell, the only quantified baseline is direct-link vs Reddit-redirect (0/10 vs 10/10), the Reddit post-content ablation and the ChemCrow trials are unquantified, and MultiOn has no reported rate because the service was offline.

title: Multi-Agent Autonomous Driving Systems with Large Language Models: A Survey of Recent Advances
evidence: Abstract: "This paper provides a frontier survey of LLM-based multi-agent ADSs."; Sec. 1: "we present a comprehensive survey of LLM-based multi-agent systems."
method: Survey and taxonomy of LLM-based multi-agent autonomous driving systems: agent-environment, agent-agent and agent-human interaction paradigms, applications, datasets, open challenges.
evaluation: None: literature survey with no original method, experiment or quantitative evaluation.
contribution: Surveys LLM-based multi-agent autonomous driving systems, organising work by interaction paradigm and noting hallucination, communication-efficiency and remote-inference latency challenges.
flag: Quotes relayed by the WebFetch reader model from the full PDF text, not seen raw - verify wording before publishing. Survey, E3 by rule. Possibly useful for snowballing: Sec. 4 (agent-human interaction), Sec. 3.2 and 5.3 (edge-cloud and remote LLM latency), Sec. 7 (hallucination risks). No takeover/handoff section as such.

title: Prompt Injection Detection and Mitigation via AI Multi-Agent NLP Frameworks
evidence: Sec 3.1: 'The Guard/Sanitizer detects and neutralizes malicious instructions while embedding metadata on detected vulnerabilities.' - it rewrites the response before it is delivered.
method: Four-agent Ollama pipeline (unfiltered Llama-2 generator, Llama-3.1 guard/sanitizer, policy enforcer, KPI evaluator) exchanging OVON JSON utterance plus whisper metadata to neutralise prompt injections.
evaluation: 500 synthetic injection prompts in 10 categories; mean TIVS 0.0506 generator, -0.0684 sanitizer, -0.0932 enforcer; no external baseline, no ablation, no accuracy/precision/recall/FPR, no latency or hardware.
contribution: A layered multi-agent sanitisation pipeline that rewrites prompt-injected LLM responses and self-scores the residual vulnerability, reporting monotonically improving injection scores across three agent stages.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - Llama guard agents sanitise a Llama generator. This is the record I most expect to be overturned to exclude-E2. No agent can halt, veto or block: the pipeline only rewrites and annotates, so (a) is a rewrite-override rather than a veto, and the paper's own 'effectively blocked' example is just the generator refusing on its own. The sole metric, TIVS, is scored by an LLM of the same model family with no ground truth, no human labels and no external baseline - the only comparison is the paper's own undefended stage 1. Aggregate ISR is never reported and is 0.0 at every stage of the one worked example. The Conclusion's headline 'reduced TIVS from -25.31 to -46.62 (a 45.7 percent improvement)' appears in no table and is on a different scale from Table 2 (-0.05 to -0.09) and from Sec 8.3 (0.12 to 0.005); the per-category results the Conclusion claims are never given; the lower-variance claim contradicts Table 3. Sec 9 admits one-shot prompts only, so multi-step injection is untested - also check E4.

title: High-Order Control Barrier Functions: Insights and a Truncated Taylor-Based Formulation
evidence: Sec IV-A: the TTCBF condition is imposed as constraint (24b) of a per-step QP whose objective tracks reference speed and lateral position, so the constraint alters the reference-tracking control near the obstacle.
method: Truncated Taylor CBF: approximates the discrete-time barrier condition by a Taylor expansion to the relative degree, needing one class-K function instead of one per order as in HOCBF.
evaluation: Simulated double-integrator robot avoiding one static circular obstacle, 2 s at dt 0.01 s; baseline standard HOCBF over a parameter sweep; mean x-speed as conservatism metric; QP averages 3 ms per step.
contribution: Reformulates high-order control barrier functions with a truncated Taylor expansion that needs a single class-K function, reducing tuning effort relative to standard HOCBF in a simulated obstacle-avoidance task.
flag: Runtime barrier constraint in a QP, but no quantitative safety metric: no collision count, minimum distance or violation rate, only mean x-speed shown in Figs 2a and 3a, so it fails the minimum evaluation for (a); maintainer may prefer E4 (single robot, one static obstacle, simulation). No separate nominal controller is described - calling it a filter is my reading. The truncation-error term gamma*dt^3 is dropped in experiments, so the formal guarantee is not what was run. The 3 ms solve time is given with no solver or hardware named and no deadline analysis, so I did not credit (d) or the latency cell. Control bounds set to +-1000 m/s^2.

title: ShieldAgent: Shielding Agents via Verifiable Safety Policy Reasoning
evidence: Sec. 3.2.4: the guard allows an action "only when the safety likelihood increases or remains within a tolerable region"; Sec. 5.2 describes it as a "post-verification module that copilots with the agent".
method: Guard agent extracts verifiable rules from policy documents into probabilistic rule circuits, then per agent action retrieves circuits, runs tools and formal verification, and returns allow or deny with violated rules.
evaluation: ShieldAgent-Bench (6 web environments, AWM agent, AgentPoison and AdvWeb attacks) plus ST-WebAgentBench, VWA-Adv, AgentHarm; vs Direct, Rule Traverse, GuardAgent; ACC 90.4/91.7, FPR 5.6/4.0, 31.1-33.8 s per sample.
contribution: Guardrail agent that verifies each web-agent action against probabilistic rule circuits built from policy text, reaching about 91% accuracy and 4.8% false positives at roughly 32 s per check.
flag: Guards ONE protected agent - not multi-agent state; (c) rests on the safety-evaluation-of-LLM-agents clause. Paper calls the guard both pre-execution gating and "post-verification", not reconciled; Fig. 19 shows action_allowed false. Latency is 31-34 s per check, far from RQ1. No hardware stated; no dedicated ablation found, baselines only. Abstract 11.3% accuracy gain not reproducible: Sec. 5.2 says 10.2% and Table 2 averages give about 9.3 points over Rule Traverse. Dataset size inconsistent (3K abstract, 2K intro, 3110 in Sec. 4 and Table 9). Online result (Table 4) is policy compliance given task success, e.g. GitLab 50.7 vs 22.8. Read chars 0-100000 of 108884.

title: DrunkAgent: Stealthy Memory Corruption in LLM-Powered Recommender Agents
evidence: Results: DrunkAgent 'always pushes the target items to the first' of the recommendation list, lifting AgentSEQ HR@1 on CDs and Vinyl from 0.0404 benign to 0.4949.
method: Black-box attack on LLM agent-based recommenders: greedy trigger search on a LLaMA-3-8B surrogate plus five memory-perturbation strategies appended to an item description to block item-agent memory updates.
evaluation: 3 Amazon datasets; victims AgentCF/AgentRAG/AgentSEQ on gpt-3.5-turbo vs 6 text-attack baselines; HR@1 0.0505 to 0.4040 (AgentCF, CDs) vs best baseline 0.0808; two-part ablation; strategy success 100 percent; paraphrasing defense fails.
contribution: DrunkAgent corrupts the memory update of item agents in LLM-based recommender agents with a surrogate-optimised trigger, raising target-item promotion from about 5 to about 40 percent HR@1.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - LLM recommender agents are the systems analysed, but nothing is guarded: this is an attack paper with no runtime mechanism, so (a) fails. TITLE MISMATCH but the SAME paper, not E6: arXiv 2503.23804 is now titled 'Get the Agents Drunk: Memory Perturbations in Autonomous Agent-based Recommender Systems', same DrunkAgent method, victims and tables - the record title should be updated. (c) is borderline: the hazard is commercial recommendation manipulation rather than safety, the primary metric is HR@1 promotion, and the multi-agent aspect is the user-agent/item-agent memory loop of AgentCF - the maintainer may well prefer exclude-E1. Universality (Fig 3), imperceptibility perplexity (Fig 4), victim-accuracy impact (Fig 5) and the paraphrasing-defense results (Fig 6) are figure-only with no numbers in the text; no latency, cost or hardware figures; the Table 6 'Q' query-count column is unlabelled.

title: Progent: Securing AI Agents with Privilege Control
evidence: Sec. 4.2: a policy-governed tool call runs only if the policy allows it and Progent "automatically switches to the fallback function when it does not" - fallbacks terminate execution, return an error, or request user inspection.
method: Progent wraps an LLM agent's tool calls in a deterministic symbolic privilege policy; forbid rules first, deny by default, fallback halts or asks the user; an LLM proposes updates and Z3 checks narrowing.
evaluation: AgentDojo, ASB, MCP real-world agents (LangChain, OpenAI SDK, OpenHands, AutoGen); baselines spotlighting, tool_filter, DataSentinel, Prompt Guard 2; ASR 39.9 to 1.0 pct and 70.3 to 3.9 pct; no latency reported.
contribution: Progent enforces least-privilege policies on every LLM-agent tool call at execution time, cutting prompt-injection attack success from 39.9 to 1.0 percent on AgentDojo with little utility loss.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - LLM tool-calling agents (black box). Check (e): it rests on an approval gate and one Manual Approval ablation (0.0 pct ASR, 75.3 utility), not a takeover or situation-awareness study. No latency or enforcement-overhead figure anywhere despite the deterministic-enforcement claim. Utility under attack reported as 54.0 vs 61.3 - check which column is Progent, since Progent is worse on one reading. Multi-agent only as one AutoGen configuration (18.7 to 0.8 pct), so (c) primacy not met.

title: LLM-Flock: LLM-Driven Decentralized Multi-Robot Flocking via Influence-Based Consensus with Collision Avoidance
evidence: App. A.2: "The plan and index are parsed via regular expressions and validated before proceeding to the consensus stage" - a format check only; safe distance is stated only in the prompt (Sec. 3.3).
method: Each robot's LLM proposes a formation plan; influence-based consensus (neighbour fraction) adopts higher-influence plans; greedy goal assignment; LLM outputs next position with prompt-stated safe distance.
evaluation: 2D simulation, 3-10 robots, 10 trials, five LLMs; Crazyflie drones (3-5) with mocap. Baseline no consensus. Metric Procrustes shape error, plotted only; no collision counts, no latency.
contribution: Proposes influence-based consensus so decentralized LLM-driven robots agree on a flocking formation plan, improving formation convergence in simulation and on Crazyflie drones.
flag: Quotes relayed by the WebFetch reader model from the full PDF text, not seen raw - verify wording before publishing. Despite 'Collision Avoidance' in the title, the reader found no collision or violation metric and no runtime guard on LLM motion commands; outcome is formation shape error, with no numeric values in the text (only in Figs. 4 and 11). App. D.2 failure case shows a robot ignoring the speed rule with nothing catching it. LLMs run on external servers (Sec. 6 limitation), so no edge deployment. E2 would be the code if the maintainer reads it as a claimed safety mechanism.

title: LLM Agents Should Employ Security Principles
evidence: Sec. 3.2 and Appendix F: the I-O Firewall checks schemas and policies on every inbound and outbound message and a blocked tool call returns a "Violation Error" (an unauthorized send_money call is rejected in the travel example).
method: AgentSandbox: agent-side sandbox applying least privilege and data minimisation - a Persistent Agent spawns per-task Ephemeral Agents behind an I-O Firewall, Data Minimizer and Response Filter.
evaluation: AgentDojo 97 tasks, gpt-4o, Important-message injection; baselines No Defense, Tool Filter, PI Detector, Delimiting, Repeat Prompt; ASR 4.34 vs 58.84 pct, benign utility 82.00 vs 83.81; no latency.
contribution: AgentSandbox applies classical security principles to LLM agents, mediating every tool call and message so prompt-injection success falls to 4.34 percent on AgentDojo at near-unchanged benign utility.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - LLM tool-calling agent. Check whether this should be exclude-E3: the paper is self-described a position paper, the authors call the evaluation preliminary, and the Firewall, Minimizer and Response Filter are given few implementation details. No ablations; main table is one model, and Appendix C extends to o3-mini and gpt-4o-mini only as figures with no reported numbers. The human-justification step (Sec. 3.2) and mixed-initiative collaboration (Appendix E) are proposed but never evaluated, so (e) is not claimed. Multi-agent is only the Persistent-Ephemeral split on single-agent AgentDojo tasks.

title: Robust and Safe Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning Framework with Communication for Autonomous Vehicles
evidence: Sec. 3.4: the CBF-based Safety Shield "filters unsafe commands before they reach the low-level controller", and Fig. 2 states "If no safe action exists, an emergency stop is triggered".
method: RSR-RSMARL: delay-robust MARL with V2V communication where a decentralised CBF-QP shield filters each agent's high-level command before actuation, with emergency stop and a reward penalty on shield interventions.
evaluation: CARLA 0.9.15 plus 1-10 scale F1TENTH hardware; baselines Safe-RMM, no-shield RSR-MARL, No-Comm, MARL-DR; 0 collisions vs 10-45 over 50 episodes; interventions 18.7 to 11.4 pct; Jetson Orin Nano 10 Hz, V2V 10-20 ms.
contribution: RSR-RSMARL couples delay-robust multi-agent RL with a decentralised control-barrier-function shield that vetoes unsafe vehicle commands before actuation, reaching zero collisions in CARLA and on F1TENTH hardware.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - a learned MARL policy guarded by a CBF-QP shield. Record title omits the subtitle "From Simulation to Hardware" and says "Framework"; the fetched paper is the same work under a renamed version. The shield is also applied during training rollouts (Algorithm 1 line 11), so check that the runtime veto is not conflated with the training constraint. Hardware Table 1 gives raw collision counts (0-5) with no rate, no variance and an undefined time unit; delays F-1 to F-5 and TV [0,5] are unitless steps and not comparable to the measured 10-20 ms V2V latency; no per-step QP solve time, so (d) rests on the 10 Hz policy rate and V2V latency only.

title: Comprehensive Vulnerability Analysis is Necessary for Trustworthy LLM-MAS
evidence: Sec. 4.1: prompt injections are placed into inter-agent communication of a planner-executor LLM-MAS at three stages, giving ASR up to 96.43 pct; Sec. 5.3 only proposes monitor agents that "detect anomalies, and intervene when necessary".
method: Position paper: a taxonomy and threat-model framework for LLM-MAS vulnerabilities, plus one preliminary injection study on a GPT-5-mini planner-executor pipeline.
evaluation: AgentDojo banking suite, GPT-5-mini planner with GPT-5-mini or GPT-5-nano executor; ASR 0.00-96.43 pct and utility 80.71-93.57 pct by injection stage; no baseline, no ablation, no trial counts or variance.
contribution: A position paper arguing that LLM multi-agent trustworthiness needs comprehensive vulnerability analysis, with a taxonomy and a small inter-agent prompt-injection study on a planner-executor pipeline.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - an LLM-MAS planner-executor is analysed, but nothing is guarded. The paper's own title begins "Position:" and the contribution is a taxonomy plus threat-model framework, hence E3; exclude-E2 applies equally since the single experiment has no baseline, no single-agent comparison and no ablation. All defences, including the monitor agents, are conceptual. Check Table 2: the Harmful and Privacy rows are identical at planner_start and executor_end. Table 1 ASRs (TAMAS 76-94 pct, AgentDojo 50 pct) are quoted from prior work, not measured here.

title: MAEBE: Multi-Agent Emergent Behavior Framework
evidence: Sec. 3.3.4: with a misaligned "red-team" supervisor in the star topology, peer pressure rose from 28.5 pct (benign) to 43.9 pct, an ensemble-level effect absent from single-agent evaluation.
method: MAEBE: an evaluation framework posing Greatest Good Benchmark questions and double-inverted variants to single agents and to six-model round-robin, homogeneous and star-supervisor ensembles, scored by an LLM judge.
evaluation: 6 frontier and open LLMs, 90 GGB questions x12 repetitions, 237k responses; single-agent baseline plus topology, length, visibility and persona ablations; Table 3 IH p=0.00 r=0.42; peer pressure 28.5 to 43.9 pct.
contribution: MAEBE shows that LLM moral preferences shift under question framing and under peer and supervisor influence in ensembles, so single-agent alignment evaluation misses emergent group risks.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: which - LLM ensembles are analysed, not guarded; there is no runtime mechanism, no tool use and no memory (Sec. 5.1), and the only stop is a four-round cap. Check the evaluation floor: no collision, violation, hazard or intervention rate exists - outcomes are GGB Likert distributions, significance tests and LLM-judge rationale shares, so exclude-E2 is defensible. Single vs round-robin first answer showed no significant difference (all p>0.20, r<=0.03), which weakens the emergence claim. Judge accuracy was never human-validated; 24.9 pct of Gemini and 23.9 pct of Llama responses were discarded. Abstract names the framework "Multi-Agent Emergent Behavior Evaluation" while the running header matches the record title.

title: Verification-Guided Falsification for Safe RL via Explainable Abstraction and Risk-Aware Exploration
evidence: Sec. 4.4 (Safety Shield): when the task policy's risk estimate exceeds the threshold "the shield intervenes and overrides the task action" with an action from a separately trained safe policy.
method: Offline pipeline: CAPS graph abstraction of an RL policy model-checked in Storm (PCTL), then risk- and uncertainty-guided falsification; a risk-critic shield then overrides unsafe actions with a safe policy.
evaluation: SAC policies on Navigation2, Maze, insulin Dosing; vs Uncertainty-Based Search and DRLFuzz; violations found, diversity, rollouts, time; shield vs no-shield ablation; AMD EPYC 8 vCPU, no step latency.
contribution: Combines model checking of an abstracted RL policy with risk-guided falsification, then adds a risk-critic shield that cuts falsifier-found violations by about a third in Maze and Navigation2.
flag: Main contribution is OFFLINE verification and falsification; the runtime shield is the last, smallest part and is evaluated only by shield vs no-shield (Maze 94->63, Navigation2 86->57 violations within a 100-episode falsification budget; Storm finds none after shielding) and not at all on Dosing. No false-intervention rate, no task-return cost of shielding, no shield latency. Single-agent; passes E4 only on the sequential aspect. Violation counts for the falsification baselines are in Fig. 4 only. Shield thresholds are deferred to Appendix A, which I did not see; PAC guarantee assumptions are not validated empirically. Read in one fetch pass.

title: Design Patterns for Securing LLM Agents against Prompt Injections
evidence: Abstract: "we propose a set of principled design patterns for building AI agents with provable resistance to prompt injection" (Abstract).
method: Six architectural design patterns (action-selector, plan-then-execute, LLM map-reduce, dual LLM, code-then-execute, context-minimization) that keep untrusted data out of an LLM agent's control flow.
evaluation: No quantitative evaluation: ten qualitative case studies (OS, SQL, email, booking, medical, software agents) mapped to patterns; no metrics, baselines, ablations, latency or hardware.
contribution: Catalogue of six design patterns that structurally bound what a prompt injection can reach in an LLM agent, illustrated by ten case studies with threat models but no measurement.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - LLM tool-calling agents. Fails the evaluation floor: no quantitative result and no theorem, lemma or proof anywhere despite the abstract claiming "provable resistance" (checked body and appendix), hence E2. Criterion (a) fails too: the patterns are architectural constraints, and user confirmation appears only as an optional best practice in Appendix A. Maintainer may prefer E3 if a design-pattern/position paper counts as tutorial-like.

title: AGENTSAFE: Benchmarking the Safety of Embodied Agents on Hazardous Instructions
evidence: Section 4.4: SAFE-AUDIT "corrects it by generating a new thought that explicitly conveys a refusal to execute the instruction" (Section 4.4).
method: Benchmark (SAFE-THOR sandbox on AI2-THOR, SAFE-VERSE hazardous-task suite, SAFE-DIAGNOSE protocol) plus SAFE-AUDIT, a zero-shot GPT-4o auditor that rewrites or refuses the agent's thought before planning.
evaluation: AI2-THOR, 45 scenes, 9 VLMs plus ReAct/ProgPrompt, 6 jailbreaks; GR/HR/PRR/PSR/TSR; baselines AgentSpec and ThinkSafe; ThinkSafe cuts normal TSR up to 14.96%, SAFE-AUDIT lifts it 2.22%, hazardous TSR 0.48%.
contribution: Benchmark of embodied VLM agents on hazardous and jailbroken instructions that separates perception, planning and execution failures, plus a thought-level auditor that cuts hazardous task success to 0.48%.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - embodied VLM agents, guarded by SAFE-AUDIT and by the AgentSpec and ThinkSafe execution-layer gates used as baselines. Check: one embodied agent per episode and no agent-to-agent interaction, so (c) rests on the LLM-agent-safety-evaluation branch rather than a multi-agent property; SAFE-AUDIT audits the global thought before planning ("rather than merely blocking them post-planning"), so (a) is borderline as an action-level veto. Abstract says 9,900 instructions while the body says 1,800 basic plus 8,100 adversarial, and Figure 2 says 1,350 interactive objects against 104 in the text. No latency, overhead or hardware figures.

title: MAGPIE: A dataset for Multi-AGent contextual PrIvacy Evaluation
evidence: Conclusion: agents commit multi-round privacy violations in 55.27% of interactions while collaborating in group chat (Conclusion; Section 5.3).
method: Dataset of 158 high-stakes scenarios in 15-16 domains where excluding private data blocks task completion; 2-4 LLM agents negotiate in a group chat for up to 10 rounds under utility prompts.
evaluation: GPT-4o, Claude-3.7-Sonnet, Mistral-Large, Llama-3-70B; misclassification 25.2-43.6% against a 10.2% human baseline; leakage 5.7-82.5% explicit, 39.7-87.0% implicit, 50.5-60.0% active; consensus 51%, task success 29.7%.
contribution: Multi-agent benchmark showing that collaborating LLM agents leak contextually private data in over half of multi-round negotiations, and that lower leakage comes at the cost of consensus and task success.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - the agents are LLM agents, but nothing guards them: no filter, shield, gate or deferral is implemented or tested, so only (c) holds and (a) fails; built-in privacy safeguards are named as future work. Weakest point against the evaluation floor is the baseline: a human misclassification rate plus cross-model and prompt-condition contrasts, no safety baseline or ablation. Internal inconsistencies: 15 vs 16 domains, "Claude-2.7-Sonnet" vs 3.7-Sonnet, Mistral implicit 39.7% in table vs 40% in text; the benchmark was generated and verified by Claude 3.7 itself; leakage is counted only on verbatim appearance of the private value, which the authors call a lower bound.

title: OpenAgentSafety: A Comprehensive Framework for Evaluating Real-World AI Agent Safety
evidence: Section 3.2: with harmful goals held by simulated coworkers under benign user intent, "unsafe rates vary from 44.9-69.2%" (Section 3.2).
method: Framework of 356 multi-turn tasks in a sandboxed workplace (bash, browser, files, code, messaging) with Sotopia-simulated LLM coworkers; rule-based environment-state checks plus a GPT-4.1 judge.
evaluation: Seven LLMs (Claude Sonnet 4/3.7, GPT-5, GPT-4o, o3-mini, DeepSeek-v3/R1); unsafe rate 49.06-72.73% by judge, 32.3-52.2% rule-based; 100-trajectory human study, 94% annotator agreement; three EC2 t3.2xlarge, 24-30 h per model.
contribution: Open framework of 356 realistic multi-turn, multi-user tool-use tasks that elicits unsafe behaviour from frontier agents in 49-73% of safety-vulnerable cases, including when only a simulated coworker is malicious.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - LLM tool-calling agents are the evaluated systems, but no guardrail, shield or approval gate is tested; "safety interventions such as guardrail agents" are explicitly future work (Section 5), so (a) fails and only (c) holds. Approval-seeking and escalation to the user are described as ideal behaviour but never counted, so (e) does not hold. No system baseline: the comparison is across seven models with Mann-Whitney tests. Tables 3 and 5 are not reconciled (Claude Sonnet 4 at 49.06% vs 29.60%), the text says five models where seven are listed, and judge-human disagreement is 39.1%, so the headline unsafe rates are soft.

title: NeHMO: Neural Hamilton-Jacobi Reachability Learning for Decentralized Safe Multi-Agent Motion Planning
evidence: "Collision Rate (CR%): Percentage of trials where any inter-arm collision occurs at any time during execution." (Section IV, metrics); "NeHMO achieves the highest success rate and lowest collision rate" (Section IV-B.3)
method: Neural Hamilton-Jacobi reachability value function (DeepReach plus symmetry and boundary-residual priors) used as a worst-case pairwise safety constraint in decentralized receding-horizon trajectory optimization, with a fail-safe control on solver timeout.
evaluation: Simulated dual/three/five UR5 and UR5-Kinova, 100 random scenarios; vs CHOMP, Ha et al. RL, DeepReach, naive; dual-UR5 SR 92% CR 2%, 36+-35 ms; Xeon w5-2455X + RTX 4070.
contribution: Learns a neural Hamilton-Jacobi reachability value for pairs of manipulators and uses it in decentralized planning, cutting dual-UR5 collision rate to 2% versus 13-34% for baselines at roughly 25 Hz.
flag: Title in the PDF is '...Decentralized Safe Multi-Arm Motion Planning' (record says Multi-Agent); same arXiv id, v2 dated 2 Jul 2026, so retitled since the 2025 record. Not a strict runtime interceptor: the HJR value is a constraint inside the planner; only the timeout/infeasible branch (FailSafeControl, eq. 6) overrides at execution, and its trigger rate is never reported - maintainer to judge yes/no. Results beyond Table II: three UR5 SR 86/CR 5 (CHOMP 68/32), five UR5 SR 66/CR 8 (CHOMP 32/68), UR5-Kinova 79/6, against reckless Kinova 47/39. Costs: about 27% longer paths than CHOMP and stuck trials (92+2 leaves 6% neither success nor collision; 26% at five arms). Planning time has std about equal to mean (36+-35 ms, 43+-52 ms) so tail latency is unbounded; no formal guarantee (authors say so). Real dual-UR5 appears only in Fig. 1 with no metrics. Assumes perfect state perception of other arms. time-to-irreversibility cell rests on the BRT/t_safe=0.3 s horizon, not an explicit time-to-collision estimate; latency cell on t_plan=0.1 s and the timeout branch - both arguable. Abstract has no numbers to verify.

title: MCPSecBench: A Systematic Security Benchmark and Playground for Testing Model Context Protocols
evidence: Section 4: "This benchmark focuses on dynamic protection mechanisms", and an attempt is scored as refused when "the MCP host or AI proactively detects and refuses the malicious action" (Section 4; Section 5.1).
method: Benchmark and playground formalising the MCP ecosystem: 17 attack types over client, protocol, server and host surfaces, driven against three hosts with two dynamic guardrails (MCIP-Guardian, FAN) toggled on.
evaluation: Claude Desktop, GPT-4.1, Cursor, 15 trials per vector; ASR and refusal rate against a No-Defense baseline; protocol attacks 100% ASR, server 75.2-78.1%; MCIP mitigates 17.9% and FAN 28.9% on average; MCIP roughly doubles cost.
contribution: Systematic MCP security benchmark that measures 17 attack types across four surfaces on three live hosts and shows two deployed runtime guardrails block under 30% of attacks and none of the protocol-level ones.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - LLM hosts and tool-calling agents, guarded by MCIP-Guardian and FAN, which refuse execution on detection. Check: the paper never describes how either guardrail intercepts a call internally, saying only that they "function by enhancing the LLM's autonomy in threat detection", so true pre-execution interception is unverified and (a) rests on the refusal outcome; FAN is classed as dynamic in Section 4 but described as operating "primarily via static rule-setting" in Section 5.3. Cost figures conflict: Section 5.3 gives $0.41 to $0.76 on Claude Desktop while Appendix E says costs stay "under $0.10 across all platforms". No latency measured; the host permission prompt is described but never measured, so (e) does not hold.

title: The Sum Leaks More Than Its Parts: Compositional Privacy Risks and Mitigations in Multi-Agent Collaboration
evidence: "a single defender's decision to block is sufficient to deny the query" (Sec. 1, CoDef description)
method: Defines compositional privacy leakage across collaborating LLM agents and adds two per-query defenses: theory-of-mind intent inference, and CoDef, a shared-state consensus vote where any defender can block.
evaluation: 119 synthetic adversarial and benign multi-agent scenarios; Qwen3-32B attacker; defenders Qwen3-32B, Gemini-2.5-pro, GPT-5; vs CoT, CoT+sensitive-set, CoT+history, ToM, self-voting; sensitive-block 86.5-89.9 pct CoDef vs 29.8-39.1 pct CoT, benign success 66.3-70.2 pct, balanced outcome up to 79.8 pct; no latency or hardware.
contribution: Shows that individually safe LLM agent answers compose into privacy leaks, and that a consensus block vote across defender agents cuts leakage while preserving most benign utility.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - LLM defender agents veto an LLM attacker's queries at inference time. title: Safe Reinforcement Learning with Receding-Horizon Safety Critic and Differentiable Action Shields
evidence: Sec. III-C: the filter "moves the action along the steepest-ascent direction a by the smallest amount needed to satisfy the constraint"; Fig. 1 caption: used "at deployment for safety-shielded control".
method: Ensemble critic predicts survival over the next H steps (CVaR-aggregated); a closed-form one-constraint QP shield with uncertainty-scaled slack corrects PPO actions; an anticipation loss trains the policy toward shielded actions.
evaluation: Sim-to-sim Unitree Go2 in MJX, flat and heightfield terrain under action noise and pushes; vs PPO, PPO with neural CBF, SafeFall predictor; horizon ablation; no latency, no real robot.
contribution: A receding-horizon ensemble safety critic with a closed-form differentiable action shield warns of quadruped falls about 30 steps ahead with half the false positives of a SafeFall-style predictor.
flag: Minimum-evaluation is THIN: success rate and return under shift appear only in figures (Figs 2,4,5,8,9), with no numeric failure, violation or intervention rate in text or tables; the only table numbers are predictor quality vs SafeFall (flat: FP 0.080 vs 0.168, FN 0.074 vs 0.016, steps before failure 29.98 vs 12.08, accuracy 0.616 vs 0.620). Note false negatives are about 4.6x WORSE than SafeFall. The abstract claim of reducing catastrophic failures is not backed by a number I could find in the body. time-to-irreversibility credited only loosely (H-step survival prediction, H=25 = 0.5 s); drop it if strict. Table I lists H=5 while experiments use H=25. Closed-form shield is claimed cheap but never timed. Single-agent, simulation only. Read in one fetch pass.

title: Trust-Weighted Adaptive Consensus: A Resilient Coordination Framework for Next-Generation Large Language Model Multi-Agent Systems
evidence: "If the resulting output confidence falls below a threshold, a Verifier Agent is invoked to double-check the result before it is finalized." (Sec 4.2 Architecture)
method: TWAC coordination layer for LLM multi-agent systems: capability-and-trust shortlisting of K=4 agents, EMA per-agent trust ledger (alpha 0.85), local consensus, and confidence-gated verifier agent before output is finalised.
evaluation: Synthetic simulation, 12 agents, 500 tasks x 30 trials, vs round-robin and centralized auction: success 0.973 vs 0.854/0.704; cascading-failure rate 0.0004 vs 0.023/0.088; 5 vs 13 messages/task; no hardware.
contribution: A trust-weighted coordination layer for LLM agent teams whose uncertainty-gated verifier checks low-confidence outputs before release, cutting simulated cascading-failure rate from 2.3% (centralized auction) to 0.04%.
flag: BORDERLINE, maintainer should decide between include and E1/E2. No LLM is ever run: agents are six-dimensional skill vectors with a noise term, so the cascading-failure numbers are properties of the authors' own simulator; code only 'available on request'. The paper's primary claim is coordination quality (success rate, messages), cascading failure is one of four metrics, so the (c) primacy test is arguable. No ablation isolates the verifier from shortlisting or trust, the confidence threshold and verifier accuracy are never given, and it is not stated what happens when the verifier rejects an output (halt, retry or reassign), so runtime_interceptor=yes rests on 'before it is finalized'. Verifier false-intervention rate and verification share not reported; latency is in abstract 'steps', equal to the auction baseline, so the verifier cost is hidden. Cascading-failure s.d. (0.0011) exceeds its mean (0.0004). Abstract says 'more than an order of magnitude' while body says about fifty times and two orders. Internal errors: Sec 6.4 refers to 'Section 8 discusses the risk of trust-ledger manipulation' but Section 8 is the reference list and no such discussion exists; MAST is cited as [8] in Sec 4.4 and 6.3 but is reference [9]; two tables are both numbered Table 1; references 15-17 (IoT sensors, bipolar disorder, ad hoc routing) are unrelated and uncited; several references lack venue. First half is a literature synthesis. IJCA is a low-barrier venue; treat as weak evidence.

title: Multi-Agent AI Systems for Autonomous Fleet Orchestration in Smart Warehouse
venue: International Journal of Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning
evidence: Cooperative A* over space-time states with a shared reservation table prevents vertex and swap conflicts (Sec. 3.3, paraphrased)
method: Simulation comparison of three deterministic dispatch policies (static zone, nearest-idle, market auction with distance/battery/congestion/fairness terms) for six warehouse AGVs with cooperative A* and heartbeat-based task reassignment.
evaluation: 20x14 grid, 6 agents, 3 policies x 6 fault conditions x 8 seeds = 144 trials; completion, wait, cycle time, recovery ticks; combined-fault completion 89.9% static vs 99.2% auction; no hardware or wall-clock latency.
contribution: Compares static, nearest-idle and auction dispatch for a six-AGV simulated warehouse under injected faults, finding adaptive policies cut wait times but the auction does not beat nearest-idle.
flag: Off-topic for (a)-(e): this is fleet task allocation and throughput under faults; collision freedom is a planner constraint (reservation table), not a measured outcome against a baseline, and no runtime override, veto or halt exists (only low-battery task exclusion and heartbeat reassignment). No human takeover. Read via one WebFetch pass of the PDF; figures 1-5 not seen. Despite the title there is no AI or learning: all policies are hand-written heuristics. Internal inconsistencies worth knowing: abstract says wait and cycle time are p<0.001 in five of six conditions but Sec. 7.2 supports four (surge p=0.034/0.044, combined wait p=0.092); abstract says static is significantly slower in every condition; breakdown event counts (35, 39, 41) exceed what the stated schedule allows (about 32) and differ by policy though the schedule is said to be policy-independent; identical recovery values within each group (40.0, 40.0, 14.0 ticks) simply mirror the timeouts; 'no collisions in 144 trials' was checked on a sample only using the planner's own table; paper calls the study 'real' though it is simulation. Reported 16,794 total orders looks about 7% above what the parameters imply (the fetch model's estimate, not mine verified). Supplementary data is referenced without a link.

title: Architectural Trust Controls in Enterprise Generative AI Platforms: A Systematic Review of Mechanisms, Frameworks, and Governance Gaps
venue: International Journal of Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning
evidence: Sec 3.1 labels the review type 'Systematic/Structured' following PRISMA; Sec 5.4 says the proposed Cognitive Gatekeeping is 'not a new technical mechanism'.
method: PRISMA-style literature review (847 retrieved, 30 synthesised, Jan 2024-May 2026) of trust controls in enterprise generative-AI platforms, with a conceptual Cognitive Gatekeeping framing; no mechanism built.
evaluation: No original evaluation. All figures are from cited works: CivicShield 72.9% detection at 2.9% false positives; AAGATE 47 ms median enforcement latency; HAAG 20-50 ms added per action.
contribution: Systematic review of architectural trust controls (fail-closed gates, refusal-first policies, human escalation) in enterprise generative-AI platforms, with a conceptual gatekeeping framework and no original experiments.

Possibly useful only for citation chasing (HAAG, CivicShield, M-PAIRS, AAGATE, Governance-as-a-Service are runtime gates with latency figures) - but many cited sources are unpublished or undated and should be verified independently. Low-quality signs: abstract names 2 databases, Sec 3.2 lists 5; two vs three reviewers; Sec 4.3.3 latency values left blank ('ms and ms') while Table 1 gives 47 ms; 65 references with several duplicates; '30-45% hallucination reduction' attributed to unspecified enterprise experiments. Read via one summarising fetch of the full PDF.

title: Turn-Based Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning Model Checking
venue: International Conference on Agents and Artificial Intelligence (ICAART)
evidence: Sec. 4: "we created a joint policy wrapper that queries the corresponding TMARL agent policy at every turn"; Table 1 then reports P(collision)=0.36 for the 3-agent Coin Collection task.
method: Turn feature added to the MDP plus a joint policy wrapper that resolves nondeterminism into an induced DTMC, built incrementally in COOL-MC and checked with Storm against PCTL hazard queries.
evaluation: Pokemon, multi-armed bandit, tic-tac-toe, Coin Collection; baseline naive monolithic model checking (out of memory past 23 bandit agents); P(collision)=0.36, P(KO)=0.0-0.001; GTX 1060, 0.5-401 s per query.
contribution: Scales probabilistic model checking of trained turn-based multi-agent RL policies by inducing a DTMC through a joint policy wrapper, yielding exact probabilities for collision and knockout hazards.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - trained TMARL agent policies are the object of verification, so the Pillar 1 carve-in for formal analysis of learned systems applies. Check (c) primacy: the headline claim is model-checking scalability (states, transitions, runtime) and the collision probability is 1 of 12 PCTL queries in toy games, with no safety metric compared to a baseline or ablation; eval floor is met only by treating the exact model-checking probabilities as proved guarantees. Analysis is offline, so runtime_interceptor is no. HP5NoHealP1 is 0.34 in Table 1 but 0.33 in the Sec. 5.2 text, and the monolithic transition count is misprinted as 51,6547,296.

title: Constrained Update Projection Approach to Safe Policy Optimization
evidence: "CUP projects the policy back onto the safe region to reconcile the constraint violation" (Sec. 1) - a projection of policy parameters during training, not of executed actions.
method: Two-step constrained policy optimisation: GAE-based surrogate improvement, then projection of the policy onto the cost-constraint set via a primal-dual update.
evaluation: Single-agent MuJoCo and Safety Gym; baselines CPO, PCPO, TRPO-L, PPO-L, FOCOPS; e.g. Ant-v3 return 1743.66 at cost 99.11 (limit 103); Humanoid 1066.83 at 19.91 (limit 20).
contribution: Constrained Update Projection trains single-agent policies that meet expected-cost limits on MuJoCo and Safety Gym with returns at or above earlier constrained-RL baselines.
flag: Training-time constraint only (prompt says a safety term in training does not meet (a)); single agent; expected-cost constraint, not per-step. Only first 100k of 187k characters read: Appendix H (compute/hardware) NOT READ, no latency figures seen. Safety Gym numbers are in figures only.

title: Provably Safe Reinforcement Learning with Step-wise Violation Constraints
evidence: Sec. 4.2 (Algorithm 1): SUCBVI estimates unsafe states optimistically and computes safe action sets by dynamic programming, then runs value iteration over those sets - constraint inside the planner.
method: SUCBVI: optimistic tabular RL that restricts value iteration to estimated safe action sets for step-wise unsafe-state constraints; SRF-UCRL is the reward-free variant.
evaluation: Tabular episodic MDPs; baselines UCBVI, OptCMDP-bonus, Optpess, Triple-Q, RF-UCRL; theory: violation O~(sqrt(ST)+S^2AH^2), regret O~(sqrt(H^3SAT)); experiment curves only, no hardware.
contribution: Gives a tabular RL algorithm with near-optimal bounds on step-wise safety violations and regret, with matching lower bounds, for single-agent episodic MDPs with unsafe states.
flag: Constraint inside planning, no runtime interceptor; the paper contrasts itself with shielding in Appendix A. Single agent (zero-sum Markov game extension is theory only, Appendix C). Regret exponent inconsistent: abstract says sqrt(H^3SAT), Theorem 4.2 as read says sqrt(H^2SAT) - check. Experiments reported as curves, no numeric values; environment details in Appendix F NOT READ (first 100k of 117k characters read).

title: MADiff: Offline Multi-agent Learning with Diffusion Models
evidence: Sec. 3.1: attention is applied across agents at each decoder layer of a shared U-Net so the model diffuses joint future observation trajectories; NBA Table 2 ADE 17.24 vs 32.07 for Baller2Vec++.
method: Attention-based diffusion model over joint multi-agent observation trajectories (shared U-Net with cross-agent attention), with an inverse dynamics model mapping predicted observations to actions, centralised or decentralised.
evaluation: Offline MPE, MA-Mujoco, SMAC, SMACv2 plus NBA prediction; baselines MA-ICQ, MA-TD3+BC, OMAR, MADT, Baller2Vec++; ADE 17.24 vs 32.07, FDE 26.69 vs 44.93; ablations on attention and teammate modelling; sampling 124-127 ms on an RTX 3090.
contribution: Shows a diffusion model with cross-agent attention can serve as a joint multi-agent world model, decoding coordinated plans and outperforming dedicated trajectory predictors on NBA forecasting.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: n-a - criterion (b) record, no safety mechanism and nothing guarded. Check Pillar 2 fit: this is generative diffusion over joint observations rather than non-generative latent prediction, and the direct predictive measure (ADE-FDE) exists only for the NBA task, while the multi-agent RL results are returns. RQ5 capped at 2 per protocol v1.6 and no hazard, collision or violation rate is reported. Sampling 124-127 ms at 15 DDIM steps on an RTX 3090 is far from sub-15 ms edge interception. MADIFF-D trails MA-ICQ on SMACv2 (10.1 vs 13.7) and the paper states it is unsuitable for tens or hundreds of agents.

title: Improving Alignment and Robustness with Circuit Breakers
evidence: Sec. 4.3 (AI agents): 100 harmful function-calling requests are evaluated and Figure 8 shows the Llama-3-8B agent harmful-action rate falling from 82 to 14 under forced function calls with circuit breakers.
method: Representation rerouting: LoRRA-style fine-tuning with a ReLU-clipped cosine loss pushes harmful-state representations toward orthogonality while an L2 retain loss preserves benign behaviour, so harmful generations derail internally.
evaluation: HarmBench attacks (GCG, AutoDAN, TAP-T, PAIR, prefilling, embedding) on Mistral-7B and Llama-3-8B, plus LLaVA multimodal and tool-calling agents; baselines refusal-trained, R2D2 adversarial training, safety prompt, harmfulness probes; average ASR 38.1 to 3.8 and 76.7 to 9.8; MT-Bench 8.05 to 8.0; WildChat refusal 2.2 to 6.2.
contribution: Circuit breakers cut jailbreak and agentic harmful-action rates by roughly an order of magnitude by rerouting harmful internal representations, at near-zero capability cost and no inference overhead.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - the LLM itself (Mistral-7B, Llama-3-8B, LLaVA-NeXT). Check (a): I ruled it out because the mechanism is a training-time representation loss baked into weights, explicitly claimed to add no inference burden; the only halting variant, a probe that stops generation (Table 2 and Sec. 4.4), is a baseline and a suggestion, not the contribution. (c) therefore rests on one subsection of tool-calling-agent evaluation (Figure 8, 100 requests, GPT-4-turbo judge), so the maintainer may rule the primacy test fails and move this to E4 or E1. The 87% and 90% average ASR reduction headline figures are derived from Table 1, not stated per attack.

title: PrivacyLens: Evaluating Privacy Norm Awareness of Language Models in Action
evidence: Sec. 3.2 and 5.1: the final action is removed from a sandboxed tool-calling trajectory and each LM must produce it (e.g. GmailSendEmail), then it is scored for privacy leakage; GPT-4 leaks in 25.68% of actions.
method: PrivacyLens expands contextual-integrity privacy seeds into vignettes and then ToolEmu-sandboxed agent trajectories via a template plus surgery-kit pipeline, and scores each LM's final tool action for leakage and helpfulness.
evaluation: 493 seeds, vignettes and trajectories plus 1,479 probing questions over 9 LMs; conditions basic vs privacy-enhancing prompt; GPT-4 LR 24.54% and LRh 25.68%, Llama-3-70B 39.15%, probing accuracy 98.99% against 25% leakage; no latency reported.
contribution: Shows LM agents that answer privacy-norm questions almost perfectly still leak sensitive information in a quarter of their actual tool actions, and that privacy prompting barely helps.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - LLM tool-calling agents are the system whose hazards are measured. Check (c): a single agent with tools, no agent-to-agent interaction and no runtime gate or override, so inclusion rests entirely on the "safety evaluation of LLM-tool-calling agents" clause and the maintainer may call it E4 wrong level. The comparison is across models and two prompt conditions rather than an ablation of a mechanism. Leakage is judged by an LM classifier (accuracy 0.92, kappa 0.82) and helpfulness by a judge with kappa only 0.56, so the headline rates inherit judge error.

title: Excluding the Irrelevant: Focusing Reinforcement Learning through Continuous Action Masking
evidence: Sec. 5.3: the authors "consider the masking as part of the policy, which creates the relevant policy", so the mask reparameterises sampling inside the policy rather than vetoing a nominal action.
method: Three continuous action masks (ray projection, zonotope generator mapping, truncated distributional sampling with hit-and-run MCMC) restrict a PPO policy to a state-dependent convex relevant action set to focus exploration.
evaluation: Seeker reach-avoid, 2D and 3D quadrotor, Walker2D, 10 seeds and 50 Optuna trials; baselines PPO and uniform replacement; returns 18.60 vs -71.03 (Seeker) and 1941.82 vs 1.19 (Walker2D); no violation rate; training hours only, Xeon 8380.
contribution: Continuous action masking confines PPO exploration to reachability-derived relevant action sets, improving returns and sample efficiency over standard PPO and naive resampling in four control tasks.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - a PPO policy, but the subject is exploration efficiency and return, not safety, and the setting is single-agent. Check (a): the abstract says only relevant actions are executed and the Seeker relevant set excludes collision-causing actions, so a reader could argue a runtime filter; I excluded because the mask lives inside the policy as a bijective reparameterisation, nothing is overridden or halted, and the paper is framed as focusing RL. No constraint-violation or collision rate is reported anywhere (collision is shown only qualitatively in Figure 5), so exclude-E2 is an alternative. Related to the authors' safe-RL and provably safe RL line, which may be queued separately.

title: GUARDIAN: Safeguarding LLM Multi-Agent Collaborations with Temporal Graph Modeling
evidence: Figure 3 caption and Section 4.1: "identify and exclude the highest-scoring anomalous node from subsequent iterations", "enables the removal of compromised agents and their connections".
method: Represents LLM debate as a temporal attributed graph; unsupervised encoder-decoder with an information bottleneck scores node and edge anomalies; highest-scoring agent is pruned from later rounds.
evaluation: MMLU, MATH, FEVER, Biographies (100 questions, 3 rounds, 3-7 agents) vs LLM Debate, DyLAN, SelfCheckGPT, Challenger, Inspector. Accuracy gain 4.2 percent average and 7.1 percent on MATH; anomaly detection rate 66.9-94.7 percent (Table 3); API calls 4.48 vs 8.00 for LLM Debate; alpha and gamma sweeps; no hardware or latency reported.
contribution: Models LLM multi-agent debate as a temporal attributed graph and prunes anomalous agents between rounds, improving accuracy under three attack types while roughly halving API calls.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - LLM multi-agent debate. Criterion (a) is borderline: GUARDIAN excludes an agent from subsequent rounds rather than vetoing one action before execution, so check whether that counts as runtime interception. The claim that detection rate "averages above 80 percent" is not supported per attack type (hallucination row averages about 78.1, communication about 78.6); check Table 3. No ablation isolates the dual decoders, the information bottleneck or incremental training; no latency, hardware, F1, AUC or human alerting.

title: Among Us: A Sandbox for Measuring and Detecting Agentic Deception
evidence: Section 1: linear probes "help us detect deception out-of-distribution with high accuracy"; Section 2.4 frames the setting as "multi-agent games impose no pre-defined ceiling on sophistication and scheming".
method: Among Us sandbox with seven LLM players; separate deception and detection Elo ratings; linear probes on the layer-20 residual stream and sparse autoencoder features used as offline deception detectors; SAE steering attempted.
evaluation: 2054 games across 18 LLMs plus 400 1v1 games (Llama-3.3-70b, Phi-4). Probes trained on TruthfulQA, DishonestQA, RepEng and in-game data; out-of-distribution AUROC 0.94 lying and 0.99 deception; on-distribution 1.000 deception and 0.863 lying; best SAE feature 0.967; ablations over layers, training-data size and input components; two 80GB A100s, about 100 GPU-hours; no latency.
contribution: Introduces an Among Us sandbox that separates LLM deception capability from detection skill via Elo, and shows linear probes flag in-game deception out-of-distribution at 0.94-0.99 AUROC.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - LLM agents in a multi-agent social deduction game. Check the (c) primacy test: the hazard is multi-agent but the detector reads a single model's residual stream, so multi-agent state is the setting rather than the detector input. No runtime gate: probes are offline and SAE steering was ineffective. Elo and win-rate values appear only in figures, not in text. The abstract claims AUROC "over 95 percent" without chain of thought, while Figure 6a action-only AUROC is 0.653 and 77 percent of those actions are non-speech.

title: WASP: Benchmarking Web Agent Security Against Prompt Injection Attacks
evidence: Abstract: "a new publicly available benchmark for end-to-end evaluation of Web Agent Security against Prompt injection attacks"; intermediate and end-to-end attack success rates are the primary measured outcomes (Section 3.4).
method: Benchmark of 84 prompt-injection tasks in self-hosted GitLab and Reddit VisualWebArena sandboxes; separates intermediate agent derailment from end-to-end attacker-goal achievement; tests defensive system prompt and instruction hierarchy.
evaluation: GPT-4o, GPT-4o-mini, o1, Claude 3.5 Sonnet v2 and 3.7 Sonnet; no-defense baseline vs system prompt vs instruction hierarchy on 84 attack and 37 utility tasks. GPT-4o intermediate ASR 0.429 to 0.167 and end-to-end 0.036 to 0.000 with utility 0.622 to 0.459; o1 intermediate 0.857 and end-to-end 0.167; URL injection 0.619 vs plain text 0.238; no hardware or latency.
contribution: Benchmarks web agents against realistic prompt injections and shows they are often derailed yet rarely complete the attacker goal, while prompt-level defenses cut attack success at a measurable utility cost.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - LLM web agents. One agent per task, so check criterion (c) primacy and whether this is exclude-E4; the multi-step web trajectory is the only non-single-input aspect. No runtime interceptor: defenses are prompt-level and the LLM judge classifies reasoning traces after execution. Both environments (GitLab, Reddit) are logical, so no cross-domain cell. Utility set is only 37 tasks and no detection rate is reported for the judge.

title: OS-Harm: A Benchmark for Measuring Safety of Computer Use Agents
evidence: Section 4.1: the OSWorld scaffolding "does not rely on external guardrails and assumes direct execution", and agents act "without asking for any user confirmation"; Table 2 reports average unsafe rates of 21-29 percent across five computer use agents.
method: OS-Harm benchmark: 150 OSWorld Ubuntu VM tasks split across deliberate misuse, prompt injection and model misbehavior, with a GPT-4.1 AER judge scoring each trace for safety violation and task completion.
evaluation: o4-mini, GPT-4.1, Claude 3.7 Sonnet, Gemini 2.5 Pro and Flash; average unsafe 27, 21, 29, 27 and 26 percent, misuse unsafe up to 70 percent, injection compliance 20 percent for o4-mini. Judge vs human F1 0.76 unsafe (precision 0.95, recall 0.64) and 0.79 completion; ablations over judge framework and model, temperature and 15-60 step limits; about 5 hours on one laptop, no per-step latency.
contribution: Provides a 150-task computer-use-agent safety benchmark spanning deliberate misuse, prompt injection and model misbehavior, with an LLM judge validated against human labels at 0.76 F1 on unsafe behavior.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - computer use agents driven by frontier LLMs. One agent per task, so check criterion (c) primacy and whether this is exclude-E4. The judge runs offline: Section 3.3 and Appendix B.5 only propose that it "can be used to detect in real time safety violations and consequently stop the agents", so the runtime guardrail is never built or measured. Judge recall 0.64 means reported unsafe rates are probably underestimates. My fetch covered 100000 of 121526 characters; the tail appendices were not read.

title: Memory Injection Attacks on LLM Agents via Query-Only Interaction
evidence: Abstract: "LLM agents with a compromised memory bank may easily produce harmful outputs"; Section 5.2 reports average injection success 98.2 percent and attack success 76.8 percent from query-only interaction.
method: MINJA attack: an ordinary user submits benign-looking queries carrying bridging reasoning steps so poisoned records enter the agent's shared memory bank and later misdirect another user's victim query.
evaluation: RAP on WebShop, EHRAgent on MIMIC-III and eICU, and a CoT QA agent on MMLU, with GPT-4 and GPT-4o. ISR 95.6-100 and ASR 57.0-98.9 with benign utility drop within 10 points; ablations over six embedding models, retrieval noise (ASR 97.8 to 95.6), 25-100 benign queries, prior poisoning and DeepSeek-R1 and Llama-2-7B; prompt-level detection 131 of 135 on MIMIC but 0 of 135 on RAP, with 34 of 50 false positives; no hardware or latency.
contribution: Shows an ordinary user can poison an LLM agent's memory bank through benign-looking queries alone, misdirecting later victim queries at 76.8 percent attack success while leaving benign-task utility intact.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - LLM agents with a RAG memory bank. Most likely overturn in this batch: it is an attack paper with no safety mechanism of its own and a single agent (shared memory across users), so the maintainer may rule exclude-E4 or exclude-E1 under the (c) primacy test. No head-to-head experimental baseline, only ablations and a conceptual comparison with AgentPoison and PANDORA. The sole tested defense is prompt-level detection, which fails completely on RAP and QA (0 of 135 and 0 of 90 with the targeted prompt). My fetch covered 100000 of 107820 characters.

title: DRIFT: Dynamic Rule-Based Defense with Injection Isolation for Securing LLM Agents
evidence: Sec. 3.2: on a deviating write/execute tool call "agents will send an approval request to user", and in evaluation "sending a user request is equivalent to rejecting the deviated function call".
method: LLM-agent defense: a secure planner derives an allowed tool trajectory and parameter checklist, a dynamic validator vetoes or approves deviating tool calls by privilege, an isolator masks injected instructions in tool outputs.
evaluation: AgentDojo, ASB, AgentDyn on GPT-4o, GPT-4o-mini, Claude-3.5; vs CaMeL, Progent, tool_filter, others; GPT-4o-mini ASR 30.7% to 1.4%, benign utility 63.55 to 57.29; tokens 0.82M to 2.37M; no latency.
contribution: DRIFT gates each tool call of an LLM agent against dynamically updated control and data constraints and strips injected instructions from tool results, cutting prompt-injection success to about 1-3% with modest utility loss.
flag: Single agent with tools, multi-agent only in the sense of criterion (c) LLM/tool-calling agent safety. Human approval is described but never exercised: evaluation treats an approval request as a rejection, so no human-handoff evidence. Overhead inconsistency: text says about 1.89x tokens but Table 3 gives 2.37M vs 0.82M (about 2.9x). ASR for GPT-4o-mini appears as 1.4% (Fig. 3) and 1.35% (Table 1). Planner-only ablation has lower ASR (2.14) than planner+validator (5.41) - validator trades security for utility. No latency, cost or hardware reported. Static-vs-dynamic ablation only as a chart. Adaptive attacks raise ASR only to about 2%. arXiv version read, may differ from the NeurIPS proceedings text.

title: Agent-Aware Zero Trust: A Framework for Securing Agentic AI in SASE and Cloud Architectures
evidence: Sec. 5.5: "Hierarchical kill-switches allow termination at the agent, domain, or system level."; Sec. 1.1: "This work is conceptual and architectural in nature".
method: Agent-aware zero-trust architecture for SASE/cloud: agent identity with continuous verification, policy envelopes bounding autonomy, trust decay with graduated privilege revocation, telemetry supervision, hierarchical kill-switches.
evaluation: None. Conceptual paper: no testbed, dataset, simulation, baseline, ablation, metric value, hardware or latency figure; authors state it is not an experimental or simulation study.
contribution: Proposes a conceptual zero-trust architecture for autonomous network/security agents with policy envelopes, trust decay and hierarchical kill-switches, without any evaluation.
flag: Full text read (WebFetch summary of the PDF; figures seen only as captions). Criterion (a) is nominal only: kill-switch and privilege revocation are described in one or two sentences each, with no trigger logic, no per-action veto/deferral and no latency. No evaluation at all, so E2. Sec. 1.1 says quantitative metrics are 'illustrative or operationally observed' but no figures appear in the body. Human oversight asserted, not operationalised. Multi-agent cascades (Sec. 4.4) are a listed threat, not a mechanism. Quality doubts: Fig. 1 and Fig. 3 reportedly share a caption; ref [5] (blockchain credential verification) is cited for an unrelated zero-trust claim; only 11 references.

title: Human-Guided Intelligent Operations for Multi-Cloud Kubernetes at Enterprise Scale
venue: Journal of Information Systems Engineering & Management
evidence: Remediation fires only when "the correlation engine exceeds a high confidence threshold and when guardrails pass"; "Closed-loop does not mean hands-off; it means the loop is closed mechanically while governance remains human." (Sec. 6)
method: Conceptual AIOps architecture for multi-cloud Kubernetes: confidence-gated auto-remediation with guardrails (scope checks, change windows, rate limits, approval policies); medium-confidence cases produce previewable plans operators approve, modify or reject.
evaluation: No evaluation protocol; anecdotal retailer deployment only: MTTD 'tens of minutes to minutes', alerts 'thousands into tens', MTTR 'improved materially'; no baseline, dataset, hardware or latency figures.
contribution: Describes a human-governed closed-loop operations design for multi-cloud Kubernetes in which automated remediation is gated by confidence thresholds, guardrails and operator approval of previewable action plans.
flag: On topic (confidence-thresholded approval gate with operator approve/modify/reject is a logical-domain deferral pattern) but there is no evaluation: no experiment, dataset, sample size, baseline or exact number; all outcome claims are order-of-magnitude phrases from an unnamed 'top global retailer'. Sec. 9 lists metrics platforms should measure (human takeover rate, operator time saved), implying they were not measured. Sec. 8 contains a garbled duplicated sentence. Does not say how an in-flight action is stopped. Low-quality venue; claims unverifiable. Figure 1 not readable. Could serve as a motivating citation only.

title: Distributed Model Predictive Control for Multi-Agent Systems: Conception and Design for Dynamic Routing Task
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
evidence: "avoidance is enforced through dynamically activated constraints, which are introduced only when predicted inter-agent distances fall below a threshold" (Abstract)
method: Sequential distributed MPC for unicycle robots on a ring communication graph; convex Manhattan-distance collision constraints with slack are activated only when predicted pairwise distance drops below a threshold.
evaluation: Gazebo with TurtleBot3, ROS 2 and ChoiRbot: two-agent crossing and four-agent intersection; minimum pairwise distance stays above 0.2 m; no baseline, no ablation, no timing, single runs.

flag: FRUCT 38 conference paper (DFKI), not a Zenodo-only item. Collision avoidance is a soft constraint inside the planner (slack variables), so strict (a) is not met. Safety is the stated outcome but evidence is two qualitative single-run scenarios with a distance plot; no baseline or ablation, no collision rate, no solve-time or hardware figures; communication assumed instantaneous. Could equally be coded E1 as a coordination planner.

title: Predictive Collision Avoidance (PCA): A Novel Pedestrian-Collision Detection System for Public-Area Mobile Robots Using Trajectory Forecasting
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
evidence: "This demonstrates that our predictive strategy provides the robot with a larger temporal margin to react before a potential collision." (Chapter 6 Results)

flag: Borderline. Bachelor thesis (Treball Final de Grau, La Salle), self-published on Zenodo, not peer reviewed. The metric is detection lead time (ACAT), not a collision or violation rate, and the avoidance module was switched off during evaluation (/coll_avoid/enabled False), so no collision is shown to be prevented; maintainer may judge this E2. The mechanism only raises costmap cost for replanning, it cannot veto or halt, hence runtime_interceptor no. Hazard is one robot vs pedestrians, multi-agent only via multiple pedestrians. Only 20 runs per configuration; Table 6.2 multi-agent scenario 2 rep 5 is all zeros (apparently a failed run) and the multi-agent PCA mean of 1.451 s does not reproduce from the table rows (about 1.33 with that row, 1.48 without). p-value given as < 0.001 in the table but '< 0.05' in the text. Simulation only: 'full deployment on the physical robot could not be conducted'. No baseline for the predictor itself. Safety margin set to 3 x ADE = 2.13 m. Long file (323k chars): read abstract, 4.1, collision evaluation in 4.2, predictor metrics in 4.3, 4.4, chapters 5-6 and 8.1-8.5; did NOT read chapters 2-3, most of 4.3, 7, 8.6, 9-10 or appendices.

title: AGORIA 3.4: A Unified Governance Framework for Cognitive and Cyber-Physical Systems with Reinforced Formal Guarantees
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
evidence: "Enforces physical invariance (hard limits) with absolute priority via CBF-QP [22, 23]." (Sec 3.1); "Without robust margin: 3 violations. Without NEXUS: 7 violations." (Sec 8.3)

flag: Borderline, weak evidence: self-published Zenodo report by a single independent researcher, citing own earlier versions. Evaluation is half a page: no description of simulator, dynamics, what counts as a violation, or how baselines were configured. NEXUS under 250 us is a computed WCET for Cortex-R5 with HSM (45 us) and is not met on Cortex-A72 (4.1 ms); experiments ran on x86/FPGA, so edge deployment is analytical not measured. No arXiv id. Paper itself concedes 1000 trials do not support the 1e-6 risk level. Maintainer may reasonably prefer exclude-E2.

title: Reflexive-Core: Single-Context Metacognitive Security for Agentic LLMs
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
evidence: "Missing or ambiguous checkpoints default to most restrictive outcome (BLOCKED)." (Sec 6.1); "Data leakage (attack cases) 58% (14/24) 0% (0/24)" (Sec 7.3.3 table)
method: System-prompt framework that splits one LLM inference into four personas (preflight, security analyst, executor, compliance validator) with fail-closed checkpoints and a final APPROVE/REVIEW/BLOCK gate parsed downstream.

flag: Borderline E4 vs include; maintainer should decide. For include: it is an execution-time approve/review/block gate on an LLM agent with a quantitative safety metric, false-positive count, baseline, and latency/cost overhead (RQ5 material). For E4: single agent, single-turn, read-only email assistant; the paper itself puts multi-agent orchestration, tool authorization and write operations out of scope; no latency constraint; REVIEW_REQUIRED human path is described but never exercised. The interceptor is the same model judging itself inside one inference, plus an output parser - weaker than an external shield, and the author concedes 'Framework-as-judge' circularity. Evidence is thin: 28 cases, n=1 per case at temperature 0.7, 4 benign cases, Claude models only, no persona ablation (listed as future work). Abstract says 0% leakage 'across all 24 attack cases on all 4 models' but the leakage table (7.3.3) is Sonnet 4.5 only; per-model leakage is not tabulated in the paper (deferred to a supplement not in this file). Opus 4.5 had 1 failure (API content filter, 0 tokens) and 89.3% strict accuracy; the 'detected but approved' failure was fixed by editing the framework after seeing results on the same test set. Baseline percentages sum to 95% (rounding; counts sum to 23 of 24). Framework adds about 4.9 s latency and 3x cost. Appendix B is an empty placeholder; released XML uses a2as tags rather than the rc tags the paper describes. Self-published on Zenodo by an independent researcher, not peer reviewed. arXiv ids appear only in the reference list.

title: Preventing Collision Avoidance Deadlocks in Multiagent Navigation for Deterministic Simulation
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
evidence: "We present Revised ORCA Logic (RORCAL), a lightweight post-processing mechanism that introduces minimal directional bias to resolve degenerate solutions" (Abstract)
method: Geometric analysis of ORCA deadlocks in symmetric configurations; RORCAL rotates a degenerate LP velocity by a small bias angle, clipped to the ORCA half-planes, to break symmetry.
evaluation: Modified RVO2 circle benchmark vs ORCA: all 29 cases n=2..30 resolved; n=250 496 vs 647 iterations; 0.359 vs 0.352 ms per iteration over 50 runs. No collision metric.

flag: Paper is about deadlock and traversal speed in game simulation, the case the protocol names as E1; collision or violation rate is never measured (collision-freedom is inherited from ORCA constraints, not tested). RORCAL does alter the candidate velocity after the LP, but for liveness, not as a safety veto, so I marked runtime_interceptor no - check if you read that differently. Abstract '23% faster' is iterations (496 vs 647 = 23.3%); wall-clock gain is 21.8% (178.30 vs 227.86 ms). Only one benchmark family (antipodal circle); the claim that the detector rarely fires in asymmetric scenes is asserted, not measured. Hardware not stated. Single industry author (Crytek), Zenodo preprint in IEEE style, no venue shown.

title: Provable and Practical Prompt Injection Resilience in Autonomous LLM Agents
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
evidence: "This preserves LLM utility when actions are already safe and intervenes only when the proposed action would violate safety." (Sec. VI-C Safety Filter)
method: UCCA: layered prompt-injection defence for LLM agents - semantic firewall, context isolation, randomized smoothing, erase-and-check, CBF-QP action filter, tool permission tokens, ZK-SNARK attestation.

Ziegler', 'Z. Greshake', 'N. Mazeika'), suggesting machine-generated text.
