I scored it E1 because the primary claim and primary outcome are coordination error, and the safe-set projection is the constrained minimiser inside the controller rather than a separate filter over a nominal policy (protocol: a constraint inside a planner does not meet a). A reader could argue the opposite: the stationarity action is projected onto safe half-spaces at every sampling instant, and min separation is reported against three baselines (PD 0.62 and LQR 0.66 fall below the 0.70 m requirement). If accepted as (a) it would pass minimum evaluation. Doubts: no collision or violation count, only one d_min figure (combined case) despite the abstract claiming separation holds for all experiments; projection activation and infeasibility counts are not reported; abstract says monotone residual decrease is proven while Sec. 5.3 concedes the measured rate is not proof; several references are unrelated to the claims they support (warehouse RPA, p-Laplacian, language learning), which suggests careless or generated writing. Scalability: 2.8 ms at 4 robots to 21.7 ms at 12, E_c 0.036 to 0.045 called almost invariant. Simulation only, no physical robots. No explicit latency constraint, so not (d). PDF found via the journal landing page; quotes relayed by the fetch tool.

title: Hijacking Robot Teams Through Adversarial Communication
evidence: Abstract: "This work presents a framework for applying black-box adversarial attacks to learned MARL policies by manipulating only the communication signals between agents."
method: Black-box attack on learned MARL communication: imitate target policies from observed traces, infer rewards from surrogate action log-likelihoods, and train an offline actor-critic to flip bits of binary messages.
evaluation: Three MADDPG domains (PCP, PO-PP, SL), 50 episodes per checkpoint, vs random bit flipping and a direct-parameterisation ablation; normalized reward score 0.11 vs 0.01, collision score 4.58 vs 0.96; Robotarium swarm over three episodes.
contribution: Shows a learned robot team can be hijacked by flipping a few bits of its binary communication using only observed traces, degrading team reward far more than equal-magnitude random noise.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: the attacked system is learned (MARL with binarised communication), but nothing is guarded - this is an attack paper with no detector, filter or defense, so (a) fails and (c) holds only if multi-agent vulnerability characterisation counts as hazard work; exclude-E1 is a reasonable overturn and this is the second most likely overturn in the batch. Note the collision metric is the task objective (predators colliding with the prey), so fewer collisions means degraded performance and not a lower hazard rate; no safety-violation rate is reported. The headline 201% reward reduction appears only in the abstract and the contributions list; Sec 5.3 reports 90.9% and 76.64% gaps against the direct-parameterisation ablation and never shows the 201% computation. The Robotarium hardware table averages only three episodes, and its PCP and PO-PP columns are identical, which looks like a copy error.

title: Multi Robot Collision Avoidance by Learning Whom to Communicate
evidence: "We define the success rate as the fraction of the total number of agents that reach the goal without colliding or getting deadlocked" (Sec. III-C, shortened)
method: DMCA: decentralized end-to-end RL navigation policy with multi-head self-attention over neighbours and Gumbel-Softmax link prediction choosing which neighbours to communicate with; collisions penalised only in reward.
evaluation: gym-collision-avoidance circle/swap/random scenes, 4-30 agents; baselines ORCA, CADRL, GA3C-CADRL, BVC, BUAVC, Long et al., SelComm; circle avg SR 0.99 vs ORCA 0.95; collision 0.00 at 30 agents; 6 ms per agent, RTX 2080 Ti.
contribution: Learns decentralized dense multi-robot navigation with attention and selective communication, reporting near-perfect success and zero collisions for up to 30 simulated agents at about 6 ms per agent per action.
flag: Semantic Scholar page and API both returned client errors; I located the paper myself as arXiv 2209.06415 (Arul, Bedi, Manocha), whose current title is 'DMCA: Dense Multi-agent Navigation using Attention and Communication' - I believe the queued title is the earlier name of the same paper but could not confirm it from an S2 record, so the maintainer should verify the match. Read from one WebFetch pass of the arXiv PDF. Borderline on (c): collision rate is tabulated against six baselines and an ablation (DMCA-LC, collision 0.32 at 30 agents vs 0.00), so the minimum evaluation would be met, but the headline claim and metric are navigation success rate (which folds in deadlock) and communication selection, and the paper itself says learned methods lack rigorous safety guarantees; under the primacy test I read it as a navigation planner, hence E1. No runtime filter: safety is a -0.25 collision reward and proximity penalty. The 6 ms figure is on a desktop GPU with no deadline, so no latency or edge cell. Abstract claim 'up to 24% improvement in success rate' is not mapped to a specific table row. Table II 0.2 m block is labelled NavSIC rather than DMCA (leftover name). Real-robot tests (2-3 robots) are qualitative only. Circle swap avg SR: DMCA 0.89, ORCA 0.85, CADRL 0.84; random scenes SR 100% at 8/16/24 robots vs SelComm 76.14/58.43/43.67.
